## Reservations that Replace Allocated Resources [#replace](https://slurm.schedmd.com/reservations.html)
By default, nodes in a reservation that are DOWN or DRAINED will be replaced,
but not nodes that are allocated to jobs. This behavior may be explicitly
requested with the REPLACE_DOWN flag.
However, you may instruct Slurm to also replace nodes which are allocated to
jobs with new idle nodes. This is done using the REPLACE flag as shown in
the example below.
The effect of this is to always maintain a constant size pool of resources.
This option is not supported for reservations specifying cores which
span more than one node, rather than full nodes. (E.g. a 1 core reservation on
node "tux1" will be moved if node "tux1" goes down, but a reservation
containing 2 cores on node "tux1" and 3 cores on "tux2" will not be moved if
"tux1" goes down.)

## Magnetic Reservations [#magnetic](https://slurm.schedmd.com/reservations.html)
The default behavior for reservations is that jobs must request a
reservation in order to run in it. The MAGNETIC flag allows you to
create a reservation that will allow jobs to run in it without requiring that
they specify the name of the reservation. The reservation will only "attract"
jobs that meet the access control requirements.
NOTE : Magnetic reservations cannot "attract" heterogeneous jobs -
heterogeneous jobs will only run in magnetic reservations if they explicitly
request the reservation.
The following example shows a reservation created on node05. The user
specified as being able to access the reservation then submits a job and
the job starts on the reserved node.
```text
$ scontrol create reservation user=user1 nodes=node05 starttime=now duration=10 flags=magnetic Reservation created: user1_850 $ scontrol show res ReservationName=user1_850 St...

## AUTHORIZATION[#SECTION_AUTHORIZATION](https://slurm.schedmd.com/scontrol.html)
Slurm generally classifies users into three authorization levels:
- Administrators include root, SlurmUser, and any users with
"AdminLevel=Administrator"
- Privileged Users include all Administrators and any users with
"AdminLevel=Operator"
- Effective Owners of a job or step include the direct owner and all
Coordinators of the corresponding account.
Note that configuring AdminLevels or Coordinators requires the use of SlurmDBD.
The authorization levels required to execute various commands are defined in the
following table.
scontrol update job: Privileged or Effective Owner
scontrol requeue: Privileged or Effective Owner
scontrol update step: Privileged or Effective Owner
scontrol suspend: Privileged or Coordinator
scontrol resume: Privileged or Coordinator
scontrol notify: Root, SlurmUser, or direct owner
scontrol write batch_script: Privileged or direct...

Summary — what --reservation does
- --reservation=<name> (sbatch/srun/salloc) tells Slurm to place the job into a named reservation so it will start on the reserved resources during the reservation window.
- By default a job will only run in a reservation if it explicitly requests that reservation (unless the reservation has the MAGNETIC flag — see below).

Key reservation properties (how reservations are defined)
- Created/managed with scontrol create/update reservation and inspected with scontrol show reservation (or scontrol show res).
- Reservations are time-bounded: StartTime, Duration or EndTime.
- Resources can be expressed as Nodes, NodeCnt, CoreCnt, TRES, etc.
- Flags control special behaviors (common ones):
  - MAGNETIC — “attracts” eligible jobs that do not explicitly name the reservation (jobs that meet the access controls may be placed into it).
  - REPLACE / REPLACE_DOWN — control whether allocated/down/drained nodes are replaced to maintain reservation size.
  - (Other flags exist; see docs for full list.)

Access control rules (the important part)
- At least one access-control field must be set when creating a reservation: Users, Groups, Accounts, QOS, or AllowedPartitions.
- Multiple access-control fields can be specified; a job must meet all specified fields to use the reservation. In other words, access-control fields are effectively ANDed. Example: Accounts=foo,QOS=high means the job must run under account foo AND use QOS high.
- Users and Groups are mutually exclusive: you may specify Users OR Groups, not both.
- Deny entries are supported by prefixing the name with a minus sign. Example: Users=-alan prevents user alan from using the reservation even if other fields would otherwise allow it (e.g., the job’s account matches).
- AllowedPartitions can restrict which partition(s) the reservation applies to (jobs must run in those partitions).
- If the reservation lists specific nodes, only those nodes are reserved.
- Jobs must request the reservation (sbatch --reservation=<name> / srun --reservation=<name> / salloc --reservation=<name>) unless the reservation is MAGNETIC.

Practical implications
- To run under a reservation, ensure the job’s account/QOS/user/partition match the reservation’s access lists exactly (or the reservation is magnetic and will “attract” the job).
- If you want a reservation that only a particular account may use, set Accounts=<acct>. If you want to allow a few specific users from that account, also set Users=<userlist> (remember Users+Accounts are ANDed).
- To prevent a single user in a permitted account from using the reservation, use Users=-baduser.
- Magnetic reservations are useful for letting eligible jobs start without each job naming the reservation; be cautious with heterogeneous jobs (magnetic reservations cannot attract heterogeneous jobs unless the job explicitly requests the reservation).

Examples
- Create a simple reservation for account teamA on nodes node01–node04 for 2 hours, usable by users alice and bob:
  scontrol create reservation ReservationName=teamA_res StartTime=now Duration=2:00 Nodes=node[01-04] Accounts=teamA Users=alice,bob
- Deny user alan even though account matches:
  scontrol create reservation ReservationName=teamA_res Accounts=teamA Users=-alan Nodes=node01 StartTime=now Duration=1:00
- Submit a job into a reservation:
  sbatch --reservation=teamA_res job.sh
- Make a reservation magnetic so eligible jobs can be placed there automatically:
  scontrol create reservation ReservationName=mag_res StartTime=now Duration=1:00 Nodes=node05 Flags=MAGNETIC Users=user1

Where to look next
- scontrol create reservation and scontrol show reservation pages (Slurm docs) for the full set of create/update fields and flags.
- Use scontrol show reservation ReservationName=<name> to inspect access lists for an existing reservation.

If you want, I can:
- show current reservations on your cluster (scontrol show reservation) or
- craft a specific scontrol create reservation command for your desired users/accounts/nodes/time.

Summary — what burst buffers are
- A burst buffer (BB) is fast intermediate storage (e.g., NVRAM/SSD/DataWarp) that Slurm can allocate for a job for staging in/out or for persistent use.
- Behavior and available options depend on the configured burst-buffer plugin (datawarp, burst_buffer, etc.). Plugin-specific directives/keywords differ (for example DataWarp supports #DW and #BB persistent commands).

How you request a burst buffer
- In a batch script: add commented BB directives near the top (they may appear before/after #SBATCH lines). Example forms (plugin-dependent):
  - Generic/BB plugin: #BB capacity=100GB pool=fast access=single-node stage_in=source_path stage_out=target_path
  - DataWarp short form: #DW capacity=100GB access=single-node path=/dw/myjob
  - Persistent create/destroy (DataWarp): #BB create_persistent name=mybuf capacity=1TB [access=...] / #BB destroy_persistent name=mybuf
- On the command line: sbatch/salloc/srun --bb="..." or sbatch/salloc/srun --bbf=file (bbf = file containing BB directives).
- Note: --bb and --bbf syntax and accepted keywords are plugin-specific. If you omit required parameters (e.g., capacity for some plugins), the job may be rejected.

Where to look for BB status
- scontrol show job <jobid>
  - If the job requested a burst buffer, this output includes fields such as BurstBufferState and the BB spec. This is the primary per-job place to see current BB state.
- scontrol show burstbuffer [name]
  - Shows the controller view of persistent burst buffers (allocation, capacity, usage, state).
- squeue / scontrol show job together
  - squeue shows the job’s Slurm state (PENDING, RUNNING). Use scontrol show job to see BB-specific states that overlay the job lifecycle.

Common BurstBufferState values and what they mean
- pending — job has been submitted and BB request is known but not yet acted on.
- allocating — (persistent BB) Slurm is allocating persistent buffer resources.
- allocated — (persistent BB) persistent buffer has been allocated.
- staging-in — data is being copied into the burst buffer before job starts.
- staged-in — staging-in finished; data present in the BB.
- pre-run — BB ready and job is about to be started.
- running — job is running and BB is active.
- suspended — BB activity suspended (job suspended).
- post-run — job finished, BB is preparing staging-out.
- staging-out — data is being copied out of the BB to backing store.
- teardown — cleaning up job-specific BB (removing temporary data, releasing metadata).
- complete — BB work done for the job.
- deleting / deleted — (persistent BB) destroying persistent buffer.
- alloc-revoke — an allocation was revoked (rare; indicates an internal error).
- teardown-fail — BB teardown failed (investigate plugin/controller logs).

Notes and troubleshooting pointers
- The job can show a BB state even while the Slurm job state is PENDING — e.g., a job waiting for staging-in to complete will be shown as PENDING (squeue) but BurstBufferState=staging-in in scontrol show job.
- If staging-in/staging-out takes long, check:
  - capacity and pool availability (plugin may be out of free capacity)
  - scontrol show burstbuffer (for persistent pools) and the plugin/controller logs
  - whether job is blocked on resources (squeue reason) vs blocked on BB staging
- alloc-revoke or teardown-fail indicates plugin/controller problems—collect scontrol show job and scontrol show burstbuffer output and check plugin/controller logs for diagnosis.
- Persistent buffers (created with create_persistent) have states allocating/allocated/deleting/deleted; job-specific buffers follow the staging→running→post-run→teardown lifecycle.

Quick commands
- Inspect BB status for a job:
  - scontrol show job <jobid>   (look for BurstBufferState, BurstBufferSpec)
- Inspect persistent burst buffers:
  - scontrol show burstbuffer [name]
- Check overall scheduler/job state:
  - squeue (job-level state and pending reason)

If you want, I can:
- Show the exact BB directives supported on your cluster (need to inspect burst_buffer.conf or the configured plugin) — ask and I’ll fetch docs from the controller, or
- Check the BB state for a particular job/reservation (give a job ID or a persistent BB name).

## Overview[#overview](https://slurm.schedmd.com/job_array.html)
Job arrays offer a mechanism for submitting and managing collections of
similar jobs quickly and easily, useful for repetitive workloads that follow a
common job pattern. This greatly improves overall performance, since job arrays
with millions of tasks can be submitted in milliseconds (subject to configured
size limits) and the scheduler can quickly identify cases when no more array
tasks are eligible to start.
All jobs must have the same initial options (e.g., size, time limit), however,
it is possible to change some of these options after the job has begun
execution using the scontrol command specifying the JobID of the array or
individual ArrayJobID .

$ scontrol update job=101 ... $ scontrol update job=101_1 ...

## System Administration [#administration](https://slurm.schedmd.com/job_array.html)
A new configuration parameter has been added to control the maximum
job array size: MaxArraySize . The smallest index that can be specified
by a user is zero and the maximum index is MaxArraySize minus one.
The default value of MaxArraySize is 1001.
The maximum MaxArraySize supported in Slurm is 4000001.
Be mindful about the value of MaxArraySize as job arrays offer an easy way
for users to submit large numbers of jobs very quickly.
The sched/backfill plugin has been modified to improve performance with

or impact the scheduling of pending jobs, the remaining elements of that job
array will be quickly skipped.

Short answer: the % part caps how many array tasks from that single job may run at once. The full sbatch array syntax is:

- --array=<index-list>[%<max_running>]

Where:
- <index-list> may be
  - a single index (e.g. 5),
  - a comma-separated list (e.g. 1,3,5,7),
  - a range (e.g. 0-99),
  - a range with step (e.g. 1-7:2 produces 1,3,5,7).
- %<max_running> is an integer that limits the maximum number of simultaneously running tasks from that job array (an absolute count, not a percent).

Documentation example (paraphrased): "--array=0-15%4" limits simultaneously running tasks from that array to 4.

Concrete examples:
- --array=0-99%10
  - Creates tasks with indices 0..99 (100 tasks total).
  - At most 10 of those tasks will be RUNNING at the same time; others wait in the array’s internal pending queue.
- --array=1-10:2%3
  - Creates tasks 1,3,5,7,9 (step=2) and allows up to 3 of them to run concurrently.
- --array=1,3,5,7%2
  - Four tasks (1,3,5,7) with at most 2 running simultaneously.

Notes and behavior:
- Array tasks are still regular jobs for limits/accounting—subject to MaxJobs, MaxSubmitJobs, QOS/account/account limits, etc.
- The smallest user-specified index may be 0 (default) and MaxArraySize (cluster config) limits the maximum array size.
- Environment variables set inside tasks include SLURM_ARRAY_JOB_ID and SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID; array elements are referenced externally as <ArrayJobID>_<TaskID> (for example 12345_7).
- squeue shows compressed array ranges by default; use squeue --array (or other options) to list elements individually.

Reference: Slurm job array docs (job_array) describing the "%" separator and examples (e.g. "--array=0-15%4").

## Initial Testing [#INITIAL_TESTING](https://slurm.schedmd.com/nss_slurm.html)
Before enabling NSS Slurm directly on the node, you should use the
-s slurm option to getent within a newly launched job step
to verify that the rest of the setup has been completed successfully. The
-s option to getent allows it to query a specific database —
even if it has not been enabled by default through the system's
nsswitch.conf . Note that nss_slurm only responds to requests from
processes within the job step itself — you must launch the getent
command within a job step to see any data returned.
As an example of a successful query:
```text
tim@blackhole:~$ srun getent -s slurm passwd tim:x:1000:1000:Tim Wickberg:/home/tim:/bin/bash tim@blackhole:~$ srun getent -s slurm group tim:x:1000:tim projecta:x:1001:tim
```

Enabling nss_slurm is as simple as adding slurm to the passwd and
group database in /etc/nsswitch.conf (only on systems that will run

the sequence in which the NSS databases will be queried, and this ensures Slurm
handles the request if able before submitting the query to other sources.
To enable cloud node name resolution slurm needs to be added to the
to hosts database in /etc/nsswitch.conf .
It is recommended that slurm is listed last.
Once enabled, test it by launching getent queries such as:
```text

sbatch submits a batch script to Slurm. The batch script may be given to
sbatch through a file name on the command line, or if no file name is specified,

## PERFORMANCE[#SECTION_PERFORMANCE](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Executing sbatch sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmctld daemon come in at once, it can result in
a degradation of performance of the slurmctld daemon, possibly resulting
in a denial of service.
Do not run sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other
programs. Ensure that programs limit calls to sbatch to the minimum
necessary for the information you are trying to gather.

## EXAMPLES[#SECTION_EXAMPLES](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Specify a batch script by filename on the command line. The batch script specifies a 1 minute time limit for the job.
```text
$ cat myscript #!/bin/sh #SBATCH --time=1 srun hostname |sort $ sbatch -N4 myscript salloc: Granted job allocation 65537 $ cat slurm-65537.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
Pass a batch script to sbatch on standard input:
```text
$ sbatch -N4 #!/bin/sh > srun hostname |sort > EOF sbatch: Submitted batch job 65541 $ cat slurm-65541.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
To create a heterogeneous job with 3 components, each allocating a unique set of nodes:
```text
$ sbatch -w node[2-3] : -w node4 : -w node[5-7] work.bash Submitted batch job 34987
```

sbatch submits a batch script to Slurm. The batch script may be given to
sbatch through a file name on the command line, or if no file name is specified,
sbatch will read in a script from standard input.
The batch script may contain one or more lines beginning with "#SBATCH" followed
by any of the CLI options documented on this page. #SBATCH directives are read
directly by Slurm, so shell-specific syntax including variable names will be
read as literal text. Once the first non-comment, non-whitespace line has been
reached in the script, no more #SBATCH directives will be processed. See example
below.

## PERFORMANCE[#SECTION_PERFORMANCE](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Executing sbatch sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmctld daemon come in at once, it can result in
a degradation of performance of the slurmctld daemon, possibly resulting
in a denial of service.
Do not run sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other
programs. Ensure that programs limit calls to sbatch to the minimum
necessary for the information you are trying to gather.

## Job Dependencies [#dependencies](https://slurm.schedmd.com/job_array.html)
A job which is to be dependent upon an entire job array should specify
itself dependent upon the ArrayJobID.
Since each array element can have a different exit code, the interpretation of
the afterok and afternotok clauses will be based upon the highest
exit code from any task in the job array.
When a job dependency specifies the job ID of a job array:
The after clause is satisfied after all tasks in the job array start.
The afterany clause is satisfied after all tasks in the job array
complete.
The aftercorr clause is satisfied after the corresponding task ID in the
specified job has completed successfully (ran to completion with an exit code of
zero).
The afterok clause is satisfied after all tasks in the job array
complete successfully.

## PAM Slurm Adopt plugin on cgroup v2 [#pam_slurm_adopt](https://slurm.schedmd.com/cgroup_v2.html)
The [pam_slurm_adopt plugin](https://slurm.schedmd.com/pam_slurm_adopt.html) has a
dependency with the API of cgroup/v1 because in some situations it relied
on the job's cgroup creation time for choosing which job id should be picked to
add your sshd pid into. With v2 we wanted to remove this dependency and not
rely on the cgroup filesystem, but simply on the job id. This won't guarantee
that the sshd session is inserted into the youngest job, but will guarantee it
will be put into the largest job id. Thanks to this we removed the dependency of
the plugin against the specific cgroup hierarchy.

## Slurm Port Numbers
The Slurm controller (slurmctld) requires a unique port for communications
as do the Slurm compute node daemons (slurmd). If not set, slurm ports
are set by checking for an entry in /etc/services and if that
fails by using an interval default set at Slurm build time.

# "Configless" Slurm
"Configless" Slurm is a feature that allows the compute nodes —
specifically the slurmd process — and user commands running on login
nodes to pull configuration information directly from the slurmctld instead of
from a pre-distributed local file. Your cluster does require a central set of
configuration files on the Slurm controllers — "configless" in Slurm's
parlance means that the compute nodes, login nodes, and other cluster hosts
do not need to be deployed with local copies of these files.
The slurmd on startup will reach out to a slurmctld that you specify and the
config files will be pulled to the node. This slurmctld can be identified by
either an explicit option, or — preferably — through DNS SRV
records defined within the cluster itself.

option.
If you are using systemd to launch slurmd, you must ensure that
"ConditionPathExists=*" is not present in the unit file or the slurmd will not
start. (The example slurmd.service file shipped in Slurm 20.02 and above does
not include this entry.)
If any of the supported config files "Include" additional config files,
the Included configs will ONLY be shipped if their "Include" filename
reference has no path separators and the file is located adjacent to slurm.conf.

## Notes[#NOTES](https://slurm.schedmd.com/configless_slurm.html)
Starting from Slurm 25.11, there's a new
SlurmctldParameters=reconfig_on_restart option that will make every
restart of slurmctld (process restart not triggered by "scontrol reconfigure")
to trigger a reconfiguration request to all slurmd and sackd daemons. For
"configless" systems this will ensure all processes are running the current
configuration. Some caution should be taken if you intend to perform rolling
upgrades on the cluster as this could lead to the daemons being upgraded sooner
than expected.
The order of precedence for determining what configuration source to use
is as follows:
- The slurmd --conf-server $host[:$port] option
- The -f $config_file option
- The SLURM_CONF environment variable (if set)
- A local slurm config file: The default slurm config file (likely /etc/slurm.conf)
- For user commands, a cached slurm config file (run/slurm/conf/slurm.conf)

Short answer
- afterany: the dependent job becomes eligible to start once the specified job(s) have finished in any way (success, failure, cancel, timeout — any exit outcome).
- afternotok: the dependent job becomes eligible only if the specified job(s) finished with a non‑zero (unsuccessful) exit — i.e., at least one of the specified jobs did not complete successfully.

Details and examples
- afterany
  - Use when you need job B to run after job A finishes, regardless of whether A succeeded or failed.
  - Example: sbatch --dependency=afterany:12345 B.sh
    - B will be released from its dependency once job 12345 completes (exit code zero or non‑zero).
- afternotok
  - Use when you want job C to run only if job A failed (non‑zero exit).
  - Example: sbatch --dependency=afternotok:12345 C.sh
    - C will be released only if job 12345 ends with a non‑zero exit (failure/abnormal termination).
- Job arrays
  - afterany on an array is satisfied after all tasks in the array complete (in any state).
  - afternotok on an array is satisfied if, after the array finishes, at least one array element did not complete successfully.
- Multiple dependencies
  - Multiple dependency clauses are evaluated together: a job will not start until all specified dependency requirements are satisfied (i.e., they act like logical AND across clauses).
- Caveats and edge cases
  - “Finish” means the job reached a terminal state; requeues or restarts change what “finished” means (the dependency uses the final termination outcome).
  - What counts as “not OK” is determined by the job’s exit/termination status (non‑zero exit code or other failure conditions).
  - If you need a job to run only after successful completion, use afterok (complement to afternotok).
  - If you need different per‑task array semantics, consider aftercorr or array‑indexed dependencies.

If you want, I can show concrete sbatch examples (including arrays or combined dependencies) for your workflow.

Good question — scontrol show job prints many fields. Below are the most important ones you’ll see and what each means, with notes on when they’re useful for debugging.

General identity and accounting
- JobId — numeric job identifier (use this to reference the job in other commands).
- JobName — user-supplied job name (helpful when reading lists).
- UserId / GroupId — submitting user and primary group (shows UID/GID and numeric id).
- Account — accounting/project the job is charged to.
- QOS — job QOS (affects limits, preemption, priority).
- Partition — partition the job was submitted to.

State, timing, and lifecycle
- JobState — current state (PENDING, RUNNING, COMPLETED, FAILED, CANCELLED, etc.). Primary field for quick status.
- Reason — why a pending job is blocked (resources, priority, reservation, dependency). Crucial for “why not starting”.
- SubmitTime — when the job was submitted.
- EligibleTime — earliest time job is eligible to run (after dependency or reservation).
- StartTime — when job started (or scheduled start).
- EndTime — completion time (for finished jobs).
- RunTime / Elapsed — elapsed runtime for running or finished jobs.
- TimeLimit — requested maximum runtime.
- TimeLeft — remaining runtime (running jobs).

Resource requests vs allocations
- ReqTRES / ReqNodes / NNodes / NTasks / CPUS — what the job requested (TRES = trackable resources; can include cpu,gpu,mem,node).
- Gres (or GRES) — requested generic resources (e.g., gres=gpu:4).
- AllocTRES / AllocNodes / NodeList / NumNodes — what Slurm actually allocated (AllocTRES shows actual allocated cpu/gpu/mem counts).
- Nodes / NodeList — node count and the actual hostnames assigned (NodeList may be a list/range).
- AllocNode:Sid — local node and system id creating the allocation (admin-level; useful for debugging allocation ownership).

I/O, environment, and control
- WorkDir — working directory used by the job.
- StdOut / StdErr — paths where stdout/stderr were written (often in job's submission output).
- Command / BatchScript — command line or script path (what is executed).
- BatchFlag — indicates sbatch/batch submission (BatchFlag=1 for sbatch); increments on requeues.

Exit and error information (after completion)
- ExitCode — exitcode formatted as <exit>:<signal> (e.g., 0:0 means clean exit).
- State after completion — COMPLETED / FAILED / TIMEOUT / CANCELLED appear in JobState.

Dependencies, preemption, and limits
- Depend — job dependencies (afterok, afterany, etc.).
- Priority / PriorityFactor(s) — scheduler priority of job (reason for being scheduled earlier/later).
- QOSLimits / OverTimeLimit / PreemptMode — policy-related fields that affect runtime/behavior.

Other useful fields
- Flags / StateFlags — internal flags (checkpointed, requeued, etc.).
- Reservation — reservation name if job is tied to a reservation (shows “reservation”).
- EligibleNodes / ReasonInfo (detailed pending information) — more granular pending diagnostics (may require more verbose show).

Practical tips
- For “why won’t this start?” look at JobState + Reason + ReqTRES/Gres + Priority + Depend + Reservation.
- For running-job resource issues check AllocTRES, NodeList, RunTime, and StdErr paths.
- ExitCode + JobState tells you whether a job failed or was killed by a signal.
- Use scontrol show job <jobid> to get these fields; add the “details”/verbose option if you need per-node allocation breakdown.

## PERFORMANCE[#SECTION_PERFORMANCE](https://slurm.schedmd.com/salloc.html)
Executing salloc sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from salloc or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmctld daemon come in at once, it can result in
a degradation of performance of the slurmctld daemon, possibly resulting
in a denial of service.
Do not run salloc or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other
programs. Ensure that programs limit calls to salloc to the minimum

## EXAMPLES[#SECTION_EXAMPLES](https://slurm.schedmd.com/salloc.html)
To get an allocation, and open a new xterm in which srun commands may be typed interactively:
```text
$ salloc -N16 xterm salloc: Granted job allocation 65537 # (at this point the xterm appears, and salloc waits for xterm to exit) salloc: Relinquishing job allocation 65537
```
To grab an allocation of nodes and launch a parallel application on one command line:
```text
$ salloc -N5 srun -n10 myprogram
```
To create a heterogeneous job with 3 components, each allocating a unique set of nodes:
```text
$ salloc -w node[2-3] : -w node4 : -w node[5-7] bash salloc: job 32294 queued and waiting for resources salloc: job 32294 has been allocated resources salloc: Granted job allocation 32294
```

Short answer
- Use sbatch to submit non-interactive batch scripts that the scheduler will queue and run later.
- Use salloc when you need an interactive allocation (a reserved set of nodes/CPUs/GPUs) to run commands, open a shell, or debug.
- Use srun to launch parallel tasks (job steps). You can run srun inside an allocation (salloc or sbatch) or use srun by itself as a one-shot allocation+launch.

When to pick each (guidelines)
- sbatch — batch workflows (default)
  - Non-interactive, reproducible jobs (training runs, large workflows, pipelines).
  - Put resource requests and commands in a script with #SBATCH lines and submit: sbatch myjob.sh
  - The scheduler assigns a job ID and runs it later; good for long-running production runs and bookkeeping.

- salloc — interactive allocations and debugging
  - You want a shell or interactive session on allocated nodes: salloc -N2 --gres=gpu:1 --time=02:00 -- q, then run commands interactively.
  - Use for debugging, interactive development, launching a GUI/xterm, or running a workload that requires interactive control.
  - After salloc grants resources you typically run srun or other commands inside that allocation. When your shell exits, the allocation is released.

- srun — launch job steps / parallel tasks
  - Use inside a batch script (sbatch) or inside an salloc session to start parallel tasks distributed across the allocation.
    Example: inside an sbatch script:
      srun -n32 ./my_mpi_program
  - Use as a one-shot launcher without a prior salloc if you want to request resources and run immediately:
      srun -N2 -n16 --gres=gpu:2 ./my_program
    (This will wait in the queue for resources like sbatch would, then run the step.)
  - Use srun to spawn MPI ranks / multi-process tasks because it integrates with Slurm’s task placement and PMI support (preferred over mpirun in many clusters).

Common patterns
- Batch, multi-step job: sbatch script that contains srun commands for each step.
- Interactive debug: salloc ... then srun --pty bash (or use srun directly with --pty if you just need a terminal).
- Quick one-off run: srun ...command... (acts like submit+run for a single step).

Notes and tips
- Resource options can be provided either as #SBATCH lines in an sbatch script or as CLI args to salloc/srun (e.g., -N, -n, --cpus-per-task, --mem, --gres).
- srun inside sbatch or salloc creates job steps that share the same allocation (same SLURM_JOBID). srun alone creates its own allocation/step and jobid.
- For MPI: prefer srun for proper Slurm integration unless your MPI distribution requires a different launcher.
- For short interactive runs, srun --pty bash can be used, but salloc is clearer when you intend to run many interactive commands.
- For automated workflows (retries, dependency trees), sbatch supports dependencies (sbatch --dependency=afterok:JOBID).

## PERFORMANCE[#SECTION_PERFORMANCE](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Executing sbatch sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmctld daemon come in at once, it can result in
a degradation of performance of the slurmctld daemon, possibly resulting
in a denial of service.
Do not run sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other
programs. Ensure that programs limit calls to sbatch to the minimum
necessary for the information you are trying to gather.

## PAM Slurm Adopt plugin on cgroup v2 [#pam_slurm_adopt](https://slurm.schedmd.com/cgroup_v2.html)
The [pam_slurm_adopt plugin](https://slurm.schedmd.com/pam_slurm_adopt.html) has a
dependency with the API of cgroup/v1 because in some situations it relied
on the job's cgroup creation time for choosing which job id should be picked to
add your sshd pid into. With v2 we wanted to remove this dependency and not
rely on the cgroup filesystem, but simply on the job id. This won't guarantee
that the sshd session is inserted into the youngest job, but will guarantee it
will be put into the largest job id. Thanks to this we removed the dependency of
the plugin against the specific cgroup hierarchy.

## Job Dependencies [#dependencies](https://slurm.schedmd.com/burst_buffer.html)
If two jobs use burst buffers and one is dependent on the other (e.g.
`sbatch --dependency=afterok:123 ...`) then the second job will not
begin until the first job completes and its burst buffer stage-out completes.
If the second job does not use a burst buffer, but is dependent upon the first
job's completion, then it will not wait for the stage-out operation of the first
job to complete.
The second job can be made to wait for the first job's stage-out operation to
complete using the "afterburstbuffer" dependency option (e.g.
`sbatch --dependency=afterburstbuffer:123 ...`).

### Main differences between cgroup/v1 and cgroup/v2 [#differences](https://slurm.schedmd.com/cgroups.html)
The three main differences between v1 and v2 are:
- Unified mode in v2 In cgroup/v1 there's a separate hierarchy for each controller, which means the job structure must be replicated and managed for every enabled controller. For example, for the same job, if using memory and freezer controllers, we will need to create the same slurm/uid/job_id/step_id/ hierarchy in both controller's directories. For example: ```text /sys/fs/cgroup/memory/slurm/uid_1000/job_1/step_0/ ``` ```text /sys/fs/cgroup/freezer/slurm/uid_1000/job_1/step_0/ ``` In cgroup/v2 we have a Unified hierarchy, where controllers are enabled at the same level and presented to the user as different files. ```text /sys/fs/cgroup/system.slice/slurmstepd.scope/job_1/step_0/ ```

## Security Considerations [#security](https://slurm.schedmd.com/metrics.html)
The metrics system has several important security implications:
- No authentication : There is no built-in authentication mechanism for metrics endpoints. Anyone with network access to the slurmctld port can query metrics.
- PrivateData dependency : The metrics feature is automatically disabled when any PrivateData parameter is set in slurm.conf to prevent exposure of sensitive information.
- Network access : Metrics are exposed through the slurmctld network interface. Consider firewall rules and network segmentation to control access.
- Information disclosure : Metrics may reveal information about cluster utilization, job patterns, and user activity that could be considered sensitive in some environments.

## PERFORMANCE[#SECTION_PERFORMANCE](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Executing sbatch sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmctld daemon come in at once, it can result in
a degradation of performance of the slurmctld daemon, possibly resulting
in a denial of service.
Do not run sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other
programs. Ensure that programs limit calls to sbatch to the minimum
necessary for the information you are trying to gather.

Summary (official Slurm docs)

- What it does
  - afterok is a job dependency type accepted by sbatch/--dependency. A job submitted with --dependency=afterok:<jobid>[:<jobid2>...] will not begin scheduling until the specified job(s) have completed successfully (i.e., exited with code 0). (sbatch doc)

- Syntax / how to use
  - On the sbatch command line:
    - sbatch --dependency=afterok:123 my.job
  - Inside a batch script:
    - #SBATCH --dependency=afterok:123
  - You may list multiple job ids separated by colons:
    - sbatch --dependency=afterok:123:124 my.job
  - For job arrays you can refer to the whole array (ArrayJobID) or specific elements (see examples below). (sbatch, job_array docs)

- Job-array behaviour (important)
  - If the dependency names a job array, afterok is satisfied only after all tasks in that array complete successfully. Because array elements may have different exit codes, the interpretation of afterok for an array is based on the highest exit code from any task in the array (so any non‑zero exit causes afterok to be unsatisfied). (job_array doc)

- Interaction with burst buffers / stage-out
  - If the first job uses burst buffers and the second job depends on it, afterok waits for the job to complete, but will not wait for the first job’s burst-buffer stage-out to finish unless you use afterburstbuffer. Use afterburstbuffer when you need the stage-out to complete before the dependent job runs. (burst_buffer doc)

- Related dependency types (quick reference)
  - after: wait until the named job(s) start.
  - afterany: wait until the named job(s) complete (any exit code).
  - afternotok: wait until the named job(s) complete with any non‑zero exit.
  - aftercorr: for arrays, wait until the corresponding task ID in the specified job completes successfully.
  - afterburstbuffer: wait until named job completes and its burst-buffer stage-out finishes.
  (See sbatch and job_array docs for full details.)

Examples (from docs)
- sbatch --dependency=afterok:123 my.job
- sbatch --depend=afterok:123_4:123_8 my.job2         (wait for specific array elements)
- sbatch --depend=afterok:123 my.job                 (wait for entire array job 123 to complete successfully)

Sources (official Slurm docs)
- sbatch (options & --dependency): https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html
- Job arrays and dependency semantics: https://slurm.schedmd.com/job_array.html
- Burst-buffer interaction with dependencies: https://slurm.schedmd.com/burst_buffer.html

## Job Priority Factors In General [#general](https://slurm.schedmd.com/priority_multifactor.html)
The job's priority at any given time will be a weighted sum of all the
factors that have been enabled in the slurm.conf file. Job priority can be
expressed as:
```text
Job_priority = site_factor + (PriorityWeightAge) * (age_factor) + (PriorityWeightAssoc) * (assoc_factor) + (PriorityWeightFairshare) * (fair-share_factor) + (PriorityWeightJobSize) * (job_size_factor) + (PriorityWeightPartition) * (priority_job_factor) + (PriorityWeightQOS) * (QOS_factor) + SUM(TRES_weight_cpu * TRES_factor_cpu, TRES_weight_ * TRES_factor_ , ...) - nice_factor
```
All of the factors in this formula are floating point numbers that
range from 0.0 to 1.0. The weights are unsigned, 32 bit integers.

Summary (live data)
- sshare (fairshare): account=research, user=alice, RawShares=0.600, NormShares=0.420, EffectvUsage=1.800.
- sprio (per-job priority rows): "No pending jobs match the filter." — there are currently no pending jobs for alice to show a per-job priority breakdown.
- Configured multifactor weights: PriorityWeightAge=1000, PriorityWeightFairshare=10000, PriorityWeightJobSize=100, PriorityWeightPartition=500, PriorityWeightQOS=1000.

What those sshare fields mean (brief)
- RawShares: the configured share weight assigned to alice (0.600).
- NormShares: that raw share normalized against other accounts/users (0.420) — this is her entitlement fraction used in fairshare calculations.
- EffectvUsage: the recent scaled usage (1.800) that Slurm uses to compare against NormShares when computing the fairshare factor.

Interpretation for alice
- Alice’s EffectvUsage (1.800) is substantially higher than her NormShares (0.420). Ratio ≈ 1.800 / 0.420 ≈ 4.3 — she has used about 4.3× her normalized share in the usage window.
- The fairshare factor (a value between 0.0 and 1.0 used by the Multifactor plugin) is derived from this comparison: users who have used significantly more than their entitlement get a much smaller fairshare factor, which reduces job priority; users who have used less get a factor closer to 1.0, increasing priority.
- Because PriorityWeightFairshare=10000 (the largest weight), the fairshare factor is the dominant term in the job-priority sum. In the priority formula:
  Job_priority = site_factor + PriorityWeightAge * age_factor + PriorityWeightFairshare * fairshare_factor + PriorityWeightJobSize * job_size_factor + PriorityWeightPartition * partition_factor + PriorityWeightQOS * qos_factor - nice_factor
  the fairshare contribution can be up to ~10000 (if fairshare_factor≈1) or near 0 (if fairshare_factor≈0). By comparison, age or QOS contributions top out at ~1000 each, partition at ~500, job size at ~100.
- Therefore, because alice’s effective usage is well above her normalized share, any queued jobs from her would be strongly deprioritized compared with users who are under-using their shares — age and QoS increases could help but would need substantial time to overcome a large fairshare penalty.

Accounting information for jobs invoked with Slurm are either logged
in the job accounting log file or saved to the Slurm database, as
configured with the AccountingStorageType parameter.

analysis. The sacct command displays information on jobs, job
steps, status, and exitcodes by default. You can tailor the output
with the use of the --format= option to specify the fields to
be shown.
Job records consist of a primary entry for the job as a whole as well as

## DEFAULT TIME WINDOW[#SECTION_DEFAULT-TIME-WINDOW](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sacct.html)
The options --starttime and --endtime define the time window between
which sacct is going to search. For historical and practical
reasons their default values (i.e. the default time window)
depends on other options: --jobs and --state.
Depending on if --jobs and/or --state are specified, the default
values of --starttime and --endtime options are:
WITHOUT EITHER --jobs NOR --state specified:
--starttime defaults to Midnight.
--endtime defaults to Now.

## FILES[#SECTION_FILES](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sacct.html)
/etc/slurm.conf [#OPT_/etc/slurm.conf](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sacct.html) Entries to this file enable job accounting and
designate the job accounting log file that collects system job accounting.
/var/log/slurm_accounting.log [#OPT_/var/log/slurm_accounting.log](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sacct.html) The default job accounting log file.
By default, this file is set to read and write permission for root only.

Good question — --format is the primary way to tailor sacct output. Below is a compact reference and practical examples you can copy.

Quick summary
- Syntax: sacct --format=FIELD[,FIELD[:WIDTH],FIELD...]
- Use FIELD names from the sacct job-accounting fields (or ALL to print every field).
- You can control parsing and headers with --parsable2, --delimiter, and --noheader (useful for scripts/CSV).
- Use other sacct options (e.g., --starttime/--endtime, --state, --jobs, --user) together with --format to limit the result set.

Field names and modifiers
- Field names: JobID, JobName, User, Account, Partition, State, ExitCode, Elapsed, Start, End, NCPUS, ReqMem, AllocNodes, AllocCPUs, TresUsage (or TresUsed), MaxRSS, MaxVMSize, AveCPU, AveRSS, etc.
- ALL prints every available field.
- Width modifier: FIELD:WIDTH sets a display width (columns will be truncated/padded to that width). Example: JobName:30
- Ave/Max/Min variants exist for some metrics (e.g., AveCPU, MaxRSS).
- Array tasks and job steps: sacct returns job and step records; use --array to expand array tasks onto separate lines, and --allocations (-X) to restrict output to allocation-level records only.

Output control for scripting
- --parsable2 (or -P) produces machine-parseable output (one record per line with the delimiter between fields and escaping rules). Good for further processing.
- --delimiter=<char> sets the delimiter used with parsable output (e.g., --delimiter=,).
- --noheader (or -n) removes the header row (useful when producing CSV).
- SACCT_FORMAT environment variable can set a default format instead of passing --format each time.

Examples
- Human-readable custom columns:
  sacct --format=JobID,JobName,User,Partition,State,ExitCode,Elapsed
- Fixed column widths to keep alignment:
  sacct --format=JobID:12,JobName:30,User:15,Elapsed:10
- Produce CSV (no header) for import into tools:
  sacct --format=JobID,User,State,Elapsed --parsable2 --delimiter=, --noheader
- Include resource-usage fields (max RSS and CPUs):
  sacct --format=JobID,JobName,User,State,Elapsed,MaxRSS,NCPUS,AveCPU --parsable2
- Time-windowed report (jobs since 2024-01-01) with selected fields:
  sacct --starttime=2024-01-01 --format=JobID,Start,End,Elapsed,State,ExitCode --parsable2 --noheader

Practical tips
- If you’re unsure of a field name, run sacct --format=ALL | less (or grep ALL output) to see all available fields and exact names.
- Use --parsable2 + --delimiter when you need robust machine parsing (it avoids column-alignment problems).
- Beware of performance: sacct queries slurmdbd; don’t call it in tight loops or repeatedly for many small queries.
- To show only allocation-level stats (no per-step details), add --allocations (or -X).
- For arrays, use --array to expand tasks; otherwise sacct may group array tasks into single lines.
- Combine with other sacct filters (--jobs, --state, --user, --starttime/--endtime) to return only the rows you need.

Short answer
- scontrol requeue <jobid> takes an existing Slurm job and places it back onto the pending queue so it will be scheduled again (instead of terminating permanently).

What it does (concise behavior)
- If the job is RUNNING: Slurm will terminate the current allocation/step(s) for that job (graceful termination where configured), mark the job as REQUEUED, free the resources, and create a pending entry so the job can be scheduled again.
- If the job is already PENDING: it will be left in the queue but treated as requeued (may affect priority/age); in practice you use it to move a running job back to PENDING.
- The job keeps its original JobID and most submission parameters (nodes, cpus, time, constraints, account, QoS, etc.).
- A requeued job may start on different nodes when it is next scheduled.

Effects you should know
- The job’s allocation is ended; unless you have checkpoint/restart configured and your job checks for/resumes from checkpoints, the job will restart from the beginning.
- For sbatch (batch) jobs, Slurm records and some flags (e.g., BatchFlag) may be updated to reflect the requeue; accounting/history will show the requeue-related records.
- For heterogeneous jobs and job arrays there are special rules: requeue operations may apply to the entire heterogeneous job leader or to array elements depending on the ID you supply—check scontrol docs for exact syntax.
- Any prolog/epilog scripts or epilog cleanup will run as configured when the allocation ends.

Permissions
- scontrol requeue requires the job owner (effective owner/coordinator) or a privileged user (operator/administrator).

When to use
- Recover a job after a transient failure (if it can restart or resume).
- Force a running job back to the queue (for debugging, resource reshuffling, testing).
- Respond to preemption policies or operator decisions to give up current allocation and try again later.

Caveats
- Requeueing does not automatically preserve in-memory state unless your job implements checkpoint/restart.
- If you want a fresh submission (new JobID) instead of reusing the same job record, cancel and sbatch again instead.

Beginning in version 21.08, Slurm now supports NVIDIA
Multi-Instance GPU (MIG) devices. This feature allows some newer NVIDIA
GPUs (like the A100) to split up a GPU into up to seven separate, isolated GPU
instances. Slurm can treat these MIG instances as individual GPUs, complete with
cgroup isolation and task binding.
To configure MIGs in Slurm, specify
`AutoDetect=nvml` in gres.conf for the
nodes with MIGs, and specify `Gres`

## Accounting [#Accounting](https://slurm.schedmd.com/gres.html)
GPU memory and GPU utilization can be tracked as
[TRES](https://slurm.schedmd.com/tres.html) for tasks using GPU
resources. If `AccountingStorageTRES=gres/gpu` is configured,
gres/gpumem and gres/gpuutil will automatically be configured and gathered from
GPU jobs. gres/gpumem and gres/gpuutil can also be set individually when
gres/gpu is not set.
gres/gpumem and gres/gpuutil are only available for NVIDIA GPUs when using
`AutoDetect=nvml`, and AMD GPUs when using
`AutoDetect=rsmi`.
NVML does not support utilization metrics for MIGs, so Slurm does not
provide gpumem or gpuutil accounting for MIG devices. See
[NVIDIA's MIG User Guide](https://docs.nvidia.com/datacenter/tesla/mig-user-guide/).

## MIG Management [#MIG_Management](https://slurm.schedmd.com/gres.html)
Beginning in version 21.08, Slurm now supports NVIDIA
Multi-Instance GPU (MIG) devices. This feature allows some newer NVIDIA
GPUs (like the A100) to split up a GPU into up to seven separate, isolated GPU
instances. Slurm can treat these MIG instances as individual GPUs, complete with
cgroup isolation and task binding.
To configure MIGs in Slurm, specify
`AutoDetect=nvml` in gres.conf for the
nodes with MIGs, and specify `Gres`
in slurm.conf as if the MIGs were regular GPUs, like this:
`NodeName=tux[1-16] gres=gpu:2`. An optional
GRES type can be specified to distinguish MIGs of different sizes from each
other, as well as from other GPUs in the cluster. This type must be a substring
of the "MIG Profile" string as reported by the node in its slurmd log under the

## AutoDetect [#AutoDetect](https://slurm.schedmd.com/gres.html)
If AutoDetect=nvml , AutoDetect=nvidia , AutoDetect=rsmi ,
AutoDetect=nrt , or AutoDetect=oneapi are set in gres.conf ,
configuration details will automatically be filled in for any system-detected
GPU. This removes the need to explicitly configure GPUs in gres.conf, though the
Gres= line in slurm.conf is still required in order to tell slurmctld how
many GRES to expect.
Note that AutoDetect=nvml , AutoDetect=rsmi ,
and AutoDetect=oneapi need their corresponding GPU management libraries
installed on the node and found during Slurm configuration in order to work.
Both AutoDetect=nvml and AutoDetect=nvidia detect NVIDIA GPUs.
AutoDetect=nvidia (added in Slurm 24.11) doesn't require the
nvml library to be installed, but doesn't detect MIGs or NVlinks.

## Configuration [#Configuration](https://slurm.schedmd.com/gres.html)
By default, no GRES are enabled in the cluster's configuration.
You must explicitly specify which GRES are to be managed in the
slurm.conf configuration file. The configuration parameters of
interest are GresTypes and Gres .
For more details, see [GresTypes](https://slurm.schedmd.com/slurm.conf.html) and [Gres](https://slurm.schedmd.com/slurm.conf.html) in the slurm.conf man page.
Note that the GRES specification for each node works in the same fashion
as the other resources managed. Nodes which are found to have fewer resources
than configured will be placed in a DRAIN state.
Snippet from an example slurm.conf file:
```text

Summary (from the official Slurm docs)
- Slurm manages “Generic RESources” (GRES) such as GPUs through two places:
  - slurm.conf: declares which GRES types the controller manages and how many of each are expected on each node.
  - gres.conf (one per node or on controller + cloud nodes): gives per-node device details (device files, core affinities, counts, AutoDetect etc.). If slurm.conf fully describes a GRES type (no File/Cores/Links needed), a per-node gres.conf may be omitted.

Key slurm.conf parameters
- GresTypes
  - A global comma-separated list of GRES type names that slurmctld will manage (for example: GresTypes=gpu,mps).
  - If you do not list a type here, Slurm will not treat it as a managed GRES.
- NodeName ... Gres=...
  - Each NodeName line may include a Gres= specification that tells slurmctld how many of a type to expect on that node.
  - Syntax examples:
    - NodeName=tux[1-16] Gres=gpu:2
    - NodeName=node01 Gres=gpu:4,mps:1
  - The Gres specification follows the same per-node resource model as other resources. If a node reports fewer resources than configured, Slurm will place the node into DRAIN.
  - For Slurm to recognize MIG partitions as separate GRES you still list them via Gres= (e.g., Gres=gpu:2) and can use an optional GRES type substring to distinguish MIG sizes (see MIG docs).

Role of gres.conf (per-node file)
- Location: same directory as slurm.conf on the node (and controller for cloud setups).
- Purpose: give detailed device mapping and metadata that slurm.conf cannot express, e.g.:
  - Name=<gres-name> (e.g. Name=gpu)
  - Type=<optional type string>
  - File=/dev/... or device list
  - Count=NN (for resources without explicit device files)
  - COREs=cpu-list (CPU affinity(s))
  - AutoDetect=<backend> (nvml, rsmi, nvidia, oneapi, nrt) — see below
- If slurm.conf already completely describes a GRES (no File/Cores/Links needed or it’s autodetected), you may omit per-node gres.conf.

AutoDetect and GPU specifics
- AutoDetect in gres.conf (e.g. AutoDetect=nvml) lets Slurm query the node’s GPU library to fill device details automatically.
- AutoDetect=nvml (or rsmi for AMD) also enables some accounting metrics; nvml/rsmi must be available on the node.
- Newer options: AutoDetect=nvidia (detects NVIDIA GPUs without nvml but won’t detect MIG or NVLink), AutoDetect=oneapi, etc.
- For NVIDIA MIGs: use AutoDetect=nvml on nodes with MIG, keep Gres= in slurm.conf to state expected counts, and optionally specify a GRES type that is a substring of the MIG profile string so Slurm can distinguish different MIG partitions.

Accounting / TRES interaction
- If you enable AccountingStorageTRES=gres/gpu (and proper AutoDetect), Slurm will collect gres/gpumem and gres/gpuutil as TRES metrics for accounting (gpuutil/gpumem only available when supported by the AutoDetect backend; MIGs have limitations).

Common pitfalls & notes
- You must list types in GresTypes and specify Gres= on NodeName lines. Omitting either will cause Slurm not to manage the devices or mark nodes DRAIN if counts don’t match.
- Mismatch between slurm.conf and actual node devices -> node is placed in DRAIN.
- Place gres.conf on each compute node (or use AutoDetect + a controller copy for cloud nodes) and ensure the slurmd can read the device files.
- Users request GRES in jobs with --gres (e.g. sbatch --gres=gpu:1), but that is a runtime usage topic—slurm.conf/gres.conf must first be configured for the scheduler to offer them.

Minimal step-by-step to enable GPUs (example)
1. In slurm.conf:
   - Add the GRES types: GresTypes=gpu
   - Add Gres= counts on NodeName lines: NodeName=node01 Gres=gpu:4
2. On each node (or use AutoDetect):
   - Create /etc/slurm/gres.conf with entries like:
     AutoDetect=nvml
     Name=gpu Type=tesla File=/dev/nvidia[0-3] COREs=0,1,2,3
   - or let AutoDetect populate details if supported.
3. Restart or reconfigure Slurm services (slurmctld/slurmd) so the controller and daemons pick up the changes (slurmctl reconfigure / service restarts as your site policy).
4. Test with scontrol show node and scontrol show config or by submitting a job that requests --gres=gpu:1.

Where to read more (official pages used)
- slurm.conf man page (GresTypes and Gres parameters)
- gres.conf man page (per-node device syntax and AutoDetect)
- GRES scheduling doc (overview, MIG guidance, accounting/TRES notes)

Snippet:
## Job Accounting Records [#job_record](https://slurm.schedmd.com/job_launch.html)
When Slurm is configured to use SlurmDBD to store job records (i.e.
AccountingStorageType=accounting_storage=slurmdbd ), there are multiple
records that get stored for each job. There is a record for the job as a
whole as well as entries for the following types of job steps:
- extern step — A step created for each job as long as you have PrologFlags=contain in your slurm.conf. Each node in the job will have a slurmstepd process created for the extern step. pam_slurm_adopt uses this step to contain external connections.
- batch step — A step created for jobs that were submitted with sbatch. The batch host, or the primary node for the job, will run an instance of slurmstepd for the batch step, which is used to run the script provided to sbatch.
- interactive step — A step created for jobs that were submitted with salloc when LaunchParameters=use_interactive...

Short answer first:
- AveCPU (sstat) = the average CPU time (user + system) used by a single task in the step. Format is a time (HH:MM:SS or similar). Multiply by task count to get approximate total CPU-time for the step.
- AveRSS (sstat) = the average Resident Set Size (resident memory) across all tasks in the step. Reported in bytes/K/MB (human-readable when printed). It is the per-task average, not the total memory used by the step.
- “Job step” metrics: sstat reports statistics per job step (batch, extern, interactive, or any srun-created step). The “Ave* / Max* / Min*” fields are computed across the tasks of that step (MaxRSS is the single task’s peak RSS, MaxRSSTask shows which task).

Details and practical notes
- “Ave* semantics”: Any Ave*, Max*, Min* field in sstat summarizes the values of each task in that step. Example: AveCPU = (sum of CPU time of each task) / (number of tasks). MaxRSS = largest RSS observed for any task in that step; MaxRSSTask gives the task index.
- Units/format:
  - AveCPU: time value (user+system), e.g. 00:25:02.000. It’s per-task average CPU-time.
  - AveRSS (and MaxRSS/AveVMSize): memory shown in human-readable units when printed (K, M, G). It’s resident memory per task.
- How to get totals:
  - Total CPU-time consumed by the step ≈ AveCPU * NTasks (use NTasks from sstat or squeue). If tasks are heterogeneous or run at different times this is an approximation.
  - Total resident memory is not a simple sum (tasks may share pages). If you need aggregate memory, consider node-level accounting or inspect each task individually (MaxRSS, per-task samples).
- Job steps:
  - Slurm creates steps for a job (extern step, batch step for sbatch, interactive for salloc/srun). sstat can show each step if you use --allsteps (-a) or address a specific step id (jobid.stepid).
  - Use sstat -j <jobid> --format=... to show step metrics. Use -p for parsable (pipe-delimited) output.
- Live vs historical data:
  - sstat reports live/step statistics (works for running/active steps). For finished jobs/steps or historic accounting use sacct (sacct stores completed step records).
- Example usage:
  - sstat -j 123 --format=JobID,StepID,AveCPU,AveRSS,AveVMSize,MaxRSS,NTasks
  - sstat -p -j 123 --format=AveCPU,AveRSS,JobID  (parsable output)
- Caveats:
  - Averages hide heterogeneity — check Max*/Min* and NTasks if tasks differ.
  - For GPU/other TRES accounting, use AllocTRES or specific fields (GPU fields) if configured.

## Block Topology[#block](https://slurm.schedmd.com/topology.html)
Slurm can be configured to allocate resources to jobs within a strictly
enforced, hierarchical block structure using
TopologyPlugin=topology/block . The block topology prioritizes the

What that means for topology placement constraints
- No cross-switch constraints: because every node is on the same switch, Slurm cannot/does not need to prefer nodes on a particular switch to reduce inter-switch latency — all nodes are already on the same fabric.
- Effective constraints come from partition, node state, and resources (GRES/CPUs/memory), not from multi-switch topology. For example, GPU jobs are limited by the gpu partition and by gpu-node-01 being down and gpu-node-02 being currently allocated — there are no idle GPU nodes available now.

- sacct shows the job failed (historical record).
- scontrol show job 2001 reports Reason=OOM killer and MinMemoryNode=128G, Partition=gpu, NumNodes=4, NumCPUs=32.

Diagnosis (what went wrong)
- The job was terminated by the Linux OOM killer while running. That means a process on one of the allocated nodes consumed more memory than the kernel (or the cgroup limit) allowed, and the kernel killed the process to free memory.
- Given MinMemoryNode=128G, the job requested 128 GB per node. Either:
  - The job actually needed more than 128 GB on at least one node (under-requested memory), or
  - Memory accounting/cgroup limits were stricter than expected and the job hit an enforced limit, or
  - The application had an unexpected memory leak or spike that exceeded the requested limit.

What to check next (actionable, read-only checks you can run)
- Inspect the job’s stderr/stdout logs for lines like "Killed process" or out-of-memory traces (the job script’s output filename, often contains %j).
- Ask the node admin or check node kernel logs for OOM messages (dmesg/journalctl) on the node(s) that ran the job — these show which process was killed and why.
- Gather memory usage stats from accounting (if enabled):
  - sacct -j 2001 -o JobID,JobName,State,Elapsed,MaxRSS,MaxVMSize,ExitCode
  - If MaxRSS is missing, check node logs or re-run with monitoring enabled.
- If you need per-process runtime stats for future runs, enable/peruse sstat while running or instrument the job to record peak RSS.

Remediation suggestions
- If the job legitimately needs more memory: increase the request (e.g., --mem= or --mem-per-cpu, or raise MinMemoryNode) and re-submit.
- If the job should fit in 128G: investigate and fix memory leaks / reduce batch sizes, use more efficient data loaders, or stream data instead of loading it all.
- If cgroups or cluster memory enforcement is unexpectedly strict: ask cluster admin to confirm cgroup memory settings and whether any system limits or node-level memory reservations are in place.
- To avoid silent kills, consider adding memory logging to the job (periodic free/top/ps outputs) and/or request a buffer above observed peak usage.

Good question — here are concise meanings and scheduling implications for the common sinfo node states you asked about.

- idle  
  - Meaning: The node is up and not currently allocated to any job.  
  - Implication: It is eligible to receive new jobs/scheduling. Shown as "idle" in sinfo.

- alloc (allocated)  
  - Meaning: The node has been allocated to one or more active jobs. You will also see variants like ALLOCATED+ when it is allocated and additional jobs are in the process of being placed.  
  - Implication: Not available for new allocations until the current allocation finishes (unless oversubscription/backfill permits).

- drain / draining / drained  
  - drain (commanded state): An admin has requested the node be removed from normal scheduling.  
  - draining: The node will not start new jobs but will let existing jobs run to completion.  
  - drained (or DRAINED): The node has no running jobs and is out of service (kept offline for maintenance or admin work).  
  - Implication: While draining/drained, the node will not be given new jobs. A reason is usually recorded by the admin when the node was drained.

- down  
  - Meaning: The node is non-responsive, has failed, or was marked unusable (hardware/network/OS fault). There are also related flags (e.g., a "not responding" marker).  
  - Implication: The scheduler will not allocate jobs to the node until it is repaired and reactivated by an administrator.

Related notes and useful checks
- You’ll see additional states/flags in sinfo output (e.g., FAIL/FAILING, MIXED, RESERVED) and suffix symbols indicating power/reboot/pending states (examples: % pending power-down, @ pending reboot, ~ powered off, ! not responding).  
- For more detail about a particular node (reason, last update, features), run: scontrol show node <nodename>. For an overview use: sinfo -N -l.

# Job Exit Codes
A job's exit code (aka exit status, return code and completion
code) is captured by Slurm and saved as part of the job record. For
sbatch jobs, the exit code that is captured is the output of the batch
script. For salloc jobs, the exit code will be the return value of
the exit call that terminates the salloc session. For srun, the exit
code will be the return value of the command that srun executes.
Any non-zero exit code will be assumed to be a job failure and will
result in a Job State of FAILED with a Reason of
"NonZeroExitCode".
The exit code is an 8 bit unsigned number ranging between 0 and
255. While it is possible for a job to return a negative exit code,
Slurm will display it as an unsigned value in the 0 - 255 range.

### Accounting[#accounting](https://slurm.schedmd.com/heterogeneous_jobs.html)
Slurm's accounting database records the het_job_id and het_job_offset
fields.
The sacct command reports job's using the format
"<het_job_id>+<het_job_offset>" and can accept a job ID
specification for filtering using the same format.
If a het_job_id value is specified as a job filter, then information about
all components of that job will be reported as shown below by default.
The --whole-hetjob=[yes|no] option can be used to force to report
the information about all the components of that job or just about the specific
component requested, no matter if the job filter includes the het_job_id
(leader) or not.
```text
$ sacct -j 67767 JobID JobName Partition Account AllocCPUS State ExitCode ------- ------- --------- ------- --------- --------- -------- 67767+0 foo debug test 2 COMPLETED 0:0 67767+1 foo debug test 4 COMPLETED 0:0 $ sacct -j 67767+1 JobID JobName...

Summary — what the two fields mean
- ExitCode (accounting field): the exit status recorded for the job (the value Slurm shows for the job or step). It is printed as "exit:signal" (for example 0:0, 1:0, 0:9). The first number is the 8‑bit exit code (0–255); the second number is the signal number if termination was by signal (0 if none).
- DerivedExitCode (accounting field): an additional field Slurm maintains in the job record that reflects Slurm’s computed/aggregated exit status for the job (initially set to the highest non‑zero exit code returned by any of the job’s steps). It has the same "code:signal" format and a free‑text comment string may be attached.

Key details and interpretation
- Format: both fields use "EXIT:SIG". Examples:
  - 0:0 → exited normally with code 0 (success).
  - 1:0 → process exited with status 1.
  - 0:9 → terminated by signal 9 (SIGKILL).
  - 255 → negative return values are shown as unsigned 0–255.
- ExitCode vs DerivedExitCode:
  - ExitCode reflects the recorded exit of the job (for sbatch this is the batch script’s return; for srun it’s the invoked command).
  - DerivedExitCode is computed by Slurm from the job’s steps (highest non‑zero step exit) so it can capture internal step failures even when the top‑level script returned 0.
- Job state implications:
  - Slurm treats a non‑zero exit as a failure (job states and reasons like FAILED / NonZeroExitCode will be set when appropriate).
  - DerivedExitCode is intended to make step failures visible in accounting even if the top‑level exit was zero.
- Admin correction:
  - An administrator can view and edit the derived fields with sjobexitmod (sjobexitmod -l <jobid> to list; -e / -r to set exit/comment). This updates the DB record (used for accounting/visibility).
- Viewing the fields:
  - sacct --format=JobID,JobName,State,ExitCode,DerivedExitCode
  - scontrol show job <jobid> (shows ExitCode in scontrol output)
  - sjobexitmod -l <jobid> (shows/edits derived exit and comment)

Practical notes
- Use DerivedExitCode when you want Slurm’s view of step‑level failures (useful for postmortem/accounting) and compare it with ExitCode to find mismatches (e.g., script returned 0 but steps failed).
- For job arrays / heterogeneous jobs, derived code is computed across the relevant steps/tasks (sacct can show per-task step ExitCode lines).
- If you need to correct accounting for a finished job (for example, mark it with an OOM code or add a comment), ask an admin to run sjobexitmod (this changes the DB record).

References
- Slurm job exit codes doc (ExitCode format, signals, derived exit code and sjobexitmod) — see Slurm documentation (sacct, job_exit_code, sjobexitmod).

## PERFORMANCE[#SECTION_PERFORMANCE](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Executing sbatch sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmctld daemon come in at once, it can result in
a degradation of performance of the slurmctld daemon, possibly resulting
in a denial of service.
Do not run sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other
programs. Ensure that programs limit calls to sbatch to the minimum
necessary for the information you are trying to gather.

## Submitting Jobs [#submitting](https://slurm.schedmd.com/heterogeneous_jobs.html)
The salloc , sbatch and srun commands can all be used
to submit heterogeneous jobs.
Resource specifications for each component of the heterogeneous job should be
separated with ":" character.
For example:
```text
$ sbatch --cpus-per-task=4 --mem-per-cpu=1 --ntasks=128 : \ --cpus-per-task=1 --mem-per-cpu=16 --ntasks=1 my.bash
```
Options specified for one component of a heterogeneous job (or job step) will
be used for subsequent components to the extent which is expected to be helpful.
Propagated options can be reset as desired for each component (e.g. a different
account name could be specified for each hetjob component.
For example, --immediate and --job-name are propagated, while
--ntasks and --mem-per-cpu are reset to default values for each
component.

## EXAMPLES[#SECTION_EXAMPLES](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Specify a batch script by filename on the command line. The batch script specifies a 1 minute time limit for the job.
```text
$ cat myscript #!/bin/sh #SBATCH --time=1 srun hostname |sort $ sbatch -N4 myscript salloc: Granted job allocation 65537 $ cat slurm-65537.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
Pass a batch script to sbatch on standard input:
```text
$ sbatch -N4 #!/bin/sh > srun hostname |sort > EOF sbatch: Submitted batch job 65541 $ cat slurm-65541.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
To create a heterogeneous job with 3 components, each allocating a unique set of nodes:
```text
$ sbatch -w node[2-3] : -w node4 : -w node[5-7] work.bash Submitted batch job 34987
```

## PERFORMANCE[#SECTION_PERFORMANCE](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Executing sbatch sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmctld daemon come in at once, it can result in
a degradation of performance of the slurmctld daemon, possibly resulting
in a denial of service.
Do not run sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other
programs. Ensure that programs limit calls to sbatch to the minimum
necessary for the information you are trying to gather.

## EXAMPLES[#SECTION_EXAMPLES](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Specify a batch script by filename on the command line. The batch script specifies a 1 minute time limit for the job.
```text
$ cat myscript #!/bin/sh #SBATCH --time=1 srun hostname |sort $ sbatch -N4 myscript salloc: Granted job allocation 65537 $ cat slurm-65537.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
Pass a batch script to sbatch on standard input:
```text
$ sbatch -N4 #!/bin/sh > srun hostname |sort > EOF sbatch: Submitted batch job 65541 $ cat slurm-65541.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
To create a heterogeneous job with 3 components, each allocating a unique set of nodes:
```text
$ sbatch -w node[2-3] : -w node4 : -w node[5-7] work.bash Submitted batch job 34987
```

## Managing Jobs[#managing](https://slurm.schedmd.com/heterogeneous_jobs.html)
Information maintained in Slurm for a heterogeneous job includes:
- job_id : Each component of a heterogeneous job will have its own unique job_id .
- het_job_id : This identification number applies to all components of the heterogeneous job. All components of the same job will have the same het_job_id value and it will be equal to the job_id of the first component. We refer to this as the "heterogeneous job leader".

If two jobs use burst buffers and one is dependent on the other (e.g.
`sbatch --dependency=afterok:123 ...`) then the second job will not

complete using the "afterburstbuffer" dependency option (e.g.

sbatch submits a batch script to Slurm. The batch script may be given to
sbatch through a file name on the command line, or if no file name is specified,
sbatch will read in a script from standard input.

by any of the CLI options documented on this page. #SBATCH directives are read
directly by Slurm, so shell-specific syntax including variable names will be
read as literal text. Once the first non-comment, non-whitespace line has been

below.

## PERFORMANCE[#SECTION_PERFORMANCE](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Executing sbatch sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmctld daemon come in at once, it can result in
a degradation of performance of the slurmctld daemon, possibly resulting
in a denial of service.
Do not run sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other
programs. Ensure that programs limit calls to sbatch to the minimum
necessary for the information you are trying to gather.

## EXAMPLES[#SECTION_EXAMPLES](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Specify a batch script by filename on the command line. The batch script specifies a 1 minute time limit for the job.
```text
$ cat myscript #!/bin/sh #SBATCH --time=1 srun hostname |sort $ sbatch -N4 myscript salloc: Granted job allocation 65537 $ cat slurm-65537.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
Pass a batch script to sbatch on standard input:
```text
$ sbatch -N4 #!/bin/sh > srun hostname |sort > EOF sbatch: Submitted batch job 65541 $ cat slurm-65541.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
To create a heterogeneous job with 3 components, each allocating a unique set of nodes:
```text
$ sbatch -w node[2-3] : -w node4 : -w node[5-7] work.bash Submitted batch job 34987
```

in a denial of service.

With the SlurmDBD, we are able to collect data from multiple
clusters in a single location.
This does impose some constraints on the user naming and IDs.
Accounting is maintained by user name (not user ID), but a
given user name should refer to the same person across all
of the computers.
Authentication relies upon user ID numbers, so those must
be uniform across all computers communicating with each
SlurmDBD, at least for users requiring authentication.
In particular, the configured SlurmUser must have the
same name and ID across all clusters.
If you plan to have administrators of user accounts, limits,
etc. they must also have consistent names and IDs across all
clusters.
If you plan to restrict access to accounting records (e.g.
only permit a user to view records of his jobs), then all

# Job Exit Codes
A job's exit code (aka exit status, return code and completion
code) is captured by Slurm and saved as part of the job record. For
sbatch jobs, the exit code that is captured is the output of the batch
script. For salloc jobs, the exit code will be the return value of
the exit call that terminates the salloc session. For srun, the exit
code will be the return value of the command that srun executes.
Any non-zero exit code will be assumed to be a job failure and will
result in a Job State of FAILED with a Reason of
"NonZeroExitCode".
The exit code is an 8 bit unsigned number ranging between 0 and
255. While it is possible for a job to return a negative exit code,
Slurm will display it as an unsigned value in the 0 - 255 range.

After reading the above description of a job's exit code, one can
imagine a scenario where a central task of a batch job fails but the
script returns an exit code of zero, indicating success. In many
cases, a user may not be able to ascertain the success or failure of a

## EXAMPLES[#SECTION_EXAMPLES](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Specify a batch script by filename on the command line. The batch script specifies a 1 minute time limit for the job.
```text
$ cat myscript #!/bin/sh #SBATCH --time=1 srun hostname |sort $ sbatch -N4 myscript salloc: Granted job allocation 65537 $ cat slurm-65537.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
Pass a batch script to sbatch on standard input:
```text
$ sbatch -N4 #!/bin/sh > srun hostname |sort > EOF sbatch: Submitted batch job 65541 $ cat slurm-65541.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
To create a heterogeneous job with 3 components, each allocating a unique set of nodes:
```text
$ sbatch -w node[2-3] : -w node4 : -w node[5-7] work.bash Submitted batch job 34987
```

salloc is used to allocate a Slurm job allocation, which is a set of resources
