## EXAMPLES[#SECTION_EXAMPLES](https://slurm.schedmd.com/salloc.html)
To get an allocation, and open a new xterm in which srun commands may be typed interactively:
```text
$ salloc -N16 xterm salloc: Granted job allocation 65537 # (at this point the xterm appears, and salloc waits for xterm to exit) salloc: Relinquishing job allocation 65537
```
To grab an allocation of nodes and launch a parallel application on one command line:
```text
$ salloc -N5 srun -n10 myprogram
```
To create a heterogeneous job with 3 components, each allocating a unique set of nodes:
```text
$ salloc -w node[2-3] : -w node4 : -w node[5-7] bash salloc: job 32294 queued and waiting for resources salloc: job 32294 has been allocated resources salloc: Granted job allocation 32294
```

Short guide — when to use sbatch, salloc, or srun

- sbatch — submit a non‑interactive batch job
  - Use when you have a job script you want queued and run later (reproducible, unattended runs).
  - Slurm returns a job ID; the job runs on allocated nodes when the scheduler starts it.
  - Typical use: production training, long experiments, cron‑style/array jobs.
  - Example: sbatch my_job.sh

- salloc — get an interactive allocation (an allocation + a shell or a command)
  - Use when you need an interactive allocation of nodes/resources for debugging, experimenting, or opening an interactive shell/xterm on allocated nodes.
  - salloc obtains the resources immediately (when available) and holds them until the requested command (or shell) exits.
  - Typical use: debug a job interactively, start an interactive MPI session, open an xterm on allocated nodes.
  - Example: salloc -N2 --time=01:00:00 --mem=64G bash

- srun — run job steps (launch tasks), either inside an allocation or by requesting a short allocation on the fly
  - Use inside a sbatch script or an salloc session to launch parallel/serial tasks across the allocated nodes (MPI/OMP/worker processes). This is the preferred launcher for MPI under Slurm.
  - srun can also be used outside an allocation to request resources and run a single command immediately (it will create a short allocation for that command).
  - Typical use: spawn the MPI program inside a batch script, or run a quick command with resources without writing a script.
  - Examples:
    - Inside a batch script: srun -n 32 ./my_mpi_program
    - Run one-off command: srun -N1 --time=00:10:00 hostname
    - Interactive pseudo-TTY: srun --pty bash

Quick decision flow
- I want a queued, repeatable job/script -> sbatch.
- I want an interactive shell or to experiment on allocated nodes -> salloc (then use srun inside it).
- I want to launch tasks on nodes that are already allocated (or quickly run a single command) -> srun.

Notes / best practices
- In batch scripts, prefer srun to launch tasks (not system mpirun) because srun integrates with Slurm’s allocation and task placement.
- salloc gives you an environment (SLURM_* variables) to use srun interactively; srun without a prior salloc may implicitly allocate resources for the command.
- Use sbatch for reproducibility and scheduling; use salloc/srun for interactive work and immediate runs.

## Partition QOS [#partition](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
A QOS can be attached to a partition. This means the partition will have all
the same limits as the QOS. This does not associate jobs with the QOS, nor does
it give the job any priority or preemption characteristics of the assigned QOS.
Jobs may separately request the same QOS or a different QOS to gain those
characteristics. However, the Partition QOS limits will override the job's QOS.
If the opposite is desired you may configure the job's QOS with
`Flags=OverPartQOS` which will reverse the order of precedence.
This functionality may be used to implement a true "floating"
partition, in which a partition may access a limited amount of resources with no
restrictions on which nodes it uses to get the resources. This is accomplished
by assigning all nodes to the partition, then configuring a Partition QOS with
`GrpTRES` set to the desired resource limits.

### Job Scheduling Priority [#priority](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
Job scheduling priority is made up of a number of factors as
described in the [priority/multifactor](https://slurm.schedmd.com/priority_multifactor.html) plugin. One
of the factors is the QOS priority. Each QOS is defined in the Slurm
database and includes an associated priority. Jobs that request and
are permitted a QOS will incorporate the priority associated with that
QOS in the job's [multi-factor priority calculation.](https://slurm.schedmd.com/priority_multifactor.html)
To enable the QOS priority component of the multi-factor priority
calculation, the "PriorityWeightQOS" configuration parameter must be
defined in the slurm.conf file and assigned an integer value greater
than zero.
A job's QOS only affects is scheduling priority when the
multi-factor plugin is loaded.

What "Reason=None" means
- "None" means the scheduler did not set a specific blocking reason for the job during the last scheduling attempt. Practically this usually indicates the job is eligible to run but is simply waiting its turn for available resources (or waiting on scheduling order/backfill). It is not on hold, not blocked by a dependency or begin time, and not explicitly limited by accounting/QOS in the last check.

Common Slurm pending reasons (brief explanations and quick remediation)
- Resources (ReqNodeNotAvail / Resources)
  - Meaning: No nodes or TRES matching the job request are currently free (e.g., not enough GPUs/CPUs/memory).
  - Fix: Check sinfo for idle nodes/partitions; adjust resource request (fewer GPUs/CPUs/memory) or wait.

- Priority
  - Meaning: Higher-priority jobs occupy the resources or the job's priority is too low to be scheduled now.
  - Fix: Check sprio/priority factors; consider raising QOS or submit time, or wait.

- BeginTime
  - Meaning: Job has an earliest start time (--begin) that hasn’t been reached.
  - Fix: Confirm requested begin time or remove the --begin setting.

- Dependency
  - Meaning: Job depends on other job(s) (afterok/afternotok/etc.) that haven’t finished.
  - Fix: Check sbatch --dependency or sacct of the dependent job(s).

- AssocGrp / MaxPerAccount / QOS limits
  - Meaning: The job would exceed per-account, association, or QOS limits (concurrent jobs, TRES usage, limits enforced by QOS).
  - Fix: Inspect account/QOS limits (sacctmgr / scontrol) or ask admins to adjust limits.

- NodeDown / NodeDrained / PartitionDown
  - Meaning: Required node(s) are down or drained and cannot satisfy the request.
  - Fix: Check sinfo and sinfo -R (sinfo_reasons) for node states; wait for nodes to be brought back or change partition.

- License
  - Meaning: A software license required by the job is not currently available (Slurm license accounting).
  - Fix: Check scontrol_license and request license or wait.

- Association/Accounting (AccountNotAllowed, AssocGrp*)
  - Meaning: Job’s account is not allowed in the partition or has hit a configured accounting limit.
  - Fix: Verify account/association and limits with sacctmgr.

When a job shows "None" but stays pending a long time
- Check cluster capacity: run sinfo to see idle nodes and their partitions.
- Check queue contention: run squeue / sprio to see competing jobs and priorities.
- For a specific job: scontrol show job <jobid> (already done) and check limits/QOS/accounting if you suspect limits.

## AUTHORIZATION[#SECTION_AUTHORIZATION](https://slurm.schedmd.com/scontrol.html)
Slurm generally classifies users into three authorization levels:
- Administrators include root, SlurmUser, and any users with
"AdminLevel=Administrator"
- Privileged Users include all Administrators and any users with
"AdminLevel=Operator"
- Effective Owners of a job or step include the direct owner and all
Coordinators of the corresponding account.
Note that configuring AdminLevels or Coordinators requires the use of SlurmDBD.
The authorization levels required to execute various commands are defined in the
following table.
scontrol update job: Privileged or Effective Owner
scontrol requeue: Privileged or Effective Owner

## Manual Power Saving[#manual](https://slurm.schedmd.com/elastic_computing.html)
A node can be manually powered up and down by setting the state of the
node to the following states using `scontrol`:
```text
scontrol update nodename= state=power_
```
`scontrol update` command actions/states of interest:
POWER_DOWN [#POWER_DOWN](https://slurm.schedmd.com/elastic_computing.html)
Will use the configured SuspendProgram program to explicitly
place a node in power saving mode. If a node is already in the process of
being powered down, the command will only change the state of the node but
won't have any effect until the configured SuspendTimeout is
reached.
POWER_DOWN_ASAP [#POWER_DOWN_ASAP](https://slurm.schedmd.com/elastic_computing.html)
Will drain the node and mark it for power down. Currently running jobs
will complete first and no additional jobs will be allocated to the
node.

node states, will be deleted. Without this option, previously running
jobs will be preserved along with node State of DOWN, DRAINED
and DRAINING nodes and the associated Reason field for those nodes.

jobs will be killed.

Short answer
- State=drain: marks the node so Slurm will not allocate any new jobs to it. If jobs are currently running the node will be left to finish those jobs; while jobs remain it is reported as DRAINING and once idle it is reported as DRAINED. No new allocations are placed on a drained node.
- State=resume (undrain): clears the drain so the node becomes allocatable again (i.e., it is returned to normal/idle/allocatable state).

Details and related semantics (from the Slurm docs)
- Drain semantics: a drain prevents new work from being scheduled on the node. Running jobs are allowed to complete; during that time the node is shown as DRAINING and after they finish it becomes DRAINED. (Power-save variants such as POWER_DOWN_ASAP combine draining with a subsequent power-down action — POWER_DOWN_ASAP “will drain the node and mark it for power down. Currently running jobs will complete first and no additional jobs will be allocated to the node.”)
- Resume/undrain: an undrain (resume) operation returns a drained node to normal so it can be allocated again. For nodes drained as part of an ASAP reboot/power-down workflow there are helper commands (for example cancel_reboot) that will undrain and clear the reason if appropriate.
- Reason and persistence: Slurm records a Reason for nodes placed into DOWN/DRAINED states (the configuration and node entries include a Reason field). slurmctld preserves DRAINED and DRAINING node states (and associated Reason) across its checkpoints/restarts.
- Reporting: sinfo and scontrol show node state flags such as DRAINING and DRAINED; these are the indicators schedulers and admins should use to understand node availability.
- What this does NOT do: draining does not forcibly kill running jobs (unless you use a force/other action). Draining only prevents new allocations and allows current work to finish (or be handled separately by admin action).

Typical usage examples (conceptual)
- scontrol update NodeName=node01 State=DRAIN  — request the node be drained (can be combined with a Reason field).
- scontrol update NodeName=node01 State=RESUME — undrain the node so it becomes allocatable.

What strigger shows (fields)
- TRIG_ID: trigger identifier
- RES_TYPE: resource type (job or node)
- RES_ID: resource identifier (job ID, host name(s), or '*' for any)
- TYPE: event type (see below)
- OFFSET: time offset in seconds (negative = before the event)
- USER: who created the trigger
- PROGRAM: program/script run when the event fires

Common trigger event types and meanings
- time (job-only): a time-based event for a job (e.g., when a job reaches its time limit or an offset before the time limit).
- fini (job-only): job termination/finish event.
- down (job or node): a node or job has entered the DOWN state (node names or job id are passed to the program).
- up (job or node): a node or job has transitioned to UP.
- drained (node-only): node has been drained (administratively taken out of service).
- idle (node-only): node has become idle.
- reconfig (node-only): a node or controller reconfiguration event occurred.
- primary_slurmctld_failure / backup_slurmctld_failure / backup_slurmctld_assumed_control / backup_slurmctld_resumed_operation: controller failover/health events (trigger when primary/backup slurmctld fails, assumes control, or resumes).
- burst_buffer: burst-buffer related error events.

Behavior notes
- When a trigger event occurs, Slurm runs the configured PROGRAM and passes the relevant resource id(s) (hostlist or job id) as arguments.
- Triggers are checked periodically (defaults to roughly every 15 seconds). Events found during an interval are compared against configured triggers and the program is executed once for that interval.
- OFFSET lets you run the program before/after the event (negative values run before the event when possible).

If you want
- List triggers yourself: strigger --get
- Create or remove triggers: strigger --set / strigger --clear

Summary — what sacctmgr changes affect
- sacctmgr talks to slurmdbd and edits the accounting database (users, accounts, associations, limits, fairshare, QOS links, etc.). These changes affect scheduling decisions (limits, fairshare), user defaults, and accounting reports site-wide.
- Most add/modify/delete operations change association metadata only. Historical job records are stored in the DB independently; they are not normally removed just by deleting an association. Explicit archive/purge operations can remove job/event records and are irreversible if configured to purge.

Safety implications and risks (by operation)

1) sacctmgr add (create user/account/cluster/association)
- Risk: accidental creation of accounts/users with wrong defaults (DefaultAccount, DefaultWCKey, AdminLevel, fairshare) so new jobs may be charged to the wrong account or inherit incorrect limits.
- Scheduling impact: adding an account with a high fairshare or a QOS association can change future scheduling/fairshare calculations.
- Mitigation: review intended defaults before adding; use sacctmgr show/list to confirm existing associations; create in a test/staging DB if available.

2) sacctmgr modify (change limits, fairshare, adminlevel, default account, etc.)
- Risk: changing per-user or per-account limits (MaxJobs, MaxWall, GrpTRES, GrpJobs, TRES limits, DefaultQOS, Fairshare, etc.) can immediately affect scheduling decisions:
  - Lowering limits may prevent queued jobs from starting (or stop future submissions).
  - Raising limits can allow resource bursts or bypass intended quotas.
  - Changing fairshare values reorders priority calculations and can shift job start order.
- Operational risk: changing DefaultAccount or AdminLevel can affect who can manage an account and which account new jobs use.
- Mitigation:
  - Inspect the existing association(s) with sacctmgr show or sacctmgr list associations (use format= to see relevant fields).
  - Apply conservative changes and monitor scheduler behavior.
  - Prefer incremental modifications and communicate with affected users.
  - When scripting changes, avoid --immediate unless you intend to commit without human confirmation.

3) sacctmgr delete (remove user/account/association)
- Risk: deleting an account or user association can:
  - Remove a billing/accounting target for future jobs (users may not be able to submit if account required).
  - Remove coordinator privileges or orphan sub-accounts.
  - Cause confusion in reports and fairshare calculations.
- Historical records: deleting an account or user association does not usually delete historical job records by default; however, archive/purge operations (sacctmgr archive/dump with purge options or slurmdbd purge settings) can remove job/event data permanently and are irreversible.
- Operational hazard: deleting an account that still has active users or policies can leave users unable to run jobs or change default accounts unexpectedly.
- Mitigation:
  - Use sacctmgr list and sacct to confirm whether there are active or recent jobs tied to the account/user.
  - Backup the SlurmDB (dump or slurmdbd DB backup) before destructive deletes.
  - Avoid running archive/purge options without a verified backup. Note from docs: archive dump with purge is irreversible.
  - Communicate deletions to affected groups and coordinate maintenance windows.

Other important safety notes and best practices
- Transaction / confirmation behavior:
  - By default sacctmgr prompts to confirm a transaction. The -i/--immediate flag commits without confirmation — use it only in tested automation.
- Backups and recovery:
  - Always backup slurmdbd data (dump or DB-level backup) before mass deletes or bulk modifications.
  - Test restore procedures in a staging environment periodically.
- Auditing & logging:
  - Changes via sacctmgr are recorded in slurmdbd logs and the DB; review logs after major changes.
- Review before change:
  - Use sacctmgr show/list (with WithAssoc or format=) to inspect the exact associations and limits you will change.
  - Use sacct and sacctmgr list associations to check for historical and active jobs related to the target account/user.
- Staging/testing:
  - Apply changes first in a staging cluster or test project to observe scheduling/fairshare effects if possible.
- Coordination:
  - Inform users when modifying limits or deleting accounts (especially if account is required to submit).
- Concurrency:
  - Concurrent sacctmgr changes can race; coordinate multi-admin operations and check the database after changes.
- Minimizing impact:
  - Prefer modifying limits on specific association rows rather than deleting and recreating entities unless necessary.
  - Use non-destructive operations (modify metadata) to achieve administrative goals when possible.

Quick checklist before running sacctmgr delete/modify/add
1. sacctmgr list/show associations for the target(s) (verify Cluster, Account, User, Partition, limits, DefaultQOS).
2. sacct -S (or sacct -u user / sacct -A account) to check historical and recent jobs tied to the entity.
3. Backup slurmdbd (DB dump).
4. Plan communication to affected users and coordination window if needed.
5. Apply change in staging if feasible; then apply in production. Avoid --immediate in interactive sessions unless confident.
6. Verify results (sacctmgr list, sshare, sprio) and monitor scheduling behavior.

If you want, I can:
- show the exact sacctmgr fields to inspect for a given account/user (examples of sacctmgr list/show commands), or
- produce a small pre-change checklist or script snippet (non-destructive) you can run to collect the necessary pre-change facts. Which would you prefer?

Short answer
- Use -C or --constraint to select nodes by their configured Feature tokens (the Feature= list on each NodeName in slurm.conf).
- The constraint value is a boolean expression of feature names; use & (AND) or comma (,) for AND, | for OR, and parentheses to group. Quote the expression so the shell doesn’t split it.

Details and examples
- Features: Nodes are tagged in slurm.conf (or helpers.conf) with Feature=token1,token2,...; --constraint matches those tokens.
- Operators:
  - & or , — logical AND (both features must be present)
  - | — logical OR (one or the other)
  - ( ) — grouping/precedence
- Quoting: put the whole expression in quotes, e.g. -C "gpu&v100" or -C "(gpu|fpga),ssd".
- Examples:
  - -C "v100" — any node with feature v100
  - -C "gpu|fpga" — nodes with gpu OR fpga
  - -C "gpu,ssd" (or -C "gpu&ssd") — nodes that have both gpu AND ssd
  - -C "(gpu|fpga),highmem" — nodes that are highmem AND either gpu or fpga

Notes
- --constraint matches the feature tokens assigned to nodes; it filters at job submission time.
- There is a separate "extra constraints" mechanism (SchedulerParameters=extra_constraints) with its own key/value syntax if your site uses node Extra fields rather than Feature tokens.

## PERFORMANCE[#SECTION_PERFORMANCE](https://slurm.schedmd.com/strigger.html)
Executing strigger sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from strigger or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmctld daemon come in at once, it can result in
a degradation of performance of the slurmctld daemon, possibly resulting
in a denial of service.
Do not run strigger or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other
programs. Ensure that programs limit calls to strigger to the minimum
necessary for the information you are trying to gather.

Summary
- strigger is the Slurm tool to set, list (get) and clear event-driven triggers. Triggers watch Slurm events (job or node events, controller/burst-buffer events) and run an arbitrary program when the event occurs.
- Typical uses: notify admins on node failures, run a cleanup/notify script shortly before a job hits its time limit, or take action when a node is drained or goes down.

How it works (behavior)
- Commands: strigger --set, --get, --clear.
- strigger registers a trigger record (resource, event type, optional offset, program to run).
- Slurm checks for trigger events periodically (default ~15 seconds). Any events that occur within that interval are checked against registered triggers and the trigger program is executed once for events in that interval.
- OFFSET is specified in seconds; negative offsets request that the program run before the event (e.g., offset=-300 means 5 minutes before a job time limit).
- RES_ID can be a job id, a hostlist, or "*" for all hosts (depending on RES_TYPE).
- Permissions: users can create triggers relevant to their resources (typical case: their jobs). Some clear/management operations and global actions are restricted to root (see manpage).

Common trigger types (TYPE)
- job-related:
  - time — when a job reaches its time limit (use OFFSET to run before the limit)
  - fini — when a job finishes/terminates
- node-related / general:
  - down — node goes down
  - up — node returns up
  - drained — node is marked drained
  - idle — node becomes idle
  - reconfig — node or partition reconfiguration
- controller / service events:
  - backup_slurmctld_assumed_control, backup_slurmctld_failure, backup_slurmctld_resumed_operation
  - burst_buffer — burst buffer error
(See strigger manpage for the full option list and exact names.)

Output / fields you’ll see with --get
- TRIG_ID — trigger identifier
- RES_TYPE — "job" or "node"
- RES_ID — job id or hostlist (or "*")
- TYPE — trigger type (time, fini, down, up, drained, idle, reconfig, etc.)
- OFFSET — seconds (negative indicates before the event)
- USER — who registered it
- PROGRAM — pathname of program to execute
- (The manpage documents the full output fields.)

Examples
- Run notify.sh 5 minutes before job 1234 hits its time limit:
  strigger --set --type=time --jobid=1234 --offset=-300 --program=/home/alice/notify.sh
- Show triggers for a node or hostlist:
  strigger --get --node=node01
- Remove a trigger by its ID:
  strigger --clear --id=42

Caveats and best practices
- Triggers are not instantaneous — they are evaluated on the periodic check interval and executed once per interval for events that happened during that period.
- Avoid tight loops calling strigger (each call is an RPC to slurmctld); excessive calls can degrade slurmctld performance.
- Test trigger programs carefully (environment, permissions, PATH) because they run under slurmctld context or the requesting user depending on configuration.

Reference
- See the strigger manpage for full syntax, all supported event names and permissions: https://slurm.schedmd.com/strigger.html

If you want, I can:
- show example strigger commands tailored to a use case (jobs vs nodes), or
- walk through a specific trigger you want to create (I’ll explain exact flags and any permission considerations).

# gres.conf
Section: Slurm Configuration File (5)
Updated: Slurm Configuration File
[Index](https://slurm.schedmd.com/gres.conf.html)

Summary — how GRES are configured

Key idea
- GRES (Generic RESources) are declared to Slurm in two places:
  1) cluster-level types in slurm.conf (GresTypes), and
  2) per-node GRES assignments either in slurm.conf (NodeName ... Gres=...) or in a per-node gres.conf file (detailed device mapping).
- slurmctld requires the slurm.conf Gres/GresTypes entries to know what to expect; gres.conf is optional only when slurm.conf fully describes the resources.

Important slurm.conf settings
- GresTypes
  - Comma-separated list of resource types that Slurm will manage (example: GresTypes=gpu,mps,license).
  - This tells the controller which GRES names are valid cluster-wide.

- Node-level Gres
  - Attach GRES counts to nodes in the NodeName lines, for example:
    NodeName=tux[1-16] Gres=gpu:2,mps:200 ...
  - Syntax is Gres=<type>:<count>[,<type2>:<count2>,...].
  - These entries tell slurmctld how many of each GRES to expect on each node.

Per-node detailed configuration — gres.conf
- If slurm.conf does not fully describe device details (per-device files, core bindings, links, etc.), put a gres.conf on each compute node (and the controller for cloud setups).
- gres.conf entries can include Name, Type, File (device path), COREs, Count, and AutoDetect options.
- Example snippets commonly used in gres.conf:
  - AutoDetect=nvml
  - Name=gpu File=/dev/nvidia[0-1] COREs=0,1
  - Name=mps Count=100 File=/dev/nvidia0 COREs=0,1
- AutoDetect (nvml/rsmi/oneapi/nvidia, depending on Slurm version) can automatically populate device details; however, slurm.conf still needs the Gres= counts so the controller knows how many resources to expect.

Behavior and gotchas
- If a node actually has fewer GRES than declared in slurm.conf, Slurm will place that node into DRAIN (node will not be used) until corrected.
- For resources like NVIDIA MPS that can be shared, slurm.conf can define the total MPS count (e.g., Gres=mps:200) and the gres.conf controls per-GPU mapping or leaves Slurm to split counts evenly across the configured GPUs if no finer mapping is provided.
- Make sure any required vendor libraries for AutoDetect (e.g., NVML) are installed on nodes if you rely on automatic detection.

User-side notes
- Users request GRES with sbatch/srun/salloc via --gres, e.g. --gres=gpu:1. The cluster GresTypes and node Gres mappings determine whether such a request can be satisfied.

Applying and verifying changes
- Changes to slurm.conf/gres.conf take effect when Slurm daemons are restarted or when the daemons receive the appropriate signal / reconfigure action (see the slurm.conf man page for exact procedures).
- Typical verification commands (run on the controller) are sinfo and scontrol show node <nodename> (see Slurm docs for exact usage).

References used
- slurm.conf man page (Gres and GresTypes parameters)
- gres.conf man page (file format, AutoDetect, Name/Count/File/COREs examples)
- GRES scheduling documentation (behavior, AutoDetect and MPS notes)

In addition to putting burst buffer directives in the batch script, the

## Heterogeneous Job Support [#het-job-support](https://slurm.schedmd.com/burst_buffer.html)
Heterogeneous jobs may request burst buffers. Burst buffer hooks will run
once for each component that has burst buffer directives. For example, if a
heterogeneous job has three components and two of them have burst buffer
directives, the burst buffer hooks will run once for each of the two components
with burst buffer directives, but not for the third component without burst
buffer directives. Further information and examples can be found in the
heterogeneous jobs page.

A burst buffer can either be persistent or linked to a specific job ID.
Since a heterogeneous job consists of multiple job IDs, a job-specific burst
buffer will be associated with only one heterogeneous job component.

Good question — here’s a compact reference for how Slurm burst buffers are requested in jobs, what status you can observe, and how to troubleshoot.

What burst buffers are in Slurm (brief)
- Burst buffers are short‑lived (or persistent, in some plugins) fast storage pools used for staging I/O in/out of jobs (e.g., NVMe, DataWarp). Slurm supports a single burst buffer plugin configured in slurm.conf (commonly datawarp or lua).

How to request burst buffers in jobs
- Requests live in the job script as commented directives (so they’re ignored by the shell but parsed by Slurm). The directive string depends on the configured plugin:
  - DataWarp plugin: common directives start with #DW (for job-specific BB) and #BB (for persistent create/destroy). Example (conceptual):
    - #DW capacity=1200GiB pool=wlm_pool access=striped dest=/mnt/bb/$SLURM_JOB_ID
    - #BB create_persistent name=alpha capacity=10 access=striped type=scratch
  - Lua plugin: default directive is #BB_LUA (or another name if set in burst_buffer.conf). The lua plugin is flexible; presence of the directive can be enough and the plugin defines options.
- Command line: salloc/srun/sbatch accept --bb and --bbf.
  - --bb lets you pass burst‑buffer directives on the command line (parsing/semantics depend on the plugin).
  - --bbf <file> reads a file containing burst buffer operations (same syntax as script directives).
  - Note: --bb cannot create/destroy persistent buffers (that’s only from script directives / plugin-specific commands where supported).

Persistent vs job-specific buffers
- Persistent buffers are typically only available with the DataWarp plugin. They are created/destroyed with #BB create_persistent / #BB destroy_persistent.
- Job‑specific buffers are allocated for the job lifetime (with stages: stage‑in → staged‑in → pre‑run → running → post‑run → stage‑out → complete).

Where to check burst buffer status
- scontrol show burst
  - Shows configured burst buffer pools, size, free/used space, flags/timeouts, and a list of allocated/persistent buffers and per-user usage. Use this to see global pool health and allocations.
- scontrol show job <jobid>
  - For jobs that requested BB, the job record includes a BurstBufferState field and burst buffer allocation details. This is the main per‑job BB status.
- sview
  - GUI has a Burst Buffer tab showing similar information.
- Plugin-specific tools
  - DataWarp often provides CLI tools (e.g., dwstat) that slurm.conf can call; the scontrol show burst output may list GetSysStatus/GetSysState commands.

Meaning of common BurstBuffer states
(from Slurm docs; appear in scontrol show job as BurstBufferState)
- pending — request recorded, waiting to be processed
- allocating — (persistent buffers) creating allocation
- allocated — (persistent buffers) allocation complete
- staging-in — plugin is moving data into the burst buffer before the job runs
- staged-in — staging in completed
- pre-run — BB is ready and job is about to start
- running — job running and BB is active
- staging-out — plugin is moving data out after job completes
- complete — BB stages and teardown finished successfully
- deleting / deleted — (persistent buffers) being removed or removed
- alloc-revoke — an allocation was revoked due to a select/plugin failure (rare; indicates a failure between node allocation and job start)
- teardown-fail — teardown failed (plugin or storage error)
- suspended / post-run / teardown — other lifecycle phases used by some plugins

Typical job lifecycle with burst buffers
- submit → BB pending/allocating → BB staged-in / allocated → pre-run → job running → post-run → staging-out → complete (persistent BBs may transition to allocated/deleting/deleted independent of job lifetime).

What you see in scontrol show burst (fields)
- Name, DefaultPool, Granularity, TotalSpace, FreeSpace, UsedSpace
- Flags and configured timeouts (StageInTimeout, StageOutTimeout, ValidateTimeout, etc.)
- Allocated Buffers: lines listing JobID, CreateTime, Pool, Size, State, UserID
- Per User Buffer Use summary

Troubleshooting tips
- If job is stuck in staging-in or staged-in never becomes pre-run:
  - Check scontrol show job <id> to read BurstBufferState and any error/Reason fields.
  - Check scontrol show burst to see pool free/used space and any allocated buffers.
  - Inspect slurmctld logs and the burst buffer plugin logs (enable DebugFlags=BurstBuffer in slurm.conf for more verbose plugin logging temporarily).
  - Check plugin/system-specific tools (e.g., DataWarp CLI dwstat) for backend errors or slow devices.
  - Timeouts: burst buffer stages honor StageInTimeout / StageOutTimeout set in config — a stage exceeding timeout will fail.
- If allocations fail due to limits:
  - Ensure AccountingStorageTres includes bb/<plugin> (for accounting of BB TRES) and check QOS/association TRES limits that may constrain bb usage.
- alloc-revoke indicates a select-plugin or allocation race/failure; investigate slurmctld/plugin logs.

Useful admin controls / integration points
- Enable plugin in slurm.conf: BurstBufferType (datawarp or lua). Only one plugin allowed.
- Configure AccountingStorageTres to include bb/datawarp or bb/lua to record usage for accounting and limits.
- Reservations: scontrol create reservation ... burstbuffer=plugin:pool:#units makes BB reservation available to reservation participants.
- Persistent buffers managed only by DataWarp plugin via #BB create_persistent/destroy_persistent.

Practical examples (conceptual)
- Minimal DataWarp job header (concept):
  - #DW capacity=100GiB pool=fast_pool access=striped dest=/bb/$SLURM_JOB_ID
  - #SBATCH --nodes=1
- Create persistent buffer (concept):
  - #BB create_persistent name=alpha capacity=1000GiB access=striped type=scratch

Commands to inspect status
- scontrol show burst
- scontrol show job <jobid>   (look for BurstBufferState and related fields)
- sview (GUI)
- plugin-specific status tools (e.g., DataWarp CLI)
- For accounting/limits: check associations/QOS and AccountingStorageTres in slurm.conf and use sacctmgr / sreport if needed.

"Resources" (the pending reason shown by squeue) means the scheduler could not find sufficient trackable resources to place your job given its request and current cluster state. It is a catch‑all that indicates a resource shortfall encountered during scheduling (CPUs, memory, GPUs/GRES, nodes, licenses, HRES, etc.), not a policy/account or dependency blockage.

What it typically means
- Not enough free CPUs or whole nodes that match the job's cpus/memory/per‑node request.
- No nodes with the requested generic resource (GRES) or GPU type (or all matching GPU nodes are allocated/drained).
- Requested memory per node exceeds what's available on any suitable node.
- Node feature/constraint (--constraint, --gres-flags, --licenses, hierarchical resources) prevents a matching allocation.
- The job requests a combination (e.g., many GPUs + large memory) that no single node or set of nodes can satisfy.
- A reservation or current allocations block placement until a future time.
- HRES (resources.yaml) definitions can also cause "Resources" when their planning rules don’t allow a match.

Important notes
- Slurm reports only the first reason encountered by the scheduler, so "Resources" may mask a more specific underlying cause (e.g., GRES shortage, memory, or a feature mismatch).
- For GPU submissions, only idle GPU nodes count as available — allocated/mixed/drained nodes are not considered free for matching.

How to diagnose (commands to run)
- See the job's reason and queue row:
  squeue -j <JOBID> -o "%i %P %j %u %t %M %R"
- Show detailed job request and TRES:
  scontrol show job <JOBID>
  (look for ReqCPUS, MinNodes/Nodes, ReqMem, Gres, TRES)
- Inspect partition/node availability:
  sinfo -l                              # partition/node states and resources
  sinfo -N -o "%N %t %C %m %G %f"       # per-node CPUs, memory, GRES, features
- If GPUs involved, check GPU node idle counts (treat idle nodes only as available).
- Check reservations that might block placement:
  scontrol show reservation
- Check scheduler/backfill diagnostics and priorities if timing is unexpected:
  sdiag
  sprio -l
- If you need runtime/resource usage of a running job to guide requests:
  sstat -j <jobid>                       (running jobs only)

Common fixes
- Lower requested resources (fewer cpus, less memory, fewer GPUs) or request nodes differently (per‑node vs per‑task).
- Remove or relax constraints/feature requests (or request a different partition).
- Request a different GPU type or omit a specific gres if not required.
- Split a large job into smaller jobs if no single allocation can satisfy it.
- Submit with a different QOS or account if limits are causing denials (but that often shows different reason codes).
- Wait for resources to free (use sinfo/squeue to estimate when), or ask admins to create a reservation if the job must run at a specific time.
- If you believe a resource is idle but Slurm does not see it, ask admins to check node state (drain, down, maintenance) or HRES configuration.

If you want next steps / preventive checks
- Verify slurmdbd is healthy: systemctl status slurmdbd and check recent /var/log/slurm/slurmdbd.log for errors.
- Confirm slurmctld is recording accounting and slurmctld → slurmdbd connectivity: check /var/log/slurm/slurmctld.log and that AccountingStorageType/Host/User in scontrol show config are correct.
- Confirm time sync across controller and compute nodes (chrony/ntpd); clock skew breaks accounting timestamps.
- Run spot checks of accounting queries: sacct (recent jobs), sreport (usage), and sacctmgr list associations/users/accounts to ensure expected associations exist.

Common accounting problems and likely remediation
- slurmdbd unreachable / DB connection errors
  - Symptoms: sacctmgr show problems or slurmdbd logs show connection or authentication errors; accounting not updating.
  - Remediation: verify DB server is up, network access/firewall, DB credentials in slurmdbd.conf, restart slurmdbd after fixing DB; inspect slurmdbd.log for specific error text.

- Corrupt or incompatible DB schema (after upgrades)
  - Symptoms: schema errors in slurmdbd.log, queries failing.
  - Remediation: run slurmdbd upgrade steps from the upgrade docs; restore DB from a known-good backup if corruption is confirmed. Coordinate maintenance window.

- Missing user/account/QOS associations
  - Symptoms: jobs show “Assoc/Account unknown” or sreport shows unexpected user/account usage.
  - Remediation: recreate associations with sacctmgr (create/modify associations, add users to accounts/QOS). Audit sacctmgr list output to verify.

- Duplicate or missing job records (partial writes)
  - Symptoms: sacct shows missing job rows or inconsistent ExitCode/Elapsed values.
  - Remediation: check slurmctld and slurmdbd logs for dropped/racy writes; if caused by outages, consider replaying logs (if available) or restoring from backup; ensure slurmdbd is configured with reliable DB storage and sufficient resources.

- Time skew across nodes
  - Symptoms: job times negative or out-of-order in sacct/sreport; quotas/usage seem wrong.
  - Remediation: correct NTP/chrony configuration and resync clocks; re-run reports after time is stable. If timestamps are permanently wrong, consult backups or accept drift in historical data.

- Permissions/role problems when running sacctmgr
  - Symptoms: permission denied on sacctmgr operations.
  - Remediation: ensure sacctmgr is run by an authorized admin or use sacctmgr --immediate with proper credentials; check slurmdbd ACLs.

# Job Exit Codes
A job's exit code (aka exit status, return code and completion
code) is captured by Slurm and saved as part of the job record. For
sbatch jobs, the exit code that is captured is the output of the batch
script. For salloc jobs, the exit code will be the return value of
the exit call that terminates the salloc session. For srun, the exit
code will be the return value of the command that srun executes.
Any non-zero exit code will be assumed to be a job failure and will
result in a Job State of FAILED with a Reason of
"NonZeroExitCode".
The exit code is an 8 bit unsigned number ranging between 0 and
255. While it is possible for a job to return a negative exit code,
Slurm will display it as an unsigned value in the 0 - 255 range.

# Job Reason Codes
These reason codes can be used to identify why a pending job has not yet been
started by the scheduler. There may be multiple reasons why a job cannot start,
in which case only the reason that was encountered by the attempted scheduling
method will be displayed. Refer to the [Scheduling Configuration Guide](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sched_config.html) for more details.

Short summary (what each field is and how to read it)

- ExitCode
  - The ExitCode field is the exit status captured for the job (or job step) and is shown in the form exit:signal (for example the docs show 0:0). The left value is the 8‑bit exit/return code, the right value is a terminating signal number when a signal caused termination.
  - Which value is captured:
    - sbatch: the return code of the batch script.
    - srun: the return code of the command run by srun (each step records its own ExitCode).
    - salloc: the return value that terminates the salloc session.
  - Semantics:
    - Exit codes are treated as unsigned 8‑bit (0–255); negative returns are displayed as their unsigned representation.
    - Any non‑zero exit code is treated as a failure and will produce a job state FAILED with reason NonZeroExitCode (unless another failure condition overrides it).

- DerivedExitCode (and the job comment)
  - The DerivedExitCode is a derived/DB field stored with the job record (and an associated comment string). It is initially set by Slurm to the highest exit code returned by the job’s steps (so it reflects step-level failures even when the top-level script returns 0).
  - The DerivedExitCode is maintained by the controller and written to the accounting DB when AccountingStorage is enabled.
  - Administrators can inspect and change the DerivedExitCode and comment with sjobexitmod (the docs show usage and examples where a job’s DerivedExitCode becomes 49:0 with a comment like "out of memory").
  - sacct can display both ExitCode and DerivedExitCode via --format.

Why both exist (practical note)
- ExitCode shows what a specific job entry or step returned; DerivedExitCode gives a concise, DB-level summary of the worst step failure for the whole job (useful when a batch script exits 0 but one of several srun steps failed). The comment field can carry a human explanation that admins or users add.

References (documented behavior)
- Slurm job exit code docs (job_exit_code) describe the exit:signal format, 8‑bit range, step exit capture, DerivedExitCode initialization, and sjobexitmod for modification.
- sacct supports showing ExitCode and DerivedExitCode in accounting output.

## Hierarchy[#hierarchy](https://slurm.schedmd.com/resource_limits.html)
Slurm's hierarchical limits are enforced in the following order
with Job QOS and Partition QOS order being reversible by using the QOS
flag 'OverPartQOS':
- Partition QOS limit
- Job QOS limit
- User association
- Account association(s), ascending the hierarchy
- Root/Cluster association
- Partition limit
- None
Note: If limits are defined at multiple points in this hierarchy,
the point in this list where the limit is first defined will be used.

- MaxJobs=20 and MaxSubmitJobs is undefined in the partition QOS

## FLAT FILE DUMP AND LOAD[#SECTION_FLAT-FILE-DUMP-AND-LOAD](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sacctmgr.html)
sacctmgr has the capability to load and dump Slurm association data to and
from a file. This method can easily add a new cluster or copy an
existing cluster's associations into a new cluster with similar
accounts. Each file contains Slurm association data for a single
cluster. Beginning with version 25.05, QOS information is included in the
dump file. Comments can be put into the file with the # character.
Each line of information must begin with one of the five titles; QOS ,
Cluster , Parent , Account or User . Following the title
is a space, dash, space, entity value, then specifications. Specifications are
colon-separated. If any variable, such as an Organization name, has a space in
it, surround the name with single or double quotes.

Short answer
- "AssocGrpGRES" (or similarly named association field shown by sacctmgr) refers to the association-level group limits that apply specifically to GRES (Generic RESources — e.g., GPUs, licenses, burst buffers). It is how Slurm records or displays the GRES-related group/TRES limits for a user/account/association.

What association (group) GRES/TRES limits are
- TRES = Trackable RESource. GRES is the TRES type for generic resources (typically gpu, license, etc.).
- Association/group limits control aggregate and per-entity use of resources for an association (user+account+cluster+optional partition).
- Common GRES-related limits:
  - GrpTRES (or Assoc group TRES): aggregate limits for the association, e.g. GrpTRES=gres/gpu=8 (at most 8 GPUs in total across that association).
  - MaxTRESPerUser / MaxTRESPerAcct: per-user or per-account maximums (can be type- and model-qualified, e.g. gres/gpu:tesla=1).
  - MaxTRESPerJob: limit of a TRES per single job (e.g. a job cannot request > 4 GPUs).
  - Other related fields: GrpJobs, MaxJobs, etc., which affect job counts rather than TRES counts.

How the limits are expressed (syntax)
- Limits are given as comma-separated TRES=VALUE pairs. Example forms:
  - GrpTRES=cpu=128,mem=512G,gres/gpu=8
  - MaxTRESPerUser=gres/gpu:tesla=1
  - MaxTRESPerJob=gres/gpu=4
- GRES type qualification: you can qualify a GRES by model/type: gres/gpu:tesla or simply gres/gpu. The qualified form targets a specific GRES subtype.

Enforcement and precedence
- When Slurm considers starting a job, it checks association/group limits. If starting that job would exceed any applicable group limit, the job is not considered for allocation (remains pending).
- Precedence order for limits: job QOS / partition QOS and association levels are checked in a defined hierarchy. In general the first-defined limit in the precedence list is used (user association → account association(s) → cluster defaults), with some exceptions documented for certain limits (see Slurm docs).
- Changing limits:
  - If you lower a limit, running jobs are not killed to satisfy the new limit; the new limit is enforced for new allocations.
  - If you delete an association, jobs belonging to it are cancelled immediately.

Important GRES caveat (common pitfall)
- Type-specific limits vs generic requests: if you set a limit for a specific GRES type (e.g., MaxTRESPerUser=gres/gpu:tesla=1) but a user submits with --gres=gpu (no model specified), Slurm may not enforce the type-specific limit. In short: a type-specific limit will not block a generic request for a different/unspecified type. This is a known design limitation; if you need strict enforcement, require users to request specific types (via job_submit plugin or policies).

How to view and change these limits
- View defined GRES types: sacctmgr show tres
- View association limits: sacctmgr show association (use format options to display TRES/GrpTRES/MaxTRES* fields)
- Set/modify limits via sacctmgr. Example (run as admin):
  - sacctmgr modify account where name=chemistry set GrpTRES=gres/gpu=16
  - sacctmgr modify user where name=alice set MaxTRESPerUser=gres/gpu:tesla=1
- To remove a TRES limit assign -1 (or use sacctmgr syntax to remove that entry).

Recommendations / best practices
- Decide whether you want generic or model-specific enforcement. If model-specific enforcement is required, either:
  - require users to request a model in --gres (enforce with job_submit plugin), or
  - implement a lua job_submit plugin to rewrite/validate requests.
- Use sacctmgr show tres and show association formats regularly to audit active limits.
- Use GrpTRES for aggregate quotas and MaxTRESPerUser/MaxTRESPerJob for per-user or per-job caps.

References / where to read more
- sacctmgr and resource_limits docs in the Slurm manual (commands: sacctmgr show tres, sacctmgr show association; docs: "Resource Limits" and "sacctmgr" pages).

### Warnings [#Warnings](https://slurm.schedmd.com/extra_constraints.html)
Whitespace characters are not treated specially. Any whitespace characters will
be considered part of a key or value. This means that the following is invalid:
```text
--extra " (a=b)"
```
The space at he beginning is parsed as a key of a request. Then the opening
parenthesis character is recognized as an invalid character for either a key
or a comparison operator. This request would result in the job being rejected.
However, this is valid:
```text
--extra "( a=b)"
```
This has a single request. The key is " a", the comparison operator is "=", and
the value is "b".
This same warning applies to single and double quotes. These are not considered
special characters, and thus are part of a string. Thus, bar and "bar" are not
equal.

## Node Extra Data [#Node_Extra_Data](https://slurm.schedmd.com/extra_constraints.html)
A node's extra data is a json formatted string. It may be initialized on
slurmd startup with the --extra flag for slurmd. For example:
```text
slurmd --extra '{ "a": 1.23, "b": true, "c": 0, "foo": "bar", "zed": 23 }'
```
Or, it may be updated with scontrol. For example:
```text
scontrol update nodename=node123 extra='{ "a": 1.23, "b": true, "c": 0, "foo": "bar", "zed": 23 }'
```
This defines the features that may be requested by the --extra option in
salloc, sbatch, and srun. Values may be any string, number, or boolean value.

## Node Extra Data [#Node_Extra_Data](https://slurm.schedmd.com/extra_constraints.html)
A node's extra data is a json formatted string. It may be initialized on
slurmd startup with the --extra flag for slurmd. For example:
```text
slurmd --extra '{ "a": 1.23, "b": true, "c": 0, "foo": "bar", "zed": 23 }'
```
Or, it may be updated with scontrol. For example:
```text
scontrol update nodename=node123 extra='{ "a": 1.23, "b": true, "c": 0, "foo": "bar", "zed": 23 }'
```
This defines the features that may be requested by the --extra option in
salloc, sbatch, and srun. Values may be any string, number, or boolean value.

### Valid and Invalid Requests [#Valid](https://slurm.schedmd.com/extra_constraints.html)
Here are some examples of valid requests:
```text
a=1.23 a= b a!=1.24 a!=1.23|foo!=blah b=200 b=true foo =0.00000001) ((c =0.1)
```
Here are some examples of invalid requests:
Invalid comparison operator:
```text
a, =0.00000001) ((c =0.1)
```
The following --extra requests are not fulfilled by this node:
```text
a!=1.23 b=0 b=false foo>baz ((c =0.00001)
```
Reminder: in order for two numbers to be considered equal, their difference
must be less than 0.0001. This is why 0.0001 is not considered equal to 0 and
thus the request `c>=0.0001` is not fulfilled,
but 0.00000001 is considered equal to 0 and thus the request
`c>=0.00000001` is fulfilled.

### Warnings [#Warnings](https://slurm.schedmd.com/extra_constraints.html)
Whitespace characters are not treated specially. Any whitespace characters will
be considered part of a key or value. This means that the following is invalid:
```text
--extra " (a=b)"
```
The space at he beginning is parsed as a key of a request. Then the opening
parenthesis character is recognized as an invalid character for either a key
or a comparison operator. This request would result in the job being rejected.
However, this is valid:
```text
--extra "( a=b)"
```
This has a single request. The key is " a", the comparison operator is "=", and
the value is "b".
This same warning applies to single and double quotes. These are not considered
special characters, and thus are part of a string. Thus, bar and "bar" are not
equal.

## Node Extra Data [#Node_Extra_Data](https://slurm.schedmd.com/extra_constraints.html)
A node's extra data is a json formatted string. It may be initialized on
slurmd startup with the --extra flag for slurmd. For example:
```text
slurmd --extra '{ "a": 1.23, "b": true, "c": 0, "foo": "bar", "zed": 23 }'
```
Or, it may be updated with scontrol. For example:
```text
scontrol update nodename=node123 extra='{ "a": 1.23, "b": true, "c": 0, "foo": "bar", "zed": 23 }'
```
This defines the features that may be requested by the --extra option in
salloc, sbatch, and srun. Values may be any string, number, or boolean value.

## Overview [#Overview](https://slurm.schedmd.com/extra_constraints.html)
Extra data may be added to a node, and jobs may request extra constraints
to filter nodes based on their extra data. This is disabled by
default, but may be enabled in slurm.conf. Warning : Slurm's backfill
scheduler cannot accurately plan nodes for jobs whose request extra constraints
are not immediately satisfied. This means that the more often extra data for
nodes is changed, the less accurate the backfill scheduler will be.

sbatch submits a batch script to Slurm. The batch script may be given to
sbatch through a file name on the command line, or if no file name is specified,
sbatch will read in a script from standard input.
The batch script may contain one or more lines beginning with "#SBATCH" followed
by any of the CLI options documented on this page. #SBATCH directives are read
directly by Slurm, so shell-specific syntax including variable names will be

below.

### Warnings [#Warnings](https://slurm.schedmd.com/extra_constraints.html)
Whitespace characters are not treated specially. Any whitespace characters will
be considered part of a key or value. This means that the following is invalid:
```text
--extra " (a=b)"
```
The space at he beginning is parsed as a key of a request. Then the opening
parenthesis character is recognized as an invalid character for either a key
or a comparison operator. This request would result in the job being rejected.
However, this is valid:
```text
--extra "( a=b)"
```
This has a single request. The key is " a", the comparison operator is "=", and
the value is "b".
This same warning applies to single and double quotes. These are not considered
special characters, and thus are part of a string. Thus, bar and "bar" are not
equal.

### Warnings [#Warnings](https://slurm.schedmd.com/extra_constraints.html)
Whitespace characters are not treated specially. Any whitespace characters will
be considered part of a key or value. This means that the following is invalid:
```text
--extra " (a=b)"
```
The space at he beginning is parsed as a key of a request. Then the opening
parenthesis character is recognized as an invalid character for either a key
or a comparison operator. This request would result in the job being rejected.
However, this is valid:
```text
--extra "( a=b)"
```
This has a single request. The key is " a", the comparison operator is "=", and
the value is "b".
This same warning applies to single and double quotes. These are not considered
special characters, and thus are part of a string. Thus, bar and "bar" are not
equal.

## DESCRIPTION[#SECTION_DESCRIPTION](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
sbatch submits a batch script to Slurm. The batch script may be given to
sbatch through a file name on the command line, or if no file name is specified,
sbatch will read in a script from standard input.
The batch script may contain one or more lines beginning with "#SBATCH" followed
by any of the CLI options documented on this page. #SBATCH directives are read
directly by Slurm, so shell-specific syntax including variable names will be
read as literal text. Once the first non-comment, non-whitespace line has been
reached in the script, no more #SBATCH directives will be processed. See example
below.
sbatch exits immediately after the script is successfully transferred to the
Slurm controller and assigned a Slurm job ID. The batch script is not

## Overview [#Overview](https://slurm.schedmd.com/extra_constraints.html)
Extra data may be added to a node, and jobs may request extra constraints
to filter nodes based on their extra data. This is disabled by
default, but may be enabled in slurm.conf. Warning : Slurm's backfill
scheduler cannot accurately plan nodes for jobs whose request extra constraints
are not immediately satisfied. This means that the more often extra data for
nodes is changed, the less accurate the backfill scheduler will be.

The following --extra requests are not fulfilled by this node:

```

must be less than 0.0001. This is why 0.0001 is not considered equal to 0 and

### Warnings [#Warnings](https://slurm.schedmd.com/extra_constraints.html)
Whitespace characters are not treated specially. Any whitespace characters will
be considered part of a key or value. This means that the following is invalid:
```text
--extra " (a=b)"
```
The space at he beginning is parsed as a key of a request. Then the opening
parenthesis character is recognized as an invalid character for either a key
or a comparison operator. This request would result in the job being rejected.
However, this is valid:
```text
--extra "( a=b)"
```
This has a single request. The key is " a", the comparison operator is "=", and
the value is "b".
This same warning applies to single and double quotes. These are not considered
special characters, and thus are part of a string. Thus, bar and "bar" are not
equal.

Short answer
- Fair Tree is Slurm’s current fair-share ranking algorithm (used by priority/multifactor). It ranks every user/association in a tree-shaped account hierarchy so that siblings are compared only to each other, then the tree is traversed (depth‑first, pre‑order) to produce a strict ranking. That ranking becomes the fairshare factor used by the scheduler (higher = higher priority).

Why Fair Tree exists / benefits
- Preserves parent/child ordering: if account A (a parent or sibling) ranks above account B, then every child/user under A ranks above every child/user under B. This prevents coordinators of sub-accounts from accidentally outranking users in other accounts.
- Stable numeric ordering: reduces precision/tie problems present in the older Classic algorithm.
- Ranks all associations (active or inactive), producing a global ordering used by the multifactor plugin.

High-level algorithm (steps)
1. For each node (association/account/user) compute a Level Fairshare value that considers only that node and its siblings (uses configured shares and each sibling’s usage).
2. For each subtree, sort the children by their Level Fairshare (highest first).
3. Build a rooted, ordered tree with children sorted left→right; perform a depth‑first pre‑order traversal:
   - Visit a child subtree fully before moving to the next sibling.
   - When you encounter a user association during traversal assign it the next rank.
4. Convert the user’s rank into the final fairshare factor: rank / total_number_of_user_associations (the top‑ranked user gets 1.0).

Important operational details
- Uses accounting DB usage and configured shares (Assoc/Account shares). Fair Tree requires the Slurm accounting DB to calculate usage-derived values.
- Priority decay: usage values are decayed using PriorityDecayHalfLife and recalculated every PriorityCalcPeriod. Those parameters control how long past usage affects fairshare.
- The multifactor plugin then multiplies the fairshare factor by PriorityWeightFairshare when computing Job_priority (see priority/multifactor).
- sshare -l shows FairShare and “Level FS” columns. Level FS may be shown as “inf” if an association has no usage.
- scontrol reconfigure does not necessarily trigger an immediate Fair Tree recompute — the algorithm runs on its scheduled calculation period; you may need to wait one PriorityCalcPeriod or force a recompute via the scheduler’s normal recalculation mechanisms.

Practical admin notes and recommendations
- Because Fair Tree produces a global strict ordering, you should pick PriorityWeightFairshare carefully (often lower than historical defaults). The docs suggest using a smaller weight (even as low as 1–2 × number_of_associations) depending on other priority factors.
- Configure PriorityDecayHalfLife and PriorityCalcPeriod to match how quickly you want past usage to fade.
- Verify results with sshare -l and sprio (or sprio --weights) to see how fairshare contributes to overall priority.
- Be aware that inactive associations are still ranked; this affects how ties and ordering behave site‑wide.

Short example intuition
- Suppose two sibling accounts A and B. If A’s Level Fairshare > B’s Level Fairshare, then during traversal all users under A will be visited before any users under B — so every child of A will have a higher fairshare rank (and thus higher fairshare factor) than every child of B. Within A, children are ordered by their own Level FS and so on down the tree.

References / commands to inspect (docs/tools)
- Docs: fair_tree algorithm page in the Slurm docs (fair_tree.html) and priority/multifactor page.
- Inspector commands: sshare -l (view fairshare and Level FS), sprio (priority factors), and check Priority* settings in slurm.conf (PriorityType, PriorityCalcPeriod, PriorityDecayHalfLife, PriorityWeightFairshare).

Brief summary
- The singleton dependency ensures at most one job with the same user + job name is allowed to be active at a time.  
- When you submit a job with --dependency=singleton (or #SBATCH --dependency=singleton), Slurm implicitly delays that job until any earlier job(s) with the same user and the same job name have finished. Once those earlier job(s) exit (in any final state), the singleton job becomes eligible to start.

Why and when to use it
- Use singleton when you want serialized execution of jobs that share the same job name (for example periodic jobs, or multiple submissions of the same workflow) and you don’t want two of them running concurrently.
- It is a lightweight alternative to manually creating after: dependencies between specific job IDs.

Behavior notes / gotchas
- The “same job” is matched by job name and submitting user. Jobs with a different name or user are not considered.
- The dependency is satisfied when the earlier job terminates in any final state (i.e., success or failure). It does not require a successful exit.
- It only affects jobs that include the singleton dependency; other jobs without that dependency are unaffected and can run concurrently.
- If you submit many singleton jobs in sequence, they will effectively run one at a time in the order Slurm resolves them.
- Don’t rely on singleton for complex ordering across different job names or users—use explicit job-ID dependencies (after, afterok, afterany, etc.) when you need precise control.

How to set it
- sbatch --dependency=singleton myscript.sh
- or in a batch script: #SBATCH --dependency=singleton

## Overview[#overview](https://slurm.schedmd.com/select_design.html)
The select plugin is responsible for selecting compute resources to be
allocated to a job, plus allocating and deallocating those resources.
The select plugin is aware of the systems topology, based upon data structures
established by the topology plugin. It can also over-subscribe resources to
support gang scheduling (time slicing of parallel jobs), if so configured.
Other architectures would rely upon the select/linear
or select/cons_tres plugins. The select/linear plugin allocates
whole nodes to jobs and is the simplest implementation.
The select/cons_tres plugin ( cons_tres is an abbreviation for
trackable resources ) can allocate individual sockets, cores, threads
or CPUs within a node. It also includes the ability to manage other generic
resources, such as GPUs.
The select/cons_tres plugin is slightly slower than
select/linear, but contains far more complex logic...

Notes and what this means
- select/cons_tres is the "consumable trackable resources" selection plugin. It lets Slurm allocate consumable resources inside a node (CPUs/cores/threads, memory, sockets/boards and generic resources such as GPUs) rather than only whole nodes. This enables co‑scheduling multiple jobs on the same node when resources permit.
- With this plugin you typically set SelectTypeParameters in slurm.conf to pick which consumable resources are tracked (examples below). If SelectTypeParameters is not present in the controller config output, it may still be present in slurm.conf.

Common SelectTypeParameters examples
- CR_CPU — track logical CPUs (cores/threads)
- CR_Core — track physical cores
- CR_Socket — track sockets
- CR_Board — track boards
- CR_CPU_Memory or CR_Core_Memory or CR_Socket_Memory — track CPU/core (or socket) together with memory per unit
- Generic resources (GPUs) are tracked viaGRES and consumable resource accounting when cons_tres is enabled

User-visible effects / requests
- Users request CPUs/memory via --cpus-per-task, --ntasks, --mem, etc.; GPUs via --gres=gpu:...

Job arrays offer a mechanism for submitting and managing collections of

## EXAMPLES[#SECTION_EXAMPLES](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Specify a batch script by filename on the command line. The batch script specifies a 1 minute time limit for the job.
```text
$ cat myscript #!/bin/sh #SBATCH --time=1 srun hostname |sort $ sbatch -N4 myscript salloc: Granted job allocation 65537 $ cat slurm-65537.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
Pass a batch script to sbatch on standard input:
```text
$ sbatch -N4 #!/bin/sh > srun hostname |sort > EOF sbatch: Submitted batch job 65541 $ cat slurm-65541.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
To create a heterogeneous job with 3 components, each allocating a unique set of nodes:
```text
$ sbatch -w node[2-3] : -w node4 : -w node[5-7] work.bash Submitted batch job 34987
```

Short answer first
- Job arrays are a single sbatch submission that creates many similar jobs (elements). The array has a single array-job ID (the "master" job allocation number) and each element has an index (task ID) and its own per-element job id.
- %A and %a are sbatch filename-replacement symbols: %A expands to the array's master job allocation number; %a expands to the element (array index) value. Use %A_%a (or SLURM_ARRAY_JOB_ID/SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID) to build unique filenames per element.

Key terms and mappings (from Slurm docs)
- Array submission: sbatch --array=1-100 myscript
  - The sbatch command returns a single array-job id (the array "master" id). Example: "Submitted batch job 36".
- Array element notation: <ArrayJobID>_<Index>
  - Example element reference: 36_4 (array 36, element index 4).
  - Referring to the whole array uses just the array id (36).
- Environment variables set for array jobs:
  - SLURM_ARRAY_JOB_ID — the job id for the array (the array's master job allocation number).
  - SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID — the array element index (the task id for this element).
  - SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_COUNT, SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_MAX, SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_MIN — summary counts/min/max for the array.
  (These are set inside the batch script environment for each element.)
- Per-element SLURM_JOB_ID:
  - Each array element behaves like a regular job and has its own SLURM_JOB_ID visible inside the element. SLURM_ARRAY_JOB_ID groups the elements; SLURM_JOB_ID is the element’s job id.

Filename replacement symbols (sbatch --output / FILENAME PATTERN)
- %A — Job array's master job allocation number (the array id).
- %a — Job array ID (index) number (the element index).
- %b — Job array ID modulo 10 (useful for sharding by last digit).
- %j — jobid of the running job (useful for non-array jobs or per-element SLURM_JOB_ID).
- %% — literal percent sign.
Use these in --output/--error/--open-mode filename patterns. Example:
- sbatch --array=1-3 --output=slurm-%A_%a.out myscript
  - If sbatch returned "Submitted batch job 36", element 1 will write slurm-36_1.out, element 2 slurm-36_2.out, etc.

Examples showing how they relate
- Inside the script for array element index 4:
  - SLURM_ARRAY_JOB_ID might be 36
  - SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID will be 4
  - SLURM_JOB_ID will be the unique job id for that element (e.g., 1024)
- Referencing elements from commands:
  - scancel 36_4 cancels element 4 of array 36
  - scancel 36 cancels all elements of array 36
  - --depend=after:123_4 (depend on element 4 of array 123), or --depend=after:123 (depend on entire array)

Notes and gotchas
- The array index values come from the --array specification and may be non-contiguous (e.g., --array=1,3,5) or have steps (--array=1-10:2).
- You can limit concurrency with --array=0-31%4 (max 4 concurrent elements).
- %A is suitable for filenames to identify the array; %a is required to distinguish elements within that array. If you use %j (per-element jobid) it may be different from the array master id.
- Use the SLURM environment variables inside the script when you need programmatic control (filename creation, logging, scancel logic, dependencies).

If you want, I can show concrete examples (sbatch lines and expected filenames) for a particular array range / output pattern you plan to use.

## Local Licenses [#local_licenses](https://slurm.schedmd.com/licenses.html)
Local licenses are defined in the slurm.conf using the Licenses
option.
slurm.conf:
```text
Licenses=fluent:30,ansys:100
```
Configured licenses can be viewed using the scontrol command.
```text
$ scontrol show lic LicenseName=ansys Total=100 Used=0 Free=100 Remote=no LicenseName=fluent Total=30 Used=0 Free=30 Remote=no
```
Requesting licenses is done by using the -L, or --licenses, submission
option.
```text
$ sbatch -L ansys:2 script.sh Submitted batch job 5212 $ scontrol show lic LicenseName=ansys Total=100 Used=2 Free=98 Remote=no LicenseName=fluent Total=30 Used=0 Free=30 Remote=no
```
Licenses may also be requested using the --tres-per-task option for
job submission. If this approach is used, the license must also be defined in
the AccountingStorageTRES option of the slurm.conf.
slurm.conf:
```text
Licenses=fluent:30 AccountingStorageTRES=license/fluent
`...

Remote licenses do not offer any kind of integration with third party

### Configuring Slurm for the use case [#configuring](https://slurm.schedmd.com/licenses.html)
Here we assume that both clusters have been configured correctly in the
slurmdbd using the sacctmgr command.
```text
$ sacctmgr show clusters format=cluster,controlhost Cluster ControlHost ---------- --------------- fluid 143.11.1.3 pdf 144.12.3.2
```
The licenses are added using the sacctmgr command, specifying the
total count of licenses and the percentage that should be allocated
to each cluster. This can be done either in one step or through a
multi-step process.
One step:
```text
$ sacctmgr add resource name=nastran cluster=fluid,pdf \ count=100 allowed=50 server=flex_host servertype=flexlm type=license Adding Resource(s) nastran@flex_host Cluster - fluid 50 Cluster - pdf 50 Settings Name = nastran Server = flex_host Description = nastran ServerType = flexlm Count = 100 Type = License
```
Multi-step:
```text
$ sacctmgr add resource name=m...

Summary — what a "license" is in Slurm
- Slurm can manage software licenses as schedulable resources (like GPUs or CPUs). Licenses are added as resources (TRES of type license) and the scheduler will account for and enforce their total counts when placing jobs.
- Admins define license pools (counts, local vs remote, cluster allocation) in Slurm’s configuration and accounting DB; users request them on job submission.

Key admin concepts
- Local licenses: configured in slurm.conf with the Licenses= option, e.g. Licenses=fluent:30,ansys:100. These are static counts known to the controller.
- AccountingStorageTRES: to record license usage in accounting, map license names to a TRES string (e.g. AccountingStorageTRES=license/fluent). This lets Slurm track license consumption in sacct/sreport.
- License resources in the accounting DB: sacctmgr add resource ... (type=License) is used to create/allocate license pools, including multi-cluster splits (allowed % per cluster) or server/serverType metadata for remote license systems.
- Remote and Dynamic licenses: Slurm can represent remote license servers (metadata only). From Slurm 23.02 onward you can update LastConsumed in the accounting DB so Slurm computes LastDeficit (licenses that must be reserved because they appear checked out to external servers). Admins typically run a periodic script that queries the real license server (lmstat or similar) and updates sacctmgr with the current consumption so Slurm’s view stays in sync.

How users request licenses (job submission)
- The supported submission option is -L or --licenses. Example:
  sbatch -L ansys:2 script.sh
  This requests 2 units from the license pool named "ansys".
- You can request multiple licenses separated by commas, and combine with other resource requests.
- Alternative: request licenses as a TRES per task with --tres-per-task=license/<name>:N. If you use this, the license name must also be present in AccountingStorageTRES so accounting and job matching work correctly.
- Requests consume the license count for the job’s lifetime (until job completes or is cancelled).

How Slurm enforces and reports licenses
- Slurm tracks Total, Used, Free for each license pool. You can view them with scontrol show lic or the scontrol_license read. Example from docs:
  scontrol show lic LicenseName=ansys Total=100 Used=2 Free=98 Remote=no
- When a job requests more licenses than are free in the pool, the scheduler will not place the job; the pending reason will reflect the resource shortage (inspect squeue to see the pending reason).
- For remote/dynamic scenarios, if the accounting DB shows fewer free licenses due to LastConsumed/LastDeficit, Slurm will reserve licenses accordingly to avoid oversubscription.

Admin operations and scripts
- Add/update license pools with sacctmgr (add resource name=<name> type=License count=<N> [cluster=... allowed=... server=...]).
- To keep remote license counts accurate, run a periodic script that queries the license server and runs sacctmgr to update lastconsumed; Slurm will incorporate those updates into scheduling decisions.
- Ensure AccountingStorageTRES includes license/<name> if you intend to use --tres-per-task to request licenses.

Practical notes / best practices
- Use -L for straightforward license requests. Use --tres-per-task when you need per-task license accounting, but ensure AccountingStorageTRES is configured.
- Treat Slurm’s license objects as “bookable slots” — they don’t automatically talk to third‑party license managers unless you implement synchronization (the remote/server fields are informational).
- Monitor license usage with scontrol show lic and include license metrics in any usage reports (sreport can summarize resource usage if configured).
- If jobs are stuck pending for licenses, check squeue to see the pending reason and inspect scontrol show lic to confirm current Free/Used counts.

References / commands (docs)
- sbatch/salloc/srun -L/--licenses option
- slurm.conf: Licenses= and AccountingStorageTRES=
- sacctmgr add resource / sacctmgr update resource (for pools and LastConsumed)
- scontrol show lic and scontrol_license to view current pools
- See Slurm “Licenses” guide and “Job Reason Codes” in the official docs for full details.

If you want, I can:
- show the current license pools on your cluster (scontrol show lic / scontrol_license), or
- walk through an example sacctmgr command to add a new license pool — which would be an admin action (I would hand that off to the operator).

Slurm's job scheduler handles GRES affinity on a socket basis internally.
However, the gres.conf interface allows administrators to specify `Cores` for GPU affinity configuration. This creates

scheduling, which it does not and never has. This can lead to issues where job

## Notes[#NOTES](https://slurm.schedmd.com/configless_slurm.html)
Starting from Slurm 25.11, there's a new
SlurmctldParameters=reconfig_on_restart option that will make every
restart of slurmctld (process restart not triggered by "scontrol reconfigure")
to trigger a reconfiguration request to all slurmd and sackd daemons. For
"configless" systems this will ensure all processes are running the current
configuration. Some caution should be taken if you intend to perform rolling
upgrades on the cluster as this could lead to the daemons being upgraded sooner
than expected.
The order of precedence for determining what configuration source to use
is as follows:
- The slurmd --conf-server $host[:$port] option
- The -f $config_file option
- The SLURM_CONF environment variable (if set)
- A local slurm config file: The default slurm config file (likely /etc/slurm.conf)

## DESCRIPTION[#SECTION_DESCRIPTION](https://slurm.schedmd.com/slurm.conf.html)
slurm.conf is an ASCII file which describes general Slurm
configuration information, the nodes to be managed, information about
how those nodes are grouped into partitions, and various scheduling
parameters associated with those partitions. This file should be
consistent across all nodes in the cluster.
The file location can be modified at execution time by setting the SLURM_CONF
environment variable. The Slurm daemons also allow you to override
both the built-in and environment-provided location using the "-f"
option on the command line.
The contents of the file are case insensitive except for the names of nodes
