## UNKILLABLE STEP PROGRAM SCRIPT[#SECTION_UNKILLABLE-STEP-PROGRAM-SCRIPT](https://slurm.schedmd.com/slurm.conf.html)
This program can be used to take special actions to clean up the unkillable
processes and/or notify system administrators.
The program will be run as SlurmdUser (usually "root") on the compute
node where UnkillableStepTimeout was triggered.
Information about the unkillable job step is passed to the script using
environment variables.
SLURM_JOB_ID [#OPT_SLURM_JOB_ID](https://slurm.schedmd.com/slurm.conf.html) Job ID.
SLURM_STEP_ID [#OPT_SLURM_STEP_ID](https://slurm.schedmd.com/slurm.conf.html) Job Step ID. Note that the special steps "batch", "interactive", and "extern"
are reported not by name but with integer Step IDs 4294967291, 4294967290, and
4294967292 respectively.

Summary — what GRES is
- GRES = Generic RESources. It’s how Slurm advertises and allocates non-CPU resources such as GPUs, MPS slots, MIG instances, license tokens, shards, etc.
- Node-level configuration lives in slurm.conf (Gres= on NodeName lines) and optionally per-node gres.conf (detailed device mapping / AutoDetect). The scheduler matches job requests against the configured GRES.

Key GRES syntax (node config)
- In slurm.conf you typically set: NodeName=node[01-08] Gres=gpu:4,mps:200
- In gres.conf each device can be described; Slurm supports AutoDetect (nvml/rsmi/oneapi) to discover GPU devices.
- GRES element format (job-side requests): name[:type:count]
  - name: GRES name (commonly "gpu")
  - type: optional string to distinguish device types (e.g., v100, a100, or a MIG profile substring)
  - count: number required (integer)
  - Examples: gpu:2   gpu:tesla:2   mps:50

Requesting GPUs at submit time
- --gres (generic): --gres=gpu[:type:count]
  - Example: sbatch --gres=gpu:2  (requests 2 GPUs per allocated node by the select plugin semantics)
  - Example with type: --gres=gpu:V100:2 (requests GPUs whose type string contains "V100")
- Convenience / GPU-specific options (shortcuts; require select/cons_tres plugin):
  - --gpus=N
    - Requests N GPUs for the job allocation (total GPUs for the job). Often equivalent to requesting --gres=gpu:N but semantics depend on whether you combine with -N/-n.
  - --gpus-per-node=N
    - Equivalent to --gres for GPUs: request N GPUs on each allocated node.
  - --gpus-per-task=N
    - Request N GPUs for each task; requires you also set a task count (e.g., --ntasks or srun task counts).
  - --gpus-per-socket, --gpus-per-core also exist for socket/core-level placement in clusters that support them.

How counts map into allocations (common patterns)
- Single-node 2 GPUs: sbatch --gpus=2 or sbatch --gres=gpu:2
- Two nodes, 1 GPU each: sbatch -N2 --gpus-per-node=1  (get 2 nodes × 1 GPU)
- MPI with one GPU per rank: sbatch --gpus-per-task=1 --ntasks-per-node=4  (4 tasks on node, each gets 1 GPU — requires enough GPUs on node)
- If you use --gpus (total) plus multiple nodes, scheduler may place them across nodes to satisfy the total; use --gpus-per-node to guarantee per-node counts.

MIG, MPS, sharding and partial-GPU resources
- MIG: Slurm supports NVIDIA MIG instances. MIG profiles can be exposed as separate GRES; type in name[:type:count] can match a MIG profile substring.
- MPS/sharding: Slurm can expose sharable resources like mps or shard in slurm.conf/gres.conf. You request them with --gres=mps:50 (counts are configured by admin). MPS/shard allocations have special semantics and require appropriate plugins.
- Note: requesting a fractional GPU (percent) is admin-configured via sharding/MPS; plain "gpu:0.5" is not supported — you request integer counts of the configured GRES units.

Environment variables and device visibility
- Slurm sets CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES for job steps to limit each step’s visible GPU devices to the ones allocated on that node. This is how Slurm ensures distinct assignments between jobs.
- The exact env vars available can vary by Slurm version and local configuration; always check your job environment if you rely on a specific variable.

Accounting and monitoring
- If AccountingStorageTRES=gres/gpu is enabled, Slurm will collect gres/gpumem and gres/gpuutil (NVML/rsmi required) for accounting.
- TRES name for GPUs is typically gres/gpu (and can show up in sacct output if accounting is configured).

Requirements & gotchas
- select/cons_tres plugin: the modern --gpus* options and many GRES features require the select/cons_tres plugin; jobs that request GPU options on systems not configured with that plugin will be rejected.
- Types must match admin configuration: if admins used a custom GRES type string in gres.conf (or used MIG profile substrings), you must match that type string when requesting specific types.
- CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES maps to device indices visible inside the job, not necessarily the physical device IDs you see with nvidia-smi on the whole node. cgroups may be used to restrict device files too.
- If your job is pending with a GPU request, use sinfo and squeue to inspect partition/node GPU availability (and pending reason). If unsure which type to request, ask your cluster admins or inspect node gres with sinfo or node slurmd logs.

Practical examples
- Simple 2-GPU batch script:
  #SBATCH --gpus=2
  #SBATCH -t 02:00:00
  ...
- Request 1 GPU per task for 8 MPI ranks (8 GPUs total, assigned per rank):
  #SBATCH --ntasks=8
  #SBATCH --gpus-per-task=1
- Two nodes, 2 GPUs per node:
  sbatch -N2 --gpus-per-node=2 myscript.sh
- Request specific GPU type:
  sbatch --gres=gpu:A100:4 my_a100_job.sh

If you want, I can:
- Show exact local examples based on your cluster’s gres configuration (I’d read sinfo/gres or show gres.conf), or
- Help convert a particular MPI/CUDA job script to the correct --gpus/--gres usage for one-GPU-per-rank or multi-GPU-per-node patterns.

Short answer
- Node features are arbitrary labels (strings) attached to nodes that describe capabilities or configuration (examples: gpu, v100, ssd, ib, highmem). They let users request nodes with particular capabilities without changing partitions.
- Jobs request features with --constraint (or -C) using a boolean expression. The scheduler filters candidate nodes to those whose feature set satisfies the expression; only those nodes are considered for placement.

What a "feature" is and how it’s stored
- Declared in slurm.conf as Feature= on NodeName lines, or provided dynamically by a NodeFeatures plugin / helper.
- Features are just tags/strings (not counted resources). Some features may be “available but not active” (common for cloud/power-managed nodes); requesting such a feature can trigger the controller to activate/power-on the node at allocation time.
- Changing some features via helpers may require a node reboot.

How to request features (constraint expressions)
- Request with sbatch/srun/salloc: --constraint=<expr> (or -C <expr>).
- Expression grammar (common operators):
  - AND: & (or comma , in some docs) — both sides must match
  - OR: | — either side matches
  - NOT: ! — node must not have that feature
  - Parentheses () to group expressions
- Examples:
  - -C gpu        → node must have feature "gpu"
  - -C "gpu&v100" → node must have both gpu and v100
  - -C "gpu|tpu"  → node with gpu OR tpu
  - -C "!infiniband" → node without feature "infiniband"
  - -C "(v100|a100)&gpu" → gpu nodes with either v100 or a100 tags

How features affect placement and scheduling behavior
- Filtering: The constraint expression filters the set of candidate nodes before the scheduler considers resources on them. If no nodes satisfy the constraint, the job remains pending.
- Availability vs activation: If a feature is listed as available but inactive (cloud/power-managed), the controller may allocate and activate the node to satisfy the job. This can increase job startup latency.
- Backfill and fragmentation: Using many, narrow, or frequently-changing features reduces the pool of eligible nodes and can fragment resources, which may increase queueing time and reduce backfill effectiveness. The Slurm docs warn that frequent changes to node extra/feature data hurt backfill accuracy.
- Features are not resource counters: Two jobs can request the same feature; Slurm still enforces resource limits (CPUs, memory, gres) per node but does not limit feature usage unless combined with other controls.
- Partition scope: Constraints are applied within the chosen partition(s). Requesting a partition plus a constraint limits placement to nodes in that partition that match the constraint.
- Interaction with GRES: Hardware that has Slurm GRES (e.g., GPUs) should normally be requested via --gres=gpu:N. Some sites also tag GPU nodes with a feature (e.g., gpu or v100). Prefer --gres for counting and allocation semantics and use features for non-counted capabilities (special NICs, accelerators that aren’t configured as GRES, licensed software, local SSD).
- Extra constraints: Slurm also supports node "Extra" fields (SchedulerParameters=extra_constraints) with richer comparison operators; these are different from simple Feature tags and use a small expression language.

Practical tips / best practices
- Use short, stable, documented feature names (alphanumeric, no operator chars).
- Prefer --gres for devices you need counted (GPUs, MICs).
- Keep the number of distinct feature combinations small to avoid fragmentation.
- For cloud/power-managed nodes, be aware requests can power-on nodes and add latency — document that to users.
- To inspect node features on your cluster: sinfo or scontrol show node (e.g., sinfo -Nl or scontrol show node <nodename>) to see the Feature list.
- If you need complex node-selection logic (e.g., key/value metadata comparisons), look at SchedulerParameters=extra_constraints and Extra node fields.

## Accounting Interpretation [#accounting-interpretation](https://slurm.schedmd.com/accounting.html)
Slurm accounting is mainly focused on parallel computing. For this reason it
gathers statistics at a "task level". A task is a set of user processes which
run in a step, which is part of a job. A user can submit a step with many
parallel tasks, e.g. by calling `srun -n`.
The [JobAcctGather](https://slurm.schedmd.com/slurm.conf.html) plugin
gathers metrics for some [Trackable Resources (TRES)](https://slurm.schedmd.com/tres.html),
like cpu, memory, energy, etc., at a given interval in the [JobAcctGatherFrequency](https://slurm.schedmd.com/slurm.conf.html)
defined in slurm.conf, or by using the `--acct-freq` option in the
command line. A poll of data is also triggered at the start or the end of a
step.
Depending on the nature of the metric, the values will be recorded as
standalone values or aggregated/calculated into a data structure.

## Infrastructure [#infrastructure](https://slurm.schedmd.com/accounting.html)
With the SlurmDBD, we are able to collect data from multiple
clusters in a single location.
This does impose some constraints on the user naming and IDs.
Accounting is maintained by user name (not user ID), but a
given user name should refer to the same person across all
of the computers.
Authentication relies upon user ID numbers, so those must
be uniform across all computers communicating with each
SlurmDBD, at least for users requiring authentication.
In particular, the configured SlurmUser must have the
same name and ID across all clusters.
If you plan to have administrators of user accounts, limits,
etc. they must also have consistent names and IDs across all
clusters.
If you plan to restrict access to accounting records (e.g.
only permit a user to view records of his jobs), then all
users should have consistent names and IDs.

Below is a focused, practical explanation of the Slurm configuration items that matter most for scheduling behavior and for accounting/enforcement. I cover where each setting lives (slurm.conf vs SlurmDBD/sacctmgr), what it does, typical knobs to tune, and quick commands you can run to inspect them.

High-level split
- Scheduling configuration: mainly in slurm.conf (SchedulerType, select/consumable-resource plugins, priority/ backfill / preemption parameters, partitions, GRES, TRES). These determine how jobs are ordered, what resources are considered, and how the scheduler backfills or preempts.
- Accounting/enforcement: SlurmDBD + sacctmgr and slurm.conf accounting plugins (AccountingStorage*, JobAcctGather*, JobCompType, AccountingStorageEnforce). These collect usage, configure accounts/QOS/limits, and enforce caps.

Key scheduling items (slurm.conf and related)
- Partitions
  - PartitionName entries in slurm.conf define which nodes/jobs belong to logical queues, default time limits, QOS visibility, and accessibility. Partitions are a fundamental scheduling scope (scheduling decisions, limits, preemption often partition-aware).
  - Inspect: scontrol show partition or sinfo.

- Node selection and resource model
  - SelectType / SelectTypeParameters (e.g., select/cons_res) — choose the resource selection plugin that models CPUs, memory, and consumable resources (TRES).
  - GRES (Generic RESources) for GPUs: configured per node and referenced in partitions; GRES entries ensure GPUs are scheduled correctly.
  - TRES (Trackable RESources): CPU, mem, gres/gpu, energy — used for accounting and limits.

- SchedulerType and backfill
  - SchedulerType (e.g., sched/backfill) selects the scheduler implementation. Backfill behavior and reservation enforcement are controlled by SchedulerParameters and scheduler plugin configuration.
  - SchedulerParameters: tune backfill, preemption, job packing and other behavior. Example knobs influence backfill aggressiveness, job packing and job re-queue handling.
  - Also relevant: MaxJobCount/MaxJobComp/DefTimeSlice for scheduler fairness and cycle behavior.

- Priorities and fairshare
  - PriorityType: which factors are used (priority/multifactor, priority/multifactor/size/fairshare, etc.).
  - PriorityWeightFairshare, PriorityWeightAge, PriorityWeightJobSize (and other PriorityWeight*): set the relative importance of fairshare, age, and job size in the final priority calculation.
  - PriorityDecayHalfLife: how quickly historical usage decays for fairshare.
  - Fairshare works against associations in the accounting DB (shares assigned to accounts/users); the scheduler multiplies that with priority weights.

- Preemption
  - PreemptType, PreemptMode, PreemptExemptTime and QOS preemption settings: control whether higher-priority jobs can preempt lower-priority ones and how that happens (suspend, requeue, checkpoint).
  - QOS entries can be marked preemptive or preemptible.

- Consumable resource enforcement
  - Ensure SelectTypeParameters are set to enable consumable resources (so memory/gpu are not double-allocated).
  - DefMemPerCPU, DefCpuPerTask, and TaskPlugin settings influence default resource accounting.

Key accounting items (SlurmDBD, sacctmgr, slurm.conf)
- Accounting storage & job accounting gathering (slurm.conf + slurmdbd)
  - AccountingStorageType / AccountingStorageHost / AccountingStorageUser etc. in slurm.conf tell slurmctld where to send accounting records (commonly slurmdbd).
  - SlurmDBD has its own slurmdbd.conf for DB connection (MySQL/MariaDB). Use SlurmDBD to centralize accounting across clusters.
  - JobAcctGatherType (e.g., jobacct_gather/linux) and JobAcctGatherFrequency control how resource usage (TRES) is sampled for jobs.
  - JobCompType: how job completion records are written (to file or to DB).

- Accounting enforcement
  - AccountingStorageEnforce: a comma-separated list of items to enforce from the DB (examples: limits, associations, qos — exact syntax depends on your Slurm version). When set, slurmctld prevents users from exceeding configured limits.
  - When enforcing, sacctmgr configured limits and QOS rules are actively applied at job submit time and/or at scheduling.

- sacctmgr associations, accounts, users and limits
  - Associations: the DB object that ties user -> account -> cluster -> optional partition.
  - sacctmgr is used to create accounts, assign users to accounts, set DefaultQOS, and set limits/weights.
  - QOS: configured via sacctmgr (or scontrol), QOS entries control Priority, MaxJobs, MaxWall, Preempt, and group resource limits.
  - Limits: per-user or per-account limits such as MaxSubmitJobs, MaxJobs, MaxJobsPerUser, MaxTRESPERUser, MaxTRESPERAccount (names vary by version). These prevent runaway usage and are enforced (if AccountingStorageEnforce includes limits).

- TRES accounting and capping
  - TRES is the canonical resource accounting unit. You can set group TRES limits (GrpTRES) or per-account/user limits to cap CPU-hours, GPU-hours, etc.
  - QOS and association settings can be used to constrain time- or resource-based usage (for example, group CPU-minutes or GPU-minutes).

Common administrative commands to inspect/configure
- View current slurm controller configuration: scontrol show config
- View partitions: scontrol show partition or sinfo
- View nodes and GRES: sinfo --Nodes or scontrol show node <node>
- Check priority/fairshare state: sprio and sshare
- View accounting DB objects: sacctmgr show associations, sacctmgr show accounts, sacctmgr show users, sacctmgr show qos
- View configured licenses: scontrol_license
- Generate usage reports: sreport (CPU-/GPU-hours, by user/account/partition)

Practical recommended settings & best practices
- Use SlurmDBD for production accounting — it centralizes usage, enables sacct/sreport, and allows enforcement.
- Enable JobAcctGatherType and an appropriate JobAcctGatherFrequency (e.g., 30–60s) so accounting reflects actual resource use (helpful for fairshare and billing).
- Model GPUs and other special hardware with GRES and ensure select/cons_res or equivalent consumable selection so resources are not double-allocated.
- Use PriorityType with PriorityWeightFairshare tuned to your sharing policy; set PriorityDecayHalfLife to match how quickly you want historical usage to wash out.
- Define QOS entries for key user groups with MaxJobs/MaxWall/GrpTRES caps rather than global hard caps; use sacctmgr to maintain accounts and associations.
- Enable AccountingStorageEnforce for the enforcement you intend (e.g., enforce=limits,qos) once your DB data and associations are correct — otherwise enforcement can reject valid submissions.
- Test preemption behavior carefully on a smaller partition before enabling cluster-wide.

Example snippets (conceptual)
- slurm.conf (examples of keys to check)
  - PriorityType=priority/multifactor
  - PriorityWeightFairshare=1000
  - PriorityWeightAge=100
  - SchedulerType=sched/backfill
  - SelectType=select/cons_res
  - JobAcctGatherType=jobacct_gather/linux
  - JobAcctGatherFrequency=30
  - AccountingStorageType=accounting_storage/slurmdbd
  - AccountingStorageHost=slurmdbd.example.com
  - AccountingStorageEnforce=limits,qos,associations

- sacctmgr examples
  - sacctmgr add account mygroup Cluster=cluster1 Description="Research"
  - sacctmgr add user alice Account=mygroup
  - sacctmgr create qos high Priority=1000 MaxJobs=50 GrpTRES=gres/gpu=100
  - sacctmgr modify account mygroup set Fairshare=100

When to check live config (I can run these reads for you)
- If you want me to inspect your cluster’s actual configuration values I can run:
  - scontrol show config (controller config)
  - sinfo (partition/node overview)
  - sacctmgr show associations/accounts/qos (accounting state)
  - sshare (current fairshare usage)
Tell me which of the above you want me to fetch and I’ll run the reads and summarize what your current settings imply for scheduling and accounting.

# Job Exit Codes
A job's exit code (aka exit status, return code and completion
code) is captured by Slurm and saved as part of the job record. For
sbatch jobs, the exit code that is captured is the output of the batch
script. For salloc jobs, the exit code will be the return value of
the exit call that terminates the salloc session. For srun, the exit
code will be the return value of the command that srun executes.
Any non-zero exit code will be assumed to be a job failure and will
result in a Job State of FAILED with a Reason of
"NonZeroExitCode".
The exit code is an 8 bit unsigned number ranging between 0 and
255. While it is possible for a job to return a negative exit code,
Slurm will display it as an unsigned value in the 0 - 255 range.

Slurm offers two ways for a queued job to preempt a running job,

### Job Scheduling Priority [#priority](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
Job scheduling priority is made up of a number of factors as
described in the [priority/multifactor](https://slurm.schedmd.com/priority_multifactor.html) plugin. One
of the factors is the QOS priority. Each QOS is defined in the Slurm
database and includes an associated priority. Jobs that request and
are permitted a QOS will incorporate the priority associated with that
QOS in the job's [multi-factor priority calculation.](https://slurm.schedmd.com/priority_multifactor.html)
To enable the QOS priority component of the multi-factor priority
calculation, the "PriorityWeightQOS" configuration parameter must be
defined in the slurm.conf file and assigned an integer value greater
than zero.
A job's QOS only affects is scheduling priority when the
multi-factor plugin is loaded.

## Hierarchy[#hierarchy](https://slurm.schedmd.com/resource_limits.html)
Slurm's hierarchical limits are enforced in the following order
with Job QOS and Partition QOS order being reversible by using the QOS
flag 'OverPartQOS':
- Partition QOS limit
- Job QOS limit
- User association
- Account association(s), ascending the hierarchy
- Root/Cluster association
- Partition limit
- None
Note: If limits are defined at multiple points in this hierarchy,
the point in this list where the limit is first defined will be used.
Consider the following example:
- MaxJobs=20 and MaxSubmitJobs is undefined in the partition QOS
- No limits are set in the job QOS and
- MaxJobs=4 and MaxSubmitJobs=50 in the user association

## Partition QOS [#partition](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
A QOS can be attached to a partition. This means the partition will have all
the same limits as the QOS. This does not associate jobs with the QOS, nor does
it give the job any priority or preemption characteristics of the assigned QOS.
Jobs may separately request the same QOS or a different QOS to gain those
characteristics. However, the Partition QOS limits will override the job's QOS.
If the opposite is desired you may configure the job's QOS with
`Flags=OverPartQOS` which will reverse the order of precedence.
This functionality may be used to implement a true "floating"
partition, in which a partition may access a limited amount of resources with no
restrictions on which nodes it uses to get the resources. This is accomplished
by assigning all nodes to the partition, then configuring a Partition QOS with
`GrpTRES` set to the desired resource limits.

Below are concise, doc-backed explanations (what the reason means, common causes, quick checks, and typical fixes) for the pending reasons you asked about. References: Slurm Job Reason Codes, Resource Limits, Priority (multifactor) and QOS docs.

1) Resources
- What it means
  - The scheduler could not find sufficient free resources to place the job (CPUs, memory, GPUs, nodes, sockets, or matching TRES/GRES).
- Common causes
  - No nodes with the requested TRES (e.g., --gres=gpu:...), not enough CPUs or memory on any single node, fragmentation across nodes, or all suitable nodes are already allocated.
  - Constraints like node features (-C / --constraint) or topology/heterogeneous requests that can't be satisfied.
- What to check
  - sinfo to see partition/node idle counts and TRES/GRES availability.
  - squeue to see what is currently running/allocating.
  - scontrol show job <jobid> for the job’s requested resources.
- Typical fixes
  - Relax resources/constraints (fewer GPUs, less memory, fewer specific features).
  - Submit with a different partition or different GRES type.
  - Wait for currently running jobs to finish or enable preemption if policy allows.

2) Priority
- What it means
  - The job is eligible but lower-priority jobs are ahead; higher-priority workload(s) currently prevent this job from being scheduled.
- Common causes
  - Other queued jobs have higher multifactor priority (age, fairshare, QOS priority, job size, partition weight, etc.).
  - QOS/association priority settings or recent account usage (fairshare) favor other jobs.
- What to check
  - sprio (shows priority components for queued jobs) and sprio --weights (configured weights).
  - squeue to identify higher-priority jobs on the partition.
  - sshare to inspect fairshare usage.
- Typical fixes
  - Request a higher QOS (if allowed).
  - Ask an admin to adjust QOS/priority weights or run under a QOS that allows preemption.
  - Wait — priority factors (age/fairshare) may escalate the job over time.

3) ReqNodeNotAvail
- What it means
  - The job requested specific node(s) or node characteristics that are currently not available or usable, so the scheduler cannot allocate them.
- Common causes
  - The job used explicit node requests (e.g., --nodelist, -w, heterogeneous node lists) and those nodes are down/drained/allocated or reserved.
  - A reservation prevents taking those nodes, or the nodes have been placed into maintenance/power-off states.
  - Node feature/constraint mismatch where nodes matching constraints are unavailable.
- What to check
  - scontrol show job <jobid> to see the exact node request.
  - sinfo (and sinfo -R / sinfo_reasons) or sinfo --Node to inspect node states (down/drain/reserved).
  - squeue --reservation=<name> if a reservation might be blocking nodes.
- Typical fixes
  - Remove explicit node list or relax constraints.
  - Wait for the nodes to come back (or ask admins to bring nodes up or clear the reservation).
  - If a reservation blocks the nodes, either use a different partition/QOS or coordinate with the reservation owner/admin.

4) QOS limits (pending reasons that indicate limit enforcement)
- What it means
  - The job would exceed a configured resource or count limit on a QOS, account, user association or partition; the scheduler set a limit-related pending reason (e.g., Max*PerAccount, AssocGrp*, MaxTRESPerUser).
- Common causes
  - Per-QOS or partition limits like MaxJobs, MaxSubmitJobs, MaxTRESPerUser (GPU/CPU hours or counts), MaxNodes, MaxWall, etc. A job can pend when it would breach a limit unless DenyOnLimit is set (then it would be denied at submission).
  - Hierarchical enforcement: Partition QOS limits are evaluated first by default; job QOS and association limits follow (OverPartQOS can change precedence).
- What to check
  - sacctmgr (sacctmgr list associations / sacctmgr show qos) to inspect QOS and association limits.
  - scontrol show job <jobid> to see the job's QOS/association.
  - Resource Limits documentation to map the pending reason to the exact configured limit name.
- Typical fixes
  - Use a different QOS or partition with sufficient limits.
  - Request limit increases from admins (via sacctmgr).
  - Change the job request (smaller resource request, fewer concurrent jobs) to fit within limits.
  - If DenyOnLimit is set and you keep hitting rejects at submit, adjust the job/QOS or ask admins to change DenyOnLimit.

Short diagnostic checklist you can run (commands)
- scontrol show job <jobid>        # job’s requested resources, QOS, node list
- squeue -j <jobid> -o "%i %P %j %u %T %M %D %R"  # queue row + reason
- sinfo -l / sinfo --Node          # partition and node availability, TRES/GRES
- sinfo -R or sinfo_reasons        # nodes in drain/down and the reasons
- sprio                             # priority breakdown for pending jobs
- sshare                            # fairshare / effective shares
- sacctmgr list qos / sacctmgr show qos  # QOS limits and flags

Local licenses are defined in the slurm.conf using the Licenses
option.
slurm.conf:

Licenses=fluent:30,ansys:100

job submission. If this approach is used, the license must also be defined in
the AccountingStorageTRES option of the slurm.conf.

Licenses=fluent:30 AccountingStorageTRES=license/fluent

## Licenses Overview [#overview](https://slurm.schedmd.com/licenses.html)
Slurm can help with software license management by assigning available
licenses to jobs at scheduling time. If the licenses are not available, jobs
are kept pending until licenses become available. Licenses in Slurm are
essentially shared resources, meaning configured resources that are not tied to
a specific host but are associated with the entire cluster.
Licenses in Slurm can be configured in two ways:
- Local Licenses: Local licenses are local to the cluster using the slurm.conf in which they are configured.
- Remote Licenses: Remote licenses are served by the database and are configured using the sacctmgr command. Remote licenses are dynamic in nature as upon running the sacctmgr command, the slurmdbd updates all clusters the licenses are assigned to.

Short answer: Slurm treats software licenses as cluster-wide allocatable resources. If your sbatch requests a license that isn’t free at schedule time, the job will stay PENDING until enough of that license becomes available.

Details — what happens and what to check
- How to request: use sbatch -L name:count (also written --licenses=name:count), or request a license via TRES (e.g., --tres-per-task=license/foo) if the license is configured in AccountingStorageTRES.
- Where licenses are defined: local licenses are configured in slurm.conf (Licenses=...), remote/dynamic licenses are configured/managed with sacctmgr.
- Scheduling behavior: the scheduler treats licenses like a shared TRES. A job that requests N of license X will only be eligible to start when at least N licenses X are free. If not enough are free, the job remains PENDING (reason will indicate resource/license unavailability).
- Allocation lifecycle: when the job starts Slurm increments Used and decrements Free for that license; when the job finishes those license units are released back to Free.
- Remote/dynamic licenses: if admins sync LastConsumed (from an external license server) into the DB, Slurm may account for deficits (LastDeficit) and withhold allocations until the deficit is resolved — this can make jobs stay pending even when the configured Total looks sufficient.
- Failure modes to watch for: requesting more licenses than Total (job will not start until changed); requesting via --tres-per-task without the AccountingStorageTRES mapping (the request may be ignored or misrouted).
- Useful commands (ask your admin or run if you have permissions): scontrol show lic (shows Total/Used/Free), sacctmgr show resource (for remote license config), and squeue / scontrol show job to see pending reason and job license request details.

Recommendation: before submitting, check the license Free count (scontrol show lic LicenseName=<name>) and request only the number you actually need (sbatch -L name:count). If jobs still stay pending and license counts look OK, contact your admins to verify remote-license sync / LastConsumed / LastDeficit settings.

## Job Priority Factors In General [#general](https://slurm.schedmd.com/priority_multifactor.html)
The job's priority at any given time will be a weighted sum of all the
factors that have been enabled in the slurm.conf file. Job priority can be
expressed as:
```text
Job_priority = site_factor + (PriorityWeightAge) * (age_factor) + (PriorityWeightAssoc) * (assoc_factor) + (PriorityWeightFairshare) * (fair-share_factor) + (PriorityWeightJobSize) * (job_size_factor) + (PriorityWeightPartition) * (priority_job_factor) + (PriorityWeightQOS) * (QOS_factor) + SUM(TRES_weight_cpu * TRES_factor_cpu, TRES_weight_ * TRES_factor_ , ...) - nice_factor
```
All of the factors in this formula are floating point numbers that
range from 0.0 to 1.0. The weights are unsigned, 32 bit integers.

## Introduction[#intro](https://slurm.schedmd.com/fair_tree.html)
Starting with Slurm 19.05, the Fair-share factor in the
[priority/multifactor plugin](https://slurm.schedmd.com/priority_multifactor.html) will
default to the Fair Tree algorithm described on this page. The previously
used [Classic algorithm](https://slurm.schedmd.com/classic_fair_share.html) can be manually
configured.
Fair Tree prioritizes users such that if accounts A and B are siblings and A
has a higher fairshare factor than B, all children of A will have higher
fairshare factors than all children of B.
Some of the benefits include:
- All users from a higher priority account receive a higher fair share factor than all users from a lower priority account.
- Users are sorted and ranked to prevent errors due to precision loss. Ties are allowed.
- Account coordinators cannot accidentally harm the priority of their users relative to users in other accounts.
- Users are ex...

Summary first
- Slurm’s queue ordering (when PriorityType=priority/multifactor) is a weighted sum of independent priority “factors” (age, fair‑share, job size, QOS, partition, TRES, site, nice, etc.). Each factor is normalized (roughly 0.0–1.0) and multiplied by a configured integer weight in slurm.conf; those products are summed to produce the final job priority score. Larger score → higher queue position.
- Fairshare is the factor that biases scheduling to favor accounts/users that are under‑served historically. The Fair Tree algorithm is the modern fairshare computation that uses the account hierarchy to produce consistent, hierarchical priorities.
- You tune behavior by changing the PriorityWeight* settings and fairshare parameters (PriorityDecayHalfLife, PriorityUsageResetPeriod, PriorityCalcPeriod) and by choosing/keeping Fair Tree.

How the multifactor priority formula works
- Concept: Job_priority = site_factor + PriorityWeightAge * age_factor + PriorityWeightAssoc * assoc_factor + PriorityWeightFairshare * fairshare_factor + PriorityWeightJobSize * job_size_factor + PriorityWeightPartition * partition_factor + PriorityWeightQOS * QOS_factor + SUM(TRES_weight_x * TRES_factor_x) - nice_factor
- Each factor is a floating point value (0.0–1.0). Each PriorityWeight* and TRES_weight_* is an unsigned integer set in slurm.conf. The final job priority is an integer (0 … 4294967295).
- Changing a weight changes the relative importance of that factor compared with the others. E.g., increasing PriorityWeightFairshare will make historical usage (fairshare) more dominant when ordering jobs.

Fairshare — the idea and behavior
- Purpose: prevent a few users/accounts from monopolizing resources by lowering priority for accounts that have already consumed more than their fair share, while boosting priority for under‑served accounts.
- It does not impose hard caps; it only changes ordering. Over‑consuming accounts can still run if nothing else is eligible.
- Fairshare requires the Slurm accounting DB to compute historical usage.
- The fairshare factor is computed from account/user “composite usage” vs. their configured shares/weights; a larger fairshare factor means the account/user is more under‑served (so its jobs get higher priority).
- Historical usage is decayed over time according to PriorityDecayHalfLife (so old usage matters less). PriorityUsageResetPeriod can periodically reset tracked usage if desired.

Fair Tree (the modern fairshare algorithm)
- Introduced in Slurm 19.05 and the default fairshare algorithm.
- Works over the account hierarchy (tree): if account A and account B are siblings and A ranks higher than B, then all children of A will rank higher than all children of B. This preserves hierarchical ordering and prevents strange inversions.
- Benefits:
  - Hierarchical consistency: parent/child relations behave intuitively.
  - Stable ordering: reduces precision errors and odd tie behaviors that could happen with the older “classic” algorithm.
  - Account coordinators can’t accidentally make some users in their account get lower effective priority relative to other accounts’ users by reassigning weights inside the account tree.
- You can still choose the older Classic algorithm if desired, but Fair Tree is generally recommended.

TRES/TRES weights and other factors
- TRES (Trackable RESources) weights let you give extra priority to jobs requesting particular resources (CPU, energy, GRES/GPU, etc.). Example: set TRES_weight_gpu higher to give GPU jobs relatively more priority.
- QOS and partition factors: PriorityWeightQOS and PriorityWeightPartition let QOS and partition membership influence priority.
- Age factor: PriorityWeightAge increases scheduling priority over time so long‑waiting jobs eventually win.

Practical tuning recommendations
- Inspect current behavior with:
  - sprio -l (shows per‑job factor contributions) — useful to see which factors dominate.
  - sshare (shows account shares/consumption).
  - scontrol show config (to view the PriorityWeight* settings and decay parameters).
- Start with moderate weights; don’t make one weight orders of magnitude larger than the others unless you want it to dominate completely.
- If fairness feels “stuck” on old usage, reduce PriorityDecayHalfLife to make recent usage matter more, or reset usage with PriorityUsageResetPeriod.
- Use TRES weights to reflect site policy: e.g., if GPU time is scarce and should be rationed differently, bump TRES_weight_gpu.
- Combine fairshare with Age weight so the system balances fairness with waiting time (avoids starvation of small/over‑used accounts).
- Monitor results (sprio, sdiag) and iterate.

Quick numeric example (illustrative)
- Suppose: PriorityWeightFairshare=1000, PriorityWeightAge=100, fairshare_factor=0.8 (under‑served), age_factor=0.2 (short wait).
  - Contribution from fairshare = 1000 * 0.8 = 800
  - Contribution from age = 100 * 0.2 = 20
  - Total (plus any other factors) → fairshare dominates ordering here.
- If you reduce PriorityWeightFairshare to 100, then age and other factors can more easily change ordering.

Useful Slurm commands for inspection
- sprio -l — show factor values and weighted contributions per queued job.
- sshare — show account share usage and entitlement.
- scontrol show config — view PriorityWeight* and PriorityDecayHalfLife settings.
- lookup docs: priority_multifactor(see Slurm docs) and fair_tree pages (for algorithm details).

If you want, I can:
- Show how your cluster’s priority factors are currently configured (scontrol show config) and show sprio -l for specific queued jobs to explain exactly why those jobs are ordered as they are. (This is a read-only request; tell me which job IDs or if you want the global view.)

"Resources" is the generic Slurm pending reason that means the scheduler could not find sufficient free resources to satisfy the job's requested resources during the scheduling attempt.

What "Resources" commonly covers
- Not enough free CPUs/cores, memory, nodes, or GPUs to meet the job's requested cpus/mem/tasks/gres.
- Fragmentation: enough aggregate resources exist but not in a layout that satisfies the job’s placement (eg. job needs 4 whole nodes but free cores are scattered).
- All candidate nodes are allocated, drained, down, or reserved.
- GRES (GPU) mismatch: the job requests a GPU type or count not present on any currently idle nodes.
- Hierarchical resources (HRES) or custom resources configured in resources.yaml are not available for the job.
- Resource/account/QOS limits that effectively prevent allocation (these may appear as other reason codes too, but can surface as Resources for the scheduling method used).
- Higher-priority jobs / reservations have blocked the resources from being used by this job.

Important notes
- Slurm only shows the first reason encountered by the scheduling method — other constraints may also be preventing start.
- "Resources" just says “not found now”; it does not indicate which specific resource is missing. Use the detailed inspection commands below to find the exact cause.

Troubleshooting checklist (commands to run and what to look for)
1. Inspect the pending reason and job details
   - squeue -j <jobid> -o "%.18i %.30j %.8u %.2t %.10M %.10L %.10R"
     -> verifies the displayed pending reason and job name/user.
   - scontrol show job <jobid>
     -> shows full job request (NumNodes, CPUs/Task, ReqMem, GRES, Constraints, QOS, Account, etc.).

2. See node/partition availability
   - sinfo -N -l or sinfo -p <partition> -l
     -> shows per-node state (idle/alloc/drain/down) and resources per node.
   - sinfo -R
     -> lists nodes in drain/down with reasons (useful if nodes are offline).

3. Check GRES (GPUs) usage and matching
   - sinfo shows GPUs per node; verify job's --gres matches an idle GPU node type.

4. Check for reservations or higher-priority jobs
   - squeue --reservation or squeue -S+P to view reservation-bound jobs.
   - scontrol show reservation <name> (if you suspect a reservation).

5. Check association / account / QOS limits
   - sacctmgr show assoc where user=<user> or scontrol show config / review QOS limits
     -> verify per-user/account per-job/per-node limits that might deny allocation.

6. Consider fragmentation/placement
   - If your job needs whole nodes or exclusive allocation, reduce tasks-per-node, request fewer nodes, or allow shared nodes (if acceptable).

7. If HRES/custom resources are used
   - Review resources.yaml and the job's resource request; missing HRES entries will block scheduling.

When to change the job
- Reduce requested resources (fewer nodes, GPUs, CPUs or less memory) or relax constraints/feature flags.
- Submit to a different partition that has free nodes.
- Wait for currently running jobs to finish or ask admin about reservations/drains.

Slurm can be used to create an advanced reservation with a start time that
remains a fixed period of time in the future.

Summary — what a Slurm reservation is
- A reservation is an administrator-created reservation of specific resources (nodes, cores, or node counts) for a fixed time window so only permitted jobs/users/accounts/QOS/partitions can run there. Reservations can also be used to block new long-running jobs before maintenance (floating reservations) or to “attract” eligible jobs without an explicit reservation request (magnetic).

Key objects/fields you’ll see in a reservation
- ReservationName — the name Slurm assigns (or you provide).
- StartTime / Duration / EndTime — when the reservation begins and how long it lasts.
- Nodes / NodeCnt / CoreCnt — which nodes, or how many nodes/cores are reserved.
- User / Account / QOS / Partition — access control: who (or which accounts/QOS/partitions) may use the reservation.
- Flags — special behaviors (MAGNETIC, REPLACE, REPLACE_DOWN, MAINT, IGNORE_JOBS, TIME_FLOAT, etc.).
- Other metadata: reason, ReservationState, and accounting tags.

Creating and inspecting reservations
- Create: use scontrol create reservation with key=value pairs. Example form from the docs:
  scontrol create reservation StartTime=now Duration=60 Nodes=node05 User=user1 Flags=magnetic
  The command will return a Reservation created: <name> string.
- Inspect/list: use scontrol show reservation (or scontrol show res) to view reservation details: start/end time, nodes, allowed users/accounts/QOS, flags, and state.

Common flags and behaviors (from the docs)
- MAGNETIC: the reservation “attracts” jobs that meet its access controls even if those jobs do not specify --reservation; useful to let eligible jobs start automatically. Note: magnetic reservations do not attract heterogeneous jobs unless the job explicitly requests the reservation.
- REPLACE / REPLACE_DOWN: control whether the reservation should replace DOWN/ DRAINED nodes (REPLACE_DOWN) or also replace allocated nodes (REPLACE) in order to maintain a constant pool. REPLACE that moves allocations has restrictions (e.g., not supported for reservations specified as cores that span nodes).
- MAINT: tag the reservation as maintenance for accounting/purpose.
- IGNORE_JOBS: allows creating a maintenance reservation even when jobs are currently running on the resources (otherwise Slurm normally only reserves resources not expected to have a running job at the reservation start).
- TIME_FLOAT: creates a “floating” reservation that keeps a start time a fixed interval in the future (used to prevent long-running jobs from being initiated on nodes before a planned future maintenance).

Access control nuances
- You can explicitly allow or deny specific users/accounts. The docs show both positive and negative forms (e.g., user=alice or user=-alan to prevent alan).
- Reservations can be limited to particular partitions and QOS.
- By default a job must request the reservation (sbatch/srun/salloc --reservation=<name>), unless the reservation is MAGNETIC.

How jobs use a reservation
- To run in a reservation explicitly: sbatch --reservation=<ReservationName> script.sh (or srun/salloc --reservation=...).
- Magnetic reservations may allow eligible jobs to be scheduled into the reserved nodes without an explicit --reservation, if the job meets the access criteria and the reservation is Magentic.

Special reservation modes/use-cases
- Maintenance reservations: use flags=maint and possibly ignore_jobs to reserve full nodes for system work; Slurm will prevent new jobs that can’t complete before the reservation start.
- Floating reservations: TIME_FLOAT prevents new long jobs from starting on nodes by keeping a reservation start time relative to now.
- Replacement behavior: use REPLACE/REPLACE_DOWN when you want the reservation to maintain a constant set of idle nodes even across node state changes.

Useful commands (docs-style examples)
- Create: scontrol create reservation StartTime=now Duration=60 Nodes=node05 User=user1 Flags=magnetic
- Show/list: scontrol show reservation or scontrol show res ReservationName=<name>
- Jobs: sbatch --reservation=<name> myjob.sh (or srun/salloc --reservation=...)

Where to read more
- The Slurm reservations guide (slurm.schedmd.com/reservations.html) provides full details and many examples (creation options, flag behaviors, and edge cases such as replacing allocated resources or magnetic reservations).

Short answer: sacctmgr add/modify/delete change the accounting database (slurmdbd) and can immediately and permanently change who can submit, what limits apply, fairshare, and associations between users/accounts/clusters/partitions. They are powerful admin actions — use them with backups, narrow where clauses, and audit logging.

What they actually change
- sacctmgr modifies the Slurm accounting DB (slurmdbd), not the job state in slurmctld. However accounting changes affect future scheduling/submit decisions (limits, QOS, fairshare) and can therefore change cluster behavior immediately.
- add creates accounts/users/associations.
- modify changes attributes (fairshare, maxjobs, maxwall, QOS, parent, etc.). Those limits are enforced for future submissions and may influence scheduler decisions (and preemption) depending on site config.
- delete removes entities or associations. Deleting an account or user can remove the association used for job submission/limits; this can block new submissions or change accounting attribution.

Key safety implications / risks
- Broad deletes are dangerous: deleting an account will remove associations for all users under it and can break submit-time validation. Deleting users/accounts in use may lead to rejections for future submissions.
- Cascading effects: account hierarchy and associations are interconnected. Deleting a parent or changing parents can affect many child accounts/users.
- Limits and QOS changes can impact scheduling immediately. Modifying limits downwards (e.g., set maxjobs=0 or reduce MaxWall) can cause users to be unable to submit, and may change preemption decisions.
- No automatic job cancellation, but scheduling/priority may change. Running jobs generally continue, but behavior may vary with site policies if QOS/limits are used for preemption or enforcement.
- Human error / incorrect where clauses can match many rows; a simple typo can delete or change many associations.
- Concurrency and availability: changes go through slurmdbd; network or DB issues can leave operations incomplete or require recovery.
- Permissions: sacctmgr requires administrative privileges — misuse by an admin is a single point of failure.

Practical safety checklist (recommended)
1. Preview before you change
   - Use list/show to inspect targets:
     - sacctmgr show associations (or sacctmgr list associations where ...)
     - sacctmgr list account, user, association to confirm exactly what will be affected
2. Avoid wildcard deletes; scope with explicit where clauses
   - Use where name=foo cluster=bar account=baz to limit scope.
3. Use interactive commit and review transactions
   - By default sacctmgr expects you to commit changes instead of immediately applying them; avoid --immediate (-i) during exploratory work.
   - After changes, review: sacctmgr list transactions to audit what changed, who did it, and when.
4. Back up the slurm DB before bulk changes
   - Use sacctmgr archive dump (or a DB backup method) to create a restore point you can load if needed.
5. Prefer deactivation over deletion
   - If you want to stop use of an account/user temporarily, consider modifying limits (e.g., set maxjobs=0 or change state/description) rather than deleting the entity.
6. Test in staging
   - For bulk or scripted changes, test on a non-production SlurmDB instance first.
7. Use explicit modifies not txt edits
   - Use sacctmgr modify ... set <attrs> with precise attribute names. Don’t script blind edits without list/show checks.
8. Be careful when automating
   - If scripting, consider non-interactive use of --immediate but ensure your script validates targets first and logs the change.
9. Keep an audit trail and inform stakeholders
   - Notify affected users before cutting their account or lowering limits. Use the transactions log for postmortem.

Recovery options if something goes wrong
- Restore from archive dump (sacctmgr archive load) or DB-level backup.
- Recreate deleted accounts/users and re-add associations if you have a dump or manual record.
- Use sacctmgr list transactions to determine exactly what changed and when; this helps construct a targeted reversal.
- For accidental limit changes, immediately modify back to prior values (if known) to restore service.

Permissions and governance
- Only users with accounting admin privileges should run sacctmgr operations.
- Implement change-control: require review/approval for mass deletes or limit reductions.

Short examples and hints
- Preview associations: sacctmgr show associations cluster=CLUSTER format=Account,User,Partition
- Temporarily block a user: sacctmgr modify user where name=alice set maxjobs=0 (safer than delete)
- Backup before bulk changes: sacctmgr archive dump file=/tmp/sacctmgr-backup.sql

## Job Dependencies [#dependencies](https://slurm.schedmd.com/burst_buffer.html)
If two jobs use burst buffers and one is dependent on the other (e.g.
`sbatch --dependency=afterok:123 ...`) then the second job will not
begin until the first job completes and its burst buffer stage-out completes.
If the second job does not use a burst buffer, but is dependent upon the first
job's completion, then it will not wait for the stage-out operation of the first
job to complete.
The second job can be made to wait for the first job's stage-out operation to
complete using the "afterburstbuffer" dependency option (e.g.
`sbatch --dependency=afterburstbuffer:123 ...`).

## PERFORMANCE[#SECTION_PERFORMANCE](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Executing sbatch sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmctld daemon come in at once, it can result in
a degradation of performance of the slurmctld daemon, possibly resulting
in a denial of service.
Do not run sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other
programs. Ensure that programs limit calls to sbatch to the minimum
necessary for the information you are trying to gather.

## PERFORMANCE[#SECTION_PERFORMANCE](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Executing sbatch sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmctld daemon come in at once, it can result in
a degradation of performance of the slurmctld daemon, possibly resulting
in a denial of service.
Do not run sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other
programs. Ensure that programs limit calls to sbatch to the minimum
necessary for the information you are trying to gather.

Summary (official Slurm behavior)
- Purpose: afterok makes a job wait until one or more other jobs complete successfully. "Successfully" means the producing job(s) finish with an exit code of zero (Slurm state COMPLETED / derived exit code = 0).
- Basic syntax: sbatch --dependency=afterok:JOBID[:JOBID... ] myscript.sh
  - You may list multiple job IDs separated by colons. Different dependency types can be combined by comma, e.g. --dependency=afterok:123,afterany:200.
- What happens at submit: sbatch returns immediately with a job ID; the dependent job is queued and will remain PENDING until the afterok condition is satisfied. The squeue pending reason will show Dependency while waiting.
- Job arrays: if you depend on an array job ID, afterok is satisfied only after all tasks in that array complete successfully. Internally Slurm uses the array's highest exit code when evaluating afterok/afternotok.
- Burst buffer nuance: if both jobs use burst buffers and the dependent job uses afterok, the dependent job will wait until the producing job completes and its burst-buffer stage-out completes. If the dependent job does not use a burst buffer, afterok does not wait for stage-out; to explicitly wait for stage-out use afterburstbuffer.
- Related dependency types (for comparison):
  - afterany: start after the specified job(s) finish for any exit code.
  - afternotok: start only if the specified job(s) finish with a non‑zero exit code (failure).
  - aftercorr / after: other variants exist (see sbatch docs and job-array doc for array-specific behaviors).

Official references
- sbatch --dependency (main syntax and options): https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html
- Job array dependency behavior: https://slurm.schedmd.com/job_array.html
- Burst buffer interaction with dependencies: https://slurm.schedmd.com/burst_buffer.html
- Job reason codes (Dependency pending reason): https://slurm.schedmd.com/job_reason_codes.html

## DESCRIPTION[#SECTION_DESCRIPTION](https://slurm.schedmd.com/strigger.html)
strigger is used to set, get or clear Slurm trigger information.
Triggers include events such as a node failing, a job reaching its
time limit or a job terminating.
These events can cause actions such as the execution of an arbitrary
script.
Typical uses include notifying system administrators of node failures
and gracefully terminating a job when its time limit is approaching.
A hostlist expression for the nodelist or job ID is passed as an argument
to the program.
Trigger events are not processed instantly, but a check is performed for
trigger events on a periodic basis (currently every 15 seconds).
Any trigger events which occur within that interval will be compared
against the trigger programs set at the end of the time interval.
The trigger program will be executed once for any event occurring in
that interval.
The record of those events (e.g. nodes which...

Result: No active triggers found.

Explanation — trigger fields you’ll see when triggers exist
- TRIG_ID: trigger identifier.
- RES_TYPE: resource type the trigger watches — "job" or "node".
- RES_ID: resource identifier (job ID, hostlist, or "*" for any).
- TYPE: event type that fires the trigger (see list below).
- OFFSET: time offset in seconds (negative = before the event).
- USER: user who created the trigger.
- PROGRAM: program/script Slurm runs when the trigger fires.

Common TYPE values and meaning
- time (job only)
  - Fires relative to a job's time limit. Use OFFSET to run a program before/after the limit (e.g., notify or checkpoint).
- fini (job only)
  - Fires when a job finishes/terminates.
- up (job or node)
  - Fires when a node or job becomes UP/available (node returns to service, or job state moves to RUNNING as applicable).
- down (job or node)
  - Fires when a node or job goes DOWN/unavailable (node failure or job abort).
- drained (node only)
  - Fires when a node enters the DRAIN or DRAINING state.
- idle (node only)
  - Fires when a node becomes IDLE (no allocations).
- reconfig (node only)
  - Fires when a node is reconfigured (scontrol reconfigure or similar).

Behavior notes
- Triggers execute the specified PROGRAM; Slurm passes a resource identifier (e.g., node list or job ID) as an argument to the program.
- Triggers are checked periodically (≈ every 15 seconds), so events are batched within that interval.
- OFFSET may be negative to run actions before the event when possible.

How to inspect and manage triggers
- List current triggers: strigger --get
- Add a trigger: strigger --set ... --program=/path/to/script
- Remove a trigger: strigger --clear --id=<TRIG_ID> (or use --jobid/--user to select)

## AUTHORIZATION[#SECTION_AUTHORIZATION](https://slurm.schedmd.com/scontrol.html)
Slurm generally classifies users into three authorization levels:
- Administrators include root, SlurmUser, and any users with
"AdminLevel=Administrator"
- Privileged Users include all Administrators and any users with
"AdminLevel=Operator"
- Effective Owners of a job or step include the direct owner and all
Coordinators of the corresponding account.
Note that configuring AdminLevels or Coordinators requires the use of SlurmDBD.
The authorization levels required to execute various commands are defined in the
following table.
scontrol update job: Privileged or Effective Owner
scontrol requeue: Privileged or Effective Owner

Job arrays offer a mechanism for submitting and managing collections of
similar jobs quickly and easily, useful for repetitive workloads that follow a
common job pattern. This greatly improves overall performance, since job arrays

Good — here’s a concise, safe reference for using scontrol update on jobs.

Basic syntax
- scontrol update job=<JobID> Field=Value [Field2=Value2 ...]
- For array jobs use either the array job id to affect all elements: job=<ArrayJobID>
  or a single element: job=<ArrayJobID>_<ArrayTaskID> (e.g., job=101_3)

Key points / safety rules
- Always identify the job explicitly with job=<id>. Do not rely on implicit context.
- Most fields can only be changed while the job is PENDING; only a subset may be changed for RUNNING or SUSPENDED jobs. Check scontrol show job=<id> first.
- Unprivileged users may only change their own jobs (and only certain fields). Privileged users (admins/operators) can change any job and may bypass policy limits.
- Some fields are read-only and cannot be updated (e.g., AllocNode:Sid, BatchFlag, ExitCode). If in doubt, use scontrol show job to inspect allowed fields and current values.
- Be conservative: change one field at a time and verify the effect with scontrol show job=<id>.
- Avoid changing state (hold/release/requeue) with generic update — use the specific scontrol_* commands or scancel as appropriate.

Common safe examples
- Rename a job:
  scontrol update job=12345 JobName=new_name
- Extend time limit (use HH:MM:SS or minutes form as your Slurm supports):
  scontrol update job=12345 TimeLimit=02:00:00
- Change QOS or Priority (requires appropriate permissions):
  scontrol update job=12345 QOS=high Priority=3000
- Change account (may be restricted by policy):
  scontrol update job=12345 Account=projectX
- Update an array element:
  scontrol update job=2000_5 TimeLimit=00:30:00

Quoting and formatting
- Values with spaces should be quoted (shell quoting), e.g., JobName="analysis run".
- Numeric fields (Priority, NumNodes) expect integers. TimeLimit accepts common Slurm time formats (consult local scontrol/sbatch docs if unsure).
- Use exact field names and capitalization as shown by scontrol show job.

Recommended safe workflow
1. Inspect the job: scontrol show job=<JobID>
2. Decide the single change you need and confirm you have permission.
3. Run the update: scontrol update job=<JobID> Field=Value
4. Confirm: scontrol show job=<JobID>
5. If multiple changes are needed, repeat steps 2–4 rather than batching many risky edits at once.

If you want, tell me a specific field or job ID you plan to change and I can point out whether it’s typically allowed for PENDING vs RUNNING jobs and any permission concerns.

Slurm's job scheduler handles GRES affinity on a socket basis internally.
However, the gres.conf interface allows administrators to specify `Cores` for GPU affinity configuration. This creates
a common misconception that Slurm will respect core-level affinity during job
scheduling, which it does not and never has. This can lead to issues where job
allocations and job steps don't align correctly, since job steps examine cores
while jobs use sockets.

Summary: --gres=gpu:N (and the newer --gpus family) request N GPU devices from Slurm for your job. Slurm allocates GPUs as generic resources (GRES) and enforces those allocations per node or per task depending on the option you choose. Slurm also sets CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES for each job step so your process sees only the GPUs assigned to it.

Key points

- Basic syntax and equivalents
  - --gres=gpu:N requests N GPUs (GRES) per node for the job allocation.
  - Modern alternatives: --gpus=N, --gpus-per-node=N (equivalent to --gres=gpu:N), --gpus-per-task=M (request per task/rank).
  - You can request a specific GPU type with name[:type:count], e.g. --gres=gpu:tesla:2.
  - These options work with sbatch, srun and salloc (they are supported by the select/cons_tres plugin).

- Per-node vs per-task vs total
  - By default --gres/gpu is "per node". Example: sbatch --nodes=2 --gres=gpu:2 → Slurm will try to give 2 GPUs on each of the 2 nodes (total 4 GPUs).
  - --gpus-per-task and --gpus-per-node change semantics:
    - --gpus-per-task=1 with --ntasks=4 on one node → 4 GPUs on that node (1 per task).
    - --gpus-per-node behaves like --gres=gpu:N (N per node).
  - There is no built-in "give me N GPUs across the whole job regardless of nodes" flag in the simple per-node syntax; you request per-node counts or per-task counts that determine the total.

- Exclusivity, sharing, and special cases
  - By default GPUs are allocated exclusively (a GPU assigned to one job will not be given to another concurrently).
  - GPU sharing is possible only if the cluster is configured for it (examples: NVIDIA MPS configured as a separate GRES type, or administrator-configured fractional/shared GRES via gres.conf). This requires admin-side configuration and the select/cons_tres plugin features.
  - MIG devices can be reported and used when AutoDetect and driver support are present; MIG handling and accounting have special considerations (NVML/MIG limits).

- How Slurm exposes allocated GPUs to your job
  - Slurm sets CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES for each job step that runs on a compute node so the process sees only the GPUs assigned to that step on that node.
  - CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES is set when tasks are launched on a compute node (each step); for sbatch it reflects node 0 of the allocation for the batch-script’s top-level environment.
  - The mapping renumbers the assigned physical GPUs to a local 0..(N-1) index in the environment. Your program sees device 0 as the first assigned physical device, etc.
  - Container runtimes that honor CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES (or NVIDIA_VISIBLE_DEVICES) will inherit the same mapping, so GPU isolation works inside containers.

- enforce-binding and affinity
  - Some Slurm configs support --gres-flags=enforce-binding which tightens assignment and binding behavior (bind GPUs to tasks/cores). Admin configuration and Slurm version determine exact behavior. When enforce-binding is active, Slurm more strictly ensures tasks are pinned to the allocated GPU(s) and sets the environment for that binding.

- Accounting and metrics
  - GPUs are tracked as a TRES (gres/gpu) when configured. If AccountingStorageTRES includes gres/gpu, Slurm can record GPU usage metrics (withnvml/rsmi support).
  - Note: NVML may not provide utilization metrics for MIG slices; accounting behavior differs for MIG.

- What happens if resources aren’t available
  - If the requested GPUs (per node or per-task) cannot be satisfied, the job remains PENDING until an allocation matching the request becomes possible.
  - Slurm’s scheduler enforces those counts when placing jobs; partial allocations that don’t meet the per-node/per-task constraint are not granted.

Examples
  - sbatch --gres=gpu:2 myjob.sh
    -> requests 2 GPUs on every node allocated to the job (common for single-node jobs).
  - sbatch --nodes=2 --gres=gpu:2 myjob.sh
    -> requests 2 GPUs on each of 2 nodes (total 4 GPUs).
  - sbatch --ntasks=4 --gpus-per-task=1 my_mpi_job.sh
    -> requests 1 GPU for each of the 4 tasks (if they are placed on one node, that node needs 4 GPUs).
  - srun --gres=gpu:1 --pty bash
    -> starts an interactive step with 1 GPU allocated on the node the step runs on.

Quick tips / troubleshooting
  - If your job still sees all GPUs (not only assigned ones): make sure you launch tasks via srun inside the allocation (srun sets per-step envs), and check cluster version/config and whether Slurm is configured to set CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES.
  - Use nvidia-smi inside the job to verify which physical device corresponds to your CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES mapping.
  - If you need GPU sharing or fractional GPUs, talk to your cluster admins — it requires special gres.conf and scheduler configuration (MPS, fractional GRES, or explicit MIG configuration).
  - If you need a GPU on only one node in a multi-node job, request per-task GPUs and control task placement, or request one node with --nodes=1 plus other nodes without GPUs.

Local licenses are defined in the slurm.conf using the Licenses
option.
slurm.conf:

Licenses=fluent:30,ansys:100

Configured licenses can be viewed using the scontrol command.
```text
$ scontrol show lic LicenseName=ansys Total=100 Used=0 Free=100 Remote=no LicenseName=fluent Total=30 Used=0 Free=30 Remote=no
```
Requesting licenses is done by using the -L, or --licenses, submission
option.
```text
$ sbatch -L ansys:2 script.sh Submitted batch job 5212 $ scontrol show lic LicenseName=ansys Total=100 Used=2 Free=98 Remote=no LicenseName=fluent Total=30 Used=0 Free=30 Remote=no

Licenses may also be requested using the --tres-per-task option for
job submission. If this approach is used, the license must also be defined in
the AccountingStorageTRES option of the slurm.conf.
slurm.conf:

Licenses=fluent:30 AccountingStorageTRES=license/fluent

## Remote Licenses [#remote_licenses](https://slurm.schedmd.com/licenses.html)
Remote licenses do not offer any kind of integration with third party
license managers by themselves. The use of the "Server" and "ServerType"
parameters when creating these licenses is just for informative purposes and

Summary — what a "license" request is
- In Slurm a "license" is a consumable resource (a TRES) that jobs can request. Administrators define license pools (counts) and Slurm will allocate those license units to jobs at submission time and keep them allocated until the job ends.
- Jobs request licenses with sbatch/srun using -L/--licenses (or by requesting a license TRES via --tres-per-task). Example: sbatch -L ansys:2 script.sh requests 2 units from the license pool named "ansys".

License pools and where they come from
- Local licenses (slurm.conf): simple static pools can be declared in slurm.conf, e.g.
  Licenses=fluent:30,ansys:100
  Slurm reports these pools via scontrol show lic LicenseName=<name>.
- Accounting DB (sacctmgr) resources: administrators can create license-type resources in the SlurmDB (sacctmgr add resource ... type=license) and set counts, cluster allocations, server metadata, and allowed percentages per cluster.
- Remote/dynamic licenses: Slurm can track licenses that are managed by an external license server. A site script can periodically sync the external server’s current usage to Slurm (sacctmgr update resource ... lastconsumed=...). Slurm uses LastConsumed/LastDeficit to account for “missing” licenses and to reserve capacity accordingly.

How to request licenses in submissions
- Short form: sbatch -L license_name:count script.sh
  Example: sbatch -L ansys:2 train.sh
- As a TRES (per-task): sbatch --tres-per-task=license/ansys=1
  If you use the TRES form, the license name must also be present in AccountingStorageTRES or configured as a resource in sacctmgr so accounting/scheduling recognize it.
- The scheduler treats license units like other consumable resources: a job will not start unless the requested license units are free.

What Slurm tracks and how to inspect it
- scontrol show lic LicenseName=<name> — shows Total, Used, Free, Remote, etc. Example output snippet:
  LicenseName=ansys Total=100 Used=2 Free=98 Remote=no
- sacctmgr show resource (or sacctmgr show resources format=...) — shows resources defined in the accounting DB, cluster allocations, server, type, count, allowed percentage.
- For dynamic/remote sync you’ll see LastConsumed and LastDeficit fields in the sacctmgr resource settings.

Scheduling behavior and implications
- Licenses are global consumable resources; the scheduler decrements the Free count when it dispatches a job and reclaims on job end.
- If insufficient license units are free, jobs will remain PENDING until license capacity is freed or the request is changed.
- Licenses can be scoped/partitioned via the accounting DB (per-cluster allocation or percentage splits) for multi-cluster deployments.
- Slurm does not itself contact external license managers (unless you add your own sync scripts); remote server and server-type fields are informational and used with site integration or scripts.

Administration: adding and managing license pools
- Add a resource in the accounting DB:
  sacctmgr add resource name=nastran cluster=clusterA,count=100 type=license server=flex_host servertype=flexlm
- Update counts or lastconsumed:
  sacctmgr update resource nastran set count=120
  sacctmgr -i update resource nastran set lastconsumed=42
  (An update to sacctmgr will be pushed to controllers so allocations change.)
- For slurm.conf Licenses=... edits you must restart/reload slurmctld appropriately.

Common operational notes and best practices
- Use descriptive license names (e.g., ansys, fluent) when defining pools; users request the same name.
- For external license managers, run a periodic sync script to set lastconsumed so Slurm’s view stays accurate (see Slurm docs’ dynamic license example).
- Monitor with scontrol show lic and sacctmgr show resource; alert if Free becomes low or LastDeficit grows.
- If you want per-task accounting of license use, use --tres-per-task=license/<name>=N and ensure AccountingStorageTRES includes license/<name>.
- Document license request syntax for users to avoid over-requesting (jobs that request more licenses than they actually need can starve others).

Troubleshooting
- Job pending with license shortage: run scontrol show lic and sacctmgr show resource to see Free/Used and whether LastDeficit is non‑zero.
- If users report licenses available on the license server but Slurm shows a deficit, check your sync process (update LastConsumed) and sacctmgr settings for allowed/allocated counts across clusters.

References / commands
- Request: sbatch -L ansys:2 script.sh or sbatch --tres-per-task=license/ansys=1
- Inspect: scontrol show lic LicenseName=ansys ; sacctmgr show resource
- Admin: sacctmgr add|update resource ... type=license

salloc is used to allocate a Slurm job allocation, which is a set of resources

## PERFORMANCE[#SECTION_PERFORMANCE](https://slurm.schedmd.com/salloc.html)
Executing salloc sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from salloc or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmctld daemon come in at once, it can result in
a degradation of performance of the slurmctld daemon, possibly resulting
in a denial of service.
Do not run salloc or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other
programs. Ensure that programs limit calls to salloc to the minimum
necessary for the information you are trying to gather.

## EXAMPLES[#SECTION_EXAMPLES](https://slurm.schedmd.com/salloc.html)
To get an allocation, and open a new xterm in which srun commands may be typed interactively:
```text
$ salloc -N16 xterm salloc: Granted job allocation 65537 # (at this point the xterm appears, and salloc waits for xterm to exit) salloc: Relinquishing job allocation 65537
```
To grab an allocation of nodes and launch a parallel application on one command line:
```text
$ salloc -N5 srun -n10 myprogram
```
To create a heterogeneous job with 3 components, each allocating a unique set of nodes:
```text
$ salloc -w node[2-3] : -w node4 : -w node[5-7] bash salloc: job 32294 queued and waiting for resources salloc: job 32294 has been allocated resources salloc: Granted job allocation 32294
```

Short answer: use sbatch to submit non‑interactive batch jobs (scripts) that Slurm will schedule and run later; use salloc when you need an interactive allocation (grab nodes/GPUs and get a shell or run commands interactively); use srun to actually launch tasks/job‑steps (either inside an allocation or as a one‑shot launcher that obtains resources).

When to pick each (practical workflow guidance)
- sbatch — scheduled, reproducible batch runs
  - Use for production training runs, pipelines, or any job you want Slurm to queue and run unattended from a script.
  - sbatch submits a batch script and returns immediately; Slurm runs the script later and records job output.
  - Typical: sbatch --nodes=2 --gres=gpu:4 --time=24:00:00 my_job.sh

- salloc — interactive allocation for debugging, development, and multi‑step interactive work
  - Use when you need an allocation you can interact with (a shell, an xterm, or run multiple srun commands inside).
  - Good for debugging, tuning, launching interactive MPI sessions, or running iterative experiments on allocated nodes.
  - Typical: salloc -N2 --gres=gpu:1 --time=02:00:00  (then you get a shell or run srun inside)

- srun — task launcher / job‑step runner (inside allocations or as a direct single‑command run)
  - Use srun to launch parallel tasks (MPI ranks, multi‑task jobs) and to create job steps inside an sbatch or salloc allocation.
  - You can also use srun directly from the command line to allocate+run a single command (acts like salloc+srun combined for a one‑off).
  - Typical inside a script or interactive allocation: srun -n 32 ./mpi_program
  - For interactive shells, srun --pty bash or srun --pty --gres=gpu:1 /bin/bash

Common patterns
- Production batch: sbatch my_job.sh (inside the script, use srun to launch MPI/parallel tasks)
- Interactive debug: salloc ... --pty bash, then srun -n... ./prog or run unit tests manually
- Quick single command: srun --nodes=1 --gres=gpu:1 --time=00:30:00 python debug.py

Notes / best practices
- Put resource requests (nodes, cpus, gres=gpu, time, partition, QOS) on the sbatch/salloc/srun command so the scheduler can allocate appropriately.
- Inside sbatch scripts prefer srun to launch tasks; it integrates with Slurm job steps and accounting.
- Use salloc when you want to keep the allocation after you run something interactively (so you can iterate).
- Avoid calling salloc/srun in tight loops (they contact slurmctld); batch large numbers of short tasks via job arrays or a single multi‑task job.
- For reproducibility and logging, prefer sbatch; for exploration and debugging, prefer salloc + srun.

If you want, tell me your concrete workflow (script vs interactive, MPI vs single‑GPU, debugging vs production) and I’ll recommend the exact command line and an example sbatch script.
