Summary — what Slurm topology/network-aware placement is
- Topology awareness means Slurm knows the cluster network switch topology (switches, parents, link speeds) and uses that information when allocating nodes so tasks are placed “close” in the network hierarchy.
- The goal is to reduce cross-switch traffic, lower latency, and avoid network contention for communication-heavy jobs (MPI, RDMA, all-reduce, etc.).

How it’s configured (administrator side)
- topology.conf + TopologyPlugin:
  - Admin supplies a topology.conf describing switches and which nodes attach to each switch (SwitchName=, Nodes=, Switches=, optional link speeds).
  - slurm.conf enables the plugin, e.g. TopologyPlugin=topology/tree (requires the select/cons_tres selection plugin).
- TopologyParam controls placement policy (examples in docs: RouteTree, TopoOptional). These affect whether jobs are restricted to nodes that share a path in the topology and how strictly that restriction is enforced.
- Tools: slurmibtopology (and similar) can help generate topology for InfiniBand fabrics.
- All nodes must be connected in the supplied topology for some policies (RouteTree) to work.

How Slurm uses topology (scheduler behavior)
- Tree/hierarchical algorithm: Slurm finds the lowest-level switch (leaf/parent) that can satisfy the job and then allocates nodes from its leaves using a best-fit algorithm.
- Best-fit may not always be strictly optimal — it chooses a compact allocation from currently idle/available nodes.
- By default a job will not span leaf switches that lack a common parent unless TopologyParam allows it (e.g., TopoOptional relaxes that restriction).
- Users (and admins) can limit how many leaf switches a job may span and how long they will wait for a compact allocation.

User controls and options
- --switches (salloc/sbatch/srun): request a maximum number of leaf switches for the job (and a wait tolerance). This asks the scheduler to try to keep your allocation within N switches.
- You can change switches constraints for pending jobs with scontrol/squeue.
- Combine topology requests with task distribution options (e.g., --distribution=block) and CPU/GPU binding to get compact allocations and correct affinity.
- If a cluster lacks topology info, these options have no effect — Slurm cannot make network-aware placement without topology.conf and the plugin enabled.

Practical effects and tuning tips
- For tightly-coupled MPI/RDMA jobs, use topology-aware allocations to keep ranks on the same switch or parent switch to reduce latency and contention.
- Request switches or compact distribution when you need minimal cross-switch traffic; allow larger switch counts if you need immediate allocation.
- Admins can include link speeds in topology.conf; Slurm uses that metadata when making placement decisions.
- Remember topology-aware placement reduces network contention but does not replace application-level tuning (MPI mapping, NCCL, etc.).

Limitations and caveats
- Topology awareness works only if the admin has configured topology.conf and enabled the plugin.
- Slurm’s allocation is based on switch-level topology, not on dynamic per-link congestion; it uses static topology+availability to pack jobs.
- The tree algorithm can allocate more switches than absolutely optimal due to current availability/best-fit behavior.
- Some TopologyParam settings can prevent jobs from running if a strictly-local allocation isn’t available (unless you allow optional spanning).

sbatch through a file name on the command line, or if no file name is specified,

below.

## PERFORMANCE[#SECTION_PERFORMANCE](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Executing sbatch sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmctld daemon come in at once, it can result in
a degradation of performance of the slurmctld daemon, possibly resulting
in a denial of service.
Do not run sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other
programs. Ensure that programs limit calls to sbatch to the minimum
necessary for the information you are trying to gather.

Snippet:
## EXAMPLES[#SECTION_EXAMPLES](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Specify a batch script by filename on the command line. The batch script specifies a 1 minute time limit for the job.
```text
$ cat myscript #!/bin/sh #SBATCH --time=1 srun hostname |sort $ sbatch -N4 myscript salloc: Granted job allocation 65537 $ cat slurm-65537.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
Pass a batch script to sbatch on standard input:
```text
$ sbatch -N4 #!/bin/sh > srun hostname |sort > EOF sbatch: Submitted batch job 65541 $ cat slurm-65541.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
To create a heterogeneous job with 3 components, each allocating a unique set of nodes:
```text
$ sbatch -w node[2-3] : -w node4 : -w node[5-7] work.bash Submitted batch job 34987
```

## EXAMPLES[#SECTION_EXAMPLES](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Specify a batch script by filename on the command line. The batch script specifies a 1 minute time limit for the job.
```text
$ cat myscript #!/bin/sh #SBATCH --time=1 srun hostname |sort $ sbatch -N4 myscript salloc: Granted job allocation 65537 $ cat slurm-65537.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
Pass a batch script to sbatch on standard input:
```text
$ sbatch -N4 #!/bin/sh > srun hostname |sort > EOF sbatch: Submitted batch job 65541 $ cat slurm-65541.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
To create a heterogeneous job with 3 components, each allocating a unique set of nodes:
```text
$ sbatch -w node[2-3] : -w node4 : -w node[5-7] work.bash Submitted batch job 34987
```

- Found one PENDING job: JobID=5004, JobName=slurm_array, User=alice. scontrol show job 5004 reports Reason=AssocGrpCPUMinutesLimit (i.e., pending for an account/group CPU-minute limit), not a dependency.

What I ran
- squeue --state=PENDING (listed pending jobs)
- scontrol show job 5004 (showed the job's Reason=AssocGrpCPUMinutesLimit)

How to find dependency‑blocked jobs (quick recipe)
1. List pending jobs and their reason:
   - squeue --states=PENDING   (look at the REASON column)
2. For any pending job whose REASON looks like a dependency (often shown as "Dependency" or similar), inspect the full job record:
   - scontrol show job <jobid>
   - In that output look for the Dependency= field (and JobState/Reason) which shows the dependency expression (for example afterok:1234).
3. Interpret the dependency expression (see types below).

Common Slurm dependency types and semantics
- after: start this job after the specified job(s) have begun running. (Waits for start.)
  - Example: --dependency=after:1234
- afterok: start after the specified job(s) complete successfully (exit code 0).
  - Example: --dependency=afterok:1234
- afternotok: start only if the specified job(s) finish with a non‑zero exit code (failure).
  - Example: --dependency=afternotok:1234
- afterany: start after the specified job(s) finish regardless of exit code.
  - Example: --dependency=afterany:1234
- singleton: delay this job until no other jobs with the same name and user are running; useful to ensure only one instance runs at a time.
  - Example: --dependency=singleton
- Multiple dependencies: you can combine types and multiple job IDs (comma separated). The job starts when the combined expression is satisfied.
  - Example: --dependency=afterok:1234,afterany:2345
- Array job dependencies: you can specify array indices or use array master IDs; dependency expressions accept array element notation.

Practical notes
- Dependency pending reason appears in the queue REASON column; scontrol show job reveals the exact Dependency= expression.
- after waits for job start; afterok/afternotok/afterany wait for job completion and evaluate exit codes accordingly—this is frequently the difference that surprises users.
- If a job is pending for a dependency that will never be satisfied (e.g., dependency points to a job that was cancelled/failed and the dependency type requires success), fix options include canceling the dependent job, modifying it (admins can change Job dependencies with scontrol), or re-submitting with adjusted dependencies.

Here’s a concise explanation of the common sinfo node states you asked about and what they mean for scheduling and troubleshooting.

- idle
  - Meaning: The node is up and not currently allocated to any job. It is available for new job allocations.
  - Scheduler implication: Jobs can be placed on the node immediately (subject to partition/QOS constraints).
  - How to inspect: sinfo -N (or sinfo -l) shows node-listed as idle.

- alloc (allocated / ALLOCATED)
  - Meaning: The node (or some of its resources) has been allocated to one or more jobs and is serving those jobs.
  - Variants: ALLOCATED+ or mixed states indicate the node is allocated to active jobs and there are jobs starting/finishing or some resources still free.
  - Scheduler implication: The scheduler will not place new allocations that conflict with the current allocation; some backfill/partial allocations may be possible depending on free resources.

- drain (DRAINING / DRAIN / DRAINED)
  - Meaning: The node has been taken out of normal service so it will not accept new allocations. Typical workflow:
    - DRAINING (often shown as drain): node set to be drained; running jobs continue until completion.
    - DRAINED: node is drained and currently has no running jobs.
  - Typical causes: Administrator-requested maintenance, upgrades, hardware repair, or to remove a node from the pool before reboot.
  - Scheduler implication: No new jobs are started on the node; existing jobs are allowed to finish (unless forcibly cancelled).
  - How to inspect reason: scontrol show node <nodename> will include the drain reason.

- down (DOWN)
  - Meaning: Slurm has determined the node is not responding or is otherwise unavailable (powered off, network unreachable, failed health check).
  - Typical causes: Node crashed, unreachable, out-of-band power-off, or repeated heartbeat failures.
  - Scheduler implication: The node will not be allocated to jobs until it is brought back up and set to an available state.
  - How to inspect reason: sinfo -R (shows nodes in DOWN/DRAIN states and reasons) or scontrol show node <nodename>.

Quick notes and useful checks
- Mixed/partial states: A node can be partially used (some CPUs/GPU allocated) and appear as MIXED/MIX in some outputs; sinfo -N or scontrol show node gives per-node resource details.
- Suffix flags: sinfo can show suffix flags like ! (not responding), ~ (powered off), @ (pending reboot), $ (reservation-maintenance) — these give additional context about node condition.
- Commands to inspect details (read-only): sinfo -N -l, sinfo -R, and scontrol show node <nodename> will show state, resource allocation, and the admin reason text.

### Job Scheduling Priority [#priority](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
Job scheduling priority is made up of a number of factors as
described in the [priority/multifactor](https://slurm.schedmd.com/priority_multifactor.html) plugin. One
of the factors is the QOS priority. Each QOS is defined in the Slurm
database and includes an associated priority. Jobs that request and
are permitted a QOS will incorporate the priority associated with that
QOS in the job's [multi-factor priority calculation.](https://slurm.schedmd.com/priority_multifactor.html)
To enable the QOS priority component of the multi-factor priority
calculation, the "PriorityWeightQOS" configuration parameter must be
defined in the slurm.conf file and assigned an integer value greater
than zero.
A job's QOS only affects is scheduling priority when the
multi-factor plugin is loaded.

There are nine factors in the Multifactor Job Priority plugin that
influence job priority:
Age
the length of time a job has been waiting in the queue, eligible to be scheduled
Association
a factor associated with each association
Fair-share
the difference between the portion of the computing resource that has been promised and the amount of resources that has been consumed
Job size
the number of nodes or CPUs a job is allocated
Nice
a factor that can be controlled by users to prioritize their own jobs.
Partition
a factor associated with each node partition
QOS
a factor associated with each Quality Of Service
Site
a factor dictated by an administrator or a site-developed job_submit or site_factor plugin

Slurm supports job preemption, the act of "stopping" one or more "low-priority"
jobs to let a "high-priority" job run.
Job preemption is implemented as a variation of Slurm's
[Gang Scheduling](https://slurm.schedmd.com/gang_scheduling.html) logic.

already allocated to one or more jobs that could be preempted by the first job,
the preemptable job(s) are preempted.

Snippet:
## Limitations of Preemption During Backfill Scheduling [#limitations](https://slurm.schedmd.com/preempt.html)
For performance reasons, the backfill scheduler reserves whole nodes for jobs,
not partial nodes. If during backfill scheduling a job preempts one or more
other jobs, the whole nodes for those preempted jobs are reserved for the
preemptor job, even if the preemptor job requested fewer resources than that.
These reserved nodes aren't available to other jobs during that backfill
cycle, even if the other jobs could fit on the nodes. Therefore, jobs may
preempt more resources during a single backfill iteration than they requested.

Summary — what QOS priority is
- A QOS (Quality of Service) is an administrator-defined class that can carry a numeric priority and many limits (timelimit, max jobs, TRES caps, etc.).  
- The QOS numeric priority is one factor used by Slurm’s multifactor priority plugin. If PriorityWeightQOS in slurm.conf > 0 then a job’s QOS priority is multiplied by that weight and added into the job’s overall scheduling score (alongside age, fairshare, job size, partition, nice, TRES, site factors, …).  
- Administrators create/inspect/modify QOS entries with sacctmgr (e.g., sacctmgr show qos; sacctmgr modify qos <name> set priority=<N>).

How QOS ties into preemption (high level)
- Preemption lets a queued “higher priority” job take resources from one or more running “lower priority” jobs so the queued job can start. Whether/how that happens is controlled by two things:
  1. PreemptType (global/slurm.conf) — determines the policy used to decide which queued jobs are allowed to preempt which running jobs (e.g., preempt/qos uses the job’s QOS relationships).  
  2. PreemptMode (partition-level or QOS-level setting) — determines the action taken to the victim job(s) when preemption happens (cancel, requeue, suspend, or gang variants).
- When PreemptType=preempt/qos, Slurm consults the QOS definitions: a QOS can be configured (via sacctmgr) with a list of other QOSs it is allowed to preempt. A queued job whose QOS is permitted to preempt the running job’s QOS can cause preemption.

PreemptMode options and their effects
- CANCEL: preempted jobs are cancelled (terminated). Good for short or expendable jobs.  
- REQUEUE: preempted jobs are requeued (returned to the queue so they can run later). Useful when you want interrupted work retried.  
- SUSPEND: preempted jobs are suspended and (when supported) will be resumed after the preemptor finishes. Requires job suspend/resume support and keeps memory/pages resident.  
- GANG variants (e.g., SUSPEND,GANG): used with gang scheduling so resources can be shared/overlapped in a coordinated way; behavior depends on select/gang logic.  
Notes: administrators set PreemptMode in the partition definition (examples in slurm.conf show PreemptMode=requeue or PreemptMode=suspend). PreemptMode may also be applied per-QOS in some setups.

How Slurm selects victims (ordering)
- The select plugin is given an ordered list of preemptable jobs for a pending candidate. That list is sorted by one of:
  - QOS priority (default when using preempt/qos),
  - partition priority combined with job size (to favor preempting smaller jobs), or
  - job start time (if PreemptParameters=youngest_first).  
- Slurm attempts to find a set of victim jobs that frees the required resources. If it finds them, it performs the configured PreemptMode action on those victims.

Practical caveats and operational concerns
- Backfill interaction: during backfill cycles, Slurm reserves whole nodes. Preemption during backfill can lead to reserving more resources than strictly requested, which can reduce packing efficiency.  
- Memory and suspended jobs: suspended jobs remain in memory; if memory accounting is not configured (SelectTypeParameter, e.g., CR_Memory or CR_Core_Memory), swapping and overcommit can occur. Configure SelectTypeParameter appropriately if you use SUSPEND.  
- Not all jobs are good candidates for suspension/requeue (no checkpoint, long startup cost). Choose PreemptMode to match the workload characteristics.  
- Preemption settings must be planned carefully: CANCEL is destructive, REQUEUE is safer but may requeue at lower priority unless you preserve priority, SUSPEND needs OS/kernel support and may require configuration tweaks.

Administrator knobs you’ll typically check or change
- View QOS and their numeric priorities: sacctmgr show qos  
- Assign which QOSs a QOS may preempt: sacctmgr (configure the preempt relationships)  
- Enable QOS weight in priority calc: set PriorityWeightQOS in slurm.conf  
- Configure preemption policy: set PreemptType in slurm.conf and PreemptMode in partition/QOS definitions  
- Tune select plugin memory tracking: SelectTypeParameter=CR_Memory or CR_Core_Memory

When to use which PreemptMode (guidelines)
- CANCEL — for very short, non-critical jobs (low admin overhead).  
- REQUEUE — when jobs are restartable and you prefer them to run later rather than be lost.  
- SUSPEND — when jobs can be suspended/resumed efficiently (good for long jobs with checkpoint/resume).  
- GANG variants — when you need coordinated multi-job resource sharing or overlap.

## Burst Buffers [#burst_buffer](https://slurm.schedmd.com/heterogeneous_jobs.html)
A burst buffer can either be persistent or linked to a specific job ID.
Since a heterogeneous job consists of multiple job IDs, a job-specific burst
buffer will be associated with only one heterogeneous job component.
Each component can have its own burst buffer directives, and they are processed
separately. Only a persistent burst buffer can be accessed by all components
of a heterogeneous job. Persistent burst buffers are only available in the
datawarp plugin. A sample batch script demonstrating this for the datawarp
plugin is appended.
```text
#!/bin/bash #SBATCH --nodes=1 --constraint=haswell #BB create_persistent name=alpha capacity=10 access=striped type=scratch #DW persistentdw name=alpha #SBATCH hetjob #SBATCH --nodes=16 --constraint=knl #DW persistentdw name=alpha ...
```

## Job Accounting Records [#job_record](https://slurm.schedmd.com/job_launch.html)
When Slurm is configured to use SlurmDBD to store job records (i.e.
AccountingStorageType=accounting_storage=slurmdbd ), there are multiple
records that get stored for each job. There is a record for the job as a
whole as well as entries for the following types of job steps:
- extern step — A step created for each job as long as you have PrologFlags=contain in your slurm.conf. Each node in the job will have a slurmstepd process created for the extern step. pam_slurm_adopt uses this step to contain external connections.
- batch step — A step created for jobs that were submitted with sbatch. The batch host, or the primary node for the job, will run an instance of slurmstepd for the batch step, which is used to run the script provided to sbatch.
- interactive step — A step created for jobs that were submitted with salloc when LaunchParameters=use_interactive...

## Node Features[#nodefeatures](https://slurm.schedmd.com/elastic_computing.html)
Features defined by [NodeFeaturesPlugins](https://slurm.schedmd.com/slurm.conf.html), and
associated to cloud nodes in the slurm.conf , will be available but not
active when the node is powered down. If a job requests available but not
active features, the controller will allocate nodes that are powered down and
have the features as available. At allocation, the features will be made
active. A cloud node will remain with the active features until the node is
powered down (i.e. the node can't be rebooted to get other features until the
node is powered down). When the node is powered down, the those features
become available but not active. Any feature not defined by
NodeFeaturesPlugins are always active.

## Node Extra Data [#Node_Extra_Data](https://slurm.schedmd.com/extra_constraints.html)
A node's extra data is a json formatted string. It may be initialized on
slurmd startup with the --extra flag for slurmd. For example:
```text
slurmd --extra '{ "a": 1.23, "b": true, "c": 0, "foo": "bar", "zed": 23 }'
```
Or, it may be updated with scontrol. For example:
```text
scontrol update nodename=node123 extra='{ "a": 1.23, "b": true, "c": 0, "foo": "bar", "zed": 23 }'
```
This defines the features that may be requested by the --extra option in
salloc, sbatch, and srun. Values may be any string, number, or boolean value.

## MPI SUPPORT[#SECTION_MPI-SUPPORT](https://slurm.schedmd.com/srun.html)
MPI use depends upon the type of MPI being used.
There are three fundamentally different modes of operation used
by these various MPI implementations.
1. Slurm directly launches the tasks and performs initialization
of communications through the PMI2 or PMIx APIs.
For example: "srun -n16 a.out".
2. Slurm creates a resource allocation for the job and then
mpirun launches tasks using Slurm's infrastructure (OpenMPI).
3. Slurm creates a resource allocation for the job and then
mpirun launches tasks using some mechanism other than Slurm,
such as SSH or RSH.
These tasks are initiated outside of Slurm's monitoring
or control. Slurm's epilog should be configured to purge
these tasks when the job's allocation is relinquished,
or the use of pam_slurm_adopt is highly recommended.

## EXAMPLES[#SECTION_EXAMPLES](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Specify a batch script by filename on the command line. The batch script specifies a 1 minute time limit for the job.
```text
$ cat myscript #!/bin/sh #SBATCH --time=1 srun hostname |sort $ sbatch -N4 myscript salloc: Granted job allocation 65537 $ cat slurm-65537.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
Pass a batch script to sbatch on standard input:
```text
$ sbatch -N4 #!/bin/sh > srun hostname |sort > EOF sbatch: Submitted batch job 65541 $ cat slurm-65541.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
To create a heterogeneous job with 3 components, each allocating a unique set of nodes:
```text
$ sbatch -w node[2-3] : -w node4 : -w node[5-7] work.bash Submitted batch job 34987
```

Executing srun sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from srun or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmctld daemon come in at once, it can result in

in a denial of service.

calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other programs. Ensure
that programs limit calls to srun to the minimum necessary for the
information you are trying to gather.

## MPI SUPPORT[#SECTION_MPI-SUPPORT](https://slurm.schedmd.com/srun.html)
MPI use depends upon the type of MPI being used.
There are three fundamentally different modes of operation used
by these various MPI implementations.
1. Slurm directly launches the tasks and performs initialization
of communications through the PMI2 or PMIx APIs.
For example: "srun -n16 a.out".
2. Slurm creates a resource allocation for the job and then
mpirun launches tasks using Slurm's infrastructure (OpenMPI).
3. Slurm creates a resource allocation for the job and then
mpirun launches tasks using some mechanism other than Slurm,
such as SSH or RSH.
These tasks are initiated outside of Slurm's monitoring
or control. Slurm's epilog should be configured to purge
these tasks when the job's allocation is relinquished,
or the use of pam_slurm_adopt is highly recommended.

## DESCRIPTION[#SECTION_DESCRIPTION](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sshare.html)
sshare is used to view Slurm share information. This command is
only viable when running with the priority/multifactor plugin.
The sshare information is derived from a database with the interface
being provided by slurmdbd (Slurm Database daemon) which is
read in from the slurmctld and used to process the shares available
to a given association. sshare provides Slurm share information of
Account, User, Raw Shares, Normalized Shares, Raw Usage, Normalized
Usage, Effective Usage, the Fair-share factor, the GrpTRESMins limit,
Partitions and accumulated currently running TRES-minutes for each association.

## PERFORMANCE[#SECTION_PERFORMANCE](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sshare.html)
Executing sshare sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from sshare or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmctld daemon come in at once, it can result in
a degradation of performance of the slurmctld daemon, possibly resulting
in a denial of service.
Do not run sshare or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other
programs. Ensure that programs limit calls to sshare to the minimum
necessary for the information you are trying to gather.

Short answer first
- RawShares: the raw (configured) share weight assigned to the user/account.
- NormShares: RawShares normalized to the relevant total (so it becomes a fraction).
- EffectvUsage: the association’s usage normalized against its parent (used with FAIR_TREE to show relative served/under‑served).

Expanded explanation and practical interpretation
- RawShares
  - What it is: the integer or weight value assigned to an association (user, account, or group) that expresses its entitlement relative to others.
  - Where it comes from: set in sacctmgr (or inherited from parent associations) as the configured share allocation.
  - Role: higher RawShares => more entitlement to resources over time.

- NormShares
  - What it is: RawShares divided by the total RawShares in the relevant scope, yielding a fraction (0..1).
  - Scope: with default fairshare it’s normalized across the full set; when PriorityFlags=FAIR_TREE it’s normalized within the association’s level in the hierarchy (siblings).
  - Meaning: NormShares is the target fraction of resources that association should receive (e.g., NormShares = 0.2 means ~20% of the share).

- EffectvUsage (Effective Usage)
  - What it is: the association’s usage expressed relative to its parent’s usage (a normalized usage metric). This field is present/meaningful when FAIR_TREE is used.
  - How it’s used: compared to NormShares to see whether an association is over‑served or under‑served relative to its entitlement.
  - Interpretation: the scheduler computes a level fairshare value (Level FS = NormShares / EffectvUsage). If Level FS > 1 the association is under‑served (should gain priority); if Level FS < 1 it is over‑served.

Related fields and behavior to keep in mind
- RawUsage: total consumed TRES‑seconds (cpu‑seconds if TRESBillingWeights unset) charged to the association. This decays over time if PriorityDecayHalfLife is configured.
- NormUsage: RawUsage normalized to the total usage (shown with sshare -l).
- Decay: PriorityDecayHalfLife causes older usage to count less, so EffectvUsage and RawUsage are time‑weighted.
- Units and display: sshare (and sshare -l) shows these fields. RawUsage units are TRES‑seconds; NormShares/NormUsage and EffectvUsage are ratios/fractions.
- Practical check: example
  - NormShares = 0.20, EffectvUsage = 0.10 -> Level FS = 0.20 / 0.10 = 2.0 (under‑served, priority boost)
  - NormShares = 0.20, EffectvUsage = 0.40 -> Level FS = 0.20 / 0.40 = 0.5 (over‑served, lower relative priority)

## PERFORMANCE[#SECTION_PERFORMANCE](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sdiag.html)
Executing sdiag sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from sdiag or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmctld daemon come in at once, it can result in
a degradation of performance of the slurmctld daemon, possibly resulting
in a denial of service.
Do not run sdiag or other Slurm client commands that send remote procedure
calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other programs. Ensure
that programs limit calls to sdiag to the minimum necessary for the
information you are trying to gather.

Good question — understanding utilization means combining historical usage (what ran) with scheduler diagnostics (how the scheduler behaved while making placements). Below I summarize the Slurm reports and diagnostics you should use, what each metric means, how to interpret common patterns, and which commands to run to gather the evidence you need.

1) Primary Slurm reports / diagnostics and what they show
- sreport cluster utilization
  - Purpose: historical resource usage/usage breakdown over a time window (CPU/GPU-hours and time nodes were Allocated, Idle, Down, PlannedDown, OverCommitted, etc.).
  - Key fields: Allocated (time nodes in use by jobs/reservations), Idle (time nodes were idle), Down (node downtime/drain), OverCommitted, TresCount/TresName (which resources: CPUs/GPUs).
  - Use for: overall usage %, account/queue share, and trends (daily/weekly/monthly usage and which accounts/users consumed most).
- sdiag (scheduler diagnostics)
  - Purpose: runtime counters describing slurmctld scheduling activity: scheduling cycle count and times, backfill statistics and windows, dispatch counts, thread count, queue depth, wait/age counters.
  - Key fields to inspect: scheduling cycle avg/median/max, queue depth, backfill opportunities used vs missed, number of jobs dispatched, number of preemptions, server thread count.
  - Use for: diagnosing scheduler bottlenecks (scheduling latency, missed backfill, high RPC load).
- sprio and sprio --weights
  - Purpose: job priority components (fairshare, age, size, qos, partition). sprio shows which factor dominates each pending job’s priority.
  - Use for: identifying why jobs aren’t starting (low priority, fairshare limits, QOS).
- sshare
  - Purpose: fairshare usage and effective shares per user/account.
  - Use for: check historical share usage and whether fairshare is starving users.
- sinfo / sinfo_reasons / sinfo_node
  - Purpose: current partition/node states (allocated/idle/drain/down) and reasons for non-availability.
  - Use for: spotting node-level causes for idle capacity (drains, down nodes, maintenance).
- squeue (with Reason column) and scontrol show job
  - Purpose: live queue: pending reasons, per-job resources, elapsed times. scontrol show job gives detailed state, constraints, and pending reason text.
  - Use for: exact pending reason codes (e.g., Resources, Priority, ReqNodeNotAvail, QOSMaxJobs, AssociationResourceLimit).

2) Important utilization metrics and how to interpret them
- Utilization % = Allocated_time / (Allocated_time + Idle_time + Down_time) (from sreport)
  - Low utilization with little Down time → not enough usable jobs (fragmentation or mismatched job sizes).
  - Low utilization with significant Down time → hardware/maintenance or misconfiguration.
- CPU/GPU-hours usage
  - Use sreport to see total CPU/GPU-hours used by accounts/users and compare against cluster capacity to spot imbalances.
- Idle time vs pending work
  - Idle time + many pending jobs usually indicates resource fragmentation (small free slots that large jobs can’t use), partitions mismatches, or constraints (gpu/generic/exclusive).
  - Idle time + zero pending jobs suggests low demand.
- Backfill efficiency (from sdiag)
  - sdiag shows backfill opportunities and whether the scheduler filled them. Low backfill usage with available small jobs implies backfill policy or job-size/constraint mismatches.
- Scheduling latency (sdiag cycle times)
  - Long average/max scheduling cycle time can cause slow job starts and missed backfill windows. High slurmctld thread counts/RPCs can also indicate overload.
- Priority/fairshare effects (sprio + sshare)
  - If sprio shows many pending jobs have low priority due to fairshare or QOS weights, users may be waiting despite free nodes. Use sshare to confirm recent share consumption.
- Reservations and planned downtime
  - Reservations will reduce available capacity; sreport and scontrol_reservation_show reveal reservation usage and effect on utilization.
- Overcommit / wasted time
  - Overcommit shows where more resources were allocated than physical capacity (misconfig), while high wasted time can come from long node idle tails from large jobs finishing asynchronously.

3) Typical diagnosis patterns and checks (what to run)
- “Cluster overall utilization is low”
  - Run: sreport cluster utilization Start=... End=...
  - Check: sinfo (are nodes drained/down?), squeue (pending jobs count), sdiag (backfill windows), sprio (are jobs low-priority?), sshare (fairshare usage).
- “Many nodes idle, but jobs pending”
  - Run: squeue -o "%.18i %.50j %.8u %.2t %.10M %.10l %.12R" (include Reason)
  - If Reason is Resources → check sinfo for states and node feature mismatches.
  - If Reason is Priority / QOS → run sprio and sshare.
  - If Reason is ReqNodeNotAvail → use sinfo_reasons to find drains or reasons.
- “Backfill opportunities are being missed”
  - Run: sdiag --all (look at backfill stats and windows), then squeue for candidate small jobs. If sdiag shows backfill windows but they’re unused, look for job constraints (gres, node feature).
- “Slow scheduling / many scheduling cycles”
  - Run: sdiag and scontrol show config (check SchedulerType, SchedulerParameters, and thread limits). High avg cycle times + high queue depth can point to tuning needs (increase threads, tune SelectTypeParameters, or reduce expensive job filters).
- “Fairshare starvation”
  - Run: sprio and sshare. If fairshare weight dominates and some users have low effective shares, consider temporary QOS bumps or adjust PriorityWeightFairshare.
- “GPU utilization low”
  - Run: sreport with TresName=GPU, scontrol_show_config, and sinfo -o to see GPU availability. Check job scripts for --gres=gpu:X vs actual usage (sstat for running jobs to measure GPU use if supported).

4) How to quantify backfill / packing efficiency (practical numbers to report)
- From sreport: total CPU/GPU usage (CPU/GPU-hours) and Allocated % for window.
- From sdiag: count of backfill opportunities, backfill jobs dispatched vs opportunities, average backfill window length.
- Useful derived metrics:
  - Utilization % (per partition).
  - Average wait time for jobs (from sreport or sacct).
  - Backfill fill ratio = (CPU-minutes actually backfilled) / (CPU-minutes available for backfill).
  - Fragmentation estimate = sum of small idle slots that cannot host the largest queued jobs (requires combining squeue and sinfo node sizes).

5) What to include when you file a utilization diagnostic to the admin/operator
- Time window and sreport output (Allocated %, Idle %, Down %, CPU/GPU-hours).
- sdiag output (scheduling cycle times, backfill stats, queue depth).
- Top pending reasons and a short squeue sample (jobid, name, user, state, time, reason).
- sprio top pending jobs and sshare snapshot.
- sinfo showing node counts by state (Allocated/Idle/Down/Drained) and any sinfo_reasons lines.
- Example: “During 2026-05-01..2026-05-03: cluster utilization 32% (sreport). sdiag shows avg cycle 120ms, max 2.3s, backfill opportunities 47 but backfill fill ratio 20%. sinfo shows 8/120 nodes drained. squeue shows 300 pending jobs; top pending reason=ReqNodeNotAvail for many GPU jobs.”
- This lets operators know whether the problem is demand (low job submission), supply (down nodes/reservations), fragmentation, or scheduler tuning.

6) Quick command checklist (copy/paste)
- Historical utilization: sreport cluster utilization Start=2026-04-01 End=2026-04-30
- Scheduler diagnostics: sdiag --all
- Queue snapshot, include Reason: squeue -o "%.18i %.50j %.8u %.2t %.10M %.10l %.12R"
- Pending job priorities: sprio
- Fairshare: sshare -l
- Node states: sinfo -R  (or sinfo -N -l)
- Job detail: scontrol show job <JOBID>
- Reservations: scontrol show reservation
- License usage: scontrol_license

7) Remedies (common fixes)
- Reduce fragmentation: encourage job array/smaller chunked jobs, enable CB- or pack-based scheduling, tune DefMemPerCPU or SelectTypeParameters to improve packing.
- Improve backfill: relax excessive constraints, allow smaller GPUs/CPU jobs into backfill via QOS or partition config.
- Fix Down/Drained nodes: repair hardware or adjust maintenance windows (reduce planned down time).
- Address starvation: adjust fairshare weights, QOS limits, or increase priority for critical users.
- Scheduler tuning: increase slurmctld thread count, adjust SchedulerParameters (e.g., MaxJobCount, scheduling frequency), or use different scheduling algorithms if needed.

- Explain any specific sdiag line or sprio field you saw, or
- Run the exact commands above on your cluster and summarize results (I’ll need permission — tell me which time window or job IDs, or say “collect sreport and sdiag now”).

Summary first
- sacctmgr supports two related but different workflows:
  1) Accounting-data archive (sacctmgr archive dump / sacctmgr archive load) — export and (optionally) purge historical Jobs/Events/etc. from the slurmdbd accounting DB into archive files, and later restore them.
  2) Flat-file association dump/load (sacctmgr dump / sacctmgr load) — export and import association metadata (Clusters, Accounts, Users, QOS, Parent relationships) to/from a human-editable cfg-style file for copying or restoring configuration.

I’ll explain each workflow, important options, examples, and best-practices.

A — Accounting archive workflow (sacctmgr archive dump)
Purpose
- Export job/event/accounting records to a flat archive file so old accounting data can be kept offline and optionally removed from the live slurmdbd DB to reduce DB size.

Key behaviors and constraints
- Archive files are written on the slurmdbd host (the machine running slurmdbd).
- You can choose which record types to archive (Jobs, Events, etc.). If you request purge, the matching records are removed from the DB permanently — this cannot be rolled back.
- If you don’t specify specific options, slurmdbd.conf defaults (ArchiveDir, Purge settings) are used.
- Archive files are not overwritten: repeated archives create new files (older files are preserved).

Important options (common)
- Directory=path  — destination directory for the archive file (must be accessible on slurmdbd host).
- Jobs=yes|no, Events=yes|no  — decide which record types to archive.
- StartTime= / EndTime=  — time window for the archive.
- Purge= yes|no (or governed by PurgeJobAfter/PurgeEventAfter in slurmdbd.conf) — remove archived records from DB.

Example (conceptual)
- sacctmgr archive dump Directory=/var/lib/slurmdbd/archives Jobs=Yes Events=No StartTime=2023-01-01 EndTime=2023-12-31 Purge=Yes

What to check before running
- Confirm ArchiveDir and slurmdbd permissions.
- Verify you really want Purge=Yes; perform a non-purging dump first to inspect the file.
- Ensure you have a good DB backup (mysqldump/pg_dump) if you may need to recover.

B — Accounting restore workflow (sacctmgr archive load)
Purpose
- Load previously archived accounting files back into the slurmdbd DB.

Key behaviors and constraints
- The archive file must exist on the slurmdbd host.
- The load will not insert records that already exist in the DB; attempting to load the same archive twice will fail or report duplicate records.
- You can control SQL insertion behavior (Insert option) and other load options.
- Archive files from prior Slurm releases can be loaded, but validate compatibility for major version changes.

Important options (common)
- File=path  — archive file to load (on slurmdbd host).
- Insert=Yes|No  — control SQL INSERT vs other behavior (check man page for details).
- Other flags to control behavior (refer to your slurm version docs).

Example (conceptual)
- sacctmgr archive load File=/var/lib/slurmdbd/archives/cluster-archive-20231231.tar

Tips for loading
- Inspect the archive file before load to confirm contents.
- If restoring after a purge, ensure no conflicting records exist; the load will skip/complain on duplicates.
- Check slurmdbd logs for errors if load fails.

C — Association dump/load workflow (flat-file) — sacctmgr dump / sacctmgr load
Purpose
- Export cluster association metadata (Cluster, Parent, Account, User, QOS) into a readable cfg-style file and import it to create or reproduce associations in another DB/cluster.

Key behaviors and constraints
- Each dump file contains association data for a single cluster.
- Since v25.05 QOS data is included in the dump.
- The file format uses lines prefixed with the entity name (QOS, Cluster, Parent, Account, User) and colon-separated specs. Comments allowed with #.
- You must be a Slurm administrator or root to run dump/load.
- sacctmgr load will reconcile imported associations with existing DB entries. Use clean=... to remove/replace existing data if you want a fresh import.

Important options (common)
- sacctmgr dump cluster=<name> file=<file.cfg>
- sacctmgr load file=<file.cfg> [clean=account,qos,user] cluster=<new_name>
  - clean controls whether to delete existing cluster/accounts/qos/users before loading.

Examples
- Dump:
  - sacctmgr dump cluster=mycluster file=mycluster.cfg
- Load:
  - sacctmgr load file=mycluster.cfg
  - sacctmgr load file=mycluster.cfg clean=account,qos,user cluster=newclustername

Use cases
- Copying account/QOS setup from one cluster to another.
- Backing up accounting associations before DB maintenance.
- Re-creating cluster associations after a DB restore.

D — Recommended workflow and best-practices
- Always take a DB backup (mysqldump/pg_dump) before any destructive operation (purge/archive with Purge=Yes).
- For archiving: run a non-purging archive first (omit Purge or set Purge=No) to examine the produced archive file.
- Confirm archive files are stored in the configured ArchiveDir and have correct ownership/permissions for slurmdbd to read/write.
- Use time windows (StartTime/EndTime) to limit the archive scope and keep archive file sizes manageable.
- When loading archives, check for duplicates and version compatibility. Don’t load the same archive twice.
- For association loads, use clean= cautiously — it can remove existing accounts/QOS/users if requested.
- Monitor slurmdbd logs for errors during archive/load and check sacct/sacctmgr queries afterward to confirm expected records are present.

E — Troubleshooting pointers
- Missing file errors: ensure File/Directory path is on the slurmdbd host and readable by slurmdbd user.
- Duplicate-record errors on load: those records already exist in DB; use a DB backup/restore workflow if you need replacement.
- If archive/load fails with DB errors, check slurmdbd logs and DB server health.
- For format/questions, consult the sacctmgr man page (sacctmgr(8)) — the archive/dump/load sections describe all supported options and exact file formats.

The job's priority at any given time will be a weighted sum of all the
factors that have been enabled in the slurm.conf file. Job priority can be
expressed as:
```text
Job_priority = site_factor + (PriorityWeightAge) * (age_factor) + (PriorityWeightAssoc) * (assoc_factor) + (PriorityWeightFairshare) * (fair-share_factor) + (PriorityWeightJobSize) * (job_size_factor) + (PriorityWeightPartition) * (priority_job_factor) + (PriorityWeightQOS) * (QOS_factor) + SUM(TRES_weight_cpu * TRES_factor_cpu, TRES_weight_ * TRES_factor_ , ...) - nice_factor
```
All of the factors in this formula are floating point numbers that
range from 0.0 to 1.0. The weights are unsigned, 32 bit integers.

Audit accounting problem reports and explain likely remediation
No accounting problems found.

I checked accounting problem reports for you.

Summary
- I ran sacctmgr show problems and found: No accounting problems found.

What that means
- The accounting DB and Slurm accounting configuration report no current consistency or configuration errors detectable by sacctmgr.
- No immediate remediation actions are required based on that check.

If you want a proactive audit or to investigate potential accounting symptoms (missing jobs, unexpected usage totals, negative balances, slow queries), here are the common accounting problem categories, how to detect them, and likely remediation steps.

1) slurmdbd unreachable / authentication / connectivity failures
- Symptoms: sacct / sacctmgr slow or empty, periodic “failed to connect” errors in logs, new jobs not appearing in accounting.
- Diagnostics to run (read-only): check slurmdbd responsiveness, slurmctld logs, and DB process:
  - systemctl status slurmdbd && journalctl -u slurmdbd
  - scontrol ping (checks slurmctld responsiveness)
  - Check slurmdbd log for DB connection/auth errors.
- Likely remediation:
  - Restart slurmdbd after resolving underlying DB connectivity or credentials issues.
  - Verify AccountingStorageType/AccountingStorageHost and DB credentials in slurm.conf and slurmdbd.conf.
  - Ensure network/firewall allows DB traffic; check DB server health and credentials.
  - If DB is down, start DB and ensure replication or backups are intact.

2) Database corruption / schema mismatch / version incompatibility
- Symptoms: sacctmgr shows schema errors, errors referencing missing tables/columns, or weird accounting totals.
- Diagnostics: inspect slurmdbd logs and DB error logs, compare slurmdbd and slurmctld versions vs DB schema expected.
- Likely remediation:
  - If schema mismatch (after upgrade), apply the Slurm DB schema upgrade procedure (use slurmdbd tools documented by SchedMD).
  - If corruption, restore from recent DB backup and re-ingest job records if needed.
  - Coordinate version upgrades: ensure slurmctld/slurmdbd and DB schema versions are compatible.

3) Job completion logging missing (JobComp plugin misconfiguration)
- Symptoms: recent jobs exist in squeue/sacct system but sacct shows missing or incomplete job records.
- Diagnostics:
  - Check JobCompType and JobAcctGatherType in slurm.conf and slurmdbd.conf.
  - Review slurmctld and slurmdbd logs for JobComp/JobAcctGather errors.
- Remediation:
  - Fix misconfigured JobComp/JobAcctGather plugin settings, restart the daemons if configuration changed.
  - Re-run accounting ingestion only after confirming stable configuration (do not re-ingest blindly).

4) Incorrect user/account/association data (wrong allocations, unexpected usage)
- Symptoms: users see unexpected usage or limits; QOS/account associations look wrong.
- Diagnostics:
  - sacctmgr show associations, sacctmgr show users, and sacctmgr show accounts
  - sshare -l for fairshare/effective shares
- Remediation:
  - Correct associations with sacctmgr (create/modify associations, set correct QOS/account).
  - Recompute shares or adjust limits; document changes.
  - For bulk errors, consider scripting safe, auditable sacctmgr changes and testing on a small set first.

5) Incorrect or missing job charging (TRES/count mismatch, GPU accounting)
- Symptoms: GPU-hours or TRES usage not matching expectation.
- Diagnostics:
  - Inspect job records with sacct -j <jobid> -o JobID,JobName,AllocTRES,Elapsed
  - Verify node TRES config in gres.conf and slurm.conf
- Remediation:
  - Fix gres.conf / slurm.conf TRES/gres definitions and restart daemons if necessary.
  - For retrospective correction, you may need to update accounting records carefully (usually via sacctmgr or DB edits) — treat as a destructive operation and plan backups.

6) Performance problems with accounting queries (slow sacct/sacctmgr)
- Symptoms: sacct or sacctmgr queries are slow or time out.
- Diagnostics:
  - Check DB server load, slow query logs, slurmdbd and MySQL/Postgres performance metrics.
- Remediation:
  - Tune DB (indexes, query plans), add resources or replica depending on load, and archive old records (use sacct or sreport with Start= to limit queries).
  - Consider purging/archiving very old accounting rows if growth is excessive (after backups).

7) Time skew / NTP issues
- Symptoms: job times inconsistent, negative elapsed times, unusual accounting windows.
- Diagnostics:
  - Check time sync (ntp/chrony) on slurmctld, slurmdbd, compute nodes.
- Remediation:
  - Fix NTP/chrony configuration and resync clocks; address any nodes with persistent skew.

8) Permission / RBAC problems for sacctmgr users
- Symptoms: operators cannot run sacctmgr or see expected rows.

Summary of what I found
- fairshare (sshare): account=research, user=alice → RawShares=0.600, NormShares=0.420, EffectiveUsage=1.800. This shows alice’s effective recent usage is ~1.8 (above 1.0), which reduces her fairshare priority credit.
- priority (sprio): the query returned “No pending jobs match the filter” — there are no pending jobs for alice to show per-job priority factors. (If you want per-job priority, submit/queue a job or tell me a job ID to inspect.)

What this means
- Fairshare: the scheduler reduces priority for users/accounts whose EffectiveUsage is high vs their share. Alice’s EffectiveUsage=1.8 indicates she has consumed more than her fair share recently, so the fairshare component of her priority is lowered.
- Other priority factors that matter: job age (wait time increases priority), QOS, partition, and job size (large jobs often get lower priority relative to small jobs / backfill opportunities).

Concrete ways to improve queue position
1) Reduce EffectiveUsage (best long-term fix)
   - run fewer simultaneous large jobs or free currently running jobs so effective usage decays.
   - split big long jobs into smaller sequential jobs so you use fewer wallclock-hours concurrently.
   - stagger workflows so you don’t accumulate large concurrent usage spikes.

2) Make jobs more backfill-friendly
   - request a shorter, more accurate walltime. Shorter jobs fit backfill windows and start sooner.
   - request fewer nodes/GPUs (if possible) so jobs can fit into smaller free slots.

3) Use QOS / account options (if available)
   - submit with a higher-priority QOS or use an account with higher shares (requires permission).
   - ask your admin to temporarily increase your QOS or adjust account associations if justified.

4) Choose a less-busy partition or special queues
   - submit to debug/small/low-priority partitions designed for short jobs (if available).
   - check partition load (sinfo) and target partitions with more idle capacity.

5) Use reservations or coordinate with admins
   - request a reservation for a time window if you need guaranteed earlier start.
   - ask admins to review fairshare weights or to grant a temporary priority boost.

6) Small tactical steps
   - submit multiple short test jobs with minimal resources to gain age-based priority quickly.
   - bundle independent tasks into arrays with modest per-task requests to improve scheduling efficiency.

enough calls from sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote

in a denial of service.

procedure calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other
programs. Ensure that programs limit calls to sbatch to the minimum
necessary for the information you are trying to gather.

If two jobs use burst buffers and one is dependent on the other (e.g.
`sbatch --dependency=afterok:123 ...`) then the second job will not
begin until the first job completes and its burst buffer stage-out completes.
If the second job does not use a burst buffer, but is dependent upon the first
job's completion, then it will not wait for the stage-out operation of the first
job to complete.
The second job can be made to wait for the first job's stage-out operation to
complete using the "afterburstbuffer" dependency option (e.g.
`sbatch --dependency=afterburstbuffer:123 ...`).

"Configless" Slurm is a feature that allows the compute nodes —
specifically the slurmd process — and user commands running on login

## Versioning [#versioning](https://slurm.schedmd.com/plugins.html)
Slurm plugins must provide a plugin_version symbol exactly matching that
of the process they are loaded into. This is to avoid any potential issues if,
e.g., an underlying struct definition is changed by a maintenance release.
It is expected that the plugins are automatically build, packaged, and
distributed alongside the libslurm library, Slurm commands, and daemons.
The only exception to this is the SPANK plugin interface which only requires
the Slurm release to match, while the maintenance release (micro version) may be
changed. This is to reflect the additional ABI stability commitment that is
maintained exclusively for that plugin interface.

Building pipelines using slurm dependencies 
 
 
 
 Quick Links 
 Introduction 
 Bash 
 Perl 
 Python 
 

 
 
 Differences between stock sbatch and sbatch on biowulf 

 
 Before discussing job dependencies we need to point out that
 sbatch on biowulf, and therefore in the examples below, is a
 wrapper script that returns just the jobid. That is different
 from stock sbatch which returns Submitted batch job 123456 .
 You can think of the wrapper doing something equivalent to 

 
#! /bin/bash

sbr="$(/path/to/real/sbatch "$@")"

if [[ "$sbr" =~ Submitted\ batch\ job\ ([0-9]+) ]]; then
 echo "${BASH_REMATCH[1]}"
 exit 0
else
 echo "sbatch failed"
 exit 1
fi
 
 

 

 
 
 Introduction 

 
Job dependencies are used to defer the start of a job until the specified
dependencies have been satisfied. They are specified with the 
 --dependency option to sbatch or swarm 
in the format
 

 
sbatch --dependency=<type:job_id[:job_id][,type:job_id[:job_id]]> ...
 

 Dependency types: 
 
 after :jobid[:jobid...] 
 job can begin after the specified jobs have started 
 
 afterany :jobid[:jobid...] 
 job can begin after the specified jobs have terminated 
 
 afternotok :jobid[:jobid...] 
 job can begin after the specified jobs have failed 
 
 afterok :jobid[:jobid...] 
 job can begin after the specified jobs have run to completion
 with an exit code of zero (see the 
 user guide for
 caveats). 
 
 singleton 
 jobs can begin execution after all previously launched jobs 
 with the same name and user have ended. This is useful to collate
 results of a swarm or to send a notification at the end of a swarm. 
 
 

 See also the Job Dependencies 
section of the User Guide . 

 To set up pipelines using job dependencies the most useful types are 
afterany, afterok and singleton. The simplest way is to use the afterok
dependency for single consecutive jobs. For example:
 
 
b2$ sbatch job1.sh 
11254323
b2$ sbatch --dependency=afterok:11254323 job2.sh 
 

 Now when job1 ends with an exit code of zero, job2 will become eligible for
scheduling. However, if job1 fails (ends with a non-zero exit code), job2 will
not be scheduled and will be canceled automatically by the scheduler.
 
 As an alternative, the afterany dependency can be used and checking for
successful execution of the prerequisites can be done in the jobscript itself.
 
 The sections below give more complicated examples of using job dependencies
for pipelines in bash, perl, and python. 

 
 
 Bash 

 The following bash script is a stylized example of some useful patterns
for using job dependencies: 

 
#! /bin/bash

# first job - no dependencies
jid1=$(sbatch --mem=12g --cpus-per-task=4 job1.sh)

# multiple jobs can depend on a single job
jid2=$(sbatch --dependency=afterany:$jid1 --mem=20g job2.sh)
jid3=$(sbatch --dependency=afterany:$jid1 --mem=20g job3.sh)

# a single job can depend on multiple jobs
jid4=$(sbatch --dependency=afterany:$jid2:$jid3 job4.sh)

# swarm can use dependencies
jid5=$(swarm --dependency=afterany:$jid4 -t 4 -g 4 -f job5.sh)

# a single job can depend on an array job
# it will start executing when all arrayjobs have finished
jid6=$(sbatch --dependency=afterany:$jid5 job6.sh)

# a single job can depend on all jobs by the same user with the same name
jid7=$(sbatch --dependency=afterany:$jid6 --job-name=dtest job7.sh)
jid8=$(sbatch --dependency=afterany:$jid6 --job-name=dtest job8.sh)
sbatch --dependency=singleton --job-name=dtest job9.sh

# show dependencies in squeue output:
squeue -u $USER -o "%.8A %.4C %.10m %.20E"

What it is
- The singleton dependency tells Slurm “only start this job once all previously launched jobs with the same job name and the same user have finished (ended).”
- In short: it serializes jobs by (user, job-name) so at most one job with that name from that user is running at a time.

How to use it
- Specify it with sbatch --dependency=singleton (the job name comes from --job-name or the script filename).
- Example:
  sbatch --dependency=singleton --job-name=mytask myscript.sh

Behavior and semantics
- “Previously launched” means jobs submitted earlier than this job. The dependent job will not become eligible until those earlier jobs with the same name and user have ended (completed, failed, cancelled, timed out — any terminal state).
- It does not require you to list job IDs; the dependency is resolved by matching job name and user.
- Ordering is by submission: later singleton jobs wait for earlier ones to terminate before running.
- It does not enforce exclusivity across different users or different job names.

When to use it
- Serializing a series of jobs that must not run concurrently (e.g., to avoid simultaneous writes to the same output file).
- Collating results or sending one notification after a swarm of jobs with the same name finishes.

Limitations / notes
- If you need a dependency tied to a specific job’s success/failure, use afterok/afternotok/afterany with job IDs instead.
- Singleton works at the (user, job-name) granularity only; it cannot enforce a cluster-wide single instance across different users.

High level: use three quick checks together to tell whether the scheduler is healthy, why jobs are stuck, and whether the scheduler itself is the bottleneck.

1) What each tool shows and why it matters
- scontrol ping
  - Purpose: basic liveness/latency check for the controller (slurmctld).
  - What to expect: a short affirmative reply (commonly "slurmctld: OK") with low RTT.
  - Interpretation: a successful, low-latency ping means the controller process is reachable. a failed/timeout or high latency suggests slurmctld is unhealthy, overloaded, or network/IPC problems; fix the controller before blaming scheduling policy.

- sdiag
  - Purpose: scheduler diagnostics — scheduling cycle stats, backfill behavior, and queue/scheduling throughput.
  - Key metrics to read:
    - scheduling cycle time (median/mean or recent cycle latency): how long each scheduling pass takes.
    - queue/depth or jobs considered per cycle: how many jobs the scheduler must examine.
    - backfill statistics (efficiency, time saved): how effectively the scheduler fills gaps.
    - counts of fast vs slow scheduling decisions (if present).
  - Interpretation:
    - Normal: short cycle times (milliseconds–low hundreds ms depending on cluster size), steady queue depth, decent backfill utilization.
    - Warning: sustained long cycle times (seconds or repeatedly high) or growing queue depth → scheduler is CPU-bound or overwhelmed with decisions.
    - Low backfill efficiency + many idle nodes → fragmentation or policy mismatch (jobs can’t be placed although capacity exists).

- queue pressure (squeue + sinfo)
  - Purpose: operational view of demand and blocking reasons.
  - Important checks:
    - pending job count and age distribution (how many are pending, how long they’ve waited).
    - per-job Pending Reason field (Resources, QOSLimit, Priority, Dependency, PartitionDown, NodeNotAvail, etc.).
    - partition/node availability and states (sinfo) — drained/down nodes reduce effective capacity.
    - ratio of RUNNING : IDLE nodes, and whether many nodes are in state MIXED/ALLOCATED.
  - Interpretation:
    - Many short-lived pending jobs or very large bursts can cause scheduler thrash.
    - If many jobs pending with reason=Resources and sinfo shows idle nodes, that suggests placement fragmentation or mismatched resource requests (e.g., exclusive node requests, GRES mismatch).
    - If reason=QOSLimit/AssocMax*Limit, it’s an accounting/quota issue, not scheduler cycles.
    - If reason=PartitionDown/NodeDown, capacity is reduced and you need node repair/resume.

2) How to combine the three to diagnose common problems
- Controller-down symptoms
  - scontrol ping fails → do not trust sdiag/squeue. Remedy: check slurmctld service, controller logs, node connectivity.
- Scheduler overloaded (backlog)
  - scontrol ping OK, sdiag shows long scheduling cycle times and increasing queue depth, and squeue shows growing pending job counts (especially many short jobs or many submissions).
  - Interpretation: scheduler can’t keep up with decision volume. Actions: throttle submissions (QOS/submit limits), increase scheduling resources (CPU/threads for slurmctld if supported), tune sched_config, or reduce job churn.
- Capacity mismatch / fragmentation
  - scontrol ping OK, sdiag cycle times normal, but squeue shows many pending jobs with reason=Resources while sinfo shows some idle nodes.
  - Interpretation: placement fragmentation, GRES/feature mismatch, or jobs request exclusive nodes/too-large resources. Actions: review requested resources, relax exclusivity, enable node sharing, or change partition config.
- Policy/accounting limits
  - Many jobs pending with reason=QOSLimit/Assoc*Limit and sprio/sshare show users/accounts exhausted.
  - Interpretation: enforce/adjust QOS or account limits, or grant temporary exceptions.
- Backfill problems
  - sdiag shows very low backfill efficiency and squeue shows small holes in node allocations.
  - Interpretation: either backfill window too small or job sizes/constraints produce fragmented free space. Actions: tune backfill parameters, allow smaller backfill windows, enable more flexible placement.

3) Practical checklist & commands to collect evidence
- Quick liveness
  - scontrol ping
    - Expect OK; capture any latency or error.
- Scheduler diagnostic snapshot
  - sdiag
    - Save the scheduling cycle times, queue depth, and backfill stats.
- Queue pressure snapshot
  - squeue --states=PENDING,RUNNING -o "%.18i %.30j %.8u %.10T %.10M %.10R"
    - Look at counts, Pending Reason, job age.
  - sinfo -R or sinfo -Nel
    - See nodes in down/drain and node reasons (sinfo_reasons if available).
- Priority/fairshare
  - sprio (and sshare) to see whether priority/fairshare is holding jobs.
- If scontrol ping fails
  - Check slurmctld logs (usually /var/log/slurmctld.log) and system service status on controller host.

4) Quick triage playbook (what to do first)
- If scontrol ping fails: isolate controller, check slurmctld, network, restart controller only after review of logs.
- If sdiag shows high cycle time: collect sdiag repeatedly (to see trends), capture slurmctld CPU/memory usage, and consider submission throttles or slurmctld resource increase.
- If squeue shows many pending + sinfo shows idle nodes: inspect Pending Reasons, job resource requests, and node feature/GRES labels.
- If many jobs blocked by limits: inspect QOS/account associations (sacctmgr/sreport) and adjust limits or grant exceptions.

5) What “healthy” looks like (concise)
- scontrol ping: responsive, low latency.
- sdiag: short scheduling cycle times for cluster size, stable queue depth, reasonable backfill efficiency.
- squeue/sinfo: pending counts small or short-lived, pending reasons meaningful (not dominated by Resources with idle nodes), few nodes down/drained.

If you want, I can:
- run the three checks now (scontrol ping, sdiag, squeue + sinfo) and summarize live health and concrete fields to act on, or
- give a short template of exact commands and parsing snippets to automate ongoing health monitoring.

## PERFORMANCE[#SECTION_PERFORMANCE](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sdiag.html)
Executing sdiag sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from sdiag or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmctld daemon come in at once, it can result in
a degradation of performance of the slurmctld daemon, possibly resulting
in a denial of service.
Do not run sdiag or other Slurm client commands that send remote procedure
calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other programs. Ensure
that programs limit calls to sdiag to the minimum necessary for the
information you are trying to gather.

The backfill scheduling plugin is loaded by default.
Without backfill scheduling, each partition is scheduled strictly in priority

sdiag reports counters and timing metrics from slurmctld that help diagnose scheduler behavior (threads, RPC/agent activity, job lifecycle, scheduling/backfill work, and cycle timing). Below are the common fields you will see and what each means.

Global / slurmctld execution
- Server thread count — number of active slurmctld threads handling RPCs and internal work; high values indicate heavy slurmctld load.
- RPC/agent counts — counts of agent/RPC activity (connections, created agents, RPC requests). spikes show increased client or controller activity.

Job lifecycle counters
- Jobs submitted / launched / completed / failed / cancelled / requeued / resumed — cumulative counters of job state transitions seen by slurmctld since the last reset. Use these to understand submission/completion rates and error volume.
- Steps created / steps completed — counts for job steps (task-level entities) created and finished.

Scheduling cycle timing and counts
- Scheduling cycle count — number of scheduler iterations (how many times the scheduler loop ran).
- Cycle time (min / avg / max) — how long scheduler iterations are taking; long or widely varying cycle times indicate expensive scheduling work or resource contention inside slurmctld.
- Work items per cycle / evaluated jobs per cycle — how much work the scheduler is doing each iteration.

Backfill and scheduling-plugin statistics
- Backfill evaluations / accepted / rejected (or similar) — how often the backfill logic examines pending jobs and whether they were allowed to run; useful to see whether backfill is effective.
- Backfill window / backfill checks — counts/metrics indicating how many potential placements the backfiller inspected; very large counts indicate heavy backfill computation.

Resource / allocation activity
- Node updates / node state changes — how many node status updates or reconfigurations slurmctld processed.
- Allocation/TRES changes — counters of resource allocation events (CPUs, GPUs, memory) handled.

Other diagnostic counters
- Preemptions / evictions / reservations handled — counts of preemption or reservation actions the scheduler took.
- Deferred/gang/heterogeneous job bookkeeping — counters related to special scheduling behaviors (if used).

Operational notes for interpretation
- sdiag shows cumulative counters reset at midnight UTC by default; use sdiag --reset to zero counters when you want to measure a fresh interval.
- High server thread count, large numbers of RPCs, or long scheduler cycle times indicate controller load; investigate submission rates, polling/monitoring clients, or expensive scheduling rules/plugins.
- Large backfill evaluation counts with few accepts can indicate inaccurate time limits on running jobs or an overly expensive backfill policy.
- Use sdiag sparingly: each invocation is an RPC to slurmctld and frequent calls can affect controller performance.

Output formats / options
- sdiag -a (default) prints the full set of counters; --json is available for machine parsing.
- There is a --reset option to clear the counters after you capture a baseline.

If you want, tell me which sdiag section you have output for (paste it) and I can explain the specific counters and what to watch for.

# Gang Scheduling
Slurm supports timesliced gang scheduling in which two or more jobs are
allocated to the same resources in the same partition and these jobs are
alternately suspended to let one job at a time have dedicated access to the
resources for a configured period of time.
Slurm also supports preemptive job scheduling that allows a job in a
higher PriorityTier partition, or in a preempting QOS, to preempt other
jobs. [Preemption](https://slurm.schedmd.com/preempt.html) is related to Gang scheduling
because SUSPEND is one of the PreemptionMode s, and it uses the Gang
scheduler to resume suspended jobs.
A workload manager that supports timeslicing can improve responsiveness
and utilization by allowing more jobs to begin running sooner.
Shorter-running jobs no longer have to wait in a queue behind longer-running
jobs.
Instead they can be run "in parallel" with the longer-running jobs, which will
allow them to start and finish quick...

## Overview[#overview](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sched_config.html)
Slurm is designed to perform a quick and simple scheduling attempt at
events such as job submission or completion and configuration changes.
During these event-triggered scheduling events, default_queue_depth
(default is 100) number of jobs will be considered.
At less frequent intervals, defined by sched_interval , the main
scheduling loop will run, considering all jobs while still honoring the
partition_job_depth limit.
In both cases, jobs are evaluated in a strict priority order and once any
job or job array task in a partition is left pending, no other jobs in that
partition will be scheduled to avoid taking resources from the higher-priority
pending job.
A more comprehensive scheduling attempt is typically done by the backfill
scheduling plugin, which considers job run time and resources required to
determine if lower-priority jobs would actually take resources need...

Short answer
- Backfill scheduling is the scheduler’s attempt to run lower‑priority jobs in “holes” (idle time and nodes) without delaying any higher‑priority job’s expected start. “Queue fit” is how well the current waiting jobs (sizes and requested runtimes) actually fit into those holes. Healthy backfill = high utilization + short wait times for short jobs + few scheduling failures due to runtime misestimates.

What backfill does (brief)
- Examines running jobs and their expected end times, then considers pending jobs (in priority order) to see which can be started now without delaying any earlier-starting job.
- Relies heavily on the expected/allocated runtime of running jobs. If those are wrong, backfill decisions become poor.

Key signals of backfill “health”
- Utilization: high sustained CPU/GPU utilization with minimal idle machine time between targeted job starts.
- Small-job responsiveness: short jobs and small allocations start quickly instead of waiting behind large jobs.
- Low fragmentation: available free resources (cores/GPU nodes) are regularly consumed rather than left unused.
- Accurate predicted start times: squeue --start (or sdiag output) shows reliable predicted starts for pending jobs.
- Few preemptions or reschedules caused by jobs exceeding their walltime estimates.
- Backfill statistics: sdiag shows backfill attempts/successes and how often the scheduler finds a fit.

Common failure modes (why backfill is “unhealthy”)
- Inaccurate walltimes: long overruns or wildly optimistic estimates cause the scheduler either to be too conservative (underutilized) or to delay higher‑priority jobs (bad fairness).
- Resource fragmentation: many nodes partially free but no pending job requests match the exact granularity, leaving gaps.
- Very large, long-running jobs at the front of the queue that reserve many nodes for long windows (small jobs can’t fit).
- Small default_queue_depth or too-frequent short scheduling windows so the scheduler doesn’t look far enough into the queue.
- Misconfigured preemption or gang-scheduling that prevents using the free slices safely.
- QoS/accounting policies that force strict ordering and prevent lower-priority jobs from running even when they could fit.

How to measure queue-fit and backfill health (practical checks)
- Check cluster-wide load and idle gaps: sinfo and squeue to see node/partition idle counts and which jobs are waiting.
- Scheduler diagnostics: sdiag — shows backfill statistics and scheduling cycle info.
- Priority and job-start reasons: sprio (priority factors), and squeue (look at REASON column for pending jobs).
- Predicted start times: squeue --start (or scontrol show job <id>) to see when the job is expected to start — compare requested duration to the available window.
- Fragmentation: sinfo --Node or sinfo -l to inspect per-node allocation patterns (many partially-used nodes is a sign).
- Walltime accuracy: sample historic jobs with sacct to compare requested TimeLimit vs actual Elapsed time and compute overrun rates.
- Utilization and responsiveness: sreport or sdiag for utilization, plus median/percentile wait times per job size class (short vs long).

Metrics to track (recommendations)
- Overall utilization (CPU/GPU) and idle seconds between job starts.
- Fraction of pending jobs that start within X minutes (e.g., 30m) — broken out by job size and runtime.
- Median and 95th percentile wait time for short jobs (<1 hour).
- Percentage of jobs that exceed their requested walltime.
- Backfill success rate from sdiag (attempted vs started).
- Number of preemptions and reschedules.

Practical tuning levers to improve fit
- Encourage or enforce accurate walltime estimates (user education, default/required time limits, incentives/penalties).
- Use job size limits or partitions (separate very large long jobs from interactive/short-job partitions).
- Tune scheduler parameters: default_queue_depth and sched_interval so the scheduler looks at a sufficiently large set of pending jobs and at appropriate cadence.
- Enable/adjust preemption or gang scheduling where appropriate (so long jobs can be suspended or higher-priority small jobs can run).
- Use QoS rules and Fairshare to prioritize short/interactive jobs for better responsiveness.
- Consolidation policies: tune resource selection so the scheduler prefers packing jobs to reduce fragmentation (e.g., SelectTypeParameters or consume‑TRES settings).
- Limit excessive node exclusivity or overuse of single-node large allocations that fragment capacity.

Short checklist to assess your cluster now
1. Run sdiag to view backfill stats (attempts, successes, cycle times).  
2. Run squeue --start and inspect pending job predicted starts and REASONs.  
3. Use sacct to compute how often jobs exceed requested walltime.  
4. Inspect sinfo/sinfo --Node to find fragmentation (many partially used nodes).  
5. Look at utilization (sreport or sdiag) and short-job wait times.  

If you want, I can:
- Walk you through specific commands and how to interpret the exact sdiag/squeue/sinfo fields on your cluster, or
- Run the diagnostics (sdiag, squeue, sacct, sinfo) now and summarize the backfill health and suggested tunings.

### Job Preemption [#preemption](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
Slurm offers two ways for a queued job to preempt a running job,
free-up the running job's resources and allocate them to the queued

A QOS can be attached to a partition. This means the partition will have all
the same limits as the QOS. This does not associate jobs with the QOS, nor does
it give the job any priority or preemption characteristics of the assigned QOS.

## Limitations of Preemption During Backfill Scheduling [#limitations](https://slurm.schedmd.com/preempt.html)
For performance reasons, the backfill scheduler reserves whole nodes for jobs,
not partial nodes. If during backfill scheduling a job preempts one or more
other jobs, the whole nodes for those preempted jobs are reserved for the
preemptor job, even if the preemptor job requested fewer resources than that.
These reserved nodes aren't available to other jobs during that backfill
cycle, even if the other jobs could fit on the nodes. Therefore, jobs may
preempt more resources during a single backfill iteration than they requested.

# Gang Scheduling
Slurm supports timesliced gang scheduling in which two or more jobs are
allocated to the same resources in the same partition and these jobs are
alternately suspended to let one job at a time have dedicated access to the
resources for a configured period of time.
Slurm also supports preemptive job scheduling that allows a job in a
higher PriorityTier partition, or in a preempting QOS, to preempt other
jobs. [Preemption](https://slurm.schedmd.com/preempt.html) is related to Gang scheduling
because SUSPEND is one of the PreemptionMode s, and it uses the Gang
scheduler to resume suspended jobs.
A workload manager that supports timeslicing can improve responsiveness
and utilization by allowing more jobs to begin running sooner.
Shorter-running jobs no longer have to wait in a queue behind longer-running
jobs.
Instead they can be run "in parallel" with the longer-running jobs, which will
allow them to start and finish quick...
