Short explanation, organized by concept and configuration points.

What QOS does for priority
- QOS (Quality of Service) is an entity you assign to jobs (and can attach to partitions). A QOS carries limits (MaxJobs, GrpTRES, MaxTRES, etc.) and a numeric priority value.
- QOS contributes to a job’s scheduling priority only when the multi-factor priority plugin is enabled and PriorityWeightQOS in slurm.conf is set > 0. The job’s priority calculation then includes the QOS priority value multiplied by that weight.
- QOS limits override association/partition limits for jobs that use that QOS (useful to enforce caps or special resources).

How to change QOS priority (admin)
- QOS priority and other attributes are managed with sacctmgr (e.g., sacctmgr modify qos <name> set priority=<int>).
- Increasing a QOS priority raises the scheduling score of jobs that request that QOS (subject to the other multifactor weights).

How preemption works (big picture)
- Preemption lets a queued (higher-priority) job cause one or more running (lower-priority) jobs to be stopped/evicted so the queued job can start.
- Two pieces govern behavior:
  1) PreemptType (slurm.conf) — which mechanism decides WHAT can preempt WHAT (common values: preempt/qos uses job QOS relationships; preempt/partition uses partition PriorityTier to decide).
  2) PreemptMode (slurm.conf, per-partition or global) — what action to take when preempting (CANCEL, REQUEUE, SUSPEND, plus GANG variants).

Preemption policy details and options
- PreemptType=preempt/qos
  - The queued job’s job-QOS is used to determine preemption eligibility. Each QOS can be configured (via sacctmgr) with a list of other QOS names that it is allowed to preempt.
- PreemptType=preempt/partition
  - Uses partition PriorityTier (and partition configuration) to decide which jobs may preempt others (higher PriorityTier can preempt lower).
- PreemptMode (action taken on preempted jobs)
  - CANCEL — preempted jobs are cancelled (terminated).
  - REQUEUE — preempted jobs are requeued (placed back into the queue to run later).
  - SUSPEND — preempted jobs are suspended (memory pages retained) and will be resumed later.
  - SUSPEND,GANG (or SUSPEND with gang scheduling) — used with gang scheduling/time-slicing so multiple jobs share resources by being suspended/resumed on a timeslice schedule.
  - Combinations/variants exist (consult PreemptMode docs for exact accepted tokens).
- PreemptParameters
  - Controls selection ordering for which running jobs are chosen to be preempted when multiple could be freed (examples: youngest_first). The selection list may be sorted by QOS priority, partition priority & job size (to favor preempting smaller jobs), or job start time.
- Ordering/selection
  - The select plugin is passed an ordered list of preemptable jobs; the order depends on configuration (QOS priority, partition priority and job size, or age with youngest_first).
- Limits and interaction
  - QOS group limits (GrpTRES, GrpJobs, etc.) are checked when considering starting a job; a pending preemptor won’t start if its group limits would be exceeded even after preempting others.
  - Backfill and preemption interact: backfill may reserve entire nodes and preemption during backfill can result in larger-than-requested reservations (whole-node effects).
  - SUSPEND keeps memory pages resident: SelectType/SelectTypeParameters should be configured to account for memory (e.g., CR_Memory) to avoid swapping when many suspended jobs remain in memory.

Practical examples (conceptual)
- To make QOS “highpri” able to preempt “normal”, an admin would use sacctmgr to assign preemption rights to highpri (e.g., set which QOS names it may preempt) and set slurm.conf PreemptType=preempt/qos; choose a PreemptMode such as REQUEUE if you want preempted jobs returned to the queue.
- To give QOS a higher scheduling impact without preemption, increase its priority and ensure PriorityWeightQOS > 0 (no preemption change is needed for priority-only effects).

Operational cautions / recommendations
- Use REQUEUE or CANCEL for simplicity; SUSPEND requires careful memory accounting and may increase resource pressure because suspended jobs keep memory resident.
- Test preemption behavior in a non-production partition first — preemption can cause application-level problems (loss of work if apps don’t checkpoint).
- Keep group and account limits consistent with preemption rules so preemptors don’t become ineligible at allocation time.

Pointers to config entries to review (admin)
- sacctmgr (show/modify qos ...)
- slurm.conf: PreemptType, PreemptMode, PreemptParameters, PriorityWeightQOS, SelectType/SelectTypeParameters, PriorityTier (partition)

Sharding provides a generic mechanism where GPUs can be

Summary — two syntaxes
- --gres=name[:type:count]  (generic resource request; treated per node)
- Convenience options equivalent to or layered on top of GRES for GPUs:
  - --gpus=<count>            (GPUs required per job)
  - --gpus-per-node=<count>   (GPUs required per node; equivalent to --gres for gpu)
  - --gpus-per-task=<count>   (GPUs required per task)

Key rules and semantics
- --gres: format is name[:type[:count]]. For GPUs the name is usually "gpu". Example forms:
  - --gres=gpu:2           (2 GPUs per node)
  - --gres=gpu:V100:2      (2 GPUs per node of type V100 — the "type" must match what is configured in gres.conf/slurm.conf)
- --gpus is a job-level request (total GPUs for the job). --gpus-per-node and --gpus-per-task express per-node or per-task counts.
- Behavior is plugin-dependent: the --gpus and --gpus-per-* shortcuts require Slurm's select/cons_tres configuration. If your cluster uses a plain GRES setup, use --gres.
- When you combine node count and per-node requests: total GPUs allocated = nodes * (gpus-per-node) (or nodes * count in --gres).
- When you use --gpus-per-task with --ntasks, Slurm will try to allocate one GPU for each task (useful for one-GPU-per-rank MPI).

Examples
- Request 2 GPUs on one node (per-node and single-node):
  #SBATCH --nodes=1
  #SBATCH --gres=gpu:2
  or
  #SBATCH --gpus=2
- Request 1 GPU on each of 4 nodes:
  #SBATCH --nodes=4
  #SBATCH --gpus-per-node=1
  or
  #SBATCH --nodes=4
  #SBATCH --gres=gpu:1
- Request 1 GPU per MPI rank (8 ranks):
  #SBATCH --ntasks=8
  #SBATCH --gpus-per-task=1
- Request specific GPU model if configured:
  #SBATCH --gres=gpu:V100:2
  (Type string must match the Type/name given in gres.conf or slurm.conf.)

Environment variables (what Slurm sets for your job)
- CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES is set for each job step so your process sees only the GPUs allocated to it (device IDs are local to the node).
- Slurm may also export variables such as SLURM_CPUS_PER_GPU when cpus-per-gpu is used; exact variables can vary by Slurm version and configuration.

Cluster-side configuration you should know
- The actual GPU names/types and counts are configured in slurm.conf and gres.conf on the nodes. If a type/name is requested that doesn't exist, the job will be rejected or remain pending.
- Features like MPS or GPU sharding require additional config (gres/mps or shard counts) and change how fractions or multiple jobs can share GPUs.
- The scheduler enforces allocations. You cannot rely on libraries enumerating all /dev/nvidia* devices; use the Slurm environment variables and CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES inside the job.

Common pitfalls & tips
- Per-node vs per-job confusion: --gres is per node; --gpus is per job. Pick the right one for multi-node jobs.
- If you ask for --gpus-per-task but don’t set ntasks as you expect, you may not get the intended mapping.
- If you need a specific model, using the type field in --gres is usually better than generic constraints, but both can work depending on how the cluster is configured.
- If you expect GPU sharing (MPS/sharding), confirm the cluster’s gres.conf and that the select/cons_tres plugin supports your intended sharing mode.
- To see what GPUs a node advertises: ask your admin or inspect sinfo / scontrol show node (your cluster may expose Gres info).

If you want, I can:
- Give ready-to-copy sbatch header templates for common workflows (single-GPU training, multi-node MPI with 1 GPU/rank, multi-GPU single-node).
- Check your cluster’s configured GPU types/counts (I can run sinfo/scontrol_show if you want me to inspect the live cluster).

## SYNOPSIS[#SECTION_SYNOPSIS](https://slurm.schedmd.com/strigger.html)
strigger --set [ OPTIONS ...]
strigger --get [ OPTIONS ...]
strigger --clear [ OPTIONS ...]

Summary
- strigger is the Slurm utility for registering event-driven “triggers”: Slurm will watch for specified cluster or job events and run a program when the event occurs.
- Typical uses: notify admins when nodes fail, run cleanup or graceful shutdown of a job shortly before its time limit, run maintenance scripts on node-state changes, etc.

How it works (conceptual)
- You register a trigger with strigger --set, specifying:
  - the resource (a job ID, user, node(s) or “*”),
  - the event type (examples below),
  - an optional time OFFSET (seconds; negative means run before the event), and
  - the PROGRAM (script or executable) to run.
- Slurm checks for trigger events periodically (default ~every 15 seconds). Any events detected within that interval are compared to active triggers at the end of the interval and the trigger program is executed once for events in that interval.
- When executed, Slurm will pass the relevant resource identifier (hostlist or jobid) as an argument to the program.

Event / trigger types (common)
- Job-related:
  - time: job reaching time limit (you can use OFFSET to run before limit)
  - fini: job termination/completion
  - up/down: job going up/down (rare for jobs; more for nodes)
- Node-related:
  - down: node entered DOWN state
  - up: node returned to UP
  - drained: node was drained
  - idle: node became idle
  - reconfig: node reconfiguration event
- Controller/cluster:
  - backup_slurmctld_failure, backup_slurmctld_assumed_control, backup_slurmctld_resumed_operation
  - burst_buffer errors, and other infrastructure events (depends on Slurm version/options)

Important fields and behavior
- TRIG_ID: numeric trigger id (returned by --get)
- RES_TYPE / RES_ID: resource type (job/node) and the identifier (jobid or hostlist; "*" allowed)
- TYPE: trigger type (time, fini, down, up, drained, idle, reconfig, etc.)
- OFFSET: seconds offset. Negative = before the event (if possible). Positive = after the event.
- USER: who created the trigger
- PROGRAM: full pathname of program/script to execute
- Triggers are executed at most once per event per interval. They are not instantaneous; timing granularity is the periodic check interval.
- A hostlist expression or jobid is passed to the program as an argument so the program can inspect/act on the affected resource.

Common command forms
- Set a trigger (job time limit 5 minutes before end):
  strigger --set --jobid=12345 --time --offset=-300 --program=/opt/bin/job_time_warn.sh
- Set a node-down notification for a set of nodes:
  strigger --set --down --node=node[01-10] --program=/usr/sbin/notify_admin
- List triggers:
  strigger --get
- Clear a trigger:
  strigger --clear --id=TRIG_ID
  (You must identify the trigger(s) to clear with --id, --jobid or --user. Clearing other users’ triggers typically requires root.)

Permissions and environment
- Some operations (clearing other users’ triggers, system-level triggers) are restricted to root or operators.
- Several options can be influenced by environment variables (SLURM_CONF, SLURM_DEBUG_FLAGS, etc.).
- Command-line options override environment variables.

Limitations and gotchas
- Granularity: because checks are periodic (≈15s), trigger timing is not real-time; short offsets smaller than the check interval may be unreliable.
- If an event occurs and the offset requires the program to run before it but the offset window has already passed, the trigger may not be able to fire “before” the event.
- Ensure trigger programs are robust and fast; they run from slurmctld context and should handle receiving a hostlist or jobid argument.

Where to read more
- The strigger man page (strigger(1)) on the Slurm documentation site has full syntax, all supported event options and examples.

If you’d like, I can:
- show exact example commands for a specific use case (notify by email, kill/notify a job X minutes before time limit, node failure alert), or
- look up precise option names/synopsis from the man page for copy-paste examples. Which would you prefer?

## Overview[#overview](https://slurm.schedmd.com/federation.html)
Slurm includes support for creating a federation of clusters
and scheduling jobs in a peer-to-peer fashion between them. Jobs submitted to a
federation receive a unique job ID that is unique among all clusters in the
federation. A job is submitted to the local cluster (the cluster defined in the
slurm.conf) and is then replicated across the clusters in the federation. Each
cluster then independently attempts to the schedule the job based off of its own
scheduling policies. The clusters coordinate with the "origin" cluster (cluster
the job was submitted to) to schedule the job.
NOTE : This is not intended as a high-throughput environment. If
scheduling more than 50,000 jobs a day, consider configuring fewer clusters that
the sibling jobs can be submitted to or directing load
to the local cluster only (e.g. --cluster-constraint= or -M submission options
could be used to do...

Federation status (from scontrol show federation):
- FederationName=mock-federation, Clusters=mock-cluster, State=ACTIVE

What that means (short):
- The federation is ACTIVE and contains the cluster(s) listed above.
- A Slurm federation enables "federated" submissions: when you submit a job to the origin cluster it is replicated as sibling jobs to the eligible clusters in the federation. Each cluster then independently attempts to schedule its sibling based on its local policies.
- Job IDs are unique across the federation (the job receives a federation-unique ID).

Can a single job span clusters?
- No. You cannot create one allocation that draws nodes from multiple federated clusters. Federation replicates the job (sibling jobs) to multiple clusters, it does not combine resources across clusters into one single allocation.
- In practice federated jobs provide multi-cluster redundancy/choice (siblings run on different clusters), not a single cross-cluster parallel allocation.

How to direct federated submissions (useful options):
- sbatch/salloc/srun support -M,--clusters=<cluster_list> and --cluster-constraint to control which clusters siblings are considered for.
- The origin cluster records the cluster list and clusters in that list are the only viable sibling targets.

Behavioral notes / caveats:
- Each cluster schedules siblings independently; results (start time, resources, completion) can differ per cluster.
- Federation is not intended for extremely high-throughput workloads (see docs for guidance).
- If a cluster is removed from the federation while jobs are running, running jobs continue as non‑federated jobs on that cluster (per docs).

Below are the main Slurm PENDING reason codes you’ll typically see and a short explanation + usual fixes — useful when jobs do appear:

- BeginTime
  - Reason: Job has a start time (–begin) in the future.
  - Fix: Wait until the specified time or remove/adjust the begin time.

- Dependency
  - Reason: Job has an sbatch dependency (afterok, afterany, etc.) that isn’t satisfied yet.
  - Fix: Check the dependent job(s); remove or change dependency if needed.

- Priority
  - Reason: Higher-priority jobs are scheduled before this one (fairshare, QOS, user/account limits affect ordering).
  - Fix: Investigate sprio/sshare; consider changing QOS or job priority or submitting with different QOS if allowed.

- Resources (or ReqMem/ReqCPUS/ReqGRES)
  - Reason: No suitable free resources (CPUs, memory, GPUs, requested TRES) meet the job request.
  - Fix: Reduce resource request, use a different partition, or wait for resources to free; check sinfo for current node availability.

- ReqNodeNotAvail (or NodeNotAvail / NotEnoughNodes)
  - Reason: Requested specific nodes/features/number of nodes aren’t available (e.g., feature mismatch, node drained or down).
  - Fix: Remove node constraints, request fewer nodes, or wait for nodes to return to service.

- QOS/Account/Assoc limits (AccountNotAllowed, Max*PerAccount, AssocGrp*)
  - Reason: The job violates account/QOS or association limits (per-account/QOS job caps, burst-buffer or billing limits).
  - Fix: Check account/QOS membership and limits (sacctmgr, scontrol); use a permitted account/QOS or ask admins to change limits.

- Reservation
  - Reason: Job is tied to a reservation that has not started or that blocks scheduling until the reservation window.
  - Fix: Inspect the reservation (scontrol show reservation) or schedule within the reservation window.

- PartitionDown/PartitionTimeLimit/Partition* (partition-related)
  - Reason: The chosen partition is offline, down, or has partition-level constraints preventing start.
  - Fix: Choose a different partition or contact admins.

- License
  - Reason: Required software license(s) are not currently available.
  - Fix: Wait for licenses to free or contact admins to increase license count; check scontrol_license for details.

- Dependency on burst buffer / BurstBuffer limits (AssocGrpBB, etc.)
  - Reason: Burst buffer allocation limits (per-association or aggregate minutes) have been reached.
  - Fix: Adjust burst buffer requests, or wait / request admin changes to limits.

- Priority preemption / Preempted or Hold-related reasons (PriorityPreempt, JobHeld)
  - Reason: Job is on hold or being preempted in favor of higher-priority work.
  - Fix: Release hold (if user-held) or change QOS/priority; contact admin if being preempted.

I checked the Slurm job state documentation (job_state_codes). Short definitions, common causes, and what to check for each state:

RUNNING
- What it means: The job has been allocated resources and its tasks are currently executing on node(s).
- Common causes why you see it: Normal execution; may also be in RUNNING while launch/cleanup flags (e.g., CONFIGURING, COMPLETING) are set briefly.
- What to check: squeue (shows elapsed time), sstat (live resource usage for a running job), stdout/stderr files, and node health. Use scontrol show job <jobid> for detailed allocation info.

PENDING
- What it means: The job is queued and waiting to start; Slurm will report a reason why it hasn’t begun.
- Common causes: waiting for free CPUs/GPUs/nodes, higher-priority jobs, unmet dependency or BeginTime, association/account/QOS limits, licenses, or partition/node state (down/drained).
- What to check: squeue (the REASON column), scontrol show job <jobid> for detailed reason, sprio or sdiag for priority/backfill info, and sinfo to inspect partition/node availability.

FAILED
- What it means: The job terminated unsuccessfully — typically finished with a non‑zero exit code or encountered a failure (launch failure, prolog/epilog error, node failure, etc.).
- Common causes: application crash, segmentation fault, failures in job prolog/launch, node problems, or resource exhaustion not captured by a dedicated state (e.g., generic failure).
- What to check: sacct -j <jobid> to see ExitCode and state history, stderr/stdout logs, scontrol show job <jobid> for any reported failure details, and node logs if a node issue is suspected.

TIMEOUT
- What it means: The job was terminated because it exceeded its configured TimeLimit.
- Common causes: actual runtime exceeded --time, unexpected hang/infinite loop, or an underestimated runtime.
- What to check: sacct/squeue to confirm TIMEOUT, your job’s requested TimeLimit (--time in sbatch/salloc/srun), job logs to see where it stopped, and consider increasing --time, adding checkpointing, or splitting the work.

Helpful sacct fields for inspecting job state, runtime, and memory — short reference and notes you can use with --format.

1) State / outcome
- State
  - What: canonical job state (COMPLETED, FAILED, CANCELLED, TIMEOUT, RUNNING, PENDING, etc.).
  - Use: primary field to know final or current job outcome.
- ExitCode
  - What: program exit code (format "code:signal" for jobs terminated by a signal).
  - Use: distinguishes user/process exit vs signal termination (e.g., OOM kill often shows a signal).
- JobID, JobName, User
  - What: identifiers to show alongside State/ExitCode for context.
  - Use: always include to avoid ambiguity when inspecting many rows.

2) Elapsed / time
- Elapsed
  - What: human-readable wall-clock time the job ran (H:MM:SS or similar).
  - Use: quick human inspection.
- ElapsedRaw
  - What: elapsed time in seconds (integer).
  - Use: preferred for arithmetic, thresholds, sorting, and scripting.
- Timelimit
  - What: the job’s requested/allocated time limit.
  - Use: compare to Elapsed/ElapsedRaw to detect time-limit kills (STATE=TIMEOUT).
- Start, End
  - What: timestamps when the job started and finished.
  - Use: reconstruct when the job ran or compute elapsed if Elapsed isn’t available.
- TotalCPU (or CPUTime)
  - What: total CPU time consumed (all tasks/threads summed).
  - Use: measure CPU usage vs wall time, detect inefficiency or I/O waiting.

3) Memory
- ReqMem
  - What: memory requested for the job (what user/submit allocates; may be per-node or per-CPU depending on how the job was submitted: --mem vs --mem-per-cpu).
  - Use: confirm requested reservation and compare to actual usage.
- MaxRSS
  - What: maximum resident set size observed for any task in the job step (the peak RAM actually used).
  - Use: primary diagnostic for OOM and for rightsizing memory requests. MaxRSSTask tells which task had the peak.
- AveRSS
  - What: average RSS across tasks.
  - Use: useful for multi-task jobs to understand typical per-task footprint.
- MaxVMSize / AveVMSize
  - What: peak/average virtual memory sizes (address space).
  - Use: catches large address-space usage even if RSS stays moderate.

Practical tips
- For scripting and comparisons use ElapsedRaw (seconds) and numeric memory fields (MaxRSS/AveRSS) rather than their human-readable forms.
- MaxRSS is reported per-task; the documented meaning is “maximum memory consumption seen by one of the tasks.” If you run many tasks, consider AveRSS or inspect per-task steps.
- To diagnose OOMs: look for State (FAILED / TIMEOUT / CANCELLED), ExitCode (signal), and MaxRSS vs ReqMem. A MaxRSS close to or above the ReqMem (or significantly above a per-cpu request) indicates under-requesting.
- Example --format to start with:
  --format=JobID,JobName,User,State,ExitCode,Elapsed,ElapsedRaw,Timelimit,Start,End,ReqMem,MaxRSS,AveRSS,TotalCPU

If you want, I can give a one-line sacct command with that --format for your cluster’s typical units/format.

## EXAMPLES[#SECTION_EXAMPLES](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Specify a batch script by filename on the command line. The batch script specifies a 1 minute time limit for the job.
```text
$ cat myscript #!/bin/sh #SBATCH --time=1 srun hostname |sort $ sbatch -N4 myscript salloc: Granted job allocation 65537 $ cat slurm-65537.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
Pass a batch script to sbatch on standard input:
```text
$ sbatch -N4 #!/bin/sh > srun hostname |sort > EOF sbatch: Submitted batch job 65541 $ cat slurm-65541.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
To create a heterogeneous job with 3 components, each allocating a unique set of nodes:
```text
$ sbatch -w node[2-3] : -w node4 : -w node[5-7] work.bash Submitted batch job 34987
```

## Node Extra Data [#Node_Extra_Data](https://slurm.schedmd.com/extra_constraints.html)
A node's extra data is a json formatted string. It may be initialized on
slurmd startup with the --extra flag for slurmd. For example:
```text
slurmd --extra '{ "a": 1.23, "b": true, "c": 0, "foo": "bar", "zed": 23 }'
```
Or, it may be updated with scontrol. For example:
```text
scontrol update nodename=node123 extra='{ "a": 1.23, "b": true, "c": 0, "foo": "bar", "zed": 23 }'
```
This defines the features that may be requested by the --extra option in
salloc, sbatch, and srun. Values may be any string, number, or boolean value.

### Warnings [#Warnings](https://slurm.schedmd.com/extra_constraints.html)
Whitespace characters are not treated specially. Any whitespace characters will
be considered part of a key or value. This means that the following is invalid:
```text
--extra " (a=b)"
```
The space at he beginning is parsed as a key of a request. Then the opening
parenthesis character is recognized as an invalid character for either a key
or a comparison operator. This request would result in the job being rejected.
However, this is valid:
```text
--extra "( a=b)"
```
This has a single request. The key is " a", the comparison operator is "=", and
the value is "b".
This same warning applies to single and double quotes. These are not considered
special characters, and thus are part of a string. Thus, bar and "bar" are not
equal.

```text

must be less than 0.0001. This is why 0.0001 is not considered equal to 0 and

## DESCRIPTION[#SECTION_DESCRIPTION](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
sbatch submits a batch script to Slurm. The batch script may be given to
sbatch through a file name on the command line, or if no file name is specified,
sbatch will read in a script from standard input.
The batch script may contain one or more lines beginning with "#SBATCH" followed
by any of the CLI options documented on this page. #SBATCH directives are read
directly by Slurm, so shell-specific syntax including variable names will be
read as literal text. Once the first non-comment, non-whitespace line has been
reached in the script, no more #SBATCH directives will be processed. See example
below.

## EXAMPLES[#SECTION_EXAMPLES](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Specify a batch script by filename on the command line. The batch script specifies a 1 minute time limit for the job.
```text
$ cat myscript #!/bin/sh #SBATCH --time=1 srun hostname |sort $ sbatch -N4 myscript salloc: Granted job allocation 65537 $ cat slurm-65537.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
Pass a batch script to sbatch on standard input:
```text
$ sbatch -N4 #!/bin/sh > srun hostname |sort > EOF sbatch: Submitted batch job 65541 $ cat slurm-65541.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
To create a heterogeneous job with 3 components, each allocating a unique set of nodes:
```text
$ sbatch -w node[2-3] : -w node4 : -w node[5-7] work.bash Submitted batch job 34987
```

### Warnings [#Warnings](https://slurm.schedmd.com/extra_constraints.html)
Whitespace characters are not treated specially. Any whitespace characters will
be considered part of a key or value. This means that the following is invalid:
```text
--extra " (a=b)"
```
The space at he beginning is parsed as a key of a request. Then the opening
parenthesis character is recognized as an invalid character for either a key
or a comparison operator. This request would result in the job being rejected.
However, this is valid:
```text
--extra "( a=b)"
```
This has a single request. The key is " a", the comparison operator is "=", and
the value is "b".
This same warning applies to single and double quotes. These are not considered
special characters, and thus are part of a string. Thus, bar and "bar" are not
equal.

a, =0.00000001) ((c =0.1)

```

thus the request `c>=0.0001` is not fulfilled,

### Step 3: Distribution of Tasks to the selected Nodes [#Step3](https://slurm.schedmd.com/cpu_management.html)
In Step 3, Slurm distributes tasks to the nodes that were selected for
the job/step in Step 1. Each task is distributed to only one node, but more than one
task may be distributed to each node. Unless overcommitment of CPUs to tasks is
specified for the job, the number of tasks distributed to a node is
constrained by the number of CPUs allocated on the node and the number of CPUs per
task. If consumable resources is configured, or resource sharing is allowed, tasks from
more than one job/step may run on the same node concurrently.
Step 3 is performed by slurmctld.

## MPI SUPPORT[#SECTION_MPI-SUPPORT](https://slurm.schedmd.com/srun.html)
MPI use depends upon the type of MPI being used.
There are three fundamentally different modes of operation used
by these various MPI implementations.
1. Slurm directly launches the tasks and performs initialization
of communications through the PMI2 or PMIx APIs.
For example: "srun -n16 a.out".
2. Slurm creates a resource allocation for the job and then
mpirun launches tasks using Slurm's infrastructure (OpenMPI).
3. Slurm creates a resource allocation for the job and then
mpirun launches tasks using some mechanism other than Slurm,
such as SSH or RSH.
These tasks are initiated outside of Slurm's monitoring
or control. Slurm's epilog should be configured to purge
these tasks when the job's allocation is relinquished,
or the use of pam_slurm_adopt is highly recommended.

## Initial Testing [#INITIAL_TESTING](https://slurm.schedmd.com/nss_slurm.html)
Before enabling NSS Slurm directly on the node, you should use the
-s slurm option to getent within a newly launched job step
to verify that the rest of the setup has been completed successfully. The
-s option to getent allows it to query a specific database —
even if it has not been enabled by default through the system's
nsswitch.conf . Note that nss_slurm only responds to requests from
processes within the job step itself — you must launch the getent
command within a job step to see any data returned.
As an example of a successful query:
```text
tim@blackhole:~$ srun getent -s slurm passwd tim:x:1000:1000:Tim Wickberg:/home/tim:/bin/bash tim@blackhole:~$ srun getent -s slurm group tim:x:1000:tim projecta:x:1001:tim
```

## NSS Configuration [#NSS_CONFIG](https://slurm.schedmd.com/nss_slurm.html)
Enabling nss_slurm is as simple as adding slurm to the passwd and
group database in /etc/nsswitch.conf (only on systems that will run
slurmd ). It is recommended that
slurm is listed first, as the order (from left to right) determines
the sequence in which the NSS databases will be queried, and this ensures Slurm
handles the request if able before submitting the query to other sources.
To enable cloud node name resolution slurm needs to be added to the
to hosts database in /etc/nsswitch.conf .
It is recommended that slurm is listed last.
Once enabled, test it by launching getent queries such as:
```text
tim@blackhole:~$ srun getent passwd tim tim:x:1000:1000:Tim Wickberg:/home/tim:/bin/bash tim@blackhole:~$ srun getent group projecta projecta:x:1001:tim
```

# "Configless" Slurm
"Configless" Slurm is a feature that allows the compute nodes —
specifically the slurmd process — and user commands running on login
nodes to pull configuration information directly from the slurmctld instead of
from a pre-distributed local file. Your cluster does require a central set of
configuration files on the Slurm controllers — "configless" in Slurm's
parlance means that the compute nodes, login nodes, and other cluster hosts
do not need to be deployed with local copies of these files.

config files will be pulled to the node. This slurmctld can be identified by
either an explicit option, or — preferably — through DNS SRV

A node's extra data is a json formatted string. It may be initialized on

slurmd --extra '{ "a": 1.23, "b": true, "c": 0, "foo": "bar", "zed": 23 }'
```
Or, it may be updated with scontrol. For example:
```text
scontrol update nodename=node123 extra='{ "a": 1.23, "b": true, "c": 0, "foo": "bar", "zed": 23 }'
```
This defines the features that may be requested by the --extra option in
salloc, sbatch, and srun. Values may be any string, number, or boolean value.

nodes is changed, the less accurate the backfill scheduler will be.

### Submitting Jobs
Why are my srun options ignored?
Everything after the command srun is
examined to determine if it is a valid option for srun. The first
token that is not a valid option for srun is considered the command
to execute and everything after that is treated as an option to
the command. For example:
srun -N2 uptime -pdebug
srun processes "-N2" as an option to itself. "uptime" is the command to
execute and "-pdebug" is treated as an option to the uptime command. Depending
on the command and options provided, you may get an invalid option message or
unexpected behavior if the options happen to be valid.
Options for srun should appear before the command to be run:
srun -N2 -pdebug uptime

### Warnings [#Warnings](https://slurm.schedmd.com/extra_constraints.html)
Whitespace characters are not treated specially. Any whitespace characters will
be considered part of a key or value. This means that the following is invalid:
```text
--extra " (a=b)"
```
The space at he beginning is parsed as a key of a request. Then the opening
parenthesis character is recognized as an invalid character for either a key
or a comparison operator. This request would result in the job being rejected.
However, this is valid:
```text
--extra "( a=b)"
```
This has a single request. The key is " a", the comparison operator is "=", and
the value is "b".
This same warning applies to single and double quotes. These are not considered
special characters, and thus are part of a string. Thus, bar and "bar" are not
equal.

Here are some examples of valid requests:
```text
a=1.23 a= b a!=1.24 a!=1.23|foo!=blah b=200 b=true foo =0.00000001) ((c =0.1)
```
Here are some examples of invalid requests:
Invalid comparison operator:
```text
a, =0.00000001) ((c =0.1)
```
The following --extra requests are not fulfilled by this node:
```text
a!=1.23 b=0 b=false foo>baz ((c =0.00001)
```
Reminder: in order for two numbers to be considered equal, their difference
must be less than 0.0001. This is why 0.0001 is not considered equal to 0 and
thus the request `c>=0.0001` is not fulfilled,
but 0.00000001 is considered equal to 0 and thus the request
`c>=0.00000001` is fulfilled.

## Overview [#Overview](https://slurm.schedmd.com/extra_constraints.html)
Extra data may be added to a node, and jobs may request extra constraints
to filter nodes based on their extra data. This is disabled by
default, but may be enabled in slurm.conf. Warning : Slurm's backfill
scheduler cannot accurately plan nodes for jobs whose request extra constraints
are not immediately satisfied. This means that the more often extra data for
nodes is changed, the less accurate the backfill scheduler will be.

If a feature is defined in the helpers.conf and is not defined on a
specific node in the helpers.conf but is defined for that node in the
slurm.conf, that feature is treated as a changeable/rebootable feature by the
controller. For example, if feature fa is defined on node node1 in
the slurm.conf but is only listed on node2 in the
helpers.conf , the feature will still trigger the node to be rebooted if
not active.
The Helper is an arbitrary program or script that reports and modifies
the feature set on a given node. The helpers are site-specific and are not
included with Slurm. Features modified by the helpers require a reboot of
the node using the RebootProgram .

## FILENAME PATTERN[#SECTION_FILENAME-PATTERN](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
sbatch allows for a filename pattern to contain one or more replacement
symbols, which are a percent sign "%" followed by a letter (e.g. %j).
\\ [#OPT_\\](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html) Do not process any of the replacement symbols.
%% [#OPT_%%](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html) The character "%".
%A [#OPT_%A](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html) Job array's master job allocation number.
%a [#OPT_%a](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html) Job array ID (index) number.
%b [#OPT_%b](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html) Job array ID (index) number modulo 10.
%J [#OPT_%J](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html) jobid.stepid of the running job (e.g. "128.0"). The stepid is only expanded for
regular steps, not for special steps like "batch" or "extern".
%j [#OPT_%j](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html) jobid of the running job.
%N [#OPT_%N](...

sbatch --parsable makes sbatch emit a single machine-readable token (the assigned Slurm job id information) instead of the human-readable line ("Submitted batch job 12345"). For plain submissions that token is the job id; for array submissions it contains the job/array identifiers in a compact, parseable form.

Why it’s useful
- easy to capture in scripts: JOBID=$(sbatch --parsable job.sh)
- safe to feed to other Slurm commands (scancel, squeue, scontrol, or sbatch --dependency=afterok:$JOBID) without brittle text parsing
- avoids locale/human-message changes and extra text that break automation

Example (script-friendly): 
JOBID=$(sbatch --parsable my_job.sh)
squeue -j "$JOBID"

Job arrays offer a mechanism for submitting and managing collections of
similar jobs quickly and easily, useful for repetitive workloads that follow a
common job pattern. This greatly improves overall performance, since job arrays
with millions of tasks can be submitted in milliseconds (subject to configured

Good question — here’s a concise explanation grounded in the sbatch/job-array docs.

What a job-array is
- A job array is a collection of similar batch jobs submitted with sbatch --array. Each element shares the same job script/options but has a distinct array index (task id).

ID terminology
- ArrayJobID (a.k.a. the job array’s master job allocation number): the job ID returned by sbatch for the array submission (this is the array “master” allocation).
- ArrayTaskID (the array index): the element index within the array (the value(s) you gave to --array, e.g. 0,1,2 or 1-10:2).
- Individual array elements can be referenced as ArrayJobID_ArrayTaskID (for example 123_4).

Environment variables (inside each array task)
- SLURM_ARRAY_JOB_ID = ArrayJobID
- SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID = ArrayTaskID
- SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_COUNT, SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_MIN, SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_MAX are also set.

Filename replacement symbols (used in --output, --error and sbatch filename patterns)
- %A — Job array’s master job allocation number (ArrayJobID). Use when you want the array’s master ID in filenames.
- %a — Job array ID (index) number (ArrayTaskID). Use when you want the per-element index in filenames.
- %b — Job array index modulo 10 (last digit of the index).
- %j — jobid of the running job.
- %J — jobid.stepid of the running job (stepid only for regular steps).
- %% — literal percent sign.

Examples
- sbatch --array=1-3 --output=job_%A_%a.out myscript.sh
  - If sbatch replies "Submitted batch job 100" (ArrayJobID=100), the files created will be:
    - job_100_1.out, job_100_2.out, job_100_3.out
  - Inside each task, SLURM_ARRAY_JOB_ID=100 and SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID will be 1, 2, or 3.

Notes / gotchas
- %A and %a are replaced by Slurm when creating/launching array tasks; they are not shell variables. If you need the values inside the script use the SLURM_* environment variables.
- For non-array jobs %A/%a aren’t meaningful; use %j (jobid) instead.
- You can combine these placeholders arbitrarily in filenames (e.g., --output=%A.%a.%j.out) and escape a literal % with %%.

## Node Features[#nodefeatures](https://slurm.schedmd.com/elastic_computing.html)
Features defined by [NodeFeaturesPlugins](https://slurm.schedmd.com/slurm.conf.html), and
associated to cloud nodes in the slurm.conf , will be available but not
active when the node is powered down. If a job requests available but not
active features, the controller will allocate nodes that are powered down and
have the features as available. At allocation, the features will be made
active. A cloud node will remain with the active features until the node is
powered down (i.e. the node can't be rebooted to get other features until the
node is powered down). When the node is powered down, the those features
become available but not active. Any feature not defined by
NodeFeaturesPlugins are always active.

## Sharding [#Sharding](https://slurm.schedmd.com/gres.html)
Sharding provides a generic mechanism where GPUs can be
shared by multiple jobs. While it does permit multiple jobs to run on a given
GPU it does not fence the processes running on the GPU, it only allows the GPU
to be shared. Sharding, therefore, works best with homogeneous workflows. It is
recommended to limit the number of shards on a node to equal the max possible
jobs that can run simultaneously on the node (i.e. cores).

### Warnings [#Warnings](https://slurm.schedmd.com/extra_constraints.html)
Whitespace characters are not treated specially. Any whitespace characters will
be considered part of a key or value. This means that the following is invalid:
```text
--extra " (a=b)"
```
The space at he beginning is parsed as a key of a request. Then the opening
parenthesis character is recognized as an invalid character for either a key
or a comparison operator. This request would result in the job being rejected.
However, this is valid:
```text
--extra "( a=b)"
```
This has a single request. The key is " a", the comparison operator is "=", and
the value is "b".
This same warning applies to single and double quotes. These are not considered
special characters, and thus are part of a string. Thus, bar and "bar" are not
equal.

Extra data may be added to a node, and jobs may request extra constraints
to filter nodes based on their extra data. This is disabled by
default, but may be enabled in slurm.conf. Warning : Slurm's backfill
scheduler cannot accurately plan nodes for jobs whose request extra constraints
are not immediately satisfied. This means that the more often extra data for
nodes is changed, the less accurate the backfill scheduler will be.

The following --extra requests are not fulfilled by this node:
```text

```
Reminder: in order for two numbers to be considered equal, their difference
must be less than 0.0001. This is why 0.0001 is not considered equal to 0 and
thus the request `c>=0.0001` is not fulfilled,
but 0.00000001 is considered equal to 0 and thus the request

## Node Extra Data [#Node_Extra_Data](https://slurm.schedmd.com/extra_constraints.html)
A node's extra data is a json formatted string. It may be initialized on
slurmd startup with the --extra flag for slurmd. For example:
```text
slurmd --extra '{ "a": 1.23, "b": true, "c": 0, "foo": "bar", "zed": 23 }'
```
Or, it may be updated with scontrol. For example:
```text
scontrol update nodename=node123 extra='{ "a": 1.23, "b": true, "c": 0, "foo": "bar", "zed": 23 }'
```
This defines the features that may be requested by the --extra option in
salloc, sbatch, and srun. Values may be any string, number, or boolean value.

Here are some examples of valid requests:
```text

Here are some examples of invalid requests:
Invalid comparison operator:

The following --extra requests are not fulfilled by this node:
```text

```
Reminder: in order for two numbers to be considered equal, their difference
must be less than 0.0001. This is why 0.0001 is not considered equal to 0 and
thus the request `c>=0.0001` is not fulfilled,
but 0.00000001 is considered equal to 0 and thus the request

## Node Extra Data [#Node_Extra_Data](https://slurm.schedmd.com/extra_constraints.html)
A node's extra data is a json formatted string. It may be initialized on
slurmd startup with the --extra flag for slurmd. For example:
```text
slurmd --extra '{ "a": 1.23, "b": true, "c": 0, "foo": "bar", "zed": 23 }'
```
Or, it may be updated with scontrol. For example:
```text
scontrol update nodename=node123 extra='{ "a": 1.23, "b": true, "c": 0, "foo": "bar", "zed": 23 }'
```
This defines the features that may be requested by the --extra option in
salloc, sbatch, and srun. Values may be any string, number, or boolean value.

### Warnings [#Warnings](https://slurm.schedmd.com/extra_constraints.html)
Whitespace characters are not treated specially. Any whitespace characters will
be considered part of a key or value. This means that the following is invalid:
```text
--extra " (a=b)"
```
The space at he beginning is parsed as a key of a request. Then the opening
parenthesis character is recognized as an invalid character for either a key
or a comparison operator. This request would result in the job being rejected.
However, this is valid:
```text
--extra "( a=b)"
```
This has a single request. The key is " a", the comparison operator is "=", and
the value is "b".
This same warning applies to single and double quotes. These are not considered
special characters, and thus are part of a string. Thus, bar and "bar" are not
equal.

Executing sacct sends a remote procedure call to slurmdbd . If
enough calls from sacct or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmdbd daemon come in at once, it can result in a
degradation of performance of the slurmdbd daemon, possibly resulting in a
denial of service.
Do not run sacct or other Slurm client commands that send remote procedure
calls to slurmdbd from loops in shell scripts or other programs. Ensure
that programs limit calls to sacct to the minimum necessary for the
information you are trying to gather.

# Job Exit Codes
A job's exit code (aka exit status, return code and completion
code) is captured by Slurm and saved as part of the job record. For
sbatch jobs, the exit code that is captured is the output of the batch
script. For salloc jobs, the exit code will be the return value of
the exit call that terminates the salloc session. For srun, the exit
code will be the return value of the command that srun executes.
Any non-zero exit code will be assumed to be a job failure and will
result in a Job State of FAILED with a Reason of
"NonZeroExitCode".
The exit code is an 8 bit unsigned number ranging between 0 and
255. While it is possible for a job to return a negative exit code,
Slurm will display it as an unsigned value in the 0 - 255 range.

## DESCRIPTION[#SECTION_DESCRIPTION](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sacct.html)
Accounting information for jobs invoked with Slurm are either logged
in the job accounting log file or saved to the Slurm database, as
configured with the AccountingStorageType parameter.
The sacct command displays job accounting data stored in the job
accounting log file or Slurm database in a variety of forms for your
analysis. The sacct command displays information on jobs, job
steps, status, and exitcodes by default. You can tailor the output
with the use of the --format= option to specify the fields to
be shown.
Job records consist of a primary entry for the job as a whole as well as
entries for job steps. The Job Launch page has a more detailed description
of each type of job step.
<[https://slurm.schedmd.com/job_launch.html#job_record](https://slurm.schedmd.com/job_launch.html)>
For the root user, the sacct command displays job accounting
data for all user...

Summary — what the two fields mean
- ExitCode: the raw exit status Slurm recorded for that job (or job step). Format is "exit:signal" where:
  - the left number is the process exit code (0–255, shown unsigned),
  - the right number is the terminating signal number (0 when none).
  Examples: "0:0" = normal success; "1:0" = process returned exit 1; "0:9" or "?:9" indicates the process was killed by SIGKILL (signal 9) and no normal exit value.
- DerivedExitCode: an aggregate/Slurm-derived value stored in the job record in the database. It is initialized by Slurm to the highest exit code observed across the job’s steps (the srun-invoked tasks) and is intended to reflect the overall job outcome after considering all steps.

How they are produced and used
- For sbatch jobs: ExitCode is the return value of the batch script when it terminates.
- For srun steps: each step’s exit code is saved to the step record; ExitCode on the job-level may reflect the batch script; DerivedExitCode aggregates across steps.
- For salloc: ExitCode is the return value that ends the salloc session.
- Any non-zero ExitCode (that Slurm records as non-zero) is treated as a failure and typically produces job state FAILED with pending/termination reason "NonZeroExitCode".
- Exit codes are 8-bit unsigned values (0–255). Negative returns are displayed as the unsigned equivalent.

Why have both fields
- ExitCode shows what the top-level process returned (or the step’s own return).
- DerivedExitCode captures Slurm’s view of the worst/most relevant step result (useful when the batch script returns 0 but an inner srun step failed), and can be used by admins/users to record a corrective/annotated outcome.

Viewing and adjusting
- sacct and scontrol show ExitCode; sacct can show DerivedExitCode via --format= (DerivedExitCode is available as a field).
- sjobexitmod can list and (if needed) modify the DerivedExitCode and the job comment string (useful to annotate a job after inspecting logs/output).

Practical troubleshooting tips
- If sacct shows ExitCode 0 but DerivedExitCode non-zero (or step records show non-zero), inspect the per-step records (sacct with step entries or scontrol show step) and the job stdout/stderr to find which srun command failed.
- If a job is marked FAILED with reason NonZeroExitCode, use the ExitCode and step records to determine whether the failure was a program exit or a signal (kill/oom).
- Use sjobexitmod only when you need to correct/annotate the derived fields in the DB (requires privileges).

Slurm can also be configured to allocate resources to jobs on a
hierarchical network to minimize network contention.
The basic algorithm is to identify the lowest level switch in the
hierarchy that can satisfy a job's request and then allocate resources
on its underlying leaf switches using a best-fit algorithm.
Use of this logic requires a configuration setting of
TopologyPlugin=topology/tree .
Note that slurm uses a best-fit algorithm on the currently
available resources. This may result in an allocation with
more than the optimum number of switches. The user can request
a maximum number of leaf switches for the job as well as a
maximum time willing to wait for that number using the `--switches`
option with the salloc, sbatch and srun commands. The parameters can

Short version
- Slurm can be made “topology aware” so the scheduler places multi-node jobs to minimize network hops and contention (important for MPI/RDMA workloads).
- This is configured by the site admin (topology.conf or topology.yaml + TopologyPlugin and TopologyParam settings). Users request topology constraints (for example a limit on how many leaf switches a job may use) and Slurm will try to satisfy them when allocating nodes.

How it works (concepts)
- Topology model: the admin describes the network as switches and children (nodes or other switches) in topology.conf/topology.yaml. Optional link speeds can be recorded. Slurm builds a tree/block model of the interconnect.
- Plugins: common plugins are topology/tree and topology/block. They change scheduling so allocation algorithms consider switch boundaries and block sizes rather than only individual idle nodes.
- Allocation goal: Slurm tries to find the smallest (lowest-level) switch or block that can satisfy a job so nodes are co‑located under common switch(es). That reduces cross-switch traffic and latency.
- Best-fit & wait: the scheduler uses a best‑fit algorithm on currently available resources. To get a better (fewer‑switch) allocation a job may be held briefly while awaiting freed nodes.
- Route/optional behavior:
  - TopologyParam=RouteTree (or similar) enforces that jobs may only be placed on nodes connected by the same fabric/path described in topology.  
  - TopologyParam=TopoOptional (or admin settings) relax enforcement so jobs may span switches when necessary.

User controls (what you can request)
- --switches=count[@time] (salloc/srun/sbatch): request a maximum number of leaf switches for the job and an optional maximum time to wait for that optimized placement (e.g. --switches=1@30s to prefer one leaf switch but wait up to 30s). The scheduler respects site limits (SchedulerParameters max_switch_wait).
- Hostlist topology functions: when topology is enabled you can use functions like switch{name}, switchwith{node}, block{name} in hostlist expressions (for example in --nodelist) to refer to topology groups.
- Normal resource request fields (--nodes, --ntasks-per-node, --cpus-per-task, --gres=gpu:4, etc.) combine with topology constraints; Slurm finds nodes matching both resource and topology constraints.

Admin-side controls (what affects placement)
- topology.conf or topology.yaml describes switches, blocks, and optionally link speeds. It can be generated (e.g. tools for IB).
- TopologyPlugin, TopologyParam, and SchedulerParameters (e.g. max_switch_wait) control algorithm and allowed waiting.
- The select plugin matters: topology plugins normally require select/cons_tres.

Practical effects
- Better locality for MPI/RDMA: fewer hops, lower latency, higher effective bandwidth, less contention on uplinks.
- Possible tradeoffs: waiting for an optimal configuration can increase queue latency; strict topology enforcement can prevent a job from starting even if idle nodes exist under different switches (unless TopoOptional is set).
- Jobs that don’t care about network locality run as before; topology is only enforced when configured and when a job requests or the policy requires it.

What topology-aware scheduling does not do automatically
- It chooses nodes to reduce network hops and fragmentation, but it does not automatically set in-job NIC selection or MPI fabric settings. You may still need to:
  - Select nodes with specific NICs via constraints/feature attributes,
  - Configure your MPI stack or RDMA environment inside the job to bind to a preferred interface,
  - Use cpu/memory binding options (--cpu-bind, --mem-bind) to improve on‑node locality.

When to use it
- Use topology awareness for tightly coupled, latency- or bandwidth-sensitive parallel jobs (MPI, NCCL, RDMA-based applications) where switch-level locality improves performance.
- If you need strict connectivity or want to avoid cross-switch traffic, use --switches and coordinate with your admin’s topology configuration.

References / further reading
- topology.conf / topology.yaml and the Topology Guide in the Slurm docs (topology/tree, topology/block).
- salloc/sbatch/srun docs for the --switches option.

"Priority" as a Slurm pending reason means: the scheduler attempted to place the job but chose other jobs first because they have higher scheduling priority. It does not by itself mean a resource limit, dependency, or begin time — it means the job lost the scheduling comparison to one or more other jobs.

What it implies
- Your job is eligible to run (no unmet dependency, begin time, or explicit account/limit block was detected for the scheduling attempt), but other jobs ranked higher and consumed the available scheduling opportunity.
- The scheduler ranks jobs by a numeric priority; higher numeric priority => scheduled earlier.

How Slurm computes that numeric priority
- By default Slurm uses the Multifactor Priority plugin. Job_priority is a weighted sum of factors such as:
  - age (how long the job has waited)
  - association/account priority
  - fairshare (historical usage)
  - job size
  - partition priority
  - QOS priority
  - TRES factors (CPU/GPU weights)
  - site/nice factors
- Each factor is normalized and multiplied by configured weights (see PriorityWeight* settings). The final priority is an integer (0 .. 4294967295); larger is better.

What to check when you see "Priority"
- Inspect the job's numeric priority and the queue ordering:
  - sprio — shows computed priority factors (per-job priority and contributing factors).
  - squeue (include PRIORITY and REASON columns) — shows which jobs are ahead of yours.
  - scontrol show job <jobid> — shows the job's Priority= value and other properties (QOS, account, nice, TRES).
- Check fairshare and effective shares:
  - sshare — to see account/user fairshare usage that may lower/increase priority.
- Check QOS and partition weights:
  - QOS or partition settings may give other jobs elevated priority (or your job lower priority).
- If preemption or backfill is in use, high-priority jobs may preempt or block lower-priority jobs from starting.

Common causes
- Many recent/high-weight jobs were submitted with higher QOS/account priority.
- Your account has low fairshare (used up entitlement), so fairshare factor reduces your priority.
- Partition or association priorities favor other users or partitions.
- Your job is large (job_size factor) and the scheduler is preferring many smaller/higher-priority jobs first (configurable by weights).

If you want help diagnosing a specific job, tell me the job ID and I can show the priority value and the jobs currently ahead of it (I'll run the appropriate Slurm reads).

Slurm's job scheduler handles GRES affinity on a socket basis internally.
However, the gres.conf interface allows administrators to specify `Cores` for GPU affinity configuration. This creates
a common misconception that Slurm will respect core-level affinity during job
scheduling, which it does not and never has. This can lead to issues where job
allocations and job steps don't align correctly, since job steps examine cores
while jobs use sockets.

  - --gpus=N (request N GPUs for the whole job)
  - --gpus-per-node=N (equivalent to --gres=gpu:N)
  - --gpus-per-task=N (request N GPUs for each task)
  - --gres=gpu:TYPE:COUNT (request GPUs of a specific type/MIG slice)
- Slurm enforces exclusivity and sets CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES (and similar per-step environment) so each job-step/task only sees its assigned GPUs.

Behavior and examples
1) --gres=gpu is per-node
- sbatch --nodes=2 --gres=gpu:2 ... => scheduler will give you 2 GPUs on each of the 2 nodes (total GPUs = 4).
- sbatch --gres=gpu:2 --nodes=1 ... => 2 GPUs on the single allocated node.

2) --gpus vs --gpus-per-node (--gres)
- sbatch --gpus=4 --nodes=2 ... => requests 4 GPUs total. Scheduler will pick nodes and distribute GPUs to satisfy the total (commonly 2+2 if each node has ≥2 GPUs), but exact packing depends on node capacities and availability.
- sbatch --gpus-per-node=2 --nodes=2 ... (same as --gres=gpu:2 --nodes=2) => rigidly 2 GPUs on every node.

3) Per-task GPU requests
- sbatch --ntasks=8 --gpus-per-task=1 ... => 1 GPU allocated to each task (8 GPUs total). Slurm will place tasks across nodes to satisfy that (spreading or packing depending on policy).
- If you instead used --gres=gpu:2 plus --ntasks=8, the scheduler gives 2 GPUs per node; how tasks map to those GPUs depends on how you launch them (srun binding) and on your tasks-per-node.

What Slurm sets for you inside the job
- For each job step launched on a node Slurm sets CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES so that processes only see the GPU device indexes assigned to them on that node. This makes it safe to run multiple jobs/steps on the same physical node without interfering.
- The exact device index values are the local device numbers as reported by the driver/NVML or as configured in gres.conf; Slurm remaps visibility so each job sees only its assigned subset.
- Note: CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES is set per-node/per-step when tasks start; interactive allocation tools (salloc) may not export a global CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES until you srun a step.

Device selection, types, and MIG
- gres supports a type field: --gres=gpu:V100:2 or --gres=gpu:MIG-<slice>:N (if your gres.conf and Slurm are configured for MIG). This lets you request particular device types or MIG slices.
- AutoDetect=nvml (common) populates device info from the driver; gres.conf can override explicit device files/affinity if needed.

Accounting and enforcement
- GPUs are tracked as a TRES (gres/gpu). If configured (AutoDetect=nvml + AccountingStorageTRES=gres/gpu) Slurm can collect gpu memory and utilization metrics (gres/gpumem, gres/gpuutil).
- Enforced access to device files is typically done via cgroups so a task cannot open other /dev/nvidia devices even if the driver enumerates them — Slurm can restrict device-node visibility.

Common gotchas and tips
- If you want a fixed total (not per-node), prefer --gpus=N; if you want per-node parity, use --gres=gpu:N or --gpus-per-node.
- For per-task GPU workloads use --gpus-per-task (or combine --ntasks with explicit resource requests) to avoid accidental oversubscription.
- Check device mapping inside the job: run nvidia-smi (or nvml-based tool) in your job step to confirm which physical GPUs you were given and the mapping to CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES.
- If your cluster uses MIG, be explicit about types if you need a particular slice.
- The select/cons_tres plugin must be in use for --gpu* options to be honored; otherwise Slurm will reject GPU requests.

- squeue: Job 2004 (gpu_test) by alice — RUNNING, 00:30:00, NODES=1, CPUS=8, MEM=16G, PARTITION=gpu.

  - cpu-node-02 — STATE=mix, CPUS(A/T)=48/64, MEM=200G/256G, PARTITION=cpu

Operational cause
- Primary cause: gpu-node-01 is marked down with a hardware failure. That removes one GPU node from service and is why the gpu partition shows 0 idle nodes.
- Secondary capacity reduction: cpu-node-01 is drained for maintenance, further lowering available CPU capacity.
- Current running job(s) continue on the remaining allocated node(s) (e.g., job 2004 is running on gpu-node-02), but there is no spare GPU capacity for new GPU jobs.

Impact
- New GPU job submissions will queue (no idle GPU nodes).
- CPU capacity is partially reduced; some CPU slots remain (cpu-node-02 mixed), but capacity is degraded.
- If gpu-node-02 fails, GPU jobs would have no place to run.

2. Repair and return node to service:

3. For the drained CPU node:

4. Communicate to users that GPU capacity is reduced until gpu-node-01 is repaired.
5. Optional short-term mitigation:

Good question — these are the fair‑share fields sshare reports. Concise definitions, how they’re computed, and what they mean for scheduling:

1) Raw Shares
- What it is: the absolute share value assigned to an association (user or account). These are the integers you set with sacctmgr (e.g., 100, 1000).
- Role: a relative entitlement value; larger RawShares → larger portion of future allocation if everything else is equal.
- Units: unitless (integer).

2) Norm Shares
- What it is: RawShares normalized into a fraction of the relevant total. In the simple (non‑FAIR_TREE) case:
  NormShares = RawShares / (sum of RawShares for all peers)
  With FAIR_TREE enabled, NormShares are normalized within the association’s level (i.e., relative to its siblings).
- Role: gives the target fraction of resources the association should receive (a proportion between 0 and 1 for that level).
- Units: unitless proportion.

3) Effectv Usage (Effective Usage)
- What it is: the association’s current usage expressed relative to its parent in the fair‑tree. Conceptually it is the association’s (decayed, TRES‑weighted) usage as a fraction of the parent’s usage.
- How it’s derived: starts from Raw Usage (TRES‑seconds; decays over time when PriorityDecayHalfLife is set, and uses TRESBillingWeights if present), then is normalized with respect to the parent node so you get a fraction (the portion of the parent’s consumption attributable to that association).
- Role: shows how much of its parent’s resources the association has actually consumed recently.

How they are used together
- sshare shows Level FS (or fairshare factor) = NormShares / EffectvUsage (for FAIR_TREE). Interpretation:
  - Level FS ≈ 1: consumption ≈ entitlement.
  - Level FS > 1: under‑served (has used less than its share) → scheduler will boost priority.
  - Level FS < 1: over‑served (has used more than its share) → priority lowered.
- Because Raw Usage decays (PriorityDecayHalfLife), EffectvUsage moves over time toward recent usage, so priorities adjust dynamically.

Concrete minimal example
- Two accounts A and B with RawShares 100 and 300 → NormShares A=0.25, B=0.75.
- If A currently consumes 50% of the parent’s usage (EffectvUsage = 0.5), then Level FS for A = 0.25 / 0.5 = 0.5 → A is over‑served; its fairshare priority is reduced.
- If A’s EffectvUsage falls to 0.1, Level FS = 0.25 / 0.1 = 2.5 → A is under‑served and will get higher priority.

Practical notes
- RawShares are configured with sacctmgr. Use sshare (e.g., sshare -l) to view RawShares, NormShares, RawUsage, NormUsage, EffectvUsage, and Level FS.
- Raw Usage is in TRES‑seconds (or cpu‑seconds if no TRES weights); TRESBillingWeights and PriorityDecayHalfLife affect the numbers you’ll see.
- EffectvUsage and Level FS only appear/behave as described when using the multifactor priority plugin and FAIR_TREE behavior.

Quick reference — what “--reservation” is and how reservation access rules work in Slurm.

What a reservation is
- A reservation reserves specific resources (nodes, cores, or TRES) for a defined time window (StartTime / Duration / EndTime) so only approved jobs may use them.
- Reservations are created/managed by the admin (scontrol create/update/delete reservation) and can be shown with scontrol show reservation or scontrol show res <name>.

How jobs use a reservation
- Submitting a job that should run in a reservation: sbatch/srun/salloc --reservation=ReservationName (or the job will start there automatically only if the reservation has the MAGNETIC flag — see below).
- By default, jobs must explicitly request the reservation name. MAGNETIC reservations “attract” matching jobs even if they don’t specify the reservation name.

Access-control fields (rules for who/what can use a reservation)
- When creating a reservation you must specify at least one access control field. Common fields:
  - Users (User= or Users=): a list of allowed users.
  - Groups (Group= or Groups=): a list of allowed Unix/GID groups.
  - Accounts (Account= or Accounts=): allowed accounting accounts.
  - QOS (QOS=): allowed Quality-of-Service values.
  - AllowedPartitions / Partition: partitions the reservation applies to.
- Important rule: Users and Groups are mutually exclusive — you cannot specify both.
- Logical combination: If you specify multiple access-control fields, a job must satisfy all of them to be allowed into the reservation. Example: Accounts=foo,QOS=high means the job must run under account foo AND request high QOS.
- Exclusions are supported: prefixing a value with '-' denies that entity (for example Users=-alice denies user alice even if their account would otherwise allow it).
- You can restrict by partition(s) and by specific nodes or node counts (Nodes=, NodeCnt=, CoreCnt=, TRES=).

Reservation behavior/flags that affect access
- MAGNETIC: jobs that meet the access controls can be scheduled into the reservation without specifying --reservation explicitly.
- REPLACE / REPLACE_DOWN: control whether nodes which are currently allocated or down are replaced to maintain reservation size.
- IGNORE_JOBS: allow creation even if running jobs overlap (useful for maintenance).
- MAINT (maintenance) flag: used to mark maintenance reservations (affects accounting/semantics).
- Other flags control exclusivity and replacement policy — check scontrol docs for the full list.

Practical examples (conceptual)
- Reserve node05 for user alice for 1 hour:
  scontrol create reservation User=alice Nodes=node05 StartTime=now Duration=60
- Reserve two nodes for account foo but exclude user bob:
  scontrol create reservation Accounts=foo Users=-bob Nodes=node[01-02] StartTime=...

Notes and tips
- A job must match all specified access controls; specifying multiple access fields is an AND, not OR.
- Use scontrol show reservation (or squeue --reservation=<name>) to inspect which jobs are tied to a reservation.
- Use MAGNETIC sparingly — it can make reservations “attract” jobs and reduce manual --reservation usage, but can interact subtly with heterogeneous jobs and backfill.
- Admins should be aware reservations affect scheduling and backfill: the scheduler will avoid starting jobs that cannot finish before a reservation start time unless the reservation allows replacement/ignore options.

Below is a concise explanation of strigger fields and the supported event (TYPE) values from the Slurm docs (strigger):

- What a trigger record contains (important fields)
  - TRIG_ID — trigger identifier.
  - RES_TYPE — resource type: job or node.
  - RES_ID — resource id: job ID, hostnames, or "*" for any host.
  - TYPE — trigger event type (see list below).
  - OFFSET — seconds offset; negative = run before the event (if applicable).
  - USER — user who set the trigger.
  - PROGRAM — program/script to execute when the trigger fires.

- How triggers are processed
  - Slurm checks trigger events periodically (≈ every 15 seconds). Any events in that interval are matched against configured triggers; each matching PROGRAM is executed once for the interval.

- Common TYPE values and what they mean (resource applicability in parentheses)
  - time (job) — a time event for a job (e.g., elapsed time reached). Often used to notify or act relative to job runtime.
  - fini (job) — job finished/terminated (job only).
  - down (node OR job) — node(s) have entered the DOWN state (or a job’s node went down); can notify admins or take recovery actions.
  - up (node OR job) — node(s) moved to UP (available) state.
  - drained (node) — node(s) were put into DRAIN state.
  - idle (node) — node(s) became IDLE (no allocations).
  - reconfig (node) — node(s) have been reconfigured (for example after a resume/maintenance).
  - controller events (cluster-wide) — e.g., primary_slurmctld_failure, backup_slurmctld_assumed_control, backup_slurmctld_failure, backup_slurmctld_resumed_operation; trigger on controller role/failure changes.
  - burst_buffer (cluster/resource) — burst buffer error events.
  - (Docs list additional specific options; use strigger --help or the strigger manpage for the full option list.)

## PERFORMANCE[#SECTION_PERFORMANCE](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sattach.html)
Executing sattach sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from sattach or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmctld daemon come in at once, it can result in
a degradation of performance of the slurmctld daemon, possibly resulting
in a denial of service.
Do not run sattach or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other
programs. Ensure that programs limit calls to sattach to the minimum
necessary for the information you are trying to gather.

sattach is the Slurm client used to attach to a running job step so you can interact with its I/O streams (stdin, stdout, stderr). Key points:

- Purpose: expose the IO streams of one job step’s tasks (so you can view output, send input, or attach a parallel debugger such as TotalView).
- Target: a running job step (srun-created/interactive steps). You specify jobid and optionally a step id (jobid[.stepid]).
- Not usable for: extern or batch steps (their IO channels are not set/forwarded), or for jobs that aren’t currently running.
- Useful options: 
  - --label: prefix output lines with task numbers
  - --input-filter / --error-filter: restrict stdin/stdout/stderr to a single task
  - --layout: request task layout from slurmctld
- How to find steps: use squeue --steps or scontrol show job <jobid> to list step ids before attaching.
- Caveats: sattach issues RPCs to slurmctld — many concurrent calls can degrade controller performance. Also requires appropriate permissions to attach to the job.

Example:
- sattach 12345         (attach to default step of job 12345)
- sattach 12345.1       (attach to step 1 of job 12345)
- sattach --label 12345

Alternatives: use srun --pty for interactive allocations, sstat/scontrol for non-interactive diagnostics, or a parallel debugger that integrates with sattach.

Summary — what "sreport cluster utilization" shows
- It’s an sreport report type that summarizes cluster resource usage (usage = accumulated resource time) over a time window.
- Output is reported in resource-time units (CPU minutes/hours, GPU minutes/hours, or other TRES units) and breaks usage into categories such as Allocated, Idle, Down, OverCommitted, PlannedDown, Reported, etc.
- The report can be grouped by account, user, QOS, or WCKey (work category), or shown as overall utilization.

Key fields you will see (common names and meanings)
- Cluster: cluster name.
- Allocated: time nodes were in use with active jobs or active reservations (does not include reservations created with MAINT or IGNORE_JOBS).
- Idle: time nodes were up but not running jobs (available).
- Down: time nodes were marked Down or fully Drained, or time slurmctld was not responding (if TrackSlurmctldDown enabled).
- OverCommitted: time resources were oversubscribed (jobs using more TRES than configured).
- PlannedDown: time set aside for planned outages/maintenance.
- Reported: total time reported by the nodes (useful as a sanity check).
- TresName / TresCount: which TRES (trackable resources) the numbers are for (for example CPU, GPU, node) and the count/unit used in the report.
- Start / End / Usage header: indicates the time window and the units used (e.g., “Usage reported in CPU Minutes”).

Typical command forms
- Basic: sreport cluster utilization Start=YYYY-MM-DD End=YYYY-MM-DD
- Example (one-hour sample): sreport cluster utilization Start=2024-04-01T00:00:00 End=2024-04-01T01:00:00
- Use named cluster: sreport --cluster=<name> cluster utilization Start=...
- Change columns/format: sreport cluster utilization Start=... End=... Format=Utilization
- Other useful cluster reports: AccountUtilizationByUser, AccountUtilizationByQOS, UserUtilizationByAccount (use the REPORT name after “cluster”).

How to interpret results
- Units matter: the header will show whether numbers are CPU minutes, GPU minutes, or node-minutes. Divide/convert as needed for CPU-hours or GPU-hours.
- Allocated vs Reported: Allocated is time in use; Reported is what nodes reported. If they differ, check node reporting or accounting settings.
- Down and PlannedDown remove capacity from the available pool — high Down time explains low utilization.
- OverCommitted > 0 means jobs were allowed to oversubscribe TRES (check oversubscribe settings or job submissions requesting more tasks than available resources).

Common filters/usage patterns
- Narrow time windows with Start= and End= to get hourly/daily reports.
- Combine with --cluster or -M to select a different named cluster in a federation.
- Use Format= to select fields or to produce Account/User breakdowns (e.g., AccountUtilizationByUser).
- For GPU-specific analysis, look at TresName=gres/gpu entries or format outputs that include TresName/TresCount.

Caveats and dependencies
- sreport reads accounting data in the SlurmDB (slurmdbd). If slurmdbd or accounting isn’t configured, reports will be incomplete or fail.
- Reservations created with MAINT or IGNORE_JOBS are not counted in Allocated.
- If node reporting is flaky or slurmctld was down, Down/Reported values may reflect that (TrackSlurmctldDown affects counting).
- Overcommitment reporting depends on how TRES accounting and job submissions are configured.

# Gang Scheduling
Slurm supports timesliced gang scheduling in which two or more jobs are
allocated to the same resources in the same partition and these jobs are
alternately suspended to let one job at a time have dedicated access to the
resources for a configured period of time.
Slurm also supports preemptive job scheduling that allows a job in a
higher PriorityTier partition, or in a preempting QOS, to preempt other
jobs. [Preemption](https://slurm.schedmd.com/preempt.html) is related to Gang scheduling
because SUSPEND is one of the PreemptionMode s, and it uses the Gang
scheduler to resume suspended jobs.
A workload manager that supports timeslicing can improve responsiveness
and utilization by allowing more jobs to begin running sooner.
Shorter-running jobs no longer have to wait in a queue behind longer-running
jobs.
Instead they can be run "in parallel" with the longer-running jobs, which will
allow them to start and finish quick...

## Backfill Scheduling [#backfill](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sched_config.html)
The backfill scheduling plugin is loaded by default.
Without backfill scheduling, each partition is scheduled strictly in priority
order, which typically results in significantly lower system utilization and
responsiveness than otherwise possible.
Backfill scheduling will start lower priority jobs if doing so does not delay
the expected start time of any higher priority jobs.
Since the expected start time of pending jobs depends upon the expected
completion time of running jobs, reasonably accurate time limits are important
for backfill scheduling to work well.
Slurm's backfill scheduler takes into consideration every running job.
It then considers pending jobs in priority order, determining when and where
each will start, taking into consideration the possibility of

## Backfill Scheduling [#backfill](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sched_config.html)
The backfill scheduling plugin is loaded by default.
Without backfill scheduling, each partition is scheduled strictly in priority
order, which typically results in significantly lower system utilization and
responsiveness than otherwise possible.

the expected start time of any higher priority jobs.

Slurm is designed to perform a quick and simple scheduling attempt at
events such as job submission or completion and configuration changes.
During these event-triggered scheduling events, default_queue_depth

plugin to use.

resources for a configured period of time.

higher PriorityTier partition, or in a preempting QOS, to preempt other

scheduler to resume suspended jobs.

and utilization by allowing more jobs to begin running sooner.
Shorter-running jobs no longer have to wait in a queue behind longer-running
jobs.

## System Administrator Information [#sys_admin](https://slurm.schedmd.com/heterogeneous_jobs.html)
The job submit plugin is invoked independently for each component of a
heterogeneous job.
The spank_init_post_opt() function is invoked once for each component of a
heterogeneous job. This permits site defined options on a per job component

## Overview[#overview](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sched_config.html)
Slurm is designed to perform a quick and simple scheduling attempt at
events such as job submission or completion and configuration changes.
During these event-triggered scheduling events, default_queue_depth
