Good question — sdiag is the Slurm scheduling-diagnostics tool that prints counters and timings from slurmctld to help you tune scheduler settings and understand scheduler behaviour. Below is a concise guide to the common sdiag sections/fields and what they mean and imply.

General notes
- Run with --all to see all counters, or --json for machine-readable output. --reset clears the counters (they also reset automatically at midnight UTC).
- sdiag issues an RPC to slurmctld; don’t poll it in tight loops (it can add load to the controller).

Top-level / control-plane fields
- Server thread count
  - Number of active slurmctld threads. High values indicate slurmctld is busy handling submissions, dispatches, RPCs, etc.
- Agent thread count
  - Threads used by scheduling/agent work (depends on build/plugins). A sustained high value means many concurrent scheduling tasks.

Scheduler loop / cycle timing
- Scheduling cycles (or Scheduling iterations)
  - How many main scheduling iterations have run (since last reset).
- Total/average/max scheduling cycle time
  - Wall-time spent running the scheduler loop (total) and per-cycle avg/max. Long/variable cycle times indicate expensive scheduling work—look at sched_interval, default_queue_depth, or expensive plugins (backfill, constraints).
- Scheduling events / event-triggered attempts
  - Counts of event-triggered scheduling attempts (e.g., job submit, job completion). Large numbers here show many reactive scheduling triggers.

Job counters
- Jobs added
  - Number of jobs the controller has ingested.
- Jobs evaluated / Jobs considered
  - How many pending jobs were evaluated by the scheduler logic.
- Jobs dispatched / Jobs started
  - How many jobs were actually dispatched/started on compute nodes.
- Jobs completed
  - Counts of job completions observed by slurmctld.

Backfill / placement statistics (sched/backfill)
- Backfill attempts / Backfill successes
  - Number of times backfill logic attempted to place lower-priority jobs and how often it succeeded.
- Backfill windows considered / backfill windows scanned
  - How many candidate backfill time windows were evaluated. Many windows scanned with few successes can indicate inaccurate time limits or fragmentation.
- Jobs started by backfill
  - How many jobs were started due to backfilling.
- Average backfill evaluation time
  - Time spent per backfill evaluation; high values suggest expensive backfill computations (consider tuning default_queue_depth, partition_job_depth, or backfill plugin parameters).

Queue-depth / evaluation depth
- default_queue_depth
  - The configured number of jobs the scheduler will consider on many events (default 100). If sdiag shows many evaluations relative to this, you may need to tune it.
- partition_job_depth
  - Per-partition depth limiting how many jobs are considered in a full scheduling pass (reflected in counters).

Preemption / requeue / timeslicing / gang-scheduler metrics
- Preemption/Preempt attempts and successes
  - How often higher-priority jobs preempt lower-priority ones and whether preemption succeeded.
- Timeslice / suspended / resumed counts (if gang/timeslicer enabled)
  - Counts of timeslice suspends/resumes; large numbers indicate frequent timeslicing activity.

Per-partition/per-plugin breakdowns
- sdiag often shows per-partition counters: scheduling attempts, backfill attempts, jobs started, evaluations. Use those to identify which partition has the most scheduling cost or backfill difficulty.
- Heterogeneous job counters if heterogeneous support is used (components deferred, expected start recorded, etc.).

Diagnostics / error counters
- Failed dispatches / failed evaluations
  - Number of times a scheduling decision failed (e.g., due to node issues or selection plugin errors). Investigate scontrol/sinfo and node reasons.

How to interpret and act
- High Server thread count + long scheduling cycle times
  - Controller is overloaded. Consider reducing sdiag frequency, increasing slurmctld resources (CPU), or tuning sched_interval/default_queue_depth/partition_job_depth.
- Many backfill attempts but few backfill starts
  - Check job time-limit accuracy (backfill relies on expected end times). Consider encouraging users to set realistic time limits or tune backfill parameters.
- Large numbers of job evaluations per event
  - Reduce default_queue_depth/partition_job_depth to limit per-event work or tune SchedulerParameters (defer, sched_interval) to prefer periodic comprehensive scheduling.
- Frequent preemption or timeslicing activity
  - Review PreemptionMode, QOS and Gang scheduling parameters; note suspended jobs can hold memory and reduce effective capacity.

When to run other tools
- For per-job pending reasons or “why is this job not starting?”: use squeue (and scontrol show job for detailed pending reason).
- For priority/fairshare: run sprio and sshare.
- For long-term usage/consumption: use sreport or sacct.

- Show an annotated example sdiag output and map each line to the explanations above, or
- Run sdiag on the cluster now and summarize the controllers’ current scheduler counters (I’ll call sdiag and report results). Which would you prefer?

## DESCRIPTION[#SECTION_DESCRIPTION](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbcast.html)
sbcast is used to transmit a file to all nodes allocated
to the currently active Slurm job.
This command should only be executed from within a Slurm batch
job or within the shell spawned after a Slurm job's resource
allocation.
SOURCE is the name of a file on the current node.
DEST should be the fully qualified pathname for the
file copy to be created on each node.
If a fully qualified pathname is not provided, the file will be created in
the directory specified in the BcastParameters parameter in the slurm.conf
file (if available) otherwise it will be created in the current working
directory from which the sbcast command is invoked.
DEST should be on a file system local to that node.
Note that parallel file systems may provide better performance
than sbcast can provide, although performance will vary
by file size, degree of parallelism, and network type.

Short answer
- sbcast copies a file from the job’s control/node to every node in the current Slurm allocation. It is run from inside a job allocation (batch script, salloc/srun shell) and writes the file to a local path on each allocated node.
- Use it when you need a file available on node-local storage (local SSD, tmpfs, /tmp) on every allocated node and either you don’t have a shared filesystem or you need local-disk performance.

What sbcast does
- Broadcasts one source file to all nodes in the active Slurm allocation (single command, Slurm coordinates delivery).
- Destination must be a path local to each node (if not given, obeys BcastParameters or current working directory).
- Can auto-collect and send dependent shared libraries (--send-libs), preserve modes (-p), compress payload (-C), and tune distribution fanout (-F).
- Implemented via RPCs to slurmctld; many concurrent calls can load slurmctld.

When sbcast helps (good use cases)
- There is no shared parallel filesystem, or it is slow/overloaded.
- You need low-latency or high-throughput access to a file from node-local storage (e.g., small executables, per-node worker config, initialization datasets cached to local SSD/tmpfs).
- The file is small-to-medium sized (single large files are OK but very large datasets may be better on a parallel FS or pre-staged by other means).
- You have many nodes and want a single coordinated broadcast rather than looping scp/rsync from the login host.
- You want to stage a binary plus its libraries to local disk (use --send-libs to include dependencies).

When sbcast is not ideal
- You already have a fast parallel/shared filesystem (Lustre, GPFS, etc.). Those often perform better than copying to each node.
- The data is very large (many GB/TB); copying across network to every node may be slower/inefficient compared to serving from a shared FS or preloading on a subset of nodes.
- You have many small files — better to tar/zip into a single file and sbcast that archive, then unpack on nodes.
- You plan to call sbcast repeatedly in a tight loop — avoid that because it stresses slurmctld.

Practical tips / options
- Run inside an allocation: e.g. salloc -N4 ... ; sbcast myprog /tmp/myprog ; srun -N4 /tmp/myprog
- Combine many small files: tar -czf bundle.tgz dir/ ; sbcast bundle.tgz /tmp/bundle.tgz ; srun tar -xzf /tmp/bundle.tgz
- Use compression: -C or --compress=lz4 to reduce network transfer
- Use --send-libs to include ELF shared-library dependencies (helpful for self-contained binaries)
- Use -p/--preserve to keep permissions and timestamps
- Tune distribution with --fanout/-F to change tree fanout if admin defaults are suboptimal
- Avoid running sbcast repeatedly; prefer one broadcast per allocation for staging
- Clean up after job: remove staged files from /tmp or local SSD if needed

Caveats and admin considerations
- sbcast invokes slurmctld RPCs; many simultaneous sbcast calls or scripted loops can overload slurmctld (risk denial-of-service).
- Destination should be local to the node; specifying a path on a shared FS defeats the local-staging purpose.
- Slurm config (BcastParameters, BcastExclude) can affect behavior; admins may tune defaults.

Alternatives
- Shared parallel filesystem (best for large shared datasets).
- rsync/scp in prolog/epilog or a central orchestration step (works if you can parallelize copies safely).
- Container images (Singularity/Apptainer) or bundling apps into an image or module.
- Use a subset of “loader” nodes that download once and then peer-distribute (custom).

Example usage
- Simple broadcast inside allocation:
  sbcast myprogram /tmp/myprogram
  srun -N4 /tmp/myprogram
- Bundle many files and broadcast:
  tar -czf bundle.tgz mydir/
  sbcast bundle.tgz /tmp/bundle.tgz
  srun -N4 bash -c 'tar -xzf /tmp/bundle.tgz -C /tmp && /tmp/mydir/run.sh'

References
- sbcast man page (Slurm docs): https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbcast.html

## File Names[#file_names](https://slurm.schedmd.com/job_array.html)
Two additional options are available to specify a job's stdin, stdout, and
stderr file names:
%A will be replaced by the value of SLURM_ARRAY_JOB_ID (as defined above)
and
%a will be replaced by the value of SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID (as defined above).
The default output file format for a job array is "slurm-%A_%a.out".
An example of explicit use of the formatting is:
sbatch -o slurm-%A_%a.out --array=1-3 -N1 tmp
which would generate output files names of this sort
"slurm-36_1.out", "slurm-36_2.out" and "slurm-36_3.out".
If these file name options are used without being part of a job array then
"%A" will be replaced by the current job ID and "%a" will be replaced by
4,294,967,294 (equivalent to 0xfffffffe or NO_VAL).

Short answer
- --array takes an index specification of the form start-end[:step][%max].
- The "%N" part is a concurrency throttle (N = maximum number of array tasks allowed to run at the same time). It is NOT a percentage; it is an absolute count.

Formal breakdown (from the Slurm sbatch / job_array docs)
- Index list: single values, comma-separated values, and ranges are all allowed:
  - 5                -> single element with index 5
  - 1,3,5,7          -> explicit indices 1,3,5,7
  - 1-7              -> indices 1,2,3,4,5,6,7
- Step: append :step to a range to select every step’th index:
  - 1-7:2            -> 1,3,5,7
- Throttle: append %max to limit simultaneous running tasks from that array:
  - 0-99%10          -> indices 0..99, but at most 10 tasks from that array may be RUNNING at once
  - 0-15%4           -> at most 4 simultaneous tasks (example from the docs)
  - %1               -> run array tasks serially (one at a time)
- Combined example:
  - --array=0-99:5%8 -> run indices 0,5,10,...,95 and allow up to 8 of those indices to run concurrently.

Other useful notes from the docs
- The smallest allowed index is 0; the global MaxArraySize (cluster config) limits the largest index/array size (default MaxArraySize is 1001 unless the admin changed it).
- Array tasks are still regular jobs for enforcement of limits like MaxJobs, MaxSubmitJobs, QOS, account limits, etc.
- Environment variables you can use inside the job script: SLURM_ARRAY_JOB_ID, SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID, SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_COUNT, SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_MIN/MAX.
- squeue prints array elements compactly (e.g., JOBID_[1-1024]); scancel can target elements with jobid_1 or jobid_[1-3].

Slurm includes support for creating a federation of clusters

## Overview[#overview](https://slurm.schedmd.com/federation.html)
Slurm includes support for creating a federation of clusters
and scheduling jobs in a peer-to-peer fashion between them. Jobs submitted to a
federation receive a unique job ID that is unique among all clusters in the
federation. A job is submitted to the local cluster (the cluster defined in the
slurm.conf) and is then replicated across the clusters in the federation. Each
cluster then independently attempts to the schedule the job based off of its own
scheduling policies. The clusters coordinate with the "origin" cluster (cluster
the job was submitted to) to schedule the job.
NOTE : This is not intended as a high-throughput environment. If
scheduling more than 50,000 jobs a day, consider configuring fewer clusters that
the sibling jobs can be submitted to or directing load
to the local cluster only (e.g. --cluster-constraint= or -M submission options
could be used to do...

Summary — what Slurm federation is
- A Slurm federation is a set of independent Slurm clusters that cooperate so jobs can be scheduled across them in a peer-to-peer fashion. Federation is configured in the accounting DB (sacctmgr) by creating a federation and adding clusters.
- Federation is intended to increase scheduling opportunity across administrative clusters, not as a high-throughput staging layer (docs warn about very high submission rates).

Key concepts and vocabulary
- Origin cluster / origin job: the cluster where the user submitted the job and the job record that “owns” the federated job.
- Sibling job(s): copies of the origin job that are submitted to other clusters in the federation.
- Sibling cluster: a cluster that received a sibling job.
- Federated job ID: a single job id unique across the federation. It encodes the origin cluster id and the local job id (bits 0–25 local id, bits 26–31 cluster origin id).
- Viable siblings / active siblings: clusters where sibling jobs are currently viable (could run) or currently running.
- Revoked (RV) state: when a sibling is explicitly revoked/removed because another cluster has started the job.

How federated job submission works (high level)
- You submit a job to your local (origin) cluster. The origin may create sibling jobs on other clusters in the federation (either all federation members or a constrained subset you specify).
- You can restrict which clusters are considered with options like -M/--clusters=<list> or --cluster-constraint=[!]<constraints>.
- Each cluster independently tries to schedule its sibling based on its local policies and resources.
- When a cluster decides it can allocate resources it asks the origin cluster to confirm no other cluster is simultaneously allocating. If allocation succeeds there, that cluster starts the job and notifies the origin.
- Once a sibling actually starts, the origin instructs other clusters to remove or revoke their sibling jobs (they enter RV or are cancelled), so only one instance runs.

Job lifecycle behaviors to know
- Only one sibling actually runs; others wait or are revoked/cancelled once one starts.
- Canceling/modifying a federated job should be coordinated through the origin; origin propagates cancellations/changes to siblings.
- If a cluster is removed from the federation, running jobs that originated there keep running as non-federated; pending siblings on the origin may remain pending as non-federated.
- Interactive jobs, arrays, requeue/cancel semantics are supported but have federation-specific behavior; the origin remains the coordination point.

Configuration and administration
- Federation objects are created/managed with sacctmgr (add/modify federation, add clusters to a federation). A cluster may be a member of only one federation at a time.
- The origin cluster is recorded in the federated job id and in the accounting DB so controllers can route coordination through the origin.

Useful commands and visibility
- squeue --sibling will show sibling rows instead of merging them.
- squeue long-format fields include: cluster, siblingsactive, siblingsviable, etc., to inspect where siblings exist and which clusters are viable.
- scontrol show job <jobid> shows detailed federated fields for a given job.
- sacctmgr can list federations and cluster membership.
- For debugging, check squeue (with sibling info) and scontrol show job; look at the cluster that is the origin if coordination messages or state transitions are unexpected.

Limitations and cautions
- Not intended for extremely high submission rates (docs give guidance ~50k/day as a threshold where federation can be problematic).
- Scheduling decisions are still local; policies, QOS, and resource availability on each cluster determine which sibling can run.
- Network/connectivity, clock skew, or accounting DB misconfiguration between clusters can cause weird behavior; ensure reliable connectivity and consistent sacctmgr configuration.
- Clusters must be explicitly configured in the federation; users normally cannot implicitly reach arbitrary clusters.

Short examples
- Submit siblings to only cluster2 and cluster3:
  sbatch -Mcluster2,cluster3 script.sh
- Constrain which clusters are viable using cluster constraints:
  sbatch --cluster-constraint=cluster2 script.sh

Where to read more
- See the Slurm Federated Scheduling Guide (Slurm docs: federation.html) for full details, job id encoding, state transitions, configuration examples, and command reference.

Slurm generally classifies users into three authorization levels:

Job arrays offer a mechanism for submitting and managing collections of
similar jobs quickly and easily, useful for repetitive workloads that follow a
common job pattern. This greatly improves overall performance, since job arrays
with millions of tasks can be submitted in milliseconds (subject to configured
size limits) and the scheduler can quickly identify cases when no more array
tasks are eligible to start.

Good question — scontrol show job prints many fields. Below are the most important ones to know, what they mean, and how to use them when inspecting or troubleshooting a job.

- JobId
  - Unique numeric job identifier. Use this when querying other Slurm commands (squeue, sacct, scontrol).

- JobName
  - Human name given at submit (sbatch --job-name). Helpful for quick identification.

- UserId / GroupId
  - Owner and group (user(uid)). Useful for filtering and ownership checks.

- Account / QOS
  - Accounting account and quality-of-service. QOS can affect priority, limits, and preemption.

- Partition
  - Partition the job was submitted to. Resource availability and policies are partition-specific.

- JobState
  - Current state (PENDING, RUNNING, COMPLETED, FAILED, CANCELLED, SUSPENDED, etc.). First field to read when diagnosing.

- Reason (or StateReason)
  - If PENDING, shows why (e.g., Resources, Priority, Dependency, QOSMaxCPU). Critical for understanding why a job won’t start.

- Dependency
  - Any job dependencies (afterok:12345, afterany:...) that must be satisfied before this job may start.

- SubmitTime / EligibleTime / StartTime / EndTime / RunTime or Elapsed
  - Timestamps for lifecycle events:
    - SubmitTime: when job was submitted.
    - EligibleTime: when it became eligible to run (after holds/dependencies).
    - StartTime: when allocation began (or N/A if not started).
    - Elapsed / RunTime: how long it has been running.
  - Compare these to TimeLimit for time usage and billing.

- TimeLimit / TimeMin
  - Requested walltime limit and minimum time. Important for expected runtime and scheduler backfill.

- Nodes / NodeList / NumNodes / NNodes
  - How many nodes requested/allocated and which nodes (NodeList). If pending due to node availability, NodeList/NumNodes shows the request shape.

- CPUs / NTasks / CPUSPerTask / TasksPerNode
  - CPU/task layout (how many tasks, cores per task). Check these against partition node capacities.

- ReqMem / ReqCPUS / ReqGRES / TRES / AllocTRES
  - Resource requests and allocations:
    - ReqMem / ReqCPUS: requested memory and CPUs.
    - ReqGRES / GRES: requested generic resources (GPUs).
    - TRES / AllocTRES: trackable resources (cpu, mem, gpu) that were allocated. Useful when investigating GPU or memory shortages.

- GresUsed / Gres
  - Which GPUs (or other GRES) were allocated/used. Useful for GPU accounting and debugging device-level failures.

- AllocNode:Sid
  - The node and system id that performed the allocation (shown for running jobs). Useful for node-level debugging.

- StdOut / StdErr / WorkDir
  - Paths to job stdout/stderr and working directory (where the batch script ran). First place to look for application logs.

- BatchFlag
  - Indicates batch-style submission (sbatch) vs interactive; increments when job is requeued. Helps reason about requeues.

- ExitCode
  - For finished jobs, exit status formatted as "rc:signal". Use to tell whether the job exited cleanly or was killed by a signal.

- Hold/HoldReason
  - Whether job is held (user/administrator hold) and why. Held jobs won't become eligible until released.

- Reservation
  - Reservation the job is tied to (if any). Reserved resources can affect scheduling eligibility.

- ArrayJobId / ArrayTaskId
  - For job arrays: array parent id and the specific task index (e.g., 1000_5).

- Priority / PriorityTier
  - Effective scheduling priority and tier. Explains ordering when resources are contested.

- Flags / Features / Constraint
  - Any special flags, required node features, or CPU architecture constraints. If constraints don’t match available nodes, the job will stay pending.

Quick troubleshooting checklist using these fields
- Job is PENDING: check JobState + Reason, Dependency, Hold, Partition, ReqGRES/TRES, and Constraints.
- Job won't get GPUs: check ReqGRES/GRES, TRES, partition GRES capacity (compare with sinfo).
- Job unexpectedly short or killed: check ExitCode, StdErr, and AllocNode:Sid to find node logs.
- Job started on wrong node-type: check NodeList, Constraint/Features, and the allocated TRES.

Good question — here are concise, safe rules and examples for using scontrol update on jobs.

Basic syntax
- scontrol update JobId=<jobid> Field1=Value1 Field2=Value2 ...
- No commas between assignments; use = with no extra spaces around the equals.
- Always target a specific job with JobId=<id> to avoid accidental mass changes. Omitting JobId or using broader selectors (JobName=..., User=...) can modify many jobs.

Authorization & safety
- scontrol update requires you be the job's effective owner (or Coordinator) or a privileged user (Operator/Administrator). Privileged users can bypass many policy limits.
- Most fields may only be changed while a job is PENDING; only a subset can be changed for RUNNING or SUSPENDED jobs. Check your local policy or try scontrol show job <id> to confirm.
- For heterogeneous jobs: update the leader (jobid) to affect all components; you can address components with jobid=123+2 (plus-sign) when applicable.
- For job arrays and array-task addressing, use the array element syntax (ArrayJobID_ArrayTaskID) where required (e.g., 345_7).

Common safe field examples
- Change time limit:
  scontrol update JobId=123 TimeLimit=02:00:00
  (TimeLimit accepts formats like MM, HH:MM:SS, or D-HH:MM:SS depending on config.)
- Change job name (usually pending jobs only):
  scontrol update JobId=123 JobName=new_name
- Change account/QOS (usually pending jobs; privileges may apply):
  scontrol update JobId=123 Account=myacct QOS=high
- Change requested priority (often restricted to privileged users):
  scontrol update JobId=123 Priority=100
- Set node list for pending allocations:
  scontrol update JobId=123 NodeList=node[01-02]
- Heterogeneous job component account change:
  scontrol update jobid=123+2 Account=abc

Best practices (to avoid mistakes)
- Always include JobId=<id>. If you mean to act on many jobs, be explicit — don’t omit JobId casually.
- Preview job state before and after:
  squeue -j <jobid>   (or) scontrol show job <jobid>
- After update, confirm with:
  scontrol show job <jobid>
- If unsure about permission or allowed fields, run the doc/help for scontrol or ask an administrator. Privileged updates can violate policy limits (e.g., extend beyond partition max time).
- When scripting: fail-safe by validating the job ID and state via squeue or scontrol show job before running scontrol update.

Notes and gotchas
- Field names are case-insensitive but use canonical names (JobId, TimeLimit, JobName, Account, QOS, NodeList, Priority).
- Quoting: values normally do not need quotes; if you must include special characters or spaces (rare for job fields), quote appropriately for your shell.
- Be careful with selectors like JobName= or User= — these will match multiple jobs if not restricted and can apply the update broadly.

# Create a two core reservation for user alan $ scontrol create reservation StartTime=now Duration=60 \ NodeCnt=1 CoreCnt=2 User=alan # Create a reservation for user brenda with two cores on # node tux8 and 4 cores on node tux9 $ scontrol create reservation StartTime=now Duration=60 \ Nodes=tux8,tux9 CoreCnt=2,4 User=brenda
```
Reservations can not only be created for the use of specific accounts and/or
QOS and/or partitions and/or users, but specific accounts and/or QOS and/or
partitions and/or users can be prevented from using them.
In the following example, a reservation is created for account foo , but
user alan is prevented from using the reservation even when using the
account foo .
```text
$ scontrol create reservation account=foo \ user=-alan partition=pdebug \ starttime=noon duration=60 nodecnt=2k,2k Reservation created: alan_9 $ scontrol show res ReservationName=alan_9 StartTime=2011-12-05T13:00:00 EndTime=2011-12-05T14:00:00...

## Reservations that Replace Allocated Resources [#replace](https://slurm.schedmd.com/reservations.html)
By default, nodes in a reservation that are DOWN or DRAINED will be replaced,
but not nodes that are allocated to jobs. This behavior may be explicitly
requested with the REPLACE_DOWN flag.
However, you may instruct Slurm to also replace nodes which are allocated to
jobs with new idle nodes. This is done using the REPLACE flag as shown in
the example below.
The effect of this is to always maintain a constant size pool of resources.
This option is not supported for reservations specifying cores which
span more than one node, rather than full nodes. (E.g. a 1 core reservation on
node "tux1" will be moved if node "tux1" goes down, but a reservation
containing 2 cores on node "tux1" and 3 cores on "tux2" will not be moved if

## Magnetic Reservations [#magnetic](https://slurm.schedmd.com/reservations.html)
The default behavior for reservations is that jobs must request a
reservation in order to run in it. The MAGNETIC flag allows you to
create a reservation that will allow jobs to run in it without requiring that
they specify the name of the reservation. The reservation will only "attract"

Below are safe, read-only steps and checks you can follow to plan and create maintenance reservations without changing cluster state. I include the recommended Slurm queries to inspect current state, guidance for choosing parameters/flags, and a short verification & rollback checklist. Do these preparatory reads first; only create or modify reservations when you’re ready and have operator approval.

1) Define the maintenance window and scope
- Choose concrete StartTime (ISO or relative like "now+2hours") and Duration.
- Decide nodes vs. partition vs. node count. Prefer a specific node list when taking nodes fully offline for maintenance.
- Decide access controls (Users, Accounts, QOS) and whether the reservation should be visible/attractive to jobs (magnetic) or marked for accounting as maintenance (flags=maint).

2) Inspect cluster state (read-only checks to run)
- Inventory partitions/nodes and per-node availability:
  - sinfo (optionally sinfo -N -l) — find idle vs allocated nodes, per-partition context.
  - sinfo_reasons — list nodes already DRAIN/ DOWN and reasons.
  - sinfo_node (partition=..., state=...) if you need node-level detail.
- Check current and pending jobs that could overlap your window:
  - squeue (filter by partition or node) — show running and pending jobs and TIME limits.
  - squeue --reservation=<name> (after a reservation exists) to see reservation queue entries.
- Find long-running or critical jobs historically:
  - sacct (e.g., sacct -S now-30days -u <user>) — identify recurring long jobs or jobs that may run into your window.
- Check existing reservations and avoid conflicts:
  - scontrol show reservation (or scontrol_reservation_show) — list current/future reservations.
- Check scheduler/backfill/fairshare effects that might impact start:
  - sdiag and sprio or sshare (if you need to understand backfill behavior and priorities).

3) Choose safe reservation flags and parameters
- flags=maint — marks it as a maintenance reservation for accounting and policy clarity.
- Avoid flags that forcibly terminate running jobs unless absolutely necessary:
  - flags=ignore_jobs will allow creation even if jobs are running, but you must manually handle or cancel those jobs later — use with caution.
  - flags=replace can cause Slurm to replace allocated nodes; use only if you understand the replacement behavior and consequences.
- For minimal disruption, prefer:
  - StartTime in the near future (gives users notice) and Duration just long enough plus buffer.
  - Not using ignore_jobs or replace unless you have a plan to cancel or migrate running jobs.
  - Optionally restrict Users/Accounts so only maintenance staff can use it.

4) Test with a small/dry approach (no state change)
- Plan a small test reservation on one non-critical node with StartTime far enough in future; verify with scontrol show reservation to see how it will be applied. There’s no true “dry-run” flag in Slurm, so creating a future reservation is the safe way to preview behavior without immediate effect.
- Verify that jobs that would start within your window are either blocked or will finish before StartTime by checking squeue elapsed/time limits and expected end times.

5) Verification right before the window (read-only)
- Re-run sinfo and squeue shortly before the StartTime to confirm nothing changed.
- Check scontrol show reservation ReservationName=<name> to confirm nodes, StartTime, Duration, and flags are correct.
- Use squeue --starttime or examine TIME left on running jobs to ensure none will overrun — if uncertain, communicate or coordinate with users.

6) Communication and coordination
- Notify affected users well in advance with the window and the exact nodes/partitions that will be impacted.
- Publish contact/rollback plan and how users can checkpoint or migrate jobs.
- Consider creating a short “maintenance reservation” announcement with ReservationName and StartTime so users can plan.

7) Execution considerations (mutating actions — operator steps, do not run yourself here)
- Typical sequence after reservation becomes active:
  - Optionally drain nodes (scontrol_node drain) if you must prevent new jobs from starting on those nodes.
  - Cancel or requeue jobs that will interfere (scancel / scontrol requeue) only after notification and approval.
  - Perform maintenance, then resume nodes (scontrol_node resume) and/or delete reservation (scontrol delete reservation <name>).
- Note: these are state-changing operations; follow your site’s change-control and call the operator / run them from an authorized admin environment.

8) Rollback and clean-up plan (prepare before making changes)
- How to abort: scontrol delete reservation ReservationName=<name>.
- How to restore service: clear node drains/resumes, verify with sinfo and a small smoke test, and notify users.
- Keep logs of actions and times for post-maintenance accounting.

9) Quick example (informational only — does not execute)
- Example create command you would run when ready:
  - scontrol create reservation ReservationName=maint_win1 StartTime=2026-05-05T02:00:00 Duration=02:00 Nodes=node[05-08] Flags=maint Users=maintteam
- Verify:
  - scontrol show reservation ReservationName=maint_win1
  - squeue --reservation=maint_win1

- [ ] Confirm no critical jobs will be interrupted (squeue + sacct history).
- [ ] Notify users and get approvals.
- [ ] Pick conservative StartTime and Duration with buffer.
- [ ] Avoid aggressive flags (ignore_jobs/replace) unless planned.
- [ ] Have rollback steps and contacts ready.

Executing sstat sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from sstat or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmctld daemon come in at once, it can result in
a degradation of performance of the slurmctld daemon, possibly resulting
in a denial of service.
Do not run sstat or other Slurm client commands that send remote procedure
calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other programs. Ensure
that programs limit calls to sstat to the minimum necessary for the
information you are trying to gather.

Summary (job 5008 — healthy_job, user=bob, partition=cpu)
- squeue: JOBID=5008, NAME=healthy_job, USER=bob, STATE=RUNNING, TIME=01:30:00, NODES=1, CPUS=8, MEM=16G, PARTITION=cpu
- step (scontrol show step): StepId=5008.0 Name=healthy_job.batch State=RUNNING Nodes=1 CPUs=8 Mem=16G
- sstat (step-level): JobID=5008 | AveCPU=00:12:30 | AveRSS=16G | AveVMSize=16G | MaxRSS=16G | NTasks=1

What each field means
- StepId / Name / State: identifies the job step (5008.0) and its step name (healthy_job.batch) and that it is RUNNING.
- Nodes / CPUs / Mem: resources allocated to the job step (1 node, 8 CPUs, 16G memory).
- NTasks: number of tasks in the step (1).
- AveCPU: average (user+system) CPU time consumed per task (00:12:30). This is per-task CPU time, not wallclock.
- AveRSS: average resident set size (physical memory) per task (16G).
- AveVMSize: average virtual memory size per task (16G).
- MaxRSS: maximum RSS seen among the tasks (16G).

Interpretation (quick math)
- Elapsed wall time = 01:30:00 = 1.5 hours.
- AveCPU 00:12:30 = 12.5 minutes = 0.2083 CPU-hours per task.
  - Per-task CPU utilization = 0.2083 / 1.5 = ~13.9% of one CPU on average.
  - Allocation CPU capacity = 8 CPUs * 1.5 h = 12 CPU-hours.
  - Allocation utilization = total used CPU-hours (0.2083) / 12 = ~1.7% of the allocated CPU capacity.
- Memory: AveRSS = 16G equals the requested 16G → the task is using essentially all of its allocated memory (MaxRSS = 16G confirms peak usage ≈ allocated memory).

Conclusions and next steps
- The job is using almost all of its allocated memory but very little CPU across the 8 cores (very low CPU utilization).
- Possible causes: the job may be I/O-bound, waiting on external resources, single-threaded work that doesn't use multiple cores, or sleeping/waiting in parts of the code.
- If you want, I can:
  - show per-task/system I/O or more sstat fields (e.g., AveDiskRead) to check I/O,
  - show step details (scontrol show step output full) or the job's stdout/stderr paths,
  - or run sstat with different fields. Which would you like?

## PERFORMANCE[#SECTION_PERFORMANCE](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Executing sbatch sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmctld daemon come in at once, it can result in
a degradation of performance of the slurmctld daemon, possibly resulting
in a denial of service.
Do not run sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other
programs. Ensure that programs limit calls to sbatch to the minimum
necessary for the information you are trying to gather.

## Node Extra Data [#Node_Extra_Data](https://slurm.schedmd.com/extra_constraints.html)
A node's extra data is a json formatted string. It may be initialized on
slurmd startup with the --extra flag for slurmd. For example:
```text
slurmd --extra '{ "a": 1.23, "b": true, "c": 0, "foo": "bar", "zed": 23 }'
```
Or, it may be updated with scontrol. For example:
```text
scontrol update nodename=node123 extra='{ "a": 1.23, "b": true, "c": 0, "foo": "bar", "zed": 23 }'
```
This defines the features that may be requested by the --extra option in
salloc, sbatch, and srun. Values may be any string, number, or boolean value.

Here’s a concise explanation of how Slurm treats partitions, constraints, and CPU availability — what to look at and how to request CPUs.

1) Partition basics
- A partition is a named queue of nodes (e.g., "cpu", "gpu", "batch"). Use --partition or -p to target one when you sbatch/salloc/srun.
- Partition availability (AVAIL) can be up, down, drain, or inact. If a partition is not "up" your jobs won’t start there.

2) Checking availability and capacity
- sinfo gives a partition/node summary. Useful fields:
  - PARTITION / AVAIL: partition name and availability (up/down/drain/inact).
  - NODES(A/I/O/T) or a similar form: counts of Allocated / Idle / Other (e.g., drained/down/doing maintenance) / Total nodes in that partition.
  - CPUS: number of CPUs per node (for the shown node set) or, with format %C, CPU(A/I/O/T) showing allocated/idle/other/total CPUs across nodes.
- Interpretation: “idle” nodes or idle CPUs are the resources eligible for new jobs. Allocated, drained, down, or reserved nodes/CPUs are not available.

3) CPU resource accounting in Slurm
- Slurm counts CPU as a TRES (Trackable RESource) named "cpu". Allocation is based on requested cpus-per-task, ntasks, tasks-per-node, and nodes.
  - Example: sbatch --partition=cpu --cpus-per-task=4 --ntasks=8 requests 8 tasks × 4 cpus/task = 32 cpu TRES.
- Key options when requesting CPU resources:
  - --cpus-per-task (or -c): threads/cores to give each task (affects CPU TRES).
  - --ntasks (or -n): number of tasks (MPI ranks).
  - --nodes: number of distinct nodes to allocate.
  - --ntasks-per-node: tasks on each node.
  - --exclusive: allocate whole node(s), preventing sharing.
- If you want a whole node, use --nodes=1 --exclusive (or request enough cpus to exceed node capacity under a restrictive policy).

4) Constraints (node selection filters)
- --constraint lets you request node features defined in slurm.conf (Feature=...) or via helpers/extra. Constraints filter which nodes can be allocated.
- Boolean operators accepted (site may differ slightly): & and comma (,) act as AND, | acts as OR. Parentheses can group expressions when supported.
  - Examples:
    - --constraint="skylake"  (nodes with feature skylake)
    - --constraint="skylake&avx512" or --constraint="skylake,avx512" (nodes must have both)
    - --constraint="skylake|haswell" (either feature)
- There is also --extra (SchedulerParameters=extra_constraints must be enabled) for JSON-style extra attributes and richer comparisons.

5) Practical checks before submitting
- Use sinfo -s or sinfo -o to see partition/node counts and CPUs:
  - sinfo -s shows partition with NODES(A/I/O/T) and quick state.
  - sinfo -o "%P %a %D %C" shows partition, availability, node count, and CPU(A/I/O/T).
- Use squeue to see current jobs consuming CPUs (per-user/partition filters).
- If you need a conditional action (e.g., submit only if idle nodes exist), first inspect sinfo (or sinfo + squeue) to confirm idle nodes/CPUs.

6) Scheduling and access caveats
- QOS, accounts, reservations, and limits can make a partition appear usable but still block your job (job held or backfilled by policy). If a partition is up and shows idle CPUs, your job still may be pending because of QOS/account limits or a reservation.
- Some systems use select/cons_tres for TRES-based allocation; that controls how CPUs/GRES are assigned.

7) Quick example requests
- Single multi-threaded task needing 8 CPU cores on cpu partition:
  sbatch --partition=cpu --cpus-per-task=8 --ntasks=1 myscript.sh
- MPI job with 16 ranks, 2 CPUs per rank:
  sbatch -p cpu --ntasks=16 --cpus-per-task=2 my_mpi_job.sh
- Force nodes with feature "highmem":
  sbatch -p cpu --constraint=highmem --cpus-per-task=4 myjob.sh

If you want, I can show the current "cpu" partition availability and CPU counts on your cluster (sinfo) or list running jobs using CPU resources (squeue). Which would you like me to check?

Short answer: sreport's "cluster utilization" reports summarize how cluster resources (CPU/GPU/memory, nodes) were used over a time window using accounting data from SlurmDB. They show usage (CPU/GPU/node minutes or hours), idle/time-down, and how usage is apportioned by account/user/QOS, so you can answer “how busy was the cluster and who used it?”

What the report contains (key fields)
- Allocated — time nodes were in use by active jobs or active reservations (this counts jobs inside reservations).
- Idle — time nodes were up and available but not running jobs.
- Down — time nodes were marked Down or fully Drained (and, optionally, time slurmctld was unresponsive if TrackSlurmctldDown is enabled).
- PlannedDown — time nodes were put into planned maintenance.
- OverCommitted — time nodes/TRES were charged beyond their physical capacity (oversubscription/shared scheduling).
- Reported / Cluster — totals/summary columns for the cluster and the reporting period.
- TresCount / TresName — which TRES (trackable resources: CPU, gres/gpu, memory, etc.) the usage numbers refer to.
- Other derived columns — depending on the sub-report you request you’ll also see Account, User, QOS, Wckey, % of cluster, etc.

Units and scope
- Usage is reported in time × resource units (the header will show the unit, commonly CPU minutes or CPU hours).
- The report is produced from SlurmDB (sreport uses accounting records), so it requires slurmdbd and accounting to be enabled and populated.

How to run common queries
- Cluster-wide utilization for a date range:
  sreport cluster Utilization Start=2024-04-01 End=2024-04-30
- Recent week:
  sreport cluster Utilization Start=now-7days
- See usage broken down by account or user:
  sreport cluster AccountUtilizationByUser Start=2024-04-01 End=2024-04-30
- Request specific output columns (FORMAT):
  sreport cluster Utilization Start=... Format=Cluster,Allocated,Idle,Down,TresCount,TresName

Interpretation tips
- Allocated + Idle + Down + PlannedDown should sum up to the total reportable node time for the period (modulo OverCommitted/reporting rounding).
- “Allocated” counts both jobs and reservations with active jobs. Reservations created with MAINT or IGNORE_JOBS are not counted as Allocated.
- OverCommitted flags indicate charged usage > physical capacity (useful to detect oversubscription or accounting oddities).
- Use TresName/TresCount to focus on GPU (gres/gpu) usage vs CPU-only usage.

Caveats and troubleshooting
- If SlurmDB is not configured or there is no historical data, sreport may return empty results.
- sreport reports what’s in accounting — if jobs were misconfigured/charged incorrectly, investigate with sacct/scontrol_show.
- For detailed per-job accounting or failed/completed histories use sacct; sreport is for aggregated usage/summary reports.

Where to read more
- The sreport reference (sreport(1)) documents all report types and FORMAT options — see the Slurm sreport manual for full field definitions and example invocations.

## Job Accounting Records [#job_record](https://slurm.schedmd.com/job_launch.html)
When Slurm is configured to use SlurmDBD to store job records (i.e.
AccountingStorageType=accounting_storage=slurmdbd ), there are multiple
records that get stored for each job. There is a record for the job as a
whole as well as entries for the following types of job steps:
- extern step — A step created for each job as long as you have PrologFlags=contain in your slurm.conf. Each node in the job will have a slurmstepd process created for the extern step. pam_slurm_adopt uses this step to contain external connections.
- batch step — A step created for jobs that were submitted with sbatch. The batch host, or the primary node for the job, will run an instance of slurmstepd for the batch step, which is used to run the script provided to sbatch.
- interactive step — A step created for jobs that were submitted with salloc when LaunchParameters=use_interactive...

Summary — what --gres=gpu:N means
- "--gres=gpu:N" requests N generic GPU resources per node for your job. It is equivalent to "--gpus-per-node N" (when Slurm is using the select/cons_tres plugin).
- There are also options with different semantics:
  - --gpus=<M> requests M GPUs per job (total across the allocation).
  - --gpus-per-node=<N> requests N GPUs per node (same as --gres=gpu:N).
  - --gpus-per-task=<k> requests k GPUs for each task (works with a task count).

How Slurm allocates those GPUs
- Allocation is done per-node (for --gres=gpu:N / --gpus-per-node) or per-job (for --gpus). If you ask for N GPUs per node and you get X nodes, total GPUs = N * X.
  - Example: #SBATCH --nodes=2 --gres=gpu:2  → 2 GPUs on each node, total 4 GPUs.
  - Example: #SBATCH --gpus=4 --nodes=2  → 4 GPUs total; Slurm will place those 4 across the allocation (not necessarily 2 per node).
- GPUs are consumable integer resources by default. Slurm reserves whole GPU devices, not fractional GPU time, unless the cluster is explicitly configured for sharing (see MPS, MIG, or custom GRES entries).
- Slurm maps specific device IDs on each node and sets CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES for each job step so the job sees only its assigned GPUs on that node. The variable is set when tasks are launched on compute nodes (sbatch’s top-level env may only reflect node 0).

Per-task behavior and task layouts
- If you run multiple tasks on a node (multiple tasks-per-node), how GPUs are divided depends on:
  - whether you used --gpus-per-task (or --gres per task) and the task count; Slurm will allocate GPUs per task accordingly, or
  - if you only requested GPUs per node, Slurm gives N GPUs to the node and it’s up to your task launcher / MPI / application to place tasks onto those GPUs.
- For deterministic per-task GPU assignment use --gpus-per-task together with --ntasks or use srun with task-affinity options.

Device naming, types, and selection
- The --gres argument accepts the form name[:type:count]. You can request a specific GPU type if configured in gres.conf (e.g., --gres=gpu:V100:2).
- Slurm uses the cluster’s gres.conf mapping (dev nodes like /dev/nvidia0, /dev/nvidia1, or MIG partitions) when assigning device indices.

Sharing (MPS / MIG / custom)
- NVIDIA MPS, MIG, or cluster-specific GRES entries can allow multiple jobs to share a physical GPU. That must be enabled/declared in gres.conf and supported by the select/cons_tres plugin. In those cases the GRES entry may represent slices or MPS capacity rather than whole devices.
- Without such configuration, jobs get exclusive GPUs.

What you will see and how to inspect
- Inside a running job step: echo $CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES shows the devices the step may use on that node.
- From the scheduler / admin view:
  - scontrol show job <jobid> shows AllocTRES / Gres and the node list for that job.
  - scontrol show node <nodename> or sinfo / sinfo -N shows per-node GRES and availability.
- If a job was rejected because the gres/cons_tres plugin isn’t configured, Slurm will reject GPU requests (look for messages from sbatch/salloc).

Common pitfalls
- Confusing “per node” vs “per job”: using --gres=gpu:N with multiple nodes multiplies the GPU count unless you intended a total-GPU request.
- Expecting fractional GPU sharing without cluster configuration (MPS/MIG) — by default Slurm reserves whole GPUs.
- Assuming CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES lists cluster-wide IDs — it’s per-node and remapped so the job only sees its local assigned GPUs.

- Show exact fields to check in scontrol show job / scontrol show node (example output fields), or
- Give example sbatch/srun lines for common layouts (4 GPUs total spanning 2 nodes, or 2 GPUs per node with 4 tasks per node).

## PERFORMANCE[#SECTION_PERFORMANCE](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Executing sbatch sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmctld daemon come in at once, it can result in
a degradation of performance of the slurmctld daemon, possibly resulting
in a denial of service.
Do not run sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other
programs. Ensure that programs limit calls to sbatch to the minimum
necessary for the information you are trying to gather.

## Initial Testing [#INITIAL_TESTING](https://slurm.schedmd.com/nss_slurm.html)
Before enabling NSS Slurm directly on the node, you should use the
-s slurm option to getent within a newly launched job step
to verify that the rest of the setup has been completed successfully. The
-s option to getent allows it to query a specific database —
even if it has not been enabled by default through the system's
nsswitch.conf . Note that nss_slurm only responds to requests from
processes within the job step itself — you must launch the getent
command within a job step to see any data returned.

tim@blackhole:~$ srun getent -s slurm passwd tim:x:1000:1000:Tim Wickberg:/home/tim:/bin/bash tim@blackhole:~$ srun getent -s slurm group tim:x:1000:tim projecta:x:1001:tim
```

# "Configless" Slurm
"Configless" Slurm is a feature that allows the compute nodes —
specifically the slurmd process — and user commands running on login
nodes to pull configuration information directly from the slurmctld instead of
from a pre-distributed local file. Your cluster does require a central set of

parlance means that the compute nodes, login nodes, and other cluster hosts
do not need to be deployed with local copies of these files.

either an explicit option, or — preferably — through DNS SRV

## Notes[#NOTES](https://slurm.schedmd.com/configless_slurm.html)
Starting from Slurm 25.11, there's a new
SlurmctldParameters=reconfig_on_restart option that will make every
restart of slurmctld (process restart not triggered by "scontrol reconfigure")
to trigger a reconfiguration request to all slurmd and sackd daemons. For
"configless" systems this will ensure all processes are running the current
configuration. Some caution should be taken if you intend to perform rolling
upgrades on the cluster as this could lead to the daemons being upgraded sooner

## PERFORMANCE[#SECTION_PERFORMANCE](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Executing sbatch sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmctld daemon come in at once, it can result in
a degradation of performance of the slurmctld daemon, possibly resulting
in a denial of service.
Do not run sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other

## PERFORMANCE[#SECTION_PERFORMANCE](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Executing sbatch sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmctld daemon come in at once, it can result in
a degradation of performance of the slurmctld daemon, possibly resulting
in a denial of service.
Do not run sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other
programs. Ensure that programs limit calls to sbatch to the minimum
necessary for the information you are trying to gather.

I looked up the official Slurm sbatch/manual docs and summarized the four dependency types you asked about. Short definitions, when they trigger, examples and typical uses:

1) after
- What it means: make the job eligible to start after the specified job(s) have started (i.e., after the referenced job(s) begin execution).
- Triggers: when the referenced job(s) have started running (does not wait for completion).
- Example: sbatch --dependency=after:12345 myjob.sh
- Use case: start something that can run concurrently once a producer has begun (e.g., start a consumer once producer is running), or coordinate start ordering without waiting for completion.

2) afterok
- What it means: start only after the specified job(s) have completed successfully (exit code 0).
- Triggers: when all referenced jobs have terminated with success (zero exit code).
- Example: sbatch --dependency=afterok:12345 next-step.sh
- Use case: multi-step workflows where later steps must run only if earlier steps succeed (build → test → deploy).

3) afterany
- What it means: start after the specified job(s) have terminated, regardless of their exit code (success or failure).
- Triggers: when all referenced jobs have finished in any terminal state.
- Example: sbatch --dependency=afterany:12345 postprocess.sh
- Use case: always-run follow-up tasks (e.g., archive logs or collect metrics) whether the upstream job succeeded or failed.

4) afternotok
- What it means: start only after the specified job(s) have terminated with a non‑zero (failing) exit code.
- Triggers: when any/all referenced jobs have finished and returned a non‑zero exit (i.e., failed).
- Example: sbatch --dependency=afternotok:12345 failure_handler.sh
- Use case: run remediation/alerting/cleanup only when an upstream job fails.

5) singleton (special)
- What it means: no job ID is passed; the job is held until all previously submitted jobs with the same user and job name have finished. Ensures only one job with that name/user runs at a time.
- Triggers: the new job becomes eligible after earlier jobs with the same name and user have terminated.
- Example: sbatch --job-name=data_proc --dependency=singleton data_proc.sh
- Use case: serialize repeated submissions of the same job (avoid parallel runs of the same job-name by the same user).

Notes and tips
- Syntax: --dependency=type:jobid[:jobid...] (singleton has no jobid).
- Combine dependencies: you can specify multiple dependencies (comma-separated) to express complex conditions.
- Choose afterok for success-only chaining, afterany when you must always continue, afternotok for failure-only handlers, after when you only need start ordering, and singleton to serialize same-name jobs.
- These definitions come from the sbatch man page / Slurm documentation.

### Job Scheduling Priority [#priority](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
Job scheduling priority is made up of a number of factors as
described in the [priority/multifactor](https://slurm.schedmd.com/priority_multifactor.html) plugin. One
of the factors is the QOS priority. Each QOS is defined in the Slurm
database and includes an associated priority. Jobs that request and
are permitted a QOS will incorporate the priority associated with that
QOS in the job's [multi-factor priority calculation.](https://slurm.schedmd.com/priority_multifactor.html)
To enable the QOS priority component of the multi-factor priority
calculation, the "PriorityWeightQOS" configuration parameter must be
defined in the slurm.conf file and assigned an integer value greater
than zero.
A job's QOS only affects is scheduling priority when the
multi-factor plugin is loaded.

A QOS can be attached to a partition. This means the partition will have all
the same limits as the QOS. This does not associate jobs with the QOS, nor does
it give the job any priority or preemption characteristics of the assigned QOS.
Jobs may separately request the same QOS or a different QOS to gain those

Below are concise, doc‑based explanations of the four Slurm pending reasons you asked about, what they mean, common causes, and how to diagnose or remediate them. Sources: Slurm job reason codes, QOS, and resource limits docs (job_reason_codes.html, qos.html, resource_limits.html).

1) Resources
- What it means
  - The job is pending because Slurm cannot currently find the compute resources (CPUs, memory, GPUs, TRES, nodes, sockets) required by the job request.
- Common causes
  - No nodes have enough free CPUs or memory to satisfy the per‑node or per‑job resource request.
  - Requested GRES (GPU type/count) are not idle on any node.
  - Exclusive/node‑level requests (e.g., --exclusive, --nodes=N with per‑node resource counts) cannot be satisfied by the available nodes.
  - Partition limits or reservations are holding the needed nodes.
- How to diagnose
  - squeue shows the pending reason (“Resources”).
  - Use sinfo (partition/node availability) and sinfo --Node or sinfo --long to see per‑node free resources.
  - Use scontrol show job <jobid> for the job’s requested TRES and details.
- Remediations
  - Reduce CPUs/memory/GPU count or change node/feature constraints.
  - Wait for running jobs to finish or request a different partition.
  - If resources are reserved/drained, consult the admin or check reservations (scontrol show reservation).

2) Priority
- What it means
  - The job is pending because other job(s) with higher scheduling priority are eligible to run before this job.
- Key notes from docs
  - Slurm computes job priority using a multi‑factor plugin (age, fairshare, QOS, job size, etc.). QOS contributes to priority if configured (PriorityWeightQOS > 0).
- Common causes
  - Newer jobs with a higher combined priority score (age, fairshare, QOS priority, etc.).
  - Your job’s account/user has lower fairshare or lower QOS priority.
- How to diagnose
  - squeue will list “Priority” as the reason and you can run sprio (or sprio --weights) to see priority factors for pending jobs.
  - sshare shows fairshare usage and effective shares.
- Remediations
  - Request a higher‑priority QOS (if permitted) or ask admins to adjust QOS/priority weights.
  - Reduce job size so it can fit into earlier backfill opportunities.
  - Wait — aging increases priority over time.

3) ReqNodeNotAvail (Requested Node Not Available)
- What it means
  - The job requested specific node(s) or node features that are not currently available (the requested node is down/drained/allocated, or feature constraints cannot be matched).
- Common causes
  - The job used node list/name constraints (e.g., --nodelist=) and that node is in use, drained, or down.
  - Feature (node feature/constraint) or partition membership mismatch (e.g., --constraint=featureX but no nodes with that feature are idle).
  - Reservation is on the node but your job isn’t matched to that reservation.
- How to diagnose
  - squeue shows the reason; use scontrol show job <jobid> to view nodelist/constraints.
  - Use sinfo and sinfo_reasons to see node states (DOWN, DRAIN) and reasons, and sinfo --Node to inspect node features and partition membership.
- Remediations
  - Remove or relax explicit node/nodelist constraints.
  - Choose a partition or constraint matching available nodes.
  - If the node is down/drained, contact admins or wait until it’s returned to service.

4) QOS limits (pending because of QOS/resource limits)
- What it means
  - The job is pending because the job’s requested resources or the job’s account/QOS would exceed configured limits (per‑QOS, per‑account, per‑partition limits). Depending on configuration, jobs that exceed limits either pend or are denied at submission.
- Key doc points
  - QOS and partition QOS can impose GrpTRES, MaxTRES, MaxJobs, MaxNodes, etc. Limits may be applied in a defined precedence (partition QOS may override job QOS unless Flags=OverPartQOS).
  - If a job request would breach a limit, by default the job will pend; if the QOS has DenyOnLimit set, the job may be denied on submission.
- Common causes
  - Your account or QOS has exceeded its allowed aggregate CPUs/GPU hours, concurrent jobs, or a per‑job/per‑node limit.
  - Partition QOS limits prevent the job from starting even if the job requests a different QOS.
- How to diagnose
  - squeue or scontrol show job <jobid> will show the pending reason (e.g., “AssocGrp”, “Max*PerAccount”, or a QOS‑related reason).
  - Use sacctmgr show qos and sacctmgr show association to inspect QOS and account limits.
  - Check resource_limits documentation for semantics of Max/Grp/PerJob/PerNode limits.
- Remediations
  - Request a different QOS or lower resource request.
  - Have an admin increase the QOS/account limits or change DenyOnLimit/OverPartQOS flags.
  - Redistribute jobs to other accounts/QOS if policy allows.

Quick troubleshooting checklist (commands to run)
- squeue -j <jobid> (confirm pending reason)
- scontrol show job <jobid> (detailed request, constraints, QOS)
- sinfo --long or sinfo --Node (node/partition availability and features)
- sprio / sprio --weights and sshare (priority/fairshare diagnostics)
- sacctmgr show qos / sacctmgr show association (QOS & limit settings)
- sinfo_reasons (if nodes are down/drained)

Starting in Slurm 23.11, a QOS may be configured to contain relative resource
limits instead of absolute limits by setting `Flags=Relative`.
When this flag is set, all resource limits are treated as percentages of the
total resources available. Values higher than 100 are interpreted as 100%.

be displayed, the limits will be enforced as a percentage (1MB = 1%).

## Hierarchy[#hierarchy](https://slurm.schedmd.com/resource_limits.html)
Slurm's hierarchical limits are enforced in the following order
with Job QOS and Partition QOS order being reversible by using the QOS
flag 'OverPartQOS':
- Partition QOS limit
- Job QOS limit
- User association
- Account association(s), ascending the hierarchy
- Root/Cluster association
- Partition limit
- None
Note: If limits are defined at multiple points in this hierarchy,
the point in this list where the limit is first defined will be used.
Consider the following example:
- MaxJobs=20 and MaxSubmitJobs is undefined in the partition QOS
- No limits are set in the job QOS and
- MaxJobs=4 and MaxSubmitJobs=50 in the user association
The limits in effect will be MaxJobs=20 and MaxSubmitJobs=50.

Job scheduling priority is made up of a number of factors as
described in the [priority/multifactor](https://slurm.schedmd.com/priority_multifactor.html) plugin. One

database and includes an associated priority. Jobs that request and
are permitted a QOS will incorporate the priority associated with that
QOS in the job's [multi-factor priority calculation.](https://slurm.schedmd.com/priority_multifactor.html)
To enable the QOS priority component of the multi-factor priority
calculation, the "PriorityWeightQOS" configuration parameter must be
defined in the slurm.conf file and assigned an integer value greater
than zero.

multi-factor plugin is loaded.

"configless" systems this will ensure all processes are running the current
configuration. Some caution should be taken if you intend to perform rolling

## Partition QOS [#partition](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
A QOS can be attached to a partition. This means the partition will have all
the same limits as the QOS. This does not associate jobs with the QOS, nor does
it give the job any priority or preemption characteristics of the assigned QOS.
Jobs may separately request the same QOS or a different QOS to gain those
characteristics. However, the Partition QOS limits will override the job's QOS.
If the opposite is desired you may configure the job's QOS with
`Flags=OverPartQOS` which will reverse the order of precedence.
This functionality may be used to implement a true "floating"
partition, in which a partition may access a limited amount of resources with no
restrictions on which nodes it uses to get the resources. This is accomplished
by assigning all nodes to the partition, then configuring a Partition QOS with
`GrpTRES` set to the desired resource limits.

### Job Preemption [#preemption](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
Slurm offers two ways for a queued job to preempt a running job,
free-up the running job's resources and allocate them to the queued
job. See the [Preemption description](https://slurm.schedmd.com/preempt.html) for
details.
The preemption method is determined by the "PreemptType"
configuration parameter defined in slurm.conf. When the "PreemptType"
is set to "preempt/qos", a queued job's QOS will be used to determine
whether it can preempt a running job. It is important to note that the QOS
used to determine if a job is eligible for preemption is the QOS associated
with the job and not a [Partition QOS](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html).
The QOS can be assigned (using sacctmgr ) a list of other
QOSs that it can preempt. When there is a queued job with a QOS that
is allowed to preempt a running job of another QOS, the Slurm
scheduler will preempt the running job.

### Job Scheduling Priority [#priority](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
Job scheduling priority is made up of a number of factors as
described in the [priority/multifactor](https://slurm.schedmd.com/priority_multifactor.html) plugin. One
of the factors is the QOS priority. Each QOS is defined in the Slurm
database and includes an associated priority. Jobs that request and
are permitted a QOS will incorporate the priority associated with that
QOS in the job's [multi-factor priority calculation.](https://slurm.schedmd.com/priority_multifactor.html)
To enable the QOS priority component of the multi-factor priority
calculation, the "PriorityWeightQOS" configuration parameter must be
defined in the slurm.conf file and assigned an integer value greater
than zero.
A job's QOS only affects is scheduling priority when the
multi-factor plugin is loaded.

## Relative QOS [#relative](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
Starting in Slurm 23.11, a QOS may be configured to contain relative resource
limits instead of absolute limits by setting `Flags=Relative`.
When this flag is set, all resource limits are treated as percentages of the
total resources available. Values higher than 100 are interpreted as 100%.
Memory limits should be set with no units. Although the default units (MB) will
be displayed, the limits will be enforced as a percentage (1MB = 1%).
NOTE : When Flags=Relative is added to a QOS, slurmctld
must be restarted or reconfigured for the flag to take effect.
Generally, the limits on a relative QOS will be calculated relative to the
resources in the whole cluster. For example, `cpu=50` would be

## Hierarchy[#hierarchy](https://slurm.schedmd.com/resource_limits.html)
Slurm's hierarchical limits are enforced in the following order
with Job QOS and Partition QOS order being reversible by using the QOS
flag 'OverPartQOS':
- Partition QOS limit
- Job QOS limit
- User association
- Account association(s), ascending the hierarchy
- Root/Cluster association
- Partition limit
- None
Note: If limits are defined at multiple points in this hierarchy,
the point in this list where the limit is first defined will be used.

- MaxJobs=20 and MaxSubmitJobs is undefined in the partition QOS

## Configuration[#config](https://slurm.schedmd.com/resource_limits.html)
Scheduling policy information must be stored in a database
as specified by the AccountingStorageType configuration parameter
in the slurm.conf configuration file.
Information can be recorded in a [MySQL](http://www.mysql.com/) or
[MariaDB](https://mariadb.org/) database.
For security and performance reasons, the use of
SlurmDBD (Slurm Database Daemon) as a front-end to the
database is strongly recommended.
SlurmDBD uses a Slurm authentication plugin (e.g. MUNGE).
SlurmDBD also uses an existing Slurm accounting storage plugin
to maximize code reuse.
SlurmDBD uses data caching and prioritization of pending requests
in order to optimize performance.
While SlurmDBD relies upon existing Slurm plugins for authentication
and database use, the other Slurm commands and daemons are not required
on the host where SlurmDBD is installed.

## Tools[#tools](https://slurm.schedmd.com/resource_limits.html)
The tool used to manage accounting policy is sacctmgr .
It can be used to create and delete cluster, user, account,
and partition records plus their combined association record.
See man sacctmgr for details on this tools and examples of
its use.
Changes made to the scheduling policy are uploaded to
the Slurm control daemons on the various clusters and take effect
immediately. When an association is deleted, all running or pending
jobs which belong to that association are immediately canceled.
When limits are lowered, running jobs will not be canceled to
satisfy the new limits, but the new lower limits will be enforced.

Short explanation of the common QOS limits and how they behave in Slurm:

- MaxWall
  - What it is: the maximum wall‑clock time (runtime) a job may request when using that QOS (format is a time value like 01:00:00).
  - Effect: it constrains the job's requested time. If a job requests more than the QOS MaxWall the cluster’s configured behavior (and QOS flags such as DenyOnLimit) determines whether the job is rejected at submission or the request is otherwise constrained/handled — administrators typically either reject the submission or enforce the smaller limit at allocation.
  - Notes: MaxWall is one of the time/node limits with special precedence rules in Slurm’s hierarchy; check the QOS and partition settings to see which limit wins.

- MaxJobs
  - What it is: the maximum number of concurrently running jobs allowed for the entity the limit is set on (a QOS, user association, account, etc.).
  - Effect: if starting a job would make the number of running jobs exceed MaxJobs for that entity, the job will not be started until resources are available. If the QOS has DenyOnLimit set, a submission that would violate MaxJobs can be rejected at submit time instead of simply pending.
  - Related limits: MaxSubmitJobs (controls number of jobs a user/account may have submitted/pending) and GrpJobs (aggregate running jobs limit for a group/account).

- GrpTRES
  - What it is: group (aggregate) limits expressed as TRES (Trackable RESources) like cpu, mem, node, or generic resources (gres). Example syntax: GrpTRES=gres/gpu=8,cpu=128,mem=512G.
  - Effect: GrpTRES limits the sum of the named resources used by all jobs in the group/association/QOS/partition. Slurm tests GrpTRES when it considers starting a job — if launching the job would push the aggregate usage over the GrpTRES value, the job will not be considered for allocation (it will remain pending). If DenyOnLimit is set the job may be rejected at submission instead.
  - Typical uses: enforce a cap on total GPUs, total CPUs, or total memory used by an account or QOS so one group can’t monopolize a resource pool.

How limits are evaluated (important rules)
- Limits are hierarchical. Slurm checks limits in a defined order (partition QOS, job QOS, user association, account, cluster, partition), and the first applicable limit wins (there are special-case exceptions for some limits like MaxWall/MaxTime).
- Grp* (group) limits are evaluated at job allocation time and are considered like a Max limit when DenyOnLimit is set.
- DenyOnLimit flag: when set for a QOS (or association), jobs that would violate a Max limit are rejected at submission time rather than pend.
- TRES names: use Slurm TRES names (cpu, mem, node, gres/gpu, etc.). You can list available TRES with sacctmgr show tres on a system.

Examples
- QOS A sets MaxJobs=10 → users or that QOS can have at most 10 running jobs at once.
- QOS B sets GrpTRES=gres/gpu=16 → the total GPUs used by all jobs tied to that QOS/account cannot exceed 16.
- QOS C sets MaxWall=12:00:00 → jobs requesting more than 12 hours will be subject to the QOS/deny policy (rejection or limit enforcement).

Commands to inspect/change (admin)
- View QOS limits: sacctmgr show qos format=... (or sacctmgr show qos)
- See available TRES: sacctmgr show tres
- Modify QOS or association limits: sacctmgr (admins only)

## Configuration[#config](https://slurm.schedmd.com/resource_limits.html)
Scheduling policy information must be stored in a database
as specified by the AccountingStorageType configuration parameter
in the slurm.conf configuration file.

For security and performance reasons, the use of
SlurmDBD (Slurm Database Daemon) as a front-end to the
database is strongly recommended.

SlurmDBD also uses an existing Slurm accounting storage plugin
to maximize code reuse.
SlurmDBD uses data caching and prioritization of pending requests

and database use, the other Slurm commands and daemons are not required
on the host where SlurmDBD is installed.

Short answer
- If the limit you’re hitting is set on your account/association (affects all users of that account, affects long‑term charging/fairshare), ask for an account/association limit change.
- If you need a temporary or user‑specific change (higher priority, different preemption, longer walltime cap, or a temporary raise that shouldn’t change the account policy) request a QOS change or a temporary QOS assignment (or reservation).

Why — the important rules
- Slurm applies limits in a hierarchy. Relevant part: Partition QOS → Job QOS → User association → Account association → cluster. The first place a limit is defined wins for that limit.
- QOS is designed for scheduling behavior (priority, preemption, grace time, deny-on-limit) and for per‑job or per‑user policy tuning. Accounts/associations are for accounting, group quotas, and persistent limits across all users in that account.

How to decide (practical checklist)
1. Which limit is actually blocking the job?
   - If the job is pending/denied with a message mentioning a QOS limit, request a QOS change.
   - If the message or admin says “account association limit” or the restriction affects everyone on that account, request an account/association change.
2. Scope of the change you want:
   - Scope = individual / temporary → QOS (or temporary QOS assignment or reservation).
   - Scope = group / permanent → account/association change.
3. Type of limit:
   - Need more concurrent jobs or submits (MaxJobs, MaxSubmitJobs) — could be set at QOS, user association, or account. Check which level currently defines it; if it’s at account level and should apply to whole group, change the account. If you only need it for yourself/one workflow, change QOS.
   - Need higher priority or different preemption/GraceTime → QOS.
   - Need larger long‑term CPU/GPU or walltime caps for the whole group → account/association.
   - Need billing/fairshare changes or permanent quota increases → account/association.
4. Temporary urgent runs:
   - Prefer a temporary QOS elevation or a reservation rather than changing account limits.

What to include in a request (to help admins decide quickly)
- Which exact limit name (MaxJobs, MaxSubmitJobs, MaxCPUs/CPUsPerUser, MaxWall/MaxTime, TRES/GPU limits, etc.), current value, and what value you request.
- Evidence (job ID and squeue / scontrol error or the denial/pending message).
- Scope: “for user bob only / for account teamX / for 7 days / permanent.”
- Justification: expected resource usage, why existing limits are inadequate, and whether this is temporary or permanent.
- Any billing/fairshare/account implications if relevant.

Examples
- Bob is getting “Denied: QOS MaxJobs exceeded” for a job he submitted: request a QOS change (or ask to be granted a different QOS) — likely quick and scoped.
- Bob’s whole research group can’t run more than N concurrent jobs because the group account has MaxSubmitJobs=50: request an account/association limit increase (affects the group).
- Bob needs higher priority to meet a deadline: request temporary higher‑priority QOS or a reservation.

If you want, I can:
- Help inspect which limit is actually being hit (what squeue/scontrol shows) if you give a job ID or the exact error message — that will tell us whether it’s QOS or account.

## PERFORMANCE[#SECTION_PERFORMANCE](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Executing sbatch sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmctld daemon come in at once, it can result in
a degradation of performance of the slurmctld daemon, possibly resulting
in a denial of service.
Do not run sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other
programs. Ensure that programs limit calls to sbatch to the minimum
necessary for the information you are trying to gather.

Specify a batch script by filename on the command line. The batch script specifies a 1 minute time limit for the job.
```text

Pass a batch script to sbatch on standard input:

```text

## Overview[#overview](https://slurm.schedmd.com/job_array.html)
Job arrays offer a mechanism for submitting and managing collections of
similar jobs quickly and easily, useful for repetitive workloads that follow a
common job pattern. This greatly improves overall performance, since job arrays
with millions of tasks can be submitted in milliseconds (subject to configured
size limits) and the scheduler can quickly identify cases when no more array
tasks are eligible to start.
All jobs must have the same initial options (e.g., size, time limit), however,
it is possible to change some of these options after the job has begun
execution using the scontrol command specifying the JobID of the array or
individual ArrayJobID .
```text
$ scontrol update job=101 ... $ scontrol update job=101_1 ...
```

A job which is to be dependent upon an entire job array should specify

## System Administration [#administration](https://slurm.schedmd.com/job_array.html)
A new configuration parameter has been added to control the maximum
job array size: MaxArraySize . The smallest index that can be specified
by a user is zero and the maximum index is MaxArraySize minus one.
The default value of MaxArraySize is 1001.
The maximum MaxArraySize supported in Slurm is 4000001.
Be mindful about the value of MaxArraySize as job arrays offer an easy way
for users to submit large numbers of jobs very quickly.

The salloc , sbatch and srun commands can all be used

be used for subsequent components to the extent which is expected to be helpful.

## PERFORMANCE[#SECTION_PERFORMANCE](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Executing sbatch sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmctld daemon come in at once, it can result in
a degradation of performance of the slurmctld daemon, possibly resulting
in a denial of service.
Do not run sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other
programs. Ensure that programs limit calls to sbatch to the minimum
necessary for the information you are trying to gather.
