## PERFORMANCE[#SECTION_PERFORMANCE](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Executing sbatch sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmctld daemon come in at once, it can result in
a degradation of performance of the slurmctld daemon, possibly resulting
in a denial of service.
Do not run sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other
programs. Ensure that programs limit calls to sbatch to the minimum
necessary for the information you are trying to gather.

## EXAMPLES[#SECTION_EXAMPLES](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Specify a batch script by filename on the command line. The batch script specifies a 1 minute time limit for the job.
```text
$ cat myscript #!/bin/sh #SBATCH --time=1 srun hostname |sort $ sbatch -N4 myscript salloc: Granted job allocation 65537 $ cat slurm-65537.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
Pass a batch script to sbatch on standard input:
```text
$ sbatch -N4 #!/bin/sh > srun hostname |sort > EOF sbatch: Submitted batch job 65541 $ cat slurm-65541.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
To create a heterogeneous job with 3 components, each allocating a unique set of nodes:
```text
$ sbatch -w node[2-3] : -w node4 : -w node[5-7] work.bash Submitted batch job 34987
```

## Submitting Jobs [#submitting](https://slurm.schedmd.com/heterogeneous_jobs.html)
The salloc , sbatch and srun commands can all be used
to submit heterogeneous jobs.
Resource specifications for each component of the heterogeneous job should be
separated with ":" character.
For example:
```text
$ sbatch --cpus-per-task=4 --mem-per-cpu=1 --ntasks=128 : \ --cpus-per-task=1 --mem-per-cpu=16 --ntasks=1 my.bash
```
Options specified for one component of a heterogeneous job (or job step) will
be used for subsequent components to the extent which is expected to be helpful.
Propagated options can be reset as desired for each component (e.g. a different
account name could be specified for each hetjob component.
For example, --immediate and --job-name are propagated, while
--ntasks and --mem-per-cpu are reset to default values for each
component.
A list of propagated options follows.
- --account
- --acctg-freq
- --begin

similar jobs quickly and easily, useful for repetitive workloads that follow a
common job pattern. This greatly improves overall performance, since job arrays

Section: Slurm Commands (1) Updated: Slurm Commands Index 

 
   
 NAME 
sbatch - Submit a batch script to Slurm.
 
   
 SYNOPSIS 
 sbatch [ OPTIONS(0) ...] [ : [ OPTIONS(N) ...]] script(0) [ args(0) ...]
 
Option(s) define multiple jobs in a co-scheduled heterogeneous job.
For more details about heterogeneous jobs see the document
 

 https://slurm.schedmd.com/heterogeneous_jobs.html 
 
   
 DESCRIPTION 
sbatch submits a batch script to Slurm. The batch script may be given to
sbatch through a file name on the command line, or if no file name is specified,
sbatch will read in a script from standard input.
 
The batch script may contain one or more lines beginning with "#SBATCH" followed
by any of the CLI options documented on this page. #SBATCH directives are read
directly by Slurm, so shell-specific syntax including variable names will be
read as literal text. Once the first non-comment, non-whitespace line has been
reached in the script, no more #SBATCH directives will be processed. See example
below.
 
sbatch exits immediately after the script is successfully transferred to the
Slurm controller and assigned a Slurm job ID. The batch script is not
necessarily granted resources immediately, it may sit in the queue of pending
jobs for some time before its required resources become available.
 
By default both standard output and standard error are directed to a file of
the name "slurm-%j.out", where the "%j" is replaced with the job allocation
number. The file will be generated on the first node of the job allocation.
Other than the batch script itself, Slurm does no movement of user files.
 
When the job allocation is finally granted for the batch script, Slurm
runs a single copy of the batch script on the first node in the set of
allocated nodes.
 
The following document describes the influence of various options on the
allocation of cpus to jobs and tasks.
 

 https://slurm.schedmd.com/cpu_management.html 
 
   
 RETURN VALUE 
sbatch will return 0 on success or error code on failure.
 
   
 SCRIPT PATH RESOLUTION 
 
The batch script is resolved in the following order:
 

 
1. If script starts with ".", then path is constructed as:
current working directory / script
 

2. If script starts with a "/", then path is considered absolute.
 

3. If script is in current working directory.
 

4. If script can be resolved through PATH. See path_resolution (7).
 

 

Current working directory is the calling process working directory unless the
 --chdir argument is passed, which will override the current working
directory.
 
   
 OPTIONS 
 

 
 
 -A , --account =< account > Charge resources used by this job to specified account.
The account is an arbitrary string. The account name may
be changed after job submission using the scontrol 
command.

This can be used to override the JobAcctGatherFrequency parameter in

# Advanced Resource Reservation Guide
Slurm has the ability to reserve resources for jobs
being executed by select users and/or QOS and/or partitions and/or select
accounts.
A resource reservation identifies the resources in that reservation
and a time period during which the reservation is available.
The resources which can be reserved include cores, nodes, licenses and/or
burst buffers.
A reservation that contains nodes or cores is associated with one partition,
and can't span resources over multiple partitions.
The only exception from this is when
the reservation is created with explicitly requested nodes.
Note that resource reservations are not compatible with Slurm's
gang scheduler plugin since the termination time of running jobs
cannot be accurately predicted.

## Magnetic Reservations [#magnetic](https://slurm.schedmd.com/reservations.html)
The default behavior for reservations is that jobs must request a
reservation in order to run in it. The MAGNETIC flag allows you to
create a reservation that will allow jobs to run in it without requiring that
they specify the name of the reservation. The reservation will only "attract"
jobs that meet the access control requirements.
NOTE : Magnetic reservations cannot "attract" heterogeneous jobs -
heterogeneous jobs will only run in magnetic reservations if they explicitly
request the reservation.
The following example shows a reservation created on node05. The user
specified as being able to access the reservation then submits a job and
the job starts on the reserved node.
```text
$ scontrol create reservation user=user1 nodes=node05 starttime=now duration=10 flags=magnetic Reservation created: user1_850 $ scontrol show res ReservationName=user1_850 St...

Below is a concise summary of the sbatch/srun --reservation option and the common reservation access rules and behaviors in Slurm.

What --reservation does
- --reservation=<name> (sbatch, srun, salloc) tells Slurm to schedule the job inside the named reservation. The job must fit completely inside the reservation’s resources and time window.
- If a job runs inside a reservation it is considered for those reserved resources first (the reservation acts as a scheduling boost), but specifying a reservation does not otherwise change a job’s base priority.
- If the reservation expires while a job is running, the job will be canceled at EndTime unless ResvOverRun (slurm.conf) or other configuration allows overrun.

How reservations are created/managed (admin only)
- Reservations are created/edited/deleted by administrators (scontrol create/delete reservation, scontrol update, etc.). Users cannot create cluster-wide reservations unless given special privileges.
- Use scontrol show reservation (or scontrol show res) to list reservation details; scontrol show reservation ReservationName=<name> shows the ACLs and resource scope.

Reservation resource types and scope
- Reservations may reserve whole nodes or specific core counts (NodeCnt/CoreCnt), licenses, or burst buffers.
- A reservation is normally tied to a single partition (unless nodes are explicitly listed when creating it).
- A job requesting a reservation must request resources that lie within the reservation (nodes, cores, mem, time); heterogeneous jobs have special limitations (see MAGNETIC notes below).

Access controls / ACLs
- A reservation can restrict who may use it by specifying one or more of:
  - Users= (allow user list)
  - Accounts= (allow account list)
  - QOS= (allow QOS list)
  - Partition= (restrict to a partition)
- ACLs are inclusive: specifying Users=alice,bob means alice OR bob may use it (job must match one).
- Exclusions are supported by prefixing a name with '-' in the ACL lists: Users=-baduser prevents that user from using the reservation even if they otherwise match an allowed account.
- If an ACL lists accounts, the job must be submitted under one of those accounts (or a user that matches Users=). If multiple ACL fields are present the job must satisfy all stated constraints.

MAGNETIC reservations (automatic attraction)
- By default, a job must explicitly name a reservation to run inside it.
- A reservation with the MAGNETIC flag “attracts” eligible jobs that meet the ACLs even when those jobs do not name the reservation; the reservation will pull matching jobs onto reserved nodes.
- Magnetic reservations do not automatically attract heterogeneous jobs — those must explicitly request the reservation name.

Other useful flags and behaviors
- REPLACE (and REPLACE_DOWN): can be used to keep a reservation’s size constant by replacing downed or allocated nodes (administrator-configurable; read the docs for limitations).
- Reservations that reserve licenses or burst buffers behave slightly differently than core/node reservations — check doc for reservation-specific details for non-core resources.
- Reservation names are typically returned/printed when created; jobs must use that exact reservation name (or rely on MAGNETIC attraction if enabled).
- Jobs that request only part of a reservation’s resources must still be fully contained (they cannot exceed the reservation’s resources or time).

How users typically request a reservation
- Explicit request: sbatch --reservation=<RESNAME> myscript.sh
- Interactive: salloc --reservation=<RESNAME> ... or srun --reservation=<RESNAME> ...
- If you try to use a reservation you are not allowed to access (ACL mismatch), Slurm will reject the job submission or place it pending with an access-related reason.

Where to check details (as a user)
- Ask your admin for the reservation name and ACLs, or run (if permitted): scontrol show reservation <name> (admins can always run this).
- If your job is pending while trying to use a reservation, check squeue for the pending reason; admins can inspect reservation internals.

If you want, I can:
- Show the reservation ACL and resource scope for a specific reservation (provide reservation name) — read-only (I’ll run scontrol/scontrol_reservation_show).
- Explain a specific pending reason you see when trying to use a reservation (provide job ID or squeue output).

## Failure Handling [#failure_handling](https://slurm.schedmd.com/prolog_epilog.html)
If the Epilog fails (returns a non-zero exit code), this will result in the
node being set to a DRAIN state.
If the EpilogSlurmctld fails (returns a non-zero exit code), this will only
be logged.
If the Prolog fails (returns a non-zero exit code), this will result in the
node being set to a DRAIN state and the job requeued. The job will be placed
in a held state unless nohold_on_prolog_fail is configured in
SchedulerParameters.
If the PrologSlurmctld fails (returns a non-zero exit code), this will cause
the job to be requeued. Only batch jobs can be requeued. Interactive jobs
(salloc and srun) will be cancelled if the PrologSlurmctld fails.
If a task epilog or srun epilog fails (returns a non-zero exit code) this
will only be logged.
If a task prolog fails (returns a non-zero exit code), the task will be

## Overview[#overview](https://slurm.schedmd.com/job_array.html)
Job arrays offer a mechanism for submitting and managing collections of
similar jobs quickly and easily, useful for repetitive workloads that follow a
common job pattern. This greatly improves overall performance, since job arrays
with millions of tasks can be submitted in milliseconds (subject to configured
size limits) and the scheduler can quickly identify cases when no more array
tasks are eligible to start.
All jobs must have the same initial options (e.g., size, time limit), however,
it is possible to change some of these options after the job has begun
execution using the scontrol command specifying the JobID of the array or
individual ArrayJobID .
```text
$ scontrol update job=101 ... $ scontrol update job=101_1 ...
```

## Job Allocation [#job_allocation](https://slurm.schedmd.com/job_launch.html)
The first step of the process is to create a job allocation, which is
a claim on compute resources. A job allocation can be created using the
salloc , sbatch or srun command. The salloc and
sbatch commands create resource allocations while the srun
command will create a resource allocation (if not already running within one)
plus launch tasks. Each of these commands will fill in a data structure
identifying the specifications of the job allocation requirement (e.g. node
count, task count, etc.) based upon command line options and environment
variables and send the RPC to the slurmctld daemon. The UID and GID of
the user launching the job will be included in a credential which will be used
later to restrict access to the job, so further steps run in the allocation

Short answer
- scontrol requeue <jobid> tells Slurm to take the specified job out of its current allocation and place it back into the pending queue so the scheduler can try to run it again (same job ID).

What actually happens
- If the job is RUNNING: Slurm terminates the job allocation (resources are released), any configured epilog/epilogSlurmctld will run, the job is marked REQUEUED while being processed, its requeue counter/flags are updated, and the job is returned to PENDING so the scheduler can reschedule it.
- If the job is PENDING: the command marks it for requeue (no allocation to terminate) and it remains eligible to be scheduled again.
- Job arrays / heterogeneous jobs: requeue on an array/heterogeneous job leader applies to all tasks/components (you may specify individual array elements with the array notation).
- Interactive allocations: interactive jobs (salloc/srun) are generally not requeued the same way as batch jobs; batch jobs are the usual target for requeue operations.
- Authorization: the command requires the job owner or a privileged user/operator.
- Side effects and limits: prolog/epilog behavior may run on termination and on the subsequent allocation; requeueing can be constrained by site policy/QOS/MaxRequeue settings, so it can be denied or limited by scheduler configuration.

When to use it
- To restart a job after a transient failure or after moving it off problematic nodes, to attempt scheduling on different nodes, or to re-run a batch job without creating a new job submission.

Example form
- scontrol requeue <jobid>

Short answer
- dependency=singleton serializes jobs so only one job from the same “singleton group” can be active at a time. Use it by passing --dependency=singleton to sbatch or srun for batch submissions.

What it does (semantics)
- When you submit a job with --dependency=singleton, Slurm will not start that job while another job in the same singleton group is still active (pending or running). The newly submitted job is held in the queue and becomes eligible only after the earlier job has finished (regardless of that job’s exit code).
- In practice the singleton group is determined by the submitting user and the job name (the job-name given with --job-name / -J). In other words, jobs with the same user and same job name are serialized by singleton.

How it differs from other dependencies
- singleton waits for completion of the earlier job(s) regardless of success or failure. Contrast that with afterok (which requires the predecessor to exit successfully) or afterany (which requires completion but is expressed with explicit job IDs).
- singleton is about preventing concurrent runs of “the same” job, not about sequencing specific job IDs.

Typical uses
- Prevent overlapping runs of a periodic task or workflow (for example, ensure a nightly data-processing job never runs concurrently with a previous run).
- Ensure only one instance of a named worker/ingest job is active per user.

Usage example
- sbatch --job-name=myjob --dependency=singleton myjob.sh

Notes and caveats
- singleton does not stop multiple submissions; it only delays start time so jobs run one at a time.
- It is enforced by the scheduler; it does not change job exit behavior or automatically cancel jobs.
- If you need sequencing that depends on success/failure, use afterok/afternotok/afterany instead.

## PERFORMANCE[#SECTION_PERFORMANCE](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Executing sbatch sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmctld daemon come in at once, it can result in
a degradation of performance of the slurmctld daemon, possibly resulting
in a denial of service.
Do not run sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other
programs. Ensure that programs limit calls to sbatch to the minimum
necessary for the information you are trying to gather.

## EXAMPLES[#SECTION_EXAMPLES](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Specify a batch script by filename on the command line. The batch script specifies a 1 minute time limit for the job.
```text

## PERFORMANCE[#SECTION_PERFORMANCE](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Executing sbatch sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmctld daemon come in at once, it can result in
a degradation of performance of the slurmctld daemon, possibly resulting
in a denial of service.
Do not run sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other
programs. Ensure that programs limit calls to sbatch to the minimum
necessary for the information you are trying to gather.

## SYNOPSIS[#SECTION_SYNOPSIS](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
sbatch [ OPTIONS(0) ...] [ : [ OPTIONS(N) ...]] script(0) [ args(0) ...]
Option(s) define multiple jobs in a co-scheduled heterogeneous job.
For more details about heterogeneous jobs see the document
[https://slurm.schedmd.com/heterogeneous_jobs.html](https://slurm.schedmd.com/heterogeneous_jobs.html)

Summary (from the official Slurm sbatch docs)

- What afterok does
  - afterok is a submission-time dependency type. A job submitted with --dependency=afterok:jobid[,jobid...] will not become eligible to run until the listed job(s) have completed successfully (i.e., exited with code 0). Only when all specified predecessor jobs finish with exit code 0 is the dependency considered satisfied.

- Syntax
  - Command-line:
    --dependency=afterok:12345
    --dependency=afterok:12345,12346
  - In a script:
    #SBATCH --dependency=afterok:12345
  - Multiple dependency specifications may be combined (comma-separated), e.g. --dependency=afterok:12345,afterany:12346

- Job arrays and task IDs
  - You may reference array tasks using the usual job array notation (e.g. afterok:1234_5). You can also reference the array master id depending on what you need.

- Typical usage patterns
  - Serial chaining:
      jid1=$(sbatch job1.sh | awk '{print $NF}')
      sbatch --dependency=afterok:$jid1 job2.sh
  - Multiple predecessors: the dependent job waits until every listed predecessor completes successfully.

- Behavior on predecessor failure
  - If any listed predecessor exits with a non‑zero status, the afterok dependency is not satisfied for that predecessor. The dependent job will remain pending on its dependency (it will not run). If you want the dependent job to run regardless of predecessor exit status, use afterany; if you want it to run only when predecessors fail, use afternotok.

- Notes / reminders from the sbatch manual
  - Dependencies are recorded at submission time by job ID(s). If you submit jobs programmatically, capture the numeric job IDs returned by sbatch and use them in the dependent sbatch call.
  - Dependency types and full --dependency syntax (multiple types, commas, etc.) are described in the sbatch man page.

- RawShares = configured share weight
- NormShares = normalized share (relative entitlement)
- EffectvUsage = effective recent usage (higher = more used; penalizes priority)

Output rows (Account / User / RawShares / NormShares / EffectvUsage)

- general / charlie / 0.100 / 0.200 / 0.400

Interpretation
- Alice’s NormShares = 0.420 but her EffectvUsage = 1.800. Her usage is ~4.29× her normalized share (1.800 / 0.420 ≈ 4.29). That means she has consumed far more than her fair share recently and will be strongly deprioritized by the fairshare factor.
- Bob and Charlie have also used more than their normalized share but to a much lesser degree (Bob ~1.84×, Charlie 2.0×), so they are less penalized than Alice.
- Root has EffectvUsage = 0.0 (no recent usage) and thus will have the highest fairshare priority.

What this means for Alice’s jobs
- New or pending jobs from alice will be scheduled with much lower priority than users with lower effective usage (e.g., root, then bob/charlie), until her effective usage decays or others’ usage increases.
- To improve scheduling priority you can: wait for usage to decay over the fairshare half-life, reduce Alice’s current running/queued usage, or change share/association settings (administrative changes).

Short answer
- The pending reason "Priority" means the scheduler attempted to place the job but did not find a placement because other jobs with higher computed priority took the available resources. In other words: your job is eligible to run but is ranked below others by Slurm’s priority system, so it waits.

What determines that priority
- Slurm’s default multifactor priority plugin computes a single numeric priority from a weighted sum of factors (site, age, association, fairshare, job size, partition, QOS, TRES factors, minus nice). See the formula in the Multifactor Priority docs.
- Priorities are integers (0 .. 4294967295). Larger = higher scheduling precedence.
- Common factors: age (older jobs gain priority), association/account priority, fairshare (historical usage), QOS and partition priority, job size (smaller/larger can be advantaged depending on config), per-account limits, and any per-user/account “priority” settings.

When Priority appears vs other reasons
- Only one reason is shown for a pending job. "Priority" is shown when the scheduler’s placement attempt fails because higher-priority jobs occupy the resources needed.
- If resources are simply not present (no free nodes), other reasons such as Resources, NodeDown, PartitionDown, or Coscheduling may appear instead.
- A job can show Priority even if resources are available overall: higher-priority jobs are first in the scheduling order and claim the available slots.

How to inspect why a job is showing Priority
- squeue (shows REASON column): check the job’s REASON.
- scontrol show job <jobid> (shows numeric Priority= value and other job fields).
- sprio (or sprio -l / sprio --weights) to see each job’s computed priority and factor contributions/weights.
- squeue + sprio will let you see the competing jobs, their priorities, and which factor(s) are giving them advantage.

Commands you can run (examples)
- squeue -o "%.18i %.9P %.20j %.8u %.2t %.10M %.R"     (show job ID, partition, name, user, state, time, REASON)
- scontrol show job <jobid>
- sprio            (or sprio -l) to list job priorities and contributing factors
- sprio --weights  (show configured factor weights)

Ways to get a job to run sooner (user-level options)
- Increase job priority indirectly: request a higher-QOS (if available) or a QOS with higher priority value.
- Use sbatch --nice to lower the job’s nice value (if your cluster allows it), or ask your admin to adjust association/account priority or QOS.
- Submit smaller jobs or change resource request to better fit available nodes (job size factor can matter).
- Wait: age factor increases over time, raising priority.

Admin-level controls (require admin)
- Adjust priority weights in slurm.conf (PriorityWeightAge, PriorityWeightFairshare, etc.) and reconfigure.
- Change association/account priority or QOS settings via sacctmgr.
- Inspect scheduler logs or use sprio_weights / scontrol show config for configured behavior.

Below is a concise guide to what “cluster utilization” means in Slurm, which Slurm reports/tools expose the important metrics, how to read them, common utilization problems and how to diagnose them, and the common levers you can use to improve utilization.

What “utilization” means
- At a basic level it’s how much of the cluster capacity is doing useful work over a time window.
  - Node/CPU/GPU utilization: fraction of node/CPU/GPU time allocated to active jobs vs total available time.
  - Job efficiency: how much of the allocated resources each job actually uses (CPU%, memory RSS, GPU usage).
  - Scheduling/backfill efficiency: how well the scheduler fills gaps in the schedule (short jobs, small jobs) without delaying larger jobs.
- Slurm expresses these as alloc-times (node-hours / cpu-hours / gpu-hours), percent utilization, and derived ratios (backfill efficiency, queue wait times).

Key Slurm tools and the metrics they provide (what to run and why)
- sreport (cluster utilization reports)
  - Best for summary usage over a time window (Allocated, Down, Idle, Utilization, CPU-hours, GPU-hours).
  - Use for accounting-level reports: utilization by account/user/QoS/partition.
  - Example: sreport cluster Utilization Start=now-7days End=now
- sinfo
  - Current partition/node states (allocated/idle/drain/down), per-node resources (CPUs, memory, GPUs).
  - Use to see physical capacity and which nodes are unavailable.
  - Example: sinfo -N -l
- squeue
  - Real-time view of running vs pending jobs and pending reasons.
  - For “why jobs aren’t starting” start with squeue (look at the REASON column).
  - Example: squeue --states=RUNNING,PENDING -o "%.18i %.20P %.20j %.8u %.2t %.10M %.10R"
- sdiag
  - Scheduler diagnostics: scheduling cycles, backfill stats, server thread count, queue depth, dispatch counters.
  - Use when you suspect scheduler throughput/backfill problems, or many short jobs.
  - Example: sdiag
- sprio and sshare
  - sprio: per-job priority factors (fairshare, age, QOS, partition) — helps explain why some jobs are low priority.
  - sshare: fairshare usage and effective shares by user/account.
- sstat (and job-level monitoring)
  - Real-time job resource usage (CPU%, memory RSS, I/O) for running jobs.
  - Use to measure actual utilization vs requested.
- sacct
  - Historical accounting: job durations, requested vs used resources, exit codes — for efficiency and waste analysis.
  - Example: sacct -S 2026-04-01 -E 2026-04-30 --format=JobID,User,JobName,State,Elapsed,ReqCPUS,MaxRSS
- scontrol show config / scontrol show node / scontrol show job
  - Inspect scheduler/node/job configuration that affects allocation and packing.
- scontrol_reservation_show
  - Shows reservations that reduce available capacity.

What each metric tells you (how to interpret)
- sreport “Allocated” and “Utilization” (over interval)
  - Allocated = time nodes were used for active jobs or reservations.
  - Utilization (%) = Allocated time / (Available time minus Down/Maintenance time). Low % means idle capacity or blocked capacity.
- sinfo NODES(A/I/D)
  - Check the A/I/D counts: if Idle (I) is high, jobs aren’t being scheduled to them (fragmentation, constraints, reservations, or pending reasons).
- squeue pending reasons
  - Common reasons: Resources, QOSLimit, Priority, Dependency, PartitionDown, ReqNodeNotAvail.
  - “Resources” + idle nodes often implies resource mismatches (gres, feature, memory) or fragmentation.
- sdiag backfill stats
  - Low backfill usage when there are gaps suggests packing/fragmentation or conservative backfill window calculations.
- sprio/sshare
  - A user’s large share deficit or low priority weight can starve smaller/short jobs — fairshare or QOS limits may be the cause.
- sstat / sacct usage vs requests
  - Jobs that request more CPUs/GPUs/memory than they use indicate over-requesting (wasteful). For example, low CPU% or MaxRSS much lower than ReqMem signals inefficiency.
- Node “Down/Drained”
  - Nodes taken out reduce usable capacity; sinfo_reasons can show why they’re down.

Common utilization problems, causes, and the diagnostic checklist
1) Low cluster utilization despite queued jobs
   - Check: squeue (REASON), sinfo (idle nodes), scontrol_reservation_show (reservations).
   - Causes: partition/node constraints (features, GRES like GPUs), reservations, oversized resource requests (job asks for full node), affinity/packing policy prevents placement, per-user/account limits, or scheduler not backfilling effectively.
2) High utilization but long queue wait times
   - Check: sdiag (scheduling throughput), sprio (priorities), sshare (fairshare), sacct (job sizes).
   - Causes: cluster is saturated with long or large jobs; priority/fairshare/QoS limits favor certain users; insufficient backfill.
3) Many nodes partially used (fragmentation)
   - Check: scontrol show config (allocation/SelectTypeParameters), sdiag, squeue.
   - Causes: allocation policy (ONE_PER_NODE vs pack), job shapes (many single-core jobs scattered), lack of node sharing.
4) Jobs use far less than requested resources
   - Check: sstat (running), sacct (historical MaxRSS, CPU), sreport usage by user.
   - Causes: users over-request resources — leads to wasted reserved capacity.
5) GPU-specific underutilization
   - Check: sinfo for GRES allocation, squeue for jobs holding GPUs, job-level GPU telemetry (nvidia-smi inside jobs).
   - Causes: jobs reserve entire GPUs but don’t use them, GPU drivers/visibility issues, or wrong gres types requested.

Practical step-by-step diagnostic workflow
- Quick snapshot: sinfo -N -l and squeue -o "%i %u %t %M %R %D" to map idle/allocated nodes to queued jobs and reasons.
- If many pending jobs: inspect the REASON column. If no reason, scontrol show job <jobid>.
- If utilization low but nodes are idle: check for reservations (scontrol_reservation_show) and node features/gres mismatches.
- If scheduler behavior suspect: run sdiag to check scheduling cycles, backfill, and dispatch counters.
- For efficiency: run sacct over the window of interest and compare ReqCPUS/ReqMem to Elapsed/MaxRSS and sum CPU/GPU-hours (sreport or sreport cluster TopUsage).
- For priority/fairshare: use sprio and sshare to see if priorities are skewed.
- For running-job efficiency: use sstat on long-running jobs to measure actual CPU% and memory use.

Tuning levers to improve utilization
- Encourage right-sizing: enforce sensible default limits, submit templates, or request review for oversized jobs; use job submit filters.
- Packing and allocation policy: adjust SelectTypeParameters and SchedulerParameters to pack tasks onto fewer nodes when desired (or conversely enable more spreading).
- Backfill tuning: adjust backfill window parameters (SchedulerParameters, bf_continue) so small jobs get scheduled into gaps.
- QOS/account limits and fairshare: change QOS weights, set per-account or per-user limits to prevent a few users from starving others.
- Reservations and maintenance scheduling: minimize use or schedule during low-demand windows.
- Preemption policies: use preemption for short/interactive jobs if acceptable.
- Elastic scaling (cloud/elastic nodes): add capacity during peak windows if supported.
- Monitoring: add finer-grained job telemetry (CPU, GPU, memory time-series) and enforce or report inefficiencies to users.

Useful example commands (summary)
- sreport cluster Utilization Start=now-30days End=now
- sinfo -N -l
- squeue --states=RUNNING,PENDING -o "%.18i %.20P %.25j %.8u %.2t %.10M %.8D %.20R"
- sdiag
- sprio
- sshare
- sacct -S YYYY-MM-DD -o JobID,User,JobName,State,Elapsed,ReqCPUS,MaxRSS

What to present to stakeholders
- Utilization headline: % node/CPU/GPU utilization over the period (from sreport).
- Waste metrics: CPU/GPU-hours requested vs used, % of jobs that underutilize requested resources (from sacct/sstat).
- Queue health: average wait time, number of pending jobs, common pending reasons (from squeue and sdiag).
- Recommendations: quick wins (enforce request sizes, tune backfill), medium-term (adjust QOS/fairshare), long-term (capacity expansion or elastic nodes).

If you want, I can:
- Run a short diagnostic on your live cluster (sinfo + squeue + sdiag + sprio) and summarize what’s currently limiting utilization — tell me which cluster/partitions to inspect or I can use defaults.

Short answer: Job 4003 (batch_inference) is pending for Reason=Resources — the scheduler cannot find the 4 GPU nodes (with 128G/node) it requested in the gpu partition.

Evidence
- squeue / job request: JOBID=4003, NODES=4, CPUS=32, MEM=128G, PARTITION=gpu.
- scontrol show job 4003: JobState=PENDING  Reason=Resources  NumNodes=4  MinMemoryNode=128G.
- sinfo for partition=gpu: partition shows NODES(A/I/D)=1/0/1 (1 allocated, 0 idle, 1 down). Node list:
  - gpu-node-01: state=mix, CPUS 16/32 allocated, MEM 64G/128G allocated (so currently partly used)
  - gpu-node-02: state=down, reason="[GPU error]"

Why that explains it
- The job needs 4 nodes but the gpu partition only has 2 nodes defined, and currently zero idle nodes. Even if both nodes were up and idle there still wouldn’t be 4 nodes to satisfy NumNodes=4.
- One node is down (gpu-node-02) and the other is partially used (gpu-node-01), so there are no idle nodes that match the request now. The per-node memory requirement (128G) further constrains placement while gpu-node-01 currently has half that memory already allocated.

Recommended remedies
- Reduce the job’s NumNodes (or memory/CPU per node) so it can fit on available hardware.
- Wait for the down node (gpu-node-02) to be repaired and returned to service (admin action).
- Submit to a different partition with sufficient nodes (if acceptable).
- Ask an admin to add more GPU nodes or fix the GPU error on gpu-node-02.

Executing sbatch sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmctld daemon come in at once, it can result in
a degradation of performance of the slurmctld daemon, possibly resulting
in a denial of service.
Do not run sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other
programs. Ensure that programs limit calls to sbatch to the minimum
necessary for the information you are trying to gather.

Short answer

- afterany: the dependent job is released when each job named in the dependency has terminated — in any final state (COMPLETED, FAILED, CANCELLED, TIMEOUT, etc.). It does not care about exit status, only that the jobs have finished.

- afternotok: the dependent job is released only when every job named in the dependency has terminated with a non‑zero / non‑OK result (i.e., they did not finish successfully). If any dependency job finished successfully (exit code 0), the afternotok condition for that dependent job is not satisfied.

Details and examples

- Syntax (example): sbatch --dependency=afterany:12345 myjob.sh or sbatch --dependency=afternotok:12345,12346 myjob.sh

- afterany semantics:
  - Waits until all listed jobs have reached a terminal state. Terminal states include COMPLETED, FAILED, CANCELLED, TIMEOUT, etc.
  - The dependent job becomes eligible regardless of whether the predecessors succeeded or failed.
  - If a listed job is still running or pending, the dependent job stays in PENDING with reason "Dependency".

- afternotok semantics:
  - Waits until all listed jobs have terminated and each terminated with a non‑zero / non‑OK result (i.e., they failed, timed out, were cancelled with a non‑zero exit code, etc.).
  - If any listed job finishes successfully (exit code 0), the afternotok condition is not met for that dependent job; the dependency is effectively unsatisfiable (the job will remain pending unless you change/cancel it).
  - Common use: run a follow-up only when prior jobs fail.

- Contrast to related types:
  - afterok: releases only if all listed jobs finished successfully (exit code 0).
  - after: releases when listed jobs have started (not when they finish).

Practical notes
- You can list multiple job IDs separated by commas. All listed jobs must satisfy the dependency rule.
- If a dependency job already finished before you submit the dependent job, its terminal state is used immediately when evaluating the dependency.
- For troubleshooting, check squeue (active queue) and sacct (historical exit codes) to see predecessors’ final states and exit codes.

If you want, I can show how to check the predecessor jobs’ states/exit codes (squeue/sacct examples) or craft a concrete sbatch example for your workflow.

Below is a compact, practical explanation of what Slurm backfill scheduling does, how to judge its “health”, what determines whether pending jobs “fit” the queue, how to diagnose problems, and common fixes/tuning steps.

1) What backfill is (high level)
- Backfill allows lower‑priority/pending jobs to start when they can run without delaying the expected start time of any higher‑priority job that has an existing reservation. Slurm computes expected start times from current allocations and job walltime requests and then fills gaps in the schedule with jobs that fit those gaps.
- It improves utilization and responsiveness compared with strictly priority‑ordered scheduling, but it depends heavily on accurate walltime estimates and predictable job runtimes.

2) How “queue fit” is determined
- Fit is purely a resource/time feasibility check: can a pending job’s requested resources (nodes/CPUs/GPU, memory, special features/licenses) be allocated on some nodes for the job’s requested duration without moving the expected start of any reserved (higher‑priority) job?
- Key inputs: requested resources (TRES), node topology/availability, job walltime, other running jobs’ expected end times, reservations, preemption/policy settings, QOS/account limits, license availability.
- A job that requests a large contiguous set of nodes or has long walltime is harder to fit into small free fragments even if overall free resources exist.

3) What “backfill health” looks like (signals & metrics)
Healthy backfill behavior tends to show:
- High overall utilization (CPUs/GPU hours used), especially low idle time on nodes.
- Many short gaps being filled with pending jobs (low wasted walltime).
- Scheduler backfill cycles making progress (some jobs started by backfill each cycle).
Unhealthy signs:
- Low utilization despite many pending jobs (lots of idle fragments).
- Many pending jobs stuck for long periods even though total free resources exist (fragmentation).
- Frequent backfill cycles with few or no starts (backfill can’t find fit).
- Large number of preemptions or backfill failures due to inaccurate walltimes.
Useful Slurm metrics/names to watch (from slurm metrics docs):
- slurm_bf_cycle_cnt, slurm_bf_active (backfill activity)
- slurm_sched_cycle_last, slurm_sched_cycle_cnt (scheduler cycle timing)
- node/partition utilization, job start rates, idle node count
- custom metrics: fraction of job starts due to backfill, avg backfill window length

4) Commands and checks to diagnose fit/health
- sinfo: partition/node availability and per-node resources (see fragmentation by node).
- squeue: pending vs running jobs, pending reason column (why jobs are waiting).
- sdiag: scheduler/backfill statistics and cycle times (good first place to get backfill health summary).
- sprio: priority factors affecting higher priority reservations/starts.
- scontrol show job <id>: detailed job resource constraints and reason for not starting.
- Slurm metrics endpoint (if enabled): /metrics and scheduler/backfill metrics.
- sreport / sshare: longer term usage/fairshare patterns if needed.
Interpretation tips:
- If sinfo shows many partially-free nodes but large pending jobs are waiting -> fragmentation.
- If squeue shows PENDING with reason “Resources” or “Priority” combined with sdiag showing few backfill successes -> fit problem.
- If sdiag shows large scheduling cycle times or many backfill cycles with zero starts -> backfill inefficient.

5) Common root causes
- Inaccurate/overestimated walltimes: jobs reserve too much future time, shrinking the backfill window.
- Fragmentation: many small free slices that don’t meet large job requests.
- Large/exclusive-node requests: jobs that need whole nodes or multiple nodes with special features are hard to pack.
- Reservations or long high‑priority jobs that create long reservations blocking gaps.
- License or specialized resource constraints (GPUs, licenses) causing local shortages.
- QOS/account/consumable limits blocking starts even when nodes are free.
- Topology requirements (e.g., contiguous nodes or same switch) that reduce fit.

6) Remediations and tuning
For users:
- Encourage accurate walltime estimates (conservative overestimates hurt backfill).
- Request only needed resources (smaller node counts, flexible memory requests).
- Use job arrays or smaller jobs where possible to improve packing.
For admins:
- Monitor metrics (sdiag + /metrics) and look at slurm_bf_cycle_cnt and start rates.
- Enforce/encourage reasonable MaxTime or walltime policies; consider a soft limit on maximum requested walltime.
- Consider backfill-related config knobs (scheduler/backfill plugin settings) and preemption settings if appropriate.
- Use topology-aware packing features (node features, gres grouping) to improve fit.
- If fragmentation is chronic, consider controlled node drains/reboots or job requeue strategies to defragment (careful: mutating actions require operator intervention).
- Tune priority weights (age/fairshare/QOS) so that “blocking” jobs aren’t always the same ones.

7) Practical quick checklist to run now (diagnostic)
- Run sdiag to see scheduler/backfill cycle and whether backfill is making progress.
- Run sinfo to inspect node partition and idle/allocated distribution.
- Run squeue --long (or with REASON) to see pending reasons for stuck jobs.
- Inspect a few representative pending jobs with scontrol show job <id> for resource constraints and reservation blocking.
- If metrics are enabled, fetch /metrics scheduler/backfill counters for trend analysis.

8) How to judge success after changes
- Increase in node utilization (CPU/GPU hours used).
- Fewer long‑waiting pending jobs; more pending jobs starting via backfill.
- Reduced average wait times and fewer scheduling cycles that start no jobs.
- Lower fragmentation as seen in sinfo (more fully utilized nodes vs many partially used nodes).

Summary
Backfill health = ability of scheduler to find real, non‑delaying fit for lower‑priority jobs and thus turn idle fragments into useful work. It depends primarily on accurate walltimes, request sizes and node topology, plus policy and reservation setup. Use sdiag/sinfo/squeue and the metrics endpoints to measure backfill activity and diagnose fragmentation. Fixes are a mixture of user education (right‑sized requests, accurate times) and admin tuning (policies, backfill/scheduler settings, topology packing).

Good question — here’s a compact reference to the common sinfo node states and what they mean for scheduling and node health. These descriptions are drawn from the Slurm documentation.

Core node states
- IDLE
  - Node is up and not running jobs. It is eligible for scheduling and will be allocated to new jobs.
- ALLOC (ALLOCATED)
  - Node is currently assigned to one or more active jobs. Not available for new allocations.
- MIXED
  - Some CPUs (or GPUs) on the node are allocated while others are idle. The node is partially in use.
- DRAINING
  - Node has been marked to stop accepting new jobs and is waiting for currently running jobs to finish. Said another way: no new allocations will be placed on the node.
- DRAIN or DRAINED
  - DRAIN: shorthand used when viewing; generally means the node is in the draining process (see DRAINING).
  - DRAINED: node has no running jobs and will not be used for scheduling until it is returned to service (often used for maintenance).
- DOWN
  - Node is not responding / unreachable and will not be allocated for new work. Usually requires admin intervention (hardware/network problem).
- FAIL / FAILING
  - Node experienced an error (jobs failed or node health checks failed). It has been flagged and is not eligible for scheduling until cleared.
- COMPLETING
  - Job(s) on the node are finishing/cleaning up; node will transition to IDLE or DRAINED when complete.
- RESERVED
  - Node is reserved for a reservation and won’t be scheduled for non-reservation jobs while the reservation applies.
- UNKNOWN
  - Slurm cannot determine the node’s status.

Common state suffix/flag symbols (appear after the state in sinfo output)
- *  — node is being powered up or configured
- !  — node is not responding (and will not be allocated)
- ~  — node is powered off
- %  — node is presently being powered down
- $  — node is in a reservation with a "maintenance" flag
- @  — node is pending reboot
- ^  — a reboot has been issued for the node
- -  — node is planned by the backfill scheduler for a higher-priority job
- +  — ALLOCATED+ indicates the node is allocated to active jobs and one or more jobs are in the process of completing or being launched (transitional allocations)

Practical notes
- “Drain” vs “Down”: draining is an administrative intent to stop new work (often for maintenance) while down means the node is unreachable/unhealthy. Draining allows current jobs to finish; down does not.
- When troubleshooting a non-starting or pending job, use sinfo to check partition/node availability and the node state flags to see if nodes are drained/down/reserved.
- Admin actions that change node state (scontrol update nodename= state=...) require cluster-admin privileges.

## Overview[#overview](https://slurm.schedmd.com/job_array.html)
Job arrays offer a mechanism for submitting and managing collections of
similar jobs quickly and easily, useful for repetitive workloads that follow a
common job pattern. This greatly improves overall performance, since job arrays
with millions of tasks can be submitted in milliseconds (subject to configured
size limits) and the scheduler can quickly identify cases when no more array
tasks are eligible to start.
All jobs must have the same initial options (e.g., size, time limit), however,
it is possible to change some of these options after the job has begun
execution using the scontrol command specifying the JobID of the array or
individual ArrayJobID .
```text
$ scontrol update job=101 ... $ scontrol update job=101_1 ...

Good question — scontrol update is powerful and can change many jobs if used incorrectly. Below is a compact, safe reference: syntax, common editable fields, examples, and safety checklist.

Basic syntax
- scontrol update job=<jobid> Key=Value Key2="Value with spaces" ...
- Key=Value pairs are separated by spaces. Quote values that contain spaces or shell-sensitive characters.
- For job arrays:
  - job=<ArrayJobID> affects the whole array.
  - job=<ArrayJobID>_<ArrayTaskID> (e.g., 1234_5) targets a single array element.

Important safety rules
- Always include the job=<jobid> argument. Omitting job= (or using a non-specific selector such as JobName alone) can modify many jobs.
- Inspect first: run scontrol show job=<jobid> (or squeue -j <jobid>) to see current state and fields before changing anything.
- Prefer changing one field at a time. Verify the result with scontrol show job=<jobid>.
- Be mindful of privileges: unprivileged users may only modify their own jobs and only certain fields; privileged users (admins/operators) can change more and can violate normal policy limits.
- Many fields are only editable while the job is PENDING. Some fields may be changed on RUNNING or SUSPENDED jobs, but this depends on the field and site policy.
- Don’t assume a change will be accepted: TimeLimit, Partition, QOS, and other changes may be constrained by account/QoS/partition limits and may be rejected unless done by a privileged user.

Commonly edited fields (examples and notes)
- TimeLimit: set runtime limit
  - Format: HH:MM:SS, MM, or D-HH:MM:SS (site may accept other forms). Example:
    - scontrol update job=12345 TimeLimit=02:00:00
  - Note: changing TimeLimit on a pending job is common; raising time over partition/account max may be blocked for non-privileged users.
- JobName:
  - scontrol update job=12345 JobName="new_name"
- QOS:
  - scontrol update job=12345 QOS=high
  - May be restricted by account/QOS associations.
- Account:
  - scontrol update job=12345 Account=myacct
- Priority:
  - scontrol update job=12345 Priority=1000
- TRES/ReqTRES (resource requests like GPUs):
  - scontrol update job=12345 TRES=gres:gpu:2
  - Typically only allowed while PENDING; changing resources for running jobs is often not allowed.
- NodeList/NumNodes:
  - scontrol update job=12345 NodeList=node01 (usually only before allocation; changing nodes for a running job is generally not possible)
- Array elements:
  - scontrol update job=2000_3 TimeLimit=01:00:00 (affects only element 3)

Fields you cannot (or normally should not) change
- AllocNode:Sid, ExitCode, BatchFlag — allocation-specific/read-only fields shown by scontrol show job.
- Many allocation/exit fields are read-only — check scontrol show job output for read-only keys.

Examples (safe, minimal)
- Inspect:
  - scontrol show job=12345
- Change time limit:
  - scontrol update job=12345 TimeLimit=03:00:00
- Rename:
  - scontrol update job=12345 JobName="analysis_v2"
- Change QOS (privileges permitting):
  - scontrol update job=12345 QOS=high

Quick verification workflow (recommended)
1. squeue -j 12345 or scontrol show job=12345 — confirm state (PENDING vs RUNNING) and current values.
2. scontrol update job=12345 <single change>
3. scontrol show job=12345 — confirm the change, and check for any scheduler messages/errors.

Final cautions
- Never run broad updates without confirming target scope. For example, using JobName=foo without job= may affect multiple users’ jobs.
- If you need to change many jobs programmatically, script carefully and test on one job first.
- When in doubt about whether a field can be changed for a given job/state, inspect with scontrol show job and consult your cluster admin or the site Slurm policy.

Summary (what the pending reason "Priority" means)
- When squeue shows a pending reason of "Priority" it means the scheduler attempted to place the job but found one or more other jobs with higher scheduling priority that are being favored for the same partition/resources. In short: the job is waiting because other job(s) have higher computed job_priority and are ahead in the scheduler's ordering.

Why that happens (how priority is computed)
- Slurm's default multifactor priority plugin computes a job priority as a weighted sum of several factors. The canonical formula (from the Slurm docs) is:
  Job_priority = site_factor + PriorityWeightAge*age_factor + PriorityWeightAssoc*assoc_factor + PriorityWeightFairshare*fairshare_factor + PriorityWeightJobSize*job_size_factor + PriorityWeightPartition*partition_factor + PriorityWeightQOS*QOS_factor + SUM(TRES_weight_* * TRES_factor_ ) - nice_factor
- Factors include (not exhaustive): age (how long job has waited), association/account priority, fairshare, job size, partition priority, QOS, TRES (resource) factors, site factors, and a "nice" adjustment. Each factor is normalized (0.0–1.0) and weightings in slurm.conf determine their influence. The final job_priority is an integer (0 .. 4294967295); larger = higher scheduling precedence.
- Because of these factors, a job may be pending for "Priority" even if resources are free for it now — the scheduler prefers to run higher-priority jobs first.

How to investigate (commands to run)
- See the pending reason in the queue: squeue -o "%i %P %j %u %T %R" (shows reason column).
- See job priority values and components: sprio (gives priorities/factors for pending jobs).
- Inspect a job's detailed priority and reason: scontrol show job <jobid> (shows JobPriority and detailed fields).
- List jobs ordered by priority to find which ones are in front: squeue --sort=-p (or use sprio combined with squeue).

Remedies / next steps
- Wait: age_factor increases over time, so the job's priority can grow and eventually run.
- If you need higher precedence, options include:
  - Submit under a higher QOS (if allowed).
  - Ask an admin to adjust association/account priority or partition priority.
  - Use sbatch --nice (or set a lower nice value) if your site permits (note: changing nice often requires privilege or configured QOS).
  - Reduce the job's requested resources or walltime so it fits available slots earlier.
  - Administrators can change priority weights in slurm.conf (PriorityWeight*) or adjust fairshare/account settings via sacctmgr — these are cluster-admin actions.
- Note: many priority changes require admin privileges (sacctmgr/scontrol/slurm.conf edits).

References (official Slurm docs)
- Job reason codes (explains "Priority" as a pending reason): https://slurm.schedmd.com/job_reason_codes.html
- Multifactor priority plugin (factors, formula, configuration): https://slurm.schedmd.com/priority_multifactor.html

- Show which jobs are currently ahead of a specific pending job (I can run sprio and squeue) — tell me the job ID to inspect.
- Or, if you want to change a job's priority or submit with a different QOS/nice, tell me what change you want and I will transfer to the operator (admin) to perform it.

Summary — how Slurm orders the queue
- Slurm’s default is the multifactor priority plugin (PriorityType=priority/multifactor). A job’s priority is a weighted sum of multiple factors (age, fairshare, job size, partition, QOS, TRES, site, nice, …). The larger the resulting integer, the higher the job is ordered in the queue and the sooner it is eligible to run.

High-level formula (concept)
- Job_priority = site_factor
  + PriorityWeightAge  * age_factor
  + PriorityWeightAssoc * assoc_factor
  + PriorityWeightFairshare * fairshare_factor
  + PriorityWeightJobSize * job_size_factor
  + PriorityWeightPartition * partition_factor
  + PriorityWeightQOS * qos_factor
  + SUM( TRES_weight_X * TRES_factor_X )
  - nice_factor
- Each factor produces a floating value roughly in [0.0, 1.0] (implementation-dependent). The configured PriorityWeight* values scale each factor’s contribution; weights are integers and the final priority is an integer (0 .. 2^32-1).

Fairshare (what it does)
- Purpose: prevent users/accounts that consumed many resources recently from always winning the scheduler. Fairshare reduces priority for heavy recent users and increases it for under-used users.
- It is driven by historical usage tracked per association (user/account), decayed over time by PriorityDecayHalfLife so older usage matters less.
- Key config knobs:
  - PriorityWeightFairshare: how strongly fairshare influences final priority (higher = more influence).
  - PriorityDecayHalfLife: how quickly historical usage decays (e.g., 7-0 is 7 days). Smaller half-life → recent use matters more.
  - PriorityUsageResetPeriod: optional periodic reset of usage counters (useful if you want hard resets).
- You can inspect fairshare-related usage with sshare (reports effective shares/usage).

Fair Tree (Fair-share algorithm starting ~19.05)
- Fair Tree is the modern fairshare algorithm used by the multifactor plugin by default.
- Behavior:
  - Hierarchical: it respects account/user/account-group hierarchies so that if parent account A ranks ahead of sibling B, then all children of A rank ahead of all children of B. That prevents accidental local re-ordering inside an account that would hurt cross-account fairness.
  - Produces stable, rank-based fairshare factors and avoids precision issues and undesirable inversions that could occur in the older Classic algorithm.
  - Tie-handling is explicit and deterministic (but ties are permitted).
- Use when you have hierarchical accounting (accounts with subaccounts) and want consistent inter-account ordering.

Configured priority weights (how they change behavior)
- Weights are the administrator’s control knobs; they scale each factor’s effect on final priority:
  - PriorityWeightFairshare (commonly big, e.g., 10000): strong influence of fairshare.
  - PriorityWeightAge (e.g., 1000): lets jobs that waited a long time climb the queue (prevents starvation).
  - PriorityWeightJobSize (e.g., 1000): can favor smaller or larger jobs depending on how job_size_factor is defined.
  - PriorityWeightPartition, PriorityWeightQOS etc.: let you prefer jobs in particular partitions or QOS classes.
  - TRES weights (TRESWeight) let CPU, GPU, memory costs change priority (e.g., deprioritize GPU-heavy jobs).
- Example numeric intuition:
  - If PriorityWeightFairshare = 10000 and fairshare_factor for alice = 0.8, that contributes ≈ 8000 points.
  - If PriorityWeightAge = 1000 and age_factor = 0.5, that contributes ≈ 500 points.
  - Final priority is the sum of all such contributions (site + assoc + fairshare + …) minus nice_factor.
- Practical tuning guidance:
  - If fairness matters most, make PriorityWeightFairshare large relative to other weights.
  - If you want long-waiting jobs to eventually run despite fairshare, increase PriorityWeightAge.
  - If small jobs should be favored to improve throughput, tune PriorityWeightJobSize or PriorityFavorSmall.
  - Use PriorityDecayHalfLife to define how much history you want (short half-life = recent use matters; long half-life = long-term quotas).
  - Avoid making all weights zero or heavily skewing one factor unless intentional.

Diagnostics and inspection
- sprio: shows per-job priority and breakdown by factor (useful to see which factors contribute most).
- sshare: shows usage and effective shares for accounts/users (helps understand fairshare state).
- scontrol show config: view the Priority* settings in slurm.conf.
- sdiag and scheduler logs: for deeper scheduler behavior and backfill diagnostics.

Common interactions and gotchas
- Fairshare vs Age: a very large fairshare weight can cause a new or low-usage user’s job to jump ahead of long-waiting jobs unless you also raise PriorityWeightAge.
- TRES weights: assigning large positive weights to a TRES increases priority for jobs consuming that TRES (or the inverse, depending on factor setup); be careful when combining TRES weights with fairshare.
- QOS and partition factors can override account-level fairness for special classes (e.g., interactive or emergency QOS).
- PriorityDecayHalfLife = 0 disables decay (usage never decays) so the usage counters must be reset periodically with PriorityUsageResetPeriod or manually.
- Priority calculations use integers and limited precision; extremely large or tiny weights can lead to unintuitive ordering—test changes in a staging environment.

- explain how to interpret sprio output for one or more real jobs, or
- suggest a tuning recipe for a cluster profile (research, bursty GPU, or throughput-focused). Which would you like?

## Command-line Job Options [#command-line](https://slurm.schedmd.com/burst_buffer.html)
In addition to putting burst buffer directives in the batch script, the
command-line options `--bb` and `--bbf` may also include
burst buffer directives. These command-line options are available for salloc,
sbatch, and srun. Note that the `--bb` option cannot create or
destroy persistent burst buffers.
The `--bbf` option takes as an argument a filename and that file
should contain a collection of burst buffer operations identical to those used
for batch jobs.
Alternatively, the `--bb` option may be used to specify burst
buffer directives as the option argument. The behavior of this option depends
on which burst buffer plugin is used. When the `--bb` option is
used, Slurm parses this option and creates a temporary burst buffer script file
that is used internally by the burst buffer plugins.

### Lua [#submit_lua](https://slurm.schedmd.com/burst_buffer.html)
The default directive for this plugin is `#BB_LUA`. The directive
used by this plugin may be changed by setting the Directive option in
burst_buffer.conf. Since the directive must always begin with a `#`
sign (which starts a comment in a shell script) this option should specify only
the string following the `#` sign. For example, if burst_buffer.conf
contains the following:
```text
Directive=BB_EXAMPLE
```
then the burst buffer directive will be `#BB_EXAMPLE`.
If the Directive option is not specified in burst_buffer.conf, then
the default directive for this plugin (`#BB_LUA`) will be used.
Since this plugin was designed to be generic and flexible, this plugin only
requires the directive to be given. If the directive is given, Slurm will run
all burst buffer stages for the job.

Overview
- A Slurm "burst buffer" is a fast (often node-local or dedicated NVMe/persistent) staging area managed by a burst‑buffer plugin (commonly datawarp or lua). Slurm coordinates allocation, stage‑in, stage‑out, and release of that storage for jobs.
- Only one burst‑buffer plugin may be configured (BurstBufferType in slurm.conf). The plugin controls directive names, available options, TRES names, and exact behavior.

Directives and CLI options
- Batch-script comment directives: burst buffer requests are normally placed as commented lines in job scripts. The directive string depends on the plugin and/or burst_buffer.conf Directive setting; common examples:
  - DataWarp plugin: lines beginning with "#DW" (job-specific) and "#BB" (used for persistent create/destroy by Slurm).
    - Example (DataWarp): #DW jobdw capacity=100GB access_mode=private pool=wlm_pool
  - Lua plugin (default directive name): "#BB_LUA" (or custom Directive value in burst_buffer.conf).
    - Example (Lua minimum): #BB_LUA <plugin-specific-ops>
- Command-line options:
  - --bb: supply burst buffer directives to sbatch/srun/salloc. Note: --bb cannot create or destroy persistent burst buffers (it creates a temporary internal script for the plugin).
  - --bbf <file>: point sbatch/srun/salloc to a file containing burst buffer operations (same syntax as inside a script).
- Persistent BB create/destroy (datawarp only via Slurm):
  - #BB create_persistent name= capacity= [access=] [pool=] [type=]
  - #BB destroy_persistent name= [hurry]
  - Persistent names must follow plugin rules (e.g., not start with a digit).

Common directive options (plugin-specific but common ideas)
- capacity (size requested: GB/TiB)
- pool (which storage pool to allocate from)
- access/access_mode (private/shared)
- type (scratch/persistent/etc.)
- name (for persistent buffers)
- hurry (for forced delete)

Job lifecycle / stages
- Allocation: Slurm (via plugin) allocates a buffer size and records the buffer as associated with the job.
- Stage‑in: data is copied into the burst buffer before the job runs (if requested).
- Run: job runs using the staged data or writing to the buffer.
- Stage‑out: on job completion (or at configured points), data is copied from buffer to the persistent storage target.
- Release/cleanup: buffer is released and cleaned up; persistent buffers remain until destroyed.

Status and how to inspect
- The plugin exposes status through Slurm tools:
  - scontrol show burst (or scontrol show burst_buffer / sview Burst Buffer tab depending on Slurm version/plugin) shows configured pools, total/free/used space, per‑job allocations, CreateTime, Size, Pool, and per‑user usage.
    - Typical fields you’ll see: Name, DefaultPool, Granularity, TotalSpace, FreeSpace, UsedSpace, Flags, StageInTimeout/StageOutTimeout, Allocated Buffers (JobID=..., Size=..., State=allocated|staged-in|staged-out), Per User Buffer Use.
  - sview’s Burst Buffer tab shows the same information in a GUI.
- Accounting/TRES:
  - If enabled, burst buffer resources are tracked in accounting with TRES names like bb/datawarp or bb/lua. Add these to AccountingStorageTres to make Slurm account for BB usage.
- Scheduling impact:
  - A job’s BB request can affect scheduling (Slurm can consider BB size when deciding placement and start order).
  - Plugins may enforce limits by QOS/association via TRES.

Interpreting buffer states
- allocated: space reserved but not yet staged in
- staged-in / staged-out: data copy stage completed or pending
- released: buffer freed (or persistent buffers show when they are still present)
- error/failed: plugin-specific; indicates stage or allocation failure

Troubleshooting pointers
- If a job is rejected or never stages:
  - Ensure BurstBufferType is configured and the plugin is running.
  - For datawarp: capacity is required for job‑specific requests; omission will reject the job.
  - Check pools and free space with scontrol show burst.
  - Verify accounting TRES (bb/...) and user quotas if jobs are denied due to limits.
  - Increase burst buffer plugin logging with DebugFlags=BurstBuffer in slurm.conf for detailed logs (only temporarily).
  - Timeouts: plugin-configured StageInTimeout/StageOutTimeout/ValidateTimeout can cause failures if operations exceed them.
- For persistent buffers:
  - Use #BB create_persistent to create; #BB destroy_persistent to delete (datawarp rules apply).
  - --bb cannot create persistent buffers; use script directives or plugin tools.

Examples (illustrative)
- In a sbatch script (DataWarp):
  - #DW jobdw capacity=200GB pool=wlm_pool access_mode=private
  - #SBATCH --time=02:00:00
  - (then the job body)
- From CLI:
  - sbatch --bb="jobdw capacity=200GB pool=wlm_pool" myscript.sh
  - sbatch --bbf=burst_ops.txt myscript.sh

Where to look for more detail
- The Slurm Burst Buffer Guide (burst_buffer.html) documents plugin-specific directives and full examples (DataWarp and Lua sections). For exact status output fields use scontrol show burst on your system.

- Job 5004 (name=slurm_array, user=alice) — state: PENDING
- scontrol_show reports Reason=AssocGrpCPUMinutesLimit
- Job request: 1 node, 4 CPUs, 8G, partition=cpu

What that reason means
- The reason code AssocGrpCPUMinutesLimit indicates the job’s association (account/group/QOS) has hit an aggregate CPU‑minutes limit. Per the Slurm docs, AssocGrp* reasons mean "the job's association has reached an aggregate limit" (e.g., CPU minutes charged to that association have exceeded the configured quota), so the scheduler will not start the job until the association is below that limit or the limit is changed.

Likely consequences and fixes
- The job will remain pending until:
  - the association’s current CPU‑minutes usage falls below its configured limit (e.g., when other jobs finish or historic usage ages out), or
  - an admin raises or removes the CPUMinutes limit for that association, or
  - you run the job under a different association/account/QOS that has available quota.
- Actions you can take:
  - Contact your cluster admin/account owner and ask them to increase the association CPUMinutes limit or explain the quota policy.
  - Re-submit under a different account/QOS if you have access to one with available quota.
  - Reduce requested resources/time so the job consumes fewer CPU‑minutes (if that helps with policy limits).

Below is a compact reference of the Slurm configuration knobs that are most relevant when you design scheduling policy and accounting. I include what each setting does, typical values or choices, and practical notes (what you must enable to get full accounting/fairshare behavior).

High-level picture
- Scheduling (slurmctld / slurm.conf): controls how jobs are prioritized/selected and when/backfill decisions are made (PriorityType, SchedulerType, SchedInterval, select/cons_res).
- Accounting (slurmdbd + slurm.conf + sacctmgr): records job completions and usage to a database, enforces association/QoS/limit policies, and enables reporting/fairshare state.
- Interaction: PriorityType can include fairshare; fairshare state is stored/updated in the accounting DB (SlurmDBD) so accurate fairshare requires accounting enabled.

Key scheduling-related slurm.conf parameters
- PriorityType
  - Defines which priority plugins are used (common plugins: priority/multifactor, priority/basic). Use multifactor to combine age, fairshare, job size, QOS, partition, etc.
  - Example: PriorityType=priority/multifactor
- Priority weights and tuning (when using multifactor)
  - PriorityWeightFairshare, PriorityWeightAge, PriorityWeightJobSize, PriorityWeightPartition, PriorityWeightQOS, etc.
  - PriorityDecayHalfLife (controls how historical usage decays for fairshare), and PriorityFlags to tweak behavior (e.g., ignore certain classes).
  - Tuning notes: raise WeightFairshare to favor users with low historical usage; adjust decay half-life to control how quickly past usage becomes irrelevant.
- SchedulerType
  - Controls which scheduler implementation runs (e.g., sched/builtin or sched/backfill). Use sched/backfill to enable backfill behavior.
  - Example: SchedulerType=sched/backfill
- SchedInterval
  - How often the scheduler rebuilds the feasible set and reorders pending jobs (seconds). Shorter interval = more responsive but more CPU used by slurmctld.
- SelectType / SelectTypeParameters
  - Resource selection plugin (select/cons_res is common). SelectTypeParameters sets how allocation is done (e.g., CR_Core, CR_Socket, CR_CPU_Memory); important for correct packing and for TRES accounting.
- Preemption / Backfill / Topology
  - You can enable preemption plugins and backfill tuning via SchedulerType and SchedulerParameters. Preemption behavior is controlled by PreemptType/PreemptMode / associated QOS settings.
- Resource definitions that affect scheduling
  - NodeName / PartitionName: node sizes, CPUs, memory, GRES (GPUs) and partitions determine which jobs are eligible.
  - DefMemPerCPU, OverSubscribe and MaxCPUsPerNode influence packing and per-job resource limits.
- TRES (Trackable RESources)
  - Slurm uses TRES names (cpu, mem, gres/gpu, license, etc.) for limits, accounting and QOS. Define GRES on nodes (e.g., Gres=gpu:4) so GPUs are visible and charged.

Key accounting-related parameters (slurm.conf + slurmdbd.conf)
- AccountingStorageType
  - Tells slurmctld how to store accounting. Typical production configuration: AccountingStorageType=accounting_storage/slurmdbd and run slurmdbd as middle tier into MySQL/MariaDB.
- AccountingStorageEnforce
  - Comma-separated enforcement options to require valid associations/limits at submission time (examples: associations and limits). Controls whether submissions are rejected or allowed to pend when they violate association/QoS/limit rules.
  - Use carefully: enabling strict enforcement can cause job submissions to be rejected if sacctmgr associations/limits are not configured.
- JobAcctGatherType (and gather plugin)
  - Controls how resource usage for running jobs is gathered (commonly jobacct_gather/linux). The gather plugin supplies per-job CPU, memory, I/O and GPU accounting used for billing/fairshare.
  - JobAcctGatherParams (plugin-specific) tune sampling frequency or enabled metrics.
- JobCompType
  - Where job completion records are sent. Use jobcomp/slurmdbd to write completion records into the accounting DB via slurmdbd.
- slurmdbd.conf (SlurmDBD)
  - DbdHost, StorageType (mysql/mariadb), StorageUser/StoragePass, LogFile, PurgeJobAfter, Archive options.
  - slurmdbd sits between slurmctld and the SQL DB; it is strongly recommended for security and scalability.
- sacctmgr (account/association/QoS setup)
  - To enable limits and enforcement you must create accounts, users, and associations with sacctmgr, and add QOS objects and limits (MaxWall, MaxTRESPerUser, GrpTRES, etc.).
- QOS and limits
  - QOS objects give per-QOS priorities and limits. QOS flags include DenyOnLimit (reject on submit if limits violated), EnforceUsageThreshold, and UsageThreshold.
  - Limits often use TRES names: MaxTRESPerUser, MaxTRESPerAccount, GrpTRES, etc.
- Fairshare / sshare
  - Fairshare state is stored in the accounting DB. Use sshare to view fairshare effective shares and historical usage. PriorityType must include fairshare and slurmdbd/accounting must be enabled for it to work correctly.
- Reporting and tools
  - sacct (historical job accounting), sreport (aggregated usage reports), sshare (fairshare view), sacctmgr (manage accounts/QoS/associations).

Minimal example (typical lines in slurm.conf)
- Scheduler/priority/accounting essentials:
  - SchedulerType=sched/backfill
  - SchedInterval=30
  - PriorityType=priority/multifactor
  - PriorityWeightFairshare=10000
  - PriorityWeightAge=1000
  - SelectType=select/cons_res
  - SelectTypeParameters=CR_Core_Memory
  - AccountingStorageType=accounting_storage/slurmdbd
  - AccountingStorageEnforce=associations,limits
  - JobAcctGatherType=jobacct_gather/linux
  - JobCompType=jobcomp/slurmdbd

What you must do to enable functional accounting + fairshare
1. Install and configure slurmdbd and a SQL database (MySQL/MariaDB). Configure slurmdbd.conf with StorageType, StorageUser, StoragePass, and DbdHost.
2. Point slurmctld at slurmdbd: set AccountingStorageType=accounting_storage/slurmdbd in slurm.conf.
3. Enable job accounting & job completion plugins: JobAcctGatherType=jobacct_gather/linux and JobCompType=jobcomp/slurmdbd.
4. Use sacctmgr to create accounts, users, and associations and to define QOS objects and limits. If you want enforcement, set AccountingStorageEnforce appropriately.
5. Tune PriorityType weights and PriorityDecayHalfLife to shape fairshare behavior; use sshare to inspect fairshare allocations.

Practical tuning tips
- Start with moderate SchedInterval (20–60s) and increase scheduler interval only if slurmctld CPU usage is a problem.
- If backfill is valuable for utilization, enable SchedulerType=sched/backfill and test with realistic job mixes.
- Test AccountingStorageEnforce in “audit” mode first (don’t immediately reject jobs) so you can verify sacctmgr associations and limits are correct.
- Use QOS DenyOnLimit for strict control of runaway submissions; use EnforceUsageThreshold for automatic throttling before hard deny.
- For GPU clusters, ensure nodes declare GRES=gpu:N and that TRES accounting is configured so fairshare and limits count GPU hours.

Where to read more (official docs)

- slurmdbd.conf (database/back-end) reference: https://slurm.schedmd.com/slurmdbd.conf.html
- QOS and resource limits: https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html
- Accounting and reporting: https://slurm.schedmd.com/accounting.html

- Topology: a single switch "switch0" connects cpu-node-01, cpu-node-02, gpu-node-01 and gpu-node-02.
- Partition/node snapshot (from sinfo):

What “topology placement constraints” mean here
- Slurm will only place tasks on nodes that are up and idle (or have free resources if the scheduler allows sharing). Nodes that are down or drained are excluded entirely.
- Partition membership, node GRES (gpu:4), and node state are hard constraints: a job requesting --partition=gpu and --gres=gpu:1 requires an idle GPU node in the gpu partition.
- Network topology (switch0) is used by the scheduler to prefer nodes with good network locality for multi-node allocations, but locality only helps if multiple eligible nodes are available and idle.

- GRES granularity: nodes advertise gpu:4 but node state (alloc/down) takes precedence; whether partial GPU allocation would be possible depends on current allocation and Slurm configuration (shared GPUs vs exclusive).

## Reservation Accounting [#account](https://slurm.schedmd.com/reservations.html)
Jobs executed within a reservation are accounted for using the appropriate
user and account. If resources within a reservation are not used, those
resources will be accounted for as being used by all users or accounts
associated with the reservation on an equal basis (e.g. if two users are
eligible to use a reservation and neither does, each user will be reported
to have used half of the reserved resources).

By default, reservations must not overlap. They must either include different
