Summary — what "--reservation" does
- --reservation=<name> (sbatch/srun/salloc) requests that Slurm place the job into a named reservation. If the reservation is not MAGNETIC, the job must explicitly specify the reservation name to run on those reserved resources.
- A job that uses a reservation must be fully contained within the reservation’s resources and time window (start/end). If the reservation ends, the job will be canceled unless controller option ResvOverRun permits an overrun.

How reservations are created (admin side)
- Reservations are created with scontrol create reservation ... and include fields such as:
  - ReservationName (auto-generated if not given)
  - StartTime / EndTime / Duration
  - Nodes / NodeCnt / CoreCnt (or explicit node list)
  - Partition (a reservation normally is tied to one partition unless explicit nodes are specified)
  - Users / Accounts / QOS (who may use the reservation)
  - Flags (MAGNETIC, OVERLAP, REPLACE, REPLACE_DOWN, etc.)
- Reservations may reserve nodes, cores, licenses, burst buffers.

Access control rules (who may run in a reservation)
- Allow lists and deny lists:
  - You can specify Users=alice,bob or Accounts=proj1,proj2 to allow only those users/accounts.
  - You can also exclude a user or account by prefacing the name with a minus sign, e.g. User=-alice or Account=-proj2. Exclusions override positive membership (i.e., prevent that entity from using the reservation even if their account is listed).
- QOS and partition may also be restricted on the reservation.
- Matching logic:
  - When a job is considered for the reservation, Slurm checks the job’s user, account, QOS and partition against the reservation’s allow/deny lists. The job must satisfy the reservation’s access constraints (and resource/partition constraints) to be eligible.
  - If the reservation is not MAGNETIC, the job must explicitly request --reservation=<name> to run in it (and still must satisfy access rules).
  - If the reservation has the MAGNETIC flag, eligible jobs that do not name the reservation may be “attracted” and started in the reservation automatically (only if they meet the reservation’s access/resource constraints). Note: MAGNETIC does not attract heterogeneous jobs unless they explicitly request the reservation.
- Partition and node constraints:
  - A reservation is normally associated with a single partition and cannot span partitions unless created with explicit node lists.
  - Reservations can be for full nodes or specific cores; some flags/behaviors differ for partial-node reservations.
- Overlap and replacement:
  - By default reservations do not overlap in time on the same nodes; use the OVERLAP flag to allow overlapping reservations.
  - REPLACE or REPLACE_DOWN flags change how reserved nodes are maintained when nodes go down or are allocated elsewhere (e.g., allow swapping in new idle nodes).
- Priority/accounting effects:
  - Using a reservation does not itself change a job’s base priority calculation, but jobs using reservations are considered for scheduling on the reserved resources before non-reserved jobs (effectively a scheduling advantage).
  - Jobs run in a reservation are accounted to the job’s user/account. If reserved resources are unused, accounting may attribute unused resources equally among the users/accounts associated with the reservation (see reservation accounting rules).

Practical examples
- Submit requesting a reservation (user-side):
  - sbatch --reservation=my_res job.sh
- Admin create example:
  - scontrol create reservation ReservationName=my_res StartTime=now Duration=60 NodeCnt=2 Users=alice,brenda Partition=gpu

Caveats & important notes
- Jobs must fit entirely inside the reservation (resource and time). Partial fits are not allowed.
- Magnetic reservations can start eligible jobs that don’t explicitly name the reservation; regular reservations require an explicit --reservation.
- Heterogeneous jobs and MAGNETIC: heterogeneous jobs are not attracted by MAGNETIC unless they explicitly request the reservation.
- If you need a reservation to span multiple partitions use explicit node lists (it’s not the normal case).
- For precise semantics, behaviors and flags see Slurm’s reservation documentation (scontrol create reservation, scontrol show reservation, and the reservations section of Slurm docs).

Summary — what the commands do
- scontrol update NodeName=<node-list> State=DRAIN[,Reason="..."]
  - Marks the specified node(s) as drained so the scheduler will not place any new allocations there.
  - Running jobs are not automatically preempted by the drain operation; they continue to run to completion (or until separately cancelled/requeued).
  - The node(s) remain in the drained state until an explicit resume/clear is performed.
  - You may supply a Reason string which is recorded and visible in node/reason listings.

- scontrol update NodeName=<node-list> State=RESUME
  - Clears the drain marking and returns the node(s) to normal scheduling eligibility (they will appear idle/allocatable and the scheduler may assign new jobs).
  - Use this to return nodes to service after maintenance.

Key notes and semantics
- Authorization: updating node state requires appropriate administrative privileges (see scontrol docs for required AdminLevel).
- Targets: NodeName accepts single names, ranges (e.g., node[01-10]) or special names (e.g., ALL).
- Drain does not implicitly kill or requeue running jobs; if you need running jobs removed you must cancel/requeue them separately.
- Drain is persistent until cleared with RESUME (or other explicit state changes); it is used for planned maintenance or to prevent new allocations.
- There are related node-state actions for power-saving and automated suspend (examples: POWER_DOWN, POWER_DOWN_ASAP, POWER_DOWN_FORCE) that combine draining semantics with node power management; POWER_DOWN_ASAP in particular will drain the node and then attempt to power it down using the configured SuspendProgram.
- Use sinfo / scontrol show node to confirm the node state and view the recorded reason.

Common examples
- Mark a node for maintenance:
  scontrol update NodeName=node01 State=DRAIN Reason="maintenance"
- Return a node to service:
  scontrol update NodeName=node01 State=RESUME

For exact syntax, authorization requirements, and the full list of node state keywords (POWER_DOWN_*, etc.), see the scontrol documentation.

## DESCRIPTION[#SECTION_DESCRIPTION](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbcast.html)
sbcast is used to transmit a file to all nodes allocated
to the currently active Slurm job.
This command should only be executed from within a Slurm batch
job or within the shell spawned after a Slurm job's resource
allocation.
SOURCE is the name of a file on the current node.
DEST should be the fully qualified pathname for the
file copy to be created on each node.
If a fully qualified pathname is not provided, the file will be created in
the directory specified in the BcastParameters parameter in the slurm.conf
file (if available) otherwise it will be created in the current working
directory from which the sbcast command is invoked.
DEST should be on a file system local to that node.
Note that parallel file systems may provide better performance
than sbcast can provide, although performance will vary
by file size, degree of parallelism, and network type.

## PERFORMANCE[#SECTION_PERFORMANCE](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbcast.html)
Executing sbcast sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from sbcast or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmctld daemon come in at once, it can result in
a degradation of performance of the slurmctld daemon, possibly resulting
in a denial of service.
Do not run sbcast or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other
programs. Ensure that programs limit calls to sbcast to the minimum
necessary for the information you are trying to gather.

Short answer
- sbcast copies a local file from the job’s submission/allocated shell to every node in the current allocation, writing it to a node-local path you specify. It’s intended for staging executables, libraries, or data onto the compute nodes of a job so tasks read from local storage instead of a shared filesystem.

What sbcast does (key facts)
- Must be run from inside a Slurm allocation (inside a job script or the job’s interactive shell).
- SOURCE is a file on the node where you run sbcast; DEST should be a fully-qualified path on each compute node (a local filesystem path is recommended).
- It sends the file via slurmctld and distributes it to all allocated nodes (tree/fanout distribution).
- Useful options: compression (-C / --compress), preserve mode/ownership (-p), control fanout (-F/--fanout), and --send-libs to include shared-library dependencies.

When sbcast helps (good use-cases)
- Avoiding an NFS/Lustre hotspot at job startup: when many ranks/tasks read the same executable/large shared file at once, copying that file once to each node’s local disk reduces load and improves startup time.
- Staging small-to-moderate sized binaries, shared libraries, or input archives that each node should use locally (e.g., MPI executables, local caches).
- When you need node-local temporary files (local SSDs) for better I/O performance than the cluster parallel filesystem.
- When you want identical files present on every node without requiring a shared filesystem mount.

When not to use sbcast (or be careful)
- Very large datasets: a parallel filesystem is often more efficient for bulk data movement; sbcast can still work but may be slower or stress slurmctld/network.
- Many small files: prefer packaging them into a single archive (tar) before sbcast to avoid extra RPC/overhead.
- Frequent repeated sbcast calls in short loops — sbcast uses RPCs to slurmctld and can overload slurmctld; don’t call it in tight loops.
- If you need the file available cluster-wide outside the allocation or permanently, use shared storage or an installation workflow instead.

Best-practice recommendations
- Run sbcast once in the job prologue (task 0 or before launching many tasks). Example in a batch script:
  - sbcast myprog /local/tmp/myprog
  - then srun --multi-prog or mpirun to launch tasks that use /local/tmp/myprog
- Combine many small files into a single archive, sbcast the archive, then extract on each node.
- Use compression (-C lz4) to reduce transfer size for compressible files; use --fanout to tune distribution for large allocations.
- Use --send-libs if you need the executable’s shared libraries copied as well; use --preserve to keep permissions.
- Check available local disk space on nodes before staging large files.

Example commands
- Copy an executable to /tmp on every allocated node:
  sbcast myprog /tmp/myprog
- Copy with compression and preserve permissions:
  sbcast -C lz4 -p myprog /local/scratch/myprog
- Send an archive and then extract on nodes (recommended for many small files):
  tar -czf archive.tgz dir/
  sbcast archive.tgz /local/tmp/archive.tgz
  srun --nodes=1 --ntasks=1 bash -c 'tar -xzf /local/tmp/archive.tgz -C /local/tmp'

Troubleshooting & performance notes
- If job startup is still slow, measure whether the shared FS is the bottleneck; sbcast helps most when many nodes simultaneously read the same file from the shared FS.
- Avoid many simultaneous sbcast calls that could cause slurmctld performance degradation.
- If you need to stage very large datasets, consider an alternative distribution mechanism (parallel filesystem, dedicated data distribution service, or preloading into node-local caches outside the job).

If you want, I can:
- Suggest an sbcast pattern for a specific job script (give me job size, file sizes, and local path),
- Or review a short job script and insert an sbcast staging step.

## EXAMPLES[#SECTION_EXAMPLES](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sreport.html)
Report number of jobs per account according to different job size bins:
```text
$ sreport job sizesbyaccount Start=11:00 -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Job Sizes 2024-08-19T11:00:00 - 2024-08-19T11:59:59 (3600 secs) Time reported in Minutes -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Cluster Account 0-49 CPUs 50-249 CPUs 250-499 CPUs 500-999 CPUs >= 1000 CPUs % of cluster --------- --------- ------------- ------------- ------------- ------------- ------------- ------------ minesofm+ root 770 0 0 0 0 100.00%
```
Report cluster utilization:
```text
$ sreport cluster utilization Start=11:00 -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Cluster Utilization 2024-08-19T11:00:00 - 2024-08-19T11:59:59 Usage reported in CPU Minutes ------------------------...

Good question — interpreting “cluster utilization” in Slurm is best done by combining sreport (historical usage), real‑time views (sinfo/squeue), and scheduler diagnostics (sdiag, sprio, sshare). Below I summarize the key metrics, what they mean, what to run to check them, how to interpret common patterns, and common mitigations.

What “utilization” means in Slurm
- sreport cluster utilization: primary authoritative metric for historical utilization. Key fields:
  - Allocated = time nodes were in use by jobs or active reservations (counts CPU/GPU minutes or node-minutes depending on format).
  - Idle = time nodes were idle/available.
  - Down/PlannedDown = maintenance or controller downtime.
  - OverCommitted = time more resources were reported used than nominal (rare).
  - TresCount/Used = concrete resource usage counts (CPU‑hours, GPU‑hours).
- Simple utilization percent ≈ Allocated / (Allocated + Idle + Down + PlannedDown). sreport prints these for you; don’t try to recompute without reading the report fields.

Real‑time checks to correlate with historical numbers
- sinfo – show partition/node states (how many nodes allocated/idle/drained/down).
- squeue – show current RUNNING vs PENDING jobs and pending reasons.
- scontrol show job <id> – detailed reason/constraints for a pending job.
- sacct – per‑job historical usage if you need job lengths, exit codes, wasted time.

Scheduler diagnostics and why they matter
- sdiag — shows scheduling cycle times, backfill efficiency, queue depth. Useful to detect:
  - Long scheduler cycles (slurmctld overloaded) => scheduling delays and apparent idle time while jobs wait.
  - Poor backfill efficiency => wasted small gaps that could have been filled by short jobs.
- sprio — shows priority components (fairshare, age, QOS). If many jobs are pending with low priority, sprio shows which factor is keeping them low.
- sshare — shows effective shares/fairshare usage (who has used their fair share).
- scontrol show config / scontrol ping — scheduler config and health; check scheduling parameters (e.g., bf_interval, MaxJobCount limits, PreemptMode, SchedulerType).

Common utilization patterns, what they mean, and checks
1) Low allocated / high idle (low utilization)
   - Possible causes: lack of jobs, users hitting job size/feature constraints, reservations, node features (GRES/GPU mismatch), user/account limits, partition restrictions.
   - Checks: squeue (few jobs), sinfo (idle nodes in partitions users submit to?), squeue --states=PENDING to see why pending, scontrol show job for pending reason.
   - Mitigations: advertise/educate users, loosen constraining features/QOS, remove unnecessary reservations, reconfigure partitions, enable backfill or better packing.

2) Idle nodes but many pending jobs
   - Possible causes: job requests don’t match free resources (e.g., need 4 GPUs but only nodes with 8 are available but reserved/exclusive?), job feature/GRES mismatches, software/license constraints, association/user limits.
   - Checks: squeue with REASON column, scontrol_show for a representative pending job, scontrol_license to check license contention.
   - Mitigations: adjust job submission scripts or partition GRES, relax exclusive node policies, adjust association limits or QOS, create reservations for important workloads.

3) High queue depth with moderate/high allocated (high contention)
   - Possible causes: cluster at steady high utilization and many jobs queued for large resource requests; fragmentation where lots of small free resources can’t satisfy big jobs.
   - Checks: sreport job sizes, sdiag backfill statistics, sacct to see distribution of job sizes/lengths.
   - Mitigations: encourage job packing (--share or --ntasks-per-node tuning), change scheduling policies to favor throughput, reserve time windows for large jobs, adjust backfill settings or enable preemption where appropriate.

4) Poor backfill efficiency
   - Symptom: sdiag shows low backfill utilization; short jobs could have run but didn’t.
   - Causes: scheduler parameters (bf_interval, bf_continue), long scheduling cycles, job constraints, large blocking jobs.
   - Checks: sdiag backfill stats, squeue to identify very large LONG jobs blocking the queue, sprio to see priorities.
   - Mitigations: tune backfill parameters, reduce block sizes or alter job priorities/partitions, allow smaller jobs to run on shared nodes.

5) Apparent low utilization because of Down/Drained nodes
   - Symptom: sreport shows significant Down time.
   - Checks: sinfo_reasons, sinfo to list nodes in DRAIN/DOWN, sinfo_node for per-node details.
   - Mitigations: repair nodes, reconfigure maintenance windows, remove or reduce planned drains during peak usage.

6) Scheduler lag / slurmctld overload
   - Symptom: sdiag shows long cycle times or backlog; many jobs waiting although resources exist.
   - Checks: sdiag cycle stats, scontrol show config for cycle timing, system metrics on slurmctld host.
   - Mitigations: increase slurmctld resources, reduce scheduling load (less frequent job submissions), tune scheduling interval and backfill params.

What specific Slurm commands to run (quick checklist)
- Get historical utilization (example):
  - sreport cluster utilization Start=2026-04-01 End=2026-04-30
- Real‑time resource state:
  - sinfo -o "%P %D %a %l %E"  (or just sinfo)
- Current queue and reasons:
  - squeue -o "%.18i %.9P %.20j %.8u %.2t %.10M %.10L %.10R"
  - For a specific pending job: scontrol show job <jobid>
- Scheduler diagnostics:
  - sdiag
  - sprio -l (or sprio --verbose)
  - sshare -l
- Node reasons:
  - sinfo -R
  - sinfo -N --long
- Licenses:
  - scontrol_license
- Historical job details:
  - sacct -u <user> --starttime=2026-04-01 --format=JobID,JobName,State,Elapsed,ReqCPUS,ReqGRES,MaxRSS

Interpreting numbers: heuristics
- Utilization > ~80% often indicates good throughput but watch queue wait times and fairness.
- Utilization < ~50% may be a sign of underuse (but acceptable for experimental clusters or for ensuring low latency).
- Backfill efficiency should be high for clusters with variable job sizes; low backfill + long queued jobs indicates tuning opportunity.

Short checklist to diagnose low utilization quickly
1. sreport cluster utilization (time window) — confirm the scale of the problem.
2. sinfo — confirm idle vs drained/down nodes and partition distribution.
3. squeue (pending reasons) — find why jobs aren’t starting.
4. sdiag + sprio + sshare — check scheduler health, backfill, and priority/fairshare reasons.
5. scontrol show job <example pending job> — detailed constraints and reasons.
6. sacct — check job size/length mix (many short jobs cause fragmentation).

When you have specific sreport, sdiag, sinfo, or squeue output I can interpret the numbers and point to exact causes and tuning options. If you want, provide an sreport/sdiag/sinfo output and I’ll analyze it and give targeted recommendations.

Summary comparison (from the Slurm docs)

Purpose
- sbatch: Submit a batch script to the scheduler (non-interactive). The script runs later as a queued batch job.
- salloc: Request an interactive job allocation (a set of nodes/CPUs). When allocation is granted, run a command (or drop you into a shell) while holding those resources.
- srun: Launch job steps / parallel tasks. Can be used inside an existing allocation (sbatch or salloc) or used standalone to obtain an allocation and run a command.

Key behavioral differences
- Interactivity
  - sbatch: non-interactive (submit-and-return; job runs later).
  - salloc: interactive (waits until resources allocated, then runs command or shell; holds allocation until command exits).
  - srun: can be interactive when run from a shell (it will run the command and return); commonly used interactively inside an salloc shell or in a batch script to create job steps.

- Allocation vs launch
  - sbatch: submits a job request (scheduler handles allocation when resources available).
  - salloc: explicitly requests an allocation now (blocks until granted), then you get to use it interactively.
  - srun: launches tasks / job steps; if not already inside an allocation it can implicitly request an allocation for the command.

- Typical usage patterns
  - sbatch: long-running or repeatable batch workflows; use job scripts with #SBATCH directives. Returns a job ID immediately.
  - salloc: debugging, interactive development, or launching an interactive parallel environment (e.g., get nodes, then run MPI tests or start an interactive job).
  - srun: start MPI/parallel tasks (srun -nN ...), used within sbatch scripts to launch steps, or used together with salloc to run on the allocated nodes.

- Relationship to each other
  - Common pattern: salloc (get allocation) → srun (launch steps interactively).
  - Common batch pattern: sbatch (submit job) → inside script use srun to run parallel tasks/steps.
  - srun can also be used as a lightweight submitter (it may create an implicit allocation and run the command immediately).

- Return/visibility
  - sbatch: prints "Submitted batch job <jobid>" and exits; job output is captured to files.
  - salloc: waits until allocation granted, prints allocation job id, then runs the command/shell; relinquishes after command exits.
  - srun: runs the command and exits when it finishes; when used standalone it behaves synchronously for that command.

When to pick which
- Use sbatch when you want to submit a non-interactive batch job or job array to run later.
- Use salloc when you need an interactive allocation (a shell or interactive environment on allocated nodes).
- Use srun to launch parallel tasks (inside sbatch or salloc) or to run a single parallel command immediately (it can also obtain resources implicitly).

Examples
- sbatch my_script.sh          # submit batch script → queued job
- salloc -N4 --time=01:00 bash  # get 4-node allocation, drop to shell on allocated nodes
- salloc -N4 srun -n16 ./a.out # get allocation and immediately run a parallel job
- srun -n8 hostname            # run 8 tasks (will allocate if not already in an allocation, or run as a step if inside one)

Notes / caveats
- Inside a batch script you typically use srun to launch the parallel program so Slurm creates job steps and accounts resources correctly.
- srun and salloc can both create allocations if none exist, but salloc is intended to hold nodes for interactive use; srun is focused on launching steps/tasks.
- Resource request flags (-N, -n, -c, --gres, --time, etc.) are accepted by all three but their meanings depend on whether you are requesting an allocation (salloc/sbatch) or launching tasks (srun).

## Partition Factor [#partition](https://slurm.schedmd.com/priority_multifactor.html)
Each node partition can be assigned an integer priority. The
larger the number, the greater the job priority will be for jobs that
request to run in this partition. This priority value is then
normalized to the highest priority of all the partitions to become the
partition factor.

"Priority" as a pending reason means the scheduler attempted to place the job but chose other jobs with higher computed priority first. In other words, there are eligible resources, but other jobs have higher priority so your job has not been selected yet.

Key points
- Job priority is a single integer (0 .. 4294967295) computed by the configured priority plugin (by default the multifactor priority plugin).
- With the multifactor plugin the priority is a weighted sum of several normalized factors, for example:
  Job_priority = site_factor + WeightAge * age_factor + WeightAssoc * assoc_factor + WeightFairshare * fairshare_factor + WeightJobSize * job_size_factor + WeightPartition * partition_factor + WeightQOS * qos_factor + SUM(TRES_weights * TRES_factors) - nice_factor
  Each factor is 0.0–1.0 and the weights come from slurm.conf (PriorityWeight* settings).
- Common factors that raise or lower priority: job age, user/account fairshare, association/account priority, job size, partition priority, QOS, requested TRES (CPUs/GPUs), and "nice".
- Only one reason is shown for a pending job: the scheduling attempt that the scheduler used found "Priority" to be the blocking reason. Other constraints (resources, licensing, reservations) might also apply but are not shown if priority was the encountered reason.

How to diagnose
- See why a specific job shows Priority: squeue -o "%i %P %j %u %T %M %R" (look at the REASON column).
- Inspect the job’s priority value and metadata: scontrol show job <jobid> (shows Priority, SubmitTime, EligibleTime, etc.).
- View factor breakdown and relative priorities: sprio -l (or sprio -j <jobid>) to see fairshare/age/QOS contributions and the computed priority.
- Check configured weights and behavior: scontrol show config (look for PriorityType and PriorityWeight* settings) or read the multifactor priority docs.

What you can do
- For users: changing job parameters that affect factors (different QOS, smaller job size, lower resource requests, or waiting for age to increase) may improve priority.
- For admins: adjust PriorityType or PriorityWeight* settings, QOS/association priorities, or fairshare settings to change scheduling behavior.

- Slurm reports the job as PENDING but gives Reason=None (no specific pending reason recorded) and SubmitTime=Unknown. That means the scheduler has not attached a standard pending reason string (like Resources, Priority, Dependency, QOSLimit, etc.).

  - Internal/controller issue or a queue-processing delay.
  - Less likely: account/QOS/association problems — those usually produce a specific reason.

The job's priority at any given time will be a weighted sum of all the
factors that have been enabled in the slurm.conf file. Job priority can be
expressed as:

Job_priority = site_factor + (PriorityWeightAge) * (age_factor) + (PriorityWeightAssoc) * (assoc_factor) + (PriorityWeightFairshare) * (fair-share_factor) + (PriorityWeightJobSize) * (job_size_factor) + (PriorityWeightPartition) * (priority_job_factor) + (PriorityWeightQOS) * (QOS_factor) + SUM(TRES_weight_cpu * TRES_factor_cpu, TRES_weight_ * TRES_factor_ , ...) - nice_factor

range from 0.0 to 1.0. The weights are unsigned, 32 bit integers.

A QOS can be attached to a partition. This means the partition will have all
the same limits as the QOS. This does not associate jobs with the QOS, nor does
it give the job any priority or preemption characteristics of the assigned QOS.
Jobs may separately request the same QOS or a different QOS to gain those
characteristics. However, the Partition QOS limits will override the job's QOS.
If the opposite is desired you may configure the job's QOS with

This functionality may be used to implement a true "floating"
partition, in which a partition may access a limited amount of resources with no
restrictions on which nodes it uses to get the resources. This is accomplished
by assigning all nodes to the partition, then configuring a Partition QOS with

### Job Scheduling Priority [#priority](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
Job scheduling priority is made up of a number of factors as
described in the [priority/multifactor](https://slurm.schedmd.com/priority_multifactor.html) plugin. One
of the factors is the QOS priority. Each QOS is defined in the Slurm
database and includes an associated priority. Jobs that request and
are permitted a QOS will incorporate the priority associated with that
QOS in the job's [multi-factor priority calculation.](https://slurm.schedmd.com/priority_multifactor.html)
To enable the QOS priority component of the multi-factor priority
calculation, the "PriorityWeightQOS" configuration parameter must be
defined in the slurm.conf file and assigned an integer value greater
than zero.
A job's QOS only affects is scheduling priority when the
multi-factor plugin is loaded.

Below is a focused, practical summary of the Slurm configuration items that actually affect scheduling decisions and accounting. I describe what each option does, where it’s configured (slurm.conf vs slurmdbd.conf / sacctmgr), typical values/choices, and short guidance on how to use them together.

1) Where things live — the big picture
- slurm.conf (on controller and nodes): the central place for scheduler plugins and cluster/partition/node parameters that control how jobs are matched to resources and how priority is calculated.
- slurmdbd.conf + slurmdbd daemon + sacctmgr: the Slurm Database Daemon and DB configuration — stores historical accounting, QOS, accounts, associations, and limits. sacct, sreport, sshare, and sacctmgr talk to the DB.
- sacct / sreport / sshare / scontrol / sdiag: tools that read schedule/accounting state (used for monitoring and troubleshooting).

2) Scheduling: key slurm.conf settings and concepts
- Priority plugin
  - PriorityType
    - Usually set to priority/multifactor (default). Enables weighted multi-factor priority computation.
    - Example: PriorityType=priority/multifactor
  - Priority factors and weights
    - PriorityWeightAge, PriorityWeightFairshare, PriorityWeightJobSize, PriorityWeightPartition, PriorityWeightQOS, etc.
    - Job_priority = weighted sum of enabled factors; larger weight => more influence.
    - Example: PriorityWeightFairshare increases fair-share effect on job order.
  - Fairshare / decay
    - PriorityDecayHalfLife controls how historical usage decays (time string, e.g. 7-0 for 7 days).
    - PriorityUsageResetPeriod resets accumulated usage (useful if you want periodic resets).
    - PriorityMaxAge sets how long the age factor ramps up.
    - Use these to tune how “past usage” penalizes heavy consumers vs new users.
- Backfill and scheduler plugin
  - SchedulerType (and plugin choice): default uses sched/backfill. Backfill allows running smaller queued jobs when they won’t delay higher priority jobs.
  - SchedulerParameters: plugin-specific tuning (depends on your Slurm version).
- Preemption
  - PreemptType and PreemptMode determine whether queued higher-priority jobs can preempt running jobs and how (suspend, requeue, kill).
  - Common pattern: PreemptType=preempt/qos to use QOS relationships; configure QOS preemption lists via sacctmgr.
- Resources and resource selection
  - SelectType / SelectTypeParameters
    - Modern clusters use select/cons_tres (or select/cons_res) to schedule on TRES (trackable resources like cpu,mem,gpu).
    - SelectTypeParameters=CR_Core_Memory or similar for older select/cons_res behavior.
  - TRES and GRES
    - TRES (trackable RESources) are slurm’s unified resource model (cpu,mem,gres/gpu,licenses).
    - GRES.conf + GresTypes controls GPU allocation details.
    - Configure TRES billing/weights if you want CPU vs GPU to affect priority or accounting.
  - DefMem, DefMemPerCPU, DefCPUPerGPU: defaults used when jobs do not request explicit mem/CPU.
- Job launch / tracking (affects accounting accuracy)
  - ProctrackType (e.g., proctrack/cgroup) and TaskPlugin (e.g., task/cgroup) with cgroup jobacct gathering
  - JobAcctGatherType and JobAcctGatherFrequency: controls how job resource usage is collected (required for accurate sacct data).
  - If you want per-process CPU/memory accounting, enable jobacct_gather/cgroup or jobacct_gather/linux.
- Partition configuration (partition-level policies)
  - PartitionName entries in slurm.conf control node groupings and default constraints (DefaultTime, MaxTime, AllowAccounts, AllowQOS).
  - Partition-level limits can be enforced or overridden by QOS/association limits.
- Misc scheduler tuning
  - SchedulerTimeSlice, FastSchedule, MaxJobCount, and other plugin parameters — tune for scheduler responsiveness and scale.

3) Quality of Service (QOS) and limits — configured in the DB (sacctmgr)
- QOS basics
  - QOS entries live in the Slurm DB and are created/modified with sacctmgr.
  - QOS attributes include: Priority (affects multi-factor priority), MaxJobs, MaxWall, MaxNodes, GrpTRES (group TRES limits), DenyOnLimit, PreemptMode, Flags (e.g., OverPartQOS).
  - Use QOS to implement buckets (premium/normal/low) with different priority, limits, and preemption rules.
- How QOS interacts with priority and scheduler
  - PriorityWeightQOS (in slurm.conf) must be non-zero to include QOS priority in the multifactor calculation.
  - If PreemptType=preempt/qos, QOS preemption settings in the DB control which QOS can preempt which.
- Association limits (users/accounts)
  - sacctmgr associations attach users to accounts and define per-association limits: MaxJobs, MaxCPUs, GrpCPUs, GrpTRES, MaxWall, etc.
  - GrpTRES can cap aggregate GPUs/CPUs for an account or user across the cluster or per partition.
- Typical workflow
  - Create accounts and users in DB (sacctmgr add account / user)
  - Create QOS entries (sacctmgr add/modify qos) and associate to accounts/users
  - Set association limits (sacctmgr modify user where=... set MaxJobs=..., GrpTRES=...).

4) Accounting architecture and slurmdbd
- slurmdbd and DB backend
  - slurmdbd (configured by slurmdbd.conf) writes accounting data to an SQL backend (MySQL/MariaDB/Postgres). slurmdbd.conf contains DB connection (StorageType, StorageHost, StorageLoc, StorageUser).
  - slurm.conf must be pointed to AccountingStorageType=accounting_storage/slurmdbd and AccountingStorageHost set appropriately (or local DB in small setups).
- What is stored / how to use it
  - sacct shows job start/stop/exitcode and resource usage (if jobacct is enabled).
  - sreport generates aggregated usage reports (CPU-hours, GPU-hours) by user/account/partition over time windows.
  - sshare displays effective fairshare values and historical usage for associations.
- Ensuring accurate accounting
  - Enable JobAcctGatherType and Proctrack/TaskPlugin appropriately (cgroup is recommended).
  - Ensure slurmd and slurmctld can communicate reliably with slurmdbd and DB (scontrol ping + slurmdbd logs help debug connectivity).
  - Configure JobAcctGatherFrequency sensibly to balance load vs timeliness.

5) Resource billing and weights
- TRES billing weights and TRESType
  - You can set billing weights so CPU-hours and GPU-hours (TRES types) count differently toward fairshare and usage (BillingWeights, TRESBillingWeights).
  - Example: set a higher weight for gres/gpu to make GPUs “more expensive” in fairshare calculations.
- sreport / sshare usage
  - Use sreport to create chargeback/usage reports by account / user / partition and to drive quota decisions.
  - Use sshare (or scontrol show assoc) to inspect the fairshare/usage numbers that influence PriorityWeightFairshare.

6) Practical tuning tips and examples
- To enable multifactor fairshare with 7-day decay:
  - slurm.conf:
    - PriorityType=priority/multifactor
    - PriorityDecayHalfLife=7-0
    - PriorityWeightFairshare=10000
    - PriorityWeightAge=1000
    - PriorityMaxAge=14-0
- To use QOS priority and preemption:
  - slurm.conf: PriorityWeightQOS=1000, PreemptType=preempt/qos
  - DB: sacctmgr add qos premium; sacctmgr modify qos premium set priority=2000, preempt_mode=REQUEUE (or specify preempt list)
- To enable accounting DB:
  - slurm.conf: AccountingStorageType=accounting_storage/slurmdbd, AccountingStorageHost=<slurmdbd host>
  - slurmdbd.conf: StorageType=accounting_storage/mysql (or account_storage/postgres), StorageUser/StoragePass/StorageLoc etc., DBDHost/DBDPort as needed.
- To account for GPUs properly:
  - Configure GRES on nodes, GresTypes=gpu in slurm.conf, GRES.conf describing GPU devices, and use TRES/GRES limits in QOS/association.

7) Common pitfalls
- Not enabling jobacct_gather + cgroup/proctrack => sacct shows little or no accurate usage.
- Forgetting to set PriorityWeightQOS to include QOS in priority calculation.
- Setting PriorityDecayHalfLife too long/short: too-long makes heavy users permanently penalized; too-short erodes fairshare effect.
- Not attaching QOS or associations correctly in DB => limits and preemption not applied.
- Mismatched slurm.conf across nodes (node resource mismatches lead to DOWN states).
- Overly aggressive JobAcctGatherFrequency or too-frequent DB writes can overload slurmdbd/DB on very large clusters.

8) Useful commands (read-only) for verification and operations
- Inspect scheduler and priorities: sdiag, sprio, scontrol show config
- Inspect fairshare and usage: sshare, sreport
- Manage QOS/accounts: sacctmgr
- Inspect accounting DB entries: sacct starttime=... format=...
- Show reservations: scontrol show reservation
(These are read-only; change operations use sacctmgr/scontrol and must be done by operators.)

9) Short checklist when deploying or changing scheduling/accounting
- Ensure slurm.conf sets the desired PriorityType and weights.
- Choose and configure SelectType (cons_tres) and GRES if you have GPUs.
- Configure cgroup/task plugins and jobacct_gather for accurate usage.
- Install slurmdbd, configure slurmdbd.conf DB connection, and point slurm.conf AccountingStorageType to slurmdbd.
- Create accounts/users and QOS/associations in DB (sacctmgr), set sensible GrpTRES/GrpCPUs limits and QOS priority.
- Test with a small set of jobs and validate sacct/sreport/sshare outputs before rolling wide.

## EXAMPLES[#SECTION_EXAMPLES](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Specify a batch script by filename on the command line. The batch script specifies a 1 minute time limit for the job.
```text
$ cat myscript #!/bin/sh #SBATCH --time=1 srun hostname |sort $ sbatch -N4 myscript salloc: Granted job allocation 65537 $ cat slurm-65537.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```

Before enabling NSS Slurm directly on the node, you should use the
-s slurm option to getent within a newly launched job step
to verify that the rest of the setup has been completed successfully. The
-s option to getent allows it to query a specific database —
even if it has not been enabled by default through the system's
nsswitch.conf . Note that nss_slurm only responds to requests from
processes within the job step itself — you must launch the getent
command within a job step to see any data returned.
As an example of a successful query:
```text
tim@blackhole:~$ srun getent -s slurm passwd tim:x:1000:1000:Tim Wickberg:/home/tim:/bin/bash tim@blackhole:~$ srun getent -s slurm group tim:x:1000:tim projecta:x:1001:tim
```

## PERFORMANCE[#SECTION_PERFORMANCE](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Executing sbatch sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmctld daemon come in at once, it can result in
a degradation of performance of the slurmctld daemon, possibly resulting
in a denial of service.
Do not run sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other
programs. Ensure that programs limit calls to sbatch to the minimum
necessary for the information you are trying to gather.

## EXAMPLES[#SECTION_EXAMPLES](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Specify a batch script by filename on the command line. The batch script specifies a 1 minute time limit for the job.
```text
$ cat myscript #!/bin/sh #SBATCH --time=1 srun hostname |sort $ sbatch -N4 myscript salloc: Granted job allocation 65537 $ cat slurm-65537.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
Pass a batch script to sbatch on standard input:
```text
$ sbatch -N4 #!/bin/sh > srun hostname |sort > EOF sbatch: Submitted batch job 65541 $ cat slurm-65541.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
To create a heterogeneous job with 3 components, each allocating a unique set of nodes:
```text
$ sbatch -w node[2-3] : -w node4 : -w node[5-7] work.bash Submitted batch job 34987
```

## Timeslicer Design and Operation [#time_slice](https://slurm.schedmd.com/gang_scheduling.html)
When enabled, the gang scheduler keeps track of the resources
allocated to all jobs. For each partition an "active bitmap" is maintained that
tracks all concurrently running jobs in the Slurm cluster. Each time a new
job is allocated to resources in a partition, the gang scheduler
compares these newly allocated resources with the resources already maintained
in the "active bitmap".
If these two sets of resources are disjoint then the new job is added to the "active bitmap". If these two sets of resources overlap then
the new job is suspended. All jobs are tracked in a per-partition job queue
within the gang scheduler logic.

A QOS can be attached to a partition. This means the partition will have all
the same limits as the QOS. This does not associate jobs with the QOS, nor does
it give the job any priority or preemption characteristics of the assigned QOS.
Jobs may separately request the same QOS or a different QOS to gain those
characteristics. However, the Partition QOS limits will override the job's QOS.
If the opposite is desired you may configure the job's QOS with
`Flags=OverPartQOS` which will reverse the order of precedence.
This functionality may be used to implement a true "floating"
partition, in which a partition may access a limited amount of resources with no
restrictions on which nodes it uses to get the resources. This is accomplished
by assigning all nodes to the partition, then configuring a Partition QOS with

## EXAMPLES[#SECTION_EXAMPLES](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Specify a batch script by filename on the command line. The batch script specifies a 1 minute time limit for the job.
```text
$ cat myscript #!/bin/sh #SBATCH --time=1 srun hostname |sort $ sbatch -N4 myscript salloc: Granted job allocation 65537 $ cat slurm-65537.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
Pass a batch script to sbatch on standard input:
```text
$ sbatch -N4 #!/bin/sh > srun hostname |sort > EOF sbatch: Submitted batch job 65541 $ cat slurm-65541.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
To create a heterogeneous job with 3 components, each allocating a unique set of nodes:
```text
$ sbatch -w node[2-3] : -w node4 : -w node[5-7] work.bash Submitted batch job 34987
```

## PERFORMANCE[#SECTION_PERFORMANCE](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Executing sbatch sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmctld daemon come in at once, it can result in
a degradation of performance of the slurmctld daemon, possibly resulting
in a denial of service.
Do not run sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other
programs. Ensure that programs limit calls to sbatch to the minimum
necessary for the information you are trying to gather.

The backfill scheduler has limitations in how it tracks usage of CPUs and

## Timeslicer Design and Operation [#time_slice](https://slurm.schedmd.com/gang_scheduling.html)
When enabled, the gang scheduler keeps track of the resources
allocated to all jobs. For each partition an "active bitmap" is maintained that
tracks all concurrently running jobs in the Slurm cluster. Each time a new
job is allocated to resources in a partition, the gang scheduler
compares these newly allocated resources with the resources already maintained
in the "active bitmap".
If these two sets of resources are disjoint then the new job is added to the "active bitmap". If these two sets of resources overlap then
the new job is suspended. All jobs are tracked in a per-partition job queue
within the gang scheduler logic.

### Jobs
How is job suspend/resume useful?
Job suspend/resume is most useful to get particularly large jobs initiated
in a timely fashion with minimal overhead. Say you want to get a full-system
job initiated. Normally you would need to either cancel all running jobs
or wait for them to terminate. Canceling jobs results in the loss of
their work to that point from their beginning.
Waiting for the jobs to terminate can take hours, depending upon your
system configuration. A more attractive alternative is to suspend the
running jobs, run the full-system job, then resume the suspended jobs.
This can easily be accomplished by configuring a special queue for
full-system jobs and using a script to control the process.
The script would stop the other partitions, suspend running jobs in those
partitions, and start the full-system partition.

Before enabling NSS Slurm directly on the node, you should use the
-s slurm option to getent within a newly launched job step
to verify that the rest of the setup has been completed successfully. The
-s option to getent allows it to query a specific database —
even if it has not been enabled by default through the system's
nsswitch.conf . Note that nss_slurm only responds to requests from
processes within the job step itself — you must launch the getent
command within a job step to see any data returned.
As an example of a successful query:
```text
tim@blackhole:~$ srun getent -s slurm passwd tim:x:1000:1000:Tim Wickberg:/home/tim:/bin/bash tim@blackhole:~$ srun getent -s slurm group tim:x:1000:tim projecta:x:1001:tim
```

## NSS Configuration [#NSS_CONFIG](https://slurm.schedmd.com/nss_slurm.html)
Enabling nss_slurm is as simple as adding slurm to the passwd and
group database in /etc/nsswitch.conf (only on systems that will run
slurmd ). It is recommended that
slurm is listed first, as the order (from left to right) determines
the sequence in which the NSS databases will be queried, and this ensures Slurm
handles the request if able before submitting the query to other sources.
To enable cloud node name resolution slurm needs to be added to the
to hosts database in /etc/nsswitch.conf .
It is recommended that slurm is listed last.
Once enabled, test it by launching getent queries such as:
```text
tim@blackhole:~$ srun getent passwd tim tim:x:1000:1000:Tim Wickberg:/home/tim:/bin/bash tim@blackhole:~$ srun getent group projecta projecta:x:1001:tim
```

## Slurm Configuration [#SLURM_CONFIG](https://slurm.schedmd.com/pam_slurm_adopt.html)
PrologFlags=contain must be set in the slurm.conf. This sets up the
"extern" step into which ssh-launched processes will be adopted. You must also
enable the task/cgroup plugin in slurm.conf. See the
[Slurm cgroups guide.](https://slurm.schedmd.com/cgroups.html)
CAUTION This option must be in place before using this module.
The module bases its checks on local steps that have already been launched. Jobs
launched without this option do not have an extern step, so pam_slurm_adopt will
not have access to those jobs.
LaunchParameters=ulimit_pam_adopt will set RLIMIT_RSS in processes
adopted by the external step, similar to tasks running in regular steps.
The UsePAM option in slurm.conf is not related to pam_slurm_adopt.
Done.

## DESCRIPTION[#SECTION_DESCRIPTION](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sacct.html)
Accounting information for jobs invoked with Slurm are either logged
in the job accounting log file or saved to the Slurm database, as
configured with the AccountingStorageType parameter.
The sacct command displays job accounting data stored in the job
accounting log file or Slurm database in a variety of forms for your
analysis. The sacct command displays information on jobs, job
steps, status, and exitcodes by default. You can tailor the output
with the use of the --format= option to specify the fields to
be shown.
Job records consist of a primary entry for the job as a whole as well as

Good question — when you inspect completed or historical jobs with sacct, these fields are the most useful for understanding job state, runtime, and memory usage. Below I list the fields, what they mean, units you can expect, and quick tips for using them.

State-related fields
- State
  - What: final job state string shown by sacct (COMPLETED, FAILED, CANCELLED, TIMEOUT, PREEMPTED, OUT_OF_MEMORY, etc.).
  - Use: primary field to know outcome; combine with ExitCode for the failure type.
- ExitCode
  - What: job exit code as "code:signal" (e.g., 0:0 for success).
  - Use: distinguishes normal exits from application errors even when State is COMPLETED.
- StateFlags / StateReason (not always present)
  - What: extra flags/reason information (e.g., OOM, REQUEUE).
  - Use: useful when you see a flagged state and want extra context.

Elapsed / time fields
- Elapsed
  - What: human-readable wall-clock runtime (format like DD-HH:MM:SS or HH:MM:SS).
  - Use: quick reading for how long the job ran.
- ElapsedRaw
  - What: elapsed time in integer seconds.
  - Use: preferred for scripted numeric comparisons, sorting, thresholds.
- Start / End
  - What: timestamp when job started and ended.
  - Use: calculate windows or correlate with system logs.
- Timelimit
  - What: job time limit requested (same human format as Elapsed).
  - Use: check whether the job hit its time limit (compare with Elapsed or check State=TIMEOUT).
- Submit
  - What: submit time; useful for ordering jobs or for “submitted before/after” queries.

Memory-related fields
- ReqMem
  - What: memory requested (reported as the request string).
  - Use: shows what the job asked for. Note: value meaning depends on how the job requested memory:
    - --mem => per node; --mem-per-cpu => per CPU.
- MaxRSS
  - What: peak resident set size (maximum physical memory used by a task).
  - Units: typically reported in KB (or with unit suffix depending on sacct version).
  - Use: primary field to see peak physical memory consumption. Useful to detect OOM or to right-size subsequent requests.
- MaxRSSTask
  - What: which task had the MaxRSS peak.
  - Use: identifies misbehaving task in multi-task jobs.
- AveRSS
  - What: average resident set size across tasks.
  - Use: good for cluster-wide averages when many tasks run.
- MaxVMSize
  - What: peak virtual memory size (address space high-water mark).
  - Use: catches large virtual allocations even if RSS was lower.

Practical tips
- Use ElapsedRaw for comparisons and scripting (e.g., detect jobs > 7200 seconds).
- Always check both State and ExitCode — ExitCode can show non-zero application exits even when State is COMPLETED (e.g., batch wrappers).
- MaxRSS is usually the most actionable memory metric; use MaxRSSTask to find which rank/task used the memory.
- ReqMem vs actual: compare ReqMem to MaxRSS to decide whether to reduce or increase requested memory.
- For pending / not-starting reasons use squeue (sacct does not show current pending reasons). For detailed per-job info use scontrol show job <id>.

Example sacct format to get a compact useful row
--format=JobID,JobName,User,State,ExitCode,Elapsed,ElapsedRaw,Start,End,Timelimit,ReqMem,AllocTRES,AllocCPUS,MaxRSS,AveRSS,MaxRSSTask

This returns state, numeric elapsed, requested memory, allocations, and peak/average memory so you can both read and script decisions from the output.

If you want, I can suggest a ready-to-copy sacct command tailored to your cluster's preferred units or to show only jobs for a specific user/time window.

Short answer
- Use squeue to view the live queue (running and pending jobs).  
- Use sacct to view accounting/history (completed, failed, cancelled jobs, exit codes, recorded resource usage).

When to pick each (doc-backed guidance)
- squeue
  - Purpose: real‑time queue view of active jobs (RUNNING, PENDING, etc.). Good for checking why a job is still pending (use the pending reason shown), seeing current node/partition allocations, and monitoring currently running jobs.
  - Typical use cases: “What is in the queue now?”, “Is job 12345 running or pending?”, “Which nodes are busy?”.
  - Common commands/examples: squeue -u alice, squeue -j 12345, squeue -p gpu.
  - Notes: squeue is fast and reads live slurmctld state.

- sacct
  - Purpose: query job accounting records stored in the job accounting log or SlurmDB (historical data about jobs and job steps). Returns exit codes, final state (COMPLETED/FAILED/CANCELLED), elapsed time, requested/consumed resources, etc.
  - Typical use cases: “What exit code did my job get?”, “How long did that completed job run?”, usage/accounting reports over a time window, user/job history.
  - Common commands/examples: sacct -j 12345 --format=JobID,JobName,State,ExitCode,Elapsed,AllocCPUs,ReqMem; sacct -u alice --starttime=2024-01-01.
  - Notes: sacct queries slurmdbd (remote procedure call). It can be slower and, if overused, can load slurmdbd — avoid calling sacct repeatedly in tight loops or scripts. sacct requires accounting storage (SlurmDB) to be configured to show historical data.

Recommended quick workflow (practical)
- Check squeue first for a job ID to see its current live state. If squeue shows no entry for that job and you need historical info (exit code, final state, elapsed), then use sacct to inspect the completed job record.
- If you need runtime resource metrics for a currently running job, use sstat (not sacct) for real‑time job resource usage; sacct is for post‑run accounting.

Other useful doc notes
- sacct shows job steps and more detailed accounting fields; use --format to tailor output.
- Because sacct contacts slurmdbd, running many sacct calls can degrade slurmdbd performance (do not loop sacct calls without limits).

Summary — what burst buffers are
- A "burst buffer" is a fast intermediate storage layer (NVMe/SSD or vendor system like DataWarp) that Slurm can allocate to jobs to speed I/O (stage-in, stage-out, scratch).
- Slurm itself delegates to a burst-buffer plugin (DataWarp, Lua-based plugins, etc.), so exact directive names and behavior depend on your cluster’s plugin and site configuration.

Where you put directives
- Burst‑buffer directives are placed as commented lines in batch scripts (they may appear before/after/interspersed with #SBATCH lines).
- You can also pass burst‑buffer options on the command line with sbatch/salloc/srun using --bb or supply a file of operations with --bbf.
- Note: --bb can request job‑local buffers but cannot create/destroy persistent buffers (that depends on the plugin).

Common directive forms and operations (plugin-dependent)
- Generic form (examples; the exact keywords vary by plugin/site):
  - Request a job buffer: #BB request pool=<pool> capacity=<size> access=<mode>
  - Stage data in/out: #BB stage_in source=<src> dest=<dest> and #BB stage_out source=<src> dest=<dest>
  - Persistent buffers (DataWarp supports persistent buffers): #BB create_persistent name=<name> capacity=<size> [pool=...] [access=...] and #BB destroy_persistent name=<name> [hurry]
- Typical parameters you’ll see:
  - pool (which burst buffer pool to use)
  - capacity / size (e.g., 100GiB or 1TiB)
  - access / access_mode (private/shared)
  - name (for persistent buffers)
  - stage_in / stage_out paths and related options
- Because plugins differ, some clusters use plugin-specific prefixes (e.g., site may document directives like #DW or other forms). Always check your site’s burst‑buffer documentation.

Life cycle / stages
- Create/allocate: Slurm (via the plugin) allocates the buffer resource for the job (or persistent buffer).
- Stage‑in: Input data is copied into the burst buffer before the job runs (if requested).
- Job runs: Job reads/writes to its burst buffer mount or path.
- Stage‑out: On job completion (or at configured times), data is flushed out to final storage.
- Release/cleanup: Buffer is freed or (for persistent buffers) left available per policy.

How to check burst‑buffer status
- scontrol show burst
  - Shows configured burst pools and current allocations. Example fields you may see (example adapted from the docs):
    - Name, DefaultPool, Granularity, TotalSpace, FreeSpace, UsedSpace, Flags, timeouts (StageInTimeout, StageOutTimeout, ...)
    - Allocated Buffers: JobID=169509 CreateTime=... Pool=wlm_pool Size=1200GiB State=allocated UserID=marshall(1017)
    - Per User Buffer Use: UserID=marshall(1017) Used=1600GiB
- sview GUI: has a “Burst Buffer” tab (if available) to view pools and allocations.
- Job-level visibility:
  - The job’s burst buffer allocation and state are reported by the plugin and can appear in scontrol show job <jobid> or in the scontrol show burst output under Allocated Buffers (exact placement depends on plugin/config).
  - Job logs / stderr may show stage‑in/stage‑out progress or failure messages.
- What status fields mean (common examples)
  - State=allocated: buffer reserved for the job
  - State=staged-in: stage‑in completed (data present in buffer)
  - Sizes: TotalSpace / FreeSpace / UsedSpace reflect pool capacity and usage
  - Timeouts: StageInTimeout and StageOutTimeout are plugin-configured timeouts you may hit if transfers are slow

Troubleshooting tips
- If stage‑in or stage‑out fails or times out:
  - Check job stderr and the plugin logs (site-specific).
  - Inspect scontrol show burst to see pool free space and the buffer’s State and timeouts.
  - Ensure you requested enough capacity and that the pool has free space.
- For persistent buffers:
  - Use the plugin’s create/destroy directives (DataWarp supports persistent buffers); remember persistent creation/destruction may require special privileges or policies.
- If you’re unsure what directive syntax your cluster accepts, consult your site’s burst‑buffer usage doc or ask admins — plugin and local conventions differ.

Quick pointers to commands (read-only)
- Inspect pools and allocations: scontrol show burst
- Inspect a job (to see if it has an allocation): scontrol show job <jobid>
- GUI: sview → Burst Buffer tab (if installed)

If you want, tell me:
- Which plugin your cluster uses (DataWarp, Lua, etc.) or paste a small example of your site’s burst‑buffer directive and I’ll translate it and show precise example lines and the exact scontrol fields to look for.

## PERFORMANCE[#SECTION_PERFORMANCE](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sacct.html)
Executing sacct sends a remote procedure call to slurmdbd . If
enough calls from sacct or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmdbd daemon come in at once, it can result in a
degradation of performance of the slurmdbd daemon, possibly resulting in a
denial of service.
Do not run sacct or other Slurm client commands that send remote procedure
calls to slurmdbd from loops in shell scripts or other programs. Ensure
that programs limit calls to sacct to the minimum necessary for the
information you are trying to gather.

Good question — sacct's --format option is how you build custom, script-friendly accounting reports. Below is a concise reference with syntax, useful fields, common modifiers, examples and important caveats.

Basics
- Syntax: --format=FIELD[,FIELD...]
- Common fields: JobID, JobName, User, Account, Partition, State, ExitCode, Elapsed, NCPUs, ReqMem, AllocCPUS, NodeList, ReqNodes, MaxRSS, MaxVMSize, Start, End
- You can use ALL to request every available field (can be very wide).

Field modifiers
- Width: FIELD:W — reserve W character width (truncates/pads for column output).
- Label: FIELD=Label — override the printed column header.
- Both combined: FIELD:W=Label (order: field, optional :width, optional =label).
- Example: JobID:12=ID, JobName:30=Command

Machine/parsible output flags (for scripts)
- --parsable2 or -P: produce a machine-parseable output variant.
- --delimiter=CHAR: change the field delimiter (useful for CSV: --delimiter=',' ). With -P the output is easier to parse.
- -n or --noheader: omit the header row.

Control which records appear
- Default shows both job and step records. Use --allocations (-X) to only show allocation-level (not steps).
- Use --array to expand array tasks onto separate lines.
- Use -S/--starttime and -E/--endtime to limit the time window.
- Filters: -u/--user, -a/--accounts, -p/--partition, -s/--state etc.

Examples
- Human-readable custom columns:
  sacct --format=JobID,JobName,User,Account,Partition,State,Elapsed,ExitCode

- CSV for scripts (no header):
  sacct -S 2026-04-01 -E 2026-04-30 --format=JobID,JobName,User,Account,State,Elapsed,ExitCode -P --delimiter=',' -n > april_report.csv

- Fixed width with custom labels:
  sacct --format=JobID:10=JOB,User:15=OWNER,JobName:30=COMMAND,State

- Include max memory and CPU usage for steps:
  sacct --format=JobID,JobName,User,State,Elapsed,MaxRSS,MaxVMSize,NCPUs

- Only allocations (no steps):
  sacct -X --format=JobID,JobName,AllocCPUS,AllocNodes,NodeList,State,Elapsed

- Expand array tasks:
  sacct --array -S 2026-05-01 --format=JobID,JobName,User,State,Elapsed

Tips & gotchas
- Quote the whole --format string if it contains spaces or special shell characters.
- Some fields (Ave*/Max*/Min*) compute across tasks/threads — e.g., MaxRSS, MaxRSSTask.
- Output field names are case-sensitive and must match documented field names.
- The SACCT_FEDERATION and SACCT_FORMAT environment variables can set defaults (SACCT_FORMAT same as --format).
- Performance: sacct queries slurmdbd; repeated/looped calls can overload slurmdbd — batch your queries or limit time windows.

Where to find the full field list
- The sacct manpage lists every job-accounting field and exact modifier syntax (search for "Job Accounting Fields" in sacct docs). Use that when you need less-common fields (AllocTRES, TresUsed, AdminComment, etc.)

Slurm can also be configured to allocate resources to jobs on a
hierarchical network to minimize network contention.

hierarchy that can satisfy a job's request and then allocate resources
on its underlying leaf switches using a best-fit algorithm.

Short version
- Slurm “topology awareness” means the scheduler knows the cluster network/switch hierarchy and uses that knowledge when placing jobs so network-sensitive jobs (MPI, RDMA, collectives) see fewer cross‑switch hops and less contention.
- “Network placement” is the practical result: Slurm will prefer nodes that share the same switch (or the fewest switches possible) and can optionally make jobs wait for an optimal placement rather than using any idle nodes anywhere.

How it works (concepts)
- Topology model: admins supply a topology.conf that describes switches, switch parents, which nodes hang off each switch, and optional link speeds. Slurm uses that to map nodes onto a hierarchical network/tree or into blocks.
- Topology plugins: Slurm provides plugins such as topology/tree and topology/block. You enable a plugin via TopologyPlugin in slurm.conf.
  - topology/tree: treats the network as a hierarchy of switches and tries to allocate nodes under the lowest common switch that satisfies the job. It uses a best‑fit algorithm on currently idle resources.
  - topology/block: treats nodes as contiguous “blocks” (bblocks/aggregated blocks) and prioritizes allocations that minimize fragmentation.
- TopologyParam options: parameters such as TopoOptional and RouteTree change strictness:
  - RouteTree (strict): jobs may only span nodes connected by the same switch fabric; nodes on separate fabrics cannot be combined.
  - TopoOptional (looser): allows spanning across switch boundaries when necessary.

User-facing controls
- --switches=count[@time] (salloc/sbatch/srun): ask Slurm to limit the allocation to at most count leaf switches; optional @time lets the job wait up to time seconds for that optimized placement. Example: --switches=1@30 requests all nodes on a single leaf switch, waiting up to 30s for that grouping.
- Hostlist topology functions: with topology plugins enabled you can use functions like switch{switchY}, block{blockX}, switchwith{nodeY}, blockwith{nodeZ} in hostlists and scripts to request nodes by topology grouping.
- Task/node distribution flags: combine topology options with --distribution or CPU/memory binding options (and --mem-bind) to control intra‑node placement for best locality.

Why it helps
- Reduces cross‑switch traffic and congestion for MPI / RDMA jobs -> better throughput and lower latency.
- Improves performance of collective operations and large all‑to‑all communication.
- Reduces fragmentation (block plugin) so many small jobs can coexist without scattering a large parallel job across many switches.

Tradeoffs and behaviors
- Waiting for optimal placement: topology-aware placement can increase queue wait time because Slurm may hold a job until sufficient nodes appear under the desired switch/block (you can cap wait with --switches@time or admins can limit via SchedulerParameters max_switch_wait).
- Best‑fit subject to current availability: Slurm uses a best‑fit heuristic and may still use more switches than an absolute optimum if nodes become available in a certain pattern.
- Requires accurate topology.conf and a consistent fabric; misconfigured topology data can cause unexpected placement or prevent spanning nodes if RouteTree is used.
- Some fabrics (multiple independent networks) may make strict routing unusable unless topology is organized appropriately.

Admin notes (how to configure)
- Create topology.conf describing switches/blocks and optional link speeds, or auto-generate for InfiniBand with tools (slurmibtopology).
- Set TopologyPlugin=topology/tree or topology/block in slurm.conf and use select/cons_tres as the select plugin.
- Tune TopologyParam (TopoOptional, RouteTree) and SchedulerParameters (e.g., max_switch_wait).
- Expose topology hostlist functions for users if desired.

When to use topology awareness
- Large MPI / RDMA jobs, jobs with heavy all‑to‑all communication, tightly coupled parallel jobs—these benefit most.
- If jobs are mostly single‑node or embarrassingly parallel, topology awareness may be less important and could add wait time.

Useful commands / next steps
- If you want, I can:
  - Show your cluster’s configured topology (requires reading topology.conf / sinfo); or
  - Explain exact sbatch/srun flags for a particular MPI application and network fabric.

# Job Exit Codes
A job's exit code (aka exit status, return code and completion
code) is captured by Slurm and saved as part of the job record. For
sbatch jobs, the exit code that is captured is the output of the batch
script. For salloc jobs, the exit code will be the return value of
the exit call that terminates the salloc session. For srun, the exit
code will be the return value of the command that srun executes.
Any non-zero exit code will be assumed to be a job failure and will
result in a Job State of FAILED with a Reason of
"NonZeroExitCode".
The exit code is an 8 bit unsigned number ranging between 0 and
255. While it is possible for a job to return a negative exit code,
Slurm will display it as an unsigned value in the 0 - 255 range.

Short answer
- ReqNodeNotAvail is a Slurm pending reason meaning “the scheduler could not find nodes that satisfy the job’s node/resource constraints right now.” In other words, nodes that would match the job’s request are not currently available (idle) so the job remains PENDING with reason ReqNodeNotAvail.

What ReqNodeNotAvail actually implies
- The scheduler tried to place the job but no node (or set of nodes) meeting the job’s requirements (partition, CPUs, memory, GPUs/GRES, features/constraints, exclusivity, node counts, topology, reservation, QOS/account limits, etc.) was free at that scheduling attempt. Only the first encountered blocking cause is shown, but multiple availability reasons may apply.

Common node-availability causes (why nodes aren’t available)
- Allocated/Busy: Nodes that match are currently RUNNING other jobs (allocated), possibly long-running or exclusive.
- Drained/Draining: Nodes are in DRAIN or DRAINING state (admin flagged for maintenance or reboot).
- Down/Failing: Nodes are DOWN, FAIL or FAILING due to hardware/network problems.
- Reserved: Nodes are reserved for a reservation; jobs not in that reservation can’t use them.
- Feature/Constraint mismatch: Job requested --constraint, --gres, or node features (eg. specific CPU, GPU type) that no idle node currently provides.
- Insufficient per-node resources: Request (eg. GPUs-per-node, CPUs-per-task, huge memory) exceeds what any single idle node can offer.
- Topology/affinity/step packing: Job requests multiple nodes with packing or contiguous topology that aren’t simultaneously free.
- GRES/GPU state: GPUs exist but are in use, isolated, or marked unusable (driver/health issues).
- Partition mismatch or partition limits: The job targeted a partition with no eligible idle nodes or partition-level limits/QOS prevented allocation.
- Account/QOS/association limits: Aggregate/account quotas or QOS limits can prevent allocation that otherwise looks node-eligible (often visible as another reason, but can manifest as ReqNodeNotAvail depending on scheduler checks).
- Licensing constraints: Software licenses required by the job are exhausted and scheduler blocks allocation where license is missing.
- Node feature mis-configuration or admin downlist: Node attributes don’t match current configuration (e.g., updated hardware/labels not reflected).
- Mixed state nodes: Nodes in MIXED state (partially allocated) may not satisfy a multi-slot request.

Quick investigation checklist (commands to run)
- See why a specific job is pending:
  - squeue -j <jobid> -o "%i %P %j %u %T %R"   (shows the pending reason column)
  - scontrol show job <jobid>                 (shows requested nodes/GRES/constraints/ReqNodeList)
- Inspect node/partition state and reasons:
  - sinfo -Nel                                (partition/node overview with states)
  - sinfo -R                                  (list nodes in DRAIN/DOWN with reasons)
  - scontrol show node <nodename>             (detailed node state, Reason, GRES, real resources)
- Check reservations and limits:
  - scontrol show reservation <name>          (if you suspect a reservation)
  - sshare / sacctmgr list                     (check fairshare, account, and association limits)
- Scheduler diagnostics:
  - sprio / sdiag                              (priority/backfill diagnostics if scheduling order is a concern)

What to try / how to resolve
- Relax constraints: drop or broaden --constraint, reduce per-node resource requests, or request fewer GPUs/CPUs.
- Try a different partition or explicitly target nodes known to have the required resources.
- Wait or contact users/admins if nodes are legitimately occupied by long jobs.
- If nodes are DRAIN/DOWN, contact admins (or check sinfo_reasons) to get an ETA or to request resume.
- Check reservations/licenses: if a reservation or license is blocking, either schedule within it or ask admin to adjust.
- If you believe the scheduler is mis-reporting, collect: squeue output, scontrol show job, sinfo, scontrol show node for candidate nodes and open an admin ticket with those outputs.

# Job Reason Codes
These reason codes can be used to identify why a pending job has not yet been
started by the scheduler. There may be multiple reasons why a job cannot start,
in which case only the reason that was encountered by the attempted scheduling
method will be displayed. Refer to the [Scheduling Configuration Guide](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sched_config.html) for more details.

Short answer
- The Slurm pending reason Resources means: the scheduler could not find the required free/eligible resources to place the job right now. That includes CPUs, memory, GPUs (GRES), consumable resources (licenses, devices), or hierarchical resources (HRES) defined in resources.yaml.

What it covers (common causes)
- No idle nodes with enough CPUs/memory to satisfy the job's ReqCPUs/ReqMem/ntasks.
- All matching GPU nodes (GRES) are already allocated or drained.
- The job requests a specific node feature/constraint (–C/--constraint) that no idle node satisfies.
- Consumable resources (licenses, specific hardware devices) are exhausted.
- Hierarchical resources (HRES) layers are insufficient where configured.
- Per-account / QOS / association limits have been reached (so resources are effectively unavailable).
- Nodes are down/drained or a reservation is consuming the needed capacity.

How to diagnose (commands to run)
- squeue -j <jobid> (or squeue -o "%i %P %j %u %t %M %R") — confirm the job’s pending reason is Resources.
- scontrol show job <jobid> — inspect requested TRES, ReqMem, partition, constraint, and other job fields.
- sinfo -Nel (or sinfo -o ...) — see partition/node counts and which nodes are idle vs allocated/drain/down.
- scontrol show node <nodename> — check AllocTRES, Available features and per-node resource counts.
- scontrol_license — check consumable license resources if licenses are used as GRES.
- sinfo -R — show nodes in drain/down states and reasons (if nodes are offline by reason).
- sshare / sacctmgr list (or ask admins) — verify account/QOS limits or associations if you suspect quotas.

How to fix or mitigate
- Reduce resource requests (fewer tasks, lower CPUs, less memory or fewer GPUs) so the scheduler can match smaller packing.
- Remove/relax node constraints (–C/--constraint) or try a different partition.
- Wait until nodes free up, or schedule during lower load.
- If consumable resources/licenses are exhausted, free up holders or request more from admin.
- Ask admins to investigate down/drained nodes or reservations that are consuming capacity.
- If HRES is in use, check resources.yaml and ensure required HRES layers have capacity or change job’s HRES request.
- Consider smaller job walltime so backfill can start it sooner, or enable preemption/QOS options if available.

Notes and gotchas
- "Resources" is a generic scheduler-level reason — it does not by itself say which resource is missing. Use scontrol show job and scontrol show node to find the specific mismatch.
- If a job requests GRES (GPUs), only nodes reported as idle in sinfo count as available for a conditional GPU submit. Allocated/drained/down/mixed nodes do not count as free.
- If you want, give me a job ID and I can run the minimal checks (squeue and scontrol show job) and summarize exactly what resource is lacking.

## AUTHORIZATION[#SECTION_AUTHORIZATION](https://slurm.schedmd.com/scontrol.html)
Slurm generally classifies users into three authorization levels:
- Administrators include root, SlurmUser, and any users with
"AdminLevel=Administrator"
- Privileged Users include all Administrators and any users with
"AdminLevel=Operator"
- Effective Owners of a job or step include the direct owner and all
Coordinators of the corresponding account.
Note that configuring AdminLevels or Coordinators requires the use of SlurmDBD.
The authorization levels required to execute various commands are defined in the
following table.
scontrol update job: Privileged or Effective Owner
scontrol requeue: Privileged or Effective Owner
scontrol update step: Privileged or Effective Owner
scontrol suspend: Privileged or Coordinator
scontrol resume: Privileged or Coordinator
scontrol notify: Root, SlurmUser, or direct owner

shut down nodes will depend upon your cluster management tools.

time limits but must have [Fault Tolerance](https://slurm.schedmd.com/elastic_computing.html). They

and start the slurmd daemon, thus the node is no longer non-responsive

## Cloud Accounting[#accounting](https://slurm.schedmd.com/power_save.html)
Information about cloud instances can be stored in the database. This can
be done by configuring instance id/type upon slurmd startup or with
scontrol update . The node's "extra" field will also be stored in the
database.
Configuring cloud information on slurmd startup:
```text
$ slurmd --instance-id=12345 --instance-type=m7g.medium --extra="arbitrary string" . . .
```
Configuring cloud information with scontrol update:
```text
$ scontrol update nodename=n1 instanceid=12345 instancetype=m7g.medium extra="arbitrary string"
```
This data can then be seen on the controller with scontrol show
node . Past and current data can be seen in the database with sacctmgr
show instance , as well as through slurmrestd with the /instance
and /instances endpoints.

The job submit plugin is invoked independently for each component of a
heterogeneous job.
The spank_init_post_opt() function is invoked once for each component of a
heterogeneous job. This permits site defined options on a per job component

## Limitations [#limitations](https://slurm.schedmd.com/heterogeneous_jobs.html)
The backfill scheduler has limitations in how it tracks usage of CPUs and
memory in the future.
This typically requires the backfill scheduler be able to allocate each
component of a heterogeneous job on a different node in order to begin its
resource allocation, even if multiple components of the job do actually get
allocated resources on the same node.
In a federation of clusters, a heterogeneous job will execute entirely on
the cluster from which the job is submitted. The heterogeneous job will not
be eligible to migrate between clusters or to have different components of
the job execute on different clusters in the federation.

### Designing Jobs
How can I run multiple jobs from within a
single script?
A Slurm job is just a resource allocation. You can execute many
job steps within that allocation, either in parallel or sequentially.
Some jobs actually launch thousands of job steps this way. The job
steps will be allocated nodes that are not already allocated to
other job steps. This essentially provides a second level of resource
management within the job for the job steps.
How can I run a job within an existing
job allocation?
There is an srun option --jobid that can be used to specify
a job's ID.
For a batch job or within an existing resource allocation, the
environment variable SLURM_JOB_ID has already been defined,
so all job steps will run within that job allocation unless
otherwise specified.

Information about cloud instances can be stored in the database. This can
be done by configuring instance id/type upon slurmd startup or with
scontrol update . The node's "extra" field will also be stored in the
database.
Configuring cloud information on slurmd startup:
```text

```text

## Node Features[#nodefeatures](https://slurm.schedmd.com/power_save.html)
Features defined by [NodeFeaturesPlugins](https://slurm.schedmd.com/slurm.conf.html), and
associated to cloud nodes in the slurm.conf , will be available but not
active when the node is powered down. If a job requests available but not
active features, the controller will allocate nodes that are powered down and
have the features as available. At allocation, the features will be made
active. A cloud node will remain with the active features until the node is
powered down (i.e. the node can't be rebooted to get other features until the
node is powered down). When the node is powered down, the those features
become available but not active. Any feature not defined by
NodeFeaturesPlugins are always active.
