## Fault Tolerance[#tolerance](https://slurm.schedmd.com/power_save.html)
If the slurmctld daemon is terminated gracefully, it will wait up
to ten seconds (or the maximum of SuspendTimeout or
ResumeTimeout if less than ten seconds) for any spawned
SuspendProgram or ResumeProgram to terminate before the daemon
terminates. If the spawned program does not terminate within that time
period, the event will be logged and slurmctld will exit in order to
permit another slurmctld daemon to be initiated. Any spawned
SuspendProgram or ResumeProgram will continue to run.
When the slurmctld daemon shuts down, any SLURM_RESUME_FILE
temporary files are no longer available, even once slurmctld restarts.
Therefore, ResumeProgram should use SLURM_RESUME_FILE within
ten seconds of starting to guarantee that it still exists.

## EXAMPLES[#SECTION_EXAMPLES](https://slurm.schedmd.com/scancel.html)
Send SIGTERM to steps 1 and 3 of job 1234:
```text
$ scancel --signal=TERM 1234.1 1234.3
```
Cancel job 1234 along with all of its steps:
```text
$ scancel 1234
```
Send SIGKILL to all steps of job 1235, but do not cancel the job itself:
```text
$ scancel --signal=KILL 1235
```
Send SIGUSR1 to the batch shell processes of job 1236:
```text
$ scancel --signal=USR1 --batch 1236
```
Cancel all pending jobs belonging to user "bob" in partition "debug":
```text
$ scancel --state=PENDING --user=bob --partition=debug
```
Cancel only array ID 4 of job array 1237
```text
$ scancel 1237_4
```

 Slurm Power Saving Guide 

 Contents 

 
 Overview 
 Configuration 
 Node Lifecycle 
 Manual Power Saving 
 Resume and Suspend Programs 
 Fault Tolerance 
 Booting Different Images 
 Use of Allocations 
 Node Features 
 Hybrid Cluster

 Overview 

 Slurm provides an integrated mechanism for nodes being suspended (powered
down, placed into power saving mode) and resumed (powered up, restored from
power saving mode) on demand or by request. Nodes that remain IDLE for
 SuspendTime will be suspended by SuspendProgram and will be
unavailable for scheduling for SuspendTimeout . Nodes will
automatically be resumed by ResumeProgram to complete work allocated
to them. Nodes that fail to register within ResumeTimeout will become
 DOWN and their allocated jobs are requeued. Node power saving can be
manually requested by scontrol update nodename=<nodename>
state=power_<down|up> . The rate of nodes being resumed or
suspended can be controlled by ResumeRate and SuspendRate . 

 Slurm can be configured to accomplish power saving by managing compute
resources in any cloud provider (e.g. Amazon
Web Services , Google Cloud
Platform , Microsoft Azure ) via
their API. These resources can be combined with an existing cluster to
process excess workload (cloud bursting) or it can operate as an independent
and self-contained cluster. 

 To enable Power Saving operation in Slurm, you must configure the
following: 

 
 ResumeProgram and SuspendProgram must be defined. Their
 value must be a valid path to a program. 

 ResumeTimeout and SuspendTimeout must be defined, either
 globally or on at least one partition. 

 SuspendTime must be defined, either globally or on at least one
 partition, and not be INFINITE or -1 . 

 ResumeRate and SuspendRate must be greater than or equal
 to 0 . 
 

 The Slurm control daemon, slurmctld , must be restarted to initially
enable Power Saving operation. Changes in the configuration parameters (e.g.
 SuspendTime ) will take effect after modifying the slurm.conf 
configuration file and executing scontrol reconfigure . 

 Configuration 

 The following configuration parameters of interest include: 

 
 DebugFlags 
 

 
 Defines specific subsystems which should provide more detailed event
 logging. Options of interest include: 

 
 Power 
 

 
 Power management plugin and power save (suspend/resume programs)
 details. 
 
 
 

 ReconfigFlags 
 

 
 Flags to control various actions that may be taken when an
 scontrol reconfigure command is issued. Options of interest
 include: 

 
 KeepPowerSaveSettings 
 

 
 If set, an scontrol reconfigure command will preserve
 the current state of SuspendExcNodes , SuspendExcParts ,
 and SuspendExcStates . 
 
 
 

 ResumeFailProgram 
 

 
 Program to be executed when nodes fail to resume by
 ResumeTimeout . The argument to the program will be the names of
 the failed nodes (using Slurm's hostlist expression format). 
 

 ResumeProgram 
 

 
 Program to be executed to restore nodes from power saving mode. The
 program executes as SlurmUser (as configured in
 slurm.conf ). The argument to the program will be the names of
 nodes to be restored from power savings mode (using Slurm's hostlist
 expression format). 

 If the slurmd daemon fails to respond within the configured
 ResumeTimeout value with an updated BootTime, the node will be
 placed in a DOWN state and the job requesting the node will be requeued.
 If the node isn't actually rebooted (e.g. when multiple-slurmd is
 configured) you can start slurmd with the "-b" option to report the node
 boot time as now. 

 A job to node mapping is available in JSON format by reading the
 temporary file specified by the SLURM_RESUME_FILE environment
 variable. This file should be used at the beginning of
 ResumeProgram - see the Fault Tolerance 
 section for more details. This program may use the scontrol show
 nodename command to ensure that a node has booted and the
 slurmd daemon started. 

 
SLURM_RESUME_FILE=/proc/1647372/fd/7:
{
 "all_nodes_resume" : "cloud[1-3,7-8]",
 "jobs" : [
 {
 "extra" : "An arbitrary string from --extra",
 "features" : "c1,c2",
 "job_id" : 140814,
 "nodes_alloc" : "cloud[1-4]",
 "nodes_resume" : "cloud[1-3]",
 "oversubscribe" : "OK",
 "partition" : "cloud",
 "reservation" : "resv_1234"
 },
 {
 "extra" : null,
 "features" : "c1,c2",
 "job_id" : 140815,
 "nodes_alloc" : "cloud[1-2]",
 "nodes_resume" : "cloud[1-2]",
 "oversubscribe" : "OK",
 "partition" : "cloud",
 "reservation" : null
 },
 {
 "extra" : null,
 "features" : null
 "job_id" : 140816,
 "nodes_alloc" : "cloud[7-8]",
 "nodes_resume" : "cloud[7-8]",
 "oversubscribe" : "NO",
 "partition" : "cloud_exclusive",
 "reservation" : null
 }
 ]
}
 

 See the squeue man page 
 for possible values for oversubscribe . 

 NOTE : The SLURM_RESUME_FILE will only exist and be
 usable if Slurm was compiled with the JSON-C serializer library. 
 

 ResumeRate 
 

 
 Maximum number of nodes to be removed from power saving mode per
 minute. A value of zero results in no limits being imposed. The default
 value is 300. Use this to prevent rapid increases in power
 consumption. 
 

 ResumeTimeout 
 

 
 Maximum time permitted (in seconds) between when a node resume request
 is issued and when the node is actually available for use. Nodes which
 fail to respond in this time frame will be marked DOWN and the jobs
 scheduled on the node requeued. Nodes which reboot after this time frame
 will be marked DOWN with a reason of "Node unexpectedly rebooted." The
 default value is 60 seconds. 
 

 SchedulerParameters 
 

 
 The interpretation of this parameter varies by SchedulerType. Multiple
 options may be comma separated. Options of interest include: 

 
 salloc_wait_nodes 
 

 
 If defined, the salloc command will wait until all allocated nodes
 are ready for use (i.e. booted) before the command returns. By
 default, salloc will return as soon as the resource allocation has
 been made. The salloc command can use the
 --wait-all-nodes option to override this configuration
 parameter. 
 

 sbatch_wait_nodes 
 

 
 If defined, the sbatch script will wait until all allocated nodes
 are ready for use (i.e. booted) before the initiation. By default,
 the sbatch script will be initiated as soon as the first node in the
 job allocation is ready. The sbatch command can use the
 --wait-all-nodes option to override this configuration
 parameter. 
 
 
 

 SlurmctldParameters 
 

 
 Comma-separated options identifying slurmctld options. Options of
 interest include: 

 
 cloud_dns 
 

 
 By default, Slurm expects that the network addresses for cloud
 nodes won't be known until creation of the node and that Slurm will
 be notified of the node's address upon registration. Since Slurm
 communications rely on the node configuration found in the
 slurm.conf, Slurm will tell the client command, after waiting for all
 nodes to boot, each node's IP address. However, in environments where
 the nodes are in DNS, this step can be avoided by configuring this
 option. 
 

 idle_on_node_suspend 
 

 
 Mark nodes as idle, regardless of current state, when suspending
 nodes with SuspendProgram so that nodes will be eligible to be
 resumed at a later time. 
 

 node_reg_mem_percent=# 
 

 
 Percentage of memory a node is allowed to register with without
 being marked as invalid with low memory. Default is 100. For
 State=CLOUD nodes, the default is 90. 
 

 power_save_interval=# 
 

 
 How often the power_save thread looks to resume and suspend nodes.
 The power_save thread will do work sooner if there are node state
 changes. Default is 10 seconds. 
 

 power_save_min_interval=# 
 

 
 How often the power_save thread, at a minimum, looks to resume and
 suspend nodes. Default is 0. 
 
 
 

 SuspendExcNodes 
 

 
 Nodes not subject to suspend/resume logic. This may be used to avoid
 suspending and resuming nodes which are not in the cloud. Alternately the
 suspend/resume programs can treat local nodes differently from nodes
 being provisioned from cloud. Use Slurm's hostlist expression to identify
 nodes with an optional ":" separator and count of nodes to exclude from
 the preceding range. For example nid[10-20]:4 will prevent 4
 usable nodes (i.e IDLE and not DOWN, DRAINING or already powered down) in
 the set nid[10-20] from being powered down. Multiple sets of
 nodes can be specified with or without counts in a comma separated list
 (e.g nid[10-20]:4,nid[80-90]:2 ). By default, no nodes are
 excluded. This value may be updated with scontrol. See
 ReconfigFlags=KeepPowerSaveSettings for setting persistence. 
 

 SuspendExcParts 
 

 
 List of partitions with nodes to never place in power saving mode.
 Multiple partitions may be specified using a comma separator. By default,
 no nodes are excluded. This value may be updated with scontrol. See
 ReconfigFlags=KeepPowerSaveSettings for setting persistence. 
 

 SuspendExcStates 
 

 
 Specifies node states that are not to be powered down automatically.
 Valid states include CLOUD, DOWN, DRAIN, DYNAMIC_FUTURE, DYNAMIC_NORM,
 FAIL, INVALID_REG, MAINTENANCE, NOT_RESPONDING, PERFCTRS, PLANNED, and
 RESERVED. By default, any of these states, if idle for
 SuspendTime , would be powered down. This value may be updated with
 scontrol. See ReconfigFlags=KeepPowerSaveSettings for setting
 persistence. 
 

 SuspendProgram 
 

 
 Program to be executed to place nodes into power saving mode. The
 program executes as SlurmUser (as configured in
 slurm.conf ). The argument to the program will be the names of
 nodes to be placed into power savings mode (using Slurm's hostlist
 expression format). 
 

 SuspendRate 
 

 
 Maximum number of nodes to be placed into power saving mode per
 minute. A value of zero results in no limits being imposed. The default
 value is 60. Use this to prevent rapid drops in power consumption. 
 

 SuspendTime 
 

 
 Nodes becomes eligible for power saving mode after being idle or down
 for this number of seconds. A negative number disables power saving mode.
 The default value is -1 (disabled). 
 

 SuspendTimeout 
 

 
 Maximum time permitted (in second) between when a node suspend request
 is issued and when the node shutdown is complete. At that time the node
 must ready for a resume request to be issued as needed for new workload.
 The default value is 30 seconds. 
 
 

 Node Configuration 

 Node parameters of interest include: 

 
 Feature 
 

 
 A node feature can be associated with resources acquired from the
 cloud and user jobs can specify their preference for resource use with
 the --constraint option. 
 

 NodeName 
 

 
 This is the name by which Slurm refers to the node. A name containing
 a numeric suffix is recommended for convenience. 
 

 State 
 

 
 Nodes which are to be added on demand should have a state of
 CLOUD . 
 

 Weight 
 

 
 Each node can be configured with a weight indicating the desirability
 of using that resource. Nodes with lower weights are used before those
 with higher weights. The default value is 1. Slurm will allocate from
 powered up nodes first, powering up nodes second and lastly powered down
 nodes -- respecting node weights in each set.
 
 

 Partition Configuration 

 Partition parameters of interest include: 

 
 PowerDownOnIdle 
 

 
 If set to YES and power saving is enabled for the partition,
 then nodes allocated from this partition will be requested to power down
 after being allocated at least one job. These nodes will not power down
 until they transition from COMPLETING to IDLE. If set to NO then
 power saving will operate as configured for the partition. The default
 value is NO . 

 The following will cause a transition from COMPLETING to
 IDLE : 

 
 Completing all running jobs without additional jobs being
 allocated. 

 ExclusiveUser=YES and after all running jobs complete but
 before another user's job is allocated. 

 OverSubscribe=EXCLUSIVE and after the running job completes
 but before another job is allocated. 
 

 NOTE : Nodes are still subject to powering down when being IDLE
 for SuspendTime when PowerDownOnIdle is set to NO. 
 

 ResumeTimeout 
 

 
 Maximum time permitted (in seconds) between when a node resume request
 is issued and when the node is actually available for use. Nodes which
 fail to respond in this time frame will be marked DOWN and the jobs
 scheduled on the node requeued. Nodes which reboot after this time frame
 will be marked DOWN with a reason of "Node unexpectedly rebooted." The
 default value is 60 seconds. 

 For nodes that are in multiple partitions with this option set, the
 highest time will take effect. If not set on any partition, the node will
 use the ResumeTimeout value set for the entire cluster. 
 

 SuspendTime 
 

 
 Nodes which remain idle or down for this number of seconds will be
 placed into power saving mode by SuspendProgram . 

 For nodes that are in multiple partitions with this option set, the
 highest time will take effect. If not set on any partition, the node will
 use the SuspendTime value set for the entire cluster. Setting
 SuspendTime to INFINITE will disable suspending of nodes in
 this partition. 
 

 SuspendTimeout 
 

 
 Maximum time permitted (in second) between when a node suspend request
 is issued and when the node shutdown is complete. At that time the node
 must ready for a resume request to be issued as needed for new workload.
 The default value is 30 seconds. 

 For nodes that are in multiple partitions with this option set, the
 highest time will take effect. If not set on any partition, the node will
 use the SuspendTimeout value set for the entire cluster. 
 
 

 Node Lifecycle 

 When Slurm is configured for Power Saving operation, nodes have an
expanded set of states associated with them. States associated with Power
Saving are generally labeled with a symbol when viewing node details with
 sinfo . 

 
 
 Figure 1. Node Lifecycle
 

 Node states of interest: 

 
 
 
 
 STATE 
 
 Power Saving Symbol 
 
 Description 
 
 

 
 POWER_DOWN 
 ! 
 Power down request. When the node is no longer running job(s),
 run the SuspendProgram . 
 

 
 POWER_UP 
   
 Power up request. When possible, run the
 ResumeProgram . 
 

 
 POWERED_DOWN 
 ~ 
 The node is powered down or in power saving mode. 
 

 
 POWERING_DOWN 
 % 
 The node is in the process of powering down, or being put into
 power saving mode, and is not capable of running any jobs for
 SuspendTimeout . 
 

 
 POWERING_UP 
 # 
 The node is in the process of powering up, or being restored from
 power saving mode. 
 
 
 
 

 Manual Power Saving 

 A node can be manually powered up and down by setting the state of the
node to the following states using scontrol : 

 
scontrol update nodename=<nodename> state=power_<down|down_asap|down_force|up>
 

 scontrol update command actions/states of interest: 

 
 POWER_DOWN 
 

 Will use the configured SuspendProgram program to explicitly
 place a node in power saving mode. If a node is already in the process of
 being powered down, the command will only change the state of the node but
 won't have any effect until the configured SuspendTimeout is
 reached. 

 POWER_DOWN_ASAP 
 

 Will drain the node and mark it for power down. Currently running jobs
 will complete first and no additional jobs will be allocated to the
 node. 

 POWER_DOWN_FORCE 
 

 Will cancel all jobs on the node, power it down, and reset its state to
 IDLE . 

 POWER_UP 
 

 Will use the configured ResumeProgram program to explicitly move
 a node out of power saving mode. If a node is already in the process of
 being powered up, the command will only change the state of the node but
 won't have any effect until the configured ResumeTimeout is
 reached. 

 RESUME 
 

 Not an actual node state, but will change a node state from DRAIN,
 DRAINING, DOWN or REBOOT to IDLE and NoResp. slurmctld will then attempt to
 contact slurmd to request that the node register itself. Once registered,
 the node state will then remove the NoResp flag and will resume normal
 operations. It will also clear the POWERING_DOWN state of a node and make
 it eligible to be allocated. 
 

 Resume and Suspend Programs 

 The ResumeProgram and SuspendProgram execute as
 SlurmUser on the node where the slurmctld daemon runs (primary
and backup server nodes). Use of sudo may be required for
 SlurmUser to power down and restart nodes. If you need to convert
Slurm's hostlist expression into individual node names, the scontrol
show hostnames command may prove useful. The commands used to boot or
shut down nodes will depend upon your cluster management tools. 

 The ResumeProgram and SuspendProgram are not subject to any
time limits but must have Fault Tolerance . They
should perform the required action, ideally verify the action (e.g. node boot
and start the slurmd daemon, thus the node is no longer non-responsive
to slurmctld ) and terminate. Long running programs will be logged by
 slurmctld , but not aborted. 

 Example ResumeProgram :

Summary
- Slurm supports integrated node power saving (suspend/resume). Nodes can be automatically suspended after idle time or manually driven through a set of power states. Suspend/Resume actions are implemented by administrator-provided SuspendProgram and ResumeProgram scripts and controlled by slurmctld configuration (SuspendTime, SuspendTimeout, ResumeTimeout, SuspendRate, ResumeRate, etc.).

Node power states (what you will see and what they mean)
- POWER_DOWN (symbol: !)
  - A power-down request. When the node has no running jobs, Slurm will run the configured SuspendProgram to place the node into power-saving mode.
- POWER_DOWN_ASAP (also shown as power_down_asap / drain+power)
  - Drain the node and mark it for power down. Currently running jobs complete; no new jobs will be allocated. After jobs finish, SuspendProgram will be run.
- POWER_DOWN_FORCE
  - Immediately cancel all jobs on the node, power it down, and reset the node state to IDLE (i.e., forceful, job-killing shutdown).
- POWERING_DOWN (symbol: %)
  - The node is in the process of being suspended/powered down and is not available for scheduling for the configured SuspendTimeout period.
- POWERED_DOWN (symbol: ~)
  - The node is powered down (in power saving mode). It will not accept jobs until resumed.
- POWER_UP
  - A power-up (resume) request. When possible Slurm will run the ResumeProgram to restore the node from power-saving mode.
- POWERING_UP (symbol: #)
  - The node is in the process of powering up (Resume in progress).
- (RESUME)
  - Note: RESUME is not a literal node state but an action that will clear DRAIN/DOWN/REBOOT flags and cause slurmctld to attempt to contact slurmd so the node can register and become IDLE/available.

How to request manual power actions
- Use scontrol update nodename=<nodelist> state=power_<...>
  - Examples:
    - scontrol update nodename=n001 state=power_down
    - scontrol update nodename=n[10-15] state=power_down_asap
    - scontrol update nodename=n2 state=power_down_force
    - scontrol update nodename=n2 state=power_up
- POWER_DOWN_ASAP and POWER_DOWN wait for running jobs to finish (ASAP means drain). POWER_DOWN_FORCE will kill jobs.

Automatic suspend/resume behavior and key config parameters
- SuspendTime
  - Idle/down duration after which nodes become eligible for suspend.
- SuspendProgram and ResumeProgram
  - Administrator-supplied scripts invoked by slurmctld to do the actual shutdown/startup (run as SlurmUser on the controller host). These receive node hostlist(s) and (for Resume) a SLURM_RESUME_FILE describing jobs/nodes to guide the resume.
- SuspendTimeout and ResumeTimeout
  - Maximum time allowed for SuspendProgram/ResumeProgram to complete. If a node fails to resume within ResumeTimeout it is marked DOWN and jobs requesting it will be requeued.
- SuspendRate and ResumeRate
  - Rate limits (nodes/minute) to avoid blasting the infrastructure with many suspend/resume ops.
- PowerDownOnIdle (partition option)
  - When YES, nodes allocated from that partition will be requested to power down after being allocated at least one job (they power down after transitioning from COMPLETING → IDLE).
- SuspendExcNodes / SuspendExcParts / SuspendExcStates
  - Lists to exclude nodes/partitions/states from automatic suspend/resume logic (useful for non-cloud or special-purpose nodes).
- idle_on_node_suspend
  - Option to mark nodes IDLE while suspending so they can be resumed later.

ResumeProgram notes and SLURM_RESUME_FILE
- ResumeProgram can examine SLURM_RESUME_FILE which lists which jobs and which nodes need to be resumed, enabling booting different images per job or other per-job actions.
- ResumeProgram and SuspendProgram must be fault tolerant; they are not killed by slurmctld but slurmctld logs long-running ones.

Behavioral consequences / cautions
- If ResumeProgram fails or nodes don’t register in ResumeTimeout, nodes are placed DOWN and jobs requeued.
- POWER_DOWN_FORCE will cancel user jobs — use carefully.
- Rate limits and timeouts help protect provider/cloud APIs and avoid thrashing.
- Node features that come from cloud/node-plugins may be inactive while a node is powered down; allocation will reactivate them when resuming.

How this appears to users/admins
- sinfo and scontrol show the expanded lifecycle and symbols (for example: ! for POWER_DOWN, % for POWERING_DOWN, # for POWERING_UP, ~ for POWERED_DOWN).
- Jobs allocated to powered-down nodes may show flags like POWER_UP_NODE while waiting for nodes to boot.

Recommended admin practice (brief)
- Provide robust ResumeProgram/SuspendProgram (with logging and error handling).
- Configure sensible Suspend/Resume timeouts and rate limits for your environment.
- Use SuspendExc* settings to protect on-prem nodes or special partitions.
- Document the behavior for users (noting POWER_DOWN_FORCE cancels jobs and that nodes may be resumed automatically for their jobs).

Slurm accounting is mainly focused on parallel computing. For this reason it
gathers statistics at a "task level". A task is a set of user processes which

parallel tasks, e.g. by calling `srun -n`.

defined in slurm.conf, or by using the `--acct-freq` option in the
command line. A poll of data is also triggered at the start or the end of a

### Accounting[#accounting](https://slurm.schedmd.com/heterogeneous_jobs.html)
Slurm's accounting database records the het_job_id and het_job_offset
fields.
The sacct command reports job's using the format
"<het_job_id>+<het_job_offset>" and can accept a job ID
specification for filtering using the same format.
If a het_job_id value is specified as a job filter, then information about
all components of that job will be reported as shown below by default.
The --whole-hetjob=[yes|no] option can be used to force to report
the information about all the components of that job or just about the specific
component requested, no matter if the job filter includes the het_job_id
(leader) or not.

Short answer first
- ExitCode and DerivedExitCode are accounting fields stored for a job (and job steps). Both use the same two-part format ee:ss where ee is the process exit status (what the process returned) and ss is the terminating signal number (0 if none). Example: 0:0 means exited normally with status 0; 1:0 means exited with status 1; 0:9 means it was killed by signal 9 (SIGKILL).

What ExitCode means
- ExitCode = ee:ss for the job/step that Slurm recorded (typically the batch script or the top-level step).  
  - ee > 0 and ss = 0 → the process exited normally with status ee.  
  - ee = 0 and ss > 0 → the process was terminated by signal ss.  
  - Both zero → normal success (0:0).
- If you inspect a process’ shell-style exit status (the value in $?), remember shells report signal-terminated processes as 128 + signal. Example: Slurm shows 0:9 (killed by SIGKILL); the shell $? would be 137 (128 + 9).

What DerivedExitCode is
- DerivedExitCode is a Slurm-determined field (same ee:ss format) that represents Slurm’s “overall” exit decision for the job. It is initially set from the highest exit code observed among the job’s steps, but slurmctld may modify it to reflect other cluster-detected conditions (prologue/epilogue failures, resource limit enforcement, OOM/job preemption, etc.).
- The job record also has a comment string which Slurm can fill with a short explanation (e.g., “out of memory”, “preempted by ...”). DerivedExitCode + comment together are the canonical way Slurm tells you why a job was considered failed even if the job script returned 0.

Common cases and what you’ll see
- Normal success: ExitCode = 0:0, DerivedExitCode = 0:0, State = COMPLETED.
- Script returned non‑zero: ExitCode = N:0, DerivedExitCode usually N:0, State = FAILED (or COMPLETED depending on script and exit handling).
- Killed by signal (SIGKILL/9): ExitCode = 0:9. Shell-style $? = 137. DerivedExitCode will normally reflect the signal (0:9) or may be adjusted.
- Step-level failure but script returned 0: ExitCode might be 0:0 while DerivedExitCode is nonzero (reflects the failed step). Check the comment to learn why Slurm overrode the plain ExitCode.
- Resource enforcement (time limit, memory): Slurm can set DerivedExitCode and comment to indicate TIME_LIMIT or OOM-related termination.

How to inspect these fields
- sacct -j <jobid> --format=JobID,JobName,State,ExitCode,DerivedExitCode,Comment
- scontrol show job <jobid>   (shows ExitCode and DerivedExitCode among other fields)
- sjobexitmod -l <jobid>     (view the derived fields) — sjobexitmod can also be used by admins to change the DerivedExitCode/comment.

Notes and tips
- For array/heterogeneous jobs look at step/component records: sacct will show component rows (jobid+offset) so you can find which step returned a nonzero exit. DerivedExitCode is computed across steps/components.
- Don’t assume ExitCode alone tells the whole story — when DerivedExitCode ≠ ExitCode, read the comment and per-step sacct rows to find the real cause.
- If you want a single numeric “shell-style” status for a signal termination, compute 128 + signal (e.g., SIGKILL → 137).

Below is a concise, practical explanation of Slurm federation and how federated jobs behave, with the key concepts, user-facing commands and admin points you’ll run into.

What is a Slurm federation
- A federation is a set of independent Slurm clusters that cooperate to schedule jobs in a peer-to-peer way. Each cluster keeps its own scheduler and policies; jobs are replicated (as “siblings”) across member clusters and each cluster independently attempts to schedule its copy.
- Use case: share/borrow capacity across administrative domains without making a single giant cluster. Not intended for extremely high job submission rates (the docs warn against >~50k jobs/day across many clusters).

Core concepts / vocabulary
- Federated job: the logical job submitted to the federation. It has a federated job ID that is unique across clusters (made from local job id + origin cluster id).
- Origin cluster / origin job: the cluster where the user submitted the job. The origin tracks the federated job and coordinates sibling state.
- Sibling job: a copy of the federated job that is submitted to each eligible member cluster (or to a subset you request). Siblings run on sibling clusters.
- Sibling cluster: a cluster that has a sibling job.
- Viable siblings: sibling jobs that are eligible to run based on constraints/policy.
- Revoked state (RV): a transient state used when the origin/scheduler coordinates sibling transitions (e.g., when a sibling elsewhere starts).
- Federated job ID format: bits are used to combine the local job ID and the origin cluster ID so job IDs are unique across the federation.

How submission and scheduling work (user view)
- You submit to your local/origin cluster as usual (sbatch, salloc, srun). The origin will submit sibling jobs to all eligible clusters in the federation (or only a list you supply).
- Directing which clusters are considered:
  - -M, --clusters=<cluster_list>: restricts the cluster list passed with the job (the submission will be made to one of the listed clusters as origin and siblings limited to that list).
  - --cluster-constraint=[!]<constraint_list>: restricts clusters based on constraints.
- Each cluster independently tries to schedule its sibling copy using its own policies (priorities, backfill, QOS, reservations).
- When one sibling starts running, the federation coordination ensures the run is reflected in the federated job state and other pending sibling copies are removed/cancelled (the origin cluster coordinates this).
- If you need to view sibling detail, squeue has federation-aware options (for example --sibling to list sibling rows, and long-format fields such as cluster, siblingsactive, siblingsviable).

Typical lifecycle events and operations
- Pending: siblings sit pending on eligible clusters until a scheduler there decides to run one.
- Start: when one sibling begins running, the origin updates federated state and remaining pending siblings are removed.
- Cancel: scancel behavior in a federation:
  - A cancel request will cancel the running sibling or pending siblings as appropriate.
  - scancel supports a --sibling=<cluster_name> option to remove a specific pending sibling from the active sibling list.
- Job modification, requeue, arrays, interactive jobs: federation supports these features, but origin coordination applies (the origin controls sibling behavior and communications).

Commands and fields useful to users
- Submit: sbatch [--clusters / -M] [--cluster-constraint] script.sh
- View federated jobs: squeue --sibling (shows sibling rows) and long-format fields:
  - cluster — which cluster is running the job/step
  - siblingsactive / siblingsactiveraw — where sibling jobs currently exist
  - siblingsviable / siblingsviableraw — where siblings remain viable to run
- Cancel: scancel <jobid> or scancel --sibling=<cluster_name> <jobid>

Admin configuration and notes
- Create/manage a federation with sacctmgr (sacctmgr add federation / modify federation, and attach clusters). A cluster may be a member of only one federation at a time.
- Removing a cluster from a federation: running jobs that originated on the removed cluster continue to run, but pending sibling jobs behavior may change (origin/pending requeue rules apply). Best practice is to drain a cluster before removing it.
- Monitoring: squeue and scontrol show extended federated info; squeue has fields and the --sibling view to inspect sibling placement.
- Limitations & cautions: federation adds cross-cluster coordination overhead and is not targeted at extreme submission rates. Network/communication interruptions can affect sibling state changes.

Troubleshooting pointers
- If a federated job isn’t starting locally, check squeue with siblingsviable/siblingsactive to see where siblings exist and which clusters are viable.
- Use squeue long-format or scontrol show job for detailed federated metadata.
- If you need to cancel only a specific pending sibling, use scancel --sibling=<cluster> <jobid>.

References / further reading
- See the Slurm “Federated Scheduling Guide” in the Slurm documentation for full details on configuration, federated job ID bits, the full set of squeue fields, admin sacctmgr commands to create/modify federations, and limitations.

Short answer: it depends on *what limit* alice is hitting.

Guidelines to decide

- Request a QOS change when the symptom is about scheduling policy, per-job limits, or priority:
  - Jobs are being denied or forced to pend with messages mentioning QOS, DenyOnLimit, or Preempt/GraceTime.
  - You need higher priority or different preemption behavior (e.g., more GraceTime, no preemption).
  - You need a larger per-job walltime or per-job node/GPU cap that is defined in a QOS (MaxWall, MaxNodes, MaxTRESPerJob, MaxGRESPerJob, MaxSubmitJobs set on a QOS).
  - You want a short-term/per-job special allowance (e.g., debugging QOS that temporarily allows bigger jobs).

- Request an account (association) limit change when the restriction is a group/account quota or long-term allocation:
  - The account is hitting aggregate quotas (MaxTRESPerAccount, GrpTRES, account-level MaxJobs/MaxSubmitJobs).
  - The issue is about project accounting, billing, or redistributing longer-term shares among group members.
  - You need a persistent change that applies to everyone on that account rather than just affecting scheduling policy/priority.

Important background (how Slurm applies limits)
- Precedence (first match wins): Partition QOS → Job QOS → User association → Account association → Cluster. That means a QOS limit will normally block a job before an account limit is consulted. So changing QOS can immediately affect submission/priority even if the account limit would also apply.

How to choose in practice
1. Inspect the error/pending reason. If the job was DENIED or PENDING with a QOS or deny reason, ask for a QOS change. If accounting messages or “exceeds account limit” appear, ask for an account (association) change.
2. If you need higher priority or different preemption/policy: request a QOS tweak.
3. If you need more aggregate resources for your project (more GPU-hours or CPU-hours for the account): request an account/allocation change.
4. If you’re unsure, include both the concrete symptom and the relevant job ID(s) when requesting changes and the admin can determine which object to edit (QOS vs account).

What to include in the request to admins (makes it faster)
- Your username (alice) and account name.
- Example job ID(s) and the exact error/pending message (or squeue/scontrol output).
- Current QOS (if known) and partition.
- What you need: e.g., “allow 4 GPUs per job instead of 1”, or “increase concurrent running jobs from 5→10”, or “increase max walltime to 72h”.
- Reason/justification and expected duration (temporary vs permanent).

Examples (mapping common needs → request)
- Need longer walltime for a single job → ask to increase MaxWall on the relevant QOS (or on account if that’s where it’s set).
- Need to run more concurrent jobs → ask to increase MaxJobs/MaxSubmitJobs on QOS or account depending which enforces your limit (check squeue/sacctmgr output).
- Need more total project GPU-hours → request account quota increase (association/account).
- Jobs being preempted / low priority → request QOS with higher priority or different preemption flags.

If you want, I can check the cluster for the exact limit that’s blocking alice (squeue or scontrol_show for a job, or sacctmgr show for account/QOS limits). Tell me a job ID or the exact error message and I’ll inspect.

Short answer
- scontrol reconfigure tells the Slurm controller (slurmctld) to re-read its configuration and request that Slurm daemons (slurmd, etc.) adopt updated settings — without restarting daemons.
- Use it when you have changed Slurm configuration files and want most settings applied immediately without a full restart of daemons.

What it does (behavior)
- Causes slurmctld to reload slurm.conf and other config files that Slurm supports being reloaded (examples in the docs: mpi.conf, burst_buffer.conf, power-save related settings, topology files, plugin parameters that are declared reloadable).
- slurmctld updates its in-memory configuration and sends RPCs to slurmd (and other daemons where applicable) so they re-read their local config as supported.
- It does not stop or requeue running jobs; allocations normally remain in place. It is a live reconfiguration mechanism rather than a restart.
- ReconfigFlags in slurm.conf control special reconfigure behaviors (for example, keep or change power-save exclusions when reconfiguring).

When to use it
- After editing slurm.conf or other reloadable Slurm config files and you want to apply the changes immediately without restarting slurmctld/slurmd.
- When you change parameters that are documented as reloadable (check the docs for the specific file/parameter).
- To propagate non-disruptive changes cluster-wide while minimizing service interruption.

When it is NOT enough / caveats
- Some settings cannot be changed via reconfigure and require a daemon restart (or a coordinated restart of slurmctld/slurmd). The docs list which parameters are reloadable; if unsure, a restart may be required.
- Certain subsystem configuration (for example accounting daemon slurmdbd settings, or changes to plugin binaries) may require restarting that daemon or a rolling restart — verify per-component docs.
- Reconfiguring frequently or running many RPCs can stress slurmctld; avoid scripting rapid repeated reconfigures.
- Complex changes to node/partition topology or node name changes may have additional operational steps; validate before applying.

Recommended workflow
1. Edit the config file(s) on the controller(s).
2. Validate syntax and expected values (review file, run any local checks your admins use).
3. Run scontrol reconfigure on the controller:
   - scontrol reconfigure
4. Verify with:
   - scontrol show config (to inspect the active configuration),
   - sinfo / scontrol show node (to confirm node/partition effects),
   - review logs if unexpected behavior appears.
5. If a setting did not take effect, consult the Slurm docs to see whether that setting requires a restart; perform a restart if necessary.

References / pointers
- See the Slurm documentation for scontrol and the specific config files (ReconfigFlags, which files/parameters are reloadable) before relying on reconfigure for critical changes.

## Age Factor[#age](https://slurm.schedmd.com/priority_multifactor.html)
Note: Computing the age factor requires the installation
and operation of the [Slurm Accounting Database](https://slurm.schedmd.com/accounting.html).
The age factor represents the length of time a job has been sitting in the
queue and eligible to run. In general, the longer a job waits in the queue, the
larger its age factor grows. However, the age factor for a dependent job will
not change while it waits for the job it depends on to complete. Also, the age
factor will not change when scheduling is withheld for a job whose node or time
limits exceed the cluster's current limits.
At some configurable length of time ( PriorityMaxAge ), the age factor
will max out to 1.0.

## Association Factor[#assoc](https://slurm.schedmd.com/priority_multifactor.html)
Each association can be assigned an integer priority. The larger the

Short answer: sprio shows the breakdown of Slurm's multifactor job priority. Each job's priority is a weighted sum of several normalized factors (0.0–1.0) multiplied by administrator-configurable integer weights. sprio can print the per-factor contributions (-n shows normalized factors, -w shows configured weights).

Details

1) The priority components (factors)
- Age — how long the job has been waiting (capped at PriorityMaxAge). Requires accounting (slurmdbd).
- Association — association/account-specific priority (association priorities are normalized).
- Fairshare — restores balance between promised vs consumed resources (depends on PriorityDecayHalfLife, usage reset, and slurmdbd).
- Job size — larger jobs can get more priority (or smaller if PriorityFavorSmall=YES).
- Nice — user-supplied nice that lowers priority (this factor is subtracted).
- Partition — per-partition priority factor.
- QOS — per-QoS priority factor.
- Site — site-defined factor (via site_factor or job_submit/site plugin).
- TRES factors — one factor per TRES type requested (CPUs, GPUs, licenses, burst buffer, etc.); more requested TRES increases that factor.

All factors themselves are floating point values normalized into the 0.0–1.0 range.

2) How weights work
- The final job priority is an integer computed roughly as:
  Job_priority = site_factor + (PriorityWeightAge * age_factor) + (PriorityWeightAssoc * assoc_factor) + (PriorityWeightFairshare * fairshare_factor) + (PriorityWeightJobSize * job_size_factor) + (PriorityWeightPartition * partition_factor) + (PriorityWeightQOS * qos_factor) + SUM( TRES_weight_X * TRES_factor_X ) - nice_factor
- Weights are unsigned integers (32-bit). The larger the weight, the more influence that factor has on the final priority.
- Factor values are 0.0–1.0, so the weight effectively scales the contribution into the integer priority space.
- The priority value range is 0 .. 4294967295 (uint32). Higher numbers = higher priority.

3) Practical notes / tuning guidance
- Default weight values in slurm.conf are small (1), but examples commonly set weights large (e.g., PriorityWeightFairshare=10000, PriorityWeightAge=1000) so differences in fractional factors produce meaningful integer differences. If weights are too small, distinct factor values may collapse to the same integer contribution.
- Use PriorityMaxAge to control how long until age_factor reaches 1.0, and PriorityDecayHalfLife / PriorityUsageResetPeriod to control fairshare behavior.
- PriorityFavorSmall controls whether small or large jobs are favored by the JobSize factor.
- TRES weights let you prioritize jobs that request certain resources (e.g., licenses, GPUs).

## Running Jobs [#Running_Jobs](https://slurm.schedmd.com/gres.html)
Jobs will not be allocated any generic resources unless specifically
requested at job submit time using the options:
--gres
Generic resources required per node
--gpus
GPUs required per job
--gpus-per-node
GPUs required per node. Equivalent to the --gres option for GPUs.
--gpus-per-socket
GPUs required per socket. Requires the job to specify a task socket.
--gpus-per-task
GPUs required per task. Requires the job to specify a task count.
All of these options are supported by the salloc , sbatch and
srun commands.
Note that all of the --gpu* options are only supported by Slurm's
select/cons_tres plugin.
Jobs requesting these options when the select/cons_tres plugin is not
configured will be rejected.

[CUDA Multi-Process Service (MPS)](https://docs.nvidia.com/deploy/pdf/CUDA_Multi_Process_Service_Overview.pdf) provides a mechanism where GPUs can be

## Sharding [#Sharding](https://slurm.schedmd.com/gres.html)
Sharding provides a generic mechanism where GPUs can be
shared by multiple jobs. While it does permit multiple jobs to run on a given
GPU it does not fence the processes running on the GPU, it only allows the GPU
to be shared. Sharding, therefore, works best with homogeneous workflows. It is
recommended to limit the number of shards on a node to equal the max possible
jobs that can run simultaneously on the node (i.e. cores).
The total count of shards available on a node should be configured in
the slurm.conf file (e.g. "NodeName=tux[1-16] Gres=gpu:2,shard:64").

## MIG Management [#MIG_Management](https://slurm.schedmd.com/gres.html)
Beginning in version 21.08, Slurm now supports NVIDIA
Multi-Instance GPU (MIG) devices. This feature allows some newer NVIDIA
GPUs (like the A100) to split up a GPU into up to seven separate, isolated GPU
instances. Slurm can treat these MIG instances as individual GPUs, complete with
cgroup isolation and task binding.
To configure MIGs in Slurm, specify
`AutoDetect=nvml` in gres.conf for the
nodes with MIGs, and specify `Gres`
in slurm.conf as if the MIGs were regular GPUs, like this:
`NodeName=tux[1-16] gres=gpu:2`. An optional
GRES type can be specified to distinguish MIGs of different sizes from each
other, as well as from other GPUs in the cluster. This type must be a substring
of the "MIG Profile" string as reported by the node in its slurmd log under the
`debug2` log level. Here is an example slurm.conf
for a system with 2 gpus, one of which is partitioned i...

Summary — what GRES is
- GRES = Generic RESources. GPUs are usually exposed to Slurm as a GRES named "gpu" (configured in slurm.conf and/or gres.conf).
- The canonical GRES request form is: name[:type:count]
  - name = resource name from configuration (commonly "gpu")
  - type = optional subtype (GPU model or MIG profile string)
  - count = how many of that resource (see “per node vs. per job” below)

Common request options (equivalent/alternate forms)
- --gres=gpu[:type:count]
  - The --gres argument is interpreted as “generic resources required per node”.
- --gpus
  - Requests GPUs per job (shorthand). Good when you want a total number of GPUs for the job, not a per-node value.
- --gpus-per-node
  - Equivalent to --gres=gpu:count (i.e., GPUs requested on each allocated node).
- --gpus-per-task / --gpus-per-socket
  - More specific granular requests (per task or per socket) and require matching task/socket layout.

Syntax details and examples
- Basic per-node request:
  - sbatch --nodes=2 --gres=gpu:2
    - Means 2 nodes, and on each node allocate 2 GPUs ⇒ total GPUs = 2 nodes * 2 GPUs = 4 GPUs.
- Request X GPUs total on one node:
  - sbatch --nodes=1 --gres=gpu:4
  - or sbatch --nodes=1 --gpus=4
- Request a specific GPU type (type must match the GRES type configured in gres.conf):
  - sbatch --gres=gpu:V100:2
    - Requests 2 GPUs of type "V100" per node.
- Per-task GPUs:
  - sbatch --ntasks=4 --gpus-per-task=1
    - This requests 1 GPU for each of 4 tasks ⇒ total 4 GPUs (Slurm will place tasks/nodes to satisfy that).
- Multiple GRES in one job:
  - sbatch --gres=gpu:2,license:matlab:1
    - Request 2 GPUs per node and 1 MATLAB license per node (example).

How counts are applied (important)
- --gres is per node. If you use --gres alone you must combine it with --nodes/--ntasks to get the total.
- --gpus (without the “per-” qualifier) typically means GPUs per job (total requested for the whole job).
- --gpus-per-node is per node (same semantic as --gres for GPUs).
- --gpus-per-task multiplies by the number of tasks to form the total GPU request.

Type field and MIG
- The optional type allows selecting a model or MIG profile: name:type:count.
- For MIG (A100) or other partitioned GPUs, the type string is matched to the configured MIG profile. Use the exact substring that the node advertises.
- If you need specific MIG instances, ensure node gres.conf and slurmd are configured to advertise them.

Sharing, sharding, MPS
- By default Slurm will allocate GPUs to jobs according to the configured counts; GPU sharing behavior depends on how the GRES is configured:
  - Exclusive allocation (one job per GPU) is typical.
  - Sharding or MPS can be configured so multiple jobs share a GPU — this requires cluster-side configuration (slurm.conf/gres.conf and select/cons_tres settings).
- If you plan to oversubscribe GPUs, check with cluster admins and the node’s gres.conf settings.

Practicals / best practices
- Always request matching CPU resources: e.g., --cpus-per-task or --ntasks-per-node so you don’t get CPU-starved while waiting for GPUs.
- If you want X GPUs total but don’t care about node packing, use --gpus=X (shorthand) and let Slurm place them.
- To force all GPUs on one node, use --nodes=1 --gpus=4 (or --gres=gpu:4).
- To see what GPUs and GRES a node advertises, use: sinfo -Nel or scontrol show node <nodename>. (These show the Gres= entries.)
- Slurm sets environment variables (e.g., CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES) inside the job so your CUDA/CuPy/PyTorch code sees only the allocated devices — code usually just works without extra binding.

Quick cheat-sheet lines to put in job headers
- 2 GPUs on any node (job-wide placement):
  - #SBATCH --gpus=2
- 2 GPUs per node across 3 nodes (total 6 GPUs):
  - #SBATCH --nodes=3
  - #SBATCH --gres=gpu:2
- 1 GPU per task, 8 tasks (total 8 GPUs):
  - #SBATCH --ntasks=8
  - #SBATCH --gpus-per-task=1
- Request specific GPU model (if supported):
  - #SBATCH --gres=gpu:V100:2

Troubleshooting / checks
- If your request is rejected, common causes:
  - Cluster not configured with select/cons_tres plugin.
  - Requested type not present on any node.
  - Not enough GPUs in the partition/node.
- To inspect cluster GRES config and availability: sinfo -Nel, scontrol show node, or ask your admin for the gres.conf entries.

If you want, I can:
- Show examples tailored to your cluster (I can run sinfo/scontrol to show what GPU types and counts are actually advertised) — tell me which partition or node to inspect.

In addition to putting burst buffer directives in the batch script, the
command-line options `--bb` and `--bbf` may also include

used, Slurm parses this option and creates a temporary burst buffer script file

## Heterogeneous Job Support [#het-job-support](https://slurm.schedmd.com/burst_buffer.html)
Heterogeneous jobs may request burst buffers. Burst buffer hooks will run
once for each component that has burst buffer directives. For example, if a
heterogeneous job has three components and two of them have burst buffer
directives, the burst buffer hooks will run once for each of the two components
with burst buffer directives, but not for the third component without burst
buffer directives. Further information and examples can be found in the
heterogeneous jobs page.

### Lua [#submit_lua](https://slurm.schedmd.com/burst_buffer.html)
The default directive for this plugin is `#BB_LUA`. The directive
used by this plugin may be changed by setting the Directive option in
burst_buffer.conf. Since the directive must always begin with a `#`
sign (which starts a comment in a shell script) this option should specify only
the string following the `#` sign. For example, if burst_buffer.conf
contains the following:
```text
Directive=BB_EXAMPLE
```
then the burst buffer directive will be `#BB_EXAMPLE`.
If the Directive option is not specified in burst_buffer.conf, then
the default directive for this plugin (`#BB_LUA`) will be used.
Since this plugin was designed to be generic and flexible, this plugin only
requires the directive to be given. If the directive is given, Slurm will run
all burst buffer stages for the job.

## Heterogeneous Job Support [#het-job-support](https://slurm.schedmd.com/burst_buffer.html)
Heterogeneous jobs may request burst buffers. Burst buffer hooks will run
once for each component that has burst buffer directives. For example, if a
heterogeneous job has three components and two of them have burst buffer
directives, the burst buffer hooks will run once for each of the two components
with burst buffer directives, but not for the third component without burst
buffer directives. Further information and examples can be found in the
heterogeneous jobs page.

### Common Configuration [#common_config](https://slurm.schedmd.com/burst_buffer.html)
- To enable a burst buffer plugin, set BurstBufferType in slurm.conf. If it is not set, then no burst buffer plugin will be loaded. Only one burst buffer plugin may be specified.
- In slurm.conf, you may set DebugFlags=BurstBuffer for detailed logging from the burst buffer plugin. This will result in very verbose logging and is not intended for prolonged use in a production system, but this may be useful for debugging.
- [TRES limits](https://slurm.schedmd.com/resource_limits.html) for burst buffers can be configured by association or QOS in the same way that TRES limits can be configured for nodes, CPUs, or any GRES. To make Slurm track burst buffer resources, add bb/datawarp (for the datawarp plugin) or bb/lua (for the lua plugin) to AccountingStorageTres in slurm.conf.
- The size of a job's burst buffer requirements can be used as a factor in setti...

Summary
- Slurm supports "burst buffers" (fast, intermediate storage) via a burst buffer plugin (commonly datawarp or lua). Jobs request burst-buffer resources with special commented directives in batch scripts or via sbatch/salloc/srun options. Runtime status is exposed with scontrol show burst (and in sview).

Where to put directives
- Put burst-buffer directives as commented lines in your sbatch script (they may appear before/after/interspersed with #SBATCH lines).
- The exact directive token depends on the plugin:
  - DataWarp: use #DW for job-specific requests; use #BB for persistent create/destroy operations.
  - Lua plugin: default directive is #BB_LUA (configurable via burst_buffer.conf Directive option).
- You can also specify directives on the command line with --bb and supply a file with --bbf (sbatch/salloc/srun). Note: --bb cannot create persistent buffers.

Directive form and common parameters
- Format: a directive keyword followed by space-separated key=value options, e.g.
  - #DW capacity=100G pool=fast access=single
  - #BB create_persistent name=mybuffer capacity=1TiB pool=wlm_pool
- Common options (plugin-dependent):
  - capacity (required for job-specific DataWarp requests) — size units like G, GiB, T, TiB
  - pool — which burst-buffer pool to use
  - name — for persistent buffers (DataWarp)
  - access — access mode (plugin-specific)
  - type — plugin-specific type field
  - hurry — for destroy_persistent to speed teardown (DataWarp)
- Lifecycle stages (hooks run at these points):
  - allocation / create — Slurm allocates the buffer for the job
  - stage-in — data staged into the burst buffer before the job starts
  - job runtime — job uses the burst buffer
  - stage-out — data is staged out after the job finishes
  - deallocate / destroy — buffer freed (unless persistent)
- Persistent buffers: only supported by certain plugins (DataWarp); must be explicitly created/destroyed (#BB create_persistent / #BB destroy_persistent). --bb cannot create persistent buffers.

Status and inspection
- scontrol show burst
  - Primary read-only status command. Shows configured burst pools, total/free/used space, flags/timeouts, and a list of allocated buffers with entries like JobID, CreateTime, Pool, Size, State (e.g., allocated, staged-in).
  - Example fields: Name, DefaultPool, Granularity, TotalSpace, FreeSpace, UsedSpace, Flags, Allocated Buffers, Per User Buffer Use.
- sview: GUI has a Burst Buffer tab showing the same info.
- scontrol show config: check BurstBufferType and other slurm.conf settings to see whether burst buffers are enabled and which plugin is in use.
- Reservations: burst-buffer resources can be reserved with scontrol create reservation burstbuffer=plugin:pool#units (Slurm will accept jobs that reference that reservation). (When discussing reservations, Slurm uses the term "reservation".)
- Accounting: if you want Slurm accounting to track BB usage, add the plugin-specific TRES (e.g., bb/datawarp or bb/lua) to AccountingStorageTres in slurm.conf.

Common status states you’ll see (plugin-dependent)
- allocated — buffer allocated for a job
- staged-in (or staged-out) — stage-in completed / stage-out completed or in that state
- released/deallocated — buffer freed
- plugin-specific states and additional metadata (timeouts, per-user usage) are shown by scontrol show burst

Practical tips and pitfalls
- Plugin must be enabled in slurm.conf (BurstBufferType). If not configured, directives are ignored and jobs requesting BB may be rejected.
- DataWarp requires capacity for job-specific requests; omission can cause job rejection.
- --bb on the command line won’t create persistent buffers; use #BB create_persistent or the plugin’s create API.
- Make sure AccountingStorageTres includes the bb TRES if you want usage tracked and limited by associations/QoS.
- Staging behavior and accepted keys/options are plugin-specific — consult your cluster’s burst_buffer.conf and the plugin docs (datawarp or lua) for exact keys and semantics.

Where to read the authoritative docs
- The Slurm Burst Buffer Guide (burst_buffer.html) — covers directives, plugin details, examples, and the status command (scontrol show burst).
- scontrol manual pages for the exact syntax of status commands and burst-related fields.

If you want, I can:
- show the exact syntax and example lines for your cluster’s configured plugin (I can read your burst_buffer.conf and slurm.conf), or
- run scontrol show burst on the cluster and explain current BB pool states — tell me which you'd like.

Here's a concise explanation of how partition constraints and GPU availability work in Slurm, what to request, and how to interpret availability when targeting a GPU partition.

1) Partitions — what they are and how they affect GPU jobs
- A partition is a logical queue grouping nodes. Partitions can differ in allowed users, time limits, QOS, limits (MaxNodes, MaxCPUsPerNode, etc.), and which nodes they include.
- Jobs are allocated entirely within a single partition. If you submit to partition "gpu" your job will only be scheduled onto nodes that are members of that partition.
- Partition configuration can also set defaults (time limit, features) and restrict who may use it.

2) How to request GPUs and node features
- --gpus=N (modern): request N GPUs total for the job (or per task when combined with task options). Preferred when supported by your cluster.
- --gres=gpu:N (older/common): request N GPUs; can include model e.g. --gres=gpu:V100:2 or --gres=gpu:2 to request specific devices.
- --constraint="feature" or --constraint="a100|v100": require nodes with a node feature (often used to pick GPU model or NIC). Multiple constraints can be combined with boolean expressions if enabled.
- Combine CPU/memory and GPU requests carefully: e.g., sbatch --partition=gpu --gpus=2 --cpus-per-task=8 --mem=64G
- If you want GPUs per task: use --gpus-per-task or --gres per task with appropriate ntasks settings.

3) How Slurm accounts and exposes GPU availability
- GRES (Generic RESources) tracks GPUs: node Gres= shows total GPUs; AllocTRES and TRES show allocated resources. scontrol show node gives detailed AllocTRES/Gres assignments.
- sinfo shows partition/node counts and resource totals; sinfo -Nel (or sinfo --Node) can show GPUs per node and states.
- In sinfo partition summaries the node counts appear as NODES(A/I/D) meaning Allocated / Idle / Down (the middle number is idle). For a new GPU job to be considered eligible in a conditional check, the idle count must be > 0.
- A GPU is considered available only when it is not already allocated to another job (or reserved). Allocated, mixed, down, or drained nodes do not count as available for a new GPU allocation.

4) Interpreting why GPU jobs are pending or not starting
- Common pending reasons: "Resources", "Priority", "ReqNodeNotAvail", "PartitionTimeLimit", "QOSMaxSubmit" — use squeue to see the pending reason. For more detail on a specific job, scontrol show job <jobid> or scontrol show node <nodename> helps.
- If the pending reason says resources, it usually means no node in the requested partition currently has the free GPUs/memory/CPUs you requested.
- If you requested a specific GPU model or used a constraint and no idle node matches, the scheduler will wait until such a node becomes free.

5) Node states that affect GPU availability
- IDLE: node has no allocated jobs (GPUs free).
- ALLOCATED/MIXED: node has at least one allocation; may still have some free GPUs depending on configuration and sharing policy.
- DRAINED/DOWN/MAINT: node is not eligible; GPUs there are not available.
- Some clusters configure exclusive node allocation for GPUs (one job per node) — then a node is either fully free or not.

6) Best practices
- Use --gpus if available (simpler and common in recent Slurm versions); fall back to --gres if needed.
- Check sinfo -Nel and squeue before submitting to understand current idle GPU nodes and pending jobs.
- If you need a particular GPU model, use both --constraint and/or --gres with model name to avoid mismatches.
- Request GPUs per task explicitly when using multi-task parallel workloads (e.g., --gpus-per-task=1 with mpirun or srun).
- If jobs remain pending, inspect the squeue reason and scontrol show node / scontrol show job for allocations and node features.
- When using extra node attributes (extra_constraints), be aware backfill accuracy can be affected and scheduler planning may be less precise.

7) Quick example requests
- Request 2 GPUs in the gpu partition (job-level): sbatch --partition=gpu --gpus=2 myscript.sh
- Request 1 GPU per MPI task, 4 tasks: sbatch --partition=gpu --ntasks=4 --gpus-per-task=1 my_mpi_job.sh
- Request specific model: sbatch --partition=gpu --gres=gpu:A100:1 --constraint="a100" myscript.sh

- inspect a specific pending GPU job to explain why it’s not starting (need the job ID).

## EXAMPLES[#SECTION_EXAMPLES](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Specify a batch script by filename on the command line. The batch script specifies a 1 minute time limit for the job.
```text
$ cat myscript #!/bin/sh #SBATCH --time=1 srun hostname |sort $ sbatch -N4 myscript salloc: Granted job allocation 65537 $ cat slurm-65537.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
Pass a batch script to sbatch on standard input:
```text
$ sbatch -N4 #!/bin/sh > srun hostname |sort > EOF sbatch: Submitted batch job 65541 $ cat slurm-65541.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
To create a heterogeneous job with 3 components, each allocating a unique set of nodes:
```text
$ sbatch -w node[2-3] : -w node4 : -w node[5-7] work.bash Submitted batch job 34987
```

## PERFORMANCE[#SECTION_PERFORMANCE](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Executing sbatch sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmctld daemon come in at once, it can result in
a degradation of performance of the slurmctld daemon, possibly resulting
in a denial of service.
Do not run sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other
programs. Ensure that programs limit calls to sbatch to the minimum
necessary for the information you are trying to gather.

## EXAMPLES[#SECTION_EXAMPLES](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Specify a batch script by filename on the command line. The batch script specifies a 1 minute time limit for the job.
```text
$ cat myscript #!/bin/sh #SBATCH --time=1 srun hostname |sort $ sbatch -N4 myscript salloc: Granted job allocation 65537 $ cat slurm-65537.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
Pass a batch script to sbatch on standard input:
```text
$ sbatch -N4 #!/bin/sh > srun hostname |sort > EOF sbatch: Submitted batch job 65541 $ cat slurm-65541.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
To create a heterogeneous job with 3 components, each allocating a unique set of nodes:
```text
$ sbatch -w node[2-3] : -w node4 : -w node[5-7] work.bash Submitted batch job 34987
```

below.

## PERFORMANCE[#SECTION_PERFORMANCE](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Executing sbatch sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmctld daemon come in at once, it can result in
a degradation of performance of the slurmctld daemon, possibly resulting
in a denial of service.
Do not run sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other
programs. Ensure that programs limit calls to sbatch to the minimum
necessary for the information you are trying to gather.

## EXAMPLES[#SECTION_EXAMPLES](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Specify a batch script by filename on the command line. The batch script specifies a 1 minute time limit for the job.
```text
$ cat myscript #!/bin/sh #SBATCH --time=1 srun hostname |sort $ sbatch -N4 myscript salloc: Granted job allocation 65537 $ cat slurm-65537.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
Pass a batch script to sbatch on standard input:
```text
$ sbatch -N4 #!/bin/sh > srun hostname |sort > EOF sbatch: Submitted batch job 65541 $ cat slurm-65541.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
To create a heterogeneous job with 3 components, each allocating a unique set of nodes:
```text
$ sbatch -w node[2-3] : -w node4 : -w node[5-7] work.bash Submitted batch job 34987
```

## PERFORMANCE[#SECTION_PERFORMANCE](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Executing sbatch sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmctld daemon come in at once, it can result in
a degradation of performance of the slurmctld daemon, possibly resulting
in a denial of service.
Do not run sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other
programs. Ensure that programs limit calls to sbatch to the minimum
necessary for the information you are trying to gather.

A burst buffer can either be persistent or linked to a specific job ID.
Since a heterogeneous job consists of multiple job IDs, a job-specific burst
buffer will be associated with only one heterogeneous job component.
Each component can have its own burst buffer directives, and they are processed
separately. Only a persistent burst buffer can be accessed by all components
of a heterogeneous job. Persistent burst buffers are only available in the
datawarp plugin. A sample batch script demonstrating this for the datawarp
plugin is appended.

## Submitting Jobs [#submitting](https://slurm.schedmd.com/heterogeneous_jobs.html)
The salloc , sbatch and srun commands can all be used
to submit heterogeneous jobs.
Resource specifications for each component of the heterogeneous job should be
separated with ":" character.
For example:
```text
$ sbatch --cpus-per-task=4 --mem-per-cpu=1 --ntasks=128 : \ --cpus-per-task=1 --mem-per-cpu=16 --ntasks=1 my.bash
```
Options specified for one component of a heterogeneous job (or job step) will
be used for subsequent components to the extent which is expected to be helpful.
Propagated options can be reset as desired for each component (e.g. a different
account name could be specified for each hetjob component.
For example, --immediate and --job-name are propagated, while
--ntasks and --mem-per-cpu are reset to default values for each
component.

The srun command is used to launch applications.
By default, the application is launched only on the first component of a
heterogeneous job, but options are available to support different behaviors.
srun's "--het-group" option defines which hetjob component(s) are to have
applications launched for them. The --het-group option takes an expression
defining which component(s) are to launch an application for an individual
execution of the srun command. The expression can contain one or more component

in a hyphen separated list. By default, an application is launched only on

## EXAMPLES[#SECTION_EXAMPLES](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Specify a batch script by filename on the command line. The batch script specifies a 1 minute time limit for the job.
```text
$ cat myscript #!/bin/sh #SBATCH --time=1 srun hostname |sort $ sbatch -N4 myscript salloc: Granted job allocation 65537 $ cat slurm-65537.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
Pass a batch script to sbatch on standard input:
```text
$ sbatch -N4 #!/bin/sh > srun hostname |sort > EOF sbatch: Submitted batch job 65541 $ cat slurm-65541.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
To create a heterogeneous job with 3 components, each allocating a unique set of nodes:
```text
$ sbatch -w node[2-3] : -w node4 : -w node[5-7] work.bash Submitted batch job 34987
```

Note that while Slurm daemons create log files and other files as needed,
it treats the lack of parent directories as a fatal error.
This prevents the daemons from running if critical file systems are
not mounted and will minimize the risk of cold-starting (starting
without preserving jobs).
Log files and job accounting files
may need to be created/owned by the "SlurmUser" uid to be successfully
accessed. Use the "chown" and "chmod" commands to set the ownership
and permissions appropriately.

about the various files and directories used by Slurm.

# "Configless" Slurm
"Configless" Slurm is a feature that allows the compute nodes —
specifically the slurmd process — and user commands running on login
nodes to pull configuration information directly from the slurmctld instead of
from a pre-distributed local file. Your cluster does require a central set of
configuration files on the Slurm controllers — "configless" in Slurm's
parlance means that the compute nodes, login nodes, and other cluster hosts
do not need to be deployed with local copies of these files.

config files will be pulled to the node. This slurmctld can be identified by

## PERFORMANCE[#SECTION_PERFORMANCE](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Executing sbatch sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmctld daemon come in at once, it can result in
a degradation of performance of the slurmctld daemon, possibly resulting
in a denial of service.
Do not run sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other
programs. Ensure that programs limit calls to sbatch to the minimum
necessary for the information you are trying to gather.

## EXAMPLES[#SECTION_EXAMPLES](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Specify a batch script by filename on the command line. The batch script specifies a 1 minute time limit for the job.
```text
$ cat myscript #!/bin/sh #SBATCH --time=1 srun hostname |sort $ sbatch -N4 myscript salloc: Granted job allocation 65537 $ cat slurm-65537.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
Pass a batch script to sbatch on standard input:
```text
$ sbatch -N4 #!/bin/sh > srun hostname |sort > EOF sbatch: Submitted batch job 65541 $ cat slurm-65541.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
To create a heterogeneous job with 3 components, each allocating a unique set of nodes:
```text
$ sbatch -w node[2-3] : -w node4 : -w node[5-7] work.bash Submitted batch job 34987
```

## EXAMPLES[#SECTION_EXAMPLES](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Specify a batch script by filename on the command line. The batch script specifies a 1 minute time limit for the job.
```text
$ cat myscript #!/bin/sh #SBATCH --time=1 srun hostname |sort $ sbatch -N4 myscript salloc: Granted job allocation 65537 $ cat slurm-65537.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
Pass a batch script to sbatch on standard input:
```text
$ sbatch -N4 #!/bin/sh > srun hostname |sort > EOF sbatch: Submitted batch job 65541 $ cat slurm-65541.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
To create a heterogeneous job with 3 components, each allocating a unique set of nodes:
```text
$ sbatch -w node[2-3] : -w node4 : -w node[5-7] work.bash Submitted batch job 34987
```

## PERFORMANCE[#SECTION_PERFORMANCE](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Executing sbatch sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmctld daemon come in at once, it can result in
a degradation of performance of the slurmctld daemon, possibly resulting
in a denial of service.
Do not run sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other
programs. Ensure that programs limit calls to sbatch to the minimum
necessary for the information you are trying to gather.

Summary
- A "hold" prevents a job from being allocated/run; the job remains in the queue (typically in PENDING) and will not be scheduled until all active holds on it are removed.
- Holds are additive: a job can have multiple hold types at once. Removing one hold does not schedule the job if any other hold remains (or other scheduling constraints still block it).

Hold types and semantics
- UserHold
  - Intended for the job owner (or a user with appropriate privileges).
  - Commonly placed at submission time with sbatch --hold or later by the job owner (or by an admin acting on behalf).
  - The job owner (and admins) can release a UserHold.
- AdminHold
  - Set by administrators (e.g., site policy or manual admin intervention).
  - Ordinary users cannot remove an AdminHold; only admins can release it.
- SystemHold
  - Placed by Slurm/system components for system-level reasons (maintenance, controller action, etc.).
  - Typically cleared by the system or by administrators when the underlying condition is resolved.

Commands and inspection
- Place a hold:
  - sbatch --hold (submit job in held state)
  - scontrol hold <jobid> (place a hold on an existing job)
- Clear a hold:
  - scontrol release <jobid> (release holds; permission rules apply — admins can clear Admin/System holds; owners can clear UserHold)
- Inspect hold/state:
  - squeue shows job state and often a reason column (held jobs display a hold-related reason).
  - scontrol show job <jobid> gives detailed job fields (including hold info).
- Job arrays and components:
  - scontrol operations on an ArrayJobID apply to all elements by default; you can target individual elements with the element-specific jobid (ArrayJobID_ArrayTaskID).

Behavioral notes / interactions
- Holds prevent scheduling even if resources are available and any dependencies are satisfied. Releasing the hold only makes the job eligible again; it may still remain pending for other reasons (resources, dependencies, QOS limits, reservations, etc.).
- Holds do not terminate or cancel a job. A held job stays in the queue until released or explicitly cancelled.
- Holding a running job is not the same as suspending it; to stop a running job you would use job suspension/requeue mechanisms (scontrol suspend/requeue), not a hold.
- Permissions matter: who can set/release which hold type follows the Owner vs Admin vs System separation; admins have broader authority.

Practical tips
- Use sbatch --hold if you want a job submitted but prevent it from starting until you explicitly release it.
- Use scontrol show job and squeue to confirm which hold type(s) are present and why a job is not starting.
- If a job remains pending after release, check resource availability, dependencies, partition/reservation constraints, and QOS/limits.

Commands referenced
- sbatch --hold
- scontrol hold <jobid>
- scontrol release <jobid>
- squeue
- scontrol show job <jobid>

## EXAMPLES[#SECTION_EXAMPLES](https://slurm.schedmd.com/salloc.html)
To get an allocation, and open a new xterm in which srun commands may be typed interactively:
```text
$ salloc -N16 xterm salloc: Granted job allocation 65537 # (at this point the xterm appears, and salloc waits for xterm to exit) salloc: Relinquishing job allocation 65537
```
To grab an allocation of nodes and launch a parallel application on one command line:
```text
$ salloc -N5 srun -n10 myprogram
```
To create a heterogeneous job with 3 components, each allocating a unique set of nodes:
```text
$ salloc -w node[2-3] : -w node4 : -w node[5-7] bash salloc: job 32294 queued and waiting for resources salloc: job 32294 has been allocated resources salloc: Granted job allocation 32294
```

Short answer
- Use sbatch to submit non‑interactive batch scripts that the scheduler will queue and run later.
- Use salloc to get an interactive allocation (a set of nodes/CPUs/GPUs) you can use yourself (shell, xterm, or multiple srun steps).
- Use srun to launch job steps (parallel tasks) inside an existing allocation — or to start a job step directly from the login node (but prefer sbatch for reproducible batch runs).

Details and typical patterns

1) sbatch — batch, reproducible, queued jobs
- What it does: submits a shell script to Slurm. sbatch returns a job ID and exits; the scheduler runs the script when resources become available.
- When to use: long or production runs, nightly jobs, training, pipelines, anything you don’t need to interact with while it runs.
- Typical pattern: put resource requests and srun calls inside the script (use srun for MPI/parallel launches).
- Example:
  sbatch --partition=gpu --gres=gpu:1 --time=04:00:00 train.sh
- Why: keeps runs reproducible, logged, and tracked by the scheduler.

2) salloc — get an interactive allocation
- What it does: requests and (when granted) holds an allocation of nodes/resources for you; it can run a command (or drop you into a shell) while the allocation is held.
- When to use: interactive debugging, interactive development, running an interactive MPI session, testing configs, opening an xterm on allocated nodes.
- Typical pattern: allocate resources, then use srun repeatedly inside that allocation to run steps/tasks.
- Example:
  salloc -N2 --ntasks-per-node=4 --gres=gpu:1 --time=02:00:00 --pty bash
- Why: lets you iterate interactively, run multiple srun steps inside the same allocation, or run a GUI/xterm on allocated nodes.

3) srun — launch job steps / parallel tasks
- What it does: launches tasks across nodes within an allocation. If there is no current allocation, srun can request an allocation for the command (behavior depends on site config), but it is commonly used inside sbatch or salloc allocations.
- When to use:
  - Inside sbatch scripts to start MPI/parallel tasks (recommended).
  - Inside an salloc interactive allocation to run single or multiple parallel steps.
  - For quick single-shot commands you want executed now (but prefer sbatch for longer or reproducible jobs).
- Typical pattern: srun --mpi=pmix -n 128 ./my_mpi_app
- Example inside a script:
  #SBATCH --nodes=4
  srun -n 256 ./mpi_program
- Why: srun manages placement, ranks, and environment for parallel tasks; using it inside a batch script or allocation is the typical pattern.

Quick decision flow
- Non‑interactive, reproducible batch job -> sbatch.
- Need an interactive allocation (debug, develop, run multiple steps) -> salloc, then srun inside it.
- Need to launch parallel tasks inside an allocation (or run a quick parallel command) -> srun.

Notes and best practices
- Prefer sbatch + srun for production workflows (keeps logs and accounting tidy).
- Use salloc for development/debugging; avoid calling salloc in tight loops (it makes RPCs to slurmctld).
- Use srun inside scripts to spawn MPI or multi‑task jobs — don’t directly mpirun unless your site specifically requires it.
- Behavior of srun when used from the login node (auto-allocation vs requiring an existing allocation) can be site-dependent; check local docs/policies.
