Quick explanation of job-array and task-level identifiers

- Array job vs element notation
  - The scheduler represents array elements as ArrayJobID_ArrayTaskID (for example 1234_5).
  - scontrol and squeue will accept that combined form to refer to a single array element; using just the ArrayJobID (1234) acts on the whole array.

- Environment variables inside an array element
  - SLURM_ARRAY_JOB_ID — the array base JobID (the first job ID of the array).
  - SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID — the array index for this element (the value from --array).
  - SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_COUNT, SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_MIN, SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_MAX — array sizing info.
  - SLURM_JOB_ID — the job id seen by the job; when running an array element you will also see SLURM_ARRAY_* vars to indicate the array identity. (You can reference the element externally as ArrayJobID_ArrayTaskID.)

- Task/rank identifiers inside multi-task jobs (MPI/ntasks)
  - SLURM_PROCID — global rank ID (0..N-1) for tasks in the job step (useful for MPI ranks).
  - SLURM_LOCALID — rank ID local to the node (0..local_ntasks-1).
  - SLURM_NTASKS, SLURM_NTASKS_PER_NODE, SLURM_CPUS_ON_NODE — counts that describe the task layout.

- How to address/cancel/operate on arrays
  - Cancel an element: scancel 1234_5
  - Cancel a range: scancel 1234_[1-10]
  - Operate on the whole array: scontrol show job 1234 (affects all elements)

- A couple of practical notes
  - If you submit sbatch --array=1-3 you get array indices 1,2,3; SLURM_ARRAY_JOB_ID will be set to the array base ID, and each running element will have SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID set to 1/2/3 respectively.
  - Slurm may create a placeholder ordering nuance: the first task submitted can be a placeholder, so JobID ordering vs task index ordering is not guaranteed to be strictly monotonic — always rely on SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID for the element index.

Good question — scontrol show job prints a lot of fields. Below are the most important ones you’ll see and what they mean, grouped for quick scanning.

Identification / ownership
- JobId — unique numeric job identifier (use this to reference the job).  
- JobName — name given at submission (sbatch --job-name).  
- UserId / User — submitting user (and UID).  
- GroupId / Group — job group/primary group.  
- Account — accounting project the job charged to.  
- Priority — scheduler priority value for the job.  
- QualityOfService (QOS) — QOS used for scheduling.

State & scheduling
- State — current job state (PENDING, RUNNING, COMPLETED, FAILED, etc.).  
- Reason — if PENDING, the scheduler’s reason string (resource/wait reason).  
- SubmitTime — when the job was submitted.  
- EligibleTime — when the job first became eligible to run.  
- StartTime — when the job started running (or “Unknown” if not started).  
- RunTime / Elapsed — how long the job has been running.  
- TimeLimit (or TimeLimitRaw) — requested walltime / job time limit.  
- EndTime (or End) — scheduled/completed end time if available.  
- Dependency — job dependencies (afterok, afterany, aftercorr, etc.).

Resources requested vs allocated
- Partition — partition the job was submitted to / allocated from.  
- NumNodes / Nodes — number of nodes requested / allocated.  
- NodeList — list or range of nodes allocated (or planned nodes).  
- NumCPUs / CPUS — number of CPUs/cores requested or allocated.  
- ReqMem / MinMemory — memory requested.  
- TRES (or ReqTRES) — requested Trackable RESources (e.g., cpu=...,mem=...,gpu=...).  
- AllocTRES — actually allocated TRES (shows what the job actually received).  
- Gres — generic resources (often gpus) requested (gres/gpu:2 etc.).  
- TresPerNode / CPUTasksPerNodel — per-node allocation details (when present).

Allocation / node details
- AllocNode:Sid — the node and system id performing the allocation (local allocator info).  
- Features / Constraint — node features or constraints used for matching (e.g., specific CPU type).  
- NumCPUsPerTask / TasksPerNode / Sockets/Cores/Threads — task/core topology if set or shown.  
- NodeList/NodeAddr (when present) — concrete node hostnames or addresses.

Job script, I/O, and environment
- Command (or BatchCommand / BatchScript path) — the command or path to the batch script (may be viewable via scontrol write batch_script).  
- StdOut / StdErr — configured stdout/stderr file paths.  
- WorkDir — working directory used for the job.  
- Environment / PassEnv — environment variables or whatever was recorded (may be limited for unprivileged users).

Exit / final state info (for completed jobs)
- ExitCode — formatted as "<exitcode>:<signal>" (e.g., 0:0 means exit 0).  
- ExitCodeDetail / Reason — more info if non-zero or signalled.

Array & batch metadata
- ArrayJobId, ArrayTaskId, ArrayTasks — job array identifiers and index range (if part of an array).  
- BatchFlag — indicates sbatch-submitted batch jobs (BatchFlag=1) and increments if requeued.  
- RequeueCount / Requeued — requeue/restart counts or flags.

Reservations / special scheduler flags
- Reservation — reservation name if the job is running under a reservation.  
- Hold/Dependency flags — HoldReasons or whether the job was submitted with a hold.  
- Flags — internal flags set on the job (internal use).

Administrative / debugging fields
- Comment / Reason (from scontrol show job -d) — extra scheduler/admin comments.  
- SuspendTime / SuspendCount — suspend-related fields if suspended.  
- PriorityFactor / FairShare info — scheduling-fairshare or priority factors (sometimes present in diagnostic output).  
- Account or QOS limits that affected scheduling (may appear in admin views).

Quick usage tips
- Use scontrol show job <jobid> to get the full record; add the "details" option (or scontrol show job -d) on systems that support it to see per-node CPU/memory allocations.  
- For a short view of state and reason use squeue; for historical exit codes and resource usage use sacct.  
- ExitCode format is important: "<code>:<signal>". If non‑zero, check StdErr and sacct for details.

If you want, I can:

## Timeslicer Design and Operation [#time_slice](https://slurm.schedmd.com/gang_scheduling.html)
When enabled, the gang scheduler keeps track of the resources
allocated to all jobs. For each partition an "active bitmap" is maintained that
tracks all concurrently running jobs in the Slurm cluster. Each time a new
job is allocated to resources in a partition, the gang scheduler
compares these newly allocated resources with the resources already maintained
in the "active bitmap".
If these two sets of resources are disjoint then the new job is added to the "active bitmap". If these two sets of resources overlap then
the new job is suspended. All jobs are tracked in a per-partition job queue
within the gang scheduler logic.

# Gang Scheduling
Slurm supports timesliced gang scheduling in which two or more jobs are
allocated to the same resources in the same partition and these jobs are
alternately suspended to let one job at a time have dedicated access to the
resources for a configured period of time.
Slurm also supports preemptive job scheduling that allows a job in a
higher PriorityTier partition, or in a preempting QOS, to preempt other
jobs. [Preemption](https://slurm.schedmd.com/preempt.html) is related to Gang scheduling
because SUSPEND is one of the PreemptionMode s, and it uses the Gang
scheduler to resume suspended jobs.
A workload manager that supports timeslicing can improve responsiveness
and utilization by allowing more jobs to begin running sooner.
Shorter-running jobs no longer have to wait in a queue behind longer-running
jobs.
Instead they can be run "in parallel" with the longer-running jobs, which will

Below is a focused explanation of how Slurm’s backfill scheduler decides whether a job “fits”, how to judge the health of backfill scheduling on your cluster, common failure modes, and practical checks / fixes you can run or apply.

What backfill is (short)
- Backfill lets lower‑priority or later‑submitted jobs start early if they will not delay the expected start time of any higher‑priority pending job. It dramatically improves utilization and responsiveness vs. strict FIFO scheduling.
- Backfill decisions use each running job’s expected completion time (based on its time limit or actual run time), the resources currently free now, and the earliest guaranteed start time of higher‑priority jobs.

How Slurm decides “fit” (the backfill window)
- Determine the earliest start time (the “reservation” or start deadline) of any job that must not be delayed (typically the highest‑priority pending job).
- Compute the time window(s) between now and those reserved start times where resources will be free (holes).
- A candidate pending job “fits” if it can be scheduled on available resources and is expected to complete before the reserved start time (i.e., its requested walltime <= available hole length and its requested resources can be mapped into a compatible set of nodes/CPUs/GPUs).
- Important inputs: requested walltime, requested TRES (CPUs, memory, GPUs), node layout/fragmentation, and whether preemption/gang scheduling is allowed.

Health signals to watch
- Utilization: overall cluster utilization (CPU/GPU hours in use). Low utilization with many pending jobs → poor backfill fit or fragmentation.
- Backfill throughput/efficiency: proportion of work done by backfilled jobs (sdiag can show backfill statistics). Good backfill increases short‑job throughput.
- Queue wait times by job size/class: short jobs should show low wait times if backfill is healthy.
- Pending reasons: many pending jobs stuck for “Resources” or “ReqNodeNotAvail” suggests fragmentation or reserved nodes.
- Fragmentation: many small free node groups (holes) that cannot satisfy medium/large job requests.
- Time limit accuracy: lots of jobs hitting TIMEOUT or running much shorter than requested time → inflates reserve windows and reduces backfill opportunities.
- Preemption / cancellations: frequent preemptions or backfill kills mean backfill policy is disruptive or misconfigured.
- Scheduler backlog / decision time: long scheduler cycle time or deep queue depth (sdiag) indicates stress.
- Priority inversion: high‑priority jobs repeatedly delayed (backfill shouldn’t delay guaranteed starts).

Common failure modes and root causes
- Overly conservative or inaccurate walltimes: users overestimate time limits → long reserved windows reduce backfill opportunities.
- Fragmented free nodes: heterogeneous or exclusive‑node allocations leave small unusable holes for jobs of varying sizes.
- Large fraction of very large jobs: large jobs monopolize capacity and create long windows that small jobs can’t use.
- Resource mismatch: users request whole nodes, specific GPUs, or strict node features that do not match available holes.
- Misconfigured scheduler parameters: too small a backfill depth, wrong SchedulerType, or disabled preemption/gang scheduling.
- Reservations or admin holds: reservations block resources and reduce backfill windows.
- Incorrect partition/QOS weights: priorities and fairshare can lead to starvation or poor start times.

Actions to improve fit & backfill health
- Enforce and educate about accurate walltimes. Consider capping maximum walltimes for certain partitions or using penalties for huge overestimates.
- Introduce or tune short‑job partitions/queues (e.g., a short‑walltime partition for interactive/short jobs).
- Enable/adjust preemption or gang scheduling for better packing of short jobs with long ones (if appropriate for your workload).
- Use job packing features or configure SelectTypeParameters (e.g., CR_Core_Memory) to allow packing multiple jobs per node when safe.
- Provide guidance on flexible resource requests (use --nodes vs --ntasks-per-node, allow multiple jobs per node when appropriate).
- Use reservations sparingly or schedule them during expected low utilization.
- Consider topology‑aware scheduling and node labeling so jobs that can share a node do not force exclusive allocations.
- Tune SchedulerParameters and backfill depth (e.g., SchedulerParameters=bf_depth,bf_resolution — check your Slurm docs and test changes).

Concrete checks and commands to run (what operators/admins commonly use)
- sdiag — scheduler/backfill diagnostics, backfill statistics and scheduling cycle times.
- sinfo — partition/node states (allocated/idle/drained), node resources and counts (helps spot fragmentation).
- squeue (with Reason column) — inspect pending job reasons and which jobs are blocking others.
- sprio — inspect priority factors (age, fairshare, QOS) that influence the “must not delay” list.
- scontrol show config | grep SchedulerType and SchedulerParameters — confirm scheduler type and backfill config.
- scontrol show job <jobid> — see a job’s requested walltime and resources.
- sshare / sreport — check fairshare and historical usage to understand priority effects and whether short jobs get scheduled.
- sacct / sreport — historical completion times and distribution of job walltimes; use this to detect systemic overestimation of runtime.

Quick diagnostic checklist (short)
1. Run sdiag; note backfill statistics and scheduling cycle times.
2. Run sinfo; inspect idle node counts and node sizes (look for many small holes).
3. Run squeue --states=PENDING -o "%i %P %j %u %t %M %R" to see pending reasons and the jobs that define earliest start times.
4. Review job walltime accuracy with sacct for a sample period (fraction of jobs that end far earlier than their requested time).
5. Inspect sprio to see whether priorities/fairshare are forcing long reservations.

Useful metrics to track (for ongoing health)
- Cluster utilization (CPU/GPU hours used / available).
- Backfill utilization or backfill job share (% of jobs started by backfill).
- Median wait time for short jobs (e.g., jobs <= 1 hour).
- Fraction of jobs that end in TIMEOUT or much earlier than requested.
- Number and size of free node gaps (fragmentation metric).

When to change scheduling configuration
- If utilization is low while many pending short jobs exist: adjust backfill parameters, enforce shorter job partitions, or improve walltime accuracy.
- If backfill jobs are being preempted frequently and users complain: consider reducing preemption aggressiveness or tuning preempt QOS.
- If the scheduler decision time is large or deep queues cause missed opportunities: consider increasing scheduling resources or tuning SchedulerParameters (with care and testing).

Summary
- Backfill works best when job walltimes are accurate and jobs’ resource requests match the cluster’s node granularity.
- Monitor utilization, backfill throughput (sdiag), pending reasons (squeue), and fragmentation (sinfo); use sacct/sreport for historical time‑accuracy analysis.
- Most problems are fixable by improving walltime accuracy, adding a short‑job partition, updating packing/selection settings, or tuning backfill/preemption policies.

If you want, I can:
- Give a short checklist you can run now (commands to paste),
- Or run live diagnostics on your cluster (sdiag, sinfo, squeue, sacct) and interpret the results — say which one you want and I’ll run them.

## Hierarchy[#hierarchy](https://slurm.schedmd.com/resource_limits.html)
Slurm's hierarchical limits are enforced in the following order
with Job QOS and Partition QOS order being reversible by using the QOS
flag 'OverPartQOS':
- Partition QOS limit
- Job QOS limit
- User association
- Account association(s), ascending the hierarchy
- Root/Cluster association
- Partition limit
- None

the point in this list where the limit is first defined will be used.

- MaxJobs=20 and MaxSubmitJobs is undefined in the partition QOS

- MaxJobs=4 and MaxSubmitJobs=50 in the user association

Slurm's job scheduler handles GRES affinity on a socket basis internally.
However, the gres.conf interface allows administrators to specify `Cores` for GPU affinity configuration. This creates
a common misconception that Slurm will respect core-level affinity during job
scheduling, which it does not and never has. This can lead to issues where job
allocations and job steps don't align correctly, since job steps examine cores

## Sharding [#Sharding](https://slurm.schedmd.com/gres.html)
Sharding provides a generic mechanism where GPUs can be
shared by multiple jobs. While it does permit multiple jobs to run on a given
GPU it does not fence the processes running on the GPU, it only allows the GPU
to be shared. Sharding, therefore, works best with homogeneous workflows. It is
recommended to limit the number of shards on a node to equal the max possible
jobs that can run simultaneously on the node (i.e. cores).
The total count of shards available on a node should be configured in
the slurm.conf file (e.g. "NodeName=tux[1-16] Gres=gpu:2,shard:64").

Short answer
- "AssocGrpGRES" (or more generally the AssocGrp* family) is a scheduler pending/reason code meaning: the job's association (user/account/partition/cluster association) has hit an aggregate GRES/TRES group limit and so the job cannot be allocated.
- GRES (generic resources, e.g. gres/gpu) are treated as TRES for accounting/limits; association-level group limits on GRES are configured via the GrpTRES (trackable resources) association/account/user/cluster fields (e.g., GrpTRES=gres/gpu=8).

Key points (what this means and how it works)
- What is being limited: association "group" limits are aggregate limits applied to an association (user+account+cluster+optional partition). They cap the total resources in-use by that association (running allocations) — e.g., GrpJobs, GrpTRES (cpu, mem, node, or generic resources like gres/gpu).
- GRES as TRES: GRES types (gpu, mps, etc.) are exposed as TRES names like gres/gpu. To limit GPUs for an association you set GrpTRES=gres/gpu=<count>.
- When the limit is checked: Grp* limits are evaluated when the scheduler considers starting a job. If starting the job would make the association exceed any Grp limit, the job is not considered eligible (it will pend). The pending reason shown by squeue will be an AssocGrp* variant (for GRES-related limits you may see names like AssocGrpGRES or AssocGrp*Limit).
- Precedence/hierarchy: limits are applied in this order (first-match wins): user association → account association(s) (hierarchy upward) → cluster/root association → partition/job/QOS specific limits as documented. If a specific association level has no setting, the next level's setting is used.
- Interaction with QOS and DenyOnLimit: QOS flags like DenyOnLimit can make a job be denied at submission if it alone violates a max. For Grp limits, the Grp limit is treated as a Max when deciding DenyOnLimit behavior (see resource_limits docs).
- Changes effect: lowering Grp limits does not kill running jobs to immediately satisfy the new limit; the new lower limit is enforced for future scheduling decisions. Deleting an association can cancel running/pending jobs that belong to it.
- Numeric and update semantics: GrpTRES entries are comma-separated TRES=value assignments (e.g., GrpTRES=cpu=32,mem=200G,gres/gpu=4). You can use "+=" / "-=" when modifying to increment/decrement. Assigning -1 removes a specific TRES limit. Using "-=" to try to make a negative value will set that TRES to 0.

How to view and set these limits (examples)
- Show current association/account limits:
  - sacctmgr show association (or sacctmgr show user/account with WithAssoc) — this displays GrpTRES, GrpJobs, etc.
- Set a GRES group limit (examples — run as an admin with sacctmgr):
  - For a user association:
    sacctmgr modify user where name=alice set GrpTRES=gres/gpu=4
  - For an account:
    sacctmgr modify account where name=chemistry set GrpTRES=gres/gpu=10
  - Or editing the association directly:
    sacctmgr modify association where user=alice account=chemistry set GrpTRES=gres/gpu=4
- Increment/decrement:
  - sacctmgr modify account where name=chemistry set GrpTRES+=gres/gpu=2
  - To remove the limit: set GrpTRES=gres/gpu=-1 (removes that TRES limit)

Troubleshooting tips
- If a job is pending with reason AssocGrp* (or AssocGrpGRES), inspect the association limits with sacctmgr show assoc (or sacctmgr show user/account) to find which GrpTRES or GrpJobs limit is blocking it.
- Remember that the scheduler tests the aggregate — even if currently some GPUs look free, the job will still pend if starting it would exceed the configured GrpTRES for that job's association.
- Check QOS/partition MaxTRES/MaxJobs settings too — a job can be blocked by a higher-priority limit at the QOS/partition level.

References / authoritative configuration names
- GrpTRES is the canonical place to set per-association aggregate limits on trackable resources (TRES), including generic resources (gres/<name>).
- The scheduler pending reason family is AssocGrp* (AssocGrpGRES being the GRES-related variant) — meaning some association-group aggregate limit was reached.
(These behaviours are described in Slurm's "Resource Limits" and "GRES" documentation; use sacctmgr show/modify to inspect and change association limits.)

## EXAMPLES[#SECTION_EXAMPLES](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Specify a batch script by filename on the command line. The batch script specifies a 1 minute time limit for the job.
```text
$ cat myscript #!/bin/sh #SBATCH --time=1 srun hostname |sort $ sbatch -N4 myscript salloc: Granted job allocation 65537 $ cat slurm-65537.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
Pass a batch script to sbatch on standard input:
```text
$ sbatch -N4 #!/bin/sh > srun hostname |sort > EOF sbatch: Submitted batch job 65541 $ cat slurm-65541.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
To create a heterogeneous job with 3 components, each allocating a unique set of nodes:
```text
$ sbatch -w node[2-3] : -w node4 : -w node[5-7] work.bash Submitted batch job 34987
```

### Warnings [#Warnings](https://slurm.schedmd.com/extra_constraints.html)
Whitespace characters are not treated specially. Any whitespace characters will
be considered part of a key or value. This means that the following is invalid:
```text
--extra " (a=b)"
```
The space at he beginning is parsed as a key of a request. Then the opening
parenthesis character is recognized as an invalid character for either a key
or a comparison operator. This request would result in the job being rejected.
However, this is valid:
```text
--extra "( a=b)"
```
This has a single request. The key is " a", the comparison operator is "=", and
the value is "b".
This same warning applies to single and double quotes. These are not considered
special characters, and thus are part of a string. Thus, bar and "bar" are not
equal.

### Valid and Invalid Requests [#Valid](https://slurm.schedmd.com/extra_constraints.html)
Here are some examples of valid requests:
```text
a=1.23 a= b a!=1.24 a!=1.23|foo!=blah b=200 b=true foo =0.00000001) ((c =0.1)
```
Here are some examples of invalid requests:
Invalid comparison operator:
```text
a, =0.00000001) ((c =0.1)
```
The following --extra requests are not fulfilled by this node:
```text
a!=1.23 b=0 b=false foo>baz ((c =0.00001)
```
Reminder: in order for two numbers to be considered equal, their difference
must be less than 0.0001. This is why 0.0001 is not considered equal to 0 and
thus the request `c>=0.0001` is not fulfilled,
but 0.00000001 is considered equal to 0 and thus the request
`c>=0.00000001` is fulfilled.

## Node Extra Data [#Node_Extra_Data](https://slurm.schedmd.com/extra_constraints.html)
A node's extra data is a json formatted string. It may be initialized on
slurmd startup with the --extra flag for slurmd. For example:
```text
slurmd --extra '{ "a": 1.23, "b": true, "c": 0, "foo": "bar", "zed": 23 }'
```
Or, it may be updated with scontrol. For example:
```text
scontrol update nodename=node123 extra='{ "a": 1.23, "b": true, "c": 0, "foo": "bar", "zed": 23 }'
```
This defines the features that may be requested by the --extra option in
salloc, sbatch, and srun. Values may be any string, number, or boolean value.

### Warnings [#Warnings](https://slurm.schedmd.com/extra_constraints.html)
Whitespace characters are not treated specially. Any whitespace characters will
be considered part of a key or value. This means that the following is invalid:
```text
--extra " (a=b)"
```
The space at he beginning is parsed as a key of a request. Then the opening
parenthesis character is recognized as an invalid character for either a key
or a comparison operator. This request would result in the job being rejected.
However, this is valid:
```text
--extra "( a=b)"
```
This has a single request. The key is " a", the comparison operator is "=", and
the value is "b".
This same warning applies to single and double quotes. These are not considered
special characters, and thus are part of a string. Thus, bar and "bar" are not
equal.

## Node Extra Data [#Node_Extra_Data](https://slurm.schedmd.com/extra_constraints.html)
A node's extra data is a json formatted string. It may be initialized on
slurmd startup with the --extra flag for slurmd. For example:
```text
slurmd --extra '{ "a": 1.23, "b": true, "c": 0, "foo": "bar", "zed": 23 }'
```
Or, it may be updated with scontrol. For example:
```text
scontrol update nodename=node123 extra='{ "a": 1.23, "b": true, "c": 0, "foo": "bar", "zed": 23 }'
```
This defines the features that may be requested by the --extra option in
salloc, sbatch, and srun. Values may be any string, number, or boolean value.

### Valid and Invalid Requests [#Valid](https://slurm.schedmd.com/extra_constraints.html)
Here are some examples of valid requests:
```text
a=1.23 a= b a!=1.24 a!=1.23|foo!=blah b=200 b=true foo =0.00000001) ((c =0.1)
```
Here are some examples of invalid requests:
Invalid comparison operator:
```text
a, =0.00000001) ((c =0.1)
```
The following --extra requests are not fulfilled by this node:
```text
a!=1.23 b=0 b=false foo>baz ((c =0.00001)
```
Reminder: in order for two numbers to be considered equal, their difference
must be less than 0.0001. This is why 0.0001 is not considered equal to 0 and
thus the request `c>=0.0001` is not fulfilled,
but 0.00000001 is considered equal to 0 and thus the request
`c>=0.00000001` is fulfilled.

to filter nodes based on their extra data. This is disabled by

sbatch submits a batch script to Slurm. The batch script may be given to
sbatch through a file name on the command line, or if no file name is specified,
sbatch will read in a script from standard input.

directly by Slurm, so shell-specific syntax including variable names will be
read as literal text. Once the first non-comment, non-whitespace line has been
reached in the script, no more #SBATCH directives will be processed. See example
below.

### Warnings [#Warnings](https://slurm.schedmd.com/extra_constraints.html)
Whitespace characters are not treated specially. Any whitespace characters will
be considered part of a key or value. This means that the following is invalid:
```text
--extra " (a=b)"
```
The space at he beginning is parsed as a key of a request. Then the opening
parenthesis character is recognized as an invalid character for either a key
or a comparison operator. This request would result in the job being rejected.
However, this is valid:
```text
--extra "( a=b)"
```
This has a single request. The key is " a", the comparison operator is "=", and
the value is "b".
This same warning applies to single and double quotes. These are not considered
special characters, and thus are part of a string. Thus, bar and "bar" are not
equal.

## SIGNALS AND ESCAPE SEQUENCES[#SECTION_SIGNALS-AND-ESCAPE-SEQUENCES](https://slurm.schedmd.com/srun.html)
Signals sent to the srun command are automatically forwarded to
the tasks it is controlling with a few exceptions. The escape sequence
<control-c> will report the state of all tasks associated with
the srun command. If <control-c> is entered twice within
one second, then the associated SIGINT signal will be sent to all tasks
and a termination sequence will be entered sending SIGCONT, SIGTERM,
and SIGKILL to all spawned tasks.
If a third <control-c> is received, the srun program will be
terminated without waiting for remote tasks to exit or their I/O to
complete.
The escape sequence <control-z> is presently ignored.

## Node Extra Data [#Node_Extra_Data](https://slurm.schedmd.com/extra_constraints.html)
A node's extra data is a json formatted string. It may be initialized on
slurmd startup with the --extra flag for slurmd. For example:
```text
slurmd --extra '{ "a": 1.23, "b": true, "c": 0, "foo": "bar", "zed": 23 }'
```
Or, it may be updated with scontrol. For example:
```text
scontrol update nodename=node123 extra='{ "a": 1.23, "b": true, "c": 0, "foo": "bar", "zed": 23 }'
```
This defines the features that may be requested by the --extra option in
salloc, sbatch, and srun. Values may be any string, number, or boolean value.

## Overview [#Overview](https://slurm.schedmd.com/extra_constraints.html)
Extra data may be added to a node, and jobs may request extra constraints
to filter nodes based on their extra data. This is disabled by
default, but may be enabled in slurm.conf. Warning : Slurm's backfill
scheduler cannot accurately plan nodes for jobs whose request extra constraints
are not immediately satisfied. This means that the more often extra data for
nodes is changed, the less accurate the backfill scheduler will be.

## Node Extra Data [#Node_Extra_Data](https://slurm.schedmd.com/extra_constraints.html)
A node's extra data is a json formatted string. It may be initialized on
slurmd startup with the --extra flag for slurmd. For example:
```text
slurmd --extra '{ "a": 1.23, "b": true, "c": 0, "foo": "bar", "zed": 23 }'
```
Or, it may be updated with scontrol. For example:
```text
scontrol update nodename=node123 extra='{ "a": 1.23, "b": true, "c": 0, "foo": "bar", "zed": 23 }'
```
This defines the features that may be requested by the --extra option in
salloc, sbatch, and srun. Values may be any string, number, or boolean value.

## DESCRIPTION[#SECTION_DESCRIPTION](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
sbatch submits a batch script to Slurm. The batch script may be given to
sbatch through a file name on the command line, or if no file name is specified,
sbatch will read in a script from standard input.
The batch script may contain one or more lines beginning with "#SBATCH" followed
by any of the CLI options documented on this page. #SBATCH directives are read
directly by Slurm, so shell-specific syntax including variable names will be
read as literal text. Once the first non-comment, non-whitespace line has been
reached in the script, no more #SBATCH directives will be processed. See example
below.

## Job Priority Factors In General [#general](https://slurm.schedmd.com/priority_multifactor.html)
The job's priority at any given time will be a weighted sum of all the
factors that have been enabled in the slurm.conf file. Job priority can be
expressed as:
```text
Job_priority = site_factor + (PriorityWeightAge) * (age_factor) + (PriorityWeightAssoc) * (assoc_factor) + (PriorityWeightFairshare) * (fair-share_factor) + (PriorityWeightJobSize) * (job_size_factor) + (PriorityWeightPartition) * (priority_job_factor) + (PriorityWeightQOS) * (QOS_factor) + SUM(TRES_weight_cpu * TRES_factor_cpu, TRES_weight_ * TRES_factor_ , ...) - nice_factor
```
All of the factors in this formula are floating point numbers that
range from 0.0 to 1.0. The weights are unsigned, 32 bit integers.

# Job Reason Codes
These reason codes can be used to identify why a pending job has not yet been
started by the scheduler. There may be multiple reasons why a job cannot start,
in which case only the reason that was encountered by the attempted scheduling
method will be displayed. Refer to the [Scheduling Configuration Guide](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sched_config.html) for more details.

Short answer
- The pending reason "Priority" means the scheduler found one or more jobs with higher priority that must be scheduled before this job. In other words, your job is waiting because other jobs score higher under Slurm’s priority algorithm for the partition/resources you requested.

Why this happens (from the official docs)
- Job reason codes doc: “Priority — One or more higher priority jobs exist for the partition associated with the job or for resources requested.” (job_reason_codes)
- Slurm uses the multifactor priority plugin by default; job priority is a weighted sum of factors such as age, fairshare, association, job size, partition, QOS, TRES factors, site factor and nice. The plugin configuration (PriorityType and the PriorityWeight* settings) determines how those factors combine into a job priority value. (priority_multifactor)

How to diagnose (commands)
- See the pending reason in the queue:
  - squeue (show the REASON column or use -o to include %R)
- Inspect the job’s priority and details:
  - scontrol show job <jobid>  (shows JobPriority and related fields)
- See per-job priority breakdown and ranking:
  - sprio -l   (or sprio for a summary) — shows priority values and factors
- Verify scheduler priority configuration:
  - scontrol show config | grep -i Priority

What you can do about it
- Wait: higher-priority jobs will run and free resources.
- Change your request: smaller resource/time requests or a different partition may allow earlier start.
- Use a different QOS (if available) that has higher priority or preemption privileges.
- If fairshare/account weighting is the cause, reducing recent usage or changing account/QOS (via admin) can help.
- Ask the cluster admin to adjust PriorityWeight settings, QOS, or to create a reservation if urgent.

References (official Slurm docs)
- Job reason codes: https://slurm.schedmd.com/job_reason_codes.html
- Multifactor Priority plugin (how priorities are computed and configured): https://slurm.schedmd.com/priority_multifactor.html

If you want, tell me a job ID and I can show the JobPriority and the current queue state for that job (squeue + scontrol); or I can run sprio to list current priority order.

## PERFORMANCE[#SECTION_PERFORMANCE](https://slurm.schedmd.com/strigger.html)
Executing strigger sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from strigger or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmctld daemon come in at once, it can result in
a degradation of performance of the slurmctld daemon, possibly resulting
in a denial of service.
Do not run strigger or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other
programs. Ensure that programs limit calls to strigger to the minimum
necessary for the information you are trying to gather.

Summary
- strigger is the Slurm client/daemon feature for defining “triggers” (actions) that run when Slurm detects certain events for jobs or nodes.
- Events include job time/finish, job/node up/down, node drained/idle/reconfig, and controller/backup controller events.
- Triggers are evaluated periodically by slurmctld (not instant — currently checked about every 15 s). Any events during that interval are compared to the configured triggers and the trigger program is executed once for matching events.

Key concepts / fields
- Resource type (RES_TYPE): job or node.
- Resource id (RES_ID): job ID, hostlist, or "*" to match any host.
- Trigger type (TYPE): examples — time, fini (job finish), down, up, drained, idle, reconfig, plus controller/backup events.
- OFFSET: time in seconds; negative values request the action before the event (e.g., OFFSET=-300 = 5 minutes before job time limit).
- PROGRAM: pathname of the program/script to execute when the trigger fires.
- TRIG_ID: numeric id assigned to the trigger (used for clearing).
- USER: the user who created/requested the trigger.

Basic commands
- Set a trigger:
  strigger --set [options]
  Example: strigger --set --jobid=12345 --type=time --offset=-300 --program=/path/to/script
  (This requests running the script 5 minutes before job 12345’s time limit.)
- List triggers:
  strigger --get [--user=USER] [--jobid=ID] [--node=NODE]
  Example: strigger --get --user=alice
- Clear a trigger:
  strigger --clear --id=TRIG_ID
  You can clear by id, jobid, or user (the --id/--jobid/--user option must be supplied).

Behavior & gotchas
- Execution is done by slurmctld when it processes trigger events; triggers are not processed instantly but on the periodic check (≈15 s), and only one execution per event per interval is performed.
- OFFSET is honored when possible — a negative OFFSET asks for the action before the event; for some events it may not be possible to guarantee exact timing.
- Beware performance: strigger calls are RPCs to slurmctld. Rapid/looped calls can overload slurmctld; avoid tight loops creating many strigger calls.
- Permissions: clearing or setting triggers may be restricted (e.g., root can manage other users’ triggers); use appropriate user/filter options when listing/clearing.

Common use cases
- Notify admin or run cleanup just before a job hits its time limit (type=time, negative OFFSET).
- Run a script when a node goes down or comes back up (type=down/up, RES_TYPE=node).
- Take automated action when a node is drained or becomes idle (type=drained/idle).
- Detect backup slurmctld failover or resume (options for backup controller events).

Where to read more
- The authoritative reference is the manpage: https://slurm.schedmd.com/strigger.html

## Overview [#Overview](https://slurm.schedmd.com/extra_constraints.html)
Extra data may be added to a node, and jobs may request extra constraints
to filter nodes based on their extra data. This is disabled by
default, but may be enabled in slurm.conf. Warning : Slurm's backfill
scheduler cannot accurately plan nodes for jobs whose request extra constraints
are not immediately satisfied. This means that the more often extra data for
nodes is changed, the less accurate the backfill scheduler will be.

## Node Extra Data [#Node_Extra_Data](https://slurm.schedmd.com/extra_constraints.html)
A node's extra data is a json formatted string. It may be initialized on
slurmd startup with the --extra flag for slurmd. For example:
```text
slurmd --extra '{ "a": 1.23, "b": true, "c": 0, "foo": "bar", "zed": 23 }'
```
Or, it may be updated with scontrol. For example:
```text
scontrol update nodename=node123 extra='{ "a": 1.23, "b": true, "c": 0, "foo": "bar", "zed": 23 }'
```
This defines the features that may be requested by the --extra option in
salloc, sbatch, and srun. Values may be any string, number, or boolean value.

associated to cloud nodes in the slurm.conf , will be available but not

active features, the controller will allocate nodes that are powered down and
have the features as available. At allocation, the features will be made
active. A cloud node will remain with the active features until the node is

sbatch submits a batch script to Slurm. The batch script may be given to
sbatch through a file name on the command line, or if no file name is specified,
sbatch will read in a script from standard input.

## Node Extra Data [#Node_Extra_Data](https://slurm.schedmd.com/extra_constraints.html)
A node's extra data is a json formatted string. It may be initialized on
slurmd startup with the --extra flag for slurmd. For example:
```text
slurmd --extra '{ "a": 1.23, "b": true, "c": 0, "foo": "bar", "zed": 23 }'
```
Or, it may be updated with scontrol. For example:
```text
scontrol update nodename=node123 extra='{ "a": 1.23, "b": true, "c": 0, "foo": "bar", "zed": 23 }'
```
This defines the features that may be requested by the --extra option in
salloc, sbatch, and srun. Values may be any string, number, or boolean value.

Short answer
- A node feature is a label/attribute attached to a node (e.g., gpu_v100, ssd_local, nvlink, large_mem). Features are used by the scheduler to filter/choose which nodes are eligible for a job; requesting a feature restricts placement to nodes that expose that feature.
- Features can be static (defined in slurm.conf) or dynamic/changeable (managed by NodeFeaturesPlugins/helpers or set via scontrol). Dynamic features may be “available” but not yet “active” (common for cloud/power-save nodes) and activating a feature can require powering/rebooting a node — which affects placement latency.
- There are two related mechanisms:
  - --constraint (feature matching / node labels): pick nodes that list the requested feature(s).
  - --extra / extra_constraints (JSON numeric/boolean attributes + expression language, only when SchedulerParameters=extra_constraints): lets you ask for numeric comparisons and Boolean expressions (e.g. gpu_mem>=16 & foo=true) for finer selection.

How features affect placement (what you should expect)
- Eligibility: Any job that requests a feature is only eligible for nodes that advertise that feature. Fewer eligible nodes usually means longer queue times.
- Fragmentation & packing: Tight feature constraints reduce the pool the scheduler can pack on and may increase fragmentation (free resources that can’t satisfy constrained jobs).
- Backfill accuracy: If you use extra_constraints or frequently-changing features, Slurm’s backfill planner may be less accurate (the docs warn that changing node extra data often harms backfill planning).
- Dynamically-changeable features can delay allocation: if the controller must power/reboot a node (or call a helper) to activate a feature, the job may be delayed until that process completes.
- Power-save / cloud nodes: features defined by NodeFeaturesPlugins are available when nodes are powered down and become active only after the node is allocated and powered on. Requesting such features tells Slurm it may allocate and power-on those nodes to satisfy the job.
- Scheduling logic: features are filters (yes/no, or expression matches). They are not resources like CPUs or GPUs (TRES). Requesting a feature does not consume it — it only restricts placement to nodes that have it.
- Heterogeneous allocations: when nodes differ in features, the scheduler may create heterogeneous job allocations (different components with different features) if the job requests multiple component types or uses nodesets.

Common examples and usage
- Define features in slurm.conf (NodeName=... Feature=f1,f2) or set/update them with scontrol:
  - scontrol update NodeName=node123 Features=ssd_local,gpu_a100
- Request a feature at submit time:
  - sbatch --constraint=gpu_a100 myjob.sh
  - You can combine feature expressions (site behavior may vary — check your local docs/policy); for more complex numeric/boolean matching use --extra with extra_constraints enabled:
    - sbatch --extra 'gpu_mem>=16 & nvlink=true' myjob.sh
- Use nodesets to group feature-selected nodes in partition config (NodeSet ... Feature=...).

How to inspect features on your cluster
- scontrol show node <nodename> — shows Features= and Extra= fields for that node.
- sinfo and scontrol show config / helpers.conf for site-level feature/plugin configuration.
- If your site uses node feature helpers, look at helpers.conf and NodeFeaturesPlugins in slurm.conf to understand which features are dynamic and whether a helper/reboot is required.

Practical recommendations / best practices
- Only request features when you need them (hardware/firmware/software or topology requirements). Unnecessary constraints hurt queue times and packing.
- For numeric or frequently-updated attributes (e.g., current GPU-free-memory), prefer a separate resource accounting or a job-side check — because frequently-changing Extra values reduce backfill accuracy.
- If your cluster defines changeable features via helpers, expect allocation delays for nodes that must be activated; coordinate with admins if you need low-latency access to particular configurations.
- Use nodesets or partition-level features for common groupings to simplify user job submission.

If you want, I can:
- Show how features are currently set on your cluster (scontrol show node / sinfo). Which node or partition should I inspect?

## PERFORMANCE[#SECTION_PERFORMANCE](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Executing sbatch sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmctld daemon come in at once, it can result in
a degradation of performance of the slurmctld daemon, possibly resulting
in a denial of service.
Do not run sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other
programs. Ensure that programs limit calls to sbatch to the minimum
necessary for the information you are trying to gather.

## EXAMPLES[#SECTION_EXAMPLES](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Specify a batch script by filename on the command line. The batch script specifies a 1 minute time limit for the job.
```text
$ cat myscript #!/bin/sh #SBATCH --time=1 srun hostname |sort $ sbatch -N4 myscript salloc: Granted job allocation 65537 $ cat slurm-65537.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
Pass a batch script to sbatch on standard input:
```text
$ sbatch -N4 #!/bin/sh > srun hostname |sort > EOF sbatch: Submitted batch job 65541 $ cat slurm-65541.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
To create a heterogeneous job with 3 components, each allocating a unique set of nodes:
```text
$ sbatch -w node[2-3] : -w node4 : -w node[5-7] work.bash Submitted batch job 34987
```

## SYNOPSIS[#SECTION_SYNOPSIS](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
sbatch [ OPTIONS(0) ...] [ : [ OPTIONS(N) ...]] script(0) [ args(0) ...]
Option(s) define multiple jobs in a co-scheduled heterogeneous job.
For more details about heterogeneous jobs see the document
[https://slurm.schedmd.com/heterogeneous_jobs.html](https://slurm.schedmd.com/heterogeneous_jobs.html)

Summary (official behavior)
- afterok is a job dependency type you can pass to sbatch (or set with #SBATCH --dependency=...).
- Meaning: the dependent job is eligible to start only after all specified jobs have finished successfully (exit code 0).
- It is checked by slurmctld at job completion; sbatch returns immediately with the dependent job ID, but that job will remain PENDING until the afterok condition is satisfied.

Syntax (from sbatch docs)
- Command-line or script directive:
  - sbatch --dependency=afterok:<jobid>[:<jobid>[:...]] myscript.sh
  - or inside a script: #SBATCH --dependency=afterok:12345:12346
- You may specify multiple job IDs separated by ':' (all listed jobs must meet the afterok condition).

Semantics and important notes
- AND semantics: when you list multiple job IDs, all must complete successfully (exit code 0) before the dependent job can run.
- Exit-code semantics: "successful" means the predecessor job(s) exited with code 0. If a predecessor fails (non‑zero exit code), times out, or is cancelled, an afterok dependency on that job will not be satisfied.
- Alternatives:
  - afterany: run after specified jobs finish regardless of exit code.
  - afternotok: run only if specified jobs finish with non‑zero exit (i.e., fail).
  - after: becomes eligible after the specified jobs have started.
- Job arrays and steps: you can reference specific job/step identifiers; consult sbatch/scontrol docs for array/step ID notation if you need element-level dependencies.
- Combining dependencies: you can express different dependency types (see sbatch docs) to build more complex conditions.

Quick examples
- Single predecessor that must succeed:
  - sbatch --dependency=afterok:12345 step2.sh
- Multiple predecessors:
  - sbatch --dependency=afterok:12345:12346 step3.sh
- Use in script:
  - #!/bin/sh
    #SBATCH --dependency=afterok:12345
    ...script body...

Reference
- Official sbatch documentation (dependency option): https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html (see --dependency and examples)

Snippet:
## Maintenance Reservations [#maint](https://slurm.schedmd.com/reservations.html)
For ease of system maintenance, you can create a reservation with the
MAINT flag that overlaps existing reservations. This is equivalent to the
OVERLAP flag but with the following distinctions:
- Reserved nodes will be shown in maint state
- Reserved nodes will not be available as replacements in other reservations
- Cluster usage reports will show this time as PlannedDown
For example, users alan and brenda might have a reservation
for some nodes daily from noon until 1PM. If there is a maintenance reservation
for all nodes starting at 12:30PM, the only jobs they may start in their
reservation would have to be completed by 12:30PM, when the maintenance
reservation begins.

Below are concise, safe, read-only steps and best practices for planning and using Slurm maintenance reservations while avoiding node state changes (drain/down) until you are explicitly ready to modify nodes.

1) Plan the window and scope
- Choose nodes (or partitions) and a maintenance window (start time + duration). Prefer low-usage windows.
- Decide whether you need to take nodes completely offline at the maintenance start (this would be a state change later) or just prevent new long-running jobs from starting.

2) Verify current and near-future usage (read-only checks you should run)
- Check current queue and running jobs: squeue (filter by nodes/partition or user).
- Check node/partition availability and counts: sinfo.
- For long-running jobs that could overlap your window, inspect historical runtimes with sacct (user or job filters).
- Check existing reservations: scontrol show reservation (or scontrol show res) and squeue --reservation=<name> to see jobs tied to a reservation.

3) Create the reservation (conceptual / best-practice options)
- Use an advanced reservation with the MAINT (maintenance) flag to mark it as maintenance. MAINT reservations are useful because:
  - They are shown as maintenance in reservation listings.
  - They may overlap other reservations but will prevent jobs that cannot finish before the MAINT start from being started.
  - They appear in usage/reporting as planned downtime.
- If you want the reservation to be a floating window relative to now, use TIME_FLOAT (start=now + offset) so it “floats.”
- Do NOT use flags=IGNORE_JOBS unless you intend to force-cancel or override running jobs — that would evict jobs and is not “safe” if you want to avoid involuntary changes.

Example (conceptual) form:
scontrol create reservation ReservationName=maint-YYYYMMDD StartTime=YYYY-MM-DDThh:mm Duration=minutes Nodes=node[01-04] Flags=MAINT Users=admin

(Do not run that command unless you intend to create the reservation — it changes cluster state.)

4) Minimize user impact without changing node state
- Set the reservation start time a little in the future so you (and users) can see it and react.
- Restrict who can use the reservation (Users= or Account=) so only maintenance jobs or admins can submit into it.
- Use small, rolling reservations (a subset of nodes) to allow staggered maintenance and reduce impact.
- Communicate the window to users and request they avoid launching jobs that exceed the window.

5) Verify effects (read-only checks after creation)
- Confirm the reservation exists and which nodes it covers: scontrol show reservation ReservationName=<name>.
- See which queued/running jobs are tied to or will be affected: squeue --reservation=<name> and squeue filtered to the nodes/partition.
- Use sinfo to see partition/node summaries; some displays will show reserved/maint counts.

6) If you ultimately need nodes idle at start (operations that require state changes)
- Two safe options:
  - Encourage users to finish jobs before the reservation and rely on the MAINT reservation to prevent new long jobs from starting.
  - At a predetermined time, explicitly change node state (e.g., drain) — note: that is a cluster-state change and must be performed deliberately with appropriate operator approval and user notice.

7) Rollback / cleanup (post-maintenance)
- After maintenance, remove or end the reservation (scontrol delete reservation=<name>) and confirm nodes return to normal scheduling. (Deleting the reservation is a mutating action.)

8) Short checklist before executing any mutating step
- Confirm active/running jobs that would be affected (squeue).
- Confirm no critical jobs are running on the targets (sacct / job owners).
- Notify affected users and operations staff.
- Use staged/reservations for rolling maintenance where possible.

Key cautions & behavior notes
- MAINT reservations will prevent starting jobs that cannot complete before the reservation start, but they do not automatically evict running jobs unless ignore_jobs or manual eviction/drain is used.
- Creating a reservation is a state change — plan and communicate before issuing it.
- If you want to avoid any immediate node state change, rely on MAINT reservations + user coordination rather than draining nodes.

References / commands you will normally use for the read-only parts
- squeue (jobs), sinfo (partitions/nodes), sacct (historical runtimes), scontrol show reservation (reservation details), squeue --reservation=<name> (jobs tied to reservation).

Slurm provides an integrated mechanism for nodes being suspended (powered
down, placed into power saving mode) and resumed (powered up, restored from
power saving mode) on demand or by request. Nodes that remain IDLE for
SuspendTime will be suspended by SuspendProgram and will be
unavailable for scheduling for SuspendTimeout . Nodes will
automatically be resumed by ResumeProgram to complete work allocated

manually requested by `scontrol update nodename= state=power_ `. The rate of nodes being resumed or

## Initial Testing [#initial_testing](https://slurm.schedmd.com/namespace.html)
An easy way to verify that the container is working is to run a job and
ensure that the /tmp directory is empty (since it normally has some other
files) and that "." is owned by the user that submitted the job.
```text
tim@slurm-ctld:~$ srun ls -al /tmp total 8 drwx------ 2 tim root 4096 Feb 10 17:14 . drwxr-xr-x 21 root root 4096 Nov 15 08:46 ..
```
While a job is running, root should be able to confirm that
`/$BasePath/$JobID/_tmp` exists and is empty. This directory is bind
mounted into the job. `/$BasePath/$JobID` should be owned by root,
and is not intended to be accessible to the user.
Additionally, when the Linux plugin is in use, you can confirm that a
PID namespace is in effect by running a job and running "ps". The only visible
PIDs should be related to the job and PID 1 will be named slurmstepd:
[${job_id}.namespace] .

The backfill scheduler has limitations in how it tracks usage of CPUs and
memory in the future.

The SelectType plugin will identify resources where a pending job can
begin execution. When PreemptMode is configured to CANCEL ,
SUSPEND or REQUEUE , the select plugin will also preempt running
jobs as needed to initiate the pending job. When
PreemptMode=SUSPEND,GANG the select plugin will initiate the pending
job and rely upon the gang scheduling logic to perform job suspend and resume,
as described below.
The select plugin is passed an ordered list of preemptable jobs to consider for

- QOS priority,
- Partition priority and job size (to favor preempting smaller jobs), or

How can I run multiple jobs from within a
single script?
A Slurm job is just a resource allocation. You can execute many
job steps within that allocation, either in parallel or sequentially.
Some jobs actually launch thousands of job steps this way. The job

## Preemption Design and Operation [#operation](https://slurm.schedmd.com/preempt.html)
The SelectType plugin will identify resources where a pending job can
begin execution. When PreemptMode is configured to CANCEL ,
SUSPEND or REQUEUE , the select plugin will also preempt running
jobs as needed to initiate the pending job. When
PreemptMode=SUSPEND,GANG the select plugin will initiate the pending
job and rely upon the gang scheduling logic to perform job suspend and resume,
as described below.
The select plugin is passed an ordered list of preemptable jobs to consider for
each pending job which is a candidate to start.
This list is sorted by either:
- QOS priority,
- Partition priority and job size (to favor preempting smaller jobs), or
- Job start time (with PreemptParameters=youngest_first ).

The job submit plugin is invoked independently for each component of a
heterogeneous job.
The spank_init_post_opt() function is invoked once for each component of a
heterogeneous job. This permits site defined options on a per job component

## Limitations [#limitations](https://slurm.schedmd.com/heterogeneous_jobs.html)
The backfill scheduler has limitations in how it tracks usage of CPUs and
memory in the future.
This typically requires the backfill scheduler be able to allocate each
component of a heterogeneous job on a different node in order to begin its
resource allocation, even if multiple components of the job do actually get
allocated resources on the same node.
In a federation of clusters, a heterogeneous job will execute entirely on
the cluster from which the job is submitted. The heterogeneous job will not
be eligible to migrate between clusters or to have different components of
the job execute on different clusters in the federation.

# Gang Scheduling
Slurm supports timesliced gang scheduling in which two or more jobs are
allocated to the same resources in the same partition and these jobs are
alternately suspended to let one job at a time have dedicated access to the
resources for a configured period of time.
Slurm also supports preemptive job scheduling that allows a job in a
higher PriorityTier partition, or in a preempting QOS, to preempt other
jobs. [Preemption](https://slurm.schedmd.com/preempt.html) is related to Gang scheduling
because SUSPEND is one of the PreemptionMode s, and it uses the Gang
scheduler to resume suspended jobs.
A workload manager that supports timeslicing can improve responsiveness
and utilization by allowing more jobs to begin running sooner.
Shorter-running jobs no longer have to wait in a queue behind longer-running
jobs.
Instead they can be run "in parallel" with the longer-running jobs, which will
allow them to start and finish quick...

### Designing Jobs
How can I run multiple jobs from within a
single script?
A Slurm job is just a resource allocation. You can execute many
job steps within that allocation, either in parallel or sequentially.
Some jobs actually launch thousands of job steps this way. The job
steps will be allocated nodes that are not already allocated to
other job steps. This essentially provides a second level of resource
management within the job for the job steps.
How can I run a job within an existing
job allocation?
There is an srun option --jobid that can be used to specify
a job's ID.
For a batch job or within an existing resource allocation, the
environment variable SLURM_JOB_ID has already been defined,
so all job steps will run within that job allocation unless
otherwise specified.

place a node in power saving mode. If a node is already in the process of

won't have any effect until the configured SuspendTimeout is

Information about cloud instances can be stored in the database. This can
be done by configuring instance id/type upon slurmd startup or with
scontrol update . The node's "extra" field will also be stored in the
database.
Configuring cloud information on slurmd startup:
```text
$ slurmd --instance-id=12345 --instance-type=m7g.medium --extra="arbitrary string" . . .

```text
$ scontrol update nodename=n1 instanceid=12345 instancetype=m7g.medium extra="arbitrary string"
```

node . Past and current data can be seen in the database with sacctmgr
show instance , as well as through slurmrestd with the /instance

Slurm provides an integrated mechanism for nodes being suspended (powered
down, placed into power saving mode) and resumed (powered up, restored from

Below is a concise summary of the node power states Slurm supports and the power‑save actions you can request (manual + automated), with the important semantics and administration notes.

1) How to request a manual power action
- Use scontrol to set a "power_" state on one or more nodes:
  scontrol update NodeName=<nodelist> state=POWER_<ACTION>
  (e.g. state=POWER_DOWN or state=POWER_UP)

2) Manual power actions (common POWER_ actions)
- POWER_DOWN
  - Request that the node enter power‑saving mode by running the configured SuspendProgram.
  - If the node is already in the process of powering down, the state change will be recorded but will not take further effect until SuspendTimeout or the current shutdown completes.
  - Intended for a graceful suspend via the suspend script.

- POWER_DOWN_ASAP
  - Drain the node and mark it for power down once current running jobs complete; no new jobs will be allocated to it.
  - Use when you want graceful completion of current work before suspending.

- POWER_DOWN_FORCE
  - Request an immediate power‑down transition. This is the “force” path — it marks the node for power down without waiting for normal idle/drain behavior.
  - Because this can interrupt normal node lifecycle, running jobs may be affected according to your Suspend/Resume configuration (they can end up requeued or fail if the node does not come back as expected). Use only for urgent cases.

- POWER_UP
  - Request the node be brought out of power saving (ResumeProgram will be executed when feasible).

(Implementations may expose additional site-specific variants; the above are the standard documented actions.)

3) Node lifecycle states you’ll see in sinfo / node listings
- POWER_DOWN — a power‑down request is recorded (symbolized in sinfo).
- POWERING_DOWN — the node is in the process of powering down and will be unavailable for scheduling for SuspendTimeout.
- POWERED_DOWN — node is powered down / in power‑saving mode.
- POWERING_UP — node is being resumed.
- POWER_UP — a power‑up request is recorded.

Symbols and exact text appear in sinfo output when PowerSave is enabled.

4) Automated power‑save components and important config knobs
- SuspendProgram: script/program slurmctld runs to suspend (power down) nodes.
- ResumeProgram: script/program slurmctld runs to boot / resume nodes.
  - These execute as SlurmUser on the controller host; sudo/root access may be required to actually power/boot nodes.
- SuspendTime: how long a node must be idle before Slurm automatically triggers SuspendProgram.
- SuspendTimeout: how long a node is considered unavailable while suspend/boot is happening (nodes are not schedulable for this time).
- ResumeTimeout: how long slurmctld waits for a node to re-register after a resume; if it fails to register the node may be set DOWN and jobs requeued.
- ResumeRate / SuspendRate: control how quickly nodes are resumed or suspended (throttling).
- PowerDownOnIdle (partition-level): when YES, nodes allocated from that partition may be requested to power down after they finish jobs (common for cloud/elastic partitions).
- SuspendExcNodes / SuspendExcParts / SuspendExcStates: configuration lists used to exclude specific nodes/partitions/states from automatic suspends.
- ResumeFailProgram / SuspendFailProgram: optional scripts to run on failure cases.

5) Scheduling & job effects
- POWER_DOWN_ASAP drains (no new allocations); running jobs finish normally.
- POWER_DOWN_FORCE / abrupt powering down can cause allocations to be interrupted; behavior for the affected jobs depends on your cluster configuration (jobs may be requeued, fail, or be treated per preemption/requeue policies). Nodes that fail to re-register within ResumeTimeout are set DOWN and allocations are requeued.
- Cloud / on‑demand nodes often use PowerSave automation to add/remove instances; features tied to nodes may be inactive while the node is powered down and re-activated on resume.

6) Operational recommendations
- Prefer POWER_DOWN_ASAP for graceful maintenance/suspend; use FORCE only for urgent/exception cases.
- Test SuspendProgram/ResumeProgram thoroughly (they run without Slurm job time limits and must be fault tolerant).
- Tune SuspendTime, SuspendTimeout, ResumeTimeout, and ResumeRate/SuspendRate to match your environment and boot/shutdown behaviour.
- Use DebugFlags=Power or logging to track power operations while testing.
- Use SuspendExc* to protect important nodes/partitions from automatic suspends.

Short answer
- ReqNodeNotAvail is a Slurm pending reason meaning "the scheduler could not find suitable/eligible nodes to satisfy the job's node/resource constraints at scheduling time." In other words, no nodes that match the job's requested partition, features, GRES/TRES, memory/CPU, exclusivity, or reservation constraints were idle/available when the scheduler tried to place the job.

Common node-availability causes (what they mean, how to check, and common fixes)
1) Nodes are DRAINED / DOWN / FAIL / FAILING
   - Meaning: nodes are administratively drained, marked down, or have failed health checks.
   - Check: sinfo -Nel (or sinfo to see partition/node states), sinfo -R (reasons), scontrol show node <nodename>.
   - Fix: operator must investigate hardware/OS and resume or clear drain (scontrol update/SD tools); contact admins.

2) Nodes are allocated / in use by other jobs
   - Meaning: all suitable nodes are currently running other jobs (allocated, MIXED).
   - Check: sinfo -Nel to see A/I counts; squeue to inspect running allocations.
   - Fix: wait, change job size/constraints, or ask for preemption/priority if available.

3) Reservation holds nodes
   - Meaning: a reservation reserves nodes for a user/group/time window.
   - Check: scontrol show reservation <name> or scontrol show reservation (list), squeue --reservation=<name> for queued entries.
   - Fix: schedule around the reservation or ask the reservation owner/admin to change it.

4) Resource mismatch (memory, CPUs, sockets, TRES limits)
   - Meaning: requested per-node memory, CPUs, or per-node TRES exceed what's free on any idle node.
   - Check: scontrol show node <node> (to inspect real node capacity), sinfo -Nel, and compare to job request (sbatch/srun args).
   - Fix: relax request (less memory/CPUs), request more nodes with smaller per-node counts, use a different partition.

5) GRES/GPU availability or GRES matching (GPU-specific)
   - Meaning: requested GPU type/feature/number not free (GPUs are allocated, or node labels/GRES mismatch).
   - Check: sinfo -Nel (shows GPUs per node), squeue to see GPU jobs, scontrol show node <node> to inspect GRES.
   - Fix: change GRES request, wait for GPUs, or target nodes that have the requested GRES. (If you intended a conditional GPU submit: check sinfo first and only submit if Idle GPU node counts > 0.)

6) Feature/constraint mismatch (node features, partitions, CPU architecture)
   - Meaning: job requested -C, --constraint, or --partition features that no idle node matches.
   - Check: sinfo -Nel (features column), scontrol show node <node>, squeue -j <jobid> (reason).
   - Fix: remove/change constraint, use a different partition, or ask admin to tag nodes appropriately.

7) Exclusive/SMT/NUMA/exact-socket placement constraints
   - Meaning: job requested exclusive node usage (--exclusive), specific sockets, or topology that reduces eligible nodes.
   - Check: job submission options and scontrol show node to see topology.
   - Fix: relax exclusivity/topology constraints or increase requested time/window.

8) Account/QOS/association limits or policy blocks
   - Meaning: account, QOS, or fairshare/accounting policy blocks scheduling on some nodes or partitions.
   - Check: squeue for the job reason, sacctmgr show associations, sacctmgr or sshare to inspect shares/limits.
   - Fix: adjust account/QOS, request admin changes, or use a different account/QOS.

9) Licenses or other external resources
   - Meaning: job requires a license or limited resource tracked by Slurm and none are free.
   - Check: scontrol license (scontrol license show / scontrol_license) or the cluster’s license tracking.
   - Fix: wait, free licenses, or use machines without that license.

10) Node reaches site-specific maintenance/evacuation (power, reboot, updates)
    - Meaning: nodes are in maintenance state (FUTURE, POWER, REBOOT).
    - Check: sinfo -Nel and sinfo -R for reasons; scontrol show node.
    - Fix: coordinate with admins; nodes will return when maintenance finishes.

Notes on interpreting the pending reason
- The scheduler only reports the first reason it encountered when attempting to schedule; there may be multiple contributing causes.
- For a specific pending job: start with squeue -j <jobid> (shows the pending reason). If you need more detail, use scontrol show job <jobid>. For node-level details, use sinfo -Nel and scontrol show node <nodename>.
- If you see ReqNodeNotAvail for a job that should be eligible, gather: the job's requested constraints (sbatch header or scontrol show job), sinfo -Nel output, and scontrol show node for candidate nodes, then contact your cluster admins with that collected info.

Quick troubleshooting checklist (for users)
1. squeue -j <jobid> (confirm reason is ReqNodeNotAvail).
2. Review job constraints: scontrol show job <jobid> or check your sbatch options.
3. sinfo -Nel (look for idle nodes matching partition/features/GRES).
4. scontrol show node <candidate_node> to compare capacities (mem, CPUs, GRES).
5. If nodes are DRAIN/DOWN/RESERVED — open a ticket with admins (include sinfo and scontrol outputs).

### User Mapping [#user_mapping](https://slurm.schedmd.com/jwt.html)
Depending on the service used to generate tokens, you may run into issues
mapping the token to a username. Slurm defaults to using the `sun`
(Slurm UserName) field. If the service uses a different field, you will need to
correct this for it to work with Slurm.
Option 1 : Change Slurm to use a different field. This can be
customized using [AuthAltParameters=userclaimfield](https://slurm.schedmd.com/slurm.conf.html). For example, using the default field
for [KeyCloak](https://www.keycloak.org/):
```text
AuthAltParameters=jwks=/local/path/to/jwks.json,userclaimfield=preferred_username
```
Option 2 : Change the identity service to use a different field. In
KeyCloak 25.0, for example, you should find this option under Clients ->
Client details -> Dedicated scopes -> Mapper details . Change the username
mapping to use the `sun` field.

## PERFORMANCE[#SECTION_PERFORMANCE](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sacct.html)
Executing sacct sends a remote procedure call to slurmdbd . If
enough calls from sacct or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmdbd daemon come in at once, it can result in a
degradation of performance of the slurmdbd daemon, possibly resulting in a
denial of service.
Do not run sacct or other Slurm client commands that send remote procedure
calls to slurmdbd from loops in shell scripts or other programs. Ensure
that programs limit calls to sacct to the minimum necessary for the
information you are trying to gather.

Two parameters are currently available to configure MCS: MCSPlugin
and MCSParameters .
- MCSPlugin Specifies which plugin should be used. Plugins are mutually exclusive, and the type of label to be associated depends on the loaded plugin.
- mcs/none is the default and disables MCS labels and functionality.
- mcs/account MCS labels can only take a value equal to the job's --account. NOTE : this option requires enabling of accounting.
- mcs/group MCS labels can only take a value equal to the job's user group.
- mcs/user MCS labels can only take a value equal to the username of the job's --uid.
- mcs/label MCS labels are arbitrary strings. Use of a job_submit plugin is recommended to manage job submissions to these labels, as no enforcement is provided otherwise.

## PERFORMANCE[#SECTION_PERFORMANCE](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sacct.html)
Executing sacct sends a remote procedure call to slurmdbd . If
enough calls from sacct or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmdbd daemon come in at once, it can result in a
degradation of performance of the slurmdbd daemon, possibly resulting in a
denial of service.
Do not run sacct or other Slurm client commands that send remote procedure
calls to slurmdbd from loops in shell scripts or other programs. Ensure
that programs limit calls to sacct to the minimum necessary for the
information you are trying to gather.

## SYNOPSIS[#SECTION_SYNOPSIS](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sacct.html)
sacct [ OPTIONS ...]

Good question — sacct's --format (alias -o) is how you build custom, column-oriented accounting output. Key points and examples:

Syntax
- Basic: --format=Field1,Field2,... (or -o Field1,Field2,...)
- Field modifiers: Field[:Width[:Label]]
  - Width sets a minimum column width.
  - Label replaces the printed column header.
  - Example: --format=JobID:12:ID,JobName:30:Name,User  
  (prints JobID in a 12‑char column with header "ID" and JobName in a 30‑char column with header "Name")

Common useful fields
- Job identifiers / status: JobID, JobName, State, ExitCode, Partition
- Times: Start, End, Elapsed
- Resources: NCPUS (or AllocCPUs), ReqMem, AllocNodes, NodeList, Tres (or ReqGRES)
- Accounting: User, Account, QOS
- Usage counters: MaxRSS, AveCPU, AveRSS, AvePages, DerivedExitCode
- Arrays/steps: JobArrayTaskID, Step, JobIDRaw
- Quick full: ALL prints every available field

Machine-friendly / parsing options
- --parsable (often -P) prints a delimiter (pipe) between fields for easier parsing.
- -n / --noheader omits the header row.
- Quick CSV: sacct -P -n -o JobID,User,Elapsed | tr '|' ',' > jobs.csv

Selection & behavior tips
- sacct queries the accounting DB (slurmdbd). Use -S/--starttime and -E/--endtime to control the time window; otherwise sacct uses a default recent range.
- Use --state= to limit by job state (COMPLETED, FAILED, CANCELLED, etc.).
- Job records include steps; if you want only the allocation (top-level job) use -X / --allocations.
- Use ALL or consult the manpage to discover field names: sacct --format=ALL or see the sacct manpage/Job Accounting Fields section.
- Avoid calling sacct in tight loops — it can overload slurmdbd.

Examples
- Human-readable summary:
  sacct --format=JobID,JobName,User,State,Elapsed -S 2026-04-01
- Fixed-width labeled columns:
  sacct -o JobID:10:JOB,User:12:USER,JobName:30:NAME,State:8:STATUS,Elapsed:10:TIME
- Parsable CSV-ish export:
  sacct -P -n -o JobID,User,Account,AllocCPUs,ReqMem,NodeList,ExitCode | tr '|' ',' > sacct_report.csv
- Only allocation rows, last 7 days, completed or failed:
  sacct -X -S now-7days -s COMPLETED,FAILED -o JobID,JobName,User,State,Elapsed,ExitCode

How to discover available field names
- sacct's manpage lists every accounting field (use lookup or man sacct). You can also run sacct --format=ALL to see names.

## Overview[#overview](https://slurm.schedmd.com/job_array.html)
Job arrays offer a mechanism for submitting and managing collections of
similar jobs quickly and easily, useful for repetitive workloads that follow a
common job pattern. This greatly improves overall performance, since job arrays
with millions of tasks can be submitted in milliseconds (subject to configured
size limits) and the scheduler can quickly identify cases when no more array

## EXAMPLES[#SECTION_EXAMPLES](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Specify a batch script by filename on the command line. The batch script specifies a 1 minute time limit for the job.
```text
$ cat myscript #!/bin/sh #SBATCH --time=1 srun hostname |sort $ sbatch -N4 myscript salloc: Granted job allocation 65537 $ cat slurm-65537.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
Pass a batch script to sbatch on standard input:
```text
$ sbatch -N4 #!/bin/sh > srun hostname |sort > EOF sbatch: Submitted batch job 65541 $ cat slurm-65541.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
To create a heterogeneous job with 3 components, each allocating a unique set of nodes:
```text
$ sbatch -w node[2-3] : -w node4 : -w node[5-7] work.bash Submitted batch job 34987
```

Summary (from the Slurm documentation)
- %A and %a are filename-replacement symbols you can use in sbatch --output/--error (and other filename pattern) strings.
  - %A — Job array's master job allocation number (the ArrayJobID). This is the job id assigned to the array as a whole (the "master" ArrayJobID).
  - %a — Job array index (the array task id / element index). This is the per-task index value from the --array specification (e.g. 0..N or 1..N).
- Environment variables set for array jobs:
  - SLURM_ARRAY_JOB_ID = first job ID of the array (ArrayJobID)
  - SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID = the array index for the running task (same as %a)
  - SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_COUNT, SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_MAX, SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_MIN are also provided.
- Other useful filename symbols:
  - %j — jobid of the running job (per-task JobID)
  - %J — jobid.stepid (e.g., "128.0")
  - %% — literal percent sign
  - %b — job array index modulo 10 (least significant digit)

Practical notes and examples
- If you submit:
  sbatch --array=1-10 --output=job-%A_%a.out myscript.sh
  and sbatch responds "Submitted batch job 12345", then task 3 will create:
  job-12345_3.out
  - %A is constant for the whole array (12345). %a varies per task (1..10).
- If you use %j instead of %A you get the task's unique job id (which can differ from the array master id). Example:
  --output=slurm-%j.out might produce slurm-12346.out for element 1, slurm-12347.out for element 2, etc.
- Use %A when you want a single identifier shared by all array elements (easy to group files). Use %a (or %j) when you need per-task unique filenames to avoid collisions.
- For dependencies and scontrol addressing, array tasks are referenced as <ArrayJobID>_<ArrayTaskID> (for example 12345_3).
- Be careful about filename collisions: don’t use a constant filename for an array without %a/%j/%A (or the job will overwrite output from concurrent tasks).
- Remember %% to place a literal % in the filename.

Behavioral caveat from the docs
- The ArrayJobID is the jobid of the first element of the array. Slurm’s internal ordering can make the first task a placeholder item; as a result the task with the lowest SLURM_JOB_ID may have the highest SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID. Use SLURM_ARRAY_JOB_ID and SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID (or %A/%a) when you need the array-specific identifiers rather than relying on ordering of SLURM_JOB_ID values.

# Job Exit Codes
A job's exit code (aka exit status, return code and completion
code) is captured by Slurm and saved as part of the job record. For
sbatch jobs, the exit code that is captured is the output of the batch
script. For salloc jobs, the exit code will be the return value of
the exit call that terminates the salloc session. For srun, the exit
code will be the return value of the command that srun executes.
Any non-zero exit code will be assumed to be a job failure and will
result in a Job State of FAILED with a Reason of
"NonZeroExitCode".
The exit code is an 8 bit unsigned number ranging between 0 and
255. While it is possible for a job to return a negative exit code,
Slurm will display it as an unsigned value in the 0 - 255 range.
