Short answer
- ReqNodeNotAvail is a Slurm pending reason that means: the scheduler could not find nodes that satisfy the job's node-related requirements (count, names, features/constraints, GRES, topology, exclusivity, etc.). In plain terms: the nodes you asked for (or nodes with the resources you requested) aren’t available right now.

What ReqNodeNotAvail commonly covers
- Nodes already allocated: the matching nodes are currently used by other jobs (allocated), so they’re not free.
- Nodes drained/maintenance: nodes are DRAINED for admin maintenance or set DRAIN with a reason.
- Nodes down / hardware failure: nodes are DOWN (failed boot, NIC, disk, health check).
- Reservations: nodes are reserved for a reservation, so they’re not available to normal jobs.
- GRES (GPU) exhaustion: requested GPUs (count, type) are already in use or not present on idle nodes.
- Feature/constraint mismatch: job constraints (e.g., --constraint=skylake, --nodelist, CPU model, node features) don’t match any idle node.
- Memory/CPU shortage: no node has the per-node memory/CPU available to satisfy the request.
- Exclusive / topology requirements: the job needs exclusive nodes, particular multi-node topology (interconnect), or colocated resources that aren’t simultaneously free.
- Licensing or managed resource limits: required software license or managed resource (BurstBuffer, special device) is exhausted.
- Power/boot state or provisioning delays: nodes are powering up, provisioning, or in a suspended/power-saving state and not yet usable.
- Admin set states or manual hold: nodes explicitly set to DRAIN/DOWN/MAINT by admins (often with a reason string).

How it differs from similar reasons
- ReqNodeNotAvail focuses on "requested nodes or node attributes cannot be satisfied." Other reasons like Priority, Dependency, or QOS/AccountNotAllowed are unrelated to node physical availability.

How to investigate (quick checklist)
- Check the job’s pending reason: squeue -j <jobid> (reason column) or scontrol show job <jobid> for more detail.
- Check partition/node summary: sinfo -Nel (shows per-node state and features) and sinfo (partition view).
- See why nodes are marked down/drain: sinfo -R (reasons) or scontrol show node <nodename>.
- Inspect GRES/licenses: scontrol show node <node> (shows Gres/AllocTRES), and scontrol_license (for license counts).
- Check reservations: scontrol show reservation (or scontrol_reservation_show).
- If multi-node topology matters, verify available nodes satisfy -N/--ntasks-per-node/affinity and interconnect requirements.
- Ask admin/logs: if nodes are down/drained for hardware/health reasons, admins will have the node reason string and logs.

Remediation ideas
- Loosen or remove strict constraints (drop --nodelist, relax --constraint or GRES requirements).
- Request fewer resources (smaller per-node memory/CPU/GPU).
- Use a different partition or node feature.
- Wait for nodes to become free, or ask the admin to clear a defective reservation or bring nodes back from DRAIN/DOWN.
- If you believe nodes should be available, provide job ID and the output of squeue -j <jobid> and sinfo -Nel to the admin so they can diagnose.

If you want, tell me a job ID and I can show the pending reason and recommended next checks.

Brief definitions (how they appear in sinfo and what they mean)

- IDLE
  - Meaning: the node is up and available for scheduling; no jobs are currently allocated.
  - Behavior: new jobs may be placed on the node according to scheduling rules.

- ALLOC (or ALLOCATED)
  - Meaning: the node has one or more running job allocations.
  - Behavior: the node’s resources are reserved for those jobs and are not available for new allocations (unless the node is shared/multi-job capable).

- DRAIN (or DRAINING / DRAINED)
  - Meaning: the node has been marked so that no new jobs will be started there. Existing running jobs are allowed to finish (unless a force option was used).
  - Why admins use it: for maintenance, software updates, graceful retire, or to remove the node from service without killing current jobs.
  - Behavior: sinfo shows the node as unavailable for new allocations; once running jobs complete the node usually becomes DRAINED (or remains in a non-allocable state) until an admin RESUMEs it.

- DOWN
  - Meaning: the node is considered unavailable because it failed (lost contact), powered off, or was administratively marked as down.
  - Behavior: the scheduler will not place jobs on it. Jobs already running may be terminated or requeued with NODE_FAIL depending on configuration. An admin must investigate/fix and then mark the node up/resume it.

Quick notes and tips
- DRAIN vs DOWN: DRAIN is for graceful removal (jobs finish); DOWN indicates a failure/unreachable state and is usually corrective-action driven.
- Mixed/partial states: a node can show as MIXED if some CPUs/GPUs are allocated while others are free. sinfo summarizations sometimes show per-node state flags.
- To see administrative reason text (why a node is DRAIN/DOWN) use sinfo -R or sinfo_reasons / scontrol show node <nodename>.

## DESCRIPTION[#SECTION_DESCRIPTION](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
sbatch submits a batch script to Slurm. The batch script may be given to
sbatch through a file name on the command line, or if no file name is specified,
sbatch will read in a script from standard input.

by any of the CLI options documented on this page. #SBATCH directives are read
directly by Slurm, so shell-specific syntax including variable names will be
read as literal text. Once the first non-comment, non-whitespace line has been
reached in the script, no more #SBATCH directives will be processed. See example
below.

## PERFORMANCE[#SECTION_PERFORMANCE](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Executing sbatch sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmctld daemon come in at once, it can result in
a degradation of performance of the slurmctld daemon, possibly resulting
in a denial of service.
Do not run sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other
programs. Ensure that programs limit calls to sbatch to the minimum
necessary for the information you are trying to gather.

## EXAMPLES[#SECTION_EXAMPLES](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Specify a batch script by filename on the command line. The batch script specifies a 1 minute time limit for the job.
```text
$ cat myscript #!/bin/sh #SBATCH --time=1 srun hostname |sort $ sbatch -N4 myscript salloc: Granted job allocation 65537 $ cat slurm-65537.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
Pass a batch script to sbatch on standard input:
```text
$ sbatch -N4 #!/bin/sh > srun hostname |sort > EOF sbatch: Submitted batch job 65541 $ cat slurm-65541.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
To create a heterogeneous job with 3 components, each allocating a unique set of nodes:
```text
$ sbatch -w node[2-3] : -w node4 : -w node[5-7] work.bash Submitted batch job 34987
```

## PERFORMANCE[#SECTION_PERFORMANCE](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Executing sbatch sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmctld daemon come in at once, it can result in
a degradation of performance of the slurmctld daemon, possibly resulting
in a denial of service.
Do not run sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other
programs. Ensure that programs limit calls to sbatch to the minimum
necessary for the information you are trying to gather.

## EXAMPLES[#SECTION_EXAMPLES](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Specify a batch script by filename on the command line. The batch script specifies a 1 minute time limit for the job.
```text
$ cat myscript #!/bin/sh #SBATCH --time=1 srun hostname |sort $ sbatch -N4 myscript salloc: Granted job allocation 65537 $ cat slurm-65537.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
Pass a batch script to sbatch on standard input:
```text
$ sbatch -N4 #!/bin/sh > srun hostname |sort > EOF sbatch: Submitted batch job 65541 $ cat slurm-65541.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
To create a heterogeneous job with 3 components, each allocating a unique set of nodes:
```text
$ sbatch -w node[2-3] : -w node4 : -w node[5-7] work.bash Submitted batch job 34987
```

Summary — what controls job email
- Two sbatch options: --mail-user=<addr> (who gets the mail) and --mail-type=<types> (which events trigger mail).
- You can set them on the sbatch command line or inside a batch script with #SBATCH lines. Command-line options override environment variables, which override #SBATCH lines in a script.
- Mail delivery uses the Slurm MailProg / configuration on the cluster; if no MailProg is configured mail may not be sent.

Flags and usage
- --mail-user=address
  - Example: --mail-user=alice@example.edu
  - Sets the email recipient. If not given, mail normally goes to the submitting user’s account (unless the site admin has changed defaults).
- --mail-type=type[,type...]
  - Provide one or more comma-separated event types. Example: --mail-type=END,FAIL

Common mail-type values and what they mean
- BEGIN — send mail when the job allocation begins (job starts running).
- END — send mail when the job terminates normally (job finished).
- FAIL — send mail when the job fails (non-zero exit, killed, etc.).
- REQUEUE — send mail when the job is requeued.
- ALL — shorthand to request mail for all supported events.
- ARRAY_TASKS — for job arrays: send mail for each individual task (rather than only the array master).
- STAGE_OUT — send mail when staged output is completed (used with burst buffers/stage-out features).
- TIME_LIMIT — notifications related to job time limits (warnings/notifications).
- TIME_LIMIT_90 (and other TIME_LIMIT_<N>) — a warning when the job reaches a percentage of its time limit (90% is common).
- STOP — send mail when the job is stopped (scontrol stop or similar).

Notes and tips
- Pick only the events you need to avoid email spam (e.g., --mail-type=END,FAIL is common).
- For job arrays, ARRAY_TASKS is useful to get per-task notifications. Without it, you may only get mail for the array master.
- Use full email addresses with --mail-user to ensure external delivery.
- If you see no mail even though options are set, check with your admin whether MailProg and MailType are configured in slurm.conf and whether outbound mail from compute nodes is allowed.

Examples
- In a script:
  #SBATCH --mail-user=alice@example.edu
  #SBATCH --mail-type=END,FAIL
- On the command line:
  sbatch --mail-user=alice@example.edu --mail-type=BEGIN,END myscript.sh

If you want, I can paste the exact manpage text or show full example scripts.

- Observer (default): Read-only monitoring, analysis, diagnosis using Slurm tools.
- Operator (via transfer_to_operator): State-changing actions requiring approval.

## Job Priority Factors In General [#general](https://slurm.schedmd.com/priority_multifactor.html)
The job's priority at any given time will be a weighted sum of all the
factors that have been enabled in the slurm.conf file. Job priority can be
expressed as:
```text
Job_priority = site_factor + (PriorityWeightAge) * (age_factor) + (PriorityWeightAssoc) * (assoc_factor) + (PriorityWeightFairshare) * (fair-share_factor) + (PriorityWeightJobSize) * (job_size_factor) + (PriorityWeightPartition) * (priority_job_factor) + (PriorityWeightQOS) * (QOS_factor) + SUM(TRES_weight_cpu * TRES_factor_cpu, TRES_weight_ * TRES_factor_ , ...) - nice_factor
```
All of the factors in this formula are floating point numbers that
range from 0.0 to 1.0. The weights are unsigned, 32 bit integers.

## Introduction[#intro](https://slurm.schedmd.com/fair_tree.html)
Starting with Slurm 19.05, the Fair-share factor in the
[priority/multifactor plugin](https://slurm.schedmd.com/priority_multifactor.html) will
default to the Fair Tree algorithm described on this page. The previously
used [Classic algorithm](https://slurm.schedmd.com/classic_fair_share.html) can be manually
configured.
Fair Tree prioritizes users such that if accounts A and B are siblings and A
has a higher fairshare factor than B, all children of A will have higher
fairshare factors than all children of B.
Some of the benefits include:
- All users from a higher priority account receive a higher fair share factor than all users from a lower priority account.
- Users are sorted and ranked to prevent errors due to precision loss. Ties are allowed.
- Account coordinators cannot accidentally harm the priority of their users relative to users in other accounts.

- sshare for alice (account "research"):
  - RawShares = 0.600
  - NormShares = 0.420
  - EffectiveUsage = 1.800

What this means
- RawShares is the configured share weight for the account/user; NormShares is that value normalized relative to other accounts/users and is what the fairshare algorithm uses to compute entitlement.
- EffectiveUsage = 1.800 means Alice has used about 1.8× her entitlement over the fairshare accounting window. Because effective usage is >1, the fairshare factor will lower Alice’s job priority (the fairshare factor is reduced for users who have used more than their share).
- Since sprio returned no pending jobs, there are currently no queued jobs for Alice whose priority could be shown; if you have a specific job ID later I can show its priority factors.

How to improve Alice’s queue position (practical options)
1) Lower EffectiveUsage (best long‑term fix)
   - Reduce recent heavy submissions or pause new large jobs so the accounting window can “decay” her usage back toward 1.0. The decay period is cluster-config dependent (see admin-controlled fairshare decay settings).
   - Ask your account coordinator/admin to increase Alice’s RawShares/NormShares if the allocation is too small for needed throughput (admin action: sacctmgr).

2) Use higher-priority QOS / reservation (admin-dependent)
   - If a higher-priority QOS or a reservation is available, use it (or ask admins to grant it) to bypass fairshare penalties. This requires admin or account-manager changes.

3) Make jobs easier to backfill
   - Request fewer CPUs/GPUs, less memory, and a shorter walltime where feasible. Smaller/shorter jobs are easier to backfill and often start sooner despite fairshare penalties.
   - Break large jobs into smaller tasks or use job arrays so portions can run earlier.

4) Exploit other priority factors
   - Age factor: a job’s priority increases while it waits. If a job is pending long enough its age will help offset fairshare penalty.
   - Job-size factor: many clusters bias toward smaller jobs. Adjusting resource requests may increase the job_size factor.
   - Avoid submitting many concurrent large jobs that push EffectiveUsage higher.

5) If you need immediate help
   - Request an admin to review shares or grant a temporary reservation / QOS bump.

## PERFORMANCE[#SECTION_PERFORMANCE](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Executing sbatch sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmctld daemon come in at once, it can result in
a degradation of performance of the slurmctld daemon, possibly resulting
in a denial of service.
Do not run sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other
programs. Ensure that programs limit calls to sbatch to the minimum
necessary for the information you are trying to gather.

sbatch provides two options to control e‑mail notifications for a job:

- --mail-user=ADDRESS
  - Set the destination e‑mail address for notifications (example: --mail-user=you@example.com).
  - Can be given on the sbatch command line or as a #SBATCH directive in the job script.

- --mail-type=TYPE[,TYPE...]
  - Select which job events trigger an e‑mail. Multiple events are provided as a comma‑separated list.
  - Common event types you will see documented and can use include: BEGIN, END, FAIL, REQUEUE, ALL, NONE, ARRAY_TASKS, TIME_LIMIT, STAGE_OUT, NODE_FAIL.
    - BEGIN: send when the job allocation starts.
    - END: send when the job finishes normally.
    - FAIL: send when the job fails (non‑zero exit or other failure conditions).
    - REQUEUE: send when the job is requeued.
    - TIME_LIMIT: send when the job reaches (or is about to reach, depending on configuration) its time limit.
    - ARRAY_TASKS: send notifications for individual array tasks rather than only the master array job.
    - ALL: shorthand for getting notifications for all (or most) events.
    - NONE: disable notifications (or omit --mail-type to get no mail).
    - STAGE_OUT / NODE_FAIL: other system/cluster-specific events may be available on some installs.
  - Use e.g. --mail-type=BEGIN,END,FAIL to get mail at start, successful end, and failure.

Examples:
- sbatch --mail-user=you@example.com --mail-type=END myscript.sh
- In a script:
  #SBATCH --mail-user=you@example.com
  #SBATCH --mail-type=BEGIN,END,FAIL

Notes and caveats:
- The cluster’s mail/send subsystem (sendmail/postfix or similar) must be configured; if the admin has disabled mail or the MTA is misconfigured you may not receive mail.
- Exact mail‑type token availability and any additional types (or short‑hands) are determined by your Slurm version/configuration; check your system’s sbatch manpage or the sbatch documentation for the full, authoritative list for your cluster.

Summary — what Fair Tree does
- Fair Tree is Slurm’s default fair-share algorithm (PriorityFlags=FAIR_TREE). It ranks all user/account associations in a hierarchical (tree) order so that under-served associations get higher fair-share factors and over-served associations get lower ones.
- The core per-level metric is Level Fairshare (LF) = S / U. Associations with LF > 1 are under-served (should get more priority); LF < 1 are over-served.

Key terms and formulas
- Raw Shares (Sraw): the shares assigned to an association (account or user).
- Norm Shares (S): Sraw normalized among siblings
  - S = Sraw_self / (sum of Sraw for self + siblings)
  - 0.0 .. 1.0
- Raw Usage (Uraw): the usage charged to that association (measured in TRES-seconds according to AccountingStorageTRES and TRESBillingWeights). This is the usage value that decays over time (see below).
- Effective Usage (U) used in LF is Uraw normalized among siblings:
  - U = Uraw_self / (sum of Uraw for self + siblings)
  - 0.0 .. 1.0
- Level Fairshare (LF):
  - LF = S / U
  - LF > 1 means under-served, LF < 1 means over-served, LF = 1 means usage matches shares at that level.
- Final FairShare factor for a user:
  - Slurm builds a rooted ordered tree of associations, computes Level FS for children at each node, sorts children by Level FS (descending), then does a depth‑first, pre‑order traversal to rank users. The user's FairShare value = rank / total_number_of_user_associations (highest rank → 1.0).

How “Raw Usage” / Effective Usage is computed and decayed
- Usage is tracked in TRES-seconds (CPU-seconds, or weighted TRES using TRESBillingWeights).
- Historical usage decays with an exponential half-life controlled by PriorityDecayHalfLife (default 7 days). Conceptually recent usage counts more; older usage decays toward zero.
- PriorityCalcPeriod controls how often the decay/recalculation runs (default every few minutes).
- If PriorityDecayHalfLife = 0, no decay is applied (usage is not aged); then PriorityUsageResetPeriod must be used to reset usage periodically.
- Because Uraw is decayed and then normalized with siblings, effective usage reflects recent resource consumption relative to siblings at the same tree level.

Practical interpretation and examples
- If two sibling accounts A and B both have S = 0.25 and S = 0.75 respectively, and their decayed usage U matches those ratios, their Level FS will be ~1.0 and neither is favored.
- Simple numeric example:
  - Shares: A=1, B=3 → S_A=0.25, S_B=0.75
  - Usage: A used 100, B used 300 (after decay) → U_A=100/400=0.25, U_B=0.75
  - LF_A = 0.25/0.25 = 1.0, LF_B = 0.75/0.75 = 1.0 → equal
  - If A had used only 50 (U_A=50/350≈0.143), LF_A≈0.25/0.143≈1.75 → A is under-served and gets higher fair-share rank.
- If an association has zero usage, tools often show Level FS as “infinity” (meaning under-served relative to siblings that have usage).

How to view these values
- Use the sshare tool (sshare -l) to view:
  - Raw Shares, Norm Shares, Raw Usage, Norm (normalized) Usage, Effective Usage (Effectv Usage), Level FS and FairShare factor.
- Note: Fair Tree calculations require Slurm accounting (slurmdbd) to have the usage data.

Admin/user implications and tuning
- PriorityWeightFairshare controls how much the fairshare factor affects overall job priority; with Fair Tree you may want to reduce this weight compared to classic setups.
- PriorityDecayHalfLife controls how quickly past usage “forgives” users. Shorter half-life returns priority faster to under‑served users; longer half-life gives long-term fairness.
- TRESBillingWeights controls which resources (GPUs, CPUs, memory) count how much in the usage metric — affects Raw Usage and therefore effective usage.
- scontrol reconfigure does not force an immediate recompute of fairshare; waits until the next PriorityCalcPeriod iteration.

Practical tips
- Check sshare -l to see which accounts/users are under- or over-served before changing shares.
- When adjusting shares, remember they are compared only among siblings at each level. Increasing a parent’s shares affects all its children relative to sibling branches.
- If you want hard enforcement of quotas rather than decayed fairness, set PriorityDecayHalfLife=0 and use usage-resetting or resource limits.

References and commands
- Read details: Slurm docs “Fair Tree” and “sshare” pages (priority_multifactor / fair_tree).
- Commands: sshare -l, review slurm.conf settings PriorityDecayHalfLife, PriorityCalcPeriod, PriorityWeightFairshare, TRESBillingWeights.

## EXAMPLES[#SECTION_EXAMPLES](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Specify a batch script by filename on the command line. The batch script specifies a 1 minute time limit for the job.
```text
$ cat myscript #!/bin/sh #SBATCH --time=1 srun hostname |sort $ sbatch -N4 myscript salloc: Granted job allocation 65537 $ cat slurm-65537.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
Pass a batch script to sbatch on standard input:
```text
$ sbatch -N4 #!/bin/sh > srun hostname |sort > EOF sbatch: Submitted batch job 65541 $ cat slurm-65541.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
To create a heterogeneous job with 3 components, each allocating a unique set of nodes:
```text
$ sbatch -w node[2-3] : -w node4 : -w node[5-7] work.bash Submitted batch job 34987
```

## Overview[#overview](https://slurm.schedmd.com/job_array.html)
Job arrays offer a mechanism for submitting and managing collections of
similar jobs quickly and easily, useful for repetitive workloads that follow a
common job pattern. This greatly improves overall performance, since job arrays
with millions of tasks can be submitted in milliseconds (subject to configured
size limits) and the scheduler can quickly identify cases when no more array
tasks are eligible to start.
All jobs must have the same initial options (e.g., size, time limit), however,
it is possible to change some of these options after the job has begun
execution using the scontrol command specifying the JobID of the array or
individual ArrayJobID .

single number of an expression identifying the entries represented by this
job record (e.g. "5-1024").
Neither field is displayed if the job is not part of a job array.
The optional job ID specified with the scontrol show job or
scontrol show step commands can identify job array elements by
specifying ArrayJobId and ArrayTaskId with an underscore between
them (e.g. <ArrayJobID>_<ArrayTaskId>).
The scontrol command will operate on all elements of a job array if the
job ID specified is ArrayJobID .
Individual job array tasks can be modified using the
ArrayJobID _ ArrayTaskID as shown below.
```tex...

Short answer (from the Slurm docs):

- Job array vs. array task
  - ArrayJobID (the job-array “master” ID): the JobID printed by sbatch when you submit an array. It identifies the whole array as a group. Slurm exposes this as SLURM_ARRAY_JOB_ID in the batch-script environment and as the ArrayJobID field in scontrol/squeue output.
  - ArrayTaskID (the array index / task ID): the index value from your --array specification (for example 1,2,3 or 0..N). Slurm exposes this as SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID in the batch-script environment and as the ArrayTaskId field in scontrol/squeue output.
  - SLURM_JOB_ID (JobID): each running array element behaves like a normal job and has a job record / JobID when it starts. The ArrayJobID is the “master” group id; individual elements may have distinct JobIDs when they get created.

- %A and %a (sbatch filename-pattern replacements)
  - %A expands to the job array’s master job allocation number (ArrayJobID).
  - %a expands to the job array index (ArrayTaskID).
  - These percent-replacements are supported in sbatch filename patterns (e.g., -o/-e and other filename places). Example:
      #SBATCH -o slurm-%A_%a.out
    If sbatch printed “Submitted batch job 36” for an array and you have array element 1, the output file becomes slurm-36_1.out.
  - Related replacements: %j is the jobid of the running job, %J is jobid.stepid, %b is the array index modulo 10, etc. (See sbatch filename-pattern docs for the full list.)

- Useful practical notes from the docs
  - Environment variables available inside array tasks: SLURM_ARRAY_JOB_ID, SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID, SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_COUNT, SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_MAX, SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_MIN (plus the normal SLURM_JOB_ID, etc.).
  - squeue displays arrays compactly (e.g. 1080_[5-1024]) by default; use squeue --array (or -r) to show one element per line.
  - Some commands accept the ArrayJobID_ArrayTaskID notation to refer to an element (for example scancel 20_4 cancels array job 20 element 4; scontrol show job 101_1 shows element 1).
  - Under normal scheduling behavior the first task submitted may be a placeholder; this can make the ordering of SLURM_JOB_ID vs. SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID non-intuitive (see job_array docs).

References: Slurm “Job Array Support” (job_array) and the sbatch man page (filename-pattern / output-environment variables).

Good question — the % in an sbatch --array specification is the job-array “throttle” (max simultaneously running tasks). Key points and examples:

- Basic index ranges and lists
  - --array=0-99 creates tasks with indices 0..99 (100 tasks).
  - You can also use comma lists and steps: --array=1,3,5,7 or --array=1-7:2 (1,3,5,7).

- Throttle syntax
  - Append %N to the array spec to limit concurrency: --array=0-99%10
    - That submits 100 tasks (indices 0..99) but only allows up to 10 tasks from that array to run at the same time. The remaining tasks stay PENDING and the scheduler starts new ones as running tasks finish.
  - The throttle applies per job-array (not globally across all arrays), and it is enforced in addition to normal cluster/user/account limits.

- What you get inside the job
  - SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID — the array index for this task (e.g., 0..99).
  - SLURM_ARRAY_JOB_ID and other array-related env vars (SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_COUNT, _TASK_MIN/_TASK_MAX).

- Useful filename substitution in scripts
  - Use %a (or %A, %j, etc.) in --output/--error patterns to include the array index or job id:
    - sbatch --array=0-9 --output=out_%a.txt myscript.sh

- Examples
  - --array=0-99%10  -> 100 tasks, max 10 running at once.
  - --array=1-20:2%4 -> tasks 1,3,5,...,19 (10 tasks total), max 4 concurrently.
  - --array=0,5,10%2 -> 3 specific tasks, at most 2 running simultaneously.

- Behavior/limits to be aware of
  - If you omit %N, the scheduler may start as many array tasks as resources/limits allow.
  - Array tasks still count toward any per-user/account/job limits (e.g., MaxJobs).
  - You can address/cancel individual array elements with jobid_index (e.g., scancel 12345_7).

Reference: Slurm job-array docs (sbatch/job_array) — the %N form is described as “limit the number of simultaneously running tasks from the job array to N.”

procedure calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other

sattach is a Slurm client that connects to an already-running job (or job step) and attaches your terminal to that job’s stdio streams so you can view and/or send standard input and see standard output and error from the job’s tasks.

Key points
- Purpose: attach to the std(in/out/err) of a running job step so you can monitor live output or interact with a running task without restarting/submitting the job.
- Scope: attaches to an existing job or job.step (you supply the jobid and optional step/task selectors).
- Not for starting jobs: sattach does not allocate resources or create a new job; it only connects to an active allocation.
- Typical uses: debug long-running jobs, inspect live logs, send input to an interactive task, or aggregate output from multiple tasks in a job step.

Basic behavior and useful options
- You can target a specific task(s) within the job step and filter streams:
  - --input-filter / --error-filter to direct stdin or show only one task’s stdout/stderr.
  - -l / --label to prefix lines with the originating task number when attaching to multiple tasks.
  - --layout to request task-to-node layout information from slurmctld.
- It contacts slurmctld (RPC). Running many sattach calls (e.g., in tight loops) can overload slurmctld — avoid automated high-frequency calls.
- Permissions: normal users can typically sattach to their own jobs; attaching to other users’ jobs usually requires admin privileges.

Examples
- Attach to job 12345’s main step:
  sattach 12345
- Attach and label output from multiple tasks:
  sattach -l 12345

When to use vs alternatives
- Use sattach when the job is already running and you want live interaction or to watch its stdout/stderr.
- Use srun --pty / salloc when you want to start an interactive allocation from scratch.
- Use sacct/scontrol/squeue/sstat for job metadata, accounting, and non-interactive diagnostics.

Caveats
- Some applications or job configurations may not expose interactive stdin/stdout in a way sattach can use.
- Because sattach sends RPCs to slurmctld, heavy/automated use can degrade scheduler performance.

Slurm generally classifies users into three authorization levels:
- Administrators include root, SlurmUser, and any users with
"AdminLevel=Administrator"
- Privileged Users include all Administrators and any users with
"AdminLevel=Operator"

## NOTES[#SECTION_NOTES](https://slurm.schedmd.com/scrontab.html)
scrontab is only available if the ScronParameters=enable option has
been enabled in the slurm.conf .
scrontab will create a temporary file in the directory set by TMPDIR
environment variable. If the variable is not set /tmp is used.
Jobs created with scrontab are assigned a single job id. When cancelled
all future runs of the job will also be cancelled. The job definition will be
commented out in the users scrontab file.
Using " scontrol requeue < job_id >" will skip the next run of the
cron job and reschedule it for the next available time based on the cron
expression.

# Job Exit Codes
A job's exit code (aka exit status, return code and completion
code) is captured by Slurm and saved as part of the job record. For
sbatch jobs, the exit code that is captured is the output of the batch
script. For salloc jobs, the exit code will be the return value of
the exit call that terminates the salloc session. For srun, the exit
code will be the return value of the command that srun executes.
Any non-zero exit code will be assumed to be a job failure and will
result in a Job State of FAILED with a Reason of
"NonZeroExitCode".
The exit code is an 8 bit unsigned number ranging between 0 and
255. While it is possible for a job to return a negative exit code,
Slurm will display it as an unsigned value in the 0 - 255 range.

Short answer
- scontrol requeue <jobid> tells Slurm to stop the job's current attempt and put the job back into the pending queue so it can be scheduled and run again.

What happens when you run it
- If the job is RUNNING: Slurm terminates the current allocation/steps for that job attempt, releases the resources, and marks the job with the REQUEUED flag. The job is then returned to the scheduler as a PENDING job to be reallocated later.
- If the job is PENDING: the command forces the job to be requeued (it becomes eligible for scheduling again). For job arrays, using the array JobID will act on all elements unless you specify a single task (e.g., 12345_7).
- The job keeps its original submission parameters (time limit, resource requests, QOS, etc.), so the requeued run will use the same request set unless you change them.
- For sbatch (batch) jobs, Slurm increments the BatchFlag when a job is requeued; this can be used to track requeue attempts.
- Authorization: you must be the job owner (or have the appropriate privileged/admin level) to run scontrol requeue.

When to use it
- Manually reschedule a job after a transient failure, preemption, or node maintenance.
- Retry a job without creating a new submission (keeps the same JobID or array structure).

Notes and cautions
- scontrol requeue is not the same as scancel. scancel permanently cancels a job; requeue requests another attempt.
- Some site-specific prolog/epilog or accounting behavior may run again on the requeued attempt (depends on local configuration).
- Preemption policies (e.g., PreemptMode=REQUEUE) can also cause automatic requeues without manual scontrol intervention.

Example
- scontrol requeue 12345
- scontrol requeue 12345_7  (single element of an array)

If you want, I can show the scontrol documentation snippet that describes authorization and BatchFlag behavior.

### Resource Limits[#limits](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
Each QOS is assigned a set of limits which will be applied to the
job. The limits mirror the limits imposed by the
user/account/cluster/partition association defined in the Slurm
database and described in the [Resource Limits page](https://slurm.schedmd.com/resource_limits.html). When limits for a QOS have been defined, they
will take precedence over the association's limits.

Short answer
- If Alice needs a temporary change (higher priority, temporary ability to burst above account limits for a few jobs, different preemption/grace settings), ask for a QOS change or assignment to a different QOS.
- If Alice needs a persistent, project-wide increase in resource allotment (higher long‑term CPU/GPU hours, higher group TRES or MaxJobs for everyone on that account), ask for an account (association) limit change.

Why (concise)
- Slurm applies limits in a hierarchy. Limits set on a QOS are applied before association/account limits, and a QOS can explicitly override partition/account limits. QOS is therefore an easy place to put job-level or short-term policy (also priority, preemption, DenyOnLimit, UsageThreshold). Account/association limits are for longer-term, per-project resource governance and apply to everyone using that account.

How to decide in practice
1. Determine exactly what is blocking Alice now:
   - Is the job being denied at submission, or is it pending? (If pending, look at squeue reason.)
   - Does any error message mention a specific limit name (MaxJobs, MaxTRESPERJOB, MaxTRESPerUser, UsageThreshold, etc.)?
2. Map the needed change:
   - Submission denied because job exceeds a QOS MaxTRESPerJob or DenyOnLimit → request QOS limit change or different QOS.
   - Jobs pending because account usage is at a UsageThreshold or group limit → request account/association increase.
   - Need higher priority or different preemption behavior for a few urgent jobs → request a temporary/higher-priority QOS.
   - Need more sustained resource share for the whole project (GPU-hours, CPU-hours) → request account/association change.
3. Consider scope & impact:
   - QOS change can be narrow (per-job or per-user via assignment) and temporary.
   - Account change affects all users of that account and should be justified with longer-term needs.

Diagnostics / commands you (or I) can run to prove which limit is active
- squeue -j <jobid> or squeue -u alice (show pending reason)
- scontrol show job <jobid> (detailed job rejection/pending info)
- scontrol show qos or sacctmgr list qos (current QOS limits)
- sacctmgr list associations user=alice account=... cluster=... (account association limits)
- sshare -l (fairshare / effective shares)

Suggested request text Alice can send to admins
- For a QOS change (temporary / per-job): “My job(s) <jobid(s)> were denied/pending with reason mentioning <limit name>. Please grant me temporary QOS <qos-name> or increase MaxTRESPerJob/MaxJobs for QOS <qos-name> from <current> to <requested> until <date>, so I can run these experiments. Job details: nodes/GPUs/CPUs/walltime.”
- For an account/association change (long term): “Our project/account <account-name> is hitting the account limit <limit name> (current=<value>). Please increase the account’s <GrpTRES/MaxJobs/UsageThreshold/etc.> to <requested value>. Justification: sustained need for X GPU-hours per week for ongoing research.”

If you want, I can:
- Check the active reason and which specific limit is being hit for Alice’s failing/pending job(s) (I’ll need the job ID(s) or permission to look up user=alice). That will show whether the QOS or the account association is enforcing the block and which field to request changed.

A QOS can be attached to a partition. This means the partition will have all
the same limits as the QOS. This does not associate jobs with the QOS, nor does
it give the job any priority or preemption characteristics of the assigned QOS.

characteristics. However, the Partition QOS limits will override the job's QOS.
If the opposite is desired you may configure the job's QOS with
`Flags=OverPartQOS` which will reverse the order of precedence.

restrictions on which nodes it uses to get the resources. This is accomplished
by assigning all nodes to the partition, then configuring a Partition QOS with

Starting in Slurm 23.11, a QOS may be configured to contain relative resource
limits instead of absolute limits by setting `Flags=Relative`.

### Job Scheduling Priority [#priority](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
Job scheduling priority is made up of a number of factors as
described in the [priority/multifactor](https://slurm.schedmd.com/priority_multifactor.html) plugin. One
of the factors is the QOS priority. Each QOS is defined in the Slurm
database and includes an associated priority. Jobs that request and
are permitted a QOS will incorporate the priority associated with that
QOS in the job's [multi-factor priority calculation.](https://slurm.schedmd.com/priority_multifactor.html)
To enable the QOS priority component of the multi-factor priority
calculation, the "PriorityWeightQOS" configuration parameter must be
defined in the slurm.conf file and assigned an integer value greater
than zero.
A job's QOS only affects is scheduling priority when the
multi-factor plugin is loaded.

### Job Preemption [#preemption](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
Slurm offers two ways for a queued job to preempt a running job,
free-up the running job's resources and allocate them to the queued
job. See the [Preemption description](https://slurm.schedmd.com/preempt.html) for
details.
The preemption method is determined by the "PreemptType"
configuration parameter defined in slurm.conf. When the "PreemptType"
is set to "preempt/qos", a queued job's QOS will be used to determine
whether it can preempt a running job. It is important to note that the QOS
used to determine if a job is eligible for preemption is the QOS associated
with the job and not a [Partition QOS](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html).

### Job Scheduling Priority [#priority](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
Job scheduling priority is made up of a number of factors as
described in the [priority/multifactor](https://slurm.schedmd.com/priority_multifactor.html) plugin. One
of the factors is the QOS priority. Each QOS is defined in the Slurm
database and includes an associated priority. Jobs that request and
are permitted a QOS will incorporate the priority associated with that
QOS in the job's [multi-factor priority calculation.](https://slurm.schedmd.com/priority_multifactor.html)
To enable the QOS priority component of the multi-factor priority
calculation, the "PriorityWeightQOS" configuration parameter must be
defined in the slurm.conf file and assigned an integer value greater
than zero.
A job's QOS only affects is scheduling priority when the
multi-factor plugin is loaded.

Starting in Slurm 23.11, a QOS may be configured to contain relative resource
limits instead of absolute limits by setting `Flags=Relative`.

## Partition QOS [#partition](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
A QOS can be attached to a partition. This means the partition will have all
the same limits as the QOS. This does not associate jobs with the QOS, nor does
it give the job any priority or preemption characteristics of the assigned QOS.
Jobs may separately request the same QOS or a different QOS to gain those
characteristics. However, the Partition QOS limits will override the job's QOS.
If the opposite is desired you may configure the job's QOS with
`Flags=OverPartQOS` which will reverse the order of precedence.
This functionality may be used to implement a true "floating"
partition, in which a partition may access a limited amount of resources with no
restrictions on which nodes it uses to get the resources. This is accomplished
by assigning all nodes to the partition, then configuring a Partition QOS with
`GrpTRES` set to the desired resource limits.

## Hierarchy[#hierarchy](https://slurm.schedmd.com/resource_limits.html)
Slurm's hierarchical limits are enforced in the following order
with Job QOS and Partition QOS order being reversible by using the QOS
flag 'OverPartQOS':
- Partition QOS limit
- Job QOS limit
- User association
- Account association(s), ascending the hierarchy
- Root/Cluster association
- Partition limit
- None
Note: If limits are defined at multiple points in this hierarchy,
the point in this list where the limit is first defined will be used.
Consider the following example:
- MaxJobs=20 and MaxSubmitJobs is undefined in the partition QOS
- No limits are set in the job QOS and
- MaxJobs=4 and MaxSubmitJobs=50 in the user association
The limits in effect will be MaxJobs=20 and MaxSubmitJobs=50.

## Configuration[#config](https://slurm.schedmd.com/resource_limits.html)
Scheduling policy information must be stored in a database
as specified by the AccountingStorageType configuration parameter
in the slurm.conf configuration file.
Information can be recorded in a [MySQL](http://www.mysql.com/) or
[MariaDB](https://mariadb.org/) database.
For security and performance reasons, the use of
SlurmDBD (Slurm Database Daemon) as a front-end to the
database is strongly recommended.
SlurmDBD uses a Slurm authentication plugin (e.g. MUNGE).
SlurmDBD also uses an existing Slurm accounting storage plugin
to maximize code reuse.
SlurmDBD uses data caching and prioritization of pending requests
in order to optimize performance.
While SlurmDBD relies upon existing Slurm plugins for authentication
and database use, the other Slurm commands and daemons are not required
on the host where SlurmDBD is installed.

The tool used to manage accounting policy is sacctmgr .
It can be used to create and delete cluster, user, account,
and partition records plus their combined association record.
See man sacctmgr for details on this tools and examples of
its use.
Changes made to the scheduling policy are uploaded to
the Slurm control daemons on the various clusters and take effect
immediately. When an association is deleted, all running or pending
jobs which belong to that association are immediately canceled.
When limits are lowered, running jobs will not be canceled to
satisfy the new limits, but the new lower limits will be enforced.

## Relative QOS [#relative](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
Starting in Slurm 23.11, a QOS may be configured to contain relative resource
limits instead of absolute limits by setting `Flags=Relative`.
When this flag is set, all resource limits are treated as percentages of the
total resources available. Values higher than 100 are interpreted as 100%.
Memory limits should be set with no units. Although the default units (MB) will
be displayed, the limits will be enforced as a percentage (1MB = 1%).
NOTE : When Flags=Relative is added to a QOS, slurmctld
must be restarted or reconfigured for the flag to take effect.
Generally, the limits on a relative QOS will be calculated relative to the
resources in the whole cluster. For example, `cpu=50` would be
interpreted as 50% of all CPUs in the cluster.

## Partition QOS [#partition](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
A QOS can be attached to a partition. This means the partition will have all
the same limits as the QOS. This does not associate jobs with the QOS, nor does
it give the job any priority or preemption characteristics of the assigned QOS.
Jobs may separately request the same QOS or a different QOS to gain those
characteristics. However, the Partition QOS limits will override the job's QOS.
If the opposite is desired you may configure the job's QOS with
`Flags=OverPartQOS` which will reverse the order of precedence.
This functionality may be used to implement a true "floating"
partition, in which a partition may access a limited amount of resources with no
restrictions on which nodes it uses to get the resources. This is accomplished
by assigning all nodes to the partition, then configuring a Partition QOS with
`GrpTRES` set to the desired resource limits.

### Job Preemption [#preemption](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
Slurm offers two ways for a queued job to preempt a running job,
free-up the running job's resources and allocate them to the queued
job. See the [Preemption description](https://slurm.schedmd.com/preempt.html) for
details.
The preemption method is determined by the "PreemptType"
configuration parameter defined in slurm.conf. When the "PreemptType"
is set to "preempt/qos", a queued job's QOS will be used to determine
whether it can preempt a running job. It is important to note that the QOS
used to determine if a job is eligible for preemption is the QOS associated
with the job and not a [Partition QOS](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html).
The QOS can be assigned (using sacctmgr ) a list of other
QOSs that it can preempt. When there is a queued job with a QOS that
is allowed to preempt a running job of another QOS, the Slurm
scheduler will preempt the running job.

Summary — how Slurm represents job arrays and the per-task identifiers

- Array vs element
  - A job array is a single submission that creates many jobs (elements). Example: sbatch --array=1-4 job.sh creates four elements.
  - The array as a whole is identified by the ArrayJobID (the JobID of the first element). Individual elements are addressed as ArrayJobID_ArrayTaskID (for example 12345_2).

- Key environment variables (set inside each array task)
  - SLURM_ARRAY_JOB_ID — the JobID of the first element (the array identifier).
  - SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID — the array index for this task (the value from --array, e.g. 2).
  - SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_COUNT / _MAX / _MIN — count and bounds of the array indices.
  - SLURM_JOB_ID — the unique Slurm job id for this particular element (you can also see the combined form 12345_2 externally).
  - SLURM_PROCID — NOT the array index; this is the MPI/parallel rank (process index) within a job step.

- How Slurm displays and references elements
  - squeue/sacct/scontrol can show array elements; they appear as ArrayJobID_ArrayTaskID (or with separate ArrayJobID/ArrayTaskID fields in scontrol show).
  - To operate on a whole array or a range:
    - scancel 12345 cancels the entire array.
    - scancel 12345_1-3 cancels tasks 1..3.
    - scontrol show job 12345_2 shows the specific element.

- sbatch substitutions and filenames
  - In sbatch scripts you can use %A -> array job id, %a -> array task id (e.g., --output=out_%A_%a.txt).

- Ordering / placeholder behavior (important caveat)
  - By default Slurm may create a “placeholder” element; the first task submitted is often a placeholder and can be scheduled last. Because of that, the numeric relationship between SLURM_JOB_ID and SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID can be non-intuitive: the element with the lowest SLURM_JOB_ID may have the highest SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID. Don’t rely on SLURM_JOB_ID ordering to infer SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID order.

- Practical tips
  - Inside a task use SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID to index per-task input files or parameters.
  - If you need to target or report on one element from outside Slurm, use the ArrayJobID_ArrayTaskID syntax (12345_7).
  - Use scontrol show job <array>_<task> for element-level details (resources, reason, exit codes).

### Job Scheduling Priority [#priority](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
Job scheduling priority is made up of a number of factors as
described in the [priority/multifactor](https://slurm.schedmd.com/priority_multifactor.html) plugin. One
of the factors is the QOS priority. Each QOS is defined in the Slurm
database and includes an associated priority. Jobs that request and
are permitted a QOS will incorporate the priority associated with that
QOS in the job's [multi-factor priority calculation.](https://slurm.schedmd.com/priority_multifactor.html)
To enable the QOS priority component of the multi-factor priority
calculation, the "PriorityWeightQOS" configuration parameter must be
defined in the slurm.conf file and assigned an integer value greater
than zero.
A job's QOS only affects is scheduling priority when the
multi-factor plugin is loaded.

# Job Exit Codes
A job's exit code (aka exit status, return code and completion
code) is captured by Slurm and saved as part of the job record. For
sbatch jobs, the exit code that is captured is the output of the batch
script. For salloc jobs, the exit code will be the return value of
the exit call that terminates the salloc session. For srun, the exit
code will be the return value of the command that srun executes.
Any non-zero exit code will be assumed to be a job failure and will
result in a Job State of FAILED with a Reason of
"NonZeroExitCode".
The exit code is an 8 bit unsigned number ranging between 0 and
255. While it is possible for a job to return a negative exit code,
Slurm will display it as an unsigned value in the 0 - 255 range.

Below are concise, doc‑based explanations of the four common pending reasons you asked about, what they mean, how to diagnose them, and common ways to resolve them.

1) Resources
- What it means
  - Slurm could not find sufficient free resources that match the job request (CPUs, memory, GPUs, TRES, nodes, or node features/constraints). This includes cases where no single node satisfies a per‑node request (e.g., --mem-per-cpu, --ntasks-per-node) or where the requested combination of resources is not available.
- How to diagnose
  - Inspect the job: scontrol show job <jobid> (look at ReqTRES, NumNodes, MinNodes, NodeList/Constraints).
  - See cluster/node availability: sinfo -Nel (per-node free/alloc counts), sinfo (partition summary).
  - Check queue rows: squeue -j <jobid> -o "%i %t %R %C %m" (reason column, requested resources).
- Typical fixes
  - Reduce resources requested (fewer CPUs, less memory, fewer GPUs, smaller node count).
  - Remove or relax constraints/--constraint/--nodelist/--exclude that force specific nodes.
  - Use a different partition with suitable nodes.
  - Wait for currently running jobs to finish or ask users/admins to free nodes.
  - For per‑node packing problems, change job layout (--ntasks-per-node, --nodes).

2) Priority
- What it means
  - The scheduler found one or more higher‑priority jobs which must run before this job. Slurm reports the first encountered blocking reason as "Priority".
- How to diagnose
  - Show job priority values: scontrol show job <jobid> (Priority field).
  - Inspect priority factors and queue ordering: sprio (or sprio -l / sprio -u <user>), sshare (fairshare usage).
  - Look for many older/higher‑QOS jobs in the same partition: squeue -p <partition> --sort=-p (or sort by priority/age).
- Typical fixes
  - Submit with a higher QOS (if permitted) or ask admin to adjust QOS/priority.
  - Reduce job size/time so it is scheduled sooner by the policy.
  - Wait—priority often resolves as higher priority jobs finish or as the job ages/fairshare changes.
  - Admin actions: change priority weights, adjust fairshare or QOS priorities.

3) ReqNodeNotAvail
- What it means
  - The specific nodes requested by the job (via --nodelist, --exclude, or a constraint that pins nodes) are not available for allocation (they may be DOWN, DRAINED, allocated to other jobs, in a reservation, or otherwise unavailable).
- How to diagnose
  - Inspect the job: scontrol show job <jobid> (NodeList, Exclude, Constraint).
  - Check node states: sinfo -Nel or sinfo --Node (or sinfo_reasons to list down/drain nodes and reasons).
  - For a named node: scontrol show node <nodename> to see state/reason.
- Typical fixes
  - Remove explicit node requests or exclusions so the scheduler can choose available nodes.
  - Choose a different partition without the unavailable nodes.
  - Wait for the named nodes to come back online or be released from other jobs.
  - If nodes are down/drained, contact the cluster admin to repair/bring them back.

4) QOS limits (jobs blocked by QOS/account limits)
- What it means
  - The job is blocked because it would violate a QOS or association/account limit. Slurm reason codes related to QOS/limits include Max*PerAccount, AssocGrp, AssocMax and similar. Limits can be per‑QOS, per‑user, per‑account, or TRES (CPU/GPU/time) caps.
- How to diagnose
  - Inspect the job fields: scontrol show job <jobid> (QOS, Account, ReqTRES).
  - Check accounting/association limits: sacctmgr show assoc / sacctmgr list associations (or ask admin to run those).
  - See fairshare/usage: sshare and sprio may help show why QOS choice affects priority.
  - The squeue reason text will often indicate the specific limit name (e.g., MaxJobsPerUser).
- Typical fixes
  - Submit under a different QOS or account with higher limits (if you have access).
  - Reduce requested resources/time to stay within the QOS limits.
  - Wait until other jobs reduce your account's current usage (free up slots).
  - Request admin changes to the QOS/account limits (this is an administrative change).

Notes and troubleshooting tips
- Only one pending reason is shown (the reason encountered during scheduling); there can be multiple underlying causes. If you need the exact, low‑level scheduler decision you can combine scontrol show job <id>, sprio, sshare, and sinfo.
- Useful quick commands: squeue -j <id> -o "%i %P %u %t %R %l %M" ; scontrol show job <id> ; sinfo -Nel ; sprio ; sshare ; sacctmgr show assoc.
- If you want, tell me a job ID and I can walk through the exact squeue/scontrol outputs you should check and what they likely mean.

Starting in Slurm 23.11, a QOS may be configured to contain relative resource
limits instead of absolute limits by setting `Flags=Relative`.
When this flag is set, all resource limits are treated as percentages of the
total resources available. Values higher than 100 are interpreted as 100%.
Memory limits should be set with no units. Although the default units (MB) will
be displayed, the limits will be enforced as a percentage (1MB = 1%).

resources in the whole cluster. For example, `cpu=50` would be

Scheduling policy information must be stored in a database
as specified by the AccountingStorageType configuration parameter
in the slurm.conf configuration file.
Information can be recorded in a [MySQL](http://www.mysql.com/) or
[MariaDB](https://mariadb.org/) database.
For security and performance reasons, the use of
SlurmDBD (Slurm Database Daemon) as a front-end to the
database is strongly recommended.
SlurmDBD uses a Slurm authentication plugin (e.g. MUNGE).
SlurmDBD also uses an existing Slurm accounting storage plugin
to maximize code reuse.
SlurmDBD uses data caching and prioritization of pending requests
in order to optimize performance.
While SlurmDBD relies upon existing Slurm plugins for authentication
and database use, the other Slurm commands and daemons are not required

### Job Scheduling Priority [#priority](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
Job scheduling priority is made up of a number of factors as
described in the [priority/multifactor](https://slurm.schedmd.com/priority_multifactor.html) plugin. One
of the factors is the QOS priority. Each QOS is defined in the Slurm
database and includes an associated priority. Jobs that request and
are permitted a QOS will incorporate the priority associated with that
QOS in the job's [multi-factor priority calculation.](https://slurm.schedmd.com/priority_multifactor.html)
To enable the QOS priority component of the multi-factor priority
calculation, the "PriorityWeightQOS" configuration parameter must be
defined in the slurm.conf file and assigned an integer value greater
than zero.
A job's QOS only affects is scheduling priority when the
multi-factor plugin is loaded.

## Partition QOS [#partition](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
A QOS can be attached to a partition. This means the partition will have all
the same limits as the QOS. This does not associate jobs with the QOS, nor does
it give the job any priority or preemption characteristics of the assigned QOS.
Jobs may separately request the same QOS or a different QOS to gain those
characteristics. However, the Partition QOS limits will override the job's QOS.
If the opposite is desired you may configure the job's QOS with
`Flags=OverPartQOS` which will reverse the order of precedence.
This functionality may be used to implement a true "floating"
partition, in which a partition may access a limited amount of resources with no
restrictions on which nodes it uses to get the resources. This is accomplished
by assigning all nodes to the partition, then configuring a Partition QOS with
`GrpTRES` set to the desired resource limits.

Before enabling NSS Slurm directly on the node, you should use the
-s slurm option to getent within a newly launched job step
to verify that the rest of the setup has been completed successfully. The
-s option to getent allows it to query a specific database —
even if it has not been enabled by default through the system's
nsswitch.conf . Note that nss_slurm only responds to requests from
processes within the job step itself — you must launch the getent
command within a job step to see any data returned.

```text
tim@blackhole:~$ srun getent -s slurm passwd tim:x:1000:1000:Tim Wickberg:/home/tim:/bin/bash tim@blackhole:~$ srun getent -s slurm group tim:x:1000:tim projecta:x:1001:tim
```

Slurm offers two ways for a queued job to preempt a running job,
free-up the running job's resources and allocate them to the queued
job. See the [Preemption description](https://slurm.schedmd.com/preempt.html) for
details.
The preemption method is determined by the "PreemptType"
configuration parameter defined in slurm.conf. When the "PreemptType"
is set to "preempt/qos", a queued job's QOS will be used to determine
whether it can preempt a running job. It is important to note that the QOS
used to determine if a job is eligible for preemption is the QOS associated
with the job and not a [Partition QOS](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html).
The QOS can be assigned (using sacctmgr ) a list of other
QOSs that it can preempt. When there is a queued job with a QOS that
is allowed to preempt a running job of another QOS, the Slurm
scheduler will preempt the running job.

## Partition QOS [#partition](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
A QOS can be attached to a partition. This means the partition will have all
the same limits as the QOS. This does not associate jobs with the QOS, nor does
it give the job any priority or preemption characteristics of the assigned QOS.
Jobs may separately request the same QOS or a different QOS to gain those
characteristics. However, the Partition QOS limits will override the job's QOS.
If the opposite is desired you may configure the job's QOS with
`Flags=OverPartQOS` which will reverse the order of precedence.
This functionality may be used to implement a true "floating"
partition, in which a partition may access a limited amount of resources with no
restrictions on which nodes it uses to get the resources. This is accomplished
by assigning all nodes to the partition, then configuring a Partition QOS with
`GrpTRES` set to the desired resource limits.

## Configuration[#config](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
To summarize the above, the QOSs and their associated limits are
defined in the Slurm database using the sacctmgr utility. The
QOS will only influence job scheduling priority when the multi-factor
priority plugin is loaded and a non-zero "PriorityWeightQOS" has been
defined in the slurm.conf file. The QOS will only determine job
preemption when the "PreemptType" is defined as "preempt/qos" in the
slurm.conf file. Limits defined for a QOS (and described above) will
override the limits of the user/account/cluster/partition
association.

## Contents[#contents](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)

Here’s a concise, doc‑based explanation of common QOS limits (with behavior notes and examples). Sources: Slurm QOS and Resource Limits pages (https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html, https://slurm.schedmd.com/resource_limits.html).

What a QOS limit is
- A QOS limit caps a resource or submission metric for jobs that request that QOS. QOS limits mirror limits that can also be set on user/account/partition/cluster associations; when a QOS defines a limit it overrides association limits (see precedence below).

Key limits (definitions)
- MaxJobs
  - Maximum number of jobs that may be concurrently active (RUNNING or PENDING as enforced) that are associated with that QOS (or that count point in the hierarchy).
  - If a submission would cause the limit to be exceeded the job will pend unless the QOS has Flags=DenyOnLimit (see DenyOnLimit).
- MaxCPUs
  - Maximum number of CPUs (cores) that may be concurrently allocated to jobs using that QOS. This is enforced against the sum of CPU allocations for matching jobs.
  - CPUs are counted as integer core units (not time-weighted).
- MaxNodes / MinNodes / Max[Time|Wall]
  - Limits on node counts or job wall time. (Note: some of these limits have special precedence rules; see hierarchy note.)
- MaxSubmitJobs, MaxSubmitJobsPerUser
  - Limits on the number of jobs that may be submitted within some context (global, per-user, etc.). These control submission rate/quantity rather than resource allocation.
- MaxTRES / GrpTRES / MaxTRESPerNode
  - TRES = Trackable RESources (e.g., cpu, mem, gres/gpu). MaxTRES can set absolute limits on TRES usage (for example cpu=2000,gpu=10,mem=100000).
  - GrpTRES limits group (aggregate) usage across the QOS.
  - MaxTRESPerNode or Max[Something]PerNode is applied per node.
- MaxGRES / GRES-related limits
  - Limits specifically for GRES (Generic RESources) such as GPUs; used when you want to constrain GPU counts.
- Flags=Relative
  - When set, numeric limits are treated as percentages of total cluster resources (e.g., cpu=50 means 50% of all CPUs). Memory limits should be set without units when using Relative (1MB = 1%).

Behavioral rules and enforcement
- Hierarchy / precedence
  - Limits are enforced according to a fixed hierarchy (partition QOS, job QOS, user association, account association(s) ascending, root/cluster association, partition limit, none). The first place a limit is defined in this list is used. You can change partition-vs-job QOS precedence with Flags=OverPartQOS.
- What happens when a limit would be exceeded
  - Default: a job that would violate a Max* limit will pend until resources are available.
  - If Flags=DenyOnLimit is set on the QOS, jobs that would violate the QOS “Max” limits will be denied at submission time (rejected), rather than pended.
  - Group (Grp) limits are treated as Max limits when DenyOnLimit is applied.
- Interaction with partitions and associations
  - A Partition QOS (a QOS attached to a partition) carries the QOS limits into the partition view and (by default) is applied before a job’s requested QOS. OverPartQOS reverses that order.
- Relative QOS nuance
  - With Flags=Relative, limits are percentages and may be computed either cluster-wide or relative to a partition when used as a partition QOS; slurmctld must be reconfigured/restarted to pick up some flag changes.
- Units and types
  - CPU limits are counts. Memory limits are normally specified with units (MB/GB) but when using Relative you should set memory with no units so it’s treated as a percentage.

Examples (from docs)
- If a partition QOS sets MaxJobs=20 and a user-association sets MaxJobs=4, the partition QOS value (20) takes effect because of the hierarchy—unless OverPartQOS is used to reverse precedence.
- If a QOS has cpu=50 and Flags=Relative, that means jobs using the QOS can consume up to 50% of total cluster CPUs (values above 100 are treated as 100).

Practical notes for admins and users
- Use MaxTRES (or specific MaxCPUs/MaxGRES) when you need precise control over specific resource types (CPUs vs GPUs vs memory).
- Use DenyOnLimit when you prefer immediate rejection at submission instead of a job silently queueing/pend-ing.
- Remember the hierarchy: setting limits at the right level (partition vs QOS vs association) matters.
- When changing QOS flags or limits, reconfiguration may be required for some flags (e.g., Relative) to take effect.

Where to read more
- QOS reference and options: https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html
- Resource limits and hierarchy: https://slurm.schedmd.com/resource_limits.html

- extract the exact sacctmgr commands to set common limits (e.g., set MaxCPUs for QOS foo) and give examples, or

As time goes on, the slurm database can grow large enough that it is hard to
manage. To maintain the database at a reasonable size, slurmdbd supports
archiving and purging data based on its age. Purged data will be deleted from
the database, but you can choose to archive the data as it is being purged.
Archived data will be placed in flat files that can later be loaded into a
slurmdbd by sacctmgr.

after setting up accounting. If purging is added after the database has already
grown to an unwieldy size, it may difficult to catch up to the desired purge
interval. Monitor table sizes and system utilization to decide how long you want
to retain data, and try to set the relevant configuration options before you

A QOS can be created, modified, and deleted with sacctmgr. These
options allow you to set the corresponding attributes or filter on them
when querying for a QOS.
NOTE : The group limits (GrpJobs, GrpTRES, etc.) are tested when a job is
being considered for being allocated resources.
If starting a job would cause any of its group limit to be exceeded,
that job will not be considered for scheduling even if that job might preempt
other jobs which would release sufficient group resources for the pending
job to be initiated.
NOTE : All TRES options (GrpTRES, MaxTRES, etc.) can also use the same

## Partition QOS [#partition](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
A QOS can be attached to a partition. This means the partition will have all
the same limits as the QOS. This does not associate jobs with the QOS, nor does
it give the job any priority or preemption characteristics of the assigned QOS.
Jobs may separately request the same QOS or a different QOS to gain those
characteristics. However, the Partition QOS limits will override the job's QOS.
If the opposite is desired you may configure the job's QOS with
`Flags=OverPartQOS` which will reverse the order of precedence.
This functionality may be used to implement a true "floating"
partition, in which a partition may access a limited amount of resources with no
restrictions on which nodes it uses to get the resources. This is accomplished
by assigning all nodes to the partition, then configuring a Partition QOS with
`GrpTRES` set to the desired resource limits.

### Job Preemption [#preemption](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
Slurm offers two ways for a queued job to preempt a running job,
free-up the running job's resources and allocate them to the queued
job. See the [Preemption description](https://slurm.schedmd.com/preempt.html) for
details.
The preemption method is determined by the "PreemptType"
configuration parameter defined in slurm.conf. When the "PreemptType"
is set to "preempt/qos", a queued job's QOS will be used to determine
whether it can preempt a running job. It is important to note that the QOS
used to determine if a job is eligible for preemption is the QOS associated
with the job and not a [Partition QOS](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html).
The QOS can be assigned (using sacctmgr ) a list of other
QOSs that it can preempt. When there is a queued job with a QOS that
is allowed to preempt a running job of another QOS, the Slurm
scheduler will preempt the running job.

Below is a focused, practical summary of the Slurm configuration knobs you should know when designing scheduling and accounting behavior. I organize it by purpose (scheduler, resource selection, enforcement & limits, accounting) and call out the related config names and where they live (slurm.conf vs slurmdbd.conf vs sacctmgr).

1) Where settings live
- slurm.conf — primary cluster config (scheduler type/parameters, partitions, select/plugin options, priority weights, AccountingStorage* entries that point at the accounting backend).
- slurmdbd.conf — Slurm Database Daemon configuration (only used if AccountingStorageType=accounting_storage/slurmdbd).
- sacctmgr — CLI for creating accounts, users, QOS, associations and limits stored in the DB (used when slurmdbd is active).
- Job completion/gather plugins — configured in slurm.conf (JobAcctGatherType, JobCompType) and may also involve files/DB.

2) Scheduling: core slurm.conf options
- SchedulerType
  - e.g., SchedulerType=sched/backfill or sched/builtin. Controls which scheduling algorithm/backfill engine is used.
- SchedulerParameters
  - Plugin-specific flags that tune backfill, job sorting, or other scheduler internals (depends on SchedulerType).
- PreemptType and PreemptMode
  - Controls whether and how queued jobs may preempt running jobs (e.g., preempt/qos).
- FastSchedule
  - FastSchedule=1 reduces evaluation overhead for large clusters (tradeoff: slightly different scheduling semantics).
- DefMemPerCPU / DefMemPerNode
  - Defaults used by scheduler for memory accounting & resource fit decisions when jobs don’t specify memory.
- Partition-specific settings
  - Partition definitions in slurm.conf can include priority, max time, nodes, and attached Partition QOS. Partition-level limits can override association/QOS limits.

3) Priority (multifactor) and job ordering
- PriorityWeight* parameters (set in slurm.conf) when using priority/multifactor:
  - PriorityWeightAge — weight for job age
  - PriorityWeightFairshare — weight for historical fairshare
  - PriorityWeightJobSize — larger jobs can be favored or penalized
  - PriorityWeightQOS, PriorityWeightPartition, PriorityWeightTRES, etc.
  - These numeric weights are combined by the multifactor priority plugin to compute job priority.
- Fairshare
  - Fairshare data is maintained (via the DB) and influences scheduling when PriorityWeightFairshare > 0.
- QOS interaction
  - QOS attributes (priority, preemptible targets, limits) are defined with sacctmgr and are only applied for scheduling when multifactor priority and the relevant weights are enabled.

4) Resource selection and accounting granularity
- SelectType and SelectTypeParameters
  - e.g., SelectType=select/cons_res and SelectTypeParameters=CR_CPU_Memory (or CR_Core_Memory). Controls resource model (TRES-based vs older core-based).
- TRES (Trackable RESources)
  - TRES are used for CPU, GPU, memory, licenses, etc. Many QOS/accounting limits are expressed as TRES.
- Enforceable defaults
  - Accurate TRES and DefMemPerCPU help ensure the scheduler fits jobs correctly and accounting records useful data.

5) Backfill and scheduling policies
- Backfill is typically enabled with sched/backfill; SchedulerParameters tune backfill window and behavior.
- Backfill policy interacts with preemption and reservations. Use PreemptType and QOS to control preemption when needed.

6) Job completion / accounting gathering (plugins in slurm.conf)
- JobAcctGatherType
  - Commonly set to jobacct_gather/linux (gathers task-level memory/CPU info) or jobacct_gather/cgroup on systems using cgroups. This plugin produces per-job resource-usage info.
- JobAcctGatherFrequency
  - How often resource usage is polled by the gatherer (controls precision vs overhead).
- JobCompType
  - Controls where Job Completion records go: jobcomp/none, jobcomp/filetxt, jobcomp/slurmdbd, etc. If using slurmdbd, use jobcomp/slurmdbd or let the slurmdbd collect records.
- JobCompLoc / JobAcctGather parameters
  - File locations for jobcomp filetxt, or plugin-specific parameters.

7) Accounting backend and enforcement (AccountingStorage* in slurm.conf and slurmdbd.conf)
- AccountingStorageType
  - e.g., accounting_storage/slurmdbd (recommended for robust DB-backed accounting). Alternatives: accounting_storage/none, accounting_storage/filetxt, etc.
- AccountingStorageHost / AccountingStorageUser / AccountingStoragePort / AccountingStorageLoc / AccountingStoragePass
  - slurm.conf entries that point the controller to the database/slurmdbd.
- AccountingStorageEnforce
  - Controls enforcement at submission/allocation time. Options include associations, limits, qos, all, etc. If you need to block a job at submit-time for exceeding limits, enable the appropriate enforcement options.
- slurmdbd.conf
  - configures DB connection parameters (MySQL/MariaDB), archive/purge and credentials. SlurmDBD must be running on the host where slurmdbd.conf is present.

8) Associations, QOS and limits (sacctmgr-managed)
- sacctmgr entities: Account, User, QOS, Association
  - Use sacctmgr to create accounts and set association limits (MaxJobs, MaxSubmitJobs, GrpTRES, MaxTRESPerUser, MaxTRESPERUSER, etc.).
- QOS
  - Define per-QOS limits and priorities; QOS can also be attached to partitions (Partition QOS). QOS controls preemption sets when PreemptType=preempt/qos.
- Common limit fields
  - GrpTRES — group TRES limits (tested at allocation time),
  - MaxTRESPerUser / MaxTRESPERUSER — caps per-user TRES consumption,
  - MaxJobs / MaxSubmitJobs — limit concurrent or queued jobs.
- Enforcement semantics
  - Many limits are checked during job start; AccountingStorageEnforce can move some checks to submission time. Group/association limits are enforced at scheduling/allocation time so they can block job start when limits are reached.

9) Reporting and tools
- sacct — historical accounting (requires job completion info in DB or filetxt)
- sreport — usage reports (CPU/GPU hours by user/account/partition)
- sstat — live resource usage for running jobs
- sacctmgr — manage accounts, QOS, associations and view limits
- scontrol show config / scontrol ping — controller diagnostics

10) Operational notes & best practices
- Consistent user names/UIDs across clusters if sharing a SlurmDBD.
- Decide retention: configure slurmdbd archive/purge before DB grows too large.
- Tune JobAcctGatherFrequency and the gather plugin to balance overhead vs accuracy.
- Use AccountingStorageEnforce to decide whether limits should block submission or only allocation.
- Restart/HUP: many slurm.conf changes take effect only after restart or SIGHUP of slurmctld (slurmdbd likewise needs restart for slurmdbd.conf changes).
- Test QOS/association limits in a staging setup — enforcement behavior (submit-time vs start-time) can be subtle.
- Use select/cons_res + TRES for modern heterogeneous clusters (GPUs, licenses, burst buffers).

11) Example (representative slurm.conf lines)
- Scheduler setup
  - SchedulerType=sched/backfill
  - SchedulerParameters=bf_continue,interactivity
- Priority weights
  - PriorityType=priority/multifactor
  - PriorityWeightAge=1000
  - PriorityWeightFairshare=10000
  - PriorityWeightJobSize=100
- Accounting backend
  - AccountingStorageType=accounting_storage/slurmdbd
  - AccountingStorageHost=slurmdbd.example.org
  - AccountingStorageUser=slurm
  - AccountingStorageEnforce=associations,limits,qos
- Job accounting plugins
  - JobAcctGatherType=jobacct_gather/linux
  - JobAcctGatherFrequency=30
  - JobCompType=jobcomp/slurmdbd

- Slurm forms a single priority score by combining factor values (fairshare, age, qos, partition, job size, etc.) multiplied by their configured weights.

# Wait for specific job array elements sbatch --depend=after:123_4 my.job sbatch --depend=afterok:123_4:123_8 my.job2 # Wait for entire job array to complete sbatch --depend=afterany:123 my.job # Wait for corresponding job array elements sbatch --depend=aftercorr:123 my.job # Wait for entire job array to complete successfully sbatch --depend=afterok:123 my.job # Wait for entire job array to complete and at least one task fails sbatch --depend=afternotok:123 my.job
```

Brief summary — syntax components
- Range/list/step: --array=0-99,5,200 or --array=1-7:2
  - 0-99 → indices 0,1,2,...,99
  - 1-7:2 → indices 1,3,5,7 (the :2 is the step)
  - Commas combine ranges and single indices
- Throttle (concurrency limit): the %N suffix
  - --array=0-99%10 limits the number of simultaneously running tasks from that array to 10.
  - The percent value is an absolute count (maximum concurrent tasks), not a percent fraction.
- Combined example: --array=1-20:2%4 → tasks 1,3,5,...,19 but only up to 4 of those run at the same time.

What this means in practice
- sbatch --array=0-99%10 submits 100 array tasks (indices 0..99) but the scheduler will only start at most 10 array tasks from that job at once. As one finishes, another pending array task will start, maintaining up to 10 running until all complete.
- Array tasks are still ordinary jobs for accounting and limits: they obey user/partition/job QOS limits, MaxJobs/MaxSubmitJobs, MaxArraySize, priorities, dependencies, etc.

How to access the index inside your script
- SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID contains the index for the running task.
- SLURM_ARRAY_JOB_ID (or %A in filename patterns) is the array master job id; %a expands to the task index in filename templates.

Examples
- sbatch --array=0-99%10 myjob.sh
  - 100 tasks (0..99), 10 concurrently running.
- #SBATCH --array=1-8:2%3
  - indices 1,3,5,7 with at most 3 running simultaneously.
- sbatch --array=0-9,20,30-39%5 myjob.sh
  - indices 0–9,20,30–39; up to 5 concurrent.

Reference
- See the Slurm "Job Array Support" and sbatch docs for full details on index syntax, % throttling, and environment variables.

create the appropriate job-specifc namespace(s).

private (or optionally shared) filesystem namespace and mount a list of
directories (defaults to /tmp and /dev/shm) inside it, giving the job a private

by 'BasePath' in the job_container.conf file.
