## Job Dependencies [#dependencies](https://slurm.schedmd.com/burst_buffer.html)
If two jobs use burst buffers and one is dependent on the other (e.g.
`sbatch --dependency=afterok:123 ...`) then the second job will not
begin until the first job completes and its burst buffer stage-out completes.
If the second job does not use a burst buffer, but is dependent upon the first
job's completion, then it will not wait for the stage-out operation of the first
job to complete.
The second job can be made to wait for the first job's stage-out operation to
complete using the "afterburstbuffer" dependency option (e.g.
`sbatch --dependency=afterburstbuffer:123 ...`).

## PERFORMANCE[#SECTION_PERFORMANCE](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Executing sbatch sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmctld daemon come in at once, it can result in
a degradation of performance of the slurmctld daemon, possibly resulting
in a denial of service.
Do not run sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other
programs. Ensure that programs limit calls to sbatch to the minimum
necessary for the information you are trying to gather.

salloc , srun and sbatch (in Slurm 21.08+) have the
'--container' argument, which can be used to request container runtime
execution. The requested job container will not be inherited by the steps
called, excluding the batch and interactive steps.

- Interactive job step 0 inside of container: ```text salloc srun --container $ABS_PATH_TO_BUNDLE bash -c "cat /etc/*rel*" ```

## Heterogeneous Steps [#het_steps](https://slurm.schedmd.com/heterogeneous_jobs.html)
Slurm version 20.11 introduces the ability to request heterogeneous job
steps from within a non-homogeneous job allocation. This allows you the
flexibility to have different layouts for job steps without requiring the
use of heterogeneous jobs, where having separate jobs for the components
may be undesirable.
Some limitations for heterogeneous steps are that the steps must be able
to run on unique nodes. You also cannot request heterogeneous steps from within
a heterogeneous job.

job_container.conf is an ASCII file which defines parameters used by
Slurm's namespace/tmpfs plugin. Based on these parameters, the plugin will
create the appropriate job-specifc namespace(s).
The namespace/tmpfs plugin creates a filesystem namespace and will construct a
private (or optionally shared) filesystem namespace and mount a list of
directories (defaults to /tmp and /dev/shm) inside it, giving the job a private

by 'BasePath' in the job_container.conf file.

The srun command is used to launch applications.

A burst buffer can either be persistent or linked to a specific job ID.
Since a heterogeneous job consists of multiple job IDs, a job-specific burst

Specify a batch script by filename on the command line. The batch script specifies a 1 minute time limit for the job.
```text
$ cat myscript #!/bin/sh #SBATCH --time=1 srun hostname |sort $ sbatch -N4 myscript salloc: Granted job allocation 65537 $ cat slurm-65537.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
Pass a batch script to sbatch on standard input:
```text
$ sbatch -N4 #!/bin/sh > srun hostname |sort > EOF sbatch: Submitted batch job 65541 $ cat slurm-65541.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
To create a heterogeneous job with 3 components, each allocating a unique set of nodes:
```text
$ sbatch -w node[2-3] : -w node4 : -w node[5-7] work.bash Submitted batch job 34987
```

Slurm environment variables will be set independently for each component of

## Heterogeneous Steps [#het_steps](https://slurm.schedmd.com/heterogeneous_jobs.html)
Slurm version 20.11 introduces the ability to request heterogeneous job
steps from within a non-homogeneous job allocation. This allows you the
flexibility to have different layouts for job steps without requiring the
use of heterogeneous jobs, where having separate jobs for the components
may be undesirable.
Some limitations for heterogeneous steps are that the steps must be able
to run on unique nodes. You also cannot request heterogeneous steps from within
a heterogeneous job.
An example scenario would be if you have a task that needs to use 1 GPU

The first step of the process is to create a job allocation, which is
a claim on compute resources. A job allocation can be created using the
salloc , sbatch or srun command. The salloc and
sbatch commands create resource allocations while the srun

## Job Dependencies [#dependencies](https://slurm.schedmd.com/burst_buffer.html)
If two jobs use burst buffers and one is dependent on the other (e.g.
`sbatch --dependency=afterok:123 ...`) then the second job will not
begin until the first job completes and its burst buffer stage-out completes.
If the second job does not use a burst buffer, but is dependent upon the first
job's completion, then it will not wait for the stage-out operation of the first
job to complete.
The second job can be made to wait for the first job's stage-out operation to
complete using the "afterburstbuffer" dependency option (e.g.
`sbatch --dependency=afterburstbuffer:123 ...`).

## Job Dependencies [#dependencies](https://slurm.schedmd.com/job_array.html)
A job which is to be dependent upon an entire job array should specify
itself dependent upon the ArrayJobID.
Since each array element can have a different exit code, the interpretation of
the afterok and afternotok clauses will be based upon the highest
exit code from any task in the job array.
When a job dependency specifies the job ID of a job array:
The after clause is satisfied after all tasks in the job array start.
The afterany clause is satisfied after all tasks in the job array
complete.
The aftercorr clause is satisfied after the corresponding task ID in the
specified job has completed successfully (ran to completion with an exit code of
zero).
The afterok clause is satisfied after all tasks in the job array

## Versioning [#versioning](https://slurm.schedmd.com/plugins.html)
Slurm plugins must provide a plugin_version symbol exactly matching that
of the process they are loaded into. This is to avoid any potential issues if,
e.g., an underlying struct definition is changed by a maintenance release.
It is expected that the plugins are automatically build, packaged, and
distributed alongside the libslurm library, Slurm commands, and daemons.
The only exception to this is the SPANK plugin interface which only requires
the Slurm release to match, while the maintenance release (micro version) may be
changed. This is to reflect the additional ABI stability commitment that is
maintained exclusively for that plugin interface.

specifically the slurmd process — and user commands running on login

# Slurm Workload Manager
Slurm is an open-source workload manager designed for Linux clusters of
all sizes.
It provides three key functions.
First it allocates exclusive and/or non-exclusive access to resources
(computer nodes) to users for some duration of time so they can perform work.
Second, it provides a framework for starting, executing, and monitoring work
(typically a parallel job) on a set of allocated nodes.
Finally, it arbitrates contention for resources by managing a queue of
pending work.
Slurm's design is very modular with dozens of optional plugins.
In its simplest configuration, it can be installed and configured in a
couple of minutes (see [Caos NSA and Perceus: All-in-one Cluster Software Stack](http://www.linux-mag.com/id/7239/1/)
by Jeffrey B. Layton).
More complex configurations can satisfy the job scheduling needs of

## Use of cgroup for Resource Specialization [#Specialization](https://slurm.schedmd.com/cgroups.html)
Resource Specialization may be used to reserve a subset of cores or a
specific amount of memory on each compute node for exclusive use by the Slurm
compute node daemon, slurmd.
If cgroup/v1 is used the reserved resources will also be used by the
slurmstepd processes. If cgroup/v2 is used, slurmstepd is not constrained by
this resource specialization. Instead the slurmstepd is constrained to the
resources allocated to the job, since it is considered part of the job and its
consumption is completely dependent on the topology of the job. For example an
MPI job can initialize many ranks with PMI and make slurmstepd consume more

The namespace/linux plugin (added 25.11) uses the configuration file
[namespace.yaml](https://slurm.schedmd.com/namespace.yaml.html). This plugin can be configured
to create user and PID namespaces in addition to a temporary filesystem
namespace. Namespaces can be configured for all nodes or for a subset of nodes.
As an example, if all nodes will be configured the same way, you could put the
following in your namespace.yaml:
```text
defaults: auto_base_path: true base_path: "/var/nvme/storage"
```
Note the following important details with this plugin:
- This plugin requires cgroup/v2 to operate correctly.
- When using user namespaces, bpf token support (added in kernel 6.9) is required to use [ConstrainDevices](https://slurm.schedmd.com/cgroup.conf.html) in cgroup.conf .

## NOTES[#SECTION_NOTES](https://slurm.schedmd.com/namespace.yaml.html)
If any parameters in namespace.yaml are changed while slurm is running, then
slurmd on the respective nodes will need to be
restarted for changes to take effect (scontrol reconfigure is not sufficient).
Additionally this can be disruptive to
jobs already running on the node. So care must be taken to make sure no jobs
are running if any changes to namespace.yaml are deployed.
Restarting slurmd is safe and non-disruptive to running jobs, as long as
namespace.yaml is not changed between restarts in which case above point
applies.

## Job Dependencies [#dependencies](https://slurm.schedmd.com/burst_buffer.html)
If two jobs use burst buffers and one is dependent on the other (e.g.
`sbatch --dependency=afterok:123 ...`) then the second job will not
begin until the first job completes and its burst buffer stage-out completes.
If the second job does not use a burst buffer, but is dependent upon the first
job's completion, then it will not wait for the stage-out operation of the first
job to complete.
The second job can be made to wait for the first job's stage-out operation to
complete using the "afterburstbuffer" dependency option (e.g.
`sbatch --dependency=afterburstbuffer:123 ...`).

## Job Submission [#jobsubmission](https://slurm.schedmd.com/federation.html)
When a federated cluster receives a job submission, it will submit copies of the
job ( sibling jobs ) to each eligible cluster. Each cluster will then
independently attempt to schedule the job.
Jobs can be directed to specific clusters in the federation using the
-M,--clusters=<cluster_list> and the new
--cluster-constraint=[!]<constraint_list> options.
Using the -M,--clusters=<cluster_list> the submission command
(sbatch, salloc, srun) will pick one cluster from the list of clusters to submit
the job to and will also pass along the list of clusters with the job. The
clusters in the list will be the only viable clusters that siblings jobs can be
submitted to. For example the submission:
```text
cluster1$ sbatch -Mcluster2,cluster3 script.sh

## PERFORMANCE[#SECTION_PERFORMANCE](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Executing sbatch sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmctld daemon come in at once, it can result in
a degradation of performance of the slurmctld daemon, possibly resulting
in a denial of service.
Do not run sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other
programs. Ensure that programs limit calls to sbatch to the minimum
necessary for the information you are trying to gather.

By default, nodes in a reservation that are DOWN or DRAINED will be replaced,
but not nodes that are allocated to jobs. This behavior may be explicitly
requested with the REPLACE_DOWN flag.
However, you may instruct Slurm to also replace nodes which are allocated to

This option is not supported for reservations specifying cores which

## Maintenance Reservations [#maint](https://slurm.schedmd.com/reservations.html)
For ease of system maintenance, you can create a reservation with the
MAINT flag that overlaps existing reservations. This is equivalent to the
OVERLAP flag but with the following distinctions:
- Reserved nodes will be shown in maint state
- Reserved nodes will not be available as replacements in other reservations
- Cluster usage reports will show this time as PlannedDown
For example, users alan and brenda might have a reservation
for some nodes daily from noon until 1PM. If there is a maintenance reservation
for all nodes starting at 12:30PM, the only jobs they may start in their
reservation would have to be completed by 12:30PM, when the maintenance
reservation begins.

Below are concise, safe steps and best practices for creating and using maintenance reservations while avoiding unintended state changes (cancels, drains, or job replacement). This is a prescriptive checklist you can follow — none of these steps change cluster state by themselves.

1) Plan the window and scope
- Decide exact nodes (or partitions), start time, and duration. Prefer reserving whole nodes for maintenance (simpler) rather than per-core reservations.
- Choose a reservation name that encodes purpose/date (e.g., maint-kernel-2026-05-10).

2) Inventory current state (read-only checks)
- Check node/partition availability: sinfo (or sinfo --Node) to list nodes and partitions.
- Check running and queued jobs on target nodes: squeue -w nodeX,nodeY (or squeue --nodes=...).
- Check existing reservations: scontrol show reservation (or scontrol_reservation_show).
- Use sacct if you need historical job/run patterns to pick low-impact times.

3) Create a reservation that does NOT force immediate disruption
- Create an advanced reservation scheduled in the future (StartTime=...) and set Duration=... so it only becomes active when you plan to maintain.
- Use Flags=MAINT to mark it as a maintenance reservation (good for accounting and planning).
- Critically: do NOT set Flags=REPLACE or Flags=IGNORE_JOBS unless you explicitly want running jobs to be replaced or ignored. Leaving those out ensures Slurm will not forcibly evict running allocations.
- Example form (adapt to your cluster’s time format and node list):
  scontrol create reservation ReservationName=maint-2026-05-10 StartTime=2026-05-10T01:00:00 Duration=120 Nodes=node[01-04] Flags=MAINT Description="kernel update"
  (This is an example—adjust fields to your environment.)

4) Use floating reservations if you want a sliding maintenance window without immediate node state changes
- TIME_FLOAT reservations can be used to create a floating maintenance window relative to now (they are treated differently in scheduling and prevent new long-running jobs).
- This is useful when you want the reservation to “float” but still block starts that would overlap the intended maintenance.

5) How reservations affect job starts (important safety behavior)
- When a reservation exists for a future period, Slurm will generally prevent new jobs from starting if they cannot complete before the reservation’s start time. This reduces the chance you’ll need to cancel running jobs.
- Creating a MAINT reservation does not, by itself, cancel or requeue currently running jobs unless you used IGNORE_JOBS or REPLACE.

6) Notify users and monitor as the window approaches
- Announce the planned maintenance window and affected nodes/users well in advance.
- Monitor squeue for jobs that will still be running as the start time approaches; follow local policy (wait, ask users to checkpoint, or cancel individual jobs).
- If you must remove running jobs, do so explicitly and with communication (scancel), do not rely on reservation flags that implicitly evict jobs unless you intended that behavior.

7) When ready to start maintenance (this is when you change state)
- If you need nodes pulled out of service immediately, change node state (for example, put nodes into DRAIN with a reason) and then stop or requeue running jobs as required. Note: these are explicit state changes and should be done only when ready.
- After maintenance, clear DRAIN and/or delete the reservation:
  scontrol delete reservation ReservationName=...

8) Clean up and accounting
- Remove the reservation when maintenance is complete (scontrol delete reservation=...).
- Confirm nodes returned to normal with sinfo and check for any blocked jobs.
- Document the maintenance (start/end times) — MAINT reservations are recorded in reports as PlannedDown.

Safety checklist (quick)
- Reserve in the future; do not set IGNORE_JOBS or REPLACE unless you understand and want eviction.
- Verify squeue for overlapping jobs before the reservation starts.
- Communicate to users and give them time to finish or checkpoint.
- Use MAINT flag for accounting; use TIME_FLOAT if you want a floating window.
- Delete reservation and clear drains after work is done.

References / notes
- MAINT reservations are intended for system maintenance and are reported as maintenance/planned down in accounting.
- Flags that will forcibly affect running jobs: IGNORE_JOBS (creates reservation even if jobs running), REPLACE (replace allocated nodes). Use these only with explicit intent.

- Draft an example scontrol command for your exact nodes/start time/duration. Which nodes/start time should I use?

## DESCRIPTION[#SECTION_DESCRIPTION](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sdiag.html)
sdiag shows information related to slurmctld execution about: threads, agents,

When enabled, the gang scheduler keeps track of the resources
allocated to all jobs. For each partition an "active bitmap" is maintained that
tracks all concurrently running jobs in the Slurm cluster. Each time a new
job is allocated to resources in a partition, the gang scheduler
compares these newly allocated resources with the resources already maintained
in the "active bitmap".

# Gang Scheduling
Slurm supports timesliced gang scheduling in which two or more jobs are
allocated to the same resources in the same partition and these jobs are
alternately suspended to let one job at a time have dedicated access to the
resources for a configured period of time.
Slurm also supports preemptive job scheduling that allows a job in a
higher PriorityTier partition, or in a preempting QOS, to preempt other
jobs. [Preemption](https://slurm.schedmd.com/preempt.html) is related to Gang scheduling
because SUSPEND is one of the PreemptionMode s, and it uses the Gang
scheduler to resume suspended jobs.
A workload manager that supports timeslicing can improve responsiveness
and utilization by allowing more jobs to begin running sooner.
Shorter-running jobs no longer have to wait in a queue behind longer-running
jobs.
Instead they can be run "in parallel" with the longer-running jobs, which will
allow them to start and finish quick...

### Archive Server[#archive](https://slurm.schedmd.com/accounting.html)
If ongoing access to Archived/Purged data is required at your site, it is
possible to create an archive instance of slurmdbd. Data previously archived
and purged from the production database can be loaded into the archive server,
keeping the production database at a manageable size while making sure old
records are still accessible.

## Sharding [#Sharding](https://slurm.schedmd.com/gres.html)
Sharding provides a generic mechanism where GPUs can be
shared by multiple jobs. While it does permit multiple jobs to run on a given
GPU it does not fence the processes running on the GPU, it only allows the GPU
to be shared. Sharding, therefore, works best with homogeneous workflows. It is
recommended to limit the number of shards on a node to equal the max possible

## Timeslicer Design and Operation [#time_slice](https://slurm.schedmd.com/gang_scheduling.html)
When enabled, the gang scheduler keeps track of the resources
allocated to all jobs. For each partition an "active bitmap" is maintained that
tracks all concurrently running jobs in the Slurm cluster. Each time a new
job is allocated to resources in a partition, the gang scheduler
compares these newly allocated resources with the resources already maintained
in the "active bitmap".
If these two sets of resources are disjoint then the new job is added to the "active bitmap". If these two sets of resources overlap then
the new job is suspended. All jobs are tracked in a per-partition job queue
within the gang scheduler logic.

## Backfill Scheduling [#backfill](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sched_config.html)
The backfill scheduling plugin is loaded by default.
Without backfill scheduling, each partition is scheduled strictly in priority
order, which typically results in significantly lower system utilization and
responsiveness than otherwise possible.
Backfill scheduling will start lower priority jobs if doing so does not delay
the expected start time of any higher priority jobs.
Since the expected start time of pending jobs depends upon the expected
completion time of running jobs, reasonably accurate time limits are important
for backfill scheduling to work well.
Slurm's backfill scheduler takes into consideration every running job.
It then considers pending jobs in priority order, determining when and where

# sdiag
Section: Slurm Commands (1)
Updated: Slurm Commands
[Index](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sdiag.html)

Good question — sdiag is the Slurm scheduling diagnostic tool that prints many counters about slurmctld activity, scheduler work, backfill, and job dispatching. Below are the common sdiag fields you’ll see (field names as printed by sdiag --all), what each means, and short guidance on interpreting them.

Global / daemon
- Server thread count  
  Number of active slurmctld threads. High values mean slurmctld is busy (submissions, dispatches, RPCs); sustained high counts → controller load/throughput issue.

- Agent thread count  
  Number of worker/agent threads (helpers used by the controller). Similar interpretation as server threads.

RPC / client activity
- RPC requests / RPC failures (or RPC messages)  
  Number of RPC calls received by slurmctld (and any failed RPCs). Spikes = many client commands or monitoring tools; failures indicate comms problems.

Job submission / lifecycle
- Jobs submitted / Jobs completed / Jobs failed / Jobs requeued  
  Counters for lifecycle events. Large numbers of failed or requeued jobs point to job-launch failures, node problems, or user-script issues.

Queue / scheduling workload
- Queue depth  
  Number of pending jobs the scheduler is considering (a snapshot of backlog). High queue depth means many jobs waiting; investigate priority/fairshare, resource shortages, or scheduling bottlenecks.

- Jobs considered / Candidates examined  
  How many pending jobs or candidate placements the scheduler evaluated per cycle. Very high values per cycle indicate expensive scheduling decisions (many partitions/nodes to scan).

Scheduling cycle / timing
- Scheduling cycles (count)  
  Number of scheduler cycles performed.

- Scheduling cycle time (min / avg / max)  
  Time spent per scheduler cycle. If avg or max is large, scheduler loop is slow — could be due to many jobs, expensive backfill computations, or a plugin/DB latency.

Dispatch / launch
- Dispatches (or Jobs dispatched)  
  Number of job dispatch attempts (start requests to nodes).

- Failed dispatches (or Launch failures)  
  How many dispatch attempts failed (node launch, proctrack, or communication problems). Non-zero values require checking node health, munge/ssh, and node daemons (slurmd) logs.

Backfill / windowing
- Backfill windows created / windows used  
  Number of backfill windows the scheduler computed and how many were actually used to start lower-priority jobs.

- Backfill attempts / Backfill failures  
  Attempts to start backfill jobs and how many failed. High failures → inaccurate job time limits, resource fragmentation, or node/launch issues.

- Largest / average backfill window (size/time)  
  Size or duration of computed windows; small windows limit ability to backfill.

Allocation scanning / node work
- Nodes scanned per allocation (or Node checks)  
  How many nodes the scheduler scanned while looking for fit. Large values indicate expensive placement decisions or large cluster size being brute-forced.

Preemption / gang/timeslice counters
- Preemptions / Suspends / Resumes (if configured)  
  Counts of preemptive actions or timeslice/gang scheduler operations. High numbers reflect active preemption policies or gang/time-slicing activity.

Priority / fairness diagnostics
- Fairshare adjustments / Priority updates (sometimes shown)  
  Counters related to priority recalculation; frequent/slow updates can affect scheduling responsiveness.

Misc / housekeeping
- Backfill lookups / Reservation checks / DB queries  
  Counts of extra work slurmctld does (checking reservations, consulting slurmdbd). Many DB queries or slow DB responses can slow scheduling.

What to watch for (practical guidance)
- High scheduling cycle times + high “jobs considered” or “nodes scanned” → scheduling is the bottleneck; consider tuning SchedulerType/SchedulerParameters, reducing expensive plugins, or limiting per-cycle work.
- Large queue depth but low dispatch count → resources constrained (no eligible nodes) or priorities/QOS preventing starts.
- Non-zero failed dispatches / launch failures → investigate node slurmd logs, node health, network/Munge, and proctrack plugin.
- Backfill windows = 0 or very small → job time limits may be inaccurate or fragmentation prevents backfill; encourage accurate time estimates or adjust backfill params.

Notes and tips
- Field names and exact output can vary by Slurm version and enabled scheduler plugins. Values are reset at midnight UTC by default; sdiag --reset clears counters immediately.
- Use sdiag --all for the full display or sdiag --json for machine-readable output.
- sdiag is an RPC to slurmctld — don’t run it in tight loops (it can add load).

If you want, paste your sdiag --all output (or run sdiag --json and paste the JSON) and I’ll interpret the specific counters and point to likely tunables or troubleshooting steps.

## Partition QOS [#partition](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
A QOS can be attached to a partition. This means the partition will have all
the same limits as the QOS. This does not associate jobs with the QOS, nor does
it give the job any priority or preemption characteristics of the assigned QOS.
Jobs may separately request the same QOS or a different QOS to gain those
characteristics. However, the Partition QOS limits will override the job's QOS.
If the opposite is desired you may configure the job's QOS with
`Flags=OverPartQOS` which will reverse the order of precedence.
This functionality may be used to implement a true "floating"
partition, in which a partition may access a limited amount of resources with no
restrictions on which nodes it uses to get the resources. This is accomplished
by assigning all nodes to the partition, then configuring a Partition QOS with
`GrpTRES` set to the desired resource limits.

Starting in Slurm 23.11, a QOS may be configured to contain relative resource
limits instead of absolute limits by setting `Flags=Relative`.

total resources available. Values higher than 100 are interpreted as 100%.

## Job Priority Factors In General [#general](https://slurm.schedmd.com/priority_multifactor.html)
The job's priority at any given time will be a weighted sum of all the
factors that have been enabled in the slurm.conf file. Job priority can be
expressed as:
```text
Job_priority = site_factor + (PriorityWeightAge) * (age_factor) + (PriorityWeightAssoc) * (assoc_factor) + (PriorityWeightFairshare) * (fair-share_factor) + (PriorityWeightJobSize) * (job_size_factor) + (PriorityWeightPartition) * (priority_job_factor) + (PriorityWeightQOS) * (QOS_factor) + SUM(TRES_weight_cpu * TRES_factor_cpu, TRES_weight_ * TRES_factor_ , ...) - nice_factor
```
All of the factors in this formula are floating point numbers that
range from 0.0 to 1.0. The weights are unsigned, 32 bit integers.

### Job Scheduling Priority [#priority](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
Job scheduling priority is made up of a number of factors as
described in the [priority/multifactor](https://slurm.schedmd.com/priority_multifactor.html) plugin. One
of the factors is the QOS priority. Each QOS is defined in the Slurm
database and includes an associated priority. Jobs that request and
are permitted a QOS will incorporate the priority associated with that
QOS in the job's [multi-factor priority calculation.](https://slurm.schedmd.com/priority_multifactor.html)
To enable the QOS priority component of the multi-factor priority
calculation, the "PriorityWeightQOS" configuration parameter must be
defined in the slurm.conf file and assigned an integer value greater
than zero.
A job's QOS only affects is scheduling priority when the
multi-factor plugin is loaded.

## Other QOS Options [#qos_other](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
- Flags Used by the slurmctld to override or enforce certain characteristics. To clear a previously set value use the modify command with a new value of -1. Valid options are: DenyOnLimit If set, jobs using this QOS will be rejected at submission time if they do not conform to the QOS 'Max' limits as stand-alone jobs. Jobs that go over these limits when other jobs are considered, but conform to the limits when considered individually will not be rejected. Short answer: sprio shows the breakdown of the Multifactor priority components that Slurm’s priority/multifactor plugin uses. A job’s composite priority is a weighted sum of several normalized factors (each 0.0–1.0) multiplied by administrator-configured integer weights. The weights live in slurm.conf (PriorityWeight*) and you can inspect current per-job components with sprio and the configured weights with sprio -w.

Canonical formula (from the plugin):
Job_priority = site_factor
+ PriorityWeightAge    * age_factor
+ PriorityWeightAssoc  * assoc_factor
+ PriorityWeightFairshare * fairshare_factor
+ PriorityWeightJobSize * job_size_factor
+ PriorityWeightPartition * partition_factor
+ PriorityWeightQOS     * qos_factor
+ SUM_over_TRES( PriorityWeightTRES_<type> * TRES_factor_<type> )
- nice_factor

Key points about components and weights
- Factors (age_factor, fairshare_factor, etc.)
  - Each is a floating point in [0.0, 1.0], normalized for that factor.
  - Represent the job’s relative value for that dimension (e.g., age_factor grows as the job waits; TRES_factor reflects requested amount of a tracked resource).
- Weights (PriorityWeight*)
  - Unsigned integers (32-bit) configured by the admin in slurm.conf.
  - Scale the importance of each factor in the final integer priority.
  - Larger weight → that factor has more influence on ordering.
  - The final Job_priority is an unsigned 32-bit integer (0 .. 4294967295); bigger = higher priority.
- The “nice” factor is subtractive: a job/user “nice” lowers priority.
- TRES factors
  - There is a factor per tracked TRES (cpu, gpu, license, burstbuffer, …). The admin configures TRES-related priority influence via PriorityWeightTRES (or per-type entries); more requested TRES can increase job priority when TRES weights are positive.
- Association factor
  - Reflects the job’s association/account/group and any association-level priority characteristics.
- Fairshare factor
  - Measures the gap between promised and consumed resources (accounting DB required); favors users/accounts below their fair share.
- Job size factor
  - Reflects job resource size (nodes/CPUs) — can be used to favor large or small jobs depending on configuration.
- Partition and QOS factors
  - Partition: per-partition configured priority adjustments.
  - QOS: each QOS can have a priority value; PriorityWeightQOS enables that contribution.

Useful commands
- sprio — show each pending job’s component contributions.
- sprio -n — show normalized factors.
- sprio -w — show the configured PriorityWeight* values.
- Edit weights in slurm.conf (PriorityWeightAge, PriorityWeightFairshare, PriorityWeightJobSize, PriorityWeightAssoc, PriorityWeightPartition, PriorityWeightQOS, PriorityWeightTRES, SiteFactor, etc.) and reconfigure/restart as needed.

How to think about tuning
- Increase PriorityWeightAge to reduce starvation (older jobs rise faster).
- Increase PriorityWeightFairshare to prioritize users/accounts underused relative to their share.
- Increase PriorityWeightJobSize to favor big parallel runs (or keep small to reduce queue fragmentation).
- Use PriorityWeightTRES to give explicit weight to GPUs, licenses, burstbuffers, etc.
- Combine weights carefully — since factors are normalized, relative weights determine trade-offs.

- show the current sprio breakdown and weights on this cluster (sprio / sprio -w), or
- suggest a recommended weight configuration for a specific policy goal (e.g., favor GPUs, reduce small-job starvation). Which would you like?

## Command-line Job Options [#command-line](https://slurm.schedmd.com/burst_buffer.html)
In addition to putting burst buffer directives in the batch script, the
command-line options `--bb` and `--bbf` may also include
burst buffer directives. These command-line options are available for salloc,
sbatch, and srun. Note that the `--bb` option cannot create or
destroy persistent burst buffers.
The `--bbf` option takes as an argument a filename and that file
should contain a collection of burst buffer operations identical to those used
for batch jobs.
Alternatively, the `--bb` option may be used to specify burst
buffer directives as the option argument. The behavior of this option depends
on which burst buffer plugin is used. When the `--bb` option is
used, Slurm parses this option and creates a temporary burst buffer script file
that is used internally by the burst buffer plugins.

- deleting
- deleted

- staged-in

- alloc-revoke

- suspended
- post-run
- staging-out
- teardown
- teardown-fail
- complete

a burst buffer. The states `allocating`, `allocated`,

contains the following:

Directive=BB_EXAMPLE

If the Directive option is not specified in burst_buffer.conf, then
the default directive for this plugin (`#BB_LUA`) will be used.

requires the directive to be given. If the directive is given, Slurm will run

## Heterogeneous Job Support [#het-job-support](https://slurm.schedmd.com/burst_buffer.html)
Heterogeneous jobs may request burst buffers. Burst buffer hooks will run
once for each component that has burst buffer directives. For example, if a
heterogeneous job has three components and two of them have burst buffer
directives, the burst buffer hooks will run once for each of the two components
with burst buffer directives, but not for the third component without burst
buffer directives. Further information and examples can be found in the

## Heterogeneous Job Support [#het-job-support](https://slurm.schedmd.com/burst_buffer.html)
Heterogeneous jobs may request burst buffers. Burst buffer hooks will run
once for each component that has burst buffer directives. For example, if a
heterogeneous job has three components and two of them have burst buffer
directives, the burst buffer hooks will run once for each of the two components
with burst buffer directives, but not for the third component without burst
buffer directives. Further information and examples can be found in the
heterogeneous jobs page.

These are the different possible burst buffer states:
- pending
- allocating
- allocated
- deleting
- deleted
- staging-in
- staged-in
- pre-run
- alloc-revoke
- running
- suspended
- post-run
- staging-out
- teardown
- teardown-fail
- complete

`scontrol show job`. This field only appears for jobs that requested
a burst buffer. The states `allocating`, `allocated`,
`deleting` and `deleted` are used

state `alloc-revoke` happens if a failure in Slurm's select plugin
occurs in between Slurm allocating resources for a job and actually starting

Below is a concise, doc-based summary of Slurm burst-buffer directives and how stage‑in / stage‑out behave. I used the official Slurm Burst Buffer Guide (burst_buffer.html) as the source.

What burst‑buffer directives are and where to put them
- Burst‑buffer directives are comment lines placed in batch scripts (they begin with #) that tell Slurm’s burst‑buffer plugin what storage to allocate and what data movement to run for the job.
- Directives may appear before, after, or interspersed with #SBATCH lines.
- The same directives can be supplied on the command line: sbatch/srun/salloc accept --bb (inline directives) and --bbf (a file of burst‑buffer operations). Note: --bb cannot create/destroy persistent buffers; --bbf points to a file formatted like the script directives.

Plugin differences (affects directive names and exact fields)
- DataWarp plugin: common directive names are #DW (job‑specific burst buffer directives) and #BB (used for persistent‑buffer create/destroy with DataWarp). DataWarp has extra, vendor-specific options; consult DataWarp docs for details.
- Lua plugin: default directive is #BB_LUA (configurable via burst_buffer.conf). The lua plugin is generic and relies on a site-provided burst_buffer.lua implementation for exact behavior.
- Exact token names and the allowed fields (stage_in, stage_out, capacity, pool, access, type, etc.) depend on the plugin; the guide documents the general fields but plugin docs (or your cluster’s burst_buffer.lua) define the precise syntax.

Job vs persistent burst buffers
- Job‑specific burst buffers: allocated for a job and released afterwards. Many plugins require a capacity; if a job requests a job‑specific buffer without specifying capacity the job may be rejected.
- Persistent burst buffers: (DataWarp only) may be created/destroyed with #BB create_persistent / destroy_persistent and survive beyond a single job.

Stage‑in / stage‑out behavior and lifecycle
- Staging occurs at defined points in the job lifecycle. Slurm tracks burst buffer states such as: pending, allocating, allocated, staging‑in, staged‑in, pre‑run, running, staging‑out, post‑run, teardown, complete (these appear in the BurstBufferState shown by scontrol show job).
- Stage‑in: data movement from the backing filesystem into the allocated burst buffer is run before the job enters the running state (the job will wait for stage‑in to finish). After successful stage‑in the job proceeds to pre‑run / run.
- Stage‑out: after the job finishes running, post‑run hooks run to move data from the burst buffer back to the target filesystem (stage‑out). Stage‑out runs during the job’s post‑run / teardown phases (the job’s completion may be delayed until stage‑out finishes).
- Timeouts: plugins expose timeout controls (e.g., StageInTimeout, StageOutTimeout in the burst‑buffer configuration/status). If staging times out or fails, the burst‑buffer plugin’s behavior depends on plugin/config (failure can lead to teardown or teardown‑fail states).
- Heterogeneous jobs: burst‑buffer hooks are run per job component that has directives — components without directives do not get burst‑buffer stages.

Typical directive components (conceptual, plugin-specific syntax varies)
- capacity=<size> (required for many job‑specific buffers)
- pool=<pool-name> (which pool to allocate from)
- stage_in=<source>:<bb-path> (request staging of source data into the buffer)
- stage_out=<bb-path>:<destination> (request staging of results out of the buffer)
- access=, type=, link/move/copy semantics — some plugins support copy vs link vs move semantics; exact names/options are plugin dependent

How to check status / diagnostics
- scontrol show job <jobid> includes a BurstBufferState field for jobs that requested burst buffers.
- scontrol show burst (or sview Burst Buffer tab) shows configured burst pools, allocated buffers, per‑job allocations, and plugin timeouts (StageInTimeout / StageOutTimeout).
- DebugFlags=BurstBuffer in slurm.conf increases burst‑buffer logging for debugging.

Practical notes and best practices
- Because stage‑in must finish before the job runs, large stage‑in operations can delay job start — account for that in scheduling and timeouts.
- Stage‑out can extend job completion time (post‑run); set StageOutTimeout appropriately and avoid leaving long, unneeded data in buffers.
- Request only the capacity you need; burst‑buffer size may affect scheduling.
- For cluster‑specific behavior and exact directive syntax/examples, consult your cluster’s burst_buffer.conf, burst_buffer.lua (if used), and the DataWarp/Lua plugin documentation in the Slurm Burst Buffer Guide.

Where to read the exact syntax
- See the official Slurm Burst Buffer Guide (burst_buffer.html) for:
  - job submission directives and command‑line options (--bb / --bbf),
  - DataWarp and Lua plugin sections,
  - persistent buffer create/destroy (#BB create_persistent ...),
  - the list of burst buffer states and example scontrol output.

## Job Accounting Records [#job_record](https://slurm.schedmd.com/job_launch.html)
When Slurm is configured to use SlurmDBD to store job records (i.e.
AccountingStorageType=accounting_storage=slurmdbd ), there are multiple
records that get stored for each job. There is a record for the job as a
whole as well as entries for the following types of job steps:
- extern step — A step created for each job as long as you have PrologFlags=contain in your slurm.conf. Each node in the job will have a slurmstepd process created for the extern step. pam_slurm_adopt uses this step to contain external connections.
- batch step — A step created for jobs that were submitted with sbatch. The batch host, or the primary node for the job, will run an instance of slurmstepd for the batch step, which is used to run the script provided to sbatch.
- interactive step — A step created for jobs that were submitted with salloc when LaunchParameters=use_interactive...

Short answer first
- sstat reports live, per-job-step resource metrics. AveCPU and AveRSS are per-task averages computed across all tasks in a job step (not cluster-wide aggregates).

What a "job step" is
- A step is a unit of execution inside a job (batch step created by sbatch, interactive step from salloc/srun, extern steps created per node, etc.). sstat shows metrics for each step.

Field meanings
- AveRSS
  - Average resident set size (physical memory in RAM) across all tasks in the step.
  - Units are bytes; sstat prints human-readable units (K, M, G).
  - Use MaxRSS and MaxRSSTask to find the single task that used the most memory — AveRSS can hide per-task spikes.
- AveCPU
  - Average CPU time (user + system) used by each task in the step.
  - Format is time (e.g., hh:mm:ss.ms). This is CPU-time, not wall-clock time.
  - If AveCPU per task is larger than the step wall time, that means tasks used multiple CPUs (multithreading or multiple cores).
- (Related) AveVMSize
  - Average virtual address space size across tasks (like AveRSS but for VM size).

How the averages are computed and caveats
- "Ave*" fields look at the measured value for each task of the step and return the average. Corresponding "Max*" and "Min*" fields report the per-task extremes; some fields also include which task had the max (e.g., MaxRSSTask).
- For MPI/parallel jobs: values are averaged across tasks on all nodes. Highly skewed per-task usage will be masked by averages.
- sstat reports live measurements for running steps. For completed jobs/steps, use sacct (historical accounting) instead.
- Sampling and timing: sstat shows current/collected statistics; very short-lived steps or infrequent sampling can produce zeros or coarse numbers.

Quick example command
- sstat -p --format=JobID,Step,AveCPU,AveRSS,MaxRSS,MaxRSSTask -j <jobid>

Quick interpretation example
- If step shows AveRSS=500M, MaxRSS=1.5G (MaxRSSTask=task-3) and AveCPU=00:10:00 while wall time = 00:05:00:
  - On average each task used 500 MiB RSS.
  - One task (task-3) used 1.5 GiB RSS.
  - Each task consumed 10 minutes of CPU time on average; since wall time is 5 minutes, tasks used ~2 CPU cores on average (10 min CPU / 5 min wall = 2).

If you want, tell me a job ID/step and I can show the live sstat fields and help interpret them.

## Federated Job IDs[#jobids](https://slurm.schedmd.com/federation.html)
When a job is submitted to a federation it gets a federated job id. Job ids in
the federation are unique across all clusters in the federation. A federated
job ID is made by utilizing an unsigned 32 bit integer to assign the cluster's
ID and the cluster's local ID.

Bits 0-25: Local Job ID Bits 26-31: Cluster Origin ID
```
Federated job IDs allow the controllers to know which cluster the job was
submitted to by looking at the cluster origin id of the job.

## Job Requeue [#jobrequeue](https://slurm.schedmd.com/federation.html)
When a federated job is requeued the origin cluster is notified and the origin
cluster will then submit new sibling jobs to viable clusters and the federated
job is eligible to start on a different cluster than the one it ran on.
slurm.conf options RequeueExit and RequeueExitHold are controlled
by the origin cluster.

Below is a concise, practical summary of Slurm federation and how federated jobs behave, with the key concepts, lifecycle, submission options, admin notes, and common pitfalls.

1) What is federation (high level)
- Federation lets multiple independent Slurm clusters cooperate so a single job submission can be attempted on many clusters (peer‑to‑peer scheduling).
- A job submitted into a federation is replicated as “sibling” jobs on eligible clusters; clusters independently try to schedule the job using their local policies.
- The cluster where the user submits the job is the origin cluster. The origin coordinates sibling activity and keeps the canonical view of the federated job.

2) Important terms
- Federated job: the job as known to the federation (unique across the federation).
- Origin job / origin cluster: the job and cluster where the submission occurred.
- Sibling job / sibling cluster: a copy of the federated job submitted to another cluster.
- Siblings viable / siblings active: clusters where siblings could run vs where sibling copies exist now.
- Revoked (RV): state used for sibling copies that must be removed once a sibling elsewhere starts.

3) Federated job IDs
- Federated job IDs are unique across the federation. Internally bits encode origin cluster ID and local job ID (e.g., low bits = local job id, high bits = cluster origin id). You can use the job ID to identify the origin cluster.

4) Job lifecycle / scheduling
- Submission: origin submits the job locally and also arranges sibling submissions to other clusters that are “viable.”
- Scheduling: each cluster independently evaluates the sibling and, when it believes it can allocate resources, coordinates with the origin to reserve/allocate.
- Start: when a cluster successfully starts the job it notifies origin; origin tells sibling clusters to revoke/remove their sibling jobs (those siblings move to a revoked state).
- Requeue: if a federated job is requeued the origin may re‑submit siblings to viable clusters; the job can later run on a different cluster.
- Cancel/Modify: cancel/modify requests are routed via the origin; canceling the federated job will remove sibling copies.
- Interactive jobs and job arrays are supported, but behavior and limitations are documented (interactive sessions still coordinate via origin).

5) How to submit and control which clusters are tried
- sbatch / salloc / srun support federation submission options:
  - -M, --clusters=<cluster_list> — submit to a chosen set of clusters (origin will pick one cluster from the list to be the origin and will only create siblings on the listed clusters).
  - --cluster-constraint=[!]<constraint_list> — constrain which clusters are viable.
- If you do not restrict clusters, the federation configuration determines which clusters are viable targets.

6) Commands and job inspection
- squeue has federation-aware options:
  - --sibling shows sibling jobs instead of merging them.
  - Long-format fields: cluster, siblingsactive, siblingsviable, siblingsactiveraw, siblingsviableraw.
- scontrol show job / scontrol show step can show detailed federated job info.
- Admins use sacctmgr to create/modify federations (sacctmgr add/modify federation; cluster membership is stored in the accounting DB).

7) Configuration and admin notes
- Federations are created with sacctmgr; clusters are added to a named federation. A cluster may be a member of only one federation at a time.
- The origin cluster must be reachable by siblings (network/connectivity).
- If a cluster is removed from a federation without draining it first, running jobs that originated there continue to run as non‑federated; pending origin jobs remain pending on origin as non‑federated while sibling jobs are re evaluated.
- Accounting/user mappings, accounts, and QOS policies should be reconciled across clusters if you expect consistent behavior and accounting. (Exact requirements depend on your site configuration.)

8) Limitations and gotchas
- Not intended for extreme job submission rates; SchedMD documentation warns about scale (e.g., very large numbers of jobs/day).
- Scheduling decisions, policies, and available resources differ per cluster — job runtime/limits or available features (GPUs, specialized hardware) may vary.
- Because coordination goes through the origin cluster, origin availability and network reliability matter.
- Sibling jobs are copies: you should be aware of any site‑specific prolog/epilog, environment, or file‑system differences that could affect execution.
- Monitoring/logging and accounting can be dispersed; use squeue/sacct and the federation fields to trace federated jobs.

9) Typical use cases
- Spread load across several cooperating clusters so users get faster starts when one site is busy.
- Provide transparent access to resources that are managed by different administrative domains but agree to cooperate.
- Allow a job to “race” on multiple clusters so the first that can run wins (useful for many interactive or short‑wait tasks).

10) Troubleshooting hints
- If siblings never start: check network connectivity between controllers and that clusters are listed as viable in squeue output (siblingsviable).
- To see where a federated job is running or which siblings exist: squeue --format=... with cluster/siblingsactive fields or squeue --sibling.
- If scheduling seems inconsistent, verify account/QOS limits and resource/FEDERATED configuration across clusters.

References and where to read more
- Slurm Federated Scheduling Guide (Slurm docs): federation.html — provides configuration examples, detailed state descriptions, submission examples, and limitations.

Slurm includes support for creating a federation of clusters
and scheduling jobs in a peer-to-peer fashion between them. Jobs submitted to a
federation receive a unique job ID that is unique among all clusters in the
federation. A job is submitted to the local cluster (the cluster defined in the
slurm.conf) and is then replicated across the clusters in the federation. Each

scheduling policies. The clusters coordinate with the "origin" cluster (cluster
the job was submitted to) to schedule the job.
NOTE : This is not intended as a high-throughput environment. If

What this means and whether jobs can span clusters
- Active federation: clusters listed (here "mock-cluster") are members and the federation controller is ACTIVE.
- Jobs are not one single allocation that spans nodes in multiple clusters. Instead, Slurm federated scheduling replicates a submitted job as "sibling" jobs across the eligible clusters. Each sibling is independently scheduled and runs entirely on a single cluster.
- The origin cluster (where you submit) coordinates the siblings and the federation assigns a unique federation-wide job ID for the job/siblings.
- You can control which clusters receive siblings using submission options:
  - sbatch/srun/salloc -M <cluster_list> (or --clusters=<list>) to limit the cluster list,
  - and --cluster-constraint to require/ban clusters by constraint.
- Practical implication: you cannot request an allocation that uses nodes from two clusters at once. If you want work to run on multiple clusters simultaneously, submit separate jobs (or let the federation create siblings); but each running sibling is confined to a single cluster.

## Job Dependencies [#dependencies](https://slurm.schedmd.com/job_array.html)
A job which is to be dependent upon an entire job array should specify
itself dependent upon the ArrayJobID.
Since each array element can have a different exit code, the interpretation of
the afterok and afternotok clauses will be based upon the highest
exit code from any task in the job array.
When a job dependency specifies the job ID of a job array:
The after clause is satisfied after all tasks in the job array start.
The afterany clause is satisfied after all tasks in the job array
complete.
The aftercorr clause is satisfied after the corresponding task ID in the
specified job has completed successfully (ran to completion with an exit code of
zero).
The afterok clause is satisfied after all tasks in the job array
complete successfully.
The afternotok clause is satisfied after all tasks in the job array
complete with at least one tasks not completing succes...

Read-only findings
- I checked the queue for PENDING jobs (squeue state=PENDING) and found no pending jobs — therefore there are no jobs currently blocked with the "Dependency" reason on this cluster right now.

Explanation — Slurm job dependency semantics (concise)

What a dependency is
- A dependency makes a job wait until one or more events for other job(s) occur. While waiting the job will normally appear PENDING with reason "Dependency".
- You can set dependencies at submission with sbatch --dependency=<type>:<jobid>[ :<jobid2>... ].

Common dependency types
- after:<jobid>[...]
  - Satisfied after the specified job(s) start running (useful to ensure ordering of start times).
- afterok:<jobid>[...]
  - Satisfied only after the specified job(s) complete successfully (exit code 0). All listed job IDs must finish with exit 0.
- afternotok:<jobid>[...]
  - Satisfied only after the specified job(s) complete with a non‑zero exit code (at least one non‑zero).
- afterany:<jobid>[...]
  - Satisfied after the specified job(s) complete, regardless of exit code.
- aftercorr:<jobid>
  - Used with job arrays; satisfied when the corresponding task index of the specified array completes successfully.
- singleton
  - Ensures only one job with the same name/user runs at a time; a later job with singleton will wait until the prior job (same name/user) finishes.
Notes:
- Multiple job IDs in one dependency clause are treated as AND: every listed job must satisfy the dependency condition.
- You can combine dependency clauses (e.g., --dependency=afterok:123,afterany:200) to create more complex waits.
- Job-array semantics: when a dependency refers to a job array, behavior depends on the dependency type:
  - after: satisfied after all tasks in the array start.
  - afterany: satisfied after all tasks complete.
  - afterok/afternotok: based on aggregate success/failure across the array (docs use the worst/aggregate exit behavior).
  - aftercorr: maps corresponding task index only.

How Slurm displays/diagnoses dependency-blocked jobs
- squeue will show pending jobs and a REASON column; dependency-blocked jobs typically show REASON=Dependency.
- For details of a job’s dependency expression use: scontrol show job <jobid>
  - That output contains a Dependency=... field showing the exact clauses and referenced job IDs.
- Example quick checks:
  - List PENDING jobs and the reason:
    squeue -t PENDING -o "%i %P %j %u %T %M %R"
    (Then look for rows where the REASON/REASON column is "Dependency".)
  - Inspect a job’s dependency detail:
    scontrol show job <jobid>

Common pitfalls and tips
- If the job you depend on was cancelled or failed, afterok will never be satisfied; use afterany or adjust workflow.
- Dependencies referencing job IDs that no longer exist (or were purged from accounting) can behave unexpectedly; scontrol show job will reveal unresolved IDs.
- Dependencies are established at submission time. To change or remove them you must modify the job (scontrol update) — that is a mutating operation and requires operator actions.
- For workflows, consider using job arrays + aftercorr for per-task chaining, or job-chaining tools (workflow managers) that can re-submit on failures.

request to run in this partition. This priority value is then
normalized to the highest priority of all the partitions to become the
partition factor.

"pending reason Priority" — what it means (from the official Slurm docs)
- Meaning: Slurm reports the pending reason "Priority" when the scheduler attempted to place the job but chose other job(s) with higher scheduling priority first. In short, your job is waiting because other work currently has a higher computed priority and gets resources before it. (See Slurm's Job Reason Codes and the Multifactor Priority Plugin docs.)

How Slurm computes that priority (brief, from the Multifactor Priority plugin)
- Job priority is a weighted sum of enabled factors:
  Job_priority = site_factor + PriorityWeightAge * age_factor + PriorityWeightAssoc * assoc_factor + PriorityWeightFairshare * fairshare_factor + PriorityWeightJobSize * job_size_factor + PriorityWeightPartition * partition_factor + PriorityWeightQOS * QOS_factor + TRES-weighted factors - nice_factor
- Each factor is normalized (typically 0.0–1.0) and weights in slurm.conf determine their relative importance. The final priority is an integer (0 .. 4294967295); larger = higher priority.

How to inspect why a specific job shows "Priority"
- View per-job priority and ordering: use sprio (or sprio <jobid>) and sprio --weights to see effective priority and the weights used by the scheduler.
- See queue and priority fields: squeue (custom output or include the PRIORITY column) or scontrol show job <jobid> for detailed job fields.
- Check association/QOS/account priorities in sacctmgr (association/account/QOS priorities may influence assoc_factor and QOS_factor).

Common ways to address it
- Wait for higher-priority jobs to finish (the scheduler will consider your job again).
- Increase your job's effective priority: request a higher QOS (if available), change the job 'nice' (lower nice value), or use an account/association with higher priority (admin action).
- Reduce resource requests or job size so the job fits earlier alongside competing jobs.
- If fairshare is reducing your priority, letting older jobs finish or requesting admin changes to fairshare/weights may help.
- Contact cluster admins if you believe priorities or priority weights (slurm.conf) need adjustment.

References (official Slurm docs)
- Job reason codes: job_reason_codes (explains "Priority" as a scheduler-chosen pending reason)
- Multifactor Priority plugin: priority_multifactor (explains the priority formula and each factor)

If you want, I can:
- Show the current priority values for one or more jobs (I would run sprio/squeue for the job IDs you give), or
- Run sprio --weights and show which factors are currently influencing priority on your cluster. Which would you like?

Audit accounting problem reports and explain likely remediation
No accounting problems found.

I ran the accounting-problem audit (sacctmgr show problems) — result: No accounting problems found.

What that means
- The Slurm accounting DB currently reports no consistency or configuration problems via sacctmgr_show_problems.
- Caveats: this check only reports the specific accounting-problem classes sacctmgr knows about. Other issues (slurmdbd outages, DB disk/permission errors, missing associations, time skew, or per-user usage anomalies) may exist but not be listed as “accounting problems.”

Recommended next checks (commands to run) — run these to detect common root causes if you suspect accounting trouble
- Check slurmdbd health and logs
  - systemctl status slurmdbd
  - journalctl -u slurmdbd --no-pager | tail -n 200
  - Check slurmdbd log file (path depends on config)
- Check DB connectivity and free space
  - mysqladmin ping (or appropriate DB tool)
  - df -h on DB host to ensure no full filesystems
  - Check DB error logs for I/O/permission problems
- Confirm controller reachability and config
  - scontrol ping
  - scontrol show config | grep -E "Slurmctld|Slurmdbd"
- Inspect associations and QOS (common cause of misattributed usage)
  - sacctmgr show associations
  - sacctmgr show users
  - sacctmgr show accounts
  - sacctmgr show qos
- Validate recent job accounting records if specific jobs are missing/wrong
  - squeue (for active jobs)
  - sacct -j <jobid> --format=JobID,JobName,User,Account,State,Start,End,Elapsed,ExitCode
- Check time sync (timestamp issues cause apparent mis-attribution)
  - timedatectl status or chronyc sourcestats / ntpq -p on controller and compute nodes
- Verify backups and maintenance
  - Confirm scheduled DB backups exist and test a restore periodically

Likely problems and concise remediation actions
1) slurmdbd down / DB unreachable
   - Symptom: new jobs not recorded, slurmdbd errors in journal.
   - Remediation: examine slurmdbd journal/logs, fix DB connectivity (network/credentials), free DB disk space, then restart slurmdbd. If DB schema/permissions broken, restore from most recent backup.

2) Database full or corrupt
   - Symptom: write errors in slurmdbd logs, sacct/sacctmgr calls failing.
   - Remediation: free space or grow storage, repair/restore DB from backup. If corruption suspected, stop slurmdbd and take DB snapshot before repair.

3) Missing or incorrect user/account/association mappings
   - Symptom: usage not charged to expected account or jobs show "Unknown" account.
   - Remediation: create/modify associations with sacctmgr (e.g., sacctmgr create user name=alice account=acct), review and fix account limits or QOS as needed.

4) QOS/account limits rejecting or throttling jobs
   - Symptom: users report job rejections or severely throttled submissions; accounting shows unexpected usage patterns.
   - Remediation: inspect sacctmgr limits/QOS and adjust (sacctmgr modify account/qos ...), or increase quotas. Check fairshare if entitlement complaints appear.

5) Time synchronization issues
   - Symptom: job start/end timestamps inconsistent across nodes / negative or huge elapsed times.
   - Remediation: enable/fix NTP/chrony on all nodes and controller, then re-evaluate affected records.

6) Backup/restore gaps
   - Symptom: inability to restore or missing historical accounting data after failure.
   - Remediation: implement/verify regular DB backups, document restore procedure, test restores periodically.

- If you want, I can run any of the checks above and return the outputs (slurmdbd status/log tail, sacctmgr show associations, sacct for specific jobs, etc.). Tell me which check(s) to run.
- If you have a concrete problem (missing job records, counts mismatching, specific users affected), give me job IDs, user/account names, or the time window and I’ll inspect those records.

Summary of trigger fields and event (TYPE) meanings (from the strigger documentation)

- Key trigger fields you’ll see
  - TRIG_ID — trigger identifier.
  - RES_TYPE — resource type: job or node.
  - RES_ID — resource identifier: job ID, hostnames, or "*" (any).
  - TYPE — event type that causes the trigger.
  - OFFSET — time offset in seconds (negative = run before the event).
  - USER — owner who created the trigger.
  - PROGRAM — script/program run when the trigger fires.

- Event TYPE values and what they mean
  - time (job only) — job has reached its time limit. Often used with a negative OFFSET to run a warning or graceful shutdown before the limit.
  - fini (job only) — job finished/terminated (completion event).
  - down (job or node) — resource moved into a DOWN state (node failure or resource down event).
  - up (job or node) — resource moved back UP (node recovered).
  - drained (node only) — node was placed into DRAIN state.
  - idle (node only) — node became idle (no jobs running).
  - reconfig (node only) — node underwent a reconfiguration (e.g., after scontrol reconfigure).

- Other notable strigger capabilities
  - There are extra event flags for controller/burst-buffer events (e.g., backup slurmctld assume/failure/resume, burst_buffer errors) that let you trigger on controller or burst-buffer conditions.
  - Triggers are checked periodically (about every 15 seconds); any events occurring within that interval are evaluated and the trigger program is executed once for events in that interval.
  - OFFSET lets you schedule before/after an event (negative OFFSET runs before the event when possible).

colon-separated. If any variable, such as an Organization name, has a space in

## SPECIFICATIONS FOR CLUSTERS[#SECTION_SPECIFICATIONS-FOR-CLUSTERS](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sacctmgr.html)
Clusters can be created, modified, and deleted with sacctmgr. These
options allow you to set the corresponding attributes or filter on them
when querying for Clusters.
Classification =< classification >[#OPT_Classification](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sacctmgr.html) Type of machine, current classifications are capability, capacity and
capapacity.
Features [+|-]=< comma_separated_list_of_feature_names >[#OPT_Features](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sacctmgr.html) Features that are specific to the cluster. Federated jobs can be directed to
clusters that contain the job requested features.
To add or remove individual features, use the += or -= operators.
To clear all existing features, set a new value of '' (two single quotes with
nothing between them).
Federation =< federation >[#OPT_Federation](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sacctmgr.html) T...

Short summary — what each command does
- sacctmgr dump: write a flat-file representation of cluster association data (Cluster, Account, User, Parent, QOS lines). Use when copying/migrating or backing up account/QOS/association configuration.
- sacctmgr load: read a previously-created dump (or archive) file and insert/reconcile its associations into the SlurmDB (slurmdbd). Can be used to restore or import cluster associations.
- sacctmgr archive dump: export historical accounting records (jobs, events, etc.) to an archive file and (optionally) purge those records from the database. This is for long-term archival and database housekeeping.
- sacctmgr archive load: import archived accounting data back into the SlurmDB from an archive file.

Key differences
- dump/load (flat-file) = cluster association metadata (accounts, users, QOS, cluster definitions). Format is human-readable lines starting with QOS/Cluster/Parent/Account/User and colon-separated specs.
- archive dump/load = accounting records (job records, events). These are archival snapshots of historical data and are used to move, back up, or purge older accounting data.

Important behaviors & options
- Permissions: sacctmgr dump/load and archive operations must be run as a Slurm administrator (or root).
- File location: archive load requires the file to exist on the slurmdbd host (not necessarily the admin’s workstation). ArchiveDir in slurmdbd.conf is the default archive directory.
- Non-destructive vs destructive:
  - sacctmgr dump is non-destructive.
  - sacctmgr archive dump can be destructive if you include purge options — once records are purged they cannot be recovered except from the archive file you created. The operation cannot be rolled back.
- Purge control: archive dump honors either explicit command-line purge options or the Purge* settings in slurmdbd.conf (examples: PurgeJobAfter, PurgeEventAfter); if you don’t specify archiving options the configured slurmdbd.conf defaults are used.
- Load idempotency/duplicates: archive load will not insert records that already exist in the DB; attempting to load the same archive twice will fail for duplicate records. For association load (dump/load), there are options such as clean= to remove existing cluster/associations before loading, and insert/SQL options in advanced cases — read the man page for exact flags.
- Version compatibility: archive files from the current or prior Slurm releases can normally be loaded.

Typical workflows (step-by-step)

1) Backup or migrate cluster associations (accounts/QOS/users)
- On source cluster:
  - sacctmgr dump cluster=<clustername> file=<clustername>.cfg
- Transfer file to destination slurmdbd host.
- On destination:
  - (optional) sacctmgr load file=<clustername>.cfg
  - Use clean=account,qos,user if you intend to replace existing data (be careful; this deletes things).
- Verify associations with sacctmgr show and in the web UI (if present).

2) Archive old accounting data and purge DB
- Decide retention policy and test in a staging DB first.
- On slurmdbd host (example):
  - sacctmgr archive dump Directory=/archive Jobs=yes Events=yes PurgeJobAfter=365d PurgeEventAfter=365d
- Confirm archive file(s) were written to Directory (ArchiveDir default if unspecified).
- Verify integrity of archive files and then confirm the DB size/records decreased.

3) Restore archived accounting records
- Ensure the archive file is present on slurmdbd host.
- sacctmgr archive load File=/archive/<archivefile>
- Note: records already in DB will not be reloaded; duplicates will cause load to fail for those records.

Practical advice / safety checklist
- Always back up the SlurmDB (database) before archive/purge or destructive load/clean operations.
- Test load/archive workflows in a staging environment first.
- Keep copies of archive files outside the slurmdbd host (off-host backups) because purge is irreversible without those files.
- Verify file ownership/permissions so slurmdbd can read archive files.
- Use sacct/sacctmgr show queries after operations to confirm expected results.
- Consult the sacctmgr man page (sacctmgr(8) or Slurm docs) for exact option names and more advanced flags (clean=, insert=, Directory=, Jobs, Events, PurgeJobAfter, PurgeEventAfter, File=, Cluster=, etc.).

## Partition QOS [#partition](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
A QOS can be attached to a partition. This means the partition will have all
the same limits as the QOS. This does not associate jobs with the QOS, nor does
it give the job any priority or preemption characteristics of the assigned QOS.
Jobs may separately request the same QOS or a different QOS to gain those
characteristics. However, the Partition QOS limits will override the job's QOS.
If the opposite is desired you may configure the job's QOS with
`Flags=OverPartQOS` which will reverse the order of precedence.
This functionality may be used to implement a true "floating"
partition, in which a partition may access a limited amount of resources with no
restrictions on which nodes it uses to get the resources. This is accomplished
by assigning all nodes to the partition, then configuring a Partition QOS with
`GrpTRES` set to the desired resource limits.

### Job Scheduling Priority [#priority](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
Job scheduling priority is made up of a number of factors as
described in the [priority/multifactor](https://slurm.schedmd.com/priority_multifactor.html) plugin. One
of the factors is the QOS priority. Each QOS is defined in the Slurm
database and includes an associated priority. Jobs that request and
are permitted a QOS will incorporate the priority associated with that
QOS in the job's [multi-factor priority calculation.](https://slurm.schedmd.com/priority_multifactor.html)
To enable the QOS priority component of the multi-factor priority
calculation, the "PriorityWeightQOS" configuration parameter must be
defined in the slurm.conf file and assigned an integer value greater
than zero.
A job's QOS only affects is scheduling priority when the
multi-factor plugin is loaded.

### Job Preemption [#preemption](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
Slurm offers two ways for a queued job to preempt a running job,
free-up the running job's resources and allocate them to the queued
job. See the [Preemption description](https://slurm.schedmd.com/preempt.html) for
details.
The preemption method is determined by the "PreemptType"
configuration parameter defined in slurm.conf. When the "PreemptType"
is set to "preempt/qos", a queued job's QOS will be used to determine
whether it can preempt a running job. It is important to note that the QOS
used to determine if a job is eligible for preemption is the QOS associated
with the job and not a [Partition QOS](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html).
The QOS can be assigned (using sacctmgr ) a list of other
QOSs that it can preempt. When there is a queued job with a QOS that
is allowed to preempt a running job of another QOS, the Slurm
scheduler will preempt the running job.

## Configuration[#config](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
To summarize the above, the QOSs and their associated limits are
defined in the Slurm database using the sacctmgr utility. The
QOS will only influence job scheduling priority when the multi-factor
priority plugin is loaded and a non-zero "PriorityWeightQOS" has been
defined in the slurm.conf file. The QOS will only determine job
preemption when the "PreemptType" is defined as "preempt/qos" in the
slurm.conf file. Limits defined for a QOS (and described above) will
override the limits of the user/account/cluster/partition
association.

## QOS examples[#examples](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
QOS manipulation examples. All QOS operations are done using
the sacctmgr command. The default output of 'sacctmgr show qos' is
very long given the large number of limits and options available
so it is best to use the format option which filters the display.
By default when a cluster is added to the database a default
qos named normal is created.
```text
$ sacctmgr show qos format=name,priority Name Priority ---------- ---------- normal 0

$ sacctmgr add qos zebra Adding QOS(s) zebra Settings Description = QOS Name $ sacctmgr show qos format=name,priority Name Priority ---------- ---------- normal 0 zebra 0
```

```text
$ sacctmgr modify qos zebra set priority=10 Modified qos... zebra $ sacctmgr show qos format=name,priority Name Priority ---------- ---------- normal 0 zebra 10
```
Set some other limits

$ sacctmgr modify qos z...

## TRES information[#SECTION_TRES-information](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sacctmgr.html)
Trackable RESources (TRES) are used in many QOS or Association limits
(GrpTRES* / MaxTRES*). When setting limits, one or more comma-separated
"TRES=value" assignments can be specified.
Each TRES can be one of the Slurm defaults (e.g., cpu , mem ,
node ), or any defined generic resource. You can see the list of available
resources by running sacctmgr show tres .
Each TRES has a different limit, e.g., "GrpTRES=cpu=16,mem=32G" would
establish 2 different limits: one for 16 CPUs and another for 32 GB of memory.
Setting a new value for a TRES type does not affect any other TRES types that
were previously specified. For example, on the same entity as above, a
subsequent assignment of "GrpTRES=gres/gpu=2" will result in
"GrpTRES=cpu=16,mem=32G,gres/gpu=2" applying to that entity.

## Partition QOS [#partition](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
A QOS can be attached to a partition. This means the partition will have all
the same limits as the QOS. This does not associate jobs with the QOS, nor does
it give the job any priority or preemption characteristics of the assigned QOS.
Jobs may separately request the same QOS or a different QOS to gain those
characteristics. However, the Partition QOS limits will override the job's QOS.
If the opposite is desired you may configure the job's QOS with

partition, in which a partition may access a limited amount of resources with no
restrictions on which nodes it uses to get the resources. This is accomplished

`GrpTRES` set to the desired resource limits.

Slurm offers two ways for a queued job to preempt a running job,
free-up the running job's resources and allocate them to the queued

### Job Scheduling Priority [#priority](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
Job scheduling priority is made up of a number of factors as
described in the [priority/multifactor](https://slurm.schedmd.com/priority_multifactor.html) plugin. One
of the factors is the QOS priority. Each QOS is defined in the Slurm
database and includes an associated priority. Jobs that request and
are permitted a QOS will incorporate the priority associated with that
QOS in the job's [multi-factor priority calculation.](https://slurm.schedmd.com/priority_multifactor.html)
To enable the QOS priority component of the multi-factor priority
calculation, the "PriorityWeightQOS" configuration parameter must be
defined in the slurm.conf file and assigned an integer value greater
than zero.
A job's QOS only affects is scheduling priority when the
multi-factor plugin is loaded.

## Configuration[#config](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
To summarize the above, the QOSs and their associated limits are
defined in the Slurm database using the sacctmgr utility. The
QOS will only influence job scheduling priority when the multi-factor

preemption when the "PreemptType" is defined as "preempt/qos" in the
slurm.conf file. Limits defined for a QOS (and described above) will
override the limits of the user/account/cluster/partition
association.

## FLAT FILE DUMP AND LOAD[#SECTION_FLAT-FILE-DUMP-AND-LOAD](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sacctmgr.html)
sacctmgr has the capability to load and dump Slurm association data to and
from a file. This method can easily add a new cluster or copy an
existing cluster's associations into a new cluster with similar
accounts. Each file contains Slurm association data for a single
cluster. Beginning with version 25.05, QOS information is included in the
dump file. Comments can be put into the file with the # character.
Each line of information must begin with one of the five titles; QOS ,
Cluster , Parent , Account or User . Following the title
is a space, dash, space, entity value, then specifications. Specifications are
colon-separated. If any variable, such as an Organization name, has a space in
it, surround the name with single or double quotes.

### Job Scheduling Priority [#priority](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
Job scheduling priority is made up of a number of factors as
described in the [priority/multifactor](https://slurm.schedmd.com/priority_multifactor.html) plugin. One
of the factors is the QOS priority. Each QOS is defined in the Slurm
database and includes an associated priority. Jobs that request and
are permitted a QOS will incorporate the priority associated with that
QOS in the job's [multi-factor priority calculation.](https://slurm.schedmd.com/priority_multifactor.html)
To enable the QOS priority component of the multi-factor priority
calculation, the "PriorityWeightQOS" configuration parameter must be
defined in the slurm.conf file and assigned an integer value greater
than zero.
A job's QOS only affects is scheduling priority when the
multi-factor plugin is loaded.
