## Partition QOS [#partition](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
A QOS can be attached to a partition. This means the partition will have all
the same limits as the QOS. This does not associate jobs with the QOS, nor does
it give the job any priority or preemption characteristics of the assigned QOS.
Jobs may separately request the same QOS or a different QOS to gain those
characteristics. However, the Partition QOS limits will override the job's QOS.
If the opposite is desired you may configure the job's QOS with
`Flags=OverPartQOS` which will reverse the order of precedence.
This functionality may be used to implement a true "floating"
partition, in which a partition may access a limited amount of resources with no
restrictions on which nodes it uses to get the resources. This is accomplished
by assigning all nodes to the partition, then configuring a Partition QOS with
`GrpTRES` set to the desired resource limits.

## Relative QOS [#relative](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
Starting in Slurm 23.11, a QOS may be configured to contain relative resource
limits instead of absolute limits by setting `Flags=Relative`.
When this flag is set, all resource limits are treated as percentages of the
total resources available. Values higher than 100 are interpreted as 100%.
Memory limits should be set with no units. Although the default units (MB) will
be displayed, the limits will be enforced as a percentage (1MB = 1%).
NOTE : When Flags=Relative is added to a QOS, slurmctld
must be restarted or reconfigured for the flag to take effect.
Generally, the limits on a relative QOS will be calculated relative to the
resources in the whole cluster. For example, `cpu=50` would be
interpreted as 50% of all CPUs in the cluster.

## Partition QOS [#partition](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
A QOS can be attached to a partition. This means the partition will have all
the same limits as the QOS. This does not associate jobs with the QOS, nor does
it give the job any priority or preemption characteristics of the assigned QOS.
Jobs may separately request the same QOS or a different QOS to gain those
characteristics. However, the Partition QOS limits will override the job's QOS.
If the opposite is desired you may configure the job's QOS with
`Flags=OverPartQOS` which will reverse the order of precedence.
This functionality may be used to implement a true "floating"
partition, in which a partition may access a limited amount of resources with no
restrictions on which nodes it uses to get the resources. This is accomplished
by assigning all nodes to the partition, then configuring a Partition QOS with
`GrpTRES` set to the desired resource limits.

Slurm offers two ways for a queued job to preempt a running job,

## Backfill Scheduling [#backfill](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sched_config.html)
The backfill scheduling plugin is loaded by default.
Without backfill scheduling, each partition is scheduled strictly in priority
order, which typically results in significantly lower system utilization and
responsiveness than otherwise possible.
Backfill scheduling will start lower priority jobs if doing so does not delay
the expected start time of any higher priority jobs.
Since the expected start time of pending jobs depends upon the expected
completion time of running jobs, reasonably accurate time limits are important
for backfill scheduling to work well.
Slurm's backfill scheduler takes into consideration every running job.
It then considers pending jobs in priority order, determining when and where
each will start, taking into consideration the possibility of

# Gang Scheduling
Slurm supports timesliced gang scheduling in which two or more jobs are
allocated to the same resources in the same partition and these jobs are
alternately suspended to let one job at a time have dedicated access to the
resources for a configured period of time.
Slurm also supports preemptive job scheduling that allows a job in a
higher PriorityTier partition, or in a preempting QOS, to preempt other
jobs. [Preemption](https://slurm.schedmd.com/preempt.html) is related to Gang scheduling
because SUSPEND is one of the PreemptionMode s, and it uses the Gang
scheduler to resume suspended jobs.
A workload manager that supports timeslicing can improve responsiveness
and utilization by allowing more jobs to begin running sooner.
Shorter-running jobs no longer have to wait in a queue behind longer-running
jobs.
Instead they can be run "in parallel" with the longer-running jobs, which will

Below is a compact, actionable guide describing what good “backfill scheduling health” looks like, how to tell whether pending jobs “fit” the backfill windows, how to diagnose common problems, and which Slurm commands to run and interpret.

What backfill is (short)
- Backfill lets lower-priority jobs start early if doing so will not delay the expected start time of any higher‑priority job. It uses expected completion times of running jobs, so reasonably accurate time limits are essential.

What “queue fit” means
- A pending job “fits” the backfill window when there is an interval of idle resources (CPU/GPU/nodes) before the next higher‑priority job needs them, long enough to run the pending job without delaying that higher‑priority job. Good fit → short jobs start quickly on spare capacity; poor fit → idle resources sit unused while short jobs wait.

Healthy backfill — observable signals
- High sustained utilization (cluster/partition usage high during working hours). Low utilization suggests missed backfill opportunities or poor packing.
- Short jobs start promptly even when big jobs are queued (i.e., waiting times for short jobs are low).
- Low fragmentation: idle nodes are usable for a variety of pending jobs (not a few nodes with odd resources).
- sdiag/backfill metrics show backfill cycles actively placing jobs (see sdiag output for backfill stats).
- Minimal queue of short jobs with “Resources” available but not starting — if that happens, scheduler fitting or config is the issue.

Useful Slurm checks (commands and what to look for)
- scontrol show config | grep -i SchedulerType
  - Verify scheduler is backfill (sched/backfill). If SchedulerType=builtin, backfill won’t run.
- sinfo -s or sinfo -o "%P %D %a %l %t %n"
  - See partition/node counts (allocated/idle/down) and per-partition resource topology.
- squeue -o "%i %P %j %u %T %M %D %R %L"
  - Look for pending jobs, their requested time limit (L), node count (D), and pending reason (R). Lots of short jobs pending while nodes are idle signals fit problems.
- sdiag
  - Shows scheduler diagnostics and backfill statistics (cycles, decisions). If sdiag shows few backfill placements or very short backfill windows, investigate causes.
- sprio [--user or --partition]
  - See priority/fairshare factors. A misconfigured priority system can prevent eligible jobs from being considered.
- scontrol show job <jobid>
  - For a specific pending job, get full Reason, ReqNodes/TimeLimit, TRES — use when squeue’s reason is missing or vague.
- sinfo -R (sinfo_reasons)
  - Shows nodes in DRAIN/DOWN and why — drained nodes reduce backfill capacity.
- sshare / sreport
  - Check fairshare/account usage and long-term usage (are some accounts hogging resources?).

Common root causes and fixes
- Inaccurate/over‑estimated walltime:
  - Cause: Users set long walltimes; backfill windows are short.
  - Fix: Enforce/encourage realistic time limits, use max walltime caps per QOS/partition, enable job runtime auto-cancel or walltime warnings.
- Large, long-running jobs fragment resources:
  - Cause: Big jobs reserve blocks that break up free nodes into unusable pockets.
  - Fix: Use node packing policies, change SelectType/SelectTypeParameters to improve packing, or add partitions for large jobs; consider preemption or reservations.
- Scheduler configuration limiting opportunities:
  - Cause: default_queue_depth too small, sched_interval too large, or backfill plugin disabled.
  - Fix: tune default_queue_depth (consider raising carefully), reduce sched_interval, verify backfill plugin is enabled.
- Reservations / maintenance / drains:
  - Cause: Reservations or drained nodes reduce windows.
  - Fix: Inspect and adjust reservations (scontrol_reservation_show); bring nodes back or reschedule maintenance.
- Priority/QOS misconfiguration:
  - Cause: Short jobs get very low effective priority.
  - Fix: tweak QOS/priority weights, increase sharing for short jobs, use preemption if appropriate.
- Insufficient information about running jobs:
  - Cause: Users omit --time or use very large default times.
  - Fix: Encourage or enforce accurate time settings; use sched/backfill only when it can trust job run times.

Practical diagnosis workflow (quick)
1. Confirm scheduler: scontrol show config | grep SchedulerType
2. Get partition/node capacity and idle counts: sinfo -s
3. Look at pending/running jobs and reasons: squeue -o ... (include TimeLimit, ReqNodes, Reason)
4. Run sdiag to see backfill decisions/stats
5. For suspicious pending jobs, run scontrol show job <id> to get the exact Reason and ReqTRES
6. Check for drains/reservations: sinfo -R; scontrol_reservation_show
7. Check priorities/fairshare: sprio and sshare

Tuning levers to improve fit
- Enforce realistic walltime (QOS limits, submit filters, user education).
- Tune scheduler params: default_queue_depth, sched_interval (careful — changes affect scheduler CPU and behavior).
- Use packing and resource topology tuning (select/cons_res/gres configs) so available fragments are usable.
- Consider preemption or gang scheduling when appropriate to increase responsiveness for short jobs.
- Create separate queues/partitions for very large jobs so small jobs can backfill more easily.
- Use job submit plugins to validate requested resources and walltime.

Operator/metrics you should collect regularly
- Partition utilization (CPU/GPU usage) and average job wait times by job size.
- Number and proportion of pending short jobs that are eligible to start given current idle nodes.
- sdiag historical snapshot (backfill placements per scheduling event).
- Distribution of requested walltimes vs actual runtimes (to target user education/policy).

## EXAMPLES[#SECTION_EXAMPLES](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Specify a batch script by filename on the command line. The batch script specifies a 1 minute time limit for the job.
```text
$ cat myscript #!/bin/sh #SBATCH --time=1 srun hostname |sort $ sbatch -N4 myscript salloc: Granted job allocation 65537 $ cat slurm-65537.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
Pass a batch script to sbatch on standard input:
```text
$ sbatch -N4 #!/bin/sh > srun hostname |sort > EOF sbatch: Submitted batch job 65541 $ cat slurm-65541.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
To create a heterogeneous job with 3 components, each allocating a unique set of nodes:
```text
$ sbatch -w node[2-3] : -w node4 : -w node[5-7] work.bash Submitted batch job 34987
```

sbatch submits a batch script to Slurm. The batch script may be given to
sbatch through a file name on the command line, or if no file name is specified,

Short answer from the Slurm docs (sbatch + Job Array pages), with examples and the exact meanings:

1) Job-array identifiers — terminology
- ArrayJobID (aka the "job array's master job allocation number")
  - This is the Slurm job ID assigned to the array as a whole (the controller’s ID for the array). The sbatch response shows this master job ID.
  - scontrol fields: ArrayJobID = JobID of the first element of the job array.
- ArrayTaskID (aka the job array index)
  - This is the index value you specified with --array (e.g. 1,2,3 or 0-9). Each array element has its ArrayTaskID.
- Full element form: <ArrayJobID>_<ArrayTaskID> (example: 12345_3). Many Slurm tools accept that form to refer to a single array element (scontrol, scancel, etc.).
- Environment variables set inside array tasks:
  - SLURM_ARRAY_JOB_ID — the array’s master job id (ArrayJobID).
  - SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID — this element’s array index (ArrayTaskID).
  - Other related variables: SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_COUNT, SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_MAX, SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_MIN.

2) Filename replacement symbols used by --output/--error (from sbatch)
- %A — Job array’s master job allocation number (ArrayJobID). Same value for every element in that array.
- %a — Job array index number (ArrayTaskID). Varies per element.
- %j — jobid of the running job (the per-element jobid).
- %J — jobid.stepid (for steps; not typically needed for simple batch scripts).
- %b — job array index modulo 10 (useful for sharding into 10 buckets).
- %% — literal percent sign (escape).

3) Practical examples
- sbatch --array=1-3 --output=slurm-%A_%a.out myjob.sh
  - If sbatch returns "Submitted batch job 36" (ArrayJobID=36), files created will be:
    - slurm-36_1.out
    - slurm-36_2.out
    - slurm-36_3.out
  - %A is 36 for all files; %a is 1,2,3 respectively.
- If you want filenames keyed by the element’s unique jobid instead:
  - sbatch --array=1-3 --output=slurm-%j.out myjob.sh
  - Each element gets its own Slurm-assigned jobid in %j (not necessarily equal to ArrayJobID).

4) When to use which:
- Use %A_%a when you want a stable, predictable mapping to the array + index that matches ArrayJobID and the requested index values.
- Use %j when you care about the actual Slurm jobid assigned to that particular element.
- Use SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID in your script if you need the index value inside the job (rather than just in the filename).

References: sbatch filename-pattern (%A, %a, %j, %% ) and Job Array docs (ArrayJobID, ArrayTaskID, SLURM_ARRAY_* env vars) from the official Slurm docs.

## Backfill Scheduling [#backfill](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sched_config.html)
The backfill scheduling plugin is loaded by default.
Without backfill scheduling, each partition is scheduled strictly in priority
order, which typically results in significantly lower system utilization and
responsiveness than otherwise possible.
Backfill scheduling will start lower priority jobs if doing so does not delay
the expected start time of any higher priority jobs.
Since the expected start time of pending jobs depends upon the expected
completion time of running jobs, reasonably accurate time limits are important
for backfill scheduling to work well.
Slurm's backfill scheduler takes into consideration every running job.
It then considers pending jobs in priority order, determining when and where
each will start, taking into consideration the possibility of

Below is a compact, practical guide to reading Slurm utilization from reports (sreport) and scheduler diagnostics (sdiag, sprio, etc.), what the key metrics mean, how to diagnose common causes of low utilization, and what to try to fix them.

What the tools show (quick map)
- sreport (historical/aggregate usage)
  - Purpose: node-/TRES- (CPU/GPU/memory) time accounting across time windows, users, accounts, QOS, partitions.
  - Key fields you’ll see: Allocated (time nodes had active jobs or active reservations), Idle (node time idle), Down (nodes fully Down/Drained or slurmctld unavailable), PlannedDown, OverCommitted, Reported, TresName/TresCount.
  - Use: get utilization percentages and trends (e.g., last 7/30/90 days), CPU-hours / GPU-hours per user/account/partition, wasted node-hours, and reservation impact.

- sdiag (scheduler diagnostics)
  - Purpose: runtime snapshot of scheduler health and efficiency.
  - Useful outputs: scheduling cycle times (avg/median/max per scheduling cycle), number of jobs considered, backfill statistics (how much time was available for backfill), queue depth, and fragmentation/backfill failures.
  - Use: detect long scheduler cycles (causes slow responses), poor backfill effectiveness, or pathological queue churn.

- sprio (priority diagnostics)
  - Purpose: shows priority scores and contributing factors (fairshare, age, job size, QOS, partition).
  - Use: understand why jobs are ordered the way they are and whether fairshare/age/QOS are suppressing particular users.

- sinfo / sinfo_reasons / sinfo_node
  - Purpose: current partition/node states and reasons for drain/down.
  - Use: find how many nodes are Idle/Allocated/Down and why (hardware, admin drain, etc.).

- squeue / scontrol show job / sstat / sacct
  - Purpose: live queue state, detailed job config, runtime resource usage, historical per-job accounting.
  - Use: verify why jobs are pending (pending reason column or scontrol show), check whether running jobs actually use requested resources (sstat) and whether time limits are accurate (sacct/sreport).

Key metrics and how to interpret them
- Allocated node-time (node-hours): time nodes were running active jobs. This is the numerator for utilization.
- Idle node-time: node-hours not doing useful work while available. Long idle time → low utilization.
- Down/Drained node-time: node-hours unavailable due to failures/maintenance → reduces capacity and can explain low allocated time.
- OverCommitted: time nodes had more requested resources than physically available (rare/misconfigured).
- Backfill efficiency: how often lower-priority jobs were scheduled into gaps without delaying higher-priority jobs. Poor backfill → unused small windows.
- Scheduling cycle time: how long the scheduler takes between decision cycles. Very long cycles reduce responsiveness and can let idle windows persist.
- Queue depth / pending job counts: many pending jobs can indicate resource shortage, but if nodes are idle while jobs pending, that points to mismatch/fragmentation or constraints.
- Priority breakdown (sprio): which factor (fairshare, age, QOS) dominates a job’s score.

High-level utilization math (conceptual)
- Simple utilization percent (over a period): Util% ≈ Allocated_node_hours / (Allocated_node_hours + Idle_node_hours + Down_node_hours + PlannedDown_node_hours)
- sreport can already compute and break this down by partition/account/user so use its “Utilization” reports for easier numbers.

How to diagnose low/odd utilization (step-by-step checklist)
1. Look at usage trends
   - Run sreport cluster Utilization Start=now-30days (or similar) to see allocated vs idle vs down by partition/account.
   - Note any large Down or PlannedDown time; those reduce capacity.

2. Confirm current state
   - sinfo to see idle vs allocated vs down node counts and per-partition sizes.
   - If many nodes are drained/down, call sinfo_reasons to get the reasons.

3. If nodes are idle but jobs are pending:
   - squeue (with reason column) to see pending reasons (Resources, Dependency, QOSLimit, Priority, PartitionState, License).
   - If squeue’s reason is empty or unclear, scontrol show job <jobid> for detailed reason.

4. Check scheduler efficiency
   - sdiag to see scheduling cycle times and backfill statistics. Long cycle times or low backfill utilization indicate scheduler-side inefficiency.
   - sprio to see if priorities keep lower-priority jobs from running even when capacity is idle.

5. Check job packing and fragmentation
   - Many small jobs that request whole nodes, or many diverse resource requests, cause fragmentation so small windows can’t be filled.
   - Use sreport or sacct to look at job shapes (NCPUs, nodes per job, runtime distributions).

6. Check actual resource usage of running jobs
   - sstat (for running jobs) or sacct (for finished jobs) to measure CPU%/GPU usage and memory. Jobs that request more resources than they use waste capacity.

7. Look for policy/limits
   - Check QOS, per-user/account limits (sacctmgr show associations), and licensing (scontrol_license) if license restrictions block jobs.
   - Confirm preemption or reservation policies that may hold nodes idle for priority jobs/reservations.

Common causes and fixes
- Inaccurate time limits → Backfill suffers. Ask users to set realistic times; enforce max runtime or use auto-cancel.
- Jobs request whole nodes but use few cores → enable multi-job packing (Node sharing) or encourage/require resource accounting and job-array/mpi wrappers.
- Small-job fragmentation → use backfill, allow smaller-job placement or node-sharing; build “short” partition for short jobs or use job arrays to consolidate.
- Long scheduler cycle times → reduce sprio/sdiag overheads: investigate complex plugins, limit over-large job churn, or tune scheduler parameters (e.g., SchedulerType, MaxJobCount considered). sdiag points to cycle time issues.
- Hardware faults/drains → fix/proactively maintain nodes; track sinfo_reasons to prioritize repairs.
- Fairshare/QOS suppressing users → review sprio output and adjust fairshare weights or QOS limits if needed.
- Licensing / other resource scarcity → scontrol_license shows license counts; if license-limited, either increase license pool or partition jobs differently.

Operational metrics to monitor continuously
- Cluster utilization % (daily/weekly/monthly) by partition and by important accounts.
- Backfill utilization (from sdiag and by comparing scheduled vs wasted backfill windows).
- Scheduler cycle times (median/95th percentile).
- Queue depth and average wait time per job size class (short vs long, small vs large).
- Node health: downtime percentages and top reasons from sinfo_reasons.
- Per-job efficiency: CPU/GPU utilization averages, and top offenders by wasted node-hours (sreport can help).

Practical commands to run for routine checks
- sreport cluster Utilization Start=now-30days
- sinfo -Nl (node-level status) and sinfo -R (reasons)
- squeue --long or squeue --format=... (include REASON) to inspect pending reasons
- sdiag
- sprio --debug or sprio -l
- sstat -j <jobid> for running-job usage; sacct -j <jobid> for finished-job accounting
- scontrol show config (to inspect scheduler timeouts and limits)
- scontrol_license (if license constraints are suspected)

Interpretation examples (what to watch for)
- High Idle + many Pending jobs → likely fragmentation, partition mismatch, or constraints (QOS/Feature/License).
- High Down time + low Allocated → capacity is reduced; fix hardware or adjust planned maintenance windows.
- Low Allocated but sdiag shows low backfill utilization → time-limit inaccuracies or scheduler itemization problem.
- Large difference between requested CPUs and sstat CPU% → users over-request resources; consider enforcing stricter job templates or CPU accounting.

Bottom line / Actionable priorities
- Use sreport for trend-level utilization and to quantify wasted node-hours (allocated vs idle vs down).
- Use sdiag and sprio to find scheduler-level inefficiencies (cycle time, backfill, priority suppression).
- Correlate sreport findings with sinfo/squeue/sstat to find whether the problem is capacity (nodes down), fragmentation/requests, or scheduling policy.
- Fixes are usually: improve job time estimates, enable better packing/node-sharing, tune scheduler/backfill settings, repair nodes faster, and adjust fairshare/QOS/policies.

- Show the exact sreport/sdiag/sprio commands and example outputs to look for, or
- Walk through your cluster’s recent sreport + sdiag outputs if you share them (I can interpret concrete numbers and give prioritized recommendations).

Short answer
- Job 5001 (cuda_training) failed because a CUDA illegal-memory-access occurred in the job, which caused the process to abort. Evidence: sacct shows stderr "CUDA error: an illegal memory access was encountered" and scontrol_show reports JobState=FAILED Reason=NonZeroExitCode with ExitCode=134:0.

What the signals/exit code mean
- ExitCode 134 is consistent with an abort triggered by the runtime (commonly SIGABRT), which is what the CUDA runtime does when it detects an unrecoverable illegal memory access. scontrol's Reason=NonZeroExitCode confirms the job exited non‑normally.

What likely went wrong (most likely causes)
- A GPU kernel performed an out‑of‑bounds read/write or used an invalid pointer (illegal device memory access).
- A race/host-device synchronization bug (e.g., launching kernels asynchronously without checking errors).
- Mismatched CUDA driver vs. runtime or incompatible library (less likely but possible).
- In multi‑node/multi‑GPU training, corrupted buffers or a NCCL/messaging bug could have caused a GPU memory error.
- Less likely: hardware/GPU fault, but that should be verified if errors repeat on the same node.

Immediate diagnostic steps to run
1. Inspect the job stderr/stdout files produced by the batch (the cluster’s job output path). The sacct row already contained the CUDA error text — capture the full stderr file for stack traces.
2. Re-run the payload under CUDA debugging tools:
   - Run with CUDA_LAUNCH_BLOCKING=1 to get a synchronous failure location.
   - Run cuda-memcheck (memcheck, racecheck) to detect illegal accesses.
3. If you can reproduce interactively on one node/GPU, run under gdb or the CUDA debuggers to get a native backtrace at the failing CUDA API call.
4. Compare CUDA driver and toolkit versions used in the job with the cluster driver (nvidia-smi / nvcc --version) and verify NCCL versions if using distributed training.
5. Try a reduced configuration (single GPU, smaller batch) to see if it is deterministic.
6. Check for core dumps or kernel logs on the nodes used (dmesg / var/log/messages) for hardware errors.
7. If it’s multi-node, test the same code on a single node first; if single-node passes but multi-node fails, focus on NCCL/IB/communication layers.

Next actions you can take
- Collect and attach the job’s full stderr/stdout (job output files) and the node(s) names where it ran if you want me to help interpret further.
- If failures repeat on the same node, open a node‑health check (dmesg, nvidia-smi) or ask an operator to inspect that node’s hardware.

Here’s a concise explanation of how partition constraints and availability work for GPU jobs in Slurm, what affects whether GPUs are usable, and what to check when you need GPU capacity.

1) Partition basics
- A partition is a named queue: it groups nodes and sets defaults/limits (time, max nodes, allowed users/accounts/QOS, etc.). Jobs are allocated within one partition.
- Nodes can belong to more than one partition; each partition may have different policies (e.g., one partition for short GPU jobs, another for long runs).

2) How GPUs are modeled and requested
- GPUs are exposed as consumable resources (GRES) and TRES (e.g., gres/gpu or gres:gpu). Common request forms:
  - Older syntax: --gres=gpu:2 (request 2 GPUs on the same node)
  - Newer shorthand: --gpus=2 or --gpus-per-node=1 (depends on Slurm version)
- You can also request specific GPU types or features using constraints and GRES names (for example --constraint="v100" or --gres=gpu:tesla_v100:2 if configured).
- By default Slurm will try to satisfy the GPU count on a single node unless you also request multiple nodes.

3) Partition constraints that affect GPU availability
- Partition membership: only nodes assigned to the GPU partition(s) are considered for jobs submitted to that partition.
- QOS / account / user limits: QOS or account associations can limit how many GPUs a user/account can consume concurrently.
- Time/size limits: partition max-time or max-nodes can prevent large GPU jobs.
- OverSubscribe / sharing: partition OverSubscribe or node config controls whether multiple jobs can share a node’s GPUs or whether GPUs are exclusive. If oversubscribe is disabled, GPUs are exclusive.
- Reservations: active reservations for a partition or specific nodes can make GPUs temporarily unavailable.
- Node features / constraints: node features (set in slurm.conf) let you constrain nodes by hardware or software (e.g., GPU model). If you use --constraint, only nodes matching those features are considered.

4) What “available” GPUs mean in practice
- For a new GPU allocation, Slurm needs idle GPUs on nodes that match your partition and constraints.
- Idle GPUs = nodes shown as idle in sinfo (not allocated, not drained, not down, not reserved for others). Allocated, mixed, drained, or down nodes are not eligible.
- If a node is in “mixed” state it has some resources allocated and some free; whether it can serve your request depends on the requested shape and the node’s remaining free GPUs (but for conditional checks many admins treat mixed as not fully free).
- Nodes in multiple partitions: even if a node is in another partition as well, availability is determined by whether it’s idle for the partition you submit to and by partition policies.

5) How the scheduler decides
- Slurm considers partition, node features/constraints, GRES inventory (gpu counts/types), per-user/account/QOS limits, reservations, and node states when placing a job.
- Backfill works only when the scheduler can predict future allocations; complex per-node extra constraints can reduce backfill accuracy.

6) Quick checks and useful commands to inspect availability
- sinfo (partition and node summary) — shows node states (idle/alloc/drain) and partition membership. Look at the idle count; NODES(A/I/D) middle number > 0 means there are idle nodes in that partition.
- squeue — shows current jobs using GPUs (who’s holding resources).
- scontrol show node <node> — shows node’s GRES inventory and current allocations.
- scontrol show reservation — shows reservations that may block nodes.
- scontrol show config / scontrol show config | grep Gres — view GRES config.

7) Common pitfalls and troubleshooting
- You request more GPUs than any single node has (Slurm will wait unless you request multiple nodes explicitly).
- You request a specific GPU model/constraint but no idle node matches that feature.
- GPUs are held by other users/accounts or blocked by a reservation or QOS cap.
- Node is drained/down for maintenance or because of a driver/hardware issue — check sinfo -R or sinfo_reasons for reasons.
- Mismatch between gres.conf and slurm.conf (Slurm must be configured with correct GRES and types).

8) Practical submission examples
- Request 2 GPUs (same node): sbatch --partition=gpu --gres=gpu:2 ...
- Request specific model (if configured as a feature): sbatch --partition=gpu --constraint=v100 --gres=gpu:2 ...
- Request 1 GPU per node across 4 nodes (newer Slurm): sbatch --partition=gpu --nodes=4 --gpus-per-node=1 ...
(Exact flags available depend on your Slurm version; check local docs.)

command-line options `--bb` and `--bbf` may also include

Heterogeneous jobs may request burst buffers. Burst buffer hooks will run
once for each component that has burst buffer directives. For example, if a
heterogeneous job has three components and two of them have burst buffer
directives, the burst buffer hooks will run once for each of the two components
with burst buffer directives, but not for the third component without burst
buffer directives. Further information and examples can be found in the
heterogeneous jobs page.

The default directive for this plugin is `#BB_LUA`. The directive
used by this plugin may be changed by setting the Directive option in
burst_buffer.conf. Since the directive must always begin with a `#`
sign (which starts a comment in a shell script) this option should specify only
the string following the `#` sign. For example, if burst_buffer.conf
contains the following:
```text
Directive=BB_EXAMPLE
```
then the burst buffer directive will be `#BB_EXAMPLE`.
If the Directive option is not specified in burst_buffer.conf, then
the default directive for this plugin (`#BB_LUA`) will be used.
Since this plugin was designed to be generic and flexible, this plugin only
requires the directive to be given. If the directive is given, Slurm will run
all burst buffer stages for the job.

## Job Dependencies [#dependencies](https://slurm.schedmd.com/burst_buffer.html)
If two jobs use burst buffers and one is dependent on the other (e.g.
`sbatch --dependency=afterok:123 ...`) then the second job will not
begin until the first job completes and its burst buffer stage-out completes.
If the second job does not use a burst buffer, but is dependent upon the first
job's completion, then it will not wait for the stage-out operation of the first
job to complete.
The second job can be made to wait for the first job's stage-out operation to
complete using the "afterburstbuffer" dependency option (e.g.
`sbatch --dependency=afterburstbuffer:123 ...`).

Summary from the official Slurm "Burst Buffer Guide" (key points and examples of behavior / directives):

What a "burst buffer" request is
- Slurm supports burst buffers via a plugin (e.g., datawarp or the generic lua plugin). The plugin is enabled with BurstBufferType in slurm.conf and governs available directive names, semantics, pools, timeouts and validation.
- Jobs request either job-specific burst buffers or (for DataWarp) create/destroy persistent burst buffers.

Where to put burst-buffer directives
- Put burst-buffer directives as commented lines in the batch script (they begin with the plugin directive string, e.g. #DW, #BB, or #BB_LUA). They may appear before, after, or mixed with #SBATCH lines.
- The directive string used for a plugin can be configured (the lua plugin uses #BB_LUA by default; DataWarp uses #DW and Slurm also supports a #BB form for persistent operations).

Command-line alternatives
- salloc, sbatch and srun accept --bb (inline directives) and --bbf (filename with burst-buffer operations). Note: --bb cannot create or destroy persistent burst buffers; behavior of --bb depends on the plugin.

Common directive fields and plugin differences
- DataWarp (plugin) commonly uses directives like #DW (job-specific) and Slurm also supports #BB create_persistent / destroy_persistent for persistent buffers. For DataWarp, a job-specific request must include a capacity; if capacity is omitted the job is rejected.
- Fields you will see in docs/examples: capacity (size requested), pool (which pool to allocate from), access (access mode), name (for persistent buffers), hurry (option when destroying).
- The lua plugin is flexible; many lua-based deployments require only the presence of the directive (the plugin then runs the configured stages). Exact parameter names and semantics can vary by plugin/config.

Stage-in / stage-out behavior and lifecycle
- Burst-buffer work is performed in distinct stages that run at specific points in the job lifecycle:
  - staging-in / staged-in / pre-run — data is staged into the buffer before the job's main workload begins
  - running — job runs while buffer is available
  - post-run / staging-out / teardown — data is staged out and buffer is torn down after job completion
  - There are other internal states (pending, allocating, allocated, deleting, deleted, alloc-revoke, suspended, teardown-fail, complete).
- Slurm tracks a job's burst-buffer state in the job's BurstBufferState field (scontrol show job will display it).
- Stage-in must complete before the job enters the running state. Stage-out is performed after the job ends; some job dependencies respect stage-out timing (see dependencies below).

Timeouts, validation and diagnostics
- The burst-buffer plugin configuration exposes timeouts (e.g., StageInTimeout, StageOutTimeout, ValidateTimeout) and other plugin-specific parameters. You can inspect plugin/pool status with scontrol show burst (example output includes pool sizes, allocated buffers, StageInTimeout/StageOutTimeout values).
- DebugFlags=BurstBuffer in slurm.conf enables verbose plugin logging for troubleshooting.

Job dependencies and stage-out
- Normal job dependencies (e.g., --dependency=afterok:JOB) wait for the dependent job to finish, but they do not necessarily wait for the first job's burst-buffer stage-out to finish.
- If you need a later job to wait until a previous job's stage-out completes, use the afterburstbuffer dependency (e.g., --dependency=afterburstbuffer:12345). This ensures the second job does not begin until the first job's stage-out is complete.

Heterogeneous jobs
- For heterogeneous jobs with multiple components, burst-buffer hooks run once per component that contains burst-buffer directives. Components without directives do not trigger burst-buffer stages.

Persistent burst buffers (DataWarp)
- With DataWarp you can create and destroy persistent burst buffers from Slurm using directives such as:
  - #BB create_persistent name=<name> capacity=<size> [access=...] [pool=...] ...
  - #BB destroy_persistent name=<name> [hurry]
- Persistent buffer lifecycle (allocating/allocated/deleting/deleted) differs from job-specific buffers.

How Slurm executes the directives
- Slurm parses the commented directive lines and hands actual stage operations to the configured plugin. The --bb option causes Slurm to create a temporary burst-buffer script internally which the plugin uses; --bbf reads a file of operations.

Useful commands for users and admins
- Inspect job burst-buffer state: scontrol show job <jobid> (look for BurstBufferState)
- Inspect configured burst buffers and pools: scontrol show burst
- Use scontrol show config / slurm.conf to see BurstBufferType and plugin config
- For debugging: enable DebugFlags=BurstBuffer and check plugin-specific logs

Practical notes / best practices
- Always check which plugin your site uses (DataWarp vs lua) because required parameters and directive names differ.
- For DataWarp jobs, always specify capacity and, if needed, pool and access to avoid job rejection.
- If downstream jobs depend on the staged-out data, use afterburstbuffer dependency so you wait for stage-out completion.
- Keep burst-buffer directives near the top of the script; placing them as comments avoids shell interpretation and ensures Slurm parses them.

## Tree Topology (Hierarchical Networks) [#hierarchical](https://slurm.schedmd.com/topology.html)
Slurm can also be configured to allocate resources to jobs on a
hierarchical network to minimize network contention.
The basic algorithm is to identify the lowest level switch in the
hierarchy that can satisfy a job's request and then allocate resources
on its underlying leaf switches using a best-fit algorithm.
Use of this logic requires a configuration setting of
TopologyPlugin=topology/tree .
Note that slurm uses a best-fit algorithm on the currently
available resources. This may result in an allocation with
more than the optimum number of switches. The user can request
a maximum number of leaf switches for the job as well as a
maximum time willing to wait for that number using the `--switches`
option with the salloc, sbatch and srun commands. The parameters can
also be changed for pending jobs using the scontrol and squeue commands.

## topology/tree[#SECTION_topology/tree](https://slurm.schedmd.com/topology.conf.html)
This plugin requires you to use the select/cons_tres plugin.
The network topology configuration, each line defining a switch name and
its children, either node names or switch names.
Slurm's hostlist expression parser is used, so the node and switch
names need not be consecutive (e.g. "Nodes=tux[0-3,12,18-20]"
and "Switches=s[0-2,4-8,12]" will parse fine).
An optional link speed may also be specified.
All nodes in the
network must be connected to at least one switch. The network must be fully
connected to use TopologyParam=RouteTree . Jobs can only span nodes
connected by the same switch fabric, even if there are available idle nodes
in other areas of the cluster.
The topology.conf file for an Infiniband switch can be
automatically generated using the slurmibtopology tool found here:
<[https://github.com/OleHolmNielsen/Slurm_tools/tree/master/slurmibt...

- All four compute nodes are assigned to a single switch: switch0 (SwitchName=switch0 Nodes=cpu-node-01,cpu-node-02,gpu-node-01,gpu-node-02). That means there is no multi-switch network boundary to worry about for placement — any job that can be satisfied by node resources may be placed without crossing a leaf-switch boundary.
- However, node states remove many resources from the pool: there are currently no fully idle nodes in either partition (sinfo shows NODES(A/I/D) gpu 1/0/1, cpu 1/0/1). Topology placement is therefore constrained by which nodes are up/idle/allocated, not by switch layout in this cluster (because all nodes share the same switch).

Current node-level details (from sinfo)
- gpu-node-01 (partition: gpu) — STATE: down, CPUS: 0/32, MEM: 0/128G, GRES: gpu:4 — excluded from placement (hardware failure).
- gpu-node-02 (partition: gpu) — STATE: alloc, CPUS: 32/32, MEM: 128G/128G, GRES: gpu:4 — fully allocated, not available.
- cpu-node-01 (partition: cpu) — STATE: drain, CPUS: 0/64, MEM: 0/256G — excluded from placement (maintenance).
- cpu-node-02 (partition: cpu) — STATE: mix, CPUS: 48/64, MEM: 200G/256G — partially available (16 CPUs free); Slurm may place additional tasks on it subject to per-job resource requests and packing policy.

How Slurm topology placement constraints apply here
- If the cluster uses the topology/tree plugin (TopologyPlugin=topology/tree), Slurm will try to allocate nodes beneath the lowest-level switch that satisfies the job (and users can request a max number of leaf switches via --switches). In this cluster that would simply be switch0.
- Because all nodes are on the same switch, switch-count constraints (--switches) are effectively a no-op: any nodes eligible by state/resources are considered on the same switch.
- The real constraint now is node availability: nodes in DOWN or DRAIN are ignored by the allocator; MIX/ALLOC nodes may still provide remaining resources but are not fully free. In the current state there are no fully idle nodes in either partition, so multi-node allocations that require idle whole nodes will be delayed until nodes become free or repaired.

Practical implications
- Multi-node jobs will not be limited by switch-crossing in this setup (all on switch0), but will be limited by the small number of available/idle nodes.
- GPU jobs that require an idle GPU node cannot be satisfied today because there are 0 idle GPU nodes (gpu-node-01 is down, gpu-node-02 is allocated).
- CPU jobs that can fit on the remaining free CPUs of cpu-node-02 may still start (if the scheduler allows packing onto a mixed node), but there are only 16 free CPUs on that node.

If you want
- I can check whether TopologyPlugin is enabled (scontrol show config) and show the exact topology plugin behavior.
- Or I can list current running/pending jobs (squeue) or show per-node allocation detail (scontrol show node cpu-node-02) to see exactly which resources are free and whether a specific job would fit. Which would you like me to do?

Short answer
- scontrol reconfigure tells the Slurm controller (slurmctld) to reread its configuration and ask the Slurm daemons (slurmd, sackd, etc.) to reload config without doing a full process restart. It is the supported way to apply many configuration changes on a running cluster with minimal disruption.

What it does (technical summary)
- Sends an RPC to slurmctld asking it to reload slurm.conf and other configuration files (cgroup.conf, burst_buffer.conf, mpi.conf, plugin configs, etc.) and to propagate the new configuration to slurmd/sackd where possible.
- Daemons may re-read files or be signalled (equivalent to a SIGHUP in many cases) so settings that are reconfigurable take effect immediately.
- Reconfig behavior is controlled by ReconfigFlags (for example KeepPowerSaveSettings affects how power‑save state is preserved across a reconfigure).
- It is not a code upgrade — it does not replace running binaries or change options that were set on daemon command lines.

When to use scontrol reconfigure
- After editing slurm.conf or one of the Slurm config files when the change is supported by dynamic reconfigure and you want to avoid a full daemon restart.
- To update scheduling, partition, qos, plugin configuration, cgroup settings, burst-buffer settings, or many runtime parameters that Slurm documents as reconfigurable.
- When you want to roll out configuration changes without interrupting running jobs (for supported parameters).

When a full restart is still required (common examples / gotchas)
- Some changes cannot be applied dynamically and require restarting the daemons. Examples include (but are not limited to):
  - Changing daemon command-line options (ports, daemon-level --conf-server/--authinfo, a different Munge socket location).
  - Major node identity changes (renaming nodes / very large topology changes) — check docs; node definition changes sometimes require restarting/reconfiguring all slurmd and slurmctld.
  - Changes to binaries (upgrades) — you must restart to run new executables.
  - Certain plugin/init behaviors or configuration parameters that the docs explicitly mark as “restart required.”
- If you are unsure whether a particular parameter can be reconfigured, check the documentation for that parameter or confirm with a staged test.

Practical guidance / safe workflow
1. Check the docs for the files/parameters you changed (the slurm.conf, cgroup.conf, burst_buffer.conf pages indicate whether scontrol reconfigure applies).
2. Make the change on the controller (and on nodes if needed).
3. Optionally run scontrol show config (and inspect logs) to confirm current settings.
4. Run scontrol reconfigure on the controller to apply the change.
5. Watch slurmctld and slurmd logs for errors and verify cluster state (sinfo, squeue) after the reconfigure.
6. Schedule reconfigures during low load if possible; avoid scripting frequent/infinite scontrol calls (it’s an RPC and can overload slurmctld).

Warnings and tips
- scontrol reconfigure is an RPC to slurmctld — many repeated calls can degrade the controller. Don’t call it in tight loops.
- Some cluster features have ReconfigFlags that change how reconfigure behaves (for example preserving power-save state). Review those flags if you use power-save or other delicate features.
- When in doubt, test on a small subset or in a staging environment; if a setting really requires a restart, plan a maintenance window.

If you want, tell me which file/parameter you changed and I can check the docs for that specific setting and say whether scontrol reconfigure should be sufficient or if a restart is required.

sacctmgr is used to view or modify Slurm account information.
The account information is maintained within a database with the interface
being provided by slurmdbd (Slurm Database daemon).
This database can serve as a central storehouse of user and
computer information for multiple computers at a single site.
Slurm account information is recorded based upon four parameters
that form what is referred to as an association .
These parameters are user , cluster , partition , and
account . user is the login name.
cluster is the name of a Slurm managed cluster as specified by
the ClusterName parameter in the slurm.conf configuration file.
partition is the name of a Slurm partition on that cluster.

sacctmgr has the capability to load and dump Slurm association data to and
from a file. This method can easily add a new cluster or copy an
existing cluster's associations into a new cluster with similar
accounts. Each file contains Slurm association data for a single
cluster. Beginning with version 25.05, QOS information is included in the
dump file. Comments can be put into the file with the # character.
Each line of information must begin with one of the five titles; QOS ,
Cluster , Parent , Account or User . Following the title
is a space, dash, space, entity value, then specifications. Specifications are
colon-separated. If any variable, such as an Organization name, has a space in
it, surround the name with single or double quotes.

sacctmgr is used to view or modify Slurm account information.
The account information is maintained within a database with the interface
being provided by slurmdbd (Slurm Database daemon).
This database can serve as a central storehouse of user and

the ClusterName parameter in the slurm.conf configuration file.
partition is the name of a Slurm partition on that cluster.

Short summary
- sacctmgr add/modify/delete change the Slurm accounting database (slurmdbd). These changes affect accounting, fairshare, QOS and association limits and therefore can change scheduling decisions immediately for pending/new jobs. They do not edit slurm.conf or node state, but can indirectly prevent or allow jobs to start.
- Treat sacctmgr writes as high-impact administrative operations: back up the DB (dump), preview changes, use interactive mode, and coordinate with users.

Concrete safety implications (what to watch for)
- Permissions/authority: sacctmgr write operations require Slurm DB (slurmdbd) admin/operator privileges. Misuse can give or remove privileges (Admin/Operator, reservation rights).
- Immediate vs interactive commit:
  - Interactive mode lets you stage several add/modify/delete commands and review before committing.
  - The -i / --immediate option commits without confirmation. Don’t use -i unless sure.
- Backups & rollback:
  - Use sacctmgr dump or archive to export associations/accounts before making changes. You can reload with sacctmgr load if needed.
  - There is no automatic transactional “undo” of arbitrary destructive edits—plan for restore from dump if needed.
- Effects on scheduling and job eligibility:
  - Limits and QOS (GrpJobs, GrpTRES, MaxTRES, DefaultQOS, etc.) are consulted when a job is considered for allocation. Modifying group limits or QOS can immediately make pending jobs ineligible to start (or eligible).
  - Changes to TRES limits using +=/-= take effect and are bounded; accidental large changes can prevent scheduling or allow excessive resource use.
  - Fairshare/fair-share allocations are taken from the DB; changing shares changes job priority ordering and can reorder the queue.
- Deleting accounts/users/associations:
  - Deleting an account or user removes the association records in the DB. This can:
    - Affect how future job submissions are validated (submission without a valid account may be refused or billed to a default account depending on your config).
    - Change how pending jobs are evaluated (they may become ineligible if their account/QOS/association no longer exists or no longer meets limits).
  - Running jobs typically continue to run; however, behavior may depend on your site configuration and federation behavior. (Because site setups vary, assume deletes may affect pending-job eligibility and accounting; test or consult site policy.)
- QOS and preemption:
  - Changing QOS flags, grace times, or group limits can cause preemption decisions or change preemption eligibility. That may terminate or preempt running jobs if policy requires.
- Federation and cluster edits:
  - Removing a cluster from a federation or changing federation associations can change behavior for federated jobs; docs explicitly note running jobs may continue but pending federated jobs’ behavior changes.
- Audit & accounting integrity:
  - AdminComment and other accounting fields can be modified only by admins; modifying these affects reports and auditing.
  - Deleting entities can make historical accounting records harder to interpret; prefer to archive before removing.

Safe workflow / checklist (recommended)
1. Inspect current state
   - list associations and limits: sacctmgr show associations (or sacctmgr list account,user,qos,cluster) and use squeue/sacct to find active or pending jobs tied to the target accounts/users.
2. Backup
   - sacctmgr dump cluster=<name> file=backup.cfg (or use archive/dump) before destructive changes.
3. Stage changes interactively
   - Run sacctmgr in interactive mode, apply add/modify/delete commands without -i, review the planned changes, then commit.
4. Preview impact on queue
   - Use squeue and sprio/sshare/sdiag to see how priority/eligibility might change. Consider running sprio and sshare after edits to validate expected priority/fairshare effects.
5. Communicate
   - Notify affected users if you’ll delete accounts or change quotas/limits. Give a maintenance window if changes may delay jobs.
6. Commit and monitor
   - Commit changes (or use --immediate if already validated) and monitor squeue, slurmctld logs, and sdiag/sprio/sstat to confirm expected results.
7. Rollback if needed
   - If something breaks, restore from the dump file (sacctmgr load file=backup.cfg) or recreate associations. Test restore in staging first where possible.

Examples of safe commands to preview and protect yourself
- Preview association(s): sacctmgr show association withassoc cluster=<cluster> account=<acct> user=<user>
- List accounts/QOS: sacctmgr list account cluster=<cluster>; sacctmgr list qos
- Dump for backup: sacctmgr dump cluster=<cluster> file=/root/backup-<date>.cfg
- Use interactive mode to stage changes: sacctmgr (then run add/modify/delete inside, review, then commit)
- Use --immediate only after review: sacctmgr modify account where name=<acct> set GrpJobs=50 --immediate

Common gotchas to call out
- Using -i/--immediate without a dump can make mistakes hard to undo.
- Deleting an account that is the DefaultAccount for users can break future job submissions for those users.
- Changing group limits/QOS can silently block large numbers of pending jobs from ever starting.
- TRES arithmetic (+=/-=) can produce very large or zero values if misused; verify with sacctmgr show after change.
- Assumptions about running jobs: some changes (especially in federated setups) may behave differently—confirm with your cluster’s policy and test.

If you want, I can:
- give a short sample interactive sacctmgr session that shows safe staging and commit steps, or
- produce a one-line checklist script (commands to run in order) you can copy to run on your cluster (I will not run them).

Short answer
- "AssocGrpGRES" is the association/group-level GRES (Generic RESource) limit entry shown in sacctmgr/association listings. It represents limits on GRES usage (for example GPUs) that apply to the association (user/account/cluster/partition association) when Slurm evaluates whether a pending job may be allocated resources.

What association (group) resource limits do
- Association limits are per-association attributes maintained with sacctmgr and tested at job allocation time. Example group limits include GrpJobs, GrpTRES (trackable resources), and GRES-specific limits.
- If starting a job would cause any group limit to be exceeded, that job will not be considered for scheduling (it will remain pending). Group limits are enforced before attempting allocation; a job will not be started simply because it could preempt others to satisfy the limit.
- Limits are hierarchical. When multiple limits exist the precedence is: job QOS/partition QOS ordering rules, then user association, account association(s), cluster/root association, then partition-level limits (the first place a limit is defined is used).

Important GRES-specific behavior and pitfalls
- GRES limits are expressed as TRES entries (e.g. gres/gpu) or in higher-level fields such as GrpTRES. You can set limits addressing a specific GRES type (for example MaxTRESPerUser=gres/gpu:tesla=1).
- Type-specific limits have a design limitation: if a user requests a generic GRES (for example --gres=gpu:2) a limit set on a specific type (gres/gpu:tesla) will not be enforced. In other words, type-scoped limits do not prevent a user from requesting an untyped generic GRES and receiving two devices of that type unless additional submit-time checking is enforced (for example via a Lua job_submit plugin).
- TRES limit modifications using "+=" or "-=" are supported; attempting to set a negative value will set the TRES to zero. Large numeric bounds are handled up to the internal limit noted in the docs.

Operational effects of changing associations/limits
- Changes made with sacctmgr are uploaded to the controllers and take effect immediately for scheduling decisions.
- Deleting an association will immediately cancel running or pending jobs that belong to that association.
- Lowering a limit does not retroactively kill running jobs to satisfy the new limit; it only affects future allocation decisions.

Where to view and manage them
- Use sacctmgr to list and modify associations and their limits (association records contain fields for GrpTRES/GrpJobs/MaxTRESPerUser and related attributes).
- The Slurm resource_limits documentation describes the precedence, semantics, and example formats; the gres documentation describes GRES configuration and limitations.

I looked up the Slurm job state docs and summarized the four states you asked about.

RUNNING
- Meaning: The job has been allocated resources and is currently executing on compute node(s).
- Typical indicators: squeue shows state=RUNNING and an ELAPSED time; sstat works for real-time resource usage on running jobs.
- Notes: A RUNNING job may also carry flags (e.g., CONFIGURING or LAUNCH_FAILED) if there are intermediate problems while launching or cleaning up.

PENDING
- Meaning: The job is queued and waiting to start (not yet allocated).
- Typical causes: lack of free resources, job dependencies, BeginTime not reached, priority or QOS limits, association/account limits, reservation constraints, or admin holds.
- How to diagnose: squeue shows PENDING and normally a REASON column explaining why. For full detail use scontrol show job <jobid> to see dependency, time window, QOS/association info and any holds.
- Notes: PENDING is the common pre-start state; resolving depends on the reason (e.g., wait for resources vs satisfy dependency).

FAILED
- Meaning: The job finished unsuccessfully — typically it exited with a non‑zero exit code or encountered another failure condition during execution.
- Typical causes: application error (non‑zero exit status), prolog/epilog or launch failures, node problems, or resource exhaustion (which might instead be OUT_OF_MEMORY or NODE_FAIL depending on cause).
- How to diagnose: use sacct -j <jobid> (shows ExitCode and State) and scontrol show job <jobid> for detailed failure messages; check STDERR and job wrapper logs referenced by the job’s job script.
- Notes: FAILED is a base state; other more specific terminal states (NODE_FAIL, OUT_OF_MEMORY, etc.) may appear instead when applicable.

TIMEOUT
- Meaning: The job was terminated because it exceeded its requested TimeLimit.
- Typical causes: job runtime exceeded the time requested with --time (or default partition limit).
- How to diagnose: sacct -j <jobid> will report State=TIMEOUT (or show TIME_LIMIT expiring) and show elapsed vs requested time; scontrol show job <jobid> includes TimeLimit and RunTime fields.
- Notes: TIMEOUT is a terminal state distinct from FAILED; the scheduler enforces time limits and will kill jobs that run past them.

# Advanced Resource Reservation Guide
Slurm has the ability to reserve resources for jobs
being executed by select users and/or QOS and/or partitions and/or select
accounts.
A resource reservation identifies the resources in that reservation
and a time period during which the reservation is available.
The resources which can be reserved include cores, nodes, licenses and/or
burst buffers.
A reservation that contains nodes or cores is associated with one partition,
and can't span resources over multiple partitions.
The only exception from this is when
the reservation is created with explicitly requested nodes.
Note that resource reservations are not compatible with Slurm's
gang scheduler plugin since the termination time of running jobs
cannot be accurately predicted.
Note that reserved burst buffers and licenses are treated somewhat
differently than reserved cores or nodes.

## Reservation Use[#use](https://slurm.schedmd.com/reservations.html)
The reservation create response includes the reservation's name.
This name is automatically generated by Slurm based upon the first
user or account name and a numeric suffix. In order to use the
reservation, the job submit request must explicitly specify that
reservation name. The job must be contained completely within the
named reservation. The job will be canceled after the reservation
reaches its EndTime. If letting the job continue execution after
the reservation EndTime, a configuration option ResvOverRun
in slurm.conf can be set to control how long the job can continue execution.
```text

Reservations are automatically purged after their end time.

NOTE : By default, when a reservation ends the reservation request will be

I looked up the local Slurm documentation on reservations and summarized the key points and common commands below.

What a reservation is
- A reservation reserves specific resources (nodes, cores, licenses, burst buffers) for a defined time window so only allowed users/accounts/QOS/partitions may use them.
- A reservation is tied to a time period (StartTime + Duration/EndTime).
- By default reservations are associated with a single partition (they cannot span partitions) unless the reservation is created with explicit node names.

Common uses
- Reserve an entire machine for maintenance.
- Reserve nodes/cores for a particular user, account, or QOS for a workshop or debugging session.
- Reserve licenses or burst buffers (these are handled slightly differently than cores/nodes).

Create a reservation (examples)
- Basic: scontrol create reservation StartTime=now Duration=60 NodeCnt=1 CoreCnt=2 User=alan
- Specific nodes: scontrol create reservation StartTime=now Duration=60 Nodes=tux8,tux9 CoreCnt=2,4 User=brenda
- Restrict/deny users: you can specify users/accounts/QOS that are allowed, or explicitly prevent specific users (e.g., user=-alan).
- Flags you’ll commonly see:
  - maint — identify the reservation as maintenance for accounting.
  - ignore_jobs — allow creating the reservation even if running jobs occupy the resources (you may cancel those jobs).
  - NO_HOLD_JOBS_AFTER_END — let jobs continue running after reservation end instead of putting them on HOLD.

Inspect a reservation
- scontrol show reservation ReservationName=<name>
- The create command returns the generated reservation name if you don’t supply one (Slurm generates a name based on the first user/account plus a suffix).

Using a reservation
- Jobs must explicitly request the reservation when submitted: sbatch --reservation=<ReservationName> ...
- The job must fit entirely within the reservation time window and resource allocation.
- Jobs in the reservation are considered for scheduling before non-reserved jobs (reservation gives scheduling preference but does not change job priority).

End of reservation and overrun
- Jobs are normally cancelled when the reservation EndTime is reached unless ResvOverRun (in slurm.conf) lets jobs continue for a configured overrun period.
- Default behavior when a reservation ends: jobs submitted to that reservation are removed from the reservation and put on HOLD (unless NO_HOLD_JOBS_AFTER_END was set).

Delete a reservation
- Reservations are automatically removed after EndTime.
- You can manually delete: scontrol delete ReservationName=<name>
- A reservation cannot be deleted while jobs are running inside it.

Limitations / notes
- Reservations cannot span multiple partitions unless you list explicit node names.
- Reservations may not be compatible with certain scheduler plugins (e.g., Slurm’s gang scheduler) because job termination timing can be affected.
- By default only resources not expected to have a running job at the reservation start can be reserved; use ignore_jobs to override.

Useful commands (quick reference)
- Create: scontrol create reservation StartTime=... Duration=... Nodes=... NodeCnt=... CoreCnt=... User=... Account=... Partition=...
- Show: scontrol show reservation ReservationName=<name>
- Delete: scontrol delete ReservationName=<name>
- Submit a job into a reservation: sbatch --reservation=<name> myscript.sh

## Partition QOS [#partition](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
A QOS can be attached to a partition. This means the partition will have all
the same limits as the QOS. This does not associate jobs with the QOS, nor does
it give the job any priority or preemption characteristics of the assigned QOS.
Jobs may separately request the same QOS or a different QOS to gain those
characteristics. However, the Partition QOS limits will override the job's QOS.
If the opposite is desired you may configure the job's QOS with
`Flags=OverPartQOS` which will reverse the order of precedence.
This functionality may be used to implement a true "floating"
partition, in which a partition may access a limited amount of resources with no
restrictions on which nodes it uses to get the resources. This is accomplished
by assigning all nodes to the partition, then configuring a Partition QOS with
`GrpTRES` set to the desired resource limits.

## Relative QOS [#relative](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
Starting in Slurm 23.11, a QOS may be configured to contain relative resource
limits instead of absolute limits by setting `Flags=Relative`.
When this flag is set, all resource limits are treated as percentages of the
total resources available. Values higher than 100 are interpreted as 100%.
Memory limits should be set with no units. Although the default units (MB) will
be displayed, the limits will be enforced as a percentage (1MB = 1%).
NOTE : When Flags=Relative is added to a QOS, slurmctld
must be restarted or reconfigured for the flag to take effect.
Generally, the limits on a relative QOS will be calculated relative to the
resources in the whole cluster. For example, `cpu=50` would be
interpreted as 50% of all CPUs in the cluster.

## Hierarchy[#hierarchy](https://slurm.schedmd.com/resource_limits.html)
Slurm's hierarchical limits are enforced in the following order
with Job QOS and Partition QOS order being reversible by using the QOS
flag 'OverPartQOS':
- Partition QOS limit
- Job QOS limit
- User association
- Account association(s), ascending the hierarchy
- Root/Cluster association
- Partition limit
- None
Note: If limits are defined at multiple points in this hierarchy,
the point in this list where the limit is first defined will be used.
Consider the following example:
- MaxJobs=20 and MaxSubmitJobs is undefined in the partition QOS
- No limits are set in the job QOS and
- MaxJobs=4 and MaxSubmitJobs=50 in the user association
The limits in effect will be MaxJobs=20 and MaxSubmitJobs=50.

enforced so it will still be possible to get two teslas.

## Configuration[#config](https://slurm.schedmd.com/resource_limits.html)
Scheduling policy information must be stored in a database
as specified by the AccountingStorageType configuration parameter
in the slurm.conf configuration file.
Information can be recorded in a [MySQL](http://www.mysql.com/) or
[MariaDB](https://mariadb.org/) database.
For security and performance reasons, the use of
SlurmDBD (Slurm Database Daemon) as a front-end to the
database is strongly recommended.
SlurmDBD uses a Slurm authentication plugin (e.g. MUNGE).
SlurmDBD also uses an existing Slurm accounting storage plugin
to maximize code reuse.
SlurmDBD uses data caching and prioritization of pending requests
in order to optimize performance.
While SlurmDBD relies upon existing Slurm plugins for authentication
and database use, the other Slurm commands and daemons are not required
on the host where SlurmDBD is installed.

## Tools[#tools](https://slurm.schedmd.com/resource_limits.html)
The tool used to manage accounting policy is sacctmgr .
It can be used to create and delete cluster, user, account,
and partition records plus their combined association record.
See man sacctmgr for details on this tools and examples of
its use.
Changes made to the scheduling policy are uploaded to
the Slurm control daemons on the various clusters and take effect
immediately. When an association is deleted, all running or pending
jobs which belong to that association are immediately canceled.
When limits are lowered, running jobs will not be canceled to
satisfy the new limits, but the new lower limits will be enforced.

Various limits and limit enforcement are described in
the [Resource Limits](https://slurm.schedmd.com/resource_limits.html) web page.
To enable any limit enforcement you must at least have
AccountingStorageEnforce=limits in your slurm.conf.

### Job Scheduling Priority [#priority](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
Job scheduling priority is made up of a number of factors as
described in the [priority/multifactor](https://slurm.schedmd.com/priority_multifactor.html) plugin. One
of the factors is the QOS priority. Each QOS is defined in the Slurm
database and includes an associated priority. Jobs that request and
are permitted a QOS will incorporate the priority associated with that
QOS in the job's [multi-factor priority calculation.](https://slurm.schedmd.com/priority_multifactor.html)
To enable the QOS priority component of the multi-factor priority
calculation, the "PriorityWeightQOS" configuration parameter must be
defined in the slurm.conf file and assigned an integer value greater
than zero.
A job's QOS only affects is scheduling priority when the
multi-factor plugin is loaded.

### Job Preemption [#preemption](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
Slurm offers two ways for a queued job to preempt a running job,
free-up the running job's resources and allocate them to the queued
job. See the [Preemption description](https://slurm.schedmd.com/preempt.html) for
details.
The preemption method is determined by the "PreemptType"
configuration parameter defined in slurm.conf. When the "PreemptType"
is set to "preempt/qos", a queued job's QOS will be used to determine
whether it can preempt a running job. It is important to note that the QOS
used to determine if a job is eligible for preemption is the QOS associated
with the job and not a [Partition QOS](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html).
The QOS can be assigned (using sacctmgr ) a list of other
QOSs that it can preempt. When there is a queued job with a QOS that
is allowed to preempt a running job of another QOS, the Slurm
scheduler will preempt the running job.

Scheduling policy information must be stored in a database
as specified by the AccountingStorageType configuration parameter
in the slurm.conf configuration file.
Information can be recorded in a [MySQL](http://www.mysql.com/) or
[MariaDB](https://mariadb.org/) database.
For security and performance reasons, the use of
SlurmDBD (Slurm Database Daemon) as a front-end to the
database is strongly recommended.
SlurmDBD uses a Slurm authentication plugin (e.g. MUNGE).
SlurmDBD also uses an existing Slurm accounting storage plugin
to maximize code reuse.
SlurmDBD uses data caching and prioritization of pending requests
in order to optimize performance.

## Job Submission [#jobsubmission](https://slurm.schedmd.com/federation.html)
When a federated cluster receives a job submission, it will submit copies of the
job ( sibling jobs ) to each eligible cluster. Each cluster will then
independently attempt to schedule the job.
Jobs can be directed to specific clusters in the federation using the
-M,--clusters=<cluster_list> and the new
--cluster-constraint=[!]<constraint_list> options.
Using the -M,--clusters=<cluster_list> the submission command
(sbatch, salloc, srun) will pick one cluster from the list of clusters to submit
the job to and will also pass along the list of clusters with the job. The
clusters in the list will be the only viable clusters that siblings jobs can be
submitted to. For example the submission:

## Hierarchy[#hierarchy](https://slurm.schedmd.com/resource_limits.html)
Slurm's hierarchical limits are enforced in the following order
with Job QOS and Partition QOS order being reversible by using the QOS
flag 'OverPartQOS':
- Partition QOS limit
- Job QOS limit

A QOS can be attached to a partition. This means the partition will have all
the same limits as the QOS. This does not associate jobs with the QOS, nor does
it give the job any priority or preemption characteristics of the assigned QOS.
Jobs may separately request the same QOS or a different QOS to gain those
characteristics. However, the Partition QOS limits will override the job's QOS.
If the opposite is desired you may configure the job's QOS with

partition, in which a partition may access a limited amount of resources with no
restrictions on which nodes it uses to get the resources. This is accomplished

The backfill scheduling plugin is loaded by default.
Without backfill scheduling, each partition is scheduled strictly in priority
order, which typically results in significantly lower system utilization and
responsiveness than otherwise possible.

Summary
- QOS limits in Slurm control how many jobs and how many resources (CPUs, memory, GPUs, etc.) a QOS, user, account, partition or cluster may consume.
- Limits are configured in the Slurm DB (sacctmgr) and follow a hierarchy (partition QOS → job QOS → user association → account → cluster → partition defaults). See the Slurm docs: resource_limits and qos pages.

Key limit types and what they mean (official-doc semantics)

1) MaxJobs / MaxSubmitJobs
- MaxJobs
  - Limits the number of jobs for the entity (commonly interpreted as the number of concurrently active jobs for that QOS/association). If starting a job would cause the MaxJobs limit to be exceeded, the job will not be considered for allocation (it will pend) unless DenyOnLimit is set (see below). (resource_limits, sacctmgr docs)
- MaxSubmitJobs
  - Controls how many jobs may be submitted/from that entity (submit-time throttling). It’s a separate cap than MaxJobs; both can be present and the effective limits follow the hierarchy rules. (resource_limits)
- Example related fields for aggregates:
  - GrpJobs — maximum number of running jobs in aggregate for that QOS (or association).

2) CPU limits (MaxCPUs and the TRES model)
- Slurm tracks consumable resources as TRES (Trackable RESources). CPU limits are expressed as the cpu TRES (cpu=N).
- Common ways to limit CPU usage via QOS/associations:
  - MaxTRESPerJob=cpu=N — maximum CPUs a single job may request.
  - MaxTRESPerUser=cpu=N — maximum CPUs a single user may have in use (or concurrently allocated), when set on the QOS/association.
  - GrpTRES=cpu=N — group aggregate CPU limit (aggregate across that QOS/account).
- Partition-level and configuration-level CPU caps exist too:
  - Partition/partition-defaults can specify MaxCPUsPerNode, MaxCPUsPerSocket, MaxNodes, etc., which affect how many CPUs can be allocated from nodes. (scontrol / partition docs; cpu_management docs)
- In practice: to limit "MaxCPUs" for a QOS you typically set MaxTRES* entries for cpu (e.g., MaxTRESPerUser=cpu=128 or MaxTRESPerJob=cpu=32), or set GrpTRES for aggregate caps. (sacctmgr / resource_limits docs)

3) Interaction, precedence, and enforcement behavior
- Precedence/hierarchy: limits defined on a Partition QOS or Job QOS will take precedence over association limits (user/account) unless Flags=OverPartQOS is used to reverse precedence. If the same limit is present in multiple places, the first point in the hierarchy is used. (resource_limits)
- Default enforcement behavior:
  - By default, if a job would exceed a limit when considered together with other jobs, the job will pend (not be denied). If you want jobs that individually would violate a “Max” limit to be rejected at submission time, set the QOS flag DenyOnLimit. (qos docs)
- Accounting enforcement:
  - Limit enforcement requires accounting enforcement to be enabled (AccountingStorageEnforce must include limits in slurm.conf). If enforcement is disabled, limits may be recorded but not enforced. (accounting/resource_limits docs)

4) Group/aggregate limits and special cases
- GrpTRES, GrpJobs, GrpSubmitJobs etc. are aggregate/group limits that are checked when attempting to start a job. If starting a job would cause a group limit to be exceeded, that job won’t be considered for scheduling. (sacctmgr docs)
- GRES (generic resources, e.g., GPUs): type-specific limits can be set (e.g., MaxTRESPerUser=gres/gpu:tesla=1) but there is a caveat: if a user requests a generic --gres=gpu:2 (without specifying type), a type-specific limit may not always be enforced (design limitation). The docs recommend using a submit plugin to enforce model-specific behavior when needed. (resource_limits)

How to view / set these (doc-guided commands)
- View QOS limits: sacctmgr show qos format=... (see sacctmgr docs and qos page).
- Set/modify limits: sacctmgr create/modify qos ... or sacctmgr modify assoc ... (sacctmgr manpage and examples in the sacctmgr docs).
- Examples in the docs:
  - sacctmgr modify user where name=<user> set MaxJobs=4 MaxTRESPerUser=cpu=64
  - sacctmgr modify qos name=<qos> set GrpTRES=cpu=200,mem=500G Flags=DenyOnLimit
  (See sacctmgr and qos documentation for precise syntax and available fields.)

Pointers to the official documentation (read first)
- QOS page (limits, DenyOnLimit, OverPartQOS): https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html
- Resource Limits (hierarchy, TRES, group limits, examples): https://slurm.schedmd.com/resource_limits.html
- sacctmgr (fields and how to create/modify QOS/associations): https://slurm.schedmd.com/sacctmgr.html
- Job reason codes (you’ll see reason codes when jobs pend due to limits): https://slurm.schedmd.com/job_reason_codes.html

Short summary of the common squeue format fields you asked about, and how to use them.

Format codes (printf-style) — examples you can pass to squeue -o:
- %i — Job ID. Prints the numeric JOBID (same as the JOBID column). You can add width/precision like "%.6i" to right‑justify/pad to 6 digits.
- %u — User. Prints the job owner’s login name (same as the USER column). Width modifiers (e.g. "%-12u") control alignment/truncation.
- %T and %t — State:
  - %T prints the full, human‑readable state name (e.g., RUNNING, PENDING, COMPLETED).
  - %t prints the short/compact state code used in the ST column (e.g., R, PD, CG). Use whichever form you prefer.
- %R — Reason. Prints the scheduler’s pending reason string (e.g., “Resources”, “Priority”) for jobs that are not yet started. For running jobs this is typically empty. Note: the special column NODELIST(REASON) will show the node list and, for pending jobs, the reason in parentheses.

Other notes:
- You may also use column names instead of percent codes (for example: squeue -o "JOBID USER STATE REASON").
- Format modifiers work like printf: width, left/right alignment, precision (e.g. "%-10u", "%10i", "%.20R").
- If you need the detailed pending reason for a single job beyond what squeue shows, scontrol show job <jobid> provides more fields.

Example usage:
- squeue -o "%i %u %T %R"
- squeue -o "%.8i %-12u %-10T %.30R"

Slurm generally classifies users into three authorization levels:
- Administrators include root, SlurmUser, and any users with

- Privileged Users include all Administrators and any users with
