Below are the scontrol show job fields that are most useful to read and why they matter. I’ve grouped them by purpose (identity, scheduling, resources, timing, I/O & control, and failure/troubleshooting).

Identity / ownership
- JobId — unique numeric job identifier (what you use with squeue/scontrol/scancel).
- JobName — human name given at submit; helpful when multiple jobs from same user exist.
- UserId / GroupId — owner and group (often shown as name(uid)); needed for access/authorization checks.

Scheduling / policy
- Partition — partition the job was submitted to (affects available resources and limits).
- Account / QOS — accounting and quality-of-service used for scheduling/limits and fairshare.
- Priority — scheduler priority value; higher is scheduled earlier.
- Reservation — name of any reservation the job is tied to (if set).

State & reason
- JobState — RUNNING / PENDING / COMPLETED / FAILED / CANCELLED / SUSPENDED / etc.
- Reason — short pending reason shown for PENDING jobs (eg, Resources, Priority, ReqNodeNotAvail). Useful for “why isn’t it starting?” troubleshooting.
- Nodes / NodeList / NumNodes — nodes allocated (for RUNNING) or requested (for pending). NodeList shows concrete node names.
- AllocNode:Sid — the node and system id that granted the allocation (useful for debugging allocation ownership).
- BatchFlag — indicates how the job was submitted (BatchFlag=1 for sbatch); increments on requeue.

Requested vs allocated resources
- TRES and ReqTRES — requested Trackable RESources (e.g., tres=cpu=4,mem=32G,gres/gpu=2). Shows what the job asked for.
- AllocTRES — resources actually allocated to the job (what the system gave). Compare AllocTRES vs ReqTRES to confirm allocations.
- NNodes / NTasks / CPUsPerTask / NumCPUs — counts of nodes, tasks, CPUs per task or total CPUs: how the job is sized across nodes.
- ReqMem / MinMemoryPerNode / MinMemoryCPU — memory request settings (per node or per job); important for OOM problems.
- Gres / ReqGRES — generic resources requested (often GPUs). If you requested GPUs, check that AllocTRES shows gres/gpu entries.

Time & timing
- SubmitTime — when the job was submitted.
- EligibleTime — when the job became eligible to run (after dependency/wait conditions).
- StartTime — actual start time (for RUNNING/COMPLETED jobs).
- EndTime — completion time (for COMPLETED/FAILED).
- TimeLimit / TimeMin — requested runtime limit and minimum time; useful to know if a job may be preempted or killed for exceeding limit.
- RunTime / Elapsed — how long the job has been running (for RUNNING jobs).

I/O, environment, control
- WorkDir — working directory where the job started.
- StdOut / StdErr — paths to stdout/stderr files (where application logs go).
- Command (or BatchScript) — the submitted command or path to batch script (so you can inspect what ran).
- Dependency — any job dependencies (afterok, afterany, etc.).
- Requeue / Reboot / Hold — flags controlling requeueing, reboot on failure, or hold status.

Exit / failure diagnostics
- ExitCode — format "<exit>:<signal>" for finished jobs; primary indicator of why a job failed.
- Reason (for COMPLETED/FAILED/CANCELLED) — may include cause text for failure.
- State and related message — together with ExitCode, tells whether the job was preempted, killed by the system, timed out, or finished normally.

Advanced / detailed fields (use scontrol show job <id> with details)
- LaunchParameters / JobStepInfo — per-step allocation details when a job uses multiple steps.
- NumCPUsAlloc / CPUSets / NUMA info — CPU placement and NUMA memory allocation (only shown with details).
- AllocNodes / NodeState info — per-node CPU/memory mapping for the job (useful for NUMA/debug performance problems).

Quick usage tips
- For “why pending” start with squeue (shows Reason column); scontrol show job <id> gives fuller fields including dependencies and requested resources.
- If a job fails, inspect ExitCode, StdErr path, and the JobState/Reason in scontrol output.
- Compare ReqTRES / ReqMem / NTasks with AllocTRES / AllocNodes to spot partial allocations or unmet requests (common with GRES/GPU requests).

- explain any specific field in more depth (which field?).

## PERFORMANCE[#SECTION_PERFORMANCE](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sdiag.html)
Executing sdiag sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from sdiag or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmctld daemon come in at once, it can result in
a degradation of performance of the slurmctld daemon, possibly resulting
in a denial of service.
Do not run sdiag or other Slurm client commands that send remote procedure
calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other programs. Ensure
that programs limit calls to sdiag to the minimum necessary for the
information you are trying to gather.

## Backfill Scheduling [#backfill](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sched_config.html)
The backfill scheduling plugin is loaded by default.
Without backfill scheduling, each partition is scheduled strictly in priority
order, which typically results in significantly lower system utilization and
responsiveness than otherwise possible.
Backfill scheduling will start lower priority jobs if doing so does not delay
the expected start time of any higher priority jobs.
Since the expected start time of pending jobs depends upon the expected
completion time of running jobs, reasonably accurate time limits are important
for backfill scheduling to work well.
Slurm's backfill scheduler takes into consideration every running job.
It then considers pending jobs in priority order, determining when and where
each will start, taking into consideration the possibility of

# Gang Scheduling
Slurm supports timesliced gang scheduling in which two or more jobs are
allocated to the same resources in the same partition and these jobs are
alternately suspended to let one job at a time have dedicated access to the
resources for a configured period of time.
Slurm also supports preemptive job scheduling that allows a job in a
higher PriorityTier partition, or in a preempting QOS, to preempt other
jobs. [Preemption](https://slurm.schedmd.com/preempt.html) is related to Gang scheduling
because SUSPEND is one of the PreemptionMode s, and it uses the Gang
scheduler to resume suspended jobs.
A workload manager that supports timeslicing can improve responsiveness
and utilization by allowing more jobs to begin running sooner.
Shorter-running jobs no longer have to wait in a queue behind longer-running
jobs.
Instead they can be run "in parallel" with the longer-running jobs, which will

## Timeslicer Design and Operation [#time_slice](https://slurm.schedmd.com/gang_scheduling.html)
When enabled, the gang scheduler keeps track of the resources
allocated to all jobs. For each partition an "active bitmap" is maintained that
tracks all concurrently running jobs in the Slurm cluster. Each time a new
job is allocated to resources in a partition, the gang scheduler
compares these newly allocated resources with the resources already maintained
in the "active bitmap".
If these two sets of resources are disjoint then the new job is added to the "active bitmap". If these two sets of resources overlap then
the new job is suspended. All jobs are tracked in a per-partition job queue
within the gang scheduler logic.

sdiag - Scheduling diagnostic tool for Slurm

sdiag
 
   
 DESCRIPTION 
sdiag shows information related to slurmctld execution about: threads, agents,
jobs, and scheduling algorithms. The goal is to obtain data from slurmctld
behavior helping to adjust configuration parameters or queues policies. The
main reason behind is to know Slurm behavior under systems with a high throughput.

and statistics explained later, and there is another execution option

Values are reset at midnight UTC time by default.
 

The first block of information is related to global slurmctld execution:
 
 
 Server thread count The number of current active slurmctld threads. A high number would mean a high
load processing events like job submissions, jobs dispatching, jobs completing,
etc. If this is often close to MAX_SERVER_THREADS it could point to a potential
bottleneck.
 
 
 Agent queue size Slurm design has scalability in mind and sending messages to thousands of nodes
is not a trivial task. The agent mechanism helps to control communication
between slurmctld and the slurmd daemons for a best effort. This value denotes
the count of enqueued outgoing RPC requests in an internal retry list.
 
 
 Agent count Number of agent threads. Each of these agent threads can create in turn a group
of up to 2 + AGENT_THREAD_COUNT active threads at a time.

separate thread. If the SlurmDBD, or database, is down then this number will
increase.

Section: Slurm Commands (1) Updated: Slurm Commands Index 

 
   
 NAME 
sdiag - Scheduling diagnostic tool for Slurm
 
   
 SYNOPSIS 
sdiag
 
   
 DESCRIPTION 
sdiag shows information related to slurmctld execution about: threads, agents,
jobs, and scheduling algorithms. The goal is to obtain data from slurmctld
behavior helping to adjust configuration parameters or queues policies. The
main reason behind is to know Slurm behavior under systems with a high throughput.
 

It has two execution modes. The default mode --all shows several counters
and statistics explained later, and there is another execution option
 --reset for resetting those values.
 

Values are reset at midnight UTC time by default.
 

The first block of information is related to global slurmctld execution:
 
 
 Server thread count The number of current active slurmctld threads. A high number would mean a high
load processing events like job submissions, jobs dispatching, jobs completing,
etc. If this is often close to MAX_SERVER_THREADS it could point to a potential
bottleneck.
 
 
 Agent queue size Slurm design has scalability in mind and sending messages to thousands of nodes
is not a trivial task. The agent mechanism helps to control communication
between slurmctld and the slurmd daemons for a best effort. This value denotes
the count of enqueued outgoing RPC requests in an internal retry list.
 
 
 Agent count Number of agent threads. Each of these agent threads can create in turn a group
of up to 2 + AGENT_THREAD_COUNT active threads at a time.
 
 
 Agent thread count Total count of active threads created by all the agent threads.
 
 
 DBD Agent queue size Slurm queues up the messages intended for the SlurmDBD and processes them in a
separate thread. If the SlurmDBD, or database, is down then this number will
increase.
 
The max queue size is configured in the slurm.conf with MaxDBDMsgs. If this number begins to grow more than half of the max queue size, the slurmdbd
and the database should be investigated immediately.
 
 
 Jobs submitted Number of jobs submitted since last reset
 
 
 Jobs started Number of jobs started since last reset. This includes backfilled jobs.
 
 
 Jobs completed Number of jobs completed since last reset.
 
 
 Jobs canceled Number of jobs canceled since last reset.
 
 
 Jobs failed Number of jobs failed due to slurmd or other internal issues since last reset.
 
 
 Job states ts: Lists the timestamp of when the following job state counts were gathered.
 
 
 Jobs pending: Number of jobs pending at the given time of the time stamp above.
 
 
 Jobs running: Number of jobs running at the given time of the time stamp above.
 
 
 
 

The next block of information is related to main scheduling algorithm based
on jobs priorities. A scheduling cycle implies to get the job_write_lock lock,
then trying to get resources for jobs pending, starting from the most priority
one and going in descending order. Once a job can not get the resources the
loop keeps going but just for jobs requesting other partitions. Jobs with
dependencies or affected by accounts limits are not processed.
 
 
 Last cycle Time in microseconds for last scheduling cycle.
 
 
 Max cycle Maximum time in microseconds for any scheduling cycle since last reset.
 
 
 Total cycles Total run time in microseconds for all scheduling cycles since last reset.
Scheduling is performed periodically and (depending upon configuration)
when a job is submitted or a job is completed.
 
 
 Mean cycle Mean time in microseconds for all scheduling cycles since last reset.
 
 
 Mean depth cycle Mean of cycle depth. Depth means number of jobs processed in a scheduling cycle.
 
 
 Cycles per minute Counter of scheduling executions per minute.
 
 
 Last queue length Length of jobs pending queue.
 
 
 
 

The next block of information is related to backfilling scheduling algorithm.
A backfilling scheduling cycle implies to get locks for jobs, nodes and
partitions objects then trying to get resources for jobs pending. Jobs are
processed based on priorities. If a job can not get resources the algorithm
calculates when it could get them obtaining a future start time for the job.
Then next job is processed and the algorithm tries to get resources for that
job but avoiding to affect the previous ones , and again it calculates
the future start time if not current resources available. The backfilling
algorithm takes more time for each new job to process since more priority jobs
can not be affected. The algorithm itself takes measures for avoiding a long
execution cycle and for taking all the locks for too long.
 
 
 Total backfilled jobs (since last slurm start) Number of jobs started thanks to backfilling since last slurm start.
 
 
 Total backfilled jobs (since last stats cycle start) Number of jobs started thanks to backfilling since last time stats where reset.
By default these values are reset at midnight UTC time.
 
 
 Total backfilled heterogeneous job components Number of heterogeneous job components started thanks to backfilling since
last Slurm start.
 
 
 Total cycles Number of backfill scheduling cycles since last reset
 
 
 Last cycle when Time when last backfill scheduling cycle happened in the format
"weekday Month MonthDay hour:minute.seconds year"
 
 
 Last cycle Time in microseconds of last backfill scheduling cycle.
It counts only execution time, removing sleep time inside a scheduling cycle
when it executes for an extended period time.
Note that locks are released during the sleep time so that other work can
proceed.
 
 
 Max cycle Time in microseconds of maximum backfill scheduling cycle execution since last reset.
It counts only execution time, removing sleep time inside a scheduling cycle
when it executes for an extended period time.
Note that locks are released during the sleep time so that other work can
proceed.
 
 
 Mean cycle Mean time in microseconds of backfilling scheduling cycles since last reset.
 
 
 Last depth cycle Number of processed jobs during last backfilling scheduling cycle. It counts
every job even if that job can not be started due to dependencies or limits.
 
 
 Last depth cycle (try sched) Number of processed jobs during last backfilling scheduling cycle. It counts
only jobs with a chance to start using available resources. These
jobs consume more scheduling time than jobs which are found can not be started
due to dependencies or limits.
 
 
 Depth Mean Mean count of jobs processed during all backfilling scheduling cycles since last
reset.
Jobs which are found to be ineligible to run when examined by the backfill
scheduler are not counted (e.g. jobs submitted to multiple partitions and
already started, jobs which have reached a QOS or account limit such as
maximum running jobs for an account, etc).
 
 
 Depth Mean (try sched) The subset of Depth Mean that the backfill scheduler attempted to schedule.
 
 
 Last queue length Number of jobs pending to be processed by backfilling algorithm.
A job is counted once for each partition it is queued to use.
A pending job array will normally be counted as one job (tasks of a job array
which have already been started/requeued or individually modified will already
have individual job records and are each counted as a separate job).
 
 
 Queue length Mean Mean count of jobs pending to be processed by backfilling algorithm.
A job is counted once for each partition it requested.
A pending job array will normally be counted as one job (tasks of a job array
which have already been started/requeued or individually modified will already
have individual job records and are each counted as a separate job).
 
 
 Last table size Count of different time slots tested by the backfill scheduler in its last
iteration.
 
 
 Mean table size Mean count of different time slots tested by the backfill scheduler.
Larger counts increase the time required for the backfill operation.
The table size is influenced by many scheduling parameters, including:
bf_min_age_reserve, bf_min_prio_reserve, bf_resolution, and bf_window.
 
 
 Latency for 1000 calls to gettimeofday() Latency of 1000 calls to the gettimeofday() syscall in microseconds,
as measured at controller startup.
 
 
 
 

The next blocks of information report the most frequently issued
remote procedure calls (RPCs), calls made for the Slurmctld daemon to perform
some action.
The fourth block reports the RPCs issued by message type.
You will need to look up those RPC codes in the Slurm source code by looking
them up in the file src/common/slurm_protocol_defs.h.
The report includes the number of times each RPC is invoked, the total time
consumed by all of those RPCs plus the average time consumed by each RPC in
microseconds.
The fifth block reports the RPCs issued by user ID, the total number of RPCs
they have issued, the total time consumed by all of those RPCs plus the average
time consumed by each RPC in microseconds.
RPCs statistics are collected for the life of the slurmctld process unless
explicitly --reset .
 
 

The sixth block of information, labeled Pending RPC Statistics, shows
information about pending outgoing RPCs on the slurmctld agent queue.
The first section of this block shows types of RPCs on the queue and the
count of each. The second section shows up to the first 25 individual RPCs
pending on the agent queue, including the type and the destination host list.
This information is cached and only refreshed on 30 second intervals.
 
   
 OPTIONS 
 
 
 -a , --all Get and report information. This is the default mode of operation.
 
 
 -M , --cluster =< string > The cluster to issue commands to. Only one cluster name may be specified.
Note that the slurmdbd must be up for this option to work properly, unless
running in a federation with FederationParameters=fed_display configured.
 
 
 -h , --help Print description of options and exit.
 
 
 --json , --json = list , --json =< data_parser > Dump information as JSON using the default data_parser plugin or explicit
data_parser with parameters. Sorting and formatting arguments will be ignored.
 
 
 --no-trunc Do not truncate long lines to 80 char.
 
 
 -r , --reset Reset scheduler and RPC counters to 0. Only supported for Slurm operators and
administrators.
 
 
 -i , --sort-by-id Sort Remote Procedure Call (RPC) data by message type ID and user ID.
 
 
 -t , --sort-by-time Sort Remote Procedure Call (RPC) data by total run time.
 
 
 -T , --sort-by-time2 Sort Remote Procedure Call (RPC) data by average run time.
 
 
 --usage Print list of options and exit.
 
 
 -V , --version Print current version number and exit.
 
 
 --yaml , --yaml = list , --yaml =< data_parser > Dump information as YAML using the default data_parser plugin or explicit
data_parser with parameters. Sorting and formatting arguments will be ignored.
 
 
 
   
 PERFORMANCE 
 

Executing sdiag sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from sdiag or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmctld daemon come in at once, it can result in
a degradation of performance of the slurmctld daemon, possibly resulting
in a denial of service.
 

Do not run sdiag or other Slurm client commands that send remote procedure
calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other programs. Ensure
that programs limit calls to sdiag to the minimum necessary for the
information you are trying to gather.
 
   
 ENVIRONMENT VARIABLES 
 

Some sdiag options may be set via environment variables. These
environment variables, along with their corresponding options, are listed below.
(Note: Command line options will always override these settings.)
 
 
 SLURM_CLUSTERS Same as --cluster 
 
 
 SLURM_CONF The location of the Slurm configuration file.
 
 SLURM_JSON Control JSON serialization:
 
 
 
 compact Output JSON as compact as possible.
 
 
 pretty Output JSON in pretty format to make it more readable.
 
 
 

 
 SLURM_YAML Control YAML serialization:
 
 
 
 compact Output YAML as compact as possible. 
 
 pretty Output YAML in pretty format to make it more readable.

Below is a concise, field-by-field explanation of the sdiag scheduler diagnostic output and what each value means / when to investigate it.

General notes
- Most timing values are in microseconds (µs) unless otherwise noted.
- Counters are either since the last reset (default: midnight UTC) or since slurmctld start (where documented).
- Use sdiag --reset as an operator to zero the counters; use --json/--yaml for machine-readable output.

1) slurmctld / agent / DBD runtime metrics
- Server thread count
  - Number of active slurmctld threads. If this is often near MAX_SERVER_THREADS in slurm.conf, slurmctld may be CPU/IO bound.
- Agent queue size
  - Number of enqueued outgoing RPCs waiting for delivery to slurmd agents (internal retry list). Growing queue → communication/backpressure.
- Agent count
  - Number of agent threads (each can spawn worker threads).
- Agent thread count
  - Total active threads created by agent threads.
- DBD Agent queue size
  - Messages queued for SlurmDBD. If this grows (especially > ~50% of MaxDBDMsgs) check slurmdbd or DB connectivity/latency.

2) Job counters
- Jobs submitted / started / completed / canceled / failed
  - Simple counters since last reset. “started” includes backfilled starts. A jump in failed or canceled can indicate slurmd/node or user/job issues.
- Job states ts / Jobs pending / Jobs running
  - Timestamp when the snapshot was taken and instantaneous counts of PENDING and RUNNING jobs.

3) Priority-based scheduling cycle (main scheduler)
- Last cycle
  - Time spent in the last scheduling cycle (µs). A single cycle does priority-ordered scheduling attempts.
- Max cycle
  - Maximum cycle time observed since reset.
- Total cycles
  - Sum of all cycle times since reset (µs).
- Mean cycle
  - Average scheduling cycle time (µs).
- Mean depth cycle
  - Average number of jobs processed per cycle (depth = jobs examined).
- Cycles per minute
  - Frequency of scheduling cycles (helpful to see if scheduler is running very frequently or rarely).
- Last queue length
  - Number of pending jobs considered in the last cycle.
Interpretation: long or frequently-spiking cycle times suggest expensive scheduling work (many jobs, heavy backfill, locks held long). Investigate large queue lengths, scheduling locks, or plugins (fairshare, multifactor priority cost).

4) Backfill scheduler block
- Total backfilled jobs (since last slurm start / since last stats reset)
  - How many jobs were started via backfilling.
- Total backfilled heterogeneous job components
  - Count for heterogeneous job components.
- Total cycles / Last cycle when / Last cycle / Max cycle / Mean cycle
  - Same semantics as main scheduler but for the backfill algorithm (µs). Backfill cycles are typically more expensive.
- Last depth cycle / Last depth cycle (try sched)
  - Number of jobs considered in the last backfill cycle; the “try sched” version counts only jobs that had a chance to start (i.e., not ineligible due to limits/dependencies).
- Depth Mean / Depth Mean (try sched)
  - Averages of the above over cycles.
- Last queue length / Queue length Mean
  - Number of jobs pending to be processed by backfill (a job is counted once per partition requested).
- Last table size / Mean table size
  - Number of distinct time slots tested by the backfill scheduler in the last iteration and mean. Larger table sizes increase backfill CPU costs. Table size is influenced by backfill settings (bf_min_age_reserve, bf_min_prio_reserve, bf_resolution, bf_window).
- Latency for 1000 gettimeofday() calls
  - Microsecond measurement of gettimeofday() syscall latency measured at controller startup; can indicate host syscall timing overhead.

When to worry: large/backfill cycle times, large table sizes, or deep backfill depths indicate backfill cost; tune bf_* settings or job time limits to reduce.

5) RPC statistics
- Frequently issued RPCs (by msg type)
  - For each RPC: count, total time consumed, average time (µs). Use these to spot expensive operations or noisy RPC types.
- RPCs by user ID
  - Which users generate many/slow RPCs (e.g., submitting many small jobs or polling).
- Pending RPC statistics
  - Types/counts of RPCs currently queued on the agent queue and up to the first 25 individual pending RPCs (type + destination host list). This is cached and refreshed every ~30s.
Interpretation: many pending RPCs or slow/expensive RPC types can indicate node communication problems, overloaded slurmds, or user-side hot loops.

6) Misc / other blocks
- Pending outgoing RPCs (detailed list)
  - Shows destination nodes and RPC types still pending; helps find problematic nodes or network partitions.
- RPCs total lifetime stats
  - These are accumulated for the slurmctld lifetime unless reset.

Troubleshooting tips (quick)
- If Server thread count ≈ MAX_SERVER_THREADS often → consider increasing MAX_SERVER_THREADS or investigate sources of high load (many submissions, RPCs).
- If DBD Agent queue grows → check slurmdbd and database responsiveness; ensure MaxDBDMsgs is appropriate.
- If backfill table size / backfill cycle time is large → tune bf_min_age_reserve, bf_resolution, bf_window or encourage more accurate per-job time limits.
- If many pending RPCs or slow RPCs → check network, slurmd health on affected nodes (sinfo, sinfo_reasons, scontrol show node), and per-node logs.
- If a particular RPC type or user dominates time → inspect user behavior (high submission rate, frequent squeue polls) or the plugin implementing that RPC.

Where to look next
- Use sinfo/sinfo_reasons and scontrol show node to inspect node health if pending RPCs point to hosts.
- Use sprio/sdiag together to correlate priority factors with scheduling cycle behavior.
- For historical patterns, run sdiag regularly or collect sdiag --json output into a monitoring system.

If you want, I can:
- Show a short example sdiag output and annotate the fields, or
- Run sdiag on your cluster and interpret the current values (I’ll call sdiag if you want a live readout).

## Accounting [#Accounting](https://slurm.schedmd.com/gres.html)
GPU memory and GPU utilization can be tracked as
[TRES](https://slurm.schedmd.com/tres.html) for tasks using GPU
resources. If `AccountingStorageTRES=gres/gpu` is configured,
gres/gpumem and gres/gpuutil will automatically be configured and gathered from
GPU jobs. gres/gpumem and gres/gpuutil can also be set individually when
gres/gpu is not set.
gres/gpumem and gres/gpuutil are only available for NVIDIA GPUs when using
`AutoDetect=nvml`, and AMD GPUs when using
`AutoDetect=rsmi`.
NVML does not support utilization metrics for MIGs, so Slurm does not
provide gpumem or gpuutil accounting for MIG devices. See

## Sharding [#Sharding](https://slurm.schedmd.com/gres.html)
Sharding provides a generic mechanism where GPUs can be
shared by multiple jobs. While it does permit multiple jobs to run on a given
GPU it does not fence the processes running on the GPU, it only allows the GPU
to be shared. Sharding, therefore, works best with homogeneous workflows. It is
recommended to limit the number of shards on a node to equal the max possible
jobs that can run simultaneously on the node (i.e. cores).
The total count of shards available on a node should be configured in
the slurm.conf file (e.g. "NodeName=tux[1-16] Gres=gpu:2,shard:64").
Several options are available for configuring shards in the gres.conf file

Good question — here’s a compact, practical guide to Slurm GRES and GPU request syntax, what Slurm does with your request, and common examples / pitfalls.

1) Basics — what GRES is
- GRES = Generic RESources. GPUs are usually configured as gres objects (Name=gpu) on each node (in slurm.conf and/or per-node gres.conf).
- The scheduler only grants GRES that are declared on nodes. The gres.conf/slurm.conf setup and the configured select plugin determine available GPU types and counts.

2) Core --gres syntax
- Form: --gres=name[:type[:count]]
  - name: resource name (usually gpu)
  - type: an optional type string (used to distinguish models, MIG sizes, etc.)
  - count: how many of that resource you request (defaults to 1 if omitted)
- Multiple different GRES can be requested by comma: --gres=gpu:tesla:2,shard:10
- Example: --gres=gpu:2  (request two GPUs; equivalent to gpu:count=2)
- Example: --gres=gpu:tesla:1  (request 1 GPU of type containing substring "tesla")

3) Convenience GPU options
- Newer Slurm provides higher-level flags (requires select/cons_tres plugin):
  - --gpus=N  (request N GPUs for the job)
  - --gpus-per-node=N  (force N GPUs on every allocated node)
  - --gpus-per-task=N  (allocate N GPUs for each task)
  - --gpus-per-socket (less common; per-socket request)
- These map to TRES/gpu accounting when the plugin is installed.

4) Request semantics (important)
- --gres=gpu:2 requests 2 GPUs per node unless using a per-job form such as --gpus (behavior depends on plugin and Slurm version). Prefer the explicit option you need:
  - To get exactly N GPUs total across job: use --gpus=N (if supported) or control with --nodes and --gpus-per-node.
  - To get N GPUs on each node: use --gres=gpu:N or --gpus-per-node=N.
  - To give each task a GPU: use --gpus-per-task=1 with --ntasks or task count.
- Slurm enforces exclusivity only if GPUs are configured as exclusive or if cgroup/device constraints are used. Shared modes (MPS, sharding, MIG) permit multiple allocations on same physical GPU depending on admin config.

5) Types, MIG, and advanced selection
- The optional type string can represent GPU model or MIG profile substring (e.g., --gres=gpu:a100-7g.10gb:1). When AutoDetect=nvml and MIG is configured, Slurm can present MIG profiles as types; the type is matched as a substring as reported by slurmd.
- You cannot generally pick a specific GPU device by its UUID via --gres; selection is by configured GRES types and counts. Admins can map device files in gres.conf which influences allocation.

6) What Slurm sets inside your job
- Slurm sets CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES for job steps so the job sees only the GPUs allocated to it (per-node, per-step).
- Newer Slurm versions also set variables like SLURM_JOB_GPUS / SLURM_STEP_GPUS (lists of allocated GPU ids/UUIDs) and SLURM_GPUS_ON_NODE, when available — check your Slurm version and configuration.
- If cgroups device/file visibility is enabled, the job cannot access GPU device files not assigned to it.

7) MPS, sharding, and sharing
- MPS: request gres=mps:N (if configured) to use CUDA MPS sharing. Admin must configure counts in slurm.conf/gres.conf.
- Sharding allows multiple jobs to share a GPU by allocating “shard” GRES; it does not fence GPU contexts and is for homogeneous workloads.
- MIG: Slurm supports NVIDIA MIG when configured (AutoDetect=nvml). Treat MIG instances as individual GPUs and use the type string to request particular MIG sizes.

8) Accounting and TRES
- GPU allocations are recorded as a TRES (tres/gpu or gres/gpu) for scheduling and accounting if AccountingStorageTRES=gres/gpu is enabled.
- gpumem and gpuutil can be reported if configured (nvml/rsmi).

9) Examples
- Batch script header (common):
  #SBATCH --gres=gpu:4
  (gives 4 GPUs per node or total depending on plugin/version; prefer --gpus for total)
- Request 2 GPUs total (if supported):
  sbatch --gpus=2 myjob.sh
- Request 1 GPU per MPI task (4 tasks):
  sbatch --ntasks=4 --gpus-per-task=1 my_mpi_job.sh
- Request 2 GPUs on each node allocated (3 nodes => 6 GPUs total):
  sbatch --nodes=3 --gpus-per-node=2 myjob.sh
- Request GPUs of a specific type (admin-defined substring):
  sbatch --gres=gpu:rtx6000:2 myjob.sh

10) Troubleshooting / tips
- If a request is rejected: check sinfo and node gres configuration (ask admin or run sinfo -R / scontrol show node).
- To see how many GPUs you have on a node: sinfo or nvidia-smi on the node (if you can access it).
- If CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES isn't what you expect, the node’s slurmd/gres/cgroup configuration may differ; ask the admin or inspect slurm.conf/gres.conf.
- Use scontrol show node <node> to inspect the node’s Gres and GresTypes if you have permission.

11) Summary recommendations
- Prefer --gpus / --gpus-per-node / --gpus-per-task when select/cons_tres is enabled — they are clearer and map to TRES.
- Use --gres=gpu[:type:count] when you need to request specific GRES types or when the cluster uses legacy GRES config.
- Rely on CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES inside the job to find which devices you can use; do not assume physical device indices match cluster-wide indices.

## Overview[#overview](https://slurm.schedmd.com/job_state_codes.html)
In the Slurm code, there are base states and state flags .
Each job has a base state and may have additional state flags set. When using

What the squeue columns above mean (summary, from Slurm docs)
- JOBID: job identifier.
- NAME: job name (sbatch --job-name / script shebang name).
- USER: submitting user.
- STATE: job state (e.g., PENDING, RUNNING, COMPLETED, FAILED). See job state codes: https://slurm.schedmd.com/job_state_codes.html
- TIME: elapsed runtime for RUNNING jobs (or 0:00 for pending).
- NODES: number of nodes allocated or requested.
- CPUS: CPU count allocated/requested.
- MEM: memory allocated/requested (format varies by site).
- PARTITION: partition the job targets.

Full squeue reference: https://slurm.schedmd.com/squeue.html

How pending reasons are shown and how to interpret them (summary from Slurm job reason docs)
- The scheduler reports a single pending reason that was encountered by the scheduling attempt; if multiple constraints block a job, only the one that was hit by the scheduler is shown.
- Common pending reasons and what they mean:
  - Priority: other jobs with higher priority are scheduled before this one.
  - Resources: no suitable free resources (CPUs/GPUs/memory/nodes) match the request.
  - PartitionDown / NodeDown / NodeNotResponding: nodes or partition are unavailable.
  - Dependency: the job has an unmet dependency (e.g., afterok).
  - QOS/Account/Association limits (AccountNotAllowed, AssocGrpBilling, etc.): job blocked by accounting, QOS, or association limits.
  - Partition/Reservation conflict: reservation or partition limits preventing placement.
- For the full list and precise reason code names: see Job Reason Codes: https://slurm.schedmd.com/job_reason_codes.html

## Maintenance Reservations [#maint](https://slurm.schedmd.com/reservations.html)
For ease of system maintenance, you can create a reservation with the
MAINT flag that overlaps existing reservations. This is equivalent to the
OVERLAP flag but with the following distinctions:
- Reserved nodes will be shown in maint state
- Reserved nodes will not be available as replacements in other reservations
- Cluster usage reports will show this time as PlannedDown
For example, users alan and brenda might have a reservation
for some nodes daily from noon until 1PM. If there is a maintenance reservation
for all nodes starting at 12:30PM, the only jobs they may start in their
reservation would have to be completed by 12:30PM, when the maintenance
reservation begins.

I looked up the local Slurm documentation on reservations and summarized the key points below (source: Slurm Advanced Resource Reservation Guide).

What a reservation is
- A reservation reserves specified resources (nodes, CPU cores, licenses, burst buffers) for a defined time window so selected users/accounts/QOS can run jobs there.
- A reservation identifies resources and a time period when those resources are available.

Scope and resource model
- Reservations that include nodes/cores are associated with a single partition and by default cannot span multiple partitions. The exception is when you explicitly specify node names — then a reservation may include nodes from different partitions.
- You can reserve full nodes or a set number of cores. Reserved burst buffers and licenses are treated slightly differently than nodes/cores.

Access control and who can use a reservation
- Reservations can be limited to particular users, accounts, or QOS values. Only jobs meeting the access controls may run in that reservation.
- By default, jobs must explicitly request the reservation (for example sbatch --reservation=<name>) to run there.

Timing and node selection
- A reservation has a start time and duration (or start and end times).
- If you don’t specify explicit nodes, Slurm will automatically select nodes to satisfy the reservation while avoiding overlaps with other reservations (unless flags change that behavior).

Important reservation flags and behaviors
- OVERLAP: allows reservations to overlap in time on the same nodes (useful for nested/reserved slices).
- MAGNETIC: makes a reservation “attract” eligible jobs even if they don’t request the reservation name. Magnetic reservations will only attract homogeneous jobs; heterogeneous jobs must explicitly request the reservation.
- MAINT (maintenance): a special overlapping reservation type for maintenance windows. Nodes in a MAINT reservation show up in maint state, won’t be used as replacements for other reservations, and time is reported as PlannedDown in usage.
- REPLACE / REPLACE_DOWN: controls whether nodes that are DOWN/DRAINED or even currently allocated to jobs should be replaced so the reservation retains a constant resource pool. REPLACE can move a reservation to new idle nodes if necessary (with caveats for reservations specified as cores across nodes).
- Default: nodes that are DOWN or DRAINED will be replaced for a reservation, but allocated nodes are not replaced unless REPLACE is used.

Limitations and notes
- Reservations are not compatible with Slurm’s gang scheduler plugin (because reservation termination times may make gang scheduling infeasible).
- Magnetic reservations will not attract heterogeneous jobs unless the job explicitly requests the reservation.
- Maintenance reservations differ from generic overlapping reservations in how they present node state and how accounting reports treat the time.

Typical commands (from the docs)
- Create: scontrol create reservation starttime=<time> duration=<mins|time> users=<userlist> nodes=<nodelist|nodecnt> flags=<flags>
  - Example (illustrative): scontrol create reservation starttime=now duration=60 users=alice nodes=node05 flags=magnetic
- View: scontrol show reservation (or scontrol show res) to inspect reservation details.
- Jobs can request a reservation when submitting: e.g., sbatch --reservation=<reservation_name> <script>
- You can view queue entries tied to a reservation with squeue --reservation=<name>.

## PERFORMANCE[#SECTION_PERFORMANCE](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sshare.html)
Executing sshare sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from sshare or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmctld daemon come in at once, it can result in
a degradation of performance of the slurmctld daemon, possibly resulting
in a denial of service.
Do not run sshare or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other
programs. Ensure that programs limit calls to sshare to the minimum
necessary for the information you are trying to gather.

Good question — these fields come from sshare and are used by Slurm’s fair-share (priority) calculations. Short definitions followed by interpretation and a small numeric example.

Definitions
- RawShares
  - The raw (configured) share weight assigned to an association (user, account, etc.). This is an administrator-set weight (via sacctmgr) and is the baseline “entitlement” value used by the fair‑share algorithm.

- NormShares (Normalized Shares)
  - The RawShares value normalized to the total shares in the same level. In other words:
    NormShares = RawShares / sum(RawShares_of_level).
  - When PriorityFlags=FAIR_TREE (the default) the normalization is done within the level (siblings under the same parent).

- EffectvUsage (Effective Usage)
  - Used with the FAIR_TREE mode. It is the association’s usage expressed relative to its parent (i.e., the association’s usage normalized with its parent). EffectvUsage therefore shows how much of the parent’s share the association has actually consumed (using decayed usage values — see Raw Usage below).

Related usage fields (for context)
- Raw Usage
  - The measured consumption expressed in TRES-seconds (or CPU-seconds if TRESBillingWeights is not defined). This usage decays over time according to PriorityDecayHalfLife.
- Norm Usage
  - Raw Usage normalized to the total Raw Usage (similar to NormShares but for usage).

How they’re used (interpretation)
- The scheduler compares the normalized entitlement (NormShares) to the association’s effective usage (EffectvUsage) to decide whether the association is over- or under-served.
- Slurm exposes a “level fair-share” metric (Level FS) = NormShares / EffectvUsage:
  - If Level FS > 1 → the association is under‑served (it has less usage than its entitlement) and will receive a boost.
  - If Level FS < 1 → the association is over‑served (it has used more than its entitlement) and will receive a penalty.
  - If Level FS ≈ 1 → usage is roughly in line with entitlement.

Small numeric example
- Parent account total RawShares = 100.
- Child A RawShares = 25 → NormShares_A = 25/100 = 0.25.
- Parent decayed Raw Usage = 1000 TRES-minutes; Child A decayed Raw Usage = 200 → EffectvUsage_A = 200/1000 = 0.20.
- Level FS_A = NormShares_A / EffectvUsage_A = 0.25 / 0.20 = 1.25 → child A is under‑served and will gain priority relative to siblings.

Notes
- Raw Usage decays with PriorityDecayHalfLife, so EffectvUsage reflects recent usage more than distant past usage.
- These fields are visible with sshare (use -l for the long listing) and are meaningful only when the priority/multifactor plugin (and slurmdbd for sshare) is configured.

Here’s a concise, practical explanation of how Slurm partitions, constraints, and GPU availability interact — what they mean, how Slurm counts “available” GPUs, common ways to request GPUs, and checks you can run.

Key concepts
- Partition: a named queue of nodes (e.g., "gpu"). Jobs use --partition= to pick which set of nodes to run on. Partitions may be restricted by accounts/QOS and can contain mixed node types.
- GRES (Generic RESources): Slurm’s mechanism for GPUs. Nodes are configured with gres=gpu:<count> in slurm.conf (and optionally detailed in gres.conf). Use --gres=gpu:N (or with a type: --gres=gpu:tesla:2) to request GPUs.
- Node features/constraints: Nodes can have feature strings (e.g., "a100", "rtx6000"). Use --constraint="feature" to restrict scheduling to nodes with that feature.
- Availability = idle GPUs on idle nodes (not allocated, mixed, drained or down). Slurm schedules only against GPUs actually free on nodes.

How Slurm reports availability
- sinfo partition summary shows NODES in the format A/I/D (per-site note: A = allocated, I = idle, D = down/drain). The middle number (I) is the count of idle nodes in that partition — for GPU submissions you need idle nodes with idle GPUs.
- A node with some GPUs already allocated (or marked mixed) is not fully “available” for a new request unless enough free GPUs remain for the job’s request and Slurm is configured to allow partial-node allocations.
- squeue shows running allocations that consume GPUs; scontrol show node <node> or scontrol show hostname will show the node’s total GRES and what’s currently assigned.

How to request GPUs (common examples)
- Request N GPUs on one node:
  --partition=gpu --gres=gpu:2 --nodes=1
- Request GPUs of a specific type (when types are configured):
  --gres=gpu:a100:1
- Use constraint to require nodes with a feature:
  --constraint="a100|rtx"  (OR/AND syntax depends on cluster config)
- Control exclusivity:
  --exclusive (take whole node even if you requested fewer GPUs)
- For MIG devices, Slurm may expose them as separate GRES types; request them by the configured GRES name.

Practical checks to determine GPU availability
- sinfo -p gpu  (or sinfo -N -p gpu -o \"%20N %10Gres %8State\") — shows partition/node availability and configured GRES.
  - Look at NODES(A/I/D); I (idle) > 0 means there are idle nodes in that partition.
- squeue --partition=gpu or squeue -o to see which jobs are using GPUs and which nodes are allocated.
- scontrol show node <node> — shows Gres and AllocTRES to see how many GPUs are free on a particular node.

Important caveats and behavior
- “Idle node” vs “idle GPU”: A node can be idle (I) or partially allocated (mixed). For conditional submissions that require free GPU nodes, only nodes with sufficient idle GPUs count as eligible.
- Mixed/allocated/drained/down nodes are not treated as available for new GPU submissions unless they have free GPUs that satisfy the job and cluster config supports partial allocation.
- Scheduling and backfill: extra constraints (features) can reduce the scheduler’s ability to backfill, potentially increasing wait time.
- Sharing GPUs: some clusters allow multiple jobs/tasks on the same GPU (shared GRES) — check site policy. Otherwise expect exclusive GPU allocation per task by default.
- Configuration matters: whether GPUs are exposed as types, whether MIG instances are enumerated, and whether GPUs can be shared or oversubscribed is determined by slurm.conf/gres.conf and site policy.

Quick example sbatch header
#SBATCH --partition=gpu
#SBATCH --nodes=1
#SBATCH --gres=gpu:2
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=8
#SBATCH --time=02:00:00
(optional) #SBATCH --constraint=a100

Short answer first:
- AveCPU (sstat) = the average CPU time (user + system) consumed by a single task in the job step.
- AveRSS (sstat) = the average resident set size (physical memory) used by a single task in the job step.
- sstat reports metrics per job step (batch/extern/interactive) and its Ave*/Max*/Min* fields aggregate across the tasks of that step (average, maximum, minimum per-task values).

Details and interpretation
- Job steps
  - A Slurm job can have multiple steps (batch step for the sbatch script, extern steps per node, interactive steps for salloc/srun).
  - sstat shows metrics for each step (use --allsteps / -a to list them).
  - Use sstat for live/running steps; for finished jobs use sacct (accounting records).

- What “Ave*” means
  - AveCPU: average (user + system) CPU time consumed by each task in the step. Format is a time value (e.g., 00:10:30 or 25:02.000). If you have N tasks, approximate total CPU time consumed ≈ AveCPU × N (useful for CPU-hours).
  - AveRSS: average resident set size (physical memory) across the tasks in the step. sstat prints this as a byte quantity (often shown in human-readable units like K/M).
  - Max*/Min*: similarly report the per-task maximum/minimum values and often include which task had the extreme (e.g., MaxRSSTask).

- How to read numbers practically
  - AveCPU = 00:10:00 on 8 tasks → roughly 8 × 10 minutes = 80 CPU-minutes consumed (1.33 CPU-hours).
  - AveRSS = 200M on 4 tasks → each task averaged ~200 MB resident memory; total resident memory in use across tasks ≈ 800 MB (if tasks are separate).

- Command examples
  - sstat -j <jobid> --format=AveCPU,AveRSS,JobID
  - sstat -a -j <jobid> --format=JobID,Step,AveCPU,AveRSS,MaxRSS

- Caveats / limitations

Summary from the Slurm docs (sbatch and job_array pages) — what job-array IDs, task IDs, and the %A / %a filename placeholders mean and how to use them.

Key concepts
- Job array: a collection of similar batch jobs submitted together via sbatch --array (or -a). Slurm treats the array as a single submission but creates per-task records as tasks start.
- Array (master) job ID: the job ID that sbatch prints when you submit the array (e.g., "Submitted batch job 36"). Slurm documentation calls this the array’s master job allocation number.
- Task (array index): the index value you request for each element of the array (for example the numbers in --array=1-100). Each element is frequently referenced as JobID_index notation (e.g., 36_1 for job 36 element 1).

Environment variables the scheduler sets (relevant ones)
- SLURM_ARRAY_JOB_ID — the array’s master job ID (the number sbatch printed for the array).
- SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID — the array index for this task (the value from --array).
- SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_COUNT — number of tasks in the array.
- SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_MAX / SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_MIN — highest / lowest index in the array.

Filename / output placeholders (percent escapes supported by sbatch)
- %A — the job array’s master job allocation number (the array job ID). Use this when you want a single identifier for the whole array.
- %a — the job array index (the task’s index value). Use this to make per-task files.
- %b — the job array index modulo 10 (rarely used; useful for simple hashing/sharding).
- %j — the jobid of the running job (generic job id expansion).
- %J — jobid.stepid (e.g., "128.0").

Examples
- sbatch --array=1-3 --output=out_%A_%a.txt my.job
  - If sbatch responded "Submitted batch job 36", the files created will be:
    out_36_1.txt, out_36_2.txt, out_36_3.txt
  - %A = 36 (array master id), %a = 1,2,3 (task indices)
- sbatch --array=0-9 --output=task_%A_%a.log --error=task_%A_%a.err ...
  - Works the same when your array indices start at 0.

Other notes / gotchas
- Indices can start at 0 or any value you specify (smallest allowed index is 0; cluster may enforce a MaxArraySize).
- To reference or operate on a particular array element in Slurm commands or dependencies, use the combined form jobid_index (e.g., 123_4). Dependencies can target an entire array (123) or a specific element (123_4).
- You can also update/query individual array elements with scontrol using job=101_1 (or the array id alone to affect the whole array).
- Using %A groups output by array submission (all tasks share the same %A), while %a gives unique names per task — usually combine them (or %a alone) depending on whether you need per-task files or a single per-array grouping.

References
- sbatch filename-pattern placeholders (%A, %a, %j, %J, %b) — sbatch documentation (FILENAME PATTERN).
- Job Array Support — job array environment variables and array semantics (job_array documentation).

## EXAMPLES[#SECTION_EXAMPLES](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Specify a batch script by filename on the command line. The batch script specifies a 1 minute time limit for the job.
```text

```
Pass a batch script to sbatch on standard input:
```text
$ sbatch -N4 #!/bin/sh > srun hostname |sort > EOF sbatch: Submitted batch job 65541 $ cat slurm-65541.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
To create a heterogeneous job with 3 components, each allocating a unique set of nodes:
```text
$ sbatch -w node[2-3] : -w node4 : -w node[5-7] work.bash Submitted batch job 34987
```

## Overview[#overview](https://slurm.schedmd.com/job_array.html)
Job arrays offer a mechanism for submitting and managing collections of
similar jobs quickly and easily, useful for repetitive workloads that follow a
common job pattern. This greatly improves overall performance, since job arrays
with millions of tasks can be submitted in milliseconds (subject to configured

Summary from the Slurm docs — concise definitions, placeholders, and examples.

Key terms
- JobID (SLURM_JOB_ID / %j): the unique Slurm job identifier for a job record/step.
- ArrayJobID (SLURM_ARRAY_JOB_ID / %A): the master job allocation number for a job array — the single job id Slurm prints when you submit the array (e.g., "Submitted batch job 12345"). Use %A in filename patterns to get that master id.
- ArrayTaskID (SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID / %a): the array index value for the current array element (the number from your --array specification). Use %a in filename patterns to get the element’s index.

Environment variables (set for array jobs)
- SLURM_JOB_ID — job id for the current job record/step.
- SLURM_ARRAY_JOB_ID — job array’s master job allocation number (the first job id of the array).
- SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID — this task’s array index.
- SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_COUNT, SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_MIN, SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_MAX — count and bounds for the array indices.

Filename replacement symbols (sbatch --output/--error pattern)
- %A — Job array's master job allocation number (ArrayJobID).
- %a — Job array index number (ArrayTaskID).
- %j — jobid (SLURM_JOB_ID).
- %J — jobid.stepid (e.g., "128.0").
- %% — literal percent sign; %b is array index modulo 10 (less commonly used).
Example:
- sbatch --array=1-10 --output=slurm-%A_%a.out myjob.sh
  - For array master id 12345 and element index 3 this expands to slurm-12345_3.out.

Addressing and operating on array elements
- scontrol and scancel accept the ArrayJobID_ArrayTaskID notation to identify one element:
  - scancel 20_4  (cancels element index 4 of array job 20)
  - scancel 20    (cancels the whole array)
- Dependencies can target single elements or whole arrays:
  - sbatch --depend=after:123_4 my.job  (depend on element 4 of job array 123)
  - sbatch --depend=afterany:123 my.job (depend on entire array)

Behavior notes / gotchas from the docs
- The --array option defines the list of indices (e.g., --array=0-31, --array=1,3,5).
- The smallest index allowed may be 0 (cluster MaxArraySize applies).
- Slurm creates a single job record for the array and creates per-element records as needed; the first task is often a placeholder and may run last — this can make the mapping between SLURM_JOB_ID and SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID non-monotonic (see docs: “the task with the lowest SLURM_JOB_ID will have the highest SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID”).
- To guarantee unique per-task output files, include both %A and %a (or %j) in the pattern.

## PERFORMANCE[#SECTION_PERFORMANCE](https://slurm.schedmd.com/strigger.html)
Executing strigger sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from strigger or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmctld daemon come in at once, it can result in
a degradation of performance of the slurmctld daemon, possibly resulting
in a denial of service.
Do not run strigger or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other
programs. Ensure that programs limit calls to strigger to the minimum
necessary for the information you are trying to gather.

High-level summary
- strigger is the Slurm trigger facility: it lets you arrange that Slurm will run a program when certain cluster or job “events” occur (node up/down/drained/idle/reconfig, job time‑limit or job finish, controller failover, burst buffer error, etc.).
- Use cases: notify admins on node failures, run a checkpoint/cleanup script a few minutes before a job hits its time limit, run automatic remediation when a node is drained, etc.

How it works (behavioral details)
- You register triggers with strigger --set, list them with strigger --get, and remove them with strigger --clear.
- Slurm checks for trigger events periodically (roughly every 15 seconds). Events that occur within that check interval are compared to the configured triggers at the end of the interval; a matched trigger’s program is executed once for the matched event(s).
- Because checks are periodic, triggers are not instantaneous — plan for that resolution when choosing offsets.

Key trigger fields and semantics
- Resource type (RES_TYPE): job or node.
- Resource ID (RES_ID): job ID, a hostlist (node name(s)), or "*" for any host.
- TYPE (event): examples
  - Jobs: time (job reaching its time limit), fini (job finished/terminated)
  - Jobs or nodes: down, up
  - Nodes only: drained, idle, reconfig
  - There are many specific flags (e.g., backup slurmctld events, burst buffer errors).
- OFFSET: seconds offset relative to the event. Negative offsets mean “before the event” (e.g., -300 = run 5 minutes before time-limit), positive means after.
- PROGRAM: pathname of the executable/script to run when the trigger fires.
- USER: user who requested the trigger; some operations/clears are restricted (administrative permissions apply).

Common examples
- Run a checkpoint script 5 minutes before a job 12345 hits its time limit:
  strigger --set --jobid=12345 --type=time --offset=-300 --program=/path/to/checkpoint.sh
- Run an admin notification on node node01 going down:
  strigger --set --node=node01 --type=down --program=/path/to/node-fail-notify.sh
- List current triggers:
  strigger --get
- Remove a trigger by its TRIG_ID (or by jobid/user):
  strigger --clear --id=<TRIG_ID>

What strigger --get shows
- Each trigger row includes TRIG_ID, RES_TYPE, RES_ID, TYPE, OFFSET, USER, PROGRAM (and related metadata).

Practical notes and best practices
- Keep trigger programs small and robust (they run from slurmctld context or as allowed by configuration). Avoid long blocking work; consider backgrounding or queuing heavier work.
- Use negative offsets to perform graceful shutdown/checkpointing before an event; positive offsets for post-event processing.
- Avoid rapid/repeated strigger RPC calls from loops — many RPCs to slurmctld can degrade controller performance (possible denial‑of‑service if abused).
- Clean up triggers when no longer needed (or use job-scoped triggers that are cleared automatically if appropriate).
- Test triggers on a non-production job/node before deploying wide automation.

Where to read more
- The official strigger manual page (strigger(1)) on slurm.schedmd.com has full options and the complete list of supported event flags and permission notes.

```text

Short answer
- Slurm uses the multifactor priority plugin (PriorityType=priority/multifactor) to compute a single numeric job priority as a weighted sum of independent factors. Three of the most important pieces that control queue ordering are: the fairshare factor (how much a user/account has recently consumed), the Fair Tree algorithm (how fairshare is computed across accounts/users), and the configured PriorityWeight* values (how strongly each factor influences ordering).

How job priority is computed (conceptual)
- Job_priority = site_factor
  + PriorityWeightAge * age_factor
  + PriorityWeightAssoc * assoc_factor
  + PriorityWeightFairshare * fairshare_factor
  + PriorityWeightJobSize * job_size_factor
  + PriorityWeightPartition * partition_factor
  + PriorityWeightQOS * qos_factor
  + SUM(TRES_weight_X * TRES_factor_X)
  - nice_factor
- Each factor is a floating value (roughly 0.0–1.0). The PriorityWeight* entries are unsigned integers; together they scale each factor’s contribution before the total is converted to the final integer priority (0 .. 4294967295).

Fairshare factor — what it means and how it behaves
- Fairshare reduces priority for users/accounts that have used more of the cluster recently; it raises priority for users/accounts that have used less.
- Fairshare values are derived from historical usage per association/account/user and are normalized into a factor used in the multifactor formula.
- Two key configuration knobs:
  - PriorityDecayHalfLife: controls how quickly past usage “decays” (short half-life forgets history quickly; long half-life keeps historical usage influential). A value of 0 disables decay (must then use PriorityUsageResetPeriod).
  - PriorityUsageResetPeriod: optionally reset usage counters on a schedule (useful for enforcing quotas or fixed-period fairness).
- Tools to inspect fairshare: sshare (shows effective shares and usage) and sprio (shows factor contributions for pending jobs).

Fair Tree (the modern fairshare algorithm)
- Since Slurm 19.05 the Fair Tree algorithm is the default method used to convert historical usage into fairshare factors.
- Fair Tree is hierarchical: if two sibling accounts A and B are ordered by fairshare, then all children of A rank above all children of B. This preserves account-level ordering and avoids precision/tie problems seen in the older Classic algorithm.
- Benefits: stable ordering across account hierarchies, predictable behavior when account coordinators adjust shares, and reduced numerical tie/precision issues.
- If you need the older "classic" behavior you can still configure that explicitly, but Fair Tree is typically preferred.

Priority weights — how to make a factor matter (or not)
- PriorityWeightFairshare, PriorityWeightAge, PriorityWeightJobSize, PriorityWeightPartition, PriorityWeightQOS, and per-TRES weights determine how strongly each factor affects final priority.
- If a weight is set to zero the corresponding factor contributes nothing.
- Typical default pattern: make PriorityWeightFairshare large relative to others so fairshare has strong influence (examples in docs use PriorityWeightFairshare=10000, others 1000).
- Example effects:
  - If PriorityWeightFairshare >> PriorityWeightAge, then users’ historical usage dominates scheduling (new jobs from under-used users jump ahead of old heavy users).
  - If PriorityWeightAge is high, long-waiting jobs will eventually win even if a user has been heavy.
- TRES weights allow bias by resource type (e.g., make GPU usage count differently than CPU usage in the fairshare calculations).

Practical tuning and debugging tips
- Decide policy first: do you want strict account-level fairness, or to allow aging to override recent usage?
- Typical levers:
  - Increase PriorityWeightFairshare to favor historical fairness.
  - Decrease PriorityDecayHalfLife to forget older usage sooner (helps new users recover).
  - Use PriorityUsageResetPeriod for hard periodic resets (monthly allocations, semester quotas).
  - Tune TRES weights to reflect relative cost/importance of GPUs vs CPUs.
- Inspect what Slurm is doing:
  - sshare — view current fairshare/usage for accounts and users.
  - sprio [--all] — show the numeric priority and per-factor contributions for pending jobs.
  - scontrol show config — see configured PriorityWeight* and decay/reset settings.
- When debugging why a particular job is low in the queue, run sprio (or scontrol show job) to see the fairshare_factor and all other factor contributions.

Short examples
- Two accounts A and B, equal job size mix, but A has consumed 4× more resources in the past week:
  - With PriorityWeightFairshare high, jobs from B will be scheduled ahead of A until usage evens out.
- If PriorityDecayHalfLife is short (e.g., 1 day), A’s advantage/penalty fades quickly and A’s jobs recover sooner.
- If PriorityWeightAge is large, even a user with poor fairshare will eventually have jobs win after waiting long enough.

Bottom line
- Fairshare (via Fair Tree) determines how recent historical consumption penalizes or boosts users/accounts.
- Priority weights control how much that fairshare (and other factors like age, job size, QOS, TRES) influence final queue ordering.
- Use sshare and sprio to inspect current effective shares and factor contributions; tune PriorityWeight* and PriorityDecayHalfLife/PriorityUsageResetPeriod to match your site’s fairness vs responsiveness goals.

If you want, I can:
- Show the current configured PriorityWeight* and fairshare settings from your cluster (scontrol show config and sshare/sprio).

## Burst Buffers [#burst_buffer](https://slurm.schedmd.com/heterogeneous_jobs.html)
A burst buffer can either be persistent or linked to a specific job ID.
Since a heterogeneous job consists of multiple job IDs, a job-specific burst
buffer will be associated with only one heterogeneous job component.
Each component can have its own burst buffer directives, and they are processed
separately. Only a persistent burst buffer can be accessed by all components
of a heterogeneous job. Persistent burst buffers are only available in the
datawarp plugin. A sample batch script demonstrating this for the datawarp
plugin is appended.
```text
#!/bin/bash #SBATCH --nodes=1 --constraint=haswell #BB create_persistent name=alpha capacity=10 access=striped type=scratch #DW persistentdw name=alpha #SBATCH hetjob #SBATCH --nodes=16 --constraint=knl #DW persistentdw name=alpha ...
```

Use of the scontrol show job option shows two new fields related to
job array support.
The JobID is a unique identifier for the job.
The ArrayJobID is the JobID of the first element of the job
array.
The ArrayTaskID is the array index of this particular entry, either a
single number of an expression identifying the entries represented by this
job record (e.g. "5-1024").

The optional job ID specified with the scontrol show job or
scontrol show step commands can identify job array elements by
specifying ArrayJobId and ArrayTaskId with an underscore between

## AUTHORIZATION[#SECTION_AUTHORIZATION](https://slurm.schedmd.com/scontrol.html)
Slurm generally classifies users into three authorization levels:
- Administrators include root, SlurmUser, and any users with
"AdminLevel=Administrator"
- Privileged Users include all Administrators and any users with
"AdminLevel=Operator"
- Effective Owners of a job or step include the direct owner and all
Coordinators of the corresponding account.
Note that configuring AdminLevels or Coordinators requires the use of SlurmDBD.
The authorization levels required to execute various commands are defined in the
following table.
scontrol update job: Privileged or Effective Owner
scontrol requeue: Privileged or Effective Owner
scontrol update step: Privileged or Effective Owner
scontrol suspend: Privileged or Coordinator
scontrol resume: Privileged or Coordinator
scontrol notify: Root, SlurmUser, or direct owner
scontrol write batch_script: Privileged or direct...

Summary: scontrol requeue <jobid> tells Slurm to stop the job’s current running allocation (if any) and place the job back into the pending queue so the scheduler can try to start it again.

Details:
- Effect on a running job: the job’s current allocation is terminated/cleaned up and the job is marked for requeueing (you may see REQUEUED or a related flag). The job’s resources (nodes/CPUs/GPUs) are released and become available to other jobs.
- Effect on scheduling: the job is put back into the pending queue and will be considered by the scheduler for a new allocation like a fresh submission (subject to priorities, QOS, constraints, reservations, etc.).
- BatchFlag: for sbatch (batch) jobs, Slurm increments BatchFlag when a job is requeued (tracking requeue attempts).
- Ownership/permissions: only the job owner (effective owner) or privileged users/operators/administrators may run scontrol requeue.
- Job arrays / heterogeneous jobs: requeue behavior applies to job arrays and heterogeneous jobs in the documented ways (requeueing a job array ID can affect all elements; heterogeneous-job leader requeue applies to components).
- Checkpointing: requeue by itself does not magically restore in-job state. Unless the job uses an application-level checkpoint/restart mechanism or Slurm checkpoint plugins are configured, the restarted job will begin from the start of the job script.
- Use cases: manually force a restart after transient node problems, move a job off nodes, or recover a job after preemption/failure (administrators often use requeue for recovery).

What to look at after running it:
- squeue and scontrol show job <id> to see the job’s new state/flags and BatchFlag changes.
- sacct for historical records of the stopped attempt and the later restarted attempt.

Below are the common Slurm pending-reason groups, what each means, and how to check/fix them. This is a general (how‑to/explanation) answer rather than a live cluster query.

1) Resource shortage (REASON often: Resources, ReqNodeNotAvail, Nodes, Gres)
- Meaning: No currently idle nodes match the job’s resource requests (CPUs, memory, GPUs, specific node features, TRES, or partition). Can also be because nodes are allocated to other jobs or drained.
- How to spot: squeue’s REASON will say Resources/ReqNodeNotAvail or show “Requires” reasons; sinfo shows partition/node idle counts.
- Fixes: reduce resource requests (fewer GPUs/CPUs/memory), relax node constraints/feature flags, choose a different partition, wait, or request a reservation.

2) Job dependency (REASON: Dependency)
- Meaning: Job has an sbatch/srun dependency (afterok, afterany, etc.) and is waiting for the predecessor(s) to finish.
- How to spot: squeue REASON shows Dependency; scontrol show job <jobid> shows Dependency field.
- Fixes: ensure predecessor job completes successfully or remove/alter the dependency.

3) Priority / Fairshare / QOS ordering (REASON: Priority or Priority) 
- Meaning: Jobs are eligible but lower priority; scheduler will start them when higher‑priority work finishes or backfill opens a window.
- How to spot: squeue REASON may show Priority; sprio / sshare show contributing factors.
- Fixes: change QOS, account, or fairshare; ask admin to adjust weights; or wait.

4) Partition/node state or configuration (REASON: PartitionDown, NodeDown, Drained, NodeNotAvailable)
- Meaning: Target partition or nodes are down/drained/maintenance; scheduler cannot allocate.
- How to spot: sinfo and sinfo -R / sinfo_reasons show down/drain lists and reasons.
- Fixes: wait for maintenance to finish or ask admins to bring nodes up.

5) QOS / account / limits (REASON: QOSMaxJobs, QOSGrpTRES, AssocLimit)
- Meaning: User/account/QOS hit limits (max jobs, TRES usage, GPU-hour caps).
- How to spot: squeue may show a limit reason; sacctmgr or sacctmgr show associations and limits.
- Fixes: reduce concurrent jobs, change account/QOS, ask accounting admin to adjust limits.

6) Licenses (REASON: License)
- Meaning: Job requests licensed software resources and no licenses are currently free.
- How to spot: squeue REASON may say License; scontrol_license shows license usage.
- Fixes: free licenses by finishing other jobs, increase license pool, or request nodes without that license requirement.

7) Holds (REASON: JobHeld, UserHold, AdminHold, SystemHold)
- Meaning: Job is placed on hold and will not run until released.
- How to spot: squeue shows STATE=PD and REASON Hold; scontrol show job <id> shows Hold information.
- Fixes: release the hold (scontrol release <jobid>) or contact the holder/admin.

8) Reservation constraints (REASON: Reservation)
- Meaning: Job is reserved for later, or a conflicting reservation says job must wait.
- How to spot: squeue REASON shows Reservation; scontrol_reservation_show lists reservations.
- Fixes: schedule within reservation, change reservation, or ask admins.

9) Job-array / throttle or per-user limits (REASON: ArrayTaskLimit, JobLimit)
- Meaning: Array concurrency or per-user job submission limits prevent starting more tasks.
- How to spot: REASON will indicate array or limit-related text; sacctmgr / squeue show array counts.
- Fixes: reduce array concurrency, consolidate tasks, or increase limits.

10) Constraint/feature mismatch (REASON: Constraint)
- Meaning: Job requested a node feature or CPU architecture that no currently idle node provides.
- How to spot: squeue REASON shows Constraint or ReqNodeNotAvail; sinfo node feature listings show which nodes have which features.
- Fixes: remove/reduce constraints or wait for matching nodes.

How to group the current pending jobs by reason (practical commands)
- List pending jobs with reason column:
  squeue -t PENDING -o "%i %u %P %j %T %R"
- For a specific job (detailed reason):
  scontrol show job <jobid>
- Check partitions / nodes:
  sinfo
  sinfo -R   (reasons for down/drain)
- Check license usage:
  scontrol license
- Check account/QOS limits:
  sacctmgr show user <user>   (or sacctmgr_list equivalent)

## Partition QOS [#partition](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
A QOS can be attached to a partition. This means the partition will have all
the same limits as the QOS. This does not associate jobs with the QOS, nor does
it give the job any priority or preemption characteristics of the assigned QOS.
Jobs may separately request the same QOS or a different QOS to gain those
characteristics. However, the Partition QOS limits will override the job's QOS.
If the opposite is desired you may configure the job's QOS with
`Flags=OverPartQOS` which will reverse the order of precedence.
This functionality may be used to implement a true "floating"
partition, in which a partition may access a limited amount of resources with no
restrictions on which nodes it uses to get the resources. This is accomplished

## Relative QOS [#relative](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
Starting in Slurm 23.11, a QOS may be configured to contain relative resource
limits instead of absolute limits by setting `Flags=Relative`.
When this flag is set, all resource limits are treated as percentages of the
total resources available. Values higher than 100 are interpreted as 100%.
Memory limits should be set with no units. Although the default units (MB) will
be displayed, the limits will be enforced as a percentage (1MB = 1%).
NOTE : When Flags=Relative is added to a QOS, slurmctld
must be restarted or reconfigured for the flag to take effect.

resources in the whole cluster. For example, `cpu=50` would be
interpreted as 50% of all CPUs in the cluster.

## Configuration[#config](https://slurm.schedmd.com/resource_limits.html)
Scheduling policy information must be stored in a database
as specified by the AccountingStorageType configuration parameter
in the slurm.conf configuration file.
Information can be recorded in a [MySQL](http://www.mysql.com/) or
[MariaDB](https://mariadb.org/) database.
For security and performance reasons, the use of
SlurmDBD (Slurm Database Daemon) as a front-end to the
database is strongly recommended.

SlurmDBD also uses an existing Slurm accounting storage plugin
to maximize code reuse.
SlurmDBD uses data caching and prioritization of pending requests
in order to optimize performance.

and database use, the other Slurm commands and daemons are not required

### Specific limits over GRES [#gres_limits](https://slurm.schedmd.com/resource_limits.html)
When a GRES has a type associated with it and a limit is applied
over this specific type (e.g. MaxTRESPerUser=gres/gpu:tesla=1 ) if a
user requests a generic gres, the type's limit will not be enforced. In this
situation an additional lua job submit plugin to check the user request may
become useful. For example, if one requests --gres=gpu:2 having a
limit set of MaxTRESPerUser=gres/gpu:tesla=1 , the limit won't be
enforced so it will still be possible to get two teslas.

## Tools[#tools](https://slurm.schedmd.com/resource_limits.html)
The tool used to manage accounting policy is sacctmgr .
It can be used to create and delete cluster, user, account,
and partition records plus their combined association record.
See man sacctmgr for details on this tools and examples of
its use.
Changes made to the scheduling policy are uploaded to
the Slurm control daemons on the various clusters and take effect
immediately. When an association is deleted, all running or pending
jobs which belong to that association are immediately canceled.
When limits are lowered, running jobs will not be canceled to
satisfy the new limits, but the new lower limits will be enforced.

## Partition QOS [#partition](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
A QOS can be attached to a partition. This means the partition will have all
the same limits as the QOS. This does not associate jobs with the QOS, nor does
it give the job any priority or preemption characteristics of the assigned QOS.
Jobs may separately request the same QOS or a different QOS to gain those
characteristics. However, the Partition QOS limits will override the job's QOS.
If the opposite is desired you may configure the job's QOS with
`Flags=OverPartQOS` which will reverse the order of precedence.
This functionality may be used to implement a true "floating"
partition, in which a partition may access a limited amount of resources with no
restrictions on which nodes it uses to get the resources. This is accomplished
by assigning all nodes to the partition, then configuring a Partition QOS with
`GrpTRES` set to the desired resource limits.

## Hierarchy[#hierarchy](https://slurm.schedmd.com/resource_limits.html)
Slurm's hierarchical limits are enforced in the following order
with Job QOS and Partition QOS order being reversible by using the QOS
flag 'OverPartQOS':
- Partition QOS limit
- Job QOS limit
- User association
- Account association(s), ascending the hierarchy
- Root/Cluster association
- Partition limit
- None
Note: If limits are defined at multiple points in this hierarchy,
the point in this list where the limit is first defined will be used.
Consider the following example:
- MaxJobs=20 and MaxSubmitJobs is undefined in the partition QOS
- No limits are set in the job QOS and
- MaxJobs=4 and MaxSubmitJobs=50 in the user association
The limits in effect will be MaxJobs=20 and MaxSubmitJobs=50.
Note: The precedence order specified above is respected except for the
following limits: Max[Time|Wall], [Min|Max]Nodes. For these limits, even
if the job is enforced with...

"Configless" Slurm is a feature that allows the compute nodes —
specifically the slurmd process — and user commands running on login
nodes to pull configuration information directly from the slurmctld instead of
from a pre-distributed local file. Your cluster does require a central set of

## Notes[#NOTES](https://slurm.schedmd.com/configless_slurm.html)
Starting from Slurm 25.11, there's a new
SlurmctldParameters=reconfig_on_restart option that will make every
restart of slurmctld (process restart not triggered by "scontrol reconfigure")
to trigger a reconfiguration request to all slurmd and sackd daemons. For
"configless" systems this will ensure all processes are running the current
configuration. Some caution should be taken if you intend to perform rolling
upgrades on the cluster as this could lead to the daemons being upgraded sooner
than expected.

- The slurmd --conf-server $host[:$port] option

- The SLURM_CONF environment variable (if set)

## Initial Testing [#INITIAL_TESTING](https://slurm.schedmd.com/nss_slurm.html)
Before enabling NSS Slurm directly on the node, you should use the
-s slurm option to getent within a newly launched job step
to verify that the rest of the setup has been completed successfully. The
-s option to getent allows it to query a specific database —
even if it has not been enabled by default through the system's
nsswitch.conf . Note that nss_slurm only responds to requests from
processes within the job step itself — you must launch the getent
command within a job step to see any data returned.
As an example of a successful query:
```text
tim@blackhole:~$ srun getent -s slurm passwd tim:x:1000:1000:Tim Wickberg:/home/tim:/bin/bash tim@blackhole:~$ srun getent -s slurm group tim:x:1000:tim projecta:x:1001:tim
```
