Enabling nss_slurm is as simple as adding slurm to the passwd and
group database in /etc/nsswitch.conf (only on systems that will run
slurmd ). It is recommended that
slurm is listed first, as the order (from left to right) determines
the sequence in which the NSS databases will be queried, and this ensures Slurm
handles the request if able before submitting the query to other sources.
To enable cloud node name resolution slurm needs to be added to the
to hosts database in /etc/nsswitch.conf .
It is recommended that slurm is listed last.
Once enabled, test it by launching getent queries such as:
```text
tim@blackhole:~$ srun getent passwd tim tim:x:1000:1000:Tim Wickberg:/home/tim:/bin/bash tim@blackhole:~$ srun getent group projecta projecta:x:1001:tim

## Hierarchy[#hierarchy](https://slurm.schedmd.com/resource_limits.html)
Slurm's hierarchical limits are enforced in the following order
with Job QOS and Partition QOS order being reversible by using the QOS
flag 'OverPartQOS':
- Partition QOS limit
- Job QOS limit
- User association
- Account association(s), ascending the hierarchy
- Root/Cluster association
- Partition limit
- None
Note: If limits are defined at multiple points in this hierarchy,
the point in this list where the limit is first defined will be used.
Consider the following example:
- MaxJobs=20 and MaxSubmitJobs is undefined in the partition QOS
- No limits are set in the job QOS and
- MaxJobs=4 and MaxSubmitJobs=50 in the user association
The limits in effect will be MaxJobs=20 and MaxSubmitJobs=50.

Scheduling policy information must be stored in a database
as specified by the AccountingStorageType configuration parameter
in the slurm.conf configuration file.
Information can be recorded in a [MySQL](http://www.mysql.com/) or
[MariaDB](https://mariadb.org/) database.
For security and performance reasons, the use of
SlurmDBD (Slurm Database Daemon) as a front-end to the
database is strongly recommended.
SlurmDBD uses a Slurm authentication plugin (e.g. MUNGE).
SlurmDBD also uses an existing Slurm accounting storage plugin
to maximize code reuse.
SlurmDBD uses data caching and prioritization of pending requests
in order to optimize performance.
While SlurmDBD relies upon existing Slurm plugins for authentication
and database use, the other Slurm commands and daemons are not required

When a GRES has a type associated with it and a limit is applied
over this specific type (e.g. MaxTRESPerUser=gres/gpu:tesla=1 ) if a
user requests a generic gres, the type's limit will not be enforced. In this

enforced so it will still be possible to get two teslas.

## Tools[#tools](https://slurm.schedmd.com/resource_limits.html)
The tool used to manage accounting policy is sacctmgr .
It can be used to create and delete cluster, user, account,
and partition records plus their combined association record.
See man sacctmgr for details on this tools and examples of
its use.
Changes made to the scheduling policy are uploaded to
the Slurm control daemons on the various clusters and take effect
immediately. When an association is deleted, all running or pending
jobs which belong to that association are immediately canceled.
When limits are lowered, running jobs will not be canceled to
satisfy the new limits, but the new lower limits will be enforced.

-c [#OPT_-c](https://slurm.schedmd.com/slurmctld.html) Clear all previous slurmctld state from its last checkpoint.
With this option, all jobs, including both running and queued, and all
node states, will be deleted. Without this option, previously running
jobs will be preserved along with node State of DOWN, DRAINED
and DRAINING nodes and the associated Reason field for those nodes.

### Job Scheduling Priority [#priority](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
Job scheduling priority is made up of a number of factors as
described in the [priority/multifactor](https://slurm.schedmd.com/priority_multifactor.html) plugin. One
of the factors is the QOS priority. Each QOS is defined in the Slurm
database and includes an associated priority. Jobs that request and
are permitted a QOS will incorporate the priority associated with that
QOS in the job's [multi-factor priority calculation.](https://slurm.schedmd.com/priority_multifactor.html)
To enable the QOS priority component of the multi-factor priority
calculation, the "PriorityWeightQOS" configuration parameter must be
defined in the slurm.conf file and assigned an integer value greater
than zero.
A job's QOS only affects is scheduling priority when the
multi-factor plugin is loaded.

Slurm offers two ways for a queued job to preempt a running job,
free-up the running job's resources and allocate them to the queued
job. See the [Preemption description](https://slurm.schedmd.com/preempt.html) for
details.
The preemption method is determined by the "PreemptType"
configuration parameter defined in slurm.conf. When the "PreemptType"
is set to "preempt/qos", a queued job's QOS will be used to determine
whether it can preempt a running job. It is important to note that the QOS
used to determine if a job is eligible for preemption is the QOS associated
with the job and not a [Partition QOS](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html).

QOSs that it can preempt. When there is a queued job with a QOS that
is allowed to preempt a running job of another QOS, the Slurm

## Partition QOS [#partition](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
A QOS can be attached to a partition. This means the partition will have all
the same limits as the QOS. This does not associate jobs with the QOS, nor does
it give the job any priority or preemption characteristics of the assigned QOS.
Jobs may separately request the same QOS or a different QOS to gain those
characteristics. However, the Partition QOS limits will override the job's QOS.
If the opposite is desired you may configure the job's QOS with
`Flags=OverPartQOS` which will reverse the order of precedence.
This functionality may be used to implement a true "floating"
partition, in which a partition may access a limited amount of resources with no
restrictions on which nodes it uses to get the resources. This is accomplished
by assigning all nodes to the partition, then configuring a Partition QOS with
`GrpTRES` set to the desired resource limits.

Starting in Slurm 23.11, a QOS may be configured to contain relative resource
limits instead of absolute limits by setting `Flags=Relative`.
When this flag is set, all resource limits are treated as percentages of the
total resources available. Values higher than 100 are interpreted as 100%.
Memory limits should be set with no units. Although the default units (MB) will
be displayed, the limits will be enforced as a percentage (1MB = 1%).

resources in the whole cluster. For example, `cpu=50` would be

## Licenses Overview [#overview](https://slurm.schedmd.com/licenses.html)
Slurm can help with software license management by assigning available
licenses to jobs at scheduling time. If the licenses are not available, jobs
are kept pending until licenses become available. Licenses in Slurm are
essentially shared resources, meaning configured resources that are not tied to
a specific host but are associated with the entire cluster.
Licenses in Slurm can be configured in two ways:
- Local Licenses: Local licenses are local to the cluster using the slurm.conf in which they are configured.
- Remote Licenses: Remote licenses are served by the database and are configured using the sacctmgr command. Remote licenses are dynamic in nature as upon running the sacctmgr command, the slurmdbd updates all clusters the licenses are assigned to.

Summary — how licenses affect an sbatch submission

- What a "license" is in Slurm
  - A license in Slurm is a cluster-wide shared resource (not tied to a specific node). Examples: license=ansys, fluent, etc.
  - Licenses are configured either in slurm.conf (local licenses) or in the SlurmDB (remote/dynamic licenses).

- How you request licenses when submitting
  - sbatch -L <name>:<count> (short) or sbatch --licenses=<name>:<count>.
    Example: sbatch -L ansys:2 script.sh
  - Alternatively you can request a license as a TRES: --tres-per-task=license/ansys=1 (requires the license be listed in AccountingStorageTRES).

- Scheduling behavior
  - The scheduler treats licenses like any other scarce shared resource. A job that requests N of a license will not be eligible to start until at least N free licenses exist.
  - If the requested license count is not available at submit/schedule time, the job remains PENDING and will be released when enough licenses become free.
  - When a job is allocated, Slurm decrements the license “Free” count and increments “Used”; when the job completes the count is returned.

- Dynamic and remote license effects
  - For remote/dynamic licenses, administrators can update the LastConsumed value (e.g., via sacctmgr) from an external license server. Slurm uses LastConsumed and computes LastDeficit to avoid overcommitting licenses that appear missing.
  - If LastDeficit indicates licenses are missing, the scheduler will reserve (set aside) those licenses and may keep jobs pending even if the total configured count looks sufficient.

- Practical consequences you should expect
  - If you submit with -L and licenses are currently in use, your job will queue and wait for licenses rather than fail.
  - If you forget to request a license that your job’s software actually needs, the job may start but later fail when the software cannot check out a license (that check is external to Slurm). Requesting the license via Slurm is the way to make scheduling respect that dependency.
  - Use --tres-per-task when you want per-task accounting of licenses; ensure the license TRES is configured in AccountingStorageTRES.

- How to check license status (admin/user commands)
  - scontrol show lic (or the scontrol_license view) shows LicenseName, Total, Used, Free.
  - Administrators use sacctmgr to add/update resources and to adjust LastConsumed for dynamic setups.

If you want, I can show the current license list/free counts on your cluster (scontrol show lic). Would you like me to check that?

------------------------------------------------------------
root         root       1.000     1.000      0.000

- alice: RawShares=0.600, NormShares=0.420, EffectvUsage=1.800
- bob:   RawShares=0.300, NormShares=0.380, EffectvUsage=0.700
- charlie: RawShares=0.100, NormShares=0.200, EffectvUsage=0.400
- root:  RawShares=1.000, NormShares=1.000, EffectvUsage=0.000

What this means (fairshare):
- NormShares indicates relative entitlement (normalized share). By that measure alice has the second-largest entitlement (0.420) after root; she is slightly above bob (0.380) and well above charlie (0.200).
- EffectvUsage is the recent/accumulated usage that the scheduler uses to reduce priority for users who have consumed more resources. Higher EffectvUsage -> lower current fairshare priority.
- Because alice’s EffectvUsage (1.800) is substantially higher than bob (0.700) and charlie (0.400), alice’s current fairshare priority is lower than those users despite her larger normalized share. root has the highest entitlement and zero usage, so root currently has the highest effective priority.

Net conclusion:
- Alice has higher entitlement than Bob and Charlie, but her much higher recent usage means she will be deprioritized by fairshare compared with them right now.

- show the current priority scores (sprio) to see the exact ordering, or

## EXAMPLES[#SECTION_EXAMPLES](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Specify a batch script by filename on the command line. The batch script specifies a 1 minute time limit for the job.
```text
$ cat myscript #!/bin/sh #SBATCH --time=1 srun hostname |sort $ sbatch -N4 myscript salloc: Granted job allocation 65537 $ cat slurm-65537.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
Pass a batch script to sbatch on standard input:
```text
$ sbatch -N4 #!/bin/sh > srun hostname |sort > EOF sbatch: Submitted batch job 65541 $ cat slurm-65541.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
To create a heterogeneous job with 3 components, each allocating a unique set of nodes:
```text
$ sbatch -w node[2-3] : -w node4 : -w node[5-7] work.bash Submitted batch job 34987
```

## EXAMPLES[#SECTION_EXAMPLES](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Specify a batch script by filename on the command line. The batch script specifies a 1 minute time limit for the job.
```text
$ cat myscript #!/bin/sh #SBATCH --time=1 srun hostname |sort $ sbatch -N4 myscript salloc: Granted job allocation 65537 $ cat slurm-65537.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
Pass a batch script to sbatch on standard input:
```text
$ sbatch -N4 #!/bin/sh > srun hostname |sort > EOF sbatch: Submitted batch job 65541 $ cat slurm-65541.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
To create a heterogeneous job with 3 components, each allocating a unique set of nodes:
```text
$ sbatch -w node[2-3] : -w node4 : -w node[5-7] work.bash Submitted batch job 34987
```

## PERFORMANCE[#SECTION_PERFORMANCE](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Executing sbatch sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmctld daemon come in at once, it can result in
a degradation of performance of the slurmctld daemon, possibly resulting
in a denial of service.
Do not run sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other
programs. Ensure that programs limit calls to sbatch to the minimum
necessary for the information you are trying to gather.

Executing sbatch sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote

in a denial of service.

procedure calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other

## EXAMPLES[#SECTION_EXAMPLES](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Specify a batch script by filename on the command line. The batch script specifies a 1 minute time limit for the job.
```text
$ cat myscript #!/bin/sh #SBATCH --time=1 srun hostname |sort $ sbatch -N4 myscript salloc: Granted job allocation 65537 $ cat slurm-65537.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
Pass a batch script to sbatch on standard input:
```text
$ sbatch -N4 #!/bin/sh > srun hostname |sort > EOF sbatch: Submitted batch job 65541 $ cat slurm-65541.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
To create a heterogeneous job with 3 components, each allocating a unique set of nodes:
```text
$ sbatch -w node[2-3] : -w node4 : -w node[5-7] work.bash Submitted batch job 34987
```

## Initial Testing [#INITIAL_TESTING](https://slurm.schedmd.com/nss_slurm.html)
Before enabling NSS Slurm directly on the node, you should use the
-s slurm option to getent within a newly launched job step
to verify that the rest of the setup has been completed successfully. The
-s option to getent allows it to query a specific database —
even if it has not been enabled by default through the system's
nsswitch.conf . Note that nss_slurm only responds to requests from
processes within the job step itself — you must launch the getent
command within a job step to see any data returned.
As an example of a successful query:
```text
tim@blackhole:~$ srun getent -s slurm passwd tim:x:1000:1000:Tim Wickberg:/home/tim:/bin/bash tim@blackhole:~$ srun getent -s slurm group tim:x:1000:tim projecta:x:1001:tim
```

## PERFORMANCE[#SECTION_PERFORMANCE](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Executing sbatch sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmctld daemon come in at once, it can result in
a degradation of performance of the slurmctld daemon, possibly resulting
in a denial of service.
Do not run sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other
programs. Ensure that programs limit calls to sbatch to the minimum
necessary for the information you are trying to gather.

## Burst Buffers [#burst_buffer](https://slurm.schedmd.com/heterogeneous_jobs.html)
A burst buffer can either be persistent or linked to a specific job ID.
Since a heterogeneous job consists of multiple job IDs, a job-specific burst
buffer will be associated with only one heterogeneous job component.
Each component can have its own burst buffer directives, and they are processed
separately. Only a persistent burst buffer can be accessed by all components
of a heterogeneous job. Persistent burst buffers are only available in the
datawarp plugin. A sample batch script demonstrating this for the datawarp
plugin is appended.

#!/bin/bash #SBATCH --nodes=1 --constraint=haswell #BB create_persistent name=alpha capacity=10 access=striped type=scratch #DW persistentdw name=alpha #SBATCH hetjob #SBATCH --nodes=16 --constraint=knl #DW persistentdw name=alpha ...

The srun command is used to launch applications.
By default, the application is launched only on the first component of a
heterogeneous job, but options are available to support different behaviors.
srun's "--het-group" option defines which hetjob component(s) are to have
applications launched for them. The --het-group option takes an expression
defining which component(s) are to launch an application for an individual
execution of the srun command. The expression can contain one or more component
index values in a comma separated list. Ranges of index values can be specified
in a hyphen separated list. By default, an application is launched only on

## DESCRIPTION[#SECTION_DESCRIPTION](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
sbatch submits a batch script to Slurm. The batch script may be given to
sbatch through a file name on the command line, or if no file name is specified,
sbatch will read in a script from standard input.
The batch script may contain one or more lines beginning with "#SBATCH" followed
by any of the CLI options documented on this page. #SBATCH directives are read
directly by Slurm, so shell-specific syntax including variable names will be
read as literal text. Once the first non-comment, non-whitespace line has been
reached in the script, no more #SBATCH directives will be processed. See example
below.

## EXAMPLES[#SECTION_EXAMPLES](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Specify a batch script by filename on the command line. The batch script specifies a 1 minute time limit for the job.
```text
$ cat myscript #!/bin/sh #SBATCH --time=1 srun hostname |sort $ sbatch -N4 myscript salloc: Granted job allocation 65537 $ cat slurm-65537.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
Pass a batch script to sbatch on standard input:
```text
$ sbatch -N4 #!/bin/sh > srun hostname |sort > EOF sbatch: Submitted batch job 65541 $ cat slurm-65541.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
To create a heterogeneous job with 3 components, each allocating a unique set of nodes:
```text
$ sbatch -w node[2-3] : -w node4 : -w node[5-7] work.bash Submitted batch job 34987

## PERFORMANCE[#SECTION_PERFORMANCE](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Executing sbatch sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmctld daemon come in at once, it can result in
a degradation of performance of the slurmctld daemon, possibly resulting
in a denial of service.
Do not run sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other
programs. Ensure that programs limit calls to sbatch to the minimum
necessary for the information you are trying to gather.

## EXAMPLES[#SECTION_EXAMPLES](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Specify a batch script by filename on the command line. The batch script specifies a 1 minute time limit for the job.
```text
$ cat myscript #!/bin/sh #SBATCH --time=1 srun hostname |sort $ sbatch -N4 myscript salloc: Granted job allocation 65537 $ cat slurm-65537.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
Pass a batch script to sbatch on standard input:
```text
$ sbatch -N4 #!/bin/sh > srun hostname |sort > EOF sbatch: Submitted batch job 65541 $ cat slurm-65541.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
To create a heterogeneous job with 3 components, each allocating a unique set of nodes:
```text
$ sbatch -w node[2-3] : -w node4 : -w node[5-7] work.bash Submitted batch job 34987
```

## PERFORMANCE[#SECTION_PERFORMANCE](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Executing sbatch sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmctld daemon come in at once, it can result in
a degradation of performance of the slurmctld daemon, possibly resulting
in a denial of service.
Do not run sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other
programs. Ensure that programs limit calls to sbatch to the minimum
necessary for the information you are trying to gather.

heterogeneous job, but options are available to support different behaviors.

## DESCRIPTION[#SECTION_DESCRIPTION](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbcast.html)
sbcast is used to transmit a file to all nodes allocated
to the currently active Slurm job.
This command should only be executed from within a Slurm batch
job or within the shell spawned after a Slurm job's resource
allocation.
SOURCE is the name of a file on the current node.
DEST should be the fully qualified pathname for the
file copy to be created on each node.
If a fully qualified pathname is not provided, the file will be created in
the directory specified in the BcastParameters parameter in the slurm.conf
file (if available) otherwise it will be created in the current working
directory from which the sbcast command is invoked.
DEST should be on a file system local to that node.
Note that parallel file systems may provide better performance
than sbcast can provide, although performance will vary
by file size, degree of parallelism, and network type.

## PERFORMANCE[#SECTION_PERFORMANCE](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbcast.html)
Executing sbcast sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from sbcast or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmctld daemon come in at once, it can result in
a degradation of performance of the slurmctld daemon, possibly resulting
in a denial of service.
Do not run sbcast or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other
programs. Ensure that programs limit calls to sbcast to the minimum
necessary for the information you are trying to gather.

Summary
- sbcast is a Slurm utility that copies (broadcasts) a file from the node where it is run to every node in the current Slurm allocation.
- It must be run inside a Slurm allocation (inside a batch job, an salloc/srun shell, or the shell spawned by an allocation).
- Destination (DEST) should be a path on a node-local filesystem (or else the configured BcastParameters directory). If DEST is not fully qualified, Slurm will place the file in the configured broadcast directory or the current working directory.

When sbcast helps (good use cases)
- No or slow shared filesystem: nodes do not share a fast parallel FS (or NFS is a hotspot). sbcast avoids many clients hitting the shared filesystem for the same file.
- Node-local staging for fast I/O: you want to copy a binary, model or dataset to node-local NVMe /tmp or $SLURM_TMPDIR before launching GPU/CPU work.
- Reducing metadata/IO pressure: many ranks/processes opening the same file from a global filesystem can overload metadata servers; staging to local disk reduces that load.
- Packaging a self-contained executable: use --send-libs to include needed shared libraries when launching on nodes that may not have the same environment.
- When launching many tasks that read the same large file in parallel from local disk (e.g., local dataset shards).

When sbcast is not the best choice
- Small files on a fast parallel filesystem: the global FS may already be faster/more convenient.
- Extremely large files (> parallel FS speed): a high-performance parallel FS may outperform node-by-node copies, or you may prefer a pre-staged dataset on local disks via a cluster data-management workflow.
- Frequent repeated sbcast calls: sbcast sends RPCs to slurmctld — many calls can degrade the controller and even resemble a DoS. Don’t call sbcast in tight loops or per-task.

Practical notes and options
- Typical flow in a job script:
  1) inside the job, copy with sbcast: sbcast ./mybinary /tmp/mybinary
  2) make it executable (chmod) and run it with srun or mpirun from the job
- Useful options:
  - --compress / -C (lz4 by default) — reduces network bytes sent for compressible files.
  - --fanout / -F — tune tree fanout for distribution topology.
  - --send-libs — auto-detect and broadcast dependent shared libraries.
  - --preserve / -p — preserve file attributes.
  - --exclude — exclude directories when autodetecting deps.
- DEST should refer to a node-local path. If you leave DEST unspecified, Slurm will use BcastParameters or the current working directory; check your cluster’s slurm.conf/BcastParameters if unsure.
- Cleanup: remove staged files in job epilog or at end of job to avoid filling local storage.

Performance/operational cautions
- sbcast triggers RPCs to slurmctld. Avoid many simultaneous sbcast calls from user scripts or at cluster scale.
- For very large data and high parallelism, test performance: sometimes a parallel filesystem or a coordinated pre-staging tool is faster.
- Do not rely on sbcast for persistent long-term storage — it is for staging within an allocation.

Example
Inside a job script:
- sbcast --compress ./model.tar /tmp/model.tar
- tar -xvf /tmp/model.tar -C /tmp/model_data
- srun --ntasks=... train --data /tmp/model_data

If you want, I can show a concrete sbcast command example tuned for your cluster (suggested DEST path, --fanout, compression) — tell me where you plan to stage files (e.g., /tmp, $SLURM_TMPDIR) and approximate file sizes.

Slurm generally classifies users into three authorization levels:
- Administrators include root, SlurmUser, and any users with
"AdminLevel=Administrator"
- Privileged Users include all Administrators and any users with
"AdminLevel=Operator"
- Effective Owners of a job or step include the direct owner and all
Coordinators of the corresponding account.
Note that configuring AdminLevels or Coordinators requires the use of SlurmDBD.

Slurm generally classifies users into three authorization levels:
- Administrators include root, SlurmUser, and any users with
"AdminLevel=Administrator"
- Privileged Users include all Administrators and any users with
"AdminLevel=Operator"

## Overview[#overview](https://slurm.schedmd.com/job_array.html)
Job arrays offer a mechanism for submitting and managing collections of
similar jobs quickly and easily, useful for repetitive workloads that follow a
common job pattern. This greatly improves overall performance, since job arrays
with millions of tasks can be submitted in milliseconds (subject to configured
size limits) and the scheduler can quickly identify cases when no more array
tasks are eligible to start.
All jobs must have the same initial options (e.g., size, time limit), however,
it is possible to change some of these options after the job has begun
execution using the scontrol command specifying the JobID of the array or
individual ArrayJobID .
```text
$ scontrol update job=101 ... $ scontrol update job=101_1 ...
```

A job which is to be dependent upon an entire job array should specify
itself dependent upon the ArrayJobID.
Since each array element can have a different exit code, the interpretation of
the afterok and afternotok clauses will be based upon the highest
exit code from any task in the job array.

## System Administration [#administration](https://slurm.schedmd.com/job_array.html)
A new configuration parameter has been added to control the maximum
job array size: MaxArraySize . The smallest index that can be specified
by a user is zero and the maximum index is MaxArraySize minus one.
The default value of MaxArraySize is 1001.
The maximum MaxArraySize supported in Slurm is 4000001.
Be mindful about the value of MaxArraySize as job arrays offer an easy way
for users to submit large numbers of jobs very quickly.
The sched/backfill plugin has been modified to improve performance with
job arrays. Once one element of a job array is discovered to not be runnable
or impact the scheduling of pending jobs, the remaining elements of that job
array will be quickly skipped.

## Other Command Use [#other_commands](https://slurm.schedmd.com/job_array.html)
The following Slurm commands do not currently recognize job arrays and their
use requires the use of Slurm job IDs, which are unique for each array element:
sbcast, sprio, sreport, sshare and sstat.

specification of either job IDs or job array elements.
The sview command has been modified to permit display of a job's ArrayJobId
and ArrayTaskId fields. Both fields are displayed with a value of "N/A" if
the job is not part of a job array.

## DESCRIPTION[#SECTION_DESCRIPTION](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
sbatch submits a batch script to Slurm. The batch script may be given to
sbatch through a file name on the command line, or if no file name is specified,
sbatch will read in a script from standard input.
The batch script may contain one or more lines beginning with "#SBATCH" followed
by any of the CLI options documented on this page. #SBATCH directives are read
directly by Slurm, so shell-specific syntax including variable names will be
read as literal text. Once the first non-comment, non-whitespace line has been
reached in the script, no more #SBATCH directives will be processed. See example
below.

## AUTHORIZATION[#SECTION_AUTHORIZATION](https://slurm.schedmd.com/scontrol.html)
Slurm generally classifies users into three authorization levels:
- Administrators include root, SlurmUser, and any users with
"AdminLevel=Administrator"
- Privileged Users include all Administrators and any users with
"AdminLevel=Operator"
- Effective Owners of a job or step include the direct owner and all
Coordinators of the corresponding account.
Note that configuring AdminLevels or Coordinators requires the use of SlurmDBD.
The authorization levels required to execute various commands are defined in the
following table.
scontrol update job: Privileged or Effective Owner
scontrol requeue: Privileged or Effective Owner
scontrol update step: Privileged or Effective Owner
scontrol suspend: Privileged or Coordinator
scontrol resume: Privileged or Coordinator
scontrol notify: Root, SlurmUser, or direct owner

Use of the scontrol show job option shows two new fields related to
job array support.
The JobID is a unique identifier for the job.
The ArrayJobID is the JobID of the first element of the job
array.
The ArrayTaskID is the array index of this particular entry, either a
single number of an expression identifying the entries represented by this
job record (e.g. "5-1024").

The optional job ID specified with the scontrol show job or
scontrol show step commands can identify job array elements by
specifying ArrayJobId and ArrayTaskId with an underscore between

# "Configless" Slurm
"Configless" Slurm is a feature that allows the compute nodes —
specifically the slurmd process — and user commands running on login
nodes to pull configuration information directly from the slurmctld instead of
from a pre-distributed local file. Your cluster does require a central set of
configuration files on the Slurm controllers — "configless" in Slurm's
parlance means that the compute nodes, login nodes, and other cluster hosts
do not need to be deployed with local copies of these files.
The slurmd on startup will reach out to a slurmctld that you specify and the
config files will be pulled to the node. This slurmctld can be identified by
either an explicit option, or — preferably — through DNS SRV

## Notes[#NOTES](https://slurm.schedmd.com/configless_slurm.html)
Starting from Slurm 25.11, there's a new
SlurmctldParameters=reconfig_on_restart option that will make every
restart of slurmctld (process restart not triggered by "scontrol reconfigure")
to trigger a reconfiguration request to all slurmd and sackd daemons. For
"configless" systems this will ensure all processes are running the current
configuration. Some caution should be taken if you intend to perform rolling
upgrades on the cluster as this could lead to the daemons being upgraded sooner
than expected.
The order of precedence for determining what configuration source to use
is as follows:
- The slurmd --conf-server $host[:$port] option
- The -f $config_file option
- The SLURM_CONF environment variable (if set)
- A local slurm config file: The default slurm config file (likely /etc/slurm.conf)

## Initial Testing [#INITIAL_TESTING](https://slurm.schedmd.com/nss_slurm.html)
Before enabling NSS Slurm directly on the node, you should use the
-s slurm option to getent within a newly launched job step
to verify that the rest of the setup has been completed successfully. The
-s option to getent allows it to query a specific database —
even if it has not been enabled by default through the system's
nsswitch.conf . Note that nss_slurm only responds to requests from
processes within the job step itself — you must launch the getent
command within a job step to see any data returned.
As an example of a successful query:
```text
tim@blackhole:~$ srun getent -s slurm passwd tim:x:1000:1000:Tim Wickberg:/home/tim:/bin/bash tim@blackhole:~$ srun getent -s slurm group tim:x:1000:tim projecta:x:1001:tim
```

## NSS Configuration [#NSS_CONFIG](https://slurm.schedmd.com/nss_slurm.html)
Enabling nss_slurm is as simple as adding slurm to the passwd and
group database in /etc/nsswitch.conf (only on systems that will run
slurmd ). It is recommended that
slurm is listed first, as the order (from left to right) determines
the sequence in which the NSS databases will be queried, and this ensures Slurm
handles the request if able before submitting the query to other sources.
To enable cloud node name resolution slurm needs to be added to the
to hosts database in /etc/nsswitch.conf .
It is recommended that slurm is listed last.
Once enabled, test it by launching getent queries such as:
```text
tim@blackhole:~$ srun getent passwd tim tim:x:1000:1000:Tim Wickberg:/home/tim:/bin/bash tim@blackhole:~$ srun getent group projecta projecta:x:1001:tim
```

The module bases its checks on local steps that have already been launched. Jobs
launched without this option do not have an extern step, so pam_slurm_adopt will
not have access to those jobs.
LaunchParameters=ulimit_pam_adopt will set RLIMIT_RSS in processes

The "show" command, when used with the "job" or "job <jobid>"
entity displays detailed information about a job or jobs. Much of
this information may be modified using the "update job" command as
described above. However, the following fields displayed by the show
job command are read-only and cannot be modified:
AllocNode:Sid [#OPT_AllocNode:Sid](https://slurm.schedmd.com/scontrol.html) Local node and system id making the resource allocation.
BatchFlag [#OPT_BatchFlag](https://slurm.schedmd.com/scontrol.html) Jobs submitted using the sbatch command have BatchFlag set to 1. The BatchFlag
will be incremented past 1 if the job is requeued due to a failure. Jobs
submitted using other commands have BatchFlag set to 0 and will not be
incremented.

Summary — what a "hold" is
- A hold prevents a job (or job-array element) from becoming eligible to run. Held jobs stay in the queue (PENDING) until the hold(s) are cleared or some other condition changes.
- Holds are separate from job dependencies and resource reasons; a job with any active hold will not be scheduled even if resources and dependencies are otherwise satisfied.

Where you see holds
- scontrol show job <jobid> (or squeue with reason) shows the Hold field/flags and squeue may show a PD reason like "JobHeld".
- sbatch --hold submits a job initially held.

Types of holds and who sets/releases them
- UserHold (or "user"): applied by the job owner (e.g., sbatch --hold or scontrol hold by owner). Owners (and privileged users) can release these.
- AdminHold (or "admin"): applied by an administrator/operator (scontrol hold by admin). Only admins/operators (or privileged users) can remove these.
- SystemHold (or "system"): set by Slurm itself (or by site scripts/plugins) for system-level reasons (e.g., account/quota enforcement, scontrol actions). Usually only admins can clear SystemHold.
- Dependency (or dependency-like states): job dependencies (--depend) are a separate mechanism that can prevent eligibility; they can appear as dependency-related hold/reasons until the dependency is satisfied.
- Note: the exact hold-label text can vary by Slurm version/site plugins (check scontrol show job for the concrete Hold= string).

Multiple holds and their effect
- Holds are cumulative/bitflags. If a job has more than one hold type set, clearing one will not make the job runnable — all active holds that block eligibility must be cleared.
- Once all holds are cleared the job becomes eligible again subject to normal scheduling (priority, resources, QOS, dependencies).

Job arrays
- You can place holds on the whole array (jobid) or on individual elements (jobid_index). scontrol hold/release accepts either form; behavior follows the same cumulative-hold rules.

Running jobs vs held jobs
- Holds are intended for pending batch jobs. Applying a hold does not generally pause/stop an already RUNNING job. To pause a running job, use suspend/resume (scontrol suspend/resume) or administrator-enforced mechanisms. (Some site-specific behavior could differ; consult your admin.)

Common commands (informational)
- Submit held: sbatch --hold myjob.sh
- Add a hold: scontrol hold <jobid>  (owner can hold own job; admin can hold any job)
- Release a hold: scontrol release <jobid>  (only allowed if you have permission to clear that hold)
- Inspect holds/detail: scontrol show job <jobid>  (look for Hold= and for the pending reason)

# Job Reason Codes

## Partition QOS [#partition](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
A QOS can be attached to a partition. This means the partition will have all
the same limits as the QOS. This does not associate jobs with the QOS, nor does
it give the job any priority or preemption characteristics of the assigned QOS.
Jobs may separately request the same QOS or a different QOS to gain those
characteristics. However, the Partition QOS limits will override the job's QOS.
If the opposite is desired you may configure the job's QOS with
`Flags=OverPartQOS` which will reverse the order of precedence.
This functionality may be used to implement a true "floating"
partition, in which a partition may access a limited amount of resources with no
restrictions on which nodes it uses to get the resources. This is accomplished
by assigning all nodes to the partition, then configuring a Partition QOS with
`GrpTRES` set to the desired resource limits.

### Job Preemption [#preemption](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
Slurm offers two ways for a queued job to preempt a running job,
free-up the running job's resources and allocate them to the queued
job. See the [Preemption description](https://slurm.schedmd.com/preempt.html) for
details.
The preemption method is determined by the "PreemptType"
configuration parameter defined in slurm.conf. When the "PreemptType"
is set to "preempt/qos", a queued job's QOS will be used to determine
whether it can preempt a running job. It is important to note that the QOS
used to determine if a job is eligible for preemption is the QOS associated
with the job and not a [Partition QOS](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html).
The QOS can be assigned (using sacctmgr ) a list of other
QOSs that it can preempt. When there is a queued job with a QOS that
is allowed to preempt a running job of another QOS, the Slurm
scheduler will preempt the running job.

### Job Scheduling Priority [#priority](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
Job scheduling priority is made up of a number of factors as
described in the [priority/multifactor](https://slurm.schedmd.com/priority_multifactor.html) plugin. One
of the factors is the QOS priority. Each QOS is defined in the Slurm
database and includes an associated priority. Jobs that request and
are permitted a QOS will incorporate the priority associated with that
QOS in the job's [multi-factor priority calculation.](https://slurm.schedmd.com/priority_multifactor.html)
To enable the QOS priority component of the multi-factor priority
calculation, the "PriorityWeightQOS" configuration parameter must be
defined in the slurm.conf file and assigned an integer value greater
than zero.
A job's QOS only affects is scheduling priority when the
multi-factor plugin is loaded.

## System Administration [#administration](https://slurm.schedmd.com/job_array.html)
A new configuration parameter has been added to control the maximum
job array size: MaxArraySize . The smallest index that can be specified
by a user is zero and the maximum index is MaxArraySize minus one.
The default value of MaxArraySize is 1001.
The maximum MaxArraySize supported in Slurm is 4000001.
Be mindful about the value of MaxArraySize as job arrays offer an easy way
for users to submit large numbers of jobs very quickly.
The sched/backfill plugin has been modified to improve performance with
job arrays. Once one element of a job array is discovered to not be runnable
or impact the scheduling of pending jobs, the remaining elements of that job
array will be quickly skipped.

## Hierarchy[#hierarchy](https://slurm.schedmd.com/resource_limits.html)
Slurm's hierarchical limits are enforced in the following order
with Job QOS and Partition QOS order being reversible by using the QOS
flag 'OverPartQOS':
- Partition QOS limit
- Job QOS limit
- User association
- Account association(s), ascending the hierarchy
- Root/Cluster association
- Partition limit
- None
Note: If limits are defined at multiple points in this hierarchy,
the point in this list where the limit is first defined will be used.
Consider the following example:
- MaxJobs=20 and MaxSubmitJobs is undefined in the partition QOS
- No limits are set in the job QOS and
- MaxJobs=4 and MaxSubmitJobs=50 in the user association
The limits in effect will be MaxJobs=20 and MaxSubmitJobs=50.

## Partition QOS [#partition](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
A QOS can be attached to a partition. This means the partition will have all
the same limits as the QOS. This does not associate jobs with the QOS, nor does
it give the job any priority or preemption characteristics of the assigned QOS.
Jobs may separately request the same QOS or a different QOS to gain those
characteristics. However, the Partition QOS limits will override the job's QOS.
If the opposite is desired you may configure the job's QOS with
`Flags=OverPartQOS` which will reverse the order of precedence.
This functionality may be used to implement a true "floating"
partition, in which a partition may access a limited amount of resources with no
restrictions on which nodes it uses to get the resources. This is accomplished
by assigning all nodes to the partition, then configuring a Partition QOS with
`GrpTRES` set to the desired resource limits.

A special privileged user, usually an account manager, that can add
users or sub-accounts to the account they are coordinator over.

## Association specific limits and scheduling policies [#assoc](https://slurm.schedmd.com/resource_limits.html)
These represent the limits and scheduling policies relevant to Associations.
When dealing with Associations, most of these limits are available

## Other Command Use [#other_commands](https://slurm.schedmd.com/job_array.html)
The following Slurm commands do not currently recognize job arrays and their
use requires the use of Slurm job IDs, which are unique for each array element:
sbcast, sprio, sreport, sshare and sstat.
The sacct, sattach and strigger commands have been modified to permit
specification of either job IDs or job array elements.
The sview command has been modified to permit display of a job's ArrayJobId
and ArrayTaskId fields. Both fields are displayed with a value of "N/A" if
the job is not part of a job array.

Short answer
- QOS MaxJobsPerUser is a QOS-enforced limit that restricts how many jobs a single user may have under that QOS. When a job would exceed a configured QOS limit the scheduler will either pend the job with a reason that indicates which limit was hit or (if the QOS has Flags=DenyOnLimit) reject it at submission.
- The pending reason you see in squeue/sview identifies which specific limit blocked the job (e.g., a per-user job count limit, a per-account TRES limit, submit-count limits, etc.). Use squeue (reason column) and scontrol show job <id> to see the exact reason for a pending job.

What MaxJobsPerUser means (and related QOS limits)
- MaxJobs, MaxJobsPerUser (per-user job counts) — limit the number of jobs allowed. If the QOS sets a MaxJobsPerUser (or the association has an equivalent per-user limit), a new job that would make that user exceed the limit will not be started.
- MaxSubmitJobs — controls how many jobs the association/QOS will allow to be submitted (queued) for a user; exceeding it can block submission or cause pending behavior depending on flags.
- MaxTRES / GrpTRES / MaxTRESPerNode / related TRES limits — resource-count limits (CPUs, GPUs, memory) applied per-QOS or per-association; hitting these yields a TRES-related pending reason.
- MaxWall / MaxTime / Min/MaxNodes — other Max* limits that can cause pending reasons when job requests exceed allowed sizes/time.

How that shows up as pending reasons
- The scheduler maps a violated limit to a reason code shown in squeue (or sview). Examples of the kinds of reason you will see:
  - a per-QOS/per-account/per-user job-count limit (MaxJobs or MaxJobsPerUser) → a MaxJobs-type reason
  - submit-count limits (MaxSubmitJobs) → a MaxSubmitJobs/submit-limit reason
  - TRES (CPU/GPU/mem) limits → MaxTRES* or AssocGrp*/AssocMax* style reasons
  - group/association aggregate limits → AssocGrp* reasons
- Only the single reason encountered by the scheduling method is shown. If multiple limits would block the job, only the first-check reason is displayed.

Important behaviors to know
- Limit precedence: Slurm evaluates limits in a hierarchy (Partition QOS, Job QOS, user association, account associations up the chain, cluster). The first level where a limit is defined is the limit that will apply.
- DenyOnLimit flag: If a QOS has Flags=DenyOnLimit, jobs violating that QOS’s Max limits will be denied at submission rather than queued and pending. If DenyOnLimit is not set, jobs that would exceed the limit will typically pend until resources/quotas free up.
- Group (Grp*) limits: Group or association aggregate limits (GrpJobs, GrpTRES) are checked when a job is considered for allocation; if starting a job would exceed a group aggregate, it will be blocked and show the corresponding AssocGrp* reason.
- Relative QOS: In newer Slurm versions a QOS can use Flags=Relative so Max limits are interpreted as percentages of cluster resources — the same reason semantics apply, but the value calculation differs.

How to diagnose a job pending for QOS limits
- squeue -o "%i %P %j %u %t %M %R" (or use sview) — check the REASON column for the pending job.
- scontrol show job <jobid> — get the job’s QOS, QOS limits in effect, and additional fields.
- sacctmgr show qos format=... or sacctmgr show association / sacctmgr show user — inspect the QOS and association limits (MaxJobs, MaxSubmitJobs, GrpTRES, Flags like DenyOnLimit).
- If you see a MaxJobs/MaxSubmitJobs/TRES-related reason, inspect how many jobs or resources the user/account currently has (squeue, sshare) to determine what’s consuming the quota.

Example troubleshooting steps
1. squeue -j <jobid>  -> note the REASON and the QOS used by the job.
2. scontrol show job <jobid> -> confirm job QOS and requested resources.
3. sacctmgr show qos <qosname> format=name,flags,maxjobs,maxsubmitjobs,max_tres,... -> see configured QOS limits and whether DenyOnLimit is set.
4. squeue -u <user> (and sshare) -> count the user’s running/pending jobs and current usage to compare against limits.

How to change limits (admin)
- Use sacctmgr to modify QOS or association limits (sacctmgr modify qos <name> set MaxJobs=..., set Flags=DenyOnLimit, etc.). Because QOS limits override association limits, be sure you understand the hierarchy before changing values.

References
- Slurm documentation: QOS and Resource Limits pages (explain QOS limits, Flags=DenyOnLimit, and the precedence order) and the Job Reason Codes page (lists the reason strings used by squeue).

If you want, tell me a job ID that is pending for you and I can show the exact squeue reason and the QOS/association limits (I will run squeue and scontrol show job as needed).

## Following systemd rules [#systemd_rules](https://slurm.schedmd.com/cgroup_v2.html)
Systemd is currently the most widely used init mechanism. For this reason
Slurm needs to find a way to coexist with the rules of systemd. The designers of
systemd have conceived a new rule called the "single-writer" rule, which implies
that every cgroup has one single owner and nobody else should write to it. Read
more about this in [systemd.io Cgroup Delegation Documentation](https://systemd.io/CGROUP_DELEGATION). In practice this means that the systemd
daemon, started when the kernel boots and which takes pid 1, will consider
itself the absolute owner and single writer of the entire cgroup tree.
This means that systemd expects that no other process should be modifying any
cgroup directly, nor should another process be creating directories or moving
pids around, without systemd being aware of it.

Short answer: scancel is a client that asks slurmctld to deliver signals; slurmctld tells the slurmd(s) on the node(s) to signal the tracked processes for the targeted job(s)/step(s). The slurmd uses the configured proctrack (e.g., proctrack/cgroup or proctrack/linux) mechanism to find the task PIDs (or the job’s cgroup) and then send the requested signals to those PIDs (or the group).

Details and important behaviors
- Targets: you can target whole jobs (1234), individual steps (1234.1), array or array-index forms (1237_4), users, partitions, states, etc. Cancelling a job step (1234.1) does not by itself cancel the whole job/allocation; cancelling the job releases the allocation.
- Default cancel sequence (no --signal): scancel jobID performs a polite cancel:
  - sends SIGCONT to all steps to wake them (if stopped),
  - then sends SIGTERM,
  - waits the KillWait time configured in slurm.conf,
  - and if processes are still running finally sends SIGKILL.
  This gives steps a chance to clean up before forcible termination.
- --signal: you can request an explicit signal (name or number) to send instead of the default cancel sequence. Example: scancel --signal=TERM 1234.1 sends SIGTERM to step 1 of job 1234.
  - If you send a SIGNAL=KILL to an entire job, Slurm will kill active steps (SIGKILL) but that signal form by itself does not necessarily show as a normal job-cancel operation (see docs for exact semantics).
- --batch (-b): by default signals other than SIGKILL are NOT sent to the batch step (the job’s shell script). Using --batch causes scancel to signal only the batch shell step (useful when the shell should trap the signal) and not other steps.
- Granularity: scancel can signal individual steps (only those will get the signal) or whole jobs (all active steps). Use the job.step syntax to address steps.
- How delivery is implemented: slurmd invokes the proctrack/cgroup or proctrack/linux plugin to enumerate the PIDs for the job/step. The proctrack plugin then issues the kernel signals (or operates via the cgroup interface) to reach every task in the job/step. On systems with cgroups/systemd, Slurm often confines tasks in a cgroup and signals the set of PIDs in that cgroup; on other systems it will signal the recorded PIDs directly.
- Cleanup vs allocation release: cancelling a job (scancel without --signal) releases the allocation. Sending a signal to steps (using --signal) may not release the allocation unless you explicitly cancel the job.

Examples
- scancel 1234
  - cancel job 1234: SIGCONT → SIGTERM → wait KillWait → SIGKILL
- scancel --signal=TERM 1234.1 1234.3
  - send SIGTERM to steps 1 and 3 only
- scancel --signal=KILL 1235
  - send SIGKILL to all steps of job 1235 (see docs: this will kill active steps but that signal form alone is treated differently from a full job cancel)
- scancel --signal=USR1 --batch 1236
  - send SIGUSR1 to the batch shell process only (so the shell can trap it)

If you want precise, version-specific edge cases (exact behavior for KILL vs cancel, or how signals interact with particular proctrack/cgroup configs), tell me your Slurm version and whether you use proctrack/cgroup (cgroups v1/v2) or proctrack/linux and I can point to the exact doc excerpts for that setup.

Extra data may be added to a node, and jobs may request extra constraints
to filter nodes based on their extra data. This is disabled by
default, but may be enabled in slurm.conf. Warning : Slurm's backfill
scheduler cannot accurately plan nodes for jobs whose request extra constraints
are not immediately satisfied. This means that the more often extra data for
nodes is changed, the less accurate the backfill scheduler will be.

## Node Extra Data [#Node_Extra_Data](https://slurm.schedmd.com/extra_constraints.html)
A node's extra data is a json formatted string. It may be initialized on
slurmd startup with the --extra flag for slurmd. For example:
```text
slurmd --extra '{ "a": 1.23, "b": true, "c": 0, "foo": "bar", "zed": 23 }'
```
Or, it may be updated with scontrol. For example:
```text
scontrol update nodename=node123 extra='{ "a": 1.23, "b": true, "c": 0, "foo": "bar", "zed": 23 }'
```
This defines the features that may be requested by the --extra option in
salloc, sbatch, and srun. Values may be any string, number, or boolean value.

## DESCRIPTION[#SECTION_DESCRIPTION](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
sbatch submits a batch script to Slurm. The batch script may be given to
sbatch through a file name on the command line, or if no file name is specified,
sbatch will read in a script from standard input.
The batch script may contain one or more lines beginning with "#SBATCH" followed
by any of the CLI options documented on this page. #SBATCH directives are read
directly by Slurm, so shell-specific syntax including variable names will be
read as literal text. Once the first non-comment, non-whitespace line has been
reached in the script, no more #SBATCH directives will be processed. See example
below.

to filter nodes based on their extra data. This is disabled by

nodes is changed, the less accurate the backfill scheduler will be.

## SIGNALS AND ESCAPE SEQUENCES[#SECTION_SIGNALS-AND-ESCAPE-SEQUENCES](https://slurm.schedmd.com/srun.html)
Signals sent to the srun command are automatically forwarded to
the tasks it is controlling with a few exceptions. The escape sequence
<control-c> will report the state of all tasks associated with
the srun command. If <control-c> is entered twice within
one second, then the associated SIGINT signal will be sent to all tasks
and a termination sequence will be entered sending SIGCONT, SIGTERM,
and SIGKILL to all spawned tasks.
If a third <control-c> is received, the srun program will be
terminated without waiting for remote tasks to exit or their I/O to
complete.
The escape sequence <control-z> is presently ignored.

### Warnings [#Warnings](https://slurm.schedmd.com/extra_constraints.html)
Whitespace characters are not treated specially. Any whitespace characters will
be considered part of a key or value. This means that the following is invalid:
```text
--extra " (a=b)"

parenthesis character is recognized as an invalid character for either a key
or a comparison operator. This request would result in the job being rejected.
However, this is valid:
```text
--extra "( a=b)"
```
This has a single request. The key is " a", the comparison operator is "=", and
the value is "b".

special characters, and thus are part of a string. Thus, bar and "bar" are not

## EXAMPLES[#SECTION_EXAMPLES](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Specify a batch script by filename on the command line. The batch script specifies a 1 minute time limit for the job.
```text
$ cat myscript #!/bin/sh #SBATCH --time=1 srun hostname |sort $ sbatch -N4 myscript salloc: Granted job allocation 65537 $ cat slurm-65537.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
Pass a batch script to sbatch on standard input:
```text
$ sbatch -N4 #!/bin/sh > srun hostname |sort > EOF sbatch: Submitted batch job 65541 $ cat slurm-65541.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
To create a heterogeneous job with 3 components, each allocating a unique set of nodes:
```text
$ sbatch -w node[2-3] : -w node4 : -w node[5-7] work.bash Submitted batch job 34987
```

## Node Extra Data [#Node_Extra_Data](https://slurm.schedmd.com/extra_constraints.html)
A node's extra data is a json formatted string. It may be initialized on
slurmd startup with the --extra flag for slurmd. For example:
```text
slurmd --extra '{ "a": 1.23, "b": true, "c": 0, "foo": "bar", "zed": 23 }'
```
Or, it may be updated with scontrol. For example:
```text
scontrol update nodename=node123 extra='{ "a": 1.23, "b": true, "c": 0, "foo": "bar", "zed": 23 }'
```
This defines the features that may be requested by the --extra option in
salloc, sbatch, and srun. Values may be any string, number, or boolean value.

## Overview [#Overview](https://slurm.schedmd.com/extra_constraints.html)
Extra data may be added to a node, and jobs may request extra constraints
to filter nodes based on their extra data. This is disabled by
default, but may be enabled in slurm.conf. Warning : Slurm's backfill
scheduler cannot accurately plan nodes for jobs whose request extra constraints
are not immediately satisfied. This means that the more often extra data for
nodes is changed, the less accurate the backfill scheduler will be.

## Overview [#Overview](https://slurm.schedmd.com/extra_constraints.html)
Extra data may be added to a node, and jobs may request extra constraints
to filter nodes based on their extra data. This is disabled by
default, but may be enabled in slurm.conf. Warning : Slurm's backfill
scheduler cannot accurately plan nodes for jobs whose request extra constraints
are not immediately satisfied. This means that the more often extra data for
nodes is changed, the less accurate the backfill scheduler will be.

### Warnings [#Warnings](https://slurm.schedmd.com/extra_constraints.html)
Whitespace characters are not treated specially. Any whitespace characters will
be considered part of a key or value. This means that the following is invalid:
```text
--extra " (a=b)"
```
The space at he beginning is parsed as a key of a request. Then the opening
parenthesis character is recognized as an invalid character for either a key
or a comparison operator. This request would result in the job being rejected.
However, this is valid:
```text
--extra "( a=b)"
```
This has a single request. The key is " a", the comparison operator is "=", and
the value is "b".
This same warning applies to single and double quotes. These are not considered
special characters, and thus are part of a string. Thus, bar and "bar" are not
equal.

## Node Extra Data [#Node_Extra_Data](https://slurm.schedmd.com/extra_constraints.html)
A node's extra data is a json formatted string. It may be initialized on
slurmd startup with the --extra flag for slurmd. For example:
```text
slurmd --extra '{ "a": 1.23, "b": true, "c": 0, "foo": "bar", "zed": 23 }'
```
Or, it may be updated with scontrol. For example:
```text
scontrol update nodename=node123 extra='{ "a": 1.23, "b": true, "c": 0, "foo": "bar", "zed": 23 }'
```
This defines the features that may be requested by the --extra option in
salloc, sbatch, and srun. Values may be any string, number, or boolean value.

### Warnings [#Warnings](https://slurm.schedmd.com/extra_constraints.html)
Whitespace characters are not treated specially. Any whitespace characters will
be considered part of a key or value. This means that the following is invalid:
```text
--extra " (a=b)"
```
The space at he beginning is parsed as a key of a request. Then the opening
parenthesis character is recognized as an invalid character for either a key
or a comparison operator. This request would result in the job being rejected.
However, this is valid:
```text
--extra "( a=b)"
```
This has a single request. The key is " a", the comparison operator is "=", and
the value is "b".
This same warning applies to single and double quotes. These are not considered
special characters, and thus are part of a string. Thus, bar and "bar" are not
equal.

## Overview [#Overview](https://slurm.schedmd.com/extra_constraints.html)

to filter nodes based on their extra data. This is disabled by
default, but may be enabled in slurm.conf. Warning : Slurm's backfill

are not immediately satisfied. This means that the more often extra data for
nodes is changed, the less accurate the backfill scheduler will be.

### Warnings [#Warnings](https://slurm.schedmd.com/extra_constraints.html)
Whitespace characters are not treated specially. Any whitespace characters will
be considered part of a key or value. This means that the following is invalid:
```text
--extra " (a=b)"
```
The space at he beginning is parsed as a key of a request. Then the opening
parenthesis character is recognized as an invalid character for either a key
or a comparison operator. This request would result in the job being rejected.
However, this is valid:
```text
--extra "( a=b)"
```
This has a single request. The key is " a", the comparison operator is "=", and
the value is "b".
This same warning applies to single and double quotes. These are not considered
special characters, and thus are part of a string. Thus, bar and "bar" are not
equal.

## Node Extra Data [#Node_Extra_Data](https://slurm.schedmd.com/extra_constraints.html)
A node's extra data is a json formatted string. It may be initialized on
slurmd startup with the --extra flag for slurmd. For example:
```text
slurmd --extra '{ "a": 1.23, "b": true, "c": 0, "foo": "bar", "zed": 23 }'
```
Or, it may be updated with scontrol. For example:
```text
scontrol update nodename=node123 extra='{ "a": 1.23, "b": true, "c": 0, "foo": "bar", "zed": 23 }'
```
This defines the features that may be requested by the --extra option in
salloc, sbatch, and srun. Values may be any string, number, or boolean value.

## Overview [#Overview](https://slurm.schedmd.com/extra_constraints.html)
Extra data may be added to a node, and jobs may request extra constraints
to filter nodes based on their extra data. This is disabled by
default, but may be enabled in slurm.conf. Warning : Slurm's backfill
scheduler cannot accurately plan nodes for jobs whose request extra constraints
are not immediately satisfied. This means that the more often extra data for
nodes is changed, the less accurate the backfill scheduler will be.

## Squeue Command Use[#squeue](https://slurm.schedmd.com/job_array.html)
When a job array is submitted to Slurm, only one job record is created.
Additional job records will only be created when the state of a task in the
job array changes, typically when a task is allocated resources or its state
is modified using the scontrol command.
By default, the squeue command will report all of the tasks associated with
a single job record on one line and use a regular expression to indicate the
"array_task_id" values as shown below.
```text
$ squeue JOBID PARTITION NAME USER ST TIME NODES NODELIST(REASON) 1080_[5-1024] debug tmp mac PD 0:00 1 (Resources) 1080_1 debug tmp mac R 0:17 1 tux0 1080_2 debug tmp mac R 0:16 1 tux1 1080_3 debug tmp mac R 0:03 1 tux2 1080_4 debug tmp mac R 0:03 1 tux3
```

## AUTHORIZATION[#SECTION_AUTHORIZATION](https://slurm.schedmd.com/scontrol.html)
Slurm generally classifies users into three authorization levels:
- Administrators include root, SlurmUser, and any users with
"AdminLevel=Administrator"
- Privileged Users include all Administrators and any users with
"AdminLevel=Operator"
- Effective Owners of a job or step include the direct owner and all
Coordinators of the corresponding account.
Note that configuring AdminLevels or Coordinators requires the use of SlurmDBD.
The authorization levels required to execute various commands are defined in the
following table.
scontrol update job: Privileged or Effective Owner
scontrol requeue: Privileged or Effective Owner
scontrol update step: Privileged or Effective Owner
scontrol suspend: Privileged or Coordinator
scontrol resume: Privileged or Coordinator

## Burst Buffers [#burst_buffer](https://slurm.schedmd.com/heterogeneous_jobs.html)
A burst buffer can either be persistent or linked to a specific job ID.
Since a heterogeneous job consists of multiple job IDs, a job-specific burst
buffer will be associated with only one heterogeneous job component.
Each component can have its own burst buffer directives, and they are processed
separately. Only a persistent burst buffer can be accessed by all components
of a heterogeneous job. Persistent burst buffers are only available in the
datawarp plugin. A sample batch script demonstrating this for the datawarp
plugin is appended.
```text
#!/bin/bash #SBATCH --nodes=1 --constraint=haswell #BB create_persistent name=alpha capacity=10 access=striped type=scratch #DW persistentdw name=alpha #SBATCH hetjob #SBATCH --nodes=16 --constraint=knl #DW persistentdw name=alpha ...
```

Quick summary — what a hold does
- A hold prevents a job from becoming eligible to be scheduled. Held jobs remain in PENDING (or in the queue) until the hold(s) that block them are removed or their other start conditions are met.
- Holds do not by themselves terminate running jobs. (To stop a running job use suspend/requeue/cancel as appropriate.)

Hold types and who sets/releases them
- UserHold
  - Set by the job owner (e.g., sbatch --hold or scontrol hold <jobid>) or by an operator acting on behalf of the user.
  - Can be released by the job owner or by privileged users (admins/operators).
- AdminHold
  - Set by administrators/operators.
  - Only privileged users (admins/operators) may remove this hold.
- SystemHold (sometimes shown as System)
  - Placed by Slurm for internal/system reasons (maintenance, controller actions, etc.).
  - Normally only the system or administrators clear this; users cannot clear SystemHold.
- Dependency hold (Dependency / DependencyHold)
  - Applied automatically when a job is submitted with a dependency (sbatch --dependency=...).
  - Cleared automatically by Slurm once the dependency condition is satisfied. Manual release is not the normal path.
- Array- and component-specific holds
  - For job arrays and heterogeneous jobs there are per-element and leader semantics; you can set/release holds on the array leader or on specific array elements (e.g., 12345 or 12345_7).

Important behavior / semantics
- Holds are cumulative: multiple hold types may be set on the same job. All holds that apply must be removed (or the condition satisfied) before the job becomes eligible to start. Removing only some of the holds does not make the job runnable if any other hold remains.
- A released job still must satisfy all normal scheduling conditions (resources available, begin time, dependencies, QOS/account limits, priority). Releasing a hold only removes that particular eligibility blocker.
- Pending reason and visibility: squeue will show the job as PENDING and usually show a reason such as JobHeld or Dependency; scontrol show job displays the Hold (Hold=...) field listing which holds are set.
- Permission model: most hold/release operations are restricted. Unprivileged users can operate on their own jobs within policy limits; privileged users (admins/operators) can place/remove holds on any job.

Common commands (conceptual)
- Submit held: sbatch --hold … (job starts in a held state)
- Place a hold: scontrol hold <jobid>  (creates a UserHold or operator-set hold)
- Release a hold: scontrol release <jobid>  (removes the specified hold(s) according to permissions)
- Inspect holds and reasons: squeue (see reason column) and scontrol show job <jobid> (see Hold= and detailed fields)

Notes and gotchas
- Putting a hold on a job does not change its submit time or some accounting fields; requeuing vs holding have different effects.
- If a job is held because of a dependency, manually releasing it (if possible) can bypass the dependency logic and may produce unexpected behavior — dependency holds are typically managed by Slurm.
- For job arrays and heterogeneous jobs use the job-array element syntax when you mean a single task (e.g., 12345_3) or operate on the leader to affect the whole group.

- Show the hold state for a particular job (I’ll need the job ID), or
- Describe exact scontrol command forms and examples for your Slurm version.

## Overview[#overview](https://slurm.schedmd.com/federation.html)
Slurm includes support for creating a federation of clusters
and scheduling jobs in a peer-to-peer fashion between them. Jobs submitted to a
federation receive a unique job ID that is unique among all clusters in the
federation. A job is submitted to the local cluster (the cluster defined in the
slurm.conf) and is then replicated across the clusters in the federation. Each
cluster then independently attempts to the schedule the job based off of its own
scheduling policies. The clusters coordinate with the "origin" cluster (cluster
the job was submitted to) to schedule the job.
NOTE : This is not intended as a high-throughput environment. If
scheduling more than 50,000 jobs a day, consider configuring fewer clusters that
the sibling jobs can be submitted to or directing load
to the local cluster only (e.g. --cluster-constraint= or -M submission options
could be used to do...

- federation: mock-federation
- clusters: mock-cluster
- state: ACTIVE

What this means for jobs
- Federation is active, but it currently contains only one cluster ("mock-cluster"). With only one member, there are no other clusters to schedule sibling jobs on, so you cannot gain cross‑cluster scheduling benefit right now.
- In general (Slurm federation behavior): a federated submission does not create one allocation that uses nodes from multiple clusters simultaneously. Instead Slurm replicates the job as independent "sibling" jobs on the clusters in the federation. Each cluster then tries to schedule its sibling according to its own policies; the origin cluster coordinates but does not merge resources across clusters.
- You can direct which clusters are eligible for siblings when submitting (example): sbatch -M clusterA,clusterB script.sh — that limits sibling submission to clusterA and clusterB. But even then each sibling is an independent allocation on its cluster, not a single job spanning nodes from both clusters.

Bottom line
- Can jobs "span clusters" (use nodes from multiple clusters in a single allocation)? No — federation uses replicated sibling jobs, not a single cross‑cluster allocation.
- In your current federation (only "mock-cluster"), there is no second cluster to submit sibling jobs to, so no cross‑cluster scheduling is possible until other clusters are added.

## PERFORMANCE[#SECTION_PERFORMANCE](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Executing sbatch sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmctld daemon come in at once, it can result in
a degradation of performance of the slurmctld daemon, possibly resulting
in a denial of service.
Do not run sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other
programs. Ensure that programs limit calls to sbatch to the minimum
necessary for the information you are trying to gather.

## Job Dependencies [#dependencies](https://slurm.schedmd.com/burst_buffer.html)
If two jobs use burst buffers and one is dependent on the other (e.g.
`sbatch --dependency=afterok:123 ...`) then the second job will not
begin until the first job completes and its burst buffer stage-out completes.
If the second job does not use a burst buffer, but is dependent upon the first
job's completion, then it will not wait for the stage-out operation of the first
job to complete.
The second job can be made to wait for the first job's stage-out operation to
complete using the "afterburstbuffer" dependency option (e.g.
`sbatch --dependency=afterburstbuffer:123 ...`).

Before enabling NSS Slurm directly on the node, you should use the
-s slurm option to getent within a newly launched job step
to verify that the rest of the setup has been completed successfully. The
-s option to getent allows it to query a specific database —
even if it has not been enabled by default through the system's
nsswitch.conf . Note that nss_slurm only responds to requests from
processes within the job step itself — you must launch the getent
command within a job step to see any data returned.

```text
tim@blackhole:~$ srun getent -s slurm passwd tim:x:1000:1000:Tim Wickberg:/home/tim:/bin/bash tim@blackhole:~$ srun getent -s slurm group tim:x:1000:tim projecta:x:1001:tim
```

Short answer

- afterany: start the dependent job after the specified job(s) have finished, regardless of their exit codes (success or failure).
- afternotok: start the dependent job after the specified job(s) have finished only if at least one of them did NOT complete successfully (i.e., at least one finished with a non‑zero/failed exit).

Details and examples

- Basic single-job dependencies
  - sbatch --dependency=afterany:123 myjob.sh
    - myjob.sh becomes eligible only after job 123 has terminated (RUN -> DONE/FAILED/CANCELLED/etc.). Exit code of 123 is ignored.
  - sbatch --dependency=afternotok:123 myjob.sh
    - myjob.sh becomes eligible only after job 123 has terminated and its termination indicates failure (non‑zero/unsuccessful). If job 123 exited with code 0, the dependency is not satisfied.

- Multiple job IDs (colon-separated list)
  - sbatch --dependency=afterany:123:124 myjob.sh
    - myjob.sh waits until both job 123 and job 124 have terminated (both must finish). The exit codes are ignored.
  - sbatch --dependency=afternotok:123:124 myjob.sh
    - myjob.sh waits until both 123 and 124 have terminated, and at least one of them must have a non‑zero/failed result. If both exit 0, the dependency is not satisfied.

- Job arrays
  - When you depend on a job array, semantics apply to the array as a whole:
    - afterany on an array is satisfied after all array tasks complete (regardless of individual exit codes).
    - afternotok on an array is satisfied after all array tasks complete and at least one task failed (i.e., at least one had a non‑zero exit).
    - (Implementation note in the docs: interpretation of afterok/afternotok for an array is based on the tasks’ exit codes taken together — effectively looking at whether any task had a non‑zero exit.)

Notes / edge cases
- “Finished” means the specified job(s) have reached a terminal state (DONE, FAILED, CANCELLED, TIMEOUT, etc.). CANCELLED/TIMEOUT produce non‑zero terminal states and will satisfy afternotok (they count as “not OK”).
- afterany differs from afterok: afterok requires successful (zero) completion of the specified jobs before the dependent job can start; afternotok requires at least one non‑successful completion.
- You can combine dependency types in more complex dependency expressions (see sbatch --dependency docs for syntax options).

Slurm environment variables will be set independently for each component of
the job by appending "_HET_GROUP_" and a sequence number to the usual name.
In addition, the "SLURM_JOB_ID" environment variable will contain the job ID
of the heterogeneous job leader and "SLURM_HET_SIZE" will contain the number of
components in the job. Note that if using srun with a single specific
het group (for instance --het-group=1) "SLURM_JOB_ID" will contain the job
ID of the heterogeneous job leader. The job ID for a specific heterogeneous
component is set in "SLURM_JOB_ID_HET_GROUP_<component_id>". For example:

## Heterogeneous Steps [#het_steps](https://slurm.schedmd.com/heterogeneous_jobs.html)
Slurm version 20.11 introduces the ability to request heterogeneous job
steps from within a non-homogeneous job allocation. This allows you the
flexibility to have different layouts for job steps without requiring the
use of heterogeneous jobs, where having separate jobs for the components
may be undesirable.
Some limitations for heterogeneous steps are that the steps must be able
to run on unique nodes. You also cannot request heterogeneous steps from within
a heterogeneous job.
An example scenario would be if you have a task that needs to use 1 GPU
per processor while another task needs all the available GPUs on a node with
only one processor. This can be accomplished like this:
```text
$ salloc -N2 --exclusive --gpus=10 salloc: Granted job allocation 61034 $ srun -N1 -n4 --gpus=4 printenv SLURMD_NODENAME : -N1 -n1 --gpus=6 printenv SLURMD_NODENAME...

## Job Accounting Records [#job_record](https://slurm.schedmd.com/job_launch.html)
When Slurm is configured to use SlurmDBD to store job records (i.e.
AccountingStorageType=accounting_storage=slurmdbd ), there are multiple
records that get stored for each job. There is a record for the job as a
whole as well as entries for the following types of job steps:
- extern step — A step created for each job as long as you have PrologFlags=contain in your slurm.conf. Each node in the job will have a slurmstepd process created for the extern step. pam_slurm_adopt uses this step to contain external connections.
- batch step — A step created for jobs that were submitted with sbatch. The batch host, or the primary node for the job, will run an instance of slurmstepd for the batch step, which is used to run the script provided to sbatch.
- interactive step — A step created for jobs that were submitted with salloc when LaunchParameters=use_interactive...

## Limitations [#LIMITATIONS](https://slurm.schedmd.com/configless_slurm.html)
Using "%n" in "SlurmdSpoolDir" or "SlurmdPidFile" will not be properly
substituted for the NodeName unless slurmd is also launched with the "-N"
option.
If you are using systemd to launch slurmd, you must ensure that
"ConditionPathExists=*" is not present in the unit file or the slurmd will not
start. (The example slurmd.service file shipped in Slurm 20.02 and above does
not include this entry.)
If any of the supported config files "Include" additional config files,

heterogeneous job, but options are available to support different behaviors.
