## Heterogeneous Steps [#het_steps](https://slurm.schedmd.com/heterogeneous_jobs.html)
Slurm version 20.11 introduces the ability to request heterogeneous job
steps from within a non-homogeneous job allocation. This allows you the
flexibility to have different layouts for job steps without requiring the
use of heterogeneous jobs, where having separate jobs for the components
may be undesirable.
Some limitations for heterogeneous steps are that the steps must be able
to run on unique nodes. You also cannot request heterogeneous steps from within
a heterogeneous job.
An example scenario would be if you have a task that needs to use 1 GPU
per processor while another task needs all the available GPUs on a node with
only one processor. This can be accomplished like this:
```text
$ salloc -N2 --exclusive --gpus=10 salloc: Granted job allocation 61034 $ srun -N1 -n4 --gpus=4 printenv SLURMD_NODENAME : -N1 -n1 --gpus=6 printenv SLURMD_NODENAME...

## Burst Buffers [#burst_buffer](https://slurm.schedmd.com/heterogeneous_jobs.html)
A burst buffer can either be persistent or linked to a specific job ID.
Since a heterogeneous job consists of multiple job IDs, a job-specific burst
buffer will be associated with only one heterogeneous job component.
Each component can have its own burst buffer directives, and they are processed
separately. Only a persistent burst buffer can be accessed by all components
of a heterogeneous job. Persistent burst buffers are only available in the
datawarp plugin. A sample batch script demonstrating this for the datawarp
plugin is appended.

job_container.conf is an ASCII file which defines parameters used by
Slurm's namespace/tmpfs plugin. Based on these parameters, the plugin will
create the appropriate job-specifc namespace(s).

private (or optionally shared) filesystem namespace and mount a list of

specifically the slurmd process — and user commands running on login

Section: Slurm Commands (1) Updated: Slurm Commands Index 

 
   
 NAME 
srun - Run parallel jobs
 
   
 SYNOPSIS 
 srun [ OPTIONS(0) ... [ executable(0) [ args(0) ...]]] [ : [ OPTIONS(N) ...]] executable(N) [ args(N) ...]
 
Option(s) define multiple jobs in a co-scheduled heterogeneous job.
For more details about heterogeneous jobs see the document
 

 https://slurm.schedmd.com/heterogeneous_jobs.html 
 
   
 DESCRIPTION 
Run a parallel job on cluster managed by Slurm. If necessary, srun will
first create a resource allocation in which to run the parallel job.
 
The following document describes the influence of various options on the
allocation of cpus to jobs and tasks.
 

 https://slurm.schedmd.com/cpu_management.html 
 
   
 RETURN VALUE 
srun will return the highest exit code of all tasks run or the highest signal
(with the high-order bit set in an 8-bit integer -- e.g. 128 + signal) of any
task that exited with a signal.
 

The value 253 is reserved for out-of-memory errors.
 
   
 EXECUTABLE PATH RESOLUTION 
 
The executable is resolved in the following order:
 

 
1. If executable starts with ".", then path is constructed as:
current working directory / executable
 

2. If executable starts with a "/", then path is considered absolute.
 

3. If executable can be resolved through PATH. See path_resolution (7).
 

4. If executable is in current working directory.
 

 

Current working directory is the calling process working directory unless the
 --chdir argument is passed, which will override the current working
directory.
 
   
 OPTIONS 
 

 
 
 -A , --account =< account > Charge resources used by this job to specified account.
The account is an arbitrary string. The account name may
be changed after job submission using the scontrol 
command. This option applies to job allocations.
 
 
 --acctg-freq =< datatype >=< interval >[,< datatype >=< interval >...] Define the job accounting and profiling sampling intervals in seconds.
This can be used to override the JobAcctGatherFrequency parameter in
the slurm.conf file. < datatype >=< interval > specifies the task
sampling interval for the jobacct_gather plugin or a
sampling interval for a profiling type by the
acct_gather_profile plugin. Multiple
comma-separated < datatype >=< interval > pairs
may be specified. Supported datatype values are:
 
 
 
 task Sampling interval for the jobacct_gather plugins and for task
profiling by the acct_gather_profile plugin.
 

 NOTE : This frequency is used to monitor memory usage. If memory limits
are enforced the highest frequency a user can request is what is configured in
the slurm.conf file. It can not be disabled.
 
 
 energy Sampling interval for energy profiling using the
acct_gather_energy plugin.
 
 
 network Sampling interval for infiniband profiling using the
acct_gather_interconnect plugin.
 
 
 filesystem Sampling interval for filesystem profiling using the
acct_gather_filesystem plugin.
 
 
 

The default value for the task sampling interval is 30 seconds.
The default value for all other intervals is 0.
An interval of 0 disables sampling of the specified type.

## Heterogeneous Steps [#het_steps](https://slurm.schedmd.com/heterogeneous_jobs.html)
Slurm version 20.11 introduces the ability to request heterogeneous job
steps from within a non-homogeneous job allocation. This allows you the
flexibility to have different layouts for job steps without requiring the
use of heterogeneous jobs, where having separate jobs for the components
may be undesirable.
Some limitations for heterogeneous steps are that the steps must be able
to run on unique nodes. You also cannot request heterogeneous steps from within
a heterogeneous job.
An example scenario would be if you have a task that needs to use 1 GPU
per processor while another task needs all the available GPUs on a node with
only one processor. This can be accomplished like this:

The srun command is used to launch applications.
By default, the application is launched only on the first component of a
heterogeneous job, but options are available to support different behaviors.
srun's "--het-group" option defines which hetjob component(s) are to have
applications launched for them. The --het-group option takes an expression
defining which component(s) are to launch an application for an individual
execution of the srun command. The expression can contain one or more component
index values in a comma separated list. Ranges of index values can be specified
in a hyphen separated list. By default, an application is launched only on
component number zero. Some examples follow:

The job submit plugin is invoked independently for each component of a
heterogeneous job.
The spank_init_post_opt() function is invoked once for each component of a
heterogeneous job. This permits site defined options on a per job component

## Burst Buffers [#burst_buffer](https://slurm.schedmd.com/heterogeneous_jobs.html)
A burst buffer can either be persistent or linked to a specific job ID.
Since a heterogeneous job consists of multiple job IDs, a job-specific burst
buffer will be associated with only one heterogeneous job component.
Each component can have its own burst buffer directives, and they are processed
separately. Only a persistent burst buffer can be accessed by all components
of a heterogeneous job. Persistent burst buffers are only available in the
datawarp plugin. A sample batch script demonstrating this for the datawarp
plugin is appended.

## DESCRIPTION[#SECTION_DESCRIPTION](https://slurm.schedmd.com/job_container.conf.html)
job_container.conf is an ASCII file which defines parameters used by
Slurm's namespace/tmpfs plugin. Based on these parameters, the plugin will
create the appropriate job-specifc namespace(s).
The namespace/tmpfs plugin creates a filesystem namespace and will construct a
private (or optionally shared) filesystem namespace and mount a list of
directories (defaults to /tmp and /dev/shm) inside it, giving the job a private
view of these directories. These paths are mounted inside the location specified
by 'BasePath' in the job_container.conf file.
When the job completes, the namespace is unmounted and all files therein are
automatically removed.
To make use of this plugin, 'PrologFlags=Contain' must also be present in
your slurm.conf file, as shown:

Summary — what scancel does when it "sends signals"
- scancel is used to either signal job steps (send an arbitrary POSIX signal) or to cancel jobs (default behavior when no --signal is given).
- You may target entire jobs, individual job steps (jobid.step), job-array elements (jobid_index), or filter sets (user, partition, state, etc.).

Canceling a job (no --signal)
- When you run scancel <jobid> (no --signal), scancel initiates an ordered termination sequence:
  1. Send SIGCONT to all steps (wake them if stopped).
  2. Send SIGTERM to all steps.
  3. Wait the KillWait duration from slurm.conf.
  4. If any steps remain, send SIGKILL.
- That sequence attempts a graceful shutdown before forcibly killing tasks.
- Canceling a job releases the allocation; cancelling a single job step does NOT release the allocation (the job must be cancelled to free resources).

Sending an explicit signal (--signal)
- scancel --signal=<SIGNAL> <targets> sends the named signal to the matching job steps (e.g., TERM, KILL, USR1, numeric signals).
- If you specify step IDs (e.g., 1234.1 1234.3) only those steps are signaled.
- Sending a signal to an entire job will signal all active steps for that job.
- Important special-case: sending "KILL" as the signal to an entire job will cancel the active job steps but does not cancel the job itself (the job record remains until explicitly cancelled).

Batch-step behavior (--batch)
- By default, signals other than SIGKILL are NOT forwarded to the batch step (the batch shell script) when a job has a batch step + child tasks.
- Use --batch to signal only the batch step (useful when the shell should trap the signal and perform cleanup). Example: scancel --signal=USR1 --batch 1236

Addressing examples
- Signal specific steps: scancel --signal=TERM 1234.1 1234.3
- Cancel job (graceful sequence): scancel 1234
- Send SIGKILL to all steps (but not cancel job record): scancel --signal=KILL 1235
- Signal the batch shell only: scancel --signal=USR1 --batch 1236

Implementation / performance notes
- scancel issues RPCs to slurmctld to request signaling. By default it may make per-job RPCs; using the --ctld option can reduce RPC count since one RPC can ask slurmctld to signal all matching jobs.

A QOS can be attached to a partition. This means the partition will have all
the same limits as the QOS. This does not associate jobs with the QOS, nor does
it give the job any priority or preemption characteristics of the assigned QOS.

- Priority: higher-priority work is scheduled first; job is waiting behind other eligible jobs. Remedy: check priority factors (sprio/sshow) or request a different QOS.
- Dependency: job has an unsatisfied dependency (afterok, afterany, etc.). Remedy: inspect sbatch dependency or sacct of the predecessor job.
- BeginTime: job was submitted with --begin and its start time hasn't arrived. Remedy: adjust begin time.
- Partition/AccountNotAllowed or PartitionQOS limits: job requests a partition or QOS it is not allowed to use, or partition-level QOS limits block it. Remedy: check job partition/QOS and account associations.

- Reservation: resources are reserved for something else; the job must wait for the reservation to end or the reservation to include the job.
- Licensing: requested licensed resources (a license tracked by Slurm) are not available. Remedy: check license usage.
- Constraint: node feature/constraint (e.g., --constraint=gpuV100) cannot be satisfied by any idle node.

Good question — both show job information but have different scopes and backends. Use this quick guide:

When to use squeue (real-time queue view)
- Immediate, live state of active jobs (RUNNING, PENDING, SUSPENDED).  
- See where a job is waiting or what nodes it’s allocated to, plus the pending REASON.  
- First tool to debug “why isn’t my job starting?” or to confirm a job is currently running.  
- Lightweight query of slurmctld (does not require slurmdbd).  
- Useful options: show partition/node, format columns, view by user or jobid.

When to use sacct (accounting / historical records)
- Historical and accounting data: completed, failed, cancelled, timed-out jobs and their ExitCode, elapsed, requested/used resources.  
- Produce reports and postmortem resource-usage queries (CPU-hours, memory, exit codes).  
- Queries slurmdbd / accounting storage (may be empty if accounting isn’t configured for your cluster).  
- Can be heavier on slurmdbd — avoid tight loops or excessive calls.

Practical rules of thumb
- To check an active job: run squeue <jobid> (if squeue shows nothing for that ID, then use sacct to find completed/failed records).  
- To investigate why a pending job isn’t starting: squeue (pending reason); if you need historical runs or exit codes, use sacct.  
- To get live resource usage for a running job (CPU%, memory): use sstat (not sacct).  
- For detailed job configuration or step-level info: use scontrol show job <id>.

Performance/behavior notes
- sacct requires accounting configured and contacts slurmdbd; it can be slower and should not be polled in tight loops.  
- squeue is the authoritative live view of the scheduler state; it does not show completed jobs.

What that means
- The job’s process aborted (ExitCode 134 = 128 + 6 → killed by signal SIGABRT) after a CUDA runtime error: an illegal memory access on the GPU.
- "illegal memory access" is a GPU-side memory violation (out-of-bounds write/read, use-after-free, or other memory-corruption inside a CUDA kernel). It usually causes the CUDA runtime to abort the process when the error is detected.

Most likely root causes (ordered by likelihood)
1. A bug in the GPU code (custom kernel or model code) causing out-of-bounds accesses or invalid pointer use.
2. A race condition / incorrect indexing in a kernel or in a multi-threaded GPU library (e.g., incorrect launch config).
3. Mismatched or incompatible versions (CUDA toolkit vs driver vs PyTorch/CUDA binary) causing runtime failures.
4. Bad input (very large batch size or tensors leading to invalid indexing or memory corruption).
5. Rare: hardware/GPU fault or driver bug (less likely but possible).

1. Inspect full stderr/stdout logs for job 5001 (the sacct snippet shows the CUDA error but full logs can have stack traces or host-side messages).

2. Reproduce locally or with a short run:
   - Run the job interactively or a reduced-version of it (smaller batch, fewer GPUs) to see if it fails quickly.
3. Enable synchronous error reporting to get a clearer backtrace:
   - Set CUDA_LAUNCH_BLOCKING=1 in the environment before running; this forces launches to be synchronous and often yields a more usable Python/C++ stack trace.
4. Run CUDA memory checks:
   - Use cuda-memcheck (or nsight tools) on the job binary or a minimal repro to catch the kernel and memory error locations.
5. Check software environment:
   - Confirm CUDA driver version matches the CUDA runtime/PyTorch CUDA build (nvidia-smi and python -c "import torch; print(torch.version.cuda)").
6. Check node/GPU health and system logs:
   - Inspect dmesg / kernel logs and nvidia-smi for ECC errors or GPU resets on the node that ran the job (if you have access to the node logs).
7. If using distributed kernels or NCCL, check for related errors (but the specific message here is a CUDA illegal memory access, not NCCL).

## Partition QOS [#partition](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
A QOS can be attached to a partition. This means the partition will have all
the same limits as the QOS. This does not associate jobs with the QOS, nor does
it give the job any priority or preemption characteristics of the assigned QOS.
Jobs may separately request the same QOS or a different QOS to gain those
characteristics. However, the Partition QOS limits will override the job's QOS.
If the opposite is desired you may configure the job's QOS with
`Flags=OverPartQOS` which will reverse the order of precedence.
This functionality may be used to implement a true "floating"
partition, in which a partition may access a limited amount of resources with no
restrictions on which nodes it uses to get the resources. This is accomplished
by assigning all nodes to the partition, then configuring a Partition QOS with
`GrpTRES` set to the desired resource limits.

### Job Scheduling Priority [#priority](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
Job scheduling priority is made up of a number of factors as
described in the [priority/multifactor](https://slurm.schedmd.com/priority_multifactor.html) plugin. One
of the factors is the QOS priority. Each QOS is defined in the Slurm
database and includes an associated priority. Jobs that request and
are permitted a QOS will incorporate the priority associated with that
QOS in the job's [multi-factor priority calculation.](https://slurm.schedmd.com/priority_multifactor.html)
To enable the QOS priority component of the multi-factor priority
calculation, the "PriorityWeightQOS" configuration parameter must be
defined in the slurm.conf file and assigned an integer value greater
than zero.
A job's QOS only affects is scheduling priority when the
multi-factor plugin is loaded.

### Job Preemption [#preemption](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
Slurm offers two ways for a queued job to preempt a running job,
free-up the running job's resources and allocate them to the queued
job. See the [Preemption description](https://slurm.schedmd.com/preempt.html) for
details.
The preemption method is determined by the "PreemptType"
configuration parameter defined in slurm.conf. When the "PreemptType"
is set to "preempt/qos", a queued job's QOS will be used to determine
whether it can preempt a running job. It is important to note that the QOS
used to determine if a job is eligible for preemption is the QOS associated
with the job and not a [Partition QOS](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html).
The QOS can be assigned (using sacctmgr ) a list of other
QOSs that it can preempt. When there is a queued job with a QOS that
is allowed to preempt a running job of another QOS, the Slurm

## Relative QOS [#relative](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
Starting in Slurm 23.11, a QOS may be configured to contain relative resource
limits instead of absolute limits by setting `Flags=Relative`.
When this flag is set, all resource limits are treated as percentages of the
total resources available. Values higher than 100 are interpreted as 100%.
Memory limits should be set with no units. Although the default units (MB) will
be displayed, the limits will be enforced as a percentage (1MB = 1%).
NOTE : When Flags=Relative is added to a QOS, slurmctld
must be restarted or reconfigured for the flag to take effect.
Generally, the limits on a relative QOS will be calculated relative to the
resources in the whole cluster. For example, `cpu=50` would be
interpreted as 50% of all CPUs in the cluster.

## TRES information[#SECTION_TRES-information](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sacctmgr.html)
Trackable RESources (TRES) are used in many QOS or Association limits
(GrpTRES* / MaxTRES*). When setting limits, one or more comma-separated
"TRES=value" assignments can be specified.
Each TRES can be one of the Slurm defaults (e.g., cpu , mem ,
node ), or any defined generic resource. You can see the list of available
resources by running sacctmgr show tres .
Each TRES has a different limit, e.g., "GrpTRES=cpu=16,mem=32G" would
establish 2 different limits: one for 16 CPUs and another for 32 GB of memory.
Setting a new value for a TRES type does not affect any other TRES types that
were previously specified. For example, on the same entity as above, a
subsequent assignment of "GrpTRES=gres/gpu=2" will result in
"GrpTRES=cpu=16,mem=32G,gres/gpu=2" applying to that entity.

A QOS can be attached to a partition. This means the partition will have all
the same limits as the QOS. This does not associate jobs with the QOS, nor does

### Job Scheduling Priority [#priority](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
Job scheduling priority is made up of a number of factors as
described in the [priority/multifactor](https://slurm.schedmd.com/priority_multifactor.html) plugin. One
of the factors is the QOS priority. Each QOS is defined in the Slurm
database and includes an associated priority. Jobs that request and
are permitted a QOS will incorporate the priority associated with that
QOS in the job's [multi-factor priority calculation.](https://slurm.schedmd.com/priority_multifactor.html)
To enable the QOS priority component of the multi-factor priority
calculation, the "PriorityWeightQOS" configuration parameter must be
defined in the slurm.conf file and assigned an integer value greater
than zero.
A job's QOS only affects is scheduling priority when the
multi-factor plugin is loaded.

## Partition QOS [#partition](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
A QOS can be attached to a partition. This means the partition will have all
the same limits as the QOS. This does not associate jobs with the QOS, nor does
it give the job any priority or preemption characteristics of the assigned QOS.
Jobs may separately request the same QOS or a different QOS to gain those
characteristics. However, the Partition QOS limits will override the job's QOS.
If the opposite is desired you may configure the job's QOS with
`Flags=OverPartQOS` which will reverse the order of precedence.
This functionality may be used to implement a true "floating"
partition, in which a partition may access a limited amount of resources with no
restrictions on which nodes it uses to get the resources. This is accomplished
by assigning all nodes to the partition, then configuring a Partition QOS with
`GrpTRES` set to the desired resource limits.

## FLAT FILE DUMP AND LOAD[#SECTION_FLAT-FILE-DUMP-AND-LOAD](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sacctmgr.html)
sacctmgr has the capability to load and dump Slurm association data to and
from a file. This method can easily add a new cluster or copy an
existing cluster's associations into a new cluster with similar
accounts. Each file contains Slurm association data for a single
cluster. Beginning with version 25.05, QOS information is included in the
dump file. Comments can be put into the file with the # character.
Each line of information must begin with one of the five titles; QOS ,
Cluster , Parent , Account or User . Following the title
is a space, dash, space, entity value, then specifications. Specifications are
colon-separated. If any variable, such as an Organization name, has a space in
it, surround the name with single or double quotes.

### Job Preemption [#preemption](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
Slurm offers two ways for a queued job to preempt a running job,
free-up the running job's resources and allocate them to the queued
job. See the [Preemption description](https://slurm.schedmd.com/preempt.html) for
details.
The preemption method is determined by the "PreemptType"
configuration parameter defined in slurm.conf. When the "PreemptType"
is set to "preempt/qos", a queued job's QOS will be used to determine
whether it can preempt a running job. It is important to note that the QOS
used to determine if a job is eligible for preemption is the QOS associated
with the job and not a [Partition QOS](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html).
The QOS can be assigned (using sacctmgr ) a list of other
QOSs that it can preempt. When there is a queued job with a QOS that
is allowed to preempt a running job of another QOS, the Slurm
scheduler will preempt the running job.

## PERFORMANCE[#SECTION_PERFORMANCE](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Executing sbatch sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmctld daemon come in at once, it can result in
a degradation of performance of the slurmctld daemon, possibly resulting
in a denial of service.
Do not run sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other
programs. Ensure that programs limit calls to sbatch to the minimum
necessary for the information you are trying to gather.

# "Configless" Slurm
"Configless" Slurm is a feature that allows the compute nodes —
specifically the slurmd process — and user commands running on login
nodes to pull configuration information directly from the slurmctld instead of
from a pre-distributed local file. Your cluster does require a central set of
configuration files on the Slurm controllers — "configless" in Slurm's
parlance means that the compute nodes, login nodes, and other cluster hosts
do not need to be deployed with local copies of these files.
The slurmd on startup will reach out to a slurmctld that you specify and the
config files will be pulled to the node. This slurmctld can be identified by
either an explicit option, or — preferably — through DNS SRV
records defined within the cluster itself.

## Notes[#NOTES](https://slurm.schedmd.com/configless_slurm.html)
Starting from Slurm 25.11, there's a new
SlurmctldParameters=reconfig_on_restart option that will make every
restart of slurmctld (process restart not triggered by "scontrol reconfigure")
to trigger a reconfiguration request to all slurmd and sackd daemons. For
"configless" systems this will ensure all processes are running the current
configuration. Some caution should be taken if you intend to perform rolling
upgrades on the cluster as this could lead to the daemons being upgraded sooner
than expected.
The order of precedence for determining what configuration source to use

- The slurmd --conf-server $host[:$port] option

- The SLURM_CONF environment variable (if set)

## DESCRIPTION[#SECTION_DESCRIPTION](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
sbatch submits a batch script to Slurm. The batch script may be given to
sbatch through a file name on the command line, or if no file name is specified,
sbatch will read in a script from standard input.
The batch script may contain one or more lines beginning with "#SBATCH" followed
by any of the CLI options documented on this page. #SBATCH directives are read
directly by Slurm, so shell-specific syntax including variable names will be
read as literal text. Once the first non-comment, non-whitespace line has been
reached in the script, no more #SBATCH directives will be processed. See example
below.

## PERFORMANCE[#SECTION_PERFORMANCE](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Executing sbatch sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmctld daemon come in at once, it can result in
a degradation of performance of the slurmctld daemon, possibly resulting
in a denial of service.
Do not run sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other
programs. Ensure that programs limit calls to sbatch to the minimum
necessary for the information you are trying to gather.

sbatch submits a batch script to Slurm. The batch script may be given to
sbatch through a file name on the command line, or if no file name is specified,
sbatch will read in a script from standard input.

by any of the CLI options documented on this page. #SBATCH directives are read
directly by Slurm, so shell-specific syntax including variable names will be
read as literal text. Once the first non-comment, non-whitespace line has been

## PERFORMANCE[#SECTION_PERFORMANCE](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Executing sbatch sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmctld daemon come in at once, it can result in
a degradation of performance of the slurmctld daemon, possibly resulting
in a denial of service.
Do not run sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other
programs. Ensure that programs limit calls to sbatch to the minimum
necessary for the information you are trying to gather.

## EXAMPLES[#SECTION_EXAMPLES](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Specify a batch script by filename on the command line. The batch script specifies a 1 minute time limit for the job.
```text
$ cat myscript #!/bin/sh #SBATCH --time=1 srun hostname |sort $ sbatch -N4 myscript salloc: Granted job allocation 65537 $ cat slurm-65537.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
Pass a batch script to sbatch on standard input:
```text
$ sbatch -N4 #!/bin/sh > srun hostname |sort > EOF sbatch: Submitted batch job 65541 $ cat slurm-65541.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
To create a heterogeneous job with 3 components, each allocating a unique set of nodes:
```text
$ sbatch -w node[2-3] : -w node4 : -w node[5-7] work.bash Submitted batch job 34987
```

slurm.conf is an ASCII file which describes general Slurm
configuration information, the nodes to be managed, information about
how those nodes are grouped into partitions, and various scheduling
parameters associated with those partitions. This file should be

## EXAMPLES[#SECTION_EXAMPLES](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Specify a batch script by filename on the command line. The batch script specifies a 1 minute time limit for the job.
```text
$ cat myscript #!/bin/sh #SBATCH --time=1 srun hostname |sort $ sbatch -N4 myscript salloc: Granted job allocation 65537 $ cat slurm-65537.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
Pass a batch script to sbatch on standard input:
```text
$ sbatch -N4 #!/bin/sh > srun hostname |sort > EOF sbatch: Submitted batch job 65541 $ cat slurm-65541.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
To create a heterogeneous job with 3 components, each allocating a unique set of nodes:
```text
$ sbatch -w node[2-3] : -w node4 : -w node[5-7] work.bash Submitted batch job 34987
```

## PERFORMANCE[#SECTION_PERFORMANCE](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Executing sbatch sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmctld daemon come in at once, it can result in
a degradation of performance of the slurmctld daemon, possibly resulting
in a denial of service.
Do not run sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other
programs. Ensure that programs limit calls to sbatch to the minimum
necessary for the information you are trying to gather.

information you are trying to gather.

## EXAMPLES[#SECTION_EXAMPLES](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Specify a batch script by filename on the command line. The batch script specifies a 1 minute time limit for the job.
```text
$ cat myscript #!/bin/sh #SBATCH --time=1 srun hostname |sort $ sbatch -N4 myscript salloc: Granted job allocation 65537 $ cat slurm-65537.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
Pass a batch script to sbatch on standard input:
```text
$ sbatch -N4 #!/bin/sh > srun hostname |sort > EOF sbatch: Submitted batch job 65541 $ cat slurm-65541.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
To create a heterogeneous job with 3 components, each allocating a unique set of nodes:
```text
$ sbatch -w node[2-3] : -w node4 : -w node[5-7] work.bash Submitted batch job 34987
```

## PERFORMANCE[#SECTION_PERFORMANCE](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Executing sbatch sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmctld daemon come in at once, it can result in
a degradation of performance of the slurmctld daemon, possibly resulting
in a denial of service.
Do not run sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other
programs. Ensure that programs limit calls to sbatch to the minimum
necessary for the information you are trying to gather.

## Partition QOS [#partition](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
A QOS can be attached to a partition. This means the partition will have all
the same limits as the QOS. This does not associate jobs with the QOS, nor does
it give the job any priority or preemption characteristics of the assigned QOS.
Jobs may separately request the same QOS or a different QOS to gain those
characteristics. However, the Partition QOS limits will override the job's QOS.
If the opposite is desired you may configure the job's QOS with
`Flags=OverPartQOS` which will reverse the order of precedence.
This functionality may be used to implement a true "floating"
partition, in which a partition may access a limited amount of resources with no
restrictions on which nodes it uses to get the resources. This is accomplished
by assigning all nodes to the partition, then configuring a Partition QOS with
`GrpTRES` set to the desired resource limits.

## Relative QOS [#relative](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
Starting in Slurm 23.11, a QOS may be configured to contain relative resource
limits instead of absolute limits by setting `Flags=Relative`.
When this flag is set, all resource limits are treated as percentages of the
total resources available. Values higher than 100 are interpreted as 100%.
Memory limits should be set with no units. Although the default units (MB) will
be displayed, the limits will be enforced as a percentage (1MB = 1%).
NOTE : When Flags=Relative is added to a QOS, slurmctld
must be restarted or reconfigured for the flag to take effect.
Generally, the limits on a relative QOS will be calculated relative to the
resources in the whole cluster. For example, `cpu=50` would be
interpreted as 50% of all CPUs in the cluster.

QOS manipulation examples. All QOS operations are done using
the sacctmgr command. The default output of 'sacctmgr show qos' is
very long given the large number of limits and options available

```text

A node can be manually powered up and down by setting the state of the

Will use the configured SuspendProgram program to explicitly

A QOS can be attached to a partition. This means the partition will have all
the same limits as the QOS. This does not associate jobs with the QOS, nor does
it give the job any priority or preemption characteristics of the assigned QOS.

Starting in Slurm 23.11, a QOS may be configured to contain relative resource
limits instead of absolute limits by setting `Flags=Relative`.

## Hierarchy[#hierarchy](https://slurm.schedmd.com/resource_limits.html)
Slurm's hierarchical limits are enforced in the following order
with Job QOS and Partition QOS order being reversible by using the QOS
flag 'OverPartQOS':
- Partition QOS limit
- Job QOS limit
- User association
- Account association(s), ascending the hierarchy
- Root/Cluster association
- Partition limit
- None
Note: If limits are defined at multiple points in this hierarchy,
the point in this list where the limit is first defined will be used.

- MaxJobs=20 and MaxSubmitJobs is undefined in the partition QOS
- No limits are set in the job QOS and
- MaxJobs=4 and MaxSubmitJobs=50 in the user association

The Slurm controller (slurmctld) requires a unique port for communications
as do the Slurm compute node daemons (slurmd). If not set, slurm ports
are set by checking for an entry in /etc/services and if that
fails by using an interval default set at Slurm build time.

# "Configless" Slurm
"Configless" Slurm is a feature that allows the compute nodes —
specifically the slurmd process — and user commands running on login
nodes to pull configuration information directly from the slurmctld instead of
from a pre-distributed local file. Your cluster does require a central set of
configuration files on the Slurm controllers — "configless" in Slurm's
parlance means that the compute nodes, login nodes, and other cluster hosts
do not need to be deployed with local copies of these files.
The slurmd on startup will reach out to a slurmctld that you specify and the
config files will be pulled to the node. This slurmctld can be identified by
either an explicit option, or — preferably — through DNS SRV
records defined within the cluster itself.

Using "%n" in "SlurmdSpoolDir" or "SlurmdPidFile" will not be properly
substituted for the NodeName unless slurmd is also launched with the "-N"
option.
If you are using systemd to launch slurmd, you must ensure that
"ConditionPathExists=*" is not present in the unit file or the slurmd will not
start. (The example slurmd.service file shipped in Slurm 20.02 and above does
not include this entry.)
If any of the supported config files "Include" additional config files,
the Included configs will ONLY be shipped if their "Include" filename
reference has no path separators and the file is located adjacent to slurm.conf.
Any additional config files will need to be shared a different way or added to

## Notes[#NOTES](https://slurm.schedmd.com/configless_slurm.html)
Starting from Slurm 25.11, there's a new
SlurmctldParameters=reconfig_on_restart option that will make every
restart of slurmctld (process restart not triggered by "scontrol reconfigure")
to trigger a reconfiguration request to all slurmd and sackd daemons. For
"configless" systems this will ensure all processes are running the current
configuration. Some caution should be taken if you intend to perform rolling
upgrades on the cluster as this could lead to the daemons being upgraded sooner
than expected.
The order of precedence for determining what configuration source to use
is as follows:
- The slurmd --conf-server $host[:$port] option
- The -f $config_file option
- The SLURM_CONF environment variable (if set)
- A local slurm config file: The default slurm config file (likely /etc/slurm.conf)

## Hierarchy[#hierarchy](https://slurm.schedmd.com/resource_limits.html)
Slurm's hierarchical limits are enforced in the following order
with Job QOS and Partition QOS order being reversible by using the QOS
flag 'OverPartQOS':
- Partition QOS limit
- Job QOS limit
- User association
- Account association(s), ascending the hierarchy
- Root/Cluster association
- Partition limit
- None
Note: If limits are defined at multiple points in this hierarchy,
the point in this list where the limit is first defined will be used.
Consider the following example:
- MaxJobs=20 and MaxSubmitJobs is undefined in the partition QOS
- No limits are set in the job QOS and
- MaxJobs=4 and MaxSubmitJobs=50 in the user association
The limits in effect will be MaxJobs=20 and MaxSubmitJobs=50.
Note: The precedence order specified above is respected except for the
following limits: Max[Time|Wall], [Min|Max]Nodes. For these limits, even

### Specific limits over GRES [#gres_limits](https://slurm.schedmd.com/resource_limits.html)
When a GRES has a type associated with it and a limit is applied
over this specific type (e.g. MaxTRESPerUser=gres/gpu:tesla=1 ) if a
user requests a generic gres, the type's limit will not be enforced. In this
situation an additional lua job submit plugin to check the user request may
become useful. For example, if one requests --gres=gpu:2 having a
limit set of MaxTRESPerUser=gres/gpu:tesla=1 , the limit won't be
enforced so it will still be possible to get two teslas.
This is due to a design limitation. The only way to enforce such a limit
is to combine the specification of the limit with a job submit plugin that

## Configuration[#config](https://slurm.schedmd.com/resource_limits.html)
Scheduling policy information must be stored in a database
as specified by the AccountingStorageType configuration parameter
in the slurm.conf configuration file.
Information can be recorded in a [MySQL](http://www.mysql.com/) or
[MariaDB](https://mariadb.org/) database.
For security and performance reasons, the use of
SlurmDBD (Slurm Database Daemon) as a front-end to the
database is strongly recommended.
SlurmDBD uses a Slurm authentication plugin (e.g. MUNGE).
SlurmDBD also uses an existing Slurm accounting storage plugin
to maximize code reuse.
SlurmDBD uses data caching and prioritization of pending requests
in order to optimize performance.
While SlurmDBD relies upon existing Slurm plugins for authentication
and database use, the other Slurm commands and daemons are not required
on the host where SlurmDBD is installed.

## Job Reason Codes [#reasons](https://slurm.schedmd.com/resource_limits.html)
When a pending job is evaluated by the scheduler but found to exceed a
configured resource limit, a corresponding reason will be assigned to the job.
More details can be found on the [Job Reason Codes](https://slurm.schedmd.com/job_reason_codes.html) page. More details about scheduling can be found in the
[Scheduling Configuration Guide](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sched_config.html).

## Manual Power Saving[#manual](https://slurm.schedmd.com/elastic_computing.html)
A node can be manually powered up and down by setting the state of the
node to the following states using `scontrol`:
```text
scontrol update nodename= state=power_
```

sacctmgr is used to view or modify Slurm account information.
The account information is maintained within a database with the interface
being provided by slurmdbd (Slurm Database daemon).

the ClusterName parameter in the slurm.conf configuration file.
partition is the name of a Slurm partition on that cluster.

Starting from Slurm 25.11, there's a new
SlurmctldParameters=reconfig_on_restart option that will make every
restart of slurmctld (process restart not triggered by "scontrol reconfigure")
to trigger a reconfiguration request to all slurmd and sackd daemons. For
"configless" systems this will ensure all processes are running the current
configuration. Some caution should be taken if you intend to perform rolling
upgrades on the cluster as this could lead to the daemons being upgraded sooner
than expected.

## Initial Testing [#INITIAL_TESTING](https://slurm.schedmd.com/nss_slurm.html)
Before enabling NSS Slurm directly on the node, you should use the
-s slurm option to getent within a newly launched job step
to verify that the rest of the setup has been completed successfully. The
-s option to getent allows it to query a specific database —
even if it has not been enabled by default through the system's
nsswitch.conf . Note that nss_slurm only responds to requests from
processes within the job step itself — you must launch the getent
command within a job step to see any data returned.
As an example of a successful query:
```text
tim@blackhole:~$ srun getent -s slurm passwd tim:x:1000:1000:Tim Wickberg:/home/tim:/bin/bash tim@blackhole:~$ srun getent -s slurm group tim:x:1000:tim projecta:x:1001:tim
```

## NSS Configuration [#NSS_CONFIG](https://slurm.schedmd.com/nss_slurm.html)
Enabling nss_slurm is as simple as adding slurm to the passwd and
group database in /etc/nsswitch.conf (only on systems that will run
slurmd ). It is recommended that
slurm is listed first, as the order (from left to right) determines
the sequence in which the NSS databases will be queried, and this ensures Slurm
handles the request if able before submitting the query to other sources.
To enable cloud node name resolution slurm needs to be added to the
to hosts database in /etc/nsswitch.conf .
It is recommended that slurm is listed last.
Once enabled, test it by launching getent queries such as:
```text
tim@blackhole:~$ srun getent passwd tim tim:x:1000:1000:Tim Wickberg:/home/tim:/bin/bash tim@blackhole:~$ srun getent group projecta projecta:x:1001:tim
```

PrologFlags=contain must be set in the slurm.conf. This sets up the
"extern" step into which ssh-launched processes will be adopted. You must also
enable the task/cgroup plugin in slurm.conf. See the
[Slurm cgroups guide.](https://slurm.schedmd.com/cgroups.html)
CAUTION This option must be in place before using this module.
The module bases its checks on local steps that have already been launched. Jobs
launched without this option do not have an extern step, so pam_slurm_adopt will
not have access to those jobs.
LaunchParameters=ulimit_pam_adopt will set RLIMIT_RSS in processes
adopted by the external step, similar to tasks running in regular steps.
The UsePAM option in slurm.conf is not related to pam_slurm_adopt.

## Partition QOS [#partition](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
A QOS can be attached to a partition. This means the partition will have all
the same limits as the QOS. This does not associate jobs with the QOS, nor does
it give the job any priority or preemption characteristics of the assigned QOS.
Jobs may separately request the same QOS or a different QOS to gain those
characteristics. However, the Partition QOS limits will override the job's QOS.
If the opposite is desired you may configure the job's QOS with
`Flags=OverPartQOS` which will reverse the order of precedence.
This functionality may be used to implement a true "floating"
partition, in which a partition may access a limited amount of resources with no
restrictions on which nodes it uses to get the resources. This is accomplished
by assigning all nodes to the partition, then configuring a Partition QOS with
`GrpTRES` set to the desired resource limits.

sacctmgr has the capability to load and dump Slurm association data to and
from a file. This method can easily add a new cluster or copy an
existing cluster's associations into a new cluster with similar
accounts. Each file contains Slurm association data for a single
cluster. Beginning with version 25.05, QOS information is included in the
dump file. Comments can be put into the file with the # character.
Each line of information must begin with one of the five titles; QOS ,
Cluster , Parent , Account or User . Following the title
is a space, dash, space, entity value, then specifications. Specifications are
colon-separated. If any variable, such as an Organization name, has a space in

### Job Preemption [#preemption](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
Slurm offers two ways for a queued job to preempt a running job,
free-up the running job's resources and allocate them to the queued
job. See the [Preemption description](https://slurm.schedmd.com/preempt.html) for
details.
The preemption method is determined by the "PreemptType"
configuration parameter defined in slurm.conf. When the "PreemptType"
is set to "preempt/qos", a queued job's QOS will be used to determine
whether it can preempt a running job. It is important to note that the QOS
used to determine if a job is eligible for preemption is the QOS associated
with the job and not a [Partition QOS](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html).
The QOS can be assigned (using sacctmgr ) a list of other
QOSs that it can preempt. When there is a queued job with a QOS that
is allowed to preempt a running job of another QOS, the Slurm
scheduler will preempt the running job.

## Licenses Overview [#overview](https://slurm.schedmd.com/licenses.html)
Slurm can help with software license management by assigning available
licenses to jobs at scheduling time. If the licenses are not available, jobs
are kept pending until licenses become available. Licenses in Slurm are
essentially shared resources, meaning configured resources that are not tied to
a specific host but are associated with the entire cluster.
Licenses in Slurm can be configured in two ways:
- Local Licenses: Local licenses are local to the cluster using the slurm.conf in which they are configured.
- Remote Licenses: Remote licenses are served by the database and are configured using the sacctmgr command. Remote licenses are dynamic in nature as upon running the sacctmgr command, the slurmdbd updates all clusters the licenses are assigned to.

## Local Licenses [#local_licenses](https://slurm.schedmd.com/licenses.html)
Local licenses are defined in the slurm.conf using the Licenses
option.
slurm.conf:
```text
Licenses=fluent:30,ansys:100
```
Configured licenses can be viewed using the scontrol command.
```text
$ scontrol show lic LicenseName=ansys Total=100 Used=0 Free=100 Remote=no LicenseName=fluent Total=30 Used=0 Free=30 Remote=no

Requesting licenses is done by using the -L, or --licenses, submission
option.
```text
$ sbatch -L ansys:2 script.sh Submitted batch job 5212 $ scontrol show lic LicenseName=ansys Total=100 Used=2 Free=98 Remote=no LicenseName=fluent Total=30 Used=0 Free=30 Remote=no
```
Licenses may also be requested using the --tres-per-task option for
job submission. If this approach is used, the license must also be defined in

slurm.conf:

Licenses=fluent:30 AccountingStorageTRES=license/fluent

Short answer
- When you request a software license in sbatch, Slurm treats that license like a shared cluster resource. If the requested license count isn't available at scheduling time, your job will remain PENDING until enough licenses are free — it will not start even if compute nodes are idle.
- Licenses are allocated at job start and released when the job (or job step) ends.

How you request a license
- Command-line: sbatch -L license_name:count script.sh
  - Example: sbatch -L ansys:2 myjob.sh
- Or request via TRES: --tres-per-task=license/<name>=N (requires that the license tres is listed in AccountingStorageTRES in slurm.conf).

Where licenses are configured
- Local licenses: configured in slurm.conf (Licenses=...). View with scontrol show lic.
- Remote/dynamic licenses: configured in the accounting DB via sacctmgr and can be periodically updated (LastConsumed/LastDeficit) so Slurm knows how many are effectively available.

How availability affects scheduling (key points)
- Scheduling requirement: Both compute resources (nodes/CPUs/GPUs) AND the requested license(s) must be available for a job to be started. If either is missing, the job stays PENDING.
- Pending reasons: A job waiting for licenses will remain PD and the squeue pending-reason will reflect resource/license constraints (check squeue for the specific reason).
- If you ask for more licenses than exist (or more than the cluster can ever provide), the job will never be satisfied and will remain pending indefinitely unless changed.
- Remote license deficits and reservations: sacctmgr/remote updates can set aside licenses (Reserved/LastDeficit/LastConsumed). Even if Total looks large, Reserved/LastDeficit can reduce Free, causing jobs to wait.

How to inspect and troubleshoot
- Check available counts: scontrol show lic (or scontrol show lic LicenseName=<name>)
  - Output has Total, Used, Free, Reserved, Remote, LastConsumed/LastDeficit for remote licenses.
- See why a specific job is pending: squeue (shows PD and a reason). For more detail, scontrol show job <jobid>.
- If jobs are stuck waiting for licenses while nodes are free, check the license counts (scontrol show lic) and talk to admins to sync with the license server (dynamic license updates via sacctmgr may be needed).

Best practices
- Request only the number of licenses actually needed.
- Prefer TRES-based license accounting if you want per-task granularity — ensure AccountingStorageTRES is configured.
- If using remote license servers, run a periodic sync/update so LastConsumed/LastDeficit reflect reality.
- If a workflow needs guaranteed access, coordinate via reservations or talk to admins to carve out license capacity.

Summary — what each command does
- sacctmgr archive dump / sacctmgr archive load
  - Purpose: archive (export) historical accounting data (jobs, step events, cluster events) to files and later restore them into the SlurmDB (slurmdbd).
  - Typical use: move old job/event records out of the live DB to shrink/trim the DB, and later restore if needed.
- sacctmgr dump / sacctmgr load
  - Purpose: export and import association/metadata (Cluster, Account, Parent, User, QOS) as a flat text file for copying or restoring the accounting configuration.
  - Typical use: clone associations to a new cluster, backup/restore cluster-account-user-QOS configuration, or move config between clusters.

Key differences
- archive (dump/load) handles accounting history (job/event records). It is about data retention and purging.
- dump/load (flat-file) handles association metadata (clusters, accounts, users, QOS). It is about configuration transfer/backup.

Important behavior & options (practical notes)
- Permissions and host:
  - Both sacctmgr dump/load and archive operations must be run as a Slurm administrator (root or slurm admin).
  - Files referenced must be accessible from the slurmdbd host (not necessarily the machine where you run the command).
- archive dump
  - Writes accounting data to archive files. Use options to control what’s archived (Jobs, Events, Directory).
  - Archiving alone does not necessarily purge records — purge occurs only if you include purge options on the command or have PurgeJobAfter / PurgeEventAfter settings in slurmdbd.conf. The command text warns this operation cannot be rolled back once purge runs.
  - Directory= lets you choose where archive files are stored (otherwise slurmdbd.conf ArchiveDir applies).
  - Be careful: archive+purge permanently removes records from the live DB unless you later restore from the archive files.
- archive load
  - Loads previously archived accounting files back into the DB.
  - The loader will not re-import records that already exist; trying to load the same archive twice will result in an error/duplicate-record refusal.
  - Archive files from current or earlier Slurm releases can be loaded (normal version compatibility caveats apply).
  - File paths must resolve on the slurmdbd host.
- dump (flat-file)
  - Exports association data to a human-readable flat file. If file not specified, a default filename using the cluster name is created.
  - File format: lines starting with one of the titles QOS, Cluster, Parent, Account, or User followed by " - <entity> <specs>" with colon-separated specs; comments allowed with #. QOS info is included (newer Slurm versions).
  - Useful to move associations between clusters or to create a source-of-truth backup.
- load (flat-file)
  - Loads association flat files into the DB. By default the data is reconciled with existing DB entries (it will merge/reconcile).
  - Options:
    - file=<filename> — which file to load (must be on slurmdbd host).
    - clean=... — remove the existing cluster (and optionally account,qos,user) before loading if you want a fresh import. Use with caution.
    - Cluster=... — override the cluster name in the file if needed.
  - Must be run as an administrator.

Typical workflows (step-by-step patterns)
1) Backing up association config (flat-file)
   - sacctmgr dump <cluster-name> file=<cluster>.cfg
   - Store cluster.cfg off-host or in version control.
   - To restore or copy to another cluster: transfer the file to the target slurmdbd host and run sacctmgr load file=<cluster>.cfg (use clean=... only if you want to remove existing associations first).

2) Archiving old accounting data (safe trim of DB)
   - Verify slurmdbd.conf settings (ArchiveDir, PurgeJobAfter, PurgeEventAfter).
   - Run: sacctmgr archive dump Directory=/path/to/dir Jobs=Yes Events=Yes Purge=Yes (options depend on your desired time filters).
   - Confirm archive files were created under ArchiveDir (or Directory you set).
   - If Purge is used, the old records will be removed from the DB — keep the archive files in a safe place to enable later restore.

3) Restoring archived history
   - Ensure the archive file(s) are present on the slurmdbd host.
   - Run: sacctmgr archive load File=/path/to/archive-file
   - If some records already exist in DB, archive load will not insert duplicates and may error if you attempt to load the same archive twice—load only once per archive file unless you clean the DB of those records first.

Best practices and cautions
- Always back up your accounting DB and archive/flat files before destructive operations.
- Understand the difference: use dump/load for association metadata, archive dump/load for historical job/event data.
- Archive+purge is irreversible for the live DB unless you have the archive files; keep those files and verify successful creation.
- Run archive/dump during low-load windows if possible and ensure sufficient disk space in ArchiveDir.
- When moving associations between clusters, check the file format and the ordering (clusters should exist or be created; sacctmgr load reconciles but read docs about clean= behavior).
- Test load on a staging DB if possible, especially when using clean= or when importing large archive files.

Useful quick examples
- Export associations: sacctmgr dump mycluster file=mycluster.cfg
- Import associations: sacctmgr load file=mycluster.cfg
- Archive accounting (example skeleton): sacctmgr archive dump Directory=/archive/path Jobs=Yes Events=Yes Purge=Yes
- Restore archived accounting: sacctmgr archive load File=/archive/path/archive-file

References
- See sacctmgr(1) archive, dump, and load documentation in the Slurm manual for full option lists and exact syntax.

# Gang Scheduling
Slurm supports timesliced gang scheduling in which two or more jobs are
allocated to the same resources in the same partition and these jobs are
alternately suspended to let one job at a time have dedicated access to the
resources for a configured period of time.
Slurm also supports preemptive job scheduling that allows a job in a
higher PriorityTier partition, or in a preempting QOS, to preempt other
jobs. [Preemption](https://slurm.schedmd.com/preempt.html) is related to Gang scheduling
because SUSPEND is one of the PreemptionMode s, and it uses the Gang
scheduler to resume suspended jobs.
A workload manager that supports timeslicing can improve responsiveness
and utilization by allowing more jobs to begin running sooner.
Shorter-running jobs no longer have to wait in a queue behind longer-running
jobs.
Instead they can be run "in parallel" with the longer-running jobs, which will

## Timeslicer Design and Operation [#time_slice](https://slurm.schedmd.com/gang_scheduling.html)
When enabled, the gang scheduler keeps track of the resources
allocated to all jobs. For each partition an "active bitmap" is maintained that
tracks all concurrently running jobs in the Slurm cluster. Each time a new
job is allocated to resources in a partition, the gang scheduler
compares these newly allocated resources with the resources already maintained
in the "active bitmap".
If these two sets of resources are disjoint then the new job is added to the "active bitmap". If these two sets of resources overlap then
the new job is suspended. All jobs are tracked in a per-partition job queue
within the gang scheduler logic.

The SchedulerType configuration parameter specifies the scheduler
plugin to use.
Options are sched/backfill, which performs backfill scheduling, and
sched/builtin, which attempts to schedule jobs in a strict priority order within
each partition/queue.

can specify a wide range of parameters as described below.

- default_queue_depth=# - Specifies the number of jobs to consider for scheduling on each event that may result in a job being scheduled. Default value is 100 jobs. Since this happens frequently, a relatively small number is generally best.
- defer - Do not attempt to schedule jobs individually at submit time. Can be useful...

Summary — what backfill is and why its “health” matters
- Backfill lets the scheduler start lower‑priority jobs in the holes of the schedule as long as they won’t delay the expected start of any higher‑priority job. It greatly improves utilization and responsiveness compared with strict priority ordering.
- Backfill health = how well the scheduler is finding and using those holes (low wasted idle time, short waits for small jobs, few missed backfill opportunities).
- “Queue fit” = how well job resource/time requests match the available capacity/fragments in the cluster (jobs that can be packed into leftover nodes/GPUs vs jobs that need large contiguous blocks).

Key things that make backfill work well (and common failure modes)
- Accurate wallclock estimates: backfill depends on expected completion times. Over‑estimates reduce backfill window size; under‑estimates can delay higher‑priority jobs. Poor time estimates are the single biggest practical problem.
- Right‑sized resource requests: asking for whole nodes when only a few cores are needed, or not specifying memory, creates fragmentation and prevents packing.
- Scheduler configuration: SchedulerType=sched/backfill and parameters (SchedulerTimeSlice, default_queue_depth, select plugin and SelectTypeParameters) affect how aggressively and efficiently backfill is computed.
- Fragmentation: many small free fragments across nodes reduce the ability to run medium/large jobs and reduce utilization.
- Preemption, reservations, and drains: frequent preemption or reserved blocks reduce usable backfill space.
- Fairshare/priority issues: jobs with low effective priority never get considered earlier even if they fit backfill holes.

How to measure backfill health (use these Slurm queries regularly)
- sdiag — shows scheduler diagnostics and backfill statistics (backfill efficiency, queue depth, scheduling cycle times). This is the single best admin‑level quick check for scheduler behavior.
- sprio (or sprio --weights) — shows why specific pending jobs are low priority (age, fairshare, QOS). Use to diagnose priority/fit issues.
- squeue -o with long format (or scontrol show job <id>) — inspect pending jobs, requested nodes/CPUs/GPUs, and TimeLimit to see whether pending jobs are small/packable.
- sinfo / sinfo -N / sinfo -R — view partition/node counts, node states, and reason lines for drains/down nodes. Look for many idle fragments vs fully idle nodes.
- sreport (or cluster accounting) — utilization and usage trends (CPU/GPU hours, wasted idle time).
- sshare — check fairshare effects that may keep jobs at low priority.

What to look for in the outputs (quick checklist)
- sdiag: very small backfill depth or low backfill efficiency → scheduler not finding useful holes.
- squeue: many small jobs pending but blocked by a few large running jobs with long remaining time → time estimates or packing problem.
- sinfo: many nodes partly idle (fragmentation) instead of few fully idle nodes → poor request shapes.
- sprio/sshare: pending jobs have low effective priority despite being small → priority/fairshare tuning or user behavior is a cause.
- sreport: high idle time during heavy queueing → wasted capacity and poor fit.

Actions to improve backfill health and queue fit
For users (quick wins)
- Request accurate walltime; prefer slight overestimate but not huge padding.
- Request only the resources you need: use --ntasks-per-node, --cpus-per-task, --mem-per-cpu (or ReqMem/ReqGRES) instead of whole nodes if possible.
- Use job arrays or small tasks so many short jobs can occupy holes.
- For GPU jobs, request exactly the number of GPUs and consider node‑local packing (e.g., one GPU per job) so leftovers can be used.
- Use checkpoints or short test runs to determine realistic runtime.

For admins / schedulers
- Ensure SchedulerType=sched/backfill is enabled and tune SchedulerTimeSlice and default_queue_depth so the scheduler evaluates a useful set of pending jobs without wasting CPU time.
- Configure SelectTypeParameters to track memory (CR_Memory or CR_Core_Memory) so the scheduler can safely pack jobs without swapping.
- Set sensible cluster/default time limits or require reasonable user-provided limits via QOS to reduce wildly overlong bounds.
- Enable/adjust preemption policies and partition QOS to allow reclaiming resources when necessary (only if acceptable to users).
- Use topology-aware packing (cons_tres) to make the scheduler aware of cores, sockets, memory and GPUs for better fits.
- Consider node-sharing policies (AllowGroups, SchedMcs, overcommit) where appropriate to increase utilization for small jobs.
- Use reservations intentionally to protect important work but minimize their footprint.

Diagnostics + remediation workflow (practical steps)
1. Run sdiag and note backfill stats (cycle time, backfill efficiency).
2. Run squeue to find what is pending and why (use squeue -o with REASON and TIME_LEFT or scontrol show job for details).
3. Run sprio and sshare to check priority/fairshare effects.
4. Run sinfo/sinfo_reasons/sinfo -N to find node fragmentation or admin holds/drains.
5. If fragmentation is the issue: encourage users to pack requests, consider adjusting select plugin parameters (memory tracking), or migrate large long jobs to dedicated partitions/reservations.
6. If time estimates are the issue: enforce or educate about walltime accuracy, set default time limits, or require jobs to use job arrays/shorter steps.
7. Re-run sdiag and sreport after changes to measure improvement (utilization, average wait, backfill efficiency).

Useful commands to run (admin checklist)
- sdiag
- squeue -o "%.18i %.9P %.8j %.8u %.2t %.10M %.6D %.6R"  (or use scontrol show job <id>)
- sprio
- sshare -l
- sinfo -N; sinfo -R
- sreport cluster Utilization Start=now-7days End=now

How to prioritize fixes
- Short term (fast impact): educate users about accurate walltimes and resource requests; enforce modest defaults via QOS.
- Mid term: tune select plugin (memory accounting), SchedulerTimeSlice, and queue depth; enable packing flags.
- Long term: rework partitions or node types (mixed vs homogeneous), change fairshare weights or QOS policies, and add/change preemption/reservation strategies.

When to call it “healthy”
- High average utilization (consistent with your site goal) with low occurrences of idle time while many jobs are pending.
- sdiag shows reasonable backfill depth and backfill work being used (not just attempted).
- Few long‑lived jobs permanently blocking many small jobs; pending queue largely moves in and out quickly.
- sprio/sshare indicate priority ordering works as intended (no large, systematic unfairness).

If you want, I can:
- Show how to interpret your sdiag output or run a set of the diagnostic commands above against your cluster (I’ll explain the results).
- Suggest exact SchedulerParameters and select plugin settings tailored to your cluster profile (CPU-only vs GPU vs mixed nodes).

Which of those would you like next? If you want live diagnosis, tell me which diagnostics to run (sdiag, squeue, sinfo, sprio, sreport) or allow me to run the standard set and I’ll analyze the results.

The nodeset configuration allows you to define a name for a specific set of
nodes which can be used to simplify the partition configuration section,
especially for heterogeneous or condo-style systems. Each nodeset may be defined
by an explicit list of nodes, and/or by filtering the nodes by a particular
configured feature. If both Feature= and Nodes= are used the

## RELOCATING CONTROLLERS[#SECTION_RELOCATING-CONTROLLERS](https://slurm.schedmd.com/slurm.conf.html)
If the cluster's computers used for the primary or backup controller
will be out of service for an extended period of time, it may be
desirable to relocate them.
In order to do so, follow this procedure:
1. Stop the Slurm daemons on the old controller and nodes.
2. Modify the slurm.conf file appropriately.
3. Copy the files from the StateSaveLocation to the new controller or ensure
that they are accessible to the new controller via a shared drive.
4. Distribute the updated slurm.conf file to all nodes.
5. Restart the Slurm daemons on the new controller and nodes.
There should be no loss of any pending jobs. Any running jobs will get the
updated host info and finish normally.
Ensure that any nodes added to the cluster have the current
slurm.conf file installed.

slurm.conf is an ASCII file which describes general Slurm
configuration information, the nodes to be managed, information about
how those nodes are grouped into partitions, and various scheduling
parameters associated with those partitions. This file should be
consistent across all nodes in the cluster.

environment variable. The Slurm daemons also allow you to override

Summary — how GRES is configured (from the Slurm docs)
- GRES (Generic RESources) describe resources like GPUs, MPS instances, FPGAs, licenses, etc. Two places hold GRES configuration:
  1. slurm.conf — cluster-wide declarations (GresTypes and per-NodeName Gres= entries)
  2. gres.conf — per-node, detailed device mapping (Name, Type, File, Count, COREs, Links, AutoDetect)
- Slurm uses those configs to advertise GRES to the scheduler and to enforce --gres requests from users (srun/sbatch --gres).

Key slurm.conf items
- GresTypes
  - Declares the names of GRES types that may be used cluster-wide.
  - Example: GresTypes=gpu,mps
- NodeName ... Gres=
  - Each NodeName entry may include a Gres= list to declare how many of each GRES that node provides.
  - Format: Gres=<name>:<count>[,<name>:<count>...]
  - Example:
    - NodeName=compute[01-04] CPUs=64 RealMemory=250000 Gres=gpu:4
- Placement/availability
  - If slurm.conf fully describes the resources (and no per-device mapping like File/COREs/Links is required), you can omit a node gres.conf; otherwise place a gres.conf on each node (or on all cloud nodes + controller for cloud).
- Applying changes
  - Changes take effect on restart of slurm daemons, on receipt of SIGHUP, or by running scontrol reconfigure (docs: slurm.conf).

Key gres.conf items (per-node detailed mapping)
- File location: same directory as slurm.conf (typically /etc/slurm/)
- Entries describe each device instance for that node. Common fields:
  - Name= (required) — resource name used by Slurm and by --gres (e.g., Name=gpu)
  - Type= (optional) — vendor/model/type string (e.g., Type=tesla)
  - File= — device file(s) (e.g., File=/dev/nvidia0 or File=/dev/nvidia[0-3])
  - Count= — logical count when you want to expose e.g. many MPS instances
  - COREs= — CPU core affinity mapping
  - Links= — symbolic link info
  - AutoDetect=nvml (or other) — let Slurm/driver autodetect GPU devices via NVML
- Example snippets (from the docs):
  - AutoDetect=nvml
    Name=gpu Type=gtx560 File=/dev/nvidia0 COREs=0,1
    Name=gpu Type=tesla File=/dev/nvidia1 COREs=2,3
  - Or explicit:
    Name=gpu Type=tesla File=/dev/nvidia[0-3] COREs=0-31

How users request GRES
- sbatch/srun/salloc: --gres=<name>:<count> (or --gres=gpu:1)
  - Example in batch script:
    #SBATCH --gres=gpu:1

Visibility and verification (commands referenced in docs)
- sinfo / scontrol / squeue show GRES info:
  - sinfo and sinfo --Node show partition/node GRES presence (sinfo displays GRES column in some formats).
  - scontrol show node <node> shows Gres and detailed node fields.
  - After jobs start, squeue shows GRES allocations for running jobs.
- Use the gres.conf and slurm.conf docs to confirm syntax and examples.

Practical checklist to add GPUs (typical flow)
1. In slurm.conf: add GresTypes=gpu (and on each NodeName add Gres=gpu:<N>).
2. On each node (or controller+cloud nodes): create /etc/slurm/gres.conf describing devices (Name=gpu File=... or AutoDetect=nvml).
3. Restart or reconfigure slurmd and slurmctld (or use scontrol reconfigure / send SIGHUP) so slurm picks up the new GRES.
4. Test: sinfo / scontrol show node / srun --gres=gpu:1 hostname.

Notes & tips from docs
- If slurm.conf fully describes a GRES type (no per-device File/COREs/Links needed), the node-level gres.conf may be omitted.
- AutoDetect=nvml is useful for NVIDIA GPUs so you don’t have to list every /dev/nvidia device.
- Use distinct names (Name=) if you want multiple GRES types (e.g., Name=gpu and Name=mps).
- Proper cgroup and device plugin configuration may also be needed to enforce device isolation (see cgroup.conf docs if you run into allocation / permissions problems).

Here are the most useful fields you’ll see in scontrol show job <jobid>, grouped and explained so you know what to check when diagnosing/summarizing a job.

Identification
- JobId — the Slurm job numeric id (e.g., 12345). Always include this when talking about a job.
- JobName — user-specified job name (sbatch --job-name).
- UserId / GroupId — owner and UNIX/GID (often shown as name(uid)).
- Account — accounting project the job is charged to.

Scheduling / policy
- Partition — partition the job was submitted to.
- QOS — quality-of-service used (affects priority/limits).
- Priority — scheduler priority value (higher = scheduled earlier).
- Dependency — job dependency string (afterok, afterany, etc.).
- Reservation — reservation name if the job is tied to one.

State & why
- JobState — current state (PENDING, RUNNING, COMPLETED, FAILED, etc.).
- Reason — short scheduler reason for PENDING (e.g., Resources, Priority, QOSLimit). First place to look when a job is stuck.
- BatchFlag — indicates sbatch/batch behavior (batch jobs set =1).
- Requeue / Restarts — whether job is eligible to be requeued and how many restarts.

Timing
- SubmitTime — when the job was submitted.
- StartTime — when the job started (or estimated start if pending).
- EndTime — end/finish time (if completed).
- RunTime (or RunTimeRaw / Elapsed) — how long the job has run.
- TimeLimit — requested walltime (sbatch --time). If running longer than this the job will be killed.

Resources requested / allocated
- NumNodes / Nodes / NodeList — requested number of nodes and the concrete node list allocated (NodeList shows names like node[01-02]).
- NumCPUs / NumTasks / CPUsPerTask — CPU/core counts and task layout (e.g., NumCPUs=32, NumTasks=8).
- ReqMem / ReqTRES — requested memory/TRES; TRES (trackable resources) string lists e.g. cpu=,mem=,gres/gpu=.
- AllocTRES — actually allocated TRES for the job (shows what the job currently holds).
- Gres / GresUsed — generic resources requested e.g. gres=gpu:1 and how many are in use.
- TresPerNode / TresPerCPU (when present) — per-node/per-CPU allocation breakdown.

Allocation details (where to look for per-node info)
- AllocNode:Sid — the local node and system id making the allocation (useful for debugging node-local issues).
- NodeAddr / NodeList — address/list of nodes allocated.
- Flags / StateFlags — extra flags describing the job/step state (suspend, restarting, etc.).
- Partition/Features — on some configs you’ll see requested node features (e.g., feature=volta) used to match nodes.

I/O & environment
- WorkDir — working directory where the job runs.
- StdOut / StdErr — paths for stdout/stderr (can be %j-expanded).
- Command / BatchScript (when shown) — the sbatch script path or submitted command (privileged users or with details).

Exit / accounting
- ExitCode — exit code and signal for completed jobs (format exit:sig). Crucial when diagnosing failures.
- TresUsage / Usage (not always shown) — actual consumption summary (CPU, memory) when available; for detailed accounting use sacct.

Job arrays & steps
- ArrayJobId / ArrayTaskId — for array elements (e.g., 2000_5).
- Steps — scontrol shows step-level info for multi-step jobs; use scontrol show step <jobid> for step details.

Useful tips
- If a pending job shows Reason=Resources, check NodeList/Partition via sinfo and current queue via squeue for contention.
- For per-node CPU/memory placement use scontrol show job <id> Details (or -d) which prints CPUs/NUMA/memory allocated per node.
- For historical resource usage or final accounting (completed jobs) use sacct — scontrol is a live-view tool.
- For very terse pending reasons use squeue first (scontrol will give more detail for some fields).

Good question — here’s a concise, safe reference for using scontrol update on jobs (documentation-backed examples and warnings).

Basic form
- scontrol update JobId=<jobid> Field1=Value1 Field2=Value2 ...
- For job arrays: use ArrayJobID to target all elements (e.g., JobId=101) or an element with an underscore (e.g., JobId=101_5).
- Multiple assignments are separated by spaces.

Examples
- Inspect first:
  - scontrol show job 12345
- Change time limit (pending jobs normally; may be restricted by QOS/account limits):
  - scontrol update JobId=12345 TimeLimit=02:00:00
  - Time formats: SS, MM:SS, HH:MM:SS, or D-HH:MM:SS (use the cluster’s accepted formats).
- Rename a job:
  - scontrol update JobId=12345 JobName="analysis-step1"
- Add/change a comment:
  - scontrol update JobId=12345 Comment="Needs longer runtime for debugging"
- Change a single array element:
  - scontrol update JobId=101_3 TimeLimit=01:00:00
- Change QOS or Priority (usually restricted — admin or owner+permissions required):
  - scontrol update JobId=12345 QOS=high
  - scontrol update JobId=12345 Priority=1000

Quoting and spacing
- If a value contains spaces or special chars, quote it: JobName="my job" Comment="needs GPU"
- Use the exact FieldName=Value form (no space around =).

What you can and cannot safely change

Audit accounting problem reports and explain likely remediation
No accounting problems found.

I ran sacctmgr show problems and found: "No accounting problems found."

What that means
- The accounting DB reports no detected consistency or integrity issues (no orphaned records, missing associations, or obvious DB-schema problems found by sacctmgr).
- It does not guarantee there are no accounting symptoms (e.g., users seeing unexpected charges or missing historical records); it means the sacctmgr self-check did not flag structural problems.

Common accounting problems and likely remediation
- Missing or incorrect user↔account associations
  - Symptom: jobs are not being charged to the expected account or show as "unaccounted".
  - Remediation: inspect associations (sacctmgr show associations), then create/modify associations with sacctmgr so users map to the correct accounts. Re-run sacctmgr show problems after fixes.

- Orphaned or inconsistent job records
  - Symptom: sacct/sacctmgr queries return unexpected job states or duplicate/partial entries.
  - Remediation: check job history with sacct for the job IDs; verify slurmctld→slurmdbd connectivity and slurmdbd logs; if records are corrupt or missing, restore from backups or apply surgical SQL fixes only after consulting backups and locking the DB.

- Database connectivity / slurmdbd problems
  - Symptom: recent jobs not appearing in accounting, errors in slurmdbd logs, or slurmdbd not accepting connections.
  - Remediation: check slurmdbd service status and logs (systemd or slurmdbd log), verify DB server is healthy (MySQL/Postgres), check network/auth config, then restart slurmdbd after fixes. Retest by submitting a small job and verifying sacct.

- Duplicate entries or broken constraints after manual DB edits
  - Symptom: unique-key violations, duplicate rows, or inconsistent limit enforcement.
  - Remediation: revert manual DB changes from a backup if available; otherwise, run careful SQL cleanup with backups and DB transaction safety; consider restoring the DB to a known-good snapshot.

- Misconfigured QOS / time/account limits or unexpected associations
  - Symptom: users hit limits unexpectedly or fairshare looks off.
  - Remediation: review QOS/account limits (sacctmgr show qos, sacctmgr show assoc), correct the configuration, and re-evaluate fairshare (sshare).

- Corrupted DB tables or engine-level problems
  - Symptom: DB-level errors (MySQL/PG) or inability for slurmdbd to query certain tables.
  - Remediation: run DB engine repair tools (mysqlcheck/pg_repair) or restore from backup; coordinate maintenance window and ensure slurmdbd is stopped or read-only while repairing.

Preventive steps and best practices
- Keep regular DB backups and test restores.
- Monitor slurmctld/slurmdbd logs and alert on slurmdbd errors or failed writes.
- Use sacctmgr show problems regularly (cron/monitoring) and review any changes to associations or DB schema carefully.
- Keep clocks synchronized (NTP) across controller and DB hosts to avoid timestamp anomalies.

- list recent accounting errors from slurmdbd logs (needs log path)
- verify slurmdbd responsiveness (scontrol_ping)
