## PERFORMANCE[#SECTION_PERFORMANCE](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Executing sbatch sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmctld daemon come in at once, it can result in
a degradation of performance of the slurmctld daemon, possibly resulting
in a denial of service.
Do not run sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other
programs. Ensure that programs limit calls to sbatch to the minimum
necessary for the information you are trying to gather.

Specify a batch script by filename on the command line. The batch script specifies a 1 minute time limit for the job.
```text
$ cat myscript #!/bin/sh #SBATCH --time=1 srun hostname |sort $ sbatch -N4 myscript salloc: Granted job allocation 65537 $ cat slurm-65537.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
Pass a batch script to sbatch on standard input:
```text
$ sbatch -N4 #!/bin/sh > srun hostname |sort > EOF sbatch: Submitted batch job 65541 $ cat slurm-65541.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
To create a heterogeneous job with 3 components, each allocating a unique set of nodes:
```text
$ sbatch -w node[2-3] : -w node4 : -w node[5-7] work.bash Submitted batch job 34987
```

## PERFORMANCE[#SECTION_PERFORMANCE](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Executing sbatch sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmctld daemon come in at once, it can result in
a degradation of performance of the slurmctld daemon, possibly resulting
in a denial of service.
Do not run sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other
programs. Ensure that programs limit calls to sbatch to the minimum
necessary for the information you are trying to gather.

procedure calls to the slurmctld daemon come in at once, it can result in
a degradation of performance of the slurmctld daemon, possibly resulting
in a denial of service.
Do not run sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other
programs. Ensure that programs limit calls to sbatch to the minimum
necessary for the information you are trying to gather.

What "Dependency" means (concise semantics)
- Slurm dependencies are declared at submit time (sbatch --dependency=...) or added/changed with scontrol. A dependency tells Slurm to hold the job until one or more conditions on other job(s) are met.
- Common dependency types:
  - after: job waits until the specified job(s) have started.
  - afterany: waits until the specified job(s) complete (any exit status).
  - afterok: waits until the specified job(s) complete successfully (exit code 0).
  - afternotok: waits until the specified job(s) complete with a non‑zero exit code.
  - aftercorr: used with job arrays — waits until the corresponding task index in the specified job array completes successfully.
  - singleton: ensures only one job with the same singleton key (often same user+name) runs at a time; later singleton jobs wait for earlier ones to finish.
- Multiple dependency clauses are combined (comma separated) and all clauses must be satisfied before the dependent job is released (i.e., dependencies are effectively ANDed).
- Job arrays: semantics are special — e.g., after waits for all tasks to start, afterany/afterok consider completion across all tasks; aftercorr matches corresponding array task IDs.

How to see exactly what job 3004 is waiting on
- Run: scontrol show job 3004
  - Look for the Dependency=... field (it will show strings like afterok:12345,afterany:23456 or ArrayJobID etc.).
- If the dependency refers to an array, interpret it using the array rules above (afterok on an array means all tasks in that array must succeed).
- If the dependency references a job that will never satisfy the condition (e.g., a missing job ID or a completed job with wrong exit code), the job will remain pending until the dependency is changed or removed.

## Reservations that Replace Allocated Resources [#replace](https://slurm.schedmd.com/reservations.html)
By default, nodes in a reservation that are DOWN or DRAINED will be replaced,
but not nodes that are allocated to jobs. This behavior may be explicitly
requested with the REPLACE_DOWN flag.
However, you may instruct Slurm to also replace nodes which are allocated to
jobs with new idle nodes. This is done using the REPLACE flag as shown in
the example below.
The effect of this is to always maintain a constant size pool of resources.
This option is not supported for reservations specifying cores which
span more than one node, rather than full nodes. (E.g. a 1 core reservation on
node "tux1" will be moved if node "tux1" goes down, but a reservation

The default behavior for reservations is that jobs must request a
reservation in order to run in it. The MAGNETIC flag allows you to
create a reservation that will allow jobs to run in it without requiring that
they specify the name of the reservation. The reservation will only "attract"
jobs that meet the access control requirements.
NOTE : Magnetic reservations cannot "attract" heterogeneous jobs -
heterogeneous jobs will only run in magnetic reservations if they explicitly
request the reservation.

specified as being able to access the reservation then submits a job and
the job starts on the reserved node.
```text

## Reservations Floating Through Time [#float](https://slurm.schedmd.com/reservations.html)
Slurm can be used to create an advanced reservation with a start time that
remains a fixed period of time in the future.
These reservation are not intended to run jobs, but to prevent long running
jobs from being initiated on specific nodes.
That node might be placed in a DRAINING state to prevent any new jobs
from being started there.
Alternately, an advanced reservation might be placed on the node to prevent
jobs exceeding some specific time limit from being started.
Attempts by users to make use of a reservation with a floating start time will
be rejected.
When ready to perform the maintenance, place the node in DRAINING state and
delete the previously created advanced reservation.
Create the reservation by using the flag value of TIME_FLOAT and a
start time that is relative to the current time (use the keyword now ).

I fetched the local Slurm documentation about reservations and summarized the key points and common usage below.

What a reservation is
- An advanced reservation reserves specific resources (nodes, cores, or counts) for a specified time window so only authorized jobs can use them during that window.
- Reservations can be scoped by user, account, QOS, partition, or explicit node lists; they can also explicitly deny users/accounts.

Key reservation fields / arguments
- ReservationName: name assigned by scontrol (or you can set one).
- StartTime / EndTime / Duration: when the reservation begins/ends (StartTime may be absolute or relative like now; Duration sets the length).
- Nodes / NodeCnt / CoreCnt / NodeList: which nodes/cores are reserved (whole nodes or specific core counts).
- Users / Accounts / QOS: who may (or may not) use the reservation; a leading "-" excludes (e.g., user=-alan).
- Partition: limit the reservation to a partition.
- Flags: special behaviors (see below).

Creating, viewing, deleting
- Create: scontrol create reservation StartTime=... Duration=... Nodes=... User=... (many other options allowed).
  Example: scontrol create reservation StartTime=now Duration=60 Nodes=node05 User=user1 Flags=magnetic
- Show: scontrol show reservation (or scontrol show res ReservationName=<name>) to view details.
- Delete: scontrol delete reservation ReservationName=<name> (or the equivalent scontrol command).

How reservations interact with scheduling and jobs
- By default jobs must explicitly request the reservation (sbatch/srun --reservation=<name>) to run inside it.
- MAGNETIC reservations: will “attract” eligible jobs that do not explicitly name the reservation (jobs still must meet access rules). Magnetic reservations do not attract heterogeneous jobs unless those jobs explicitly request the reservation.
- Time-safety: as a reservation start approaches, Slurm will not start new jobs that cannot finish before the reservation (to avoid jobs overlapping the reservation).
- Creation constraints: by default Slurm will not allow creating a reservation that conflicts with resources expected to be busy at the start time (i.e., resources with running jobs that won’t finish). The IGNORE_JOBS flag can be used for maintenance reservations where you plan to cancel running jobs manually.
- REPLACE / REPLACE_DOWN flags:
  - REPLACE_DOWN: causes DOWN or DRAINED nodes in a reservation to be replaced.
  - REPLACE: attempts to replace nodes that are allocated to jobs with idle nodes to maintain a steady reservation size (not supported for reservations defined as cores spread over multiple nodes).
- TIME_FLOAT: creates a “floating” reservation whose start time is relative (keeps the reservation at a fixed offset into the future). Useful for scheduling maintenance windows that float with time. Floating reservations aren’t usable by normal job submissions until they become active.

How users request a reservation when submitting jobs
- sbatch --reservation=<ReservationName> script.sh
- srun --reservation=<ReservationName> ...
- If the reservation is MAGNETIC, users who meet the access control may get scheduled into it without naming it (subject to compatibility).

Monitoring reservations
- scontrol show reservation (details)
- squeue --reservation=<name> (jobs bound to that reservation)
- scontrol show res (short/reserved resource view)

Access control and special cases
- You can grant and deny access by user/account/QOS with the Users/Accounts fields (use a minus prefix to deny).
- Reservations may be full-node or per-core; some flags (e.g., REPLACE) have limits when reservations span multiple nodes with partial core allocations.
- Use the MAINT flag for maintenance-style reservations (accounting/identification).

Examples (from the docs)
- Create a simple user reservation:
  scontrol create reservation StartTime=now Duration=60 NodeCnt=1 CoreCnt=2 User=alan
- Create a magnetic reservation on node05 for user1:
  scontrol create reservation User=user1 Nodes=node05 StartTime=now Duration=10 Flags=magnetic

Where to read more
- The local Slurm reservations guide (reservations.html) has the full reference and many examples: it documents all reservation keywords and flags (MAGNETIC, REPLACE, TIME_FLOAT, IGNORE_JOBS, MAINT, etc.), plus examples for per-node and per-core reservations.

## DESCRIPTION[#SECTION_DESCRIPTION](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sacctmgr.html)
sacctmgr is used to view or modify Slurm account information.
The account information is maintained within a database with the interface
being provided by slurmdbd (Slurm Database daemon).
This database can serve as a central storehouse of user and
computer information for multiple computers at a single site.
Slurm account information is recorded based upon four parameters
that form what is referred to as an association .
These parameters are user , cluster , partition , and
account . user is the login name.

Summary — what to watch for
- sacctmgr modifies the Slurm accounting DB (slurmdbd) — associations are the Cluster+Account+User(+Partition) records that the scheduler uses for limits, fairshare, default QOS, etc. Changes to accounts/users/QOS/limits affect scheduling and future job submissions, and can change which pending jobs are eligible to start.
- Unsafe edits can: block users from submitting, make pending jobs unschedulable, change priorities/fairshare, remove coordinator/admin privileges, orphan or remove associations, or otherwise change accounting and reporting. Because these are DB changes, mistakes can require restoring a backup.

Concrete safety implications by action
- sacctmgr add (create)
  - Low risk for existing jobs: adding accounts/users/QOS generally enables capabilities (new account, new association, more privileges). It won’t retroactively break running jobs.
  - Use-case risks: accidentally creating duplicate or misconfigured associations (wrong cluster/partition/account) can confuse accounting or allow unintentional access.
  - Safety tips: specify cluster/account/partition explicitly, and verify with sacctmgr list/show after adding.

- sacctmgr modify
  - Scheduling & limits: changes to limits (MaxJobs, MaxTRES, GrpJobs, GrpTRES, MaxWall, DefaultQOS, Fairshare, etc.) influence scheduler decisions. The docs note group limits (GrpJobs, GrpTRES…) are tested when a job is considered for allocation — i.e., limits primarily affect scheduling of new/pending jobs.
  - Permissions & roles: changing AdminLevel, coordinator flags, or UsersAreCoords changes who can manage accounts.
  - Potential surprises: lowering group limits or per-user limits can make already-pending jobs unschedulable; raising limits can allow a flood of new jobs to start. Some attributes are inherited by child accounts so modifying a parent can have broad scope.
  - Safety tips: preview existing values with sacctmgr show/list and sshare (fairshare view); prefer targeted modify with a precise where clause; test changes in interactive mode before committing.

- sacctmgr delete
  - Broad impact: deleting an account, user, or association removes that entity from the Slurm accounting DB. That prevents future submissions using that account/association and can remove coordinator privileges.
  - Running jobs: the documentation treats associations and accounts as DB metadata used by the scheduler. It does not describe deletion as automatically killing running jobs; however deleting an account or association can prevent future accounting or make re-association awkward. Deleting entities with children (account hierarchies) may fail or produce unexpected consequences if not done in the proper order.
  - Danger: a too-broad delete (missing or incorrect where clause) can remove many associations at once.
  - Safety tips: always use an explicit where clause (cluster=..., account=..., user=...), list associations first, and prefer deleting only the specific association or leaf account. Don’t delete parent accounts before children.

Operational controls and safety procedures
- Interactive mode vs immediate:
  - Run sacctmgr without --immediate to use interactive mode; you can stage commands and then run commit to apply changes. This is safer for reviewing batched edits.
  - Use --immediate (or -i) only when you are sure — it commits without confirmation.
- Preview and verify:
  - Use sacctmgr list/show (and sacctmgr list associations, sacctmgr show account/user/qos) to inspect current state before changes.
  - Check scheduler effects with squeue/sinfo/sshare after committing if you expect scheduling or fairshare changes.
- Back up the accounting DB:
  - Use sacctmgr archive dump (or the DB backup mechanism for slurmdbd) to export a flat-file snapshot before destructive changes so you can restore with archive load if needed.
- Narrow, auditable changes:
  - Use precise where= filters to scope add/modify/delete.
  - Log/record the exact commands and rationale; prefer small, incremental changes.
- Test-first:
  - If possible, test the change in a staging cluster or with non-production accounts/users.
- Recovery plan:
  - Have a DB dump or snapshot ready. Know how to load it (sacctmgr archive load) and involve DB/Slurm admins if you need to recover.
- Communicate:
  - Inform affected users before making changes that affect submission ability, limits, or fairshare. Coordinate if you will remove or change accounts.

Examples of common mistakes
- Running sacctmgr delete account name=X cluster=Y without verifying children → accidentally remove sub-accounts or associations.
- Lowering GrpJobs/GrpTRES too far → many pending jobs become unschedulable.
- Removing a coordinator flag or AdminLevel without warning → users lose management ability unexpectedly.
- Using --immediate for a multi-change script with a bug → immediate commit of many unwanted changes.

Useful commands to run before/after edits
- Preview: sacctmgr list associations cluster=<cluster> format=Account,User,Partition,Fairshare,...
- Inspect entity: sacctmgr show account name=<acct> ; sacctmgr show user name=<user> cluster=<cluster>
- Backup: sacctmgr archive dump file=<file>
- Interactive: sacctmgr (enter interactive mode), make edits, then commit
- Recover: sacctmgr archive load file=<file> (restore from dump)

Bottom line (short)
- Adds are relatively safe but check names/associations.
- Modifies change scheduler behavior for new/pending jobs — preview and stage changes.
- Deletes are highest risk — back up, scope narrowly, review associations, and use interactive/commit workflow.

## Job Accounting Records [#job_record](https://slurm.schedmd.com/job_launch.html)
When Slurm is configured to use SlurmDBD to store job records (i.e.
AccountingStorageType=accounting_storage=slurmdbd ), there are multiple
records that get stored for each job. There is a record for the job as a

## Task Launch [#task_launch](https://slurm.schedmd.com/job_launch.html)
The srun command builds a task launch request data structure
including the credential, executable name, file names, etc. and sends it to
the slurmd daemon on node zero of the job step allocation. The
slurmd daemon validates the signature and forwards the request to the
slurmd daemons on other nodes to launch tasks for that job step. The
degree of fanout in this message forwarding is configurable using the
TreeWidth parameter. Each slurmd daemon tests that the job has
not been cancelled since the credential was issued (due to a possible race
condition) and spawns a slurmstepd program to manage the job step.
Note that the slurmctld daemon is not directly involved in task
launch in order to minimize the overhead on this critical resource.

```text

Cancel job 1234 along with all of its steps:

$ scancel --signal=KILL 1235

## NOTES[#SECTION_NOTES](https://slurm.schedmd.com/scancel.html)
If multiple filters are supplied (e.g. --partition and --name )
only the jobs satisfying all of the filtering options will be signaled.
Cancelling a job step will not result in the job being terminated.
The job must be cancelled to release a resource allocation.
To cancel a job, invoke scancel without --signal option. This
will send first a SIGCONT to all steps to eventually wake them up followed by
a SIGTERM, then wait the KillWait duration defined in the slurm.conf file
and finally if they have not terminated send a SIGKILL. This gives
time for the running job/step(s) to clean up.
If a signal value of "KILL" is sent to an entire job, this will cancel
the active job steps but not cancel the job itself.

## ARGUMENTS[#SECTION_ARGUMENTS](https://slurm.schedmd.com/scancel.html)
job_id [#OPT_job_id](https://slurm.schedmd.com/scancel.html) The Slurm job ID to be signaled.
step_id [#OPT_step_id](https://slurm.schedmd.com/scancel.html) The step ID of the job step to be signaled.
If not specified, the operation is performed at the level of a job.
If neither --batch nor --signal are used,
the entire job will be terminated.
When --batch is used, the batch shell processes will be signaled.
The child processes of the shell will not be signaled by Slurm, but
the shell may forward the signal.
When --batch is not used but --signal is used,
then all job steps will be signaled, but the batch script itself
will not be signaled.

Summary — what scancel does when it sends signals
- scancel can send arbitrary POSIX signals (name or number) to jobs or individual job steps with --signal (e.g., --signal=TERM, --signal=KILL, --signal=USR1).
- You may address an individual step with jobid.step (e.g., 1234.1) or job-array elements with the array syntax (e.g., 1237_4).

Behavior details
- Canceling a job (invoking scancel without --signal) is a controlled termination sequence:
  - scancel first sends SIGCONT to all steps to wake sleeping processes,
  - then sends SIGTERM,
  - waits the KillWait duration from slurm.conf,
  - and if processes remain, sends SIGKILL. This sequence both signals steps and results in the job being cancelled and its allocation released.
- Sending a specific signal with --signal only delivers that signal; it does not by itself perform the full cancel sequence unless you send the signals that cause termination. Note: sending signal=KILL to an entire job will kill active job steps but will not mark the job as cancelled (it does not perform the normal cancel/release sequence).
- Signaling a job vs signaling steps:
  - If you signal a job-level ID (e.g., scancel --signal=TERM 1234) the signal is delivered to job steps according to the rules above.
  - If you signal a specific step (e.g., scancel --signal=TERM 1234.1) only that step is signaled. Cancelling a job step does not cancel the job; the job allocation remains until the job is cancelled.
- --batch option:
  - By default, signals other than SIGKILL are not sent to the batch step (the shell script) when you signal a job/steps.
  - With --batch, scancel signals only the batch step (the shell process). Children of that shell are not directly signaled by Slurm (the shell might forward the signal if it traps it).
  - Conversely, if you use --signal but not --batch, scancel signals all job steps but not the batch script itself.
- Performance note (operational): scancel normally makes RPCs to slurmctld to determine matching jobs and then sends per-job signal RPCs. Using --ctld can reduce the number of RPCs for large sets of targets.

Examples
- scancel 1234
  - Cancel job 1234: wake (SIGCONT), SIGTERM, wait KillWait, then SIGKILL if needed — job and allocation released.
- scancel --signal=TERM 1234.1
  - Send SIGTERM only to step 1 of job 1234; job remains unless you cancel it.
- scancel --signal=KILL 1235
  - Send SIGKILL to all steps of job 1235; active steps are killed but the job may not be marked cancelled.
- scancel --signal=USR1 --batch 1236
  - Send SIGUSR1 to the batch shell (script) of job 1236 only.

Good — here’s a concise explanation of what “partition constraints” and “availability” mean for the debug partition, how they affect job scheduling, and the quick checks you can run.

What a partition (e.g., "debug") can constrain
- Timelimit (TIMELIMIT): max walltime a job may request in that partition (debug often very short, e.g., 30m). Jobs requesting longer than this will be refused or placed in a different partition.
- Job size limits: max/min nodes, tasks, CPUs or memory per job that the partition allows.
- Access controls: which accounts, users, groups, or QOS can submit to the partition (AllowAccounts/AllowGroups/Default/RootOnly).
- Node membership: which nodes are in the partition (Nodes or NodeSet). Nodes may be shared across partitions but with different limits.
- Features/GRES expectations: the partition may be intended for nodes with specific features (e.g., gpu, fastnet). Jobs that use --constraint or --gres must match available node attributes.
- QOS/priority limits: a partition may be associated with particular QOS that impose MaxJobs, MaxWall, or other limits taking effect before user/account limits.
- Reservation and maintenance flags: reservations may reserve debug nodes for a time window; nodes can be drained/down for maintenance and removed from availability.

What “availability” (as shown by sinfo) means and how to read it
- Use sinfo to inspect partition state:
  - sinfo -s or sinfo --partition=debug --long
- Key columns you’ll see:
  - AVAIL / State: whether the partition is administratively up/down and usable.
  - TIMELIMIT: the partition walltime limit.
  - NODES(A/I/O/T) or NODES column: summary of nodes and states. NODES(A/I/O/T) typically shown as Allocated/Idle/Other/Total.
    - Allocated (A): nodes currently running jobs for that partition.
    - Idle (I): nodes free for immediate allocation — these are the nodes eligible for new jobs.
    - Other (O): nodes in other states (drain, down, reserved, etc.).
    - Total (T): total nodes assigned to the partition.
- Example sinfo summary and interpretation:
  - debug up 30:00 0/8/0/8 dev[0-7]
    - TIMELIMIT 30:00, 8 total nodes, 0 allocated, 8 idle → 8 nodes available for new jobs.
  - debug up 30:00 0/0/8/8 dev[0-7]
    - 0 idle, 8 in "other" (likely drained/down/reserved) → no nodes currently available to schedule jobs.

Common reasons debug jobs don’t start (check in this order)
1. Walltime or size exceeds partition limits (request shorter time or smaller node count).
2. Job’s constraints/features do not match any idle node (job used --constraint, --gres, or requested a feature not present).
3. No idle nodes (allocated or reserved) — check NODES(A/I/O/T) in sinfo.
4. Reservation holds the nodes (check scontrol show reservation / squeue --reservation=<name>).
5. User/account/QoS limits or association caps prevent scheduling (check sacctmgr or QOS).
6. Nodes are in DRAIN/DOWN for maintenance (sinfo --states=drain,down or sinfo -N).
7. Pending reasons from the queue (use squeue -p debug to see pending reason strings; for a single job use scontrol show job <jobid> to get the detailed reason).

Quick commands to inspect the debug partition and a job
- Partition/node status:
  - sinfo -s                  # short summary for all partitions
  - sinfo --partition=debug --long
  - sinfo -N --partition=debug   # one line per node
  - sinfo --states=drained,down --partition=debug
- Queue and pending reasons:
  - squeue -p debug
  - squeue -p debug -o "%.18i %.9P %.8j %.8u %.2t %.10M %.10l %.6D %R"  # custom format including REASON
  - scontrol show job <jobid>   # detailed job info & pending reason
- Reservations and access:
  - scontrol show reservation
  - scontrol show partition debug   # if available on your system for partition details
  - sacctmgr list associations or sacctmgr show user <user>  # for account / association limits

Practical tips
- Debug partitions are typically configured to favor very short, small runs: ask for the lowest necessary walltime and node count.

## PERFORMANCE[#SECTION_PERFORMANCE](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Executing sbatch sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmctld daemon come in at once, it can result in
a degradation of performance of the slurmctld daemon, possibly resulting
in a denial of service.
Do not run sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other
programs. Ensure that programs limit calls to sbatch to the minimum
necessary for the information you are trying to gather.

## EXAMPLES[#SECTION_EXAMPLES](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Specify a batch script by filename on the command line. The batch script specifies a 1 minute time limit for the job.
```text
$ cat myscript #!/bin/sh #SBATCH --time=1 srun hostname |sort $ sbatch -N4 myscript salloc: Granted job allocation 65537 $ cat slurm-65537.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
Pass a batch script to sbatch on standard input:
```text
$ sbatch -N4 #!/bin/sh > srun hostname |sort > EOF sbatch: Submitted batch job 65541 $ cat slurm-65541.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
To create a heterogeneous job with 3 components, each allocating a unique set of nodes:
```text
$ sbatch -w node[2-3] : -w node4 : -w node[5-7] work.bash Submitted batch job 34987
```

The configuration of nodes (or machines) to be managed by Slurm is
also specified in /etc/slurm.conf .
Changes in node configuration (e.g. adding nodes, changing their
processor count, etc.) require restarting or reconfiguring all slurmctld
and slurmd daemons.
All slurmd daemons must know each node in the system to forward
messages in support of hierarchical communications.
Only the NodeName must be supplied in the configuration file.
All other node configuration information is optional.
It is advisable to establish baseline node configurations,
especially if the cluster is heterogeneous.

## PERFORMANCE[#SECTION_PERFORMANCE](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Executing sbatch sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmctld daemon come in at once, it can result in
a degradation of performance of the slurmctld daemon, possibly resulting
in a denial of service.
Do not run sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other
programs. Ensure that programs limit calls to sbatch to the minimum
necessary for the information you are trying to gather.

## EXAMPLES[#SECTION_EXAMPLES](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Specify a batch script by filename on the command line. The batch script specifies a 1 minute time limit for the job.
```text
$ cat myscript #!/bin/sh #SBATCH --time=1 srun hostname |sort $ sbatch -N4 myscript salloc: Granted job allocation 65537 $ cat slurm-65537.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
Pass a batch script to sbatch on standard input:
```text
$ sbatch -N4 #!/bin/sh > srun hostname |sort > EOF sbatch: Submitted batch job 65541 $ cat slurm-65541.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
To create a heterogeneous job with 3 components, each allocating a unique set of nodes:
```text
$ sbatch -w node[2-3] : -w node4 : -w node[5-7] work.bash Submitted batch job 34987
```

## Preemption Design and Operation [#operation](https://slurm.schedmd.com/preempt.html)
The SelectType plugin will identify resources where a pending job can
begin execution. When PreemptMode is configured to CANCEL ,
SUSPEND or REQUEUE , the select plugin will also preempt running
jobs as needed to initiate the pending job. When
PreemptMode=SUSPEND,GANG the select plugin will initiate the pending
job and rely upon the gang scheduling logic to perform job suspend and resume,
as described below.
The select plugin is passed an ordered list of preemptable jobs to consider for
each pending job which is a candidate to start.
This list is sorted by either:
- QOS priority,
- Partition priority and job size (to favor preempting smaller jobs), or
- Job start time (with PreemptParameters=youngest_first ).

Batch jobs with –requeue=expedite will automatically requeue on node failure, or if the batch script returns a non-zero exit code and one or more Epilog scripts fail. Expedited requeue jobs are eligible to restart immediately, are treated as the highest priority job in the system, and their previously allocated set of nodes will be prevented from launching other work.

## PERFORMANCE[#SECTION_PERFORMANCE](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Executing sbatch sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmctld daemon come in at once, it can result in
a degradation of performance of the slurmctld daemon, possibly resulting
in a denial of service.
Do not run sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other
programs. Ensure that programs limit calls to sbatch to the minimum
necessary for the information you are trying to gather.

## EXAMPLES[#SECTION_EXAMPLES](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Specify a batch script by filename on the command line. The batch script specifies a 1 minute time limit for the job.
```text
$ cat myscript #!/bin/sh #SBATCH --time=1 srun hostname |sort $ sbatch -N4 myscript salloc: Granted job allocation 65537 $ cat slurm-65537.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
Pass a batch script to sbatch on standard input:
```text
$ sbatch -N4 #!/bin/sh > srun hostname |sort > EOF sbatch: Submitted batch job 65541 $ cat slurm-65541.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
To create a heterogeneous job with 3 components, each allocating a unique set of nodes:
```text
$ sbatch -w node[2-3] : -w node4 : -w node[5-7] work.bash Submitted batch job 34987
```

## EXAMPLES[#SECTION_EXAMPLES](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Specify a batch script by filename on the command line. The batch script specifies a 1 minute time limit for the job.
```text
$ cat myscript #!/bin/sh #SBATCH --time=1 srun hostname |sort $ sbatch -N4 myscript salloc: Granted job allocation 65537 $ cat slurm-65537.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
Pass a batch script to sbatch on standard input:
```text
$ sbatch -N4 #!/bin/sh > srun hostname |sort > EOF sbatch: Submitted batch job 65541 $ cat slurm-65541.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
To create a heterogeneous job with 3 components, each allocating a unique set of nodes:
```text
$ sbatch -w node[2-3] : -w node4 : -w node[5-7] work.bash Submitted batch job 34987
```

### Task Data[#task](https://slurm.schedmd.com/hdf5_profile_user_guide.html)
JobAcctGatherType =jobacct_gather/linux
is required in slurm.conf to collect task data.
Appropriately set task=freq in either JobAcctGatherFrequency in slurm.conf
or in --acctg-freq on the command line.
Each data sample in the Task Time Series contains the following data
items.
Date Time
Time of day at which the data sample was taken. This can be used to
correlate activity with other sources such as logs.
Time
Elapsed time since the beginning of the step.
CPU Frequency
CPU Frequency at time of sample.
CPU Time
Seconds of CPU time used during the sample.
CPU Utilization
CPU Utilization during the interval.
RSS
Value of RSS at time of sample.
VM Size
Value of VM Size at time of sample.
Pages
Pages used in sample.
Read Megabytes
Number of megabytes read from local disk.
Write Megabytes
Number of megabytes written to local disk.

## PERFORMANCE[#SECTION_PERFORMANCE](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Executing sbatch sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmctld daemon come in at once, it can result in
a degradation of performance of the slurmctld daemon, possibly resulting
in a denial of service.
Do not run sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other
programs. Ensure that programs limit calls to sbatch to the minimum
necessary for the information you are trying to gather.

## PERFORMANCE[#SECTION_PERFORMANCE](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Executing sbatch sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmctld daemon come in at once, it can result in
a degradation of performance of the slurmctld daemon, possibly resulting
in a denial of service.
Do not run sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other
programs. Ensure that programs limit calls to sbatch to the minimum
necessary for the information you are trying to gather.

## EXAMPLES[#SECTION_EXAMPLES](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Specify a batch script by filename on the command line. The batch script specifies a 1 minute time limit for the job.
```text
$ cat myscript #!/bin/sh #SBATCH --time=1 srun hostname |sort $ sbatch -N4 myscript salloc: Granted job allocation 65537 $ cat slurm-65537.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
Pass a batch script to sbatch on standard input:
```text
$ sbatch -N4 #!/bin/sh > srun hostname |sort > EOF sbatch: Submitted batch job 65541 $ cat slurm-65541.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
To create a heterogeneous job with 3 components, each allocating a unique set of nodes:
```text
$ sbatch -w node[2-3] : -w node4 : -w node[5-7] work.bash Submitted batch job 34987
```

## SPECIFICATIONS FOR USERS[#SECTION_SPECIFICATIONS-FOR-USERS](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sacctmgr.html)
Users can be created, modified, and deleted with sacctmgr. These
options allow you to set the corresponding attributes or filter on them
when querying for Users.
It is important to recognize the difference between a User and an Association.
There is a User entity that exists for each unique username. However, there
can be multiple User Associations for the same User. The combination of a
Cluster, Account, User, and optionally a Partition constitute a User
Association. When adding an existing User to another Account, you are creating
an additional User Association rather than modifying an existing User.

## Partition QOS [#partition](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
A QOS can be attached to a partition. This means the partition will have all
the same limits as the QOS. This does not associate jobs with the QOS, nor does
it give the job any priority or preemption characteristics of the assigned QOS.
Jobs may separately request the same QOS or a different QOS to gain those
characteristics. However, the Partition QOS limits will override the job's QOS.
If the opposite is desired you may configure the job's QOS with

# Preemption
Slurm supports job preemption, the act of "stopping" one or more "low-priority"
jobs to let a "high-priority" job run.
Job preemption is implemented as a variation of Slurm's
[Gang Scheduling](https://slurm.schedmd.com/gang_scheduling.html) logic.

The SelectType plugin will identify resources where a pending job can

## Limitations of Preemption During Backfill Scheduling [#limitations](https://slurm.schedmd.com/preempt.html)
For performance reasons, the backfill scheduler reserves whole nodes for jobs,
not partial nodes. If during backfill scheduling a job preempts one or more
other jobs, the whole nodes for those preempted jobs are reserved for the
preemptor job, even if the preemptor job requested fewer resources than that.
These reserved nodes aren't available to other jobs during that backfill
cycle, even if the other jobs could fit on the nodes. Therefore, jobs may
preempt more resources during a single backfill iteration than they requested.

# Gang Scheduling
Slurm supports timesliced gang scheduling in which two or more jobs are
allocated to the same resources in the same partition and these jobs are
alternately suspended to let one job at a time have dedicated access to the
resources for a configured period of time.
Slurm also supports preemptive job scheduling that allows a job in a
higher PriorityTier partition, or in a preempting QOS, to preempt other
jobs. [Preemption](https://slurm.schedmd.com/preempt.html) is related to Gang scheduling
because SUSPEND is one of the PreemptionMode s, and it uses the Gang
scheduler to resume suspended jobs.
A workload manager that supports timeslicing can improve responsiveness
and utilization by allowing more jobs to begin running sooner.
Shorter-running jobs no longer have to wait in a queue behind longer-running
jobs.
Instead they can be run "in parallel" with the longer-running jobs, which will

## Timeslicer Design and Operation [#time_slice](https://slurm.schedmd.com/gang_scheduling.html)
When enabled, the gang scheduler keeps track of the resources
allocated to all jobs. For each partition an "active bitmap" is maintained that
tracks all concurrently running jobs in the Slurm cluster. Each time a new
job is allocated to resources in a partition, the gang scheduler
compares these newly allocated resources with the resources already maintained
in the "active bitmap".
If these two sets of resources are disjoint then the new job is added to the "active bitmap". If these two sets of resources overlap then
the new job is suspended. All jobs are tracked in a per-partition job queue
within the gang scheduler logic.
A separate timeslicer thread is spawned by the gang scheduler
on startup. This thread sleeps for the configured SchedulerTimeSlice
interval. When it wakes up, it checks each partition for suspended jobs. If

# Preemption
Slurm supports job preemption, the act of "stopping" one or more "low-priority"
jobs to let a "high-priority" job run.
Job preemption is implemented as a variation of Slurm's
[Gang Scheduling](https://slurm.schedmd.com/gang_scheduling.html) logic.
When a job that can preempt others is allocated resources that are
already allocated to one or more jobs that could be preempted by the first job,
the preemptable job(s) are preempted.
Based on the configuration the preempted job(s) can be cancelled, or can be
requeued and started using other resources, or suspended and resumed once the
preemptor job completes, or can even share resources with the preemptor using
Gang Scheduling.
The PriorityTier of the Partition of the job or its Quality Of Service (QOS)
can be used to identify which jobs can preempt or be preempted by other jobs.

The SelectType plugin will identify resources where a pending job can
begin execution. When PreemptMode is configured to CANCEL ,
SUSPEND or REQUEUE , the select plugin will also preempt running

job and rely upon the gang scheduling logic to perform job suspend and resume,
as described below.

## Limitations of Preemption During Backfill Scheduling [#limitations](https://slurm.schedmd.com/preempt.html)
For performance reasons, the backfill scheduler reserves whole nodes for jobs,
not partial nodes. If during backfill scheduling a job preempts one or more
other jobs, the whole nodes for those preempted jobs are reserved for the
preemptor job, even if the preemptor job requested fewer resources than that.
These reserved nodes aren't available to other jobs during that backfill
cycle, even if the other jobs could fit on the nodes. Therefore, jobs may
preempt more resources during a single backfill iteration than they requested.

Summary — what QOS priority is
- QOS (Quality of Service) is a database-configured entity you can assign to jobs (and also attach limits to partitions). A QOS carries a numeric priority and many limits (GrpTRES, MaxJobs, MaxWall, etc.).
- The QOS priority is one factor in Slurm’s multifactor scheduling priority. It only affects scheduling priority when the multifactor priority plugin is enabled and PriorityWeightQOS in slurm.conf is non‑zero. Higher numeric QOS.priority -> higher contribution to job priority.
- QOS assigned to a job (job QOS) is what gives a job the QOS priority and preemption behavior. A Partition QOS only supplies limits to the partition; it does not by itself change a job’s scheduling priority unless you configure Flags=OverPartQOS or the job explicitly requests that QOS.

How to set QOS priority (example)
- Create/modify with sacctmgr, e.g.:
  - sacctmgr add qos high
  - sacctmgr modify qos high set priority=100
(That numeric value becomes part of the multifactor priority calculation when enabled.)

Preemption — concepts and configurable pieces
- Preemption = allowing a higher-priority queued job to stop one or more running lower-priority jobs so the queued job can run.
- Decision points are split across:
  1. PreemptType (which attribute(s) determine who can preempt whom — common is preempt/qos so job QOS relationships are used).
  2. PreemptMode (what to do to preempted jobs: CANCEL, REQUEUE, SUSPEND, or SUSPEND,GANG).
  3. Select/placement logic and PreemptParameters (how candidate preemptable jobs are ordered for preemption, e.g., youngest_first).
  4. Partition PriorityTier and QOS configuration (which QOSs are allowed to preempt which others).

Key configuration knobs (common values)
- PreemptType=preempt/qos
  - Use the job’s QOS and QOS preemption lists to determine eligibility. QOS objects can be given an allow-list of other QOSs they may preempt (configured via sacctmgr).
- PreemptMode=...
  - CANCEL — preempted jobs are killed.
  - REQUEUE — preempted jobs are requeued (so they will run again later).
  - SUSPEND — preempted jobs are suspended; they can resume after the preemptor finishes.
  - SUSPEND,GANG — used with the gang scheduler to timeslice/schedule competing jobs on the same resources.
- PreemptParameters=youngest_first (optional)
  - Controls ordering of candidates (e.g., prefer preempting the youngest running jobs).
- PriorityWeightQOS (in slurm.conf)
  - Must be >0 for QOS.priority to count in the multifactor priority calculation.

How Slurm chooses which jobs to preempt
- The select plugin is given an ordered list of preemptable running jobs for a pending preemptor. That order can be by:
  - QOS priority,
  - partition priority + job size (to prefer preempting smaller jobs), or
  - job start time (youngest_first),
  depending on PreemptType/parameters.
- If resources need to be freed, Slurm will preempt enough jobs (following the ordering/rules) to start the pending job.

Effects, tradeoffs, and operational notes
- CANCEL — simplest but loses in-progress work.
- REQUEUE — preserves job for a later attempt, but restart may still cost time and data; job state is dropped from the node.
- SUSPEND — preserves working memory/state and lets the job resume, but suspended jobs continue to occupy memory (can cause overcommit/swap). Requires appropriate SelectType/SelectTypeParameters and system/kernel support for suspension.
- SUSPEND,GANG — enables gang scheduling/timeslicing where multiple jobs share nodes by alternating active periods; more complex to configure but can improve responsiveness.
- Backfill and whole-node reservations: the backfill scheduler reserves whole nodes, so preemption during backfill can reserve more nodes than the preemptor requested (limits on partial-node preemption).
- Resource accounting: when using suspend or timeslicing, configure SelectTypeParameter to track memory (e.g., CR_Memory or CR_Core_Memory) to avoid swapping and incorrect overcommit.
- Test your chosen mode: preemption semantics are disruptive; pick the mode that matches your policy (e.g., SLAs favor CANCEL for strict isolation, SUSPEND/GANG for interactive responsiveness, REQUEUE for checkpointable batch jobs).

Practical example snippets
- Enable QOS priority in slurm.conf:
  - PriorityWeightQOS=100
- Make QOS preempt others (job-side preemption based on QOS), set slurm.conf:
  - PreemptType=preempt/qos
  - PreemptMode=REQUEUE   (or CANCEL, SUSPEND, SUSPEND,GANG)
  - (optionally) PreemptParameters=youngest_first
- Configure which QOS can preempt which (sacctmgr):
  - sacctmgr modify qos high set preempt=normal,low
  - sacctmgr modify qos high set priority=200

When to use which preemption policy
- CANCEL: when you cannot tolerate suspended/queued state or checkpointing is not widely used and you prefer resource predictability.
- REQUEUE: when jobs can be restarted safely and you want to avoid losing job records.
- SUSPEND / SUSPEND,GANG: when preserving job execution state is needed and you have the memory/OS/kernel support and SelectType configured to handle suspended memory.

## PERFORMANCE[#SECTION_PERFORMANCE](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Executing sbatch sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmctld daemon come in at once, it can result in
a degradation of performance of the slurmctld daemon, possibly resulting
in a denial of service.
Do not run sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other
programs. Ensure that programs limit calls to sbatch to the minimum
necessary for the information you are trying to gather.

## Notes[#NOTES](https://slurm.schedmd.com/configless_slurm.html)
Starting from Slurm 25.11, there's a new
SlurmctldParameters=reconfig_on_restart option that will make every
restart of slurmctld (process restart not triggered by "scontrol reconfigure")
to trigger a reconfiguration request to all slurmd and sackd daemons. For
"configless" systems this will ensure all processes are running the current
configuration. Some caution should be taken if you intend to perform rolling
upgrades on the cluster as this could lead to the daemons being upgraded sooner
than expected.
The order of precedence for determining what configuration source to use
is as follows:
- The slurmd --conf-server $host[:$port] option
- The -f $config_file option
- The SLURM_CONF environment variable (if set)
- A local slurm config file: The default slurm config file (likely /etc/slurm.conf)

## Initial Testing [#INITIAL_TESTING](https://slurm.schedmd.com/nss_slurm.html)
Before enabling NSS Slurm directly on the node, you should use the
-s slurm option to getent within a newly launched job step
to verify that the rest of the setup has been completed successfully. The
-s option to getent allows it to query a specific database —
even if it has not been enabled by default through the system's
nsswitch.conf . Note that nss_slurm only responds to requests from
processes within the job step itself — you must launch the getent
command within a job step to see any data returned.
As an example of a successful query:
```text
tim@blackhole:~$ srun getent -s slurm passwd tim:x:1000:1000:Tim Wickberg:/home/tim:/bin/bash tim@blackhole:~$ srun getent -s slurm group tim:x:1000:tim projecta:x:1001:tim
```

## NSS Configuration [#NSS_CONFIG](https://slurm.schedmd.com/nss_slurm.html)
Enabling nss_slurm is as simple as adding slurm to the passwd and
group database in /etc/nsswitch.conf (only on systems that will run
slurmd ). It is recommended that
slurm is listed first, as the order (from left to right) determines
the sequence in which the NSS databases will be queried, and this ensures Slurm
handles the request if able before submitting the query to other sources.
To enable cloud node name resolution slurm needs to be added to the
to hosts database in /etc/nsswitch.conf .
It is recommended that slurm is listed last.
Once enabled, test it by launching getent queries such as:
```text
tim@blackhole:~$ srun getent passwd tim tim:x:1000:1000:Tim Wickberg:/home/tim:/bin/bash tim@blackhole:~$ srun getent group projecta projecta:x:1001:tim
```

## PERFORMANCE[#SECTION_PERFORMANCE](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Executing sbatch sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmctld daemon come in at once, it can result in
a degradation of performance of the slurmctld daemon, possibly resulting
in a denial of service.
Do not run sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other
programs. Ensure that programs limit calls to sbatch to the minimum
necessary for the information you are trying to gather.

## PERFORMANCE[#SECTION_PERFORMANCE](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Executing sbatch sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmctld daemon come in at once, it can result in
a degradation of performance of the slurmctld daemon, possibly resulting
in a denial of service.
Do not run sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other
programs. Ensure that programs limit calls to sbatch to the minimum
necessary for the information you are trying to gather.

## EXAMPLES[#SECTION_EXAMPLES](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Specify a batch script by filename on the command line. The batch script specifies a 1 minute time limit for the job.
```text
$ cat myscript #!/bin/sh #SBATCH --time=1 srun hostname |sort $ sbatch -N4 myscript salloc: Granted job allocation 65537 $ cat slurm-65537.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
Pass a batch script to sbatch on standard input:
```text
$ sbatch -N4 #!/bin/sh > srun hostname |sort > EOF sbatch: Submitted batch job 65541 $ cat slurm-65541.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
To create a heterogeneous job with 3 components, each allocating a unique set of nodes:
```text
$ sbatch -w node[2-3] : -w node4 : -w node[5-7] work.bash Submitted batch job 34987
```

## Burst Buffers [#burst_buffer](https://slurm.schedmd.com/heterogeneous_jobs.html)
A burst buffer can either be persistent or linked to a specific job ID.
Since a heterogeneous job consists of multiple job IDs, a job-specific burst
buffer will be associated with only one heterogeneous job component.
Each component can have its own burst buffer directives, and they are processed
separately. Only a persistent burst buffer can be accessed by all components
of a heterogeneous job. Persistent burst buffers are only available in the
datawarp plugin. A sample batch script demonstrating this for the datawarp
plugin is appended.

#!/bin/bash #SBATCH --nodes=1 --constraint=haswell #BB create_persistent name=alpha capacity=10 access=striped type=scratch #DW persistentdw name=alpha #SBATCH hetjob #SBATCH --nodes=16 --constraint=knl #DW persistentdw name=alpha ...

## Launching Applications (Job Steps) [#job_steps](https://slurm.schedmd.com/heterogeneous_jobs.html)
The srun command is used to launch applications.
By default, the application is launched only on the first component of a
heterogeneous job, but options are available to support different behaviors.
srun's "--het-group" option defines which hetjob component(s) are to have
applications launched for them. The --het-group option takes an expression
defining which component(s) are to launch an application for an individual
execution of the srun command. The expression can contain one or more component
index values in a comma separated list. Ranges of index values can be specified
in a hyphen separated list. By default, an application is launched only on
component number zero. Some examples follow:

When a job array is submitted to Slurm, only one job record is created.
Additional job records will only be created when the state of a task in the
job array changes, typically when a task is allocated resources or its state
is modified using the scontrol command.

a single job record on one line and use a regular expression to indicate the

## Submitting Jobs [#submitting](https://slurm.schedmd.com/heterogeneous_jobs.html)
The salloc , sbatch and srun commands can all be used
to submit heterogeneous jobs.
Resource specifications for each component of the heterogeneous job should be
separated with ":" character.
For example:
```text
$ sbatch --cpus-per-task=4 --mem-per-cpu=1 --ntasks=128 : \ --cpus-per-task=1 --mem-per-cpu=16 --ntasks=1 my.bash
```
Options specified for one component of a heterogeneous job (or job step) will
be used for subsequent components to the extent which is expected to be helpful.
Propagated options can be reset as desired for each component (e.g. a different
account name could be specified for each hetjob component.
For example, --immediate and --job-name are propagated, while
--ntasks and --mem-per-cpu are reset to default values for each
component.

## PERFORMANCE[#SECTION_PERFORMANCE](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Executing sbatch sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmctld daemon come in at once, it can result in
a degradation of performance of the slurmctld daemon, possibly resulting
in a denial of service.
Do not run sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other
programs. Ensure that programs limit calls to sbatch to the minimum
necessary for the information you are trying to gather.

## EXAMPLES[#SECTION_EXAMPLES](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Specify a batch script by filename on the command line. The batch script specifies a 1 minute time limit for the job.
```text
$ cat myscript #!/bin/sh #SBATCH --time=1 srun hostname |sort $ sbatch -N4 myscript salloc: Granted job allocation 65537 $ cat slurm-65537.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
Pass a batch script to sbatch on standard input:
```text
$ sbatch -N4 #!/bin/sh > srun hostname |sort > EOF sbatch: Submitted batch job 65541 $ cat slurm-65541.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
To create a heterogeneous job with 3 components, each allocating a unique set of nodes:
```text
$ sbatch -w node[2-3] : -w node4 : -w node[5-7] work.bash Submitted batch job 34987
```

## LOGGING[#SECTION_LOGGING](https://slurm.schedmd.com/slurm.conf.html)
Note that while Slurm daemons create log files and other files as needed,
it treats the lack of parent directories as a fatal error.
This prevents the daemons from running if critical file systems are
not mounted and will minimize the risk of cold-starting (starting
without preserving jobs).
Log files and job accounting files
may need to be created/owned by the "SlurmUser" uid to be successfully
accessed. Use the "chown" and "chmod" commands to set the ownership
and permissions appropriately.
See the section FILE AND DIRECTORY PERMISSIONS for information
about the various files and directories used by Slurm.
It is recommended that the logrotate utility be used to ensure that
various log files do not become too large.
This also applies to text files used for accounting,

## EXAMPLES[#SECTION_EXAMPLES](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Specify a batch script by filename on the command line. The batch script specifies a 1 minute time limit for the job.
```text
$ cat myscript #!/bin/sh #SBATCH --time=1 srun hostname |sort $ sbatch -N4 myscript salloc: Granted job allocation 65537 $ cat slurm-65537.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
Pass a batch script to sbatch on standard input:
```text
$ sbatch -N4 #!/bin/sh > srun hostname |sort > EOF sbatch: Submitted batch job 65541 $ cat slurm-65541.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
To create a heterogeneous job with 3 components, each allocating a unique set of nodes:
```text
$ sbatch -w node[2-3] : -w node4 : -w node[5-7] work.bash Submitted batch job 34987
```

sbatch through a file name on the command line, or if no file name is specified,

## PERFORMANCE[#SECTION_PERFORMANCE](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Executing sbatch sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmctld daemon come in at once, it can result in
a degradation of performance of the slurmctld daemon, possibly resulting
in a denial of service.
Do not run sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other
programs. Ensure that programs limit calls to sbatch to the minimum
necessary for the information you are trying to gather.

## Burst Buffers [#burst_buffer](https://slurm.schedmd.com/heterogeneous_jobs.html)
A burst buffer can either be persistent or linked to a specific job ID.
Since a heterogeneous job consists of multiple job IDs, a job-specific burst
buffer will be associated with only one heterogeneous job component.
Each component can have its own burst buffer directives, and they are processed
separately. Only a persistent burst buffer can be accessed by all components
of a heterogeneous job. Persistent burst buffers are only available in the
datawarp plugin. A sample batch script demonstrating this for the datawarp
plugin is appended.

```

## Submitting Jobs [#submitting](https://slurm.schedmd.com/heterogeneous_jobs.html)
The salloc , sbatch and srun commands can all be used
to submit heterogeneous jobs.
Resource specifications for each component of the heterogeneous job should be
separated with ":" character.
For example:
```text
$ sbatch --cpus-per-task=4 --mem-per-cpu=1 --ntasks=128 : \ --cpus-per-task=1 --mem-per-cpu=16 --ntasks=1 my.bash
```
Options specified for one component of a heterogeneous job (or job step) will
be used for subsequent components to the extent which is expected to be helpful.
Propagated options can be reset as desired for each component (e.g. a different
account name could be specified for each hetjob component.
For example, --immediate and --job-name are propagated, while
--ntasks and --mem-per-cpu are reset to default values for each
component.
A list of propagated options follows.
- --account
- --acctg-freq
- --begin
- --cluster-constraint

When a job array is submitted to Slurm, only one job record is created.
Additional job records will only be created when the state of a task in the
job array changes, typically when a task is allocated resources or its state
is modified using the scontrol command.
By default, the squeue command will report all of the tasks associated with
a single job record on one line and use a regular expression to indicate the
"array_task_id" values as shown below.

By default, the application is launched only on the first component of a
heterogeneous job, but options are available to support different behaviors.
srun's "--het-group" option defines which hetjob component(s) are to have
applications launched for them. The --het-group option takes an expression
defining which component(s) are to launch an application for an individual
execution of the srun command. The expression can contain one or more component
index values in a comma separated list. Ranges of index values can be specified
in a hyphen separated list. By default, an application is launched only on
component number zero. Some examples follow:
- --het-group=2

## Job Allocation [#job_allocation](https://slurm.schedmd.com/job_launch.html)
The first step of the process is to create a job allocation, which is
a claim on compute resources. A job allocation can be created using the
salloc , sbatch or srun command. The salloc and
sbatch commands create resource allocations while the srun
command will create a resource allocation (if not already running within one)
plus launch tasks. Each of these commands will fill in a data structure

variables and send the RPC to the slurmctld daemon. The UID and GID of

## PERFORMANCE[#SECTION_PERFORMANCE](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Executing sbatch sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmctld daemon come in at once, it can result in
a degradation of performance of the slurmctld daemon, possibly resulting
in a denial of service.
Do not run sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other
programs. Ensure that programs limit calls to sbatch to the minimum
necessary for the information you are trying to gather.

## EXAMPLES[#SECTION_EXAMPLES](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Specify a batch script by filename on the command line. The batch script specifies a 1 minute time limit for the job.
```text
$ cat myscript #!/bin/sh #SBATCH --time=1 srun hostname |sort $ sbatch -N4 myscript salloc: Granted job allocation 65537 $ cat slurm-65537.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
Pass a batch script to sbatch on standard input:
```text
$ sbatch -N4 #!/bin/sh > srun hostname |sort > EOF sbatch: Submitted batch job 65541 $ cat slurm-65541.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
To create a heterogeneous job with 3 components, each allocating a unique set of nodes:
```text
$ sbatch -w node[2-3] : -w node4 : -w node[5-7] work.bash Submitted batch job 34987
```

## EXAMPLES[#SECTION_EXAMPLES](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Specify a batch script by filename on the command line. The batch script specifies a 1 minute time limit for the job.
```text
$ cat myscript #!/bin/sh #SBATCH --time=1 srun hostname |sort $ sbatch -N4 myscript salloc: Granted job allocation 65537 $ cat slurm-65537.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
Pass a batch script to sbatch on standard input:
```text
$ sbatch -N4 #!/bin/sh > srun hostname |sort > EOF sbatch: Submitted batch job 65541 $ cat slurm-65541.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
To create a heterogeneous job with 3 components, each allocating a unique set of nodes:
```text
$ sbatch -w node[2-3] : -w node4 : -w node[5-7] work.bash Submitted batch job 34987
```

## File Names[#file_names](https://slurm.schedmd.com/job_array.html)
Two additional options are available to specify a job's stdin, stdout, and
stderr file names:
%A will be replaced by the value of SLURM_ARRAY_JOB_ID (as defined above)
and
%a will be replaced by the value of SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID (as defined above).
The default output file format for a job array is "slurm-%A_%a.out".
An example of explicit use of the formatting is:
sbatch -o slurm-%A_%a.out --array=1-3 -N1 tmp
which would generate output files names of this sort
"slurm-36_1.out", "slurm-36_2.out" and "slurm-36_3.out".
If these file name options are used without being part of a job array then
"%A" will be replaced by the current job ID and "%a" will be replaced by
4,294,967,294 (equivalent to 0xfffffffe or NO_VAL).

## RETURN VALUE[#SECTION_RETURN-VALUE](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
sbatch will return 0 on success or error code on failure.

sbatch --parsable makes sbatch print a machine-readable job identifier instead of the human text "Submitted batch job <id>". Concretely:

- For a normal batch submission it prints the job ID only (no extra words).
- For job arrays it emits identifiers in Slurm's array notation (the array/master/element identifiers) in a consistent, script-friendly form.

Why it's useful
- Easy to capture in scripts: jid=$(sbatch --parsable my.job) reliably returns the job id with no text to strip.
- Feed directly to other Slurm commands: use that id for dependencies (--dependency), cancellations (scancel), queries (squeue/scontrol), or bookkeeping.
- Avoids fragile text parsing of sbatch's human-readable output when automating job workflows.

## PERFORMANCE[#SECTION_PERFORMANCE](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Executing sbatch sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmctld daemon come in at once, it can result in
a degradation of performance of the slurmctld daemon, possibly resulting
in a denial of service.
Do not run sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other
programs. Ensure that programs limit calls to sbatch to the minimum
necessary for the information you are trying to gather.

## EXAMPLES[#SECTION_EXAMPLES](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Specify a batch script by filename on the command line. The batch script specifies a 1 minute time limit for the job.
```text
$ cat myscript #!/bin/sh #SBATCH --time=1 srun hostname |sort $ sbatch -N4 myscript salloc: Granted job allocation 65537 $ cat slurm-65537.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
Pass a batch script to sbatch on standard input:
```text
$ sbatch -N4 #!/bin/sh > srun hostname |sort > EOF sbatch: Submitted batch job 65541 $ cat slurm-65541.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
To create a heterogeneous job with 3 components, each allocating a unique set of nodes:
```text
$ sbatch -w node[2-3] : -w node4 : -w node[5-7] work.bash Submitted batch job 34987
```

## EXAMPLES[#SECTION_EXAMPLES](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Specify a batch script by filename on the command line. The batch script specifies a 1 minute time limit for the job.
```text
$ cat myscript #!/bin/sh #SBATCH --time=1 srun hostname |sort $ sbatch -N4 myscript salloc: Granted job allocation 65537 $ cat slurm-65537.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
Pass a batch script to sbatch on standard input:
```text
$ sbatch -N4 #!/bin/sh > srun hostname |sort > EOF sbatch: Submitted batch job 65541 $ cat slurm-65541.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
To create a heterogeneous job with 3 components, each allocating a unique set of nodes:
```text
$ sbatch -w node[2-3] : -w node4 : -w node[5-7] work.bash Submitted batch job 34987
```

## PERFORMANCE[#SECTION_PERFORMANCE](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Executing sbatch sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmctld daemon come in at once, it can result in
a degradation of performance of the slurmctld daemon, possibly resulting
in a denial of service.
Do not run sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other
programs. Ensure that programs limit calls to sbatch to the minimum
necessary for the information you are trying to gather.

## EXAMPLES[#SECTION_EXAMPLES](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Specify a batch script by filename on the command line. The batch script specifies a 1 minute time limit for the job.
```text
$ cat myscript #!/bin/sh #SBATCH --time=1 srun hostname |sort $ sbatch -N4 myscript salloc: Granted job allocation 65537 $ cat slurm-65537.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
Pass a batch script to sbatch on standard input:
```text
$ sbatch -N4 #!/bin/sh > srun hostname |sort > EOF sbatch: Submitted batch job 65541 $ cat slurm-65541.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
To create a heterogeneous job with 3 components, each allocating a unique set of nodes:
```text
$ sbatch -w node[2-3] : -w node4 : -w node[5-7] work.bash Submitted batch job 34987
```

  - 4003 — batch_inference — Reason=Resources
  - 4006 — stuck_job — Reason=Priority

How I looked
- squeue (state=PENDING) to find jobs and their REASON.
- scontrol show job <jobid> for details (the detailed job output shows the Reason=... field).

What "Dependency" means (Slurm semantics)
- A job with Reason=Dependency is waiting because it had a --dependency=... set at submission time and the dependency condition has not yet been satisfied.
- Common dependency types:
  - after: start after the listed job(s) have started.
  - afterok: start after the listed job(s) finish successfully (exit code 0).
  - afternotok: start after the listed job(s) finish with non‑zero exit (failed).
  - afterany: start after the listed job(s) finish (any exit code).
  - singleton: only one job with this name may run; this job waits until other singleton jobs with the same name complete.
- Dependencies can reference one or more job IDs (type:jobid[,jobid...]) and job arrays; multiple dependencies are combined per the dependency type semantics.
- If you depend on a job that already finished, Slurm evaluates the dependency against that job's final result immediately — e.g., afterok is satisfied only if the earlier job exited with success.
- squeue shows only the single reason encountered by the scheduler (the REASON column). A job could also be blocked by resources or priority, but squeue will display the one reason the scheduler encountered first.
- To see the actual dependency expression for a job, inspect the job details: scontrol show job <jobid> (look for the Dependency=... field).

How to find dependency-blocked jobs yourself
- Quick: squeue -t PENDING -o "%.18i %.30j %.10T %.20R" | grep Dependency
  (lists PENDING jobs and filters for rows whose Reason column contains "Dependency")
- For each candidate job, run: scontrol show job <jobid> to view the Dependency=... line and full details.
- If the dependency target finished already, use sacct -j <jobid> to see its final state/exit code.

Troubleshooting dependency-blocked jobs
- If dependency target failed but you still want the dependent job to run: cancel and resubmit the dependent job without the dependency, or edit/remove the dependency (requires admin/operator action).
- If dependency target is still running or pending, wait or investigate that job's blocking reason (squeue / scontrol show job / sacct for history).
- If a job is stuck with Reason=Dependency but its dependency target looks satisfied, check whether the dependency referenced a different job ID (typo) or an array element — use scontrol show job to confirm the exact Dependency value.

Next steps

  - re-run a filtered squeue command to search for dependency-blocked jobs for a specific user, partition, or time window (tell me the filter you want), or

## Overview[#overview](https://slurm.schedmd.com/job_array.html)
Job arrays offer a mechanism for submitting and managing collections of
similar jobs quickly and easily, useful for repetitive workloads that follow a
common job pattern. This greatly improves overall performance, since job arrays
with millions of tasks can be submitted in milliseconds (subject to configured
size limits) and the scheduler can quickly identify cases when no more array
tasks are eligible to start.
All jobs must have the same initial options (e.g., size, time limit), however,
it is possible to change some of these options after the job has begun
execution using the scontrol command specifying the JobID of the array or
individual ArrayJobID .

$ scontrol update job=101 ... $ scontrol update job=101_1 ...

When a job array is submitted to Slurm, only one job record is created.
Additional job records will only be created when the state of a task in the
job array changes, typically when a task is allocated resources or its state
is modified using the scontrol command.
By default, the squeue command will report all of the tasks associated with
a single job record on one line and use a regular expression to indicate the
"array_task_id" values as shown below.

```

What you should know about job arrays and task-level identifiers
- Array element identifier format:
  - Individual array tasks are referenced as JOBID_INDEX, e.g. 5004_1, 5004_2, … .

- Environment variables visible inside array tasks (use these in your batch script):
  - SLURM_ARRAY_JOB_ID — the job-id that identifies the array as a whole (the array’s base job id).
  - SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID — the array index for the current task (use this to pick different inputs/parameters).
  - SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_COUNT, SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_MIN, SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_MAX — counts/range of the array indices.
  - Note: array-aware scripts should normally use SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID to pick work for each element.

- squeue / display behavior:
  - By default squeue often collapses array info into a single line showing the index range (e.g., 5004_[1-100]) and will only show separate lines for elements when their state changes (allocated, running, failed, etc.).

## PERFORMANCE[#SECTION_PERFORMANCE](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sdiag.html)
Executing sdiag sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from sdiag or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmctld daemon come in at once, it can result in
a degradation of performance of the slurmctld daemon, possibly resulting
in a denial of service.
Do not run sdiag or other Slurm client commands that send remote procedure
calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other programs. Ensure
that programs limit calls to sdiag to the minimum necessary for the
information you are trying to gather.

## PERFORMANCE[#SECTION_PERFORMANCE](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sdiag.html)
Executing sdiag sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from sdiag or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmctld daemon come in at once, it can result in
a degradation of performance of the slurmctld daemon, possibly resulting
in a denial of service.
Do not run sdiag or other Slurm client commands that send remote procedure
calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other programs. Ensure
that programs limit calls to sdiag to the minimum necessary for the
information you are trying to gather.

The job submit plugin is invoked independently for each component of a
heterogeneous job.
The spank_init_post_opt() function is invoked once for each component of a
heterogeneous job. This permits site defined options on a per job component
basis.
Scheduling of heterogeneous jobs is performed only by the sched/backfill

time or deferred. The pending reason of heterogeneous jobs isn't set until

## Limitations [#limitations](https://slurm.schedmd.com/heterogeneous_jobs.html)
The backfill scheduler has limitations in how it tracks usage of CPUs and
memory in the future.
This typically requires the backfill scheduler be able to allocate each
component of a heterogeneous job on a different node in order to begin its
resource allocation, even if multiple components of the job do actually get
allocated resources on the same node.
