## NAME[#SECTION_NAME](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sdiag.html)
sdiag - Scheduling diagnostic tool for Slurm

Good — here’s a concise field-by-field explanation of the common sdiag (scheduler diagnostics) output and how to interpret each metric.

General notes
- sdiag --all is the usual mode; sdiag --reset clears the counters (they’re also reset automatically at midnight UTC by default).
- You can emit JSON (--json) for programmatic parsing.
- sdiag reports counters and timing information about slurmctld behavior (threads, RPCs/agents, scheduling cycles, backfill/reservations, job dispatching). High counts or long times generally indicate load or scheduler work that may need tuning.

Primary fields and meaning

- Server thread count
  - Number of active slurmctld threads. A higher number means slurmctld is processing many concurrent tasks (submits, completions, RPCs). Persistently high values can indicate heavy load.

- Agent thread count
  - Number of worker/agent threads used by slurmctld to perform asynchronous work. Similar interpretation to server threads; growth signals concurrent internal work.

- Scheduling cycle count (or Scheduler cycles)
  - How many scheduling iterations the controller has performed. Each cycle examines the queue and attempts to dispatch eligible jobs.

- Avg / Min / Max scheduling cycle time
  - Timing statistics (often in microseconds or milliseconds) for scheduling iterations:
    - Avg cycle time: typical cost of a scheduler iteration.
    - Max cycle time: worst-case iteration — useful to spot occasional expensive computations.
  - Long average or large max times mean the scheduler is spending a lot of CPU/time evaluating the queue (could be many jobs, complex constraints, or expensive backfill evaluation).

- Jobs considered / Jobs examined (per cycle or total)
  - How many pending jobs the scheduler looked at while deciding what to start. High ratio of considered→started indicates wasted work if many are repeatedly re-examined but never run.

- Jobs started / Jobs dispatched
  - Number of jobs the scheduler actually launched. Compare to “jobs considered” to judge efficiency.

- Jobs rejected / Jobs deferred / Jobs failed to start
  - Jobs that could not be scheduled (due to policies, resources, time limits, or heterogeneous constraints) or that failed during allocation. Use these to find scheduling bottlenecks or misconfigurations.

- Backfill statistics (Backfill windows / Backfill attempts / Backfill jobs started / Backfill failures)
  - Counts/timings for the backfill algorithm:
    - How many candidate backfill windows were evaluated.
    - How many backfill-starts succeeded vs. deferred/failed.
  - Large numbers of attempted windows with few starts suggest fragmentation or unsuitable job time limits.

- Reservation checks / Reservation evaluations
  - How often reservations are consulted during scheduling. Useful if you use advance/reservation-based allocations.

- Queue scan totals / Queue scan time
  - Aggregate time spent scanning the job queue (often separate from cycle time). High values point to expensive queue evaluation (many jobs, complex constraints).

- RPC / Event counters
  - Counts of RPCs or events processed by slurmctld (client requests, plugin calls, etc.). High RPC rates may indicate heavy client activity or monitoring tools over-querying slurmctld.

- Priority/fairshare evaluations (if present)
  - Number/timing of priority calculations. Expensive priority computations (many users/accounts) will increase scheduler cycle time.

How to use sdiag data
- Look for correlations: high Avg cycle time + many jobs considered + few jobs started = inefficient scheduling or resource fragmentation.
- Use Max cycle time to find occasional expensive iterations (helps track down specific problematic jobs or constraints).
- If backfill is expensive (many windows tried), encourage users to set realistic time limits or tune backfill parameters.
- If RPC or thread counts are high, investigate frequent client calls (monitoring scripts, polling) or scale scheduler resources.
- Use --json for automation and --reset to get a fresh baseline after making config changes.

## Job Priority Factors In General [#general](https://slurm.schedmd.com/priority_multifactor.html)
The job's priority at any given time will be a weighted sum of all the
factors that have been enabled in the slurm.conf file. Job priority can be
expressed as:
```text
Job_priority = site_factor + (PriorityWeightAge) * (age_factor) + (PriorityWeightAssoc) * (assoc_factor) + (PriorityWeightFairshare) * (fair-share_factor) + (PriorityWeightJobSize) * (job_size_factor) + (PriorityWeightPartition) * (priority_job_factor) + (PriorityWeightQOS) * (QOS_factor) + SUM(TRES_weight_cpu * TRES_factor_cpu, TRES_weight_ * TRES_factor_ , ...) - nice_factor
```
All of the factors in this formula are floating point numbers that
range from 0.0 to 1.0. The weights are unsigned, 32 bit integers.

## Job Priority Factors In General [#general](https://slurm.schedmd.com/priority_multifactor.html)
The job's priority at any given time will be a weighted sum of all the
factors that have been enabled in the slurm.conf file. Job priority can be
expressed as:
```text
Job_priority = site_factor + (PriorityWeightAge) * (age_factor) + (PriorityWeightAssoc) * (assoc_factor) + (PriorityWeightFairshare) * (fair-share_factor) + (PriorityWeightJobSize) * (job_size_factor) + (PriorityWeightPartition) * (priority_job_factor) + (PriorityWeightQOS) * (QOS_factor) + SUM(TRES_weight_cpu * TRES_factor_cpu, TRES_weight_ * TRES_factor_ , ...) - nice_factor
```
All of the factors in this formula are floating point numbers that
range from 0.0 to 1.0. The weights are unsigned, 32 bit integers.
The job's priority is an integer that ranges between 0 and
4294967295. The larger the number, the higher the job will be
positioned in the queue, and the sooner the j...

What the pending reason "Priority" means
- When squeue shows a pending job with reason "Priority" it means the scheduler attempted to place the job but found one or more other jobs with higher scheduling priority for the same partition/resources. The scheduler will schedule those higher‑priority jobs before this one, so your job is waiting on priority order rather than (for example) an immediate lack of nodes or a dependency.

Why that can happen (how Slurm computes priority)
- Slurm (by default) uses the multifactor priority plugin. A job’s priority is a weighted sum of a set of factors such as:
  - age (how long the job has been waiting)
  - association/account priority
  - fairshare
  - job size (smaller jobs often favored)
  - partition priority
  - QOS factor
  - TRES (resource) factors (CPU/GPU weights)
  - site factor and a user “nice” factor
- Factors are normalized 0.0–1.0 and weights (PriorityWeight*) in slurm.conf scale them; the final job priority is an integer (0..4294967295). The Priority pending reason simply means other jobs have higher numeric priority at the time the scheduler tried to place your job.

Important notes
- Only one pending reason is shown even when multiple conditions apply; "Priority" is the reason encountered by the scheduling attempt.
- “Priority” does not necessarily mean resources are currently free — it means priority ordering prevents your job from being scheduled ahead of others.
- Cluster config (PriorityType, PriorityWeight* values, whether preemption is enabled) controls behavior.

How to investigate (use these commands)
- sprio -l or sprio <jobid> — show per-job priority score and factor breakdown (sprio -l gives verbose factor details).
- scontrol show job <jobid> — view job fields (QOS, Account, TRES, Priority as recorded).
- squeue -j <jobid> -o "%.18i %.9P %.20j %.8u %.2t %.10M %.8D %R" — view the job row including the REASON column (replace format as you prefer).
- scontrol show config | egrep "Priority|PriorityWeight" — see which priority factors are enabled and their weights.
- squeue (or sprio) for competing jobs — list other jobs in the partition to see which have higher priority.

What you can do
- Wait — age and fairshare often raise a job’s priority over time.
- Reduce requested resources or change partition to improve relative priority.
- Submit with a higher QOS or different account if permitted.
- Talk to your admins if you think weights or fairshare settings are unfair or need adjustment (they can change PriorityWeight* or PriorityType, or enable preemption/QOS changes).

If you want, I can:
- Inspect a specific pending job (show its priority breakdown and the competing jobs) — tell me the job ID and I’ll run the appropriate reads.

## PERFORMANCE[#SECTION_PERFORMANCE](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sattach.html)
Executing sattach sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from sattach or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmctld daemon come in at once, it can result in
a degradation of performance of the slurmctld daemon, possibly resulting
in a denial of service.
Do not run sattach or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other
programs. Ensure that programs limit calls to sattach to the minimum
necessary for the information you are trying to gather.

## EXAMPLES[#SECTION_EXAMPLES](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sattach.html)
Attach to job 15, step 0:
```text
$ sattach 15.0
```
Limit the output to the 5th task of job 65386, step 15:
```text
$ sattach --output-filter 5 65386.15
```

sattach is a Slurm client used to attach to an already‑running job step so you can view and/or interact with its standard input, output, and error streams.

Key points
- Purpose: connect to an existing running job step (jobid.stepid) to watch stdout/stderr or send stdin, or to inspect output from particular tasks inside a multi‑task job (MPI, srun tasks).
- Typical usage: sattach <jobid>.<stepid> (step 0 is commonly used), e.g. sattach 12345.0
- Useful options:
  - --input-filter / --output-filter / --error-filter: limit stdin/out/err to a single task number.
  - -l, --label: prefix lines with the originating task number (helpful for multi‑task jobs).
  - --layout: request task layout from slurmctld for nicer formatting.
- Behavior: it attaches to an existing allocation/step — it does not create an allocation or start a new job/step.
- Limits & cautions:
  - Only works for running job steps (cannot attach to completed or not‑started steps).
  - It performs an RPC to slurmctld; excessive or scripted calls can degrade controller performance.
  - Permissions/policy: whether you may attach to another user’s job depends on cluster configuration and admin policy.
- Common use cases: debugging live MPI/srun tasks, collecting output from a particular task in a multi‑task job, or interactively sending input into a running process.

Example:
- Attach to job 65386 step 15 and show output only from task 5:
  sattach --output-filter 5 65386.15

## PERFORMANCE[#SECTION_PERFORMANCE](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Executing sbatch sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmctld daemon come in at once, it can result in
a degradation of performance of the slurmctld daemon, possibly resulting
in a denial of service.
Do not run sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other
programs. Ensure that programs limit calls to sbatch to the minimum
necessary for the information you are trying to gather.

## EXAMPLES[#SECTION_EXAMPLES](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Specify a batch script by filename on the command line. The batch script specifies a 1 minute time limit for the job.
```text
$ cat myscript #!/bin/sh #SBATCH --time=1 srun hostname |sort $ sbatch -N4 myscript salloc: Granted job allocation 65537 $ cat slurm-65537.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
Pass a batch script to sbatch on standard input:
```text
$ sbatch -N4 #!/bin/sh > srun hostname |sort > EOF sbatch: Submitted batch job 65541 $ cat slurm-65541.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
To create a heterogeneous job with 3 components, each allocating a unique set of nodes:
```text
$ sbatch -w node[2-3] : -w node4 : -w node[5-7] work.bash Submitted batch job 34987
```

A new configuration parameter has been added to control the maximum
job array size: MaxArraySize . The smallest index that can be specified
by a user is zero and the maximum index is MaxArraySize minus one.
The default value of MaxArraySize is 1001.
The maximum MaxArraySize supported in Slurm is 4000001.
Be mindful about the value of MaxArraySize as job arrays offer an easy way
for users to submit large numbers of jobs very quickly.
The sched/backfill plugin has been modified to improve performance with
job arrays. Once one element of a job array is discovered to not be runnable
or impact the scheduling of pending jobs, the remaining elements of that job

sbatch supports a small set of mail-related options you use to tell Slurm when to send job-status email and where to send it.

How to set them
- On the sbatch command line:
  - --mail-user=<address>
  - --mail-type=<type>[,<type>...]
- In a batch script use #SBATCH directives:
  - #SBATCH --mail-user=you@example.com
  - #SBATCH --mail-type=BEGIN,END,FAIL
- Environment variables are also supported (e.g., SBATCH_MAIL_USER, SBATCH_MAIL_TYPE). Note the precedence: command-line options override environment variables, and environment variables override #SBATCH directives in the script.

Common mail-type values and meaning
- NONE — do not send any mail.
- BEGIN — send mail when the job begins (allocation granted / job started).
- END — send mail when the job finishes (regardless of success/failure).
- FAIL — send mail when the job fails (abnormal exit/failed).
- REQUEUE — send mail if the job is requeued.
- ALL — shorthand to request all the common notifications (convenience alias).
- TIME_LIMIT / TIME_LIMIT_xx (percent thresholds) — send warning when job is approaching its time limit (clusters may provide variants like TIME_LIMIT_90 etc.; exact names available in your Slurm docs/config).
- ARRAY_TASKS — affects array-element notifications (send per-array-element notices).

Usage notes and tips
- You can supply multiple types as a comma-separated list (e.g., --mail-type=BEGIN,END,FAIL).
- Use --mail-user to give one or more recipient addresses (site policy may affect allowed formats).
- Email notifications depend on MTA/configuration on your cluster; administrators can disable or alter mail delivery.
- For job arrays, use the array-specific mail-type (or ARRAY_TASKS) to control element-level messages.
- If you need fine-grained control beyond these built-in events, consider writing a small wrapper in your batch script to send mail (mailx, sendmail, curl to an alert webhook) at any programmatic point.

## Local Licenses [#local_licenses](https://slurm.schedmd.com/licenses.html)
Local licenses are defined in the slurm.conf using the Licenses
option.
slurm.conf:
```text
Licenses=fluent:30,ansys:100
```
Configured licenses can be viewed using the scontrol command.
```text
$ scontrol show lic LicenseName=ansys Total=100 Used=0 Free=100 Remote=no LicenseName=fluent Total=30 Used=0 Free=30 Remote=no
```
Requesting licenses is done by using the -L, or --licenses, submission
option.
```text
$ sbatch -L ansys:2 script.sh Submitted batch job 5212 $ scontrol show lic LicenseName=ansys Total=100 Used=2 Free=98 Remote=no LicenseName=fluent Total=30 Used=0 Free=30 Remote=no
```
Licenses may also be requested using the --tres-per-task option for
job submission. If this approach is used, the license must also be defined in
the AccountingStorageTRES option of the slurm.conf.

## Remote Licenses [#remote_licenses](https://slurm.schedmd.com/licenses.html)
Remote licenses do not offer any kind of integration with third party
license managers by themselves. The use of the "Server" and "ServerType"
parameters when creating these licenses is just for informative purposes and
does not imply any kind of automatic license management with those servers.
It is the responsibility of the system administrator to implement any
integration needed with these systems. For example, that would include ensuring
that only users requesting remote licenses through Slurm can check out licenses
from the license server, or making sure that Slurm's license count stays
synchronized with license server's
(see [Dynamic Licenses](https://slurm.schedmd.com/licenses.html)).

Summary
- In Slurm, "licenses" are tracked consumable resources (like CPUs or GPUs) that the scheduler can allocate to jobs to prevent oversubscription of commercial-software licenses.
- Admins define license pools (local or remote) and counts; users request licenses at job submission with -L/--licenses or as a TRES (license/<name>).
- Slurm enforces license counts in scheduling: a job requesting licenses will not start until the requested license count is available.

Key concepts
- License pool: a named resource (e.g., ansys, matlab) with a Total count and runtime counters (Used, Free, Reserved). Pools can be configured in slurm.conf (local licenses) or in the accounting DB via sacctmgr (managed/remote).
- Local vs Remote:
  - Local licenses are declared in slurm.conf with the Licenses option (example: Licenses=fluent:30,ansys:100). These are visible to the controller directly.
  - Remote licenses are managed via sacctmgr as resources and can include server/serverType metadata. Slurm itself doesn’t automatically query third‑party license servers; admins can integrate with them (see “dynamic licenses”).
- Dynamic licenses: admins can periodically update LastConsumed using sacctmgr (e.g., from lmstat), and Slurm will use LastConsumed/LastDeficit to account for external checkouts.
- TRES mapping: license resources are tracked as TRES when configured (AccountingStorageTRES can include license/<name>) so you can also request them via --tres-per-task. When used as TRES, they integrate with accounting and TRES-based scheduling.

How users request licenses
- sbatch/salloc/srun: use -L or --licenses
  - Syntax (common forms): -L name[:count] or -L name@server[:count]
  - Examples:
    - sbatch -L ansys:2 job.sh  (request 2 ansys licenses)
    - sbatch -L nastran@flex_host job.sh  (request remote nastran license)
- As TRES:
  - --tres-per-task=license/<name>=N (requires license be configured in AccountingStorageTRES)
  - Useful when you want per-task accounting rather than top-level job request.

Admin commands / inspection
- scontrol show lic  — see license pools and state (fields: LicenseName, Total, Used, Free, Reserved, Remote, LastConsumed, LastDeficit, LastUpdate).
  - Example output fragment: LicenseName=ansys Total=100 Used=2 Free=98 Remote=no
- sacctmgr add/modify resource — add license resources to the accounting DB, distribute counts across clusters, set server/serverType, allowed percentage, etc.
  - Example: sacctmgr add resource name=nastran cluster=fluid,pdf count=100 allowed=50 server=flex_host type=license
- To implement dynamic updates, admins run a script that polls the external license server and updates sacctmgr (set lastconsumed=...), which the controller uses to compute deficits/reservations.

Scheduler behavior / effects
- Jobs requesting license counts consume those resources when they are allocated (Used increases, Free decreases).
- If insufficient Free licenses exist, the job will remain PENDING until licenses are freed or counts are updated; the pending reason will reflect resource shortages.
- Reserved shows admin-held licenses that are not available to normal scheduling.
- Slurm will not automatically check out licenses from third‑party servers—admins must synchronize counts for remote/dynamic licenses.

Troubleshooting & tips
- If jobs remain pending and you suspect license exhaustion: run scontrol show lic to inspect Free/Used/Reserved and verify the correct license name was requested.
- For external license managers, set up a periodic sync that updates sacctmgr LastConsumed so Slurm’s view matches the license server.
- Use --tres-per-task when you need per-task license accounting or when integrating with TRES-based limits/quotas.
- Be explicit with server-qualified names for remote licenses (name@server) to avoid ambiguity across clusters.

Quick examples
- Submit requesting two ansys licenses:
  - sbatch -L ansys:2 job.sh
- Check license pools:

## Licenses Overview [#overview](https://slurm.schedmd.com/licenses.html)
Slurm can help with software license management by assigning available
licenses to jobs at scheduling time. If the licenses are not available, jobs
are kept pending until licenses become available. Licenses in Slurm are
essentially shared resources, meaning configured resources that are not tied to
a specific host but are associated with the entire cluster.
Licenses in Slurm can be configured in two ways:
- Local Licenses: Local licenses are local to the cluster using the slurm.conf in which they are configured.
- Remote Licenses: Remote licenses are served by the database and are configured using the sacctmgr command. Remote licenses are dynamic in nature as upon running the sacctmgr command, the slurmdbd updates all clusters the licenses are assigned to.

Short answer
- If a job requests a software license when you run sbatch (for example sbatch -L ansys:2), the scheduler treats that license as a cluster resource (a TRES). The job may be accepted but will remain PENDING until the requested license count is available. Slurm will not start the job unless it can allocate the requested licenses.

What happens end-to-end
1. Admin config
   - Licenses are configured either in slurm.conf (local licenses) or in the accounting DB via sacctmgr (remote/dynamic licenses). Each license has a Total count; Slurm tracks Used and Free counts.
   - If you use license requests via TRES (--tres-per-task or --tres), the license name must also appear in AccountingStorageTRES so usage is recorded.

2. How users request licenses
   - Short form: sbatch -L license_name:count script.sh
   - TRES form: sbatch --tres-per-task=license/license_name=count (or --tres=...) depending on your site
   - Either method declares the job’s license needs to the scheduler.

3. Scheduling and start-time behavior
   - The scheduler checks license availability when considering a job for allocation. If the Free count for that license is less than the job’s request, the job stays PENDING.
   - Jobs do not consume license counts until they are allocated/started; Used counts update when the allocation is made (you can see this with scontrol show lic).
   - Backfill/priority still respects license counts: a lower-priority job can only start if enough licenses are free at the time it would start.

4. Local vs remote/dynamic licenses
   - Local licenses (configured in slurm.conf) are static counts maintained by slurmctld.
   - Remote/dynamic licenses can be updated from an external license server (via sacctmgr updates). Slurm uses LastConsumed/LastDeficit info to avoid oversubscription; administrators can push dynamic counts into Slurm so scheduling reflects real license availability.

5. Effects on users and common outcomes
   - Submission is usually accepted; the job becomes PENDING with a reason related to resources/licenses until licenses free up.
   - Jobs do not fail just because licenses are unavailable at submit time; they wait.
   - If you over-request licenses (request more than Total), the job will never start until the request or the license counts are changed.

How to check and troubleshoot
- Check configured and current counts: scontrol show lic  (or scontrol show lic LicenseName=ansys)
- See why a job is pending: squeue -j <jobid> (look at the REASON column) and for more detail scontrol show job <jobid>
- Admins can inspect/adjust license resources with sacctmgr (add/update resource) and push dynamic counts if integrated with a license server.

Example
- Cluster has Licenses=ansys:10, 8 are used → Free=2.
- sbatch -L ansys:3 script.sh → job accepted but stays PENDING until at least 3 licenses are free (e.g., when other jobs release them).

If you want, I can show current license counts on this cluster (scontrol show lic) or explain how to convert an sbatch -L request into a --tres request for your site.

## Relative QOS [#relative](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
Starting in Slurm 23.11, a QOS may be configured to contain relative resource
limits instead of absolute limits by setting `Flags=Relative`.
When this flag is set, all resource limits are treated as percentages of the
total resources available. Values higher than 100 are interpreted as 100%.
Memory limits should be set with no units. Although the default units (MB) will
be displayed, the limits will be enforced as a percentage (1MB = 1%).
NOTE : When Flags=Relative is added to a QOS, slurmctld
must be restarted or reconfigured for the flag to take effect.
Generally, the limits on a relative QOS will be calculated relative to the
resources in the whole cluster. For example, `cpu=50` would be
interpreted as 50% of all CPUs in the cluster.
However, when a relative QOS is also assigned as a partition QOS, some unique
conditions will apply:
- Limits will be calculated relative t...

Short answer
- If Alice’s problem is that her user/account is hitting per-user or per-account resource caps (e.g., too many concurrent jobs, too many GPUs/CPUs charged to the account), ask for an account/association limit change.
- If the problem is cluster-wide scheduling policy, job priority, or a QOS-specific cap (for example jobs are denied/pending specifically because of a QOS’s MaxJobs/MaxTRES or you need preemption/priority changes), ask for a QOS change.
- If you’re unsure, include the current pending/denied message and the exact limit name shown by Slurm — that tells the admin whether the association/account or a QOS is enforcing the limit.

How to decide (short decision checklist)
1. Look at the error/pending reason shown by Slurm (or the admin’s logs).
   - If it says something like “Association limit reached”, “GrpTRES…”, or references your account/user, it’s an account/association limit.
   - If it references a QOS name or the job was denied/pended because of QOS Max* or DenyOnLimit, it’s a QOS limit.
2. Who should be affected?
   - Single user or single project/account only → change the account association.
   - Multiple users/projects, or you need different scheduling behavior (priority, preemption, grace time, DenyOnLimit, relative caps) → change or create a QOS.
3. Scope and permanence:
   - Short-term spike / deadline → ask for a temporary account limit increase or a temporary higher-QOS allocation.
   - Long-term change in policy or priority → ask for a QOS update (admins can tune flags like Priority, Preempt, GraceTime, or Relative limits).
4. Precedence: QOS limits can override association limits. If both exist, the first place a limit is found in Slurm’s hierarchy is enforced. Ask admins to check both QOS and association values.

Typical limits you might request changing
- MaxJobs, MaxSubmitJobs (concurrent/submit throttling)
- MaxTRESPERUSER, MaxTRESPERACCOUNT, GrpTRES (total GPU/CPU/memory caps)
- MaxTRESPerNode or MaxNodes / MinNodes (node-level caps)
- Priority/QOS flags (Priority, Preempt, DenyOnLimit, GraceTime, Relative)

What Alice should include in the request to admins (so they can act quickly)
- Your username and account/project name.
- Exact text of the Slurm pending/deny message (or squeue output row) and the job ID if applicable.
- Which limit you think to raise (e.g., “increase MaxTRESPERUSER for gres/gpu from 4 to 8” or “increase MaxJobs from 50 to 150”).
- Why (expected job mix, deadlines, number of simultaneous runs, temporary or permanent).
- Time window if temporary (start/end).
- Whether you also need increased priority or preemption behavior (i.e., do you need a QOS change instead).

Examples (phrasing to use)
- Account change: “Please increase my account’s MaxTRESPERUSER (gres/gpu) from 4 to 8 for 2 weeks; we need to run 6 concurrent GPU jobs for an urgent experiment.”
- QOS change: “Please create/update a QOS to allow up to 200 concurrent jobs and give it higher priority for project X, with GraceTime=00:10:00 and Flags=Preempt to allow preemption by production jobs.”

When to ask for both
- If your job uses a particular QOS and that QOS has strict caps, you may need a QOS change even if the account also has room. Conversely, increasing the account without changing a restrictive QOS may have no effect. If in doubt, tell the admin the job’s requested QOS and the account so they can inspect both.

If you want, I can:
- Tell you exactly what to include in a short email to your admins (I can draft it), or
- If you want me to diagnose which limit is being hit, run the checks needed (I’ll need the job ID or squeue/sacct output) and then advise which change to request.

## AUTHORIZATION[#SECTION_AUTHORIZATION](https://slurm.schedmd.com/scontrol.html)
Slurm generally classifies users into three authorization levels:
- Administrators include root, SlurmUser, and any users with
"AdminLevel=Administrator"
- Privileged Users include all Administrators and any users with
"AdminLevel=Operator"
- Effective Owners of a job or step include the direct owner and all
Coordinators of the corresponding account.
Note that configuring AdminLevels or Coordinators requires the use of SlurmDBD.
The authorization levels required to execute various commands are defined in the
following table.
scontrol update job: Privileged or Effective Owner
scontrol requeue: Privileged or Effective Owner
scontrol update step: Privileged or Effective Owner
scontrol suspend: Privileged or Coordinator
scontrol resume: Privileged or Coordinator
scontrol notify: Root, SlurmUser, or direct owner

## Overview[#overview](https://slurm.schedmd.com/job_array.html)
Job arrays offer a mechanism for submitting and managing collections of
similar jobs quickly and easily, useful for repetitive workloads that follow a
common job pattern. This greatly improves overall performance, since job arrays
with millions of tasks can be submitted in milliseconds (subject to configured
size limits) and the scheduler can quickly identify cases when no more array
tasks are eligible to start.
All jobs must have the same initial options (e.g., size, time limit), however,
it is possible to change some of these options after the job has begun
execution using the scontrol command specifying the JobID of the array or
individual ArrayJobID .
```text
$ scontrol update job=101 ... $ scontrol update job=101_1 ...
```

Summary (from the official Slurm docs)

- Job-array identifiers
  - ArrayJobID: the job id assigned to the array allocation (the "master" job allocation). In sbatch output this is the id printed when the array is submitted (e.g., "Submitted batch job 36").
  - ArrayTaskID (array index): the index value for the particular element of the array (the numbers you passed to --array, e.g. 1,2,3 or 0-7).
  - Environment variables set for array jobs:
    - SLURM_ARRAY_JOB_ID = the ArrayJobID (first job id of the array)
    - SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID = the ArrayTaskID (the element index)
    - SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_COUNT, _TASK_MAX, _TASK_MIN are also provided.

- Addressing array elements to Slurm tools
  - Use ArrayJobID_ArrayTaskID (e.g. 12345_7) to refer to a specific element with scontrol or squeue. scontrol show job will report ArrayJobID and ArrayTaskID fields.

- Filename pattern placeholders for --output/--error (percent substitutions)
  - %A — Job array's master job allocation number (ArrayJobID)
  - %a — Job array ID (index) number (ArrayTaskID)
  - %b — Job array ID modulo 10
  - %j — jobid of the running job
  - %J — jobid.stepid of the running job (e.g. 128.0)
  - %% — a literal percent sign
  (These are documented under "FILENAME PATTERN" in the sbatch manual.)

Practical implications / examples
- If you submit:
    sbatch --array=1-3 --output=slurm-%A_%a.out my.job
  and sbatch prints "Submitted batch job 36", Slurm will create per-task files:
    slurm-36_1.out, slurm-36_2.out, slurm-36_3.out
  (%A expands to 36, %a to 1/2/3).

- To avoid output-file collisions you should include either %a (per-element index) or %j/%J (task-specific job id/step) in the filename when writing per-element output.

Caveats
- Array job internals and job-id assignment order can make JobID numbers and array indexes appear non-linear (see job array docs). Use the documented placeholders or the SLURM_ARRAY_* env vars inside the job script for robust per-task naming/logic.

## Relative QOS [#relative](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
Starting in Slurm 23.11, a QOS may be configured to contain relative resource
limits instead of absolute limits by setting `Flags=Relative`.

### Job Scheduling Priority [#priority](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
Job scheduling priority is made up of a number of factors as
described in the [priority/multifactor](https://slurm.schedmd.com/priority_multifactor.html) plugin. One
of the factors is the QOS priority. Each QOS is defined in the Slurm
database and includes an associated priority. Jobs that request and
are permitted a QOS will incorporate the priority associated with that
QOS in the job's [multi-factor priority calculation.](https://slurm.schedmd.com/priority_multifactor.html)
To enable the QOS priority component of the multi-factor priority
calculation, the "PriorityWeightQOS" configuration parameter must be
defined in the slurm.conf file and assigned an integer value greater
than zero.
A job's QOS only affects is scheduling priority when the
multi-factor plugin is loaded.

Below are concise, doc-backed explanations (what the scheduler means, common causes, and what to check/fix) for the pending reasons you asked about. All behavior below is from the Slurm documentation (job reason codes, QOS and resource-limits pages).

1) Resources
- What it means:
  - The scheduler could not find sufficient free resources to start the job given its request (CPUs, memory, GPU/GRES, TRES, sockets, cores, exclusive nodes, etc.). This is the generic “no suitable resources available now” reason.
- Common causes:
  - Not enough idle CPUs, memory, or GPUs in the partition; per-node resources are insufficient for the job’s per-node request.  
  - Nodes with the required features/constraints are busy, down, drained, or reserved.  
  - TRES/GRES (e.g., gpus) are already allocated to other jobs or are limited by association/QOS limits.
- What to check:
  - sinfo to view partition/node free vs allocated counts and node features.  
  - squeue to see currently running jobs consuming resources.  
  - scontrol show job <jobid> for the job’s requested TRES/features and the scheduler’s allocation attempt details.
- How to resolve:
  - Wait for resources to free, reduce resource request (fewer CPUs/GPU or less memory), remove/relax constraints, or request different partition. Admins can add capacity, change reservations, or adjust preemption/QOS settings.

2) Priority
- What it means:
  - The job is pending because one or more jobs with higher scheduling priority are eligible to run first. Slurm’s multifactor priority calculation (age, fairshare, QOS priority, job size, etc.) determines which jobs the scheduler prefers.
- Common causes:
  - Other jobs have higher QOS or higher multifactor priority (older jobs, favorable fairshare, higher QOS priority).  
  - Backfill/packing rules allow higher priority jobs to take the next available window.
- What to check:
  - sprio (or sprio --weights) to inspect job priorities and which factors dominate.  
  - squeue sorted by priority to see which jobs are scheduled ahead.  
  - sshare to inspect fairshare usage if that may be lowering your priority.
- How to resolve:
  - Request a higher QOS (if allowed), change job size/time to fit backfill windows, or wait. Admins can tune priority weights or QOS priorities.

3) ReqNodeNotAvail
- What it means:
  - The job requested specific node(s) or node constraints (via --nodelist, --exclude, --constraint, features, or a node-count requirement) and no currently usable node satisfies that request. Unlike the generic Resources reason, this explicitly indicates the requested node(s) or constrained set are unavailable.
- Common causes:
  - You requested explicit node names that are down/drained/allocated or excluded.  
  - The constraint string or feature request matches no idle nodes.  
  - A node is reserved or otherwise not offered (maintenance/reservation).
- What to check:
  - scontrol show job <jobid> to see NodeList/ReqNodes/Constraints in the job request.  
  - sinfo (or sinfo_reasons / sinfo_node) to see node states, drains, and reasons.  
  - scontrol show node <nodename> for node details and reason fields.
- How to resolve:
  - Remove or relax the node list/constraint, correct the requested node names, or wait / ask admins to clear reservations or bring nodes back (if appropriate).

4) QOS limits (how they cause pending/rejection)
- What it means:
  - The job is being held back by configured QOS/association/account limits (MaxTRES, MaxJobs, MaxWall, GrpTRES, usage thresholds, etc.). Limits can apply per user, account, or QOS and may cause a job to pend until the cluster/association usage is under the limit.
- Important doc behaviors to know:
  - By default, if a job would breach a QOS limit when considered together with currently running jobs, the job will pend until resources or quota free up.  
  - If the QOS has Flags=“DenyOnLimit”, then jobs that violate the QOS Max limits as stand‑alone requests are rejected at submission time instead of pending. (Group limits are treated similarly when DenyOnLimit applies.)  
  - Partition-level QOS limits are applied before the job’s requested QOS unless OverPartQOS changes that behavior.  
  - There are also relative QOS modes (Flags=Relative) where limits are percentages of total cluster resources.
- What to check:
  - sacctmgr show qos (or sacctmgr show assoc) to inspect QOS limits and flags (MaxJobs, MaxTRESPerUser/PerAccount, DenyOnLimit, UsageThreshold, etc.).  
  - squeue/sacct to see current running usage and whether an account/association has hit a limit.  
  - scontrol show config for OverPartQOS / priority weight settings if behavior seems unexpected.
- How to resolve:
  - Request a different QOS without those limits, reduce job resource usage, wait for usage to drop, or ask admins to raise limits or change DenyOnLimit/OverPartQOS behavior.

## Important Notes[#notes](https://slurm.schedmd.com/fair_tree.html)
- As the Fair Tree algorithm ranks all users, active or not, the administrator must carefully consider how to apply other priority weights in the priority/multifactor plugin. The PriorityWeightFairshare can be usefully set to a much smaller value than usual, possibly as low as 1 or 2 times the number of user associations.
- Fair Tree requires the [Slurm Accounting Database](https://slurm.schedmd.com/accounting.html) to provide usage information and the assigned shares values.
- scontrol reconfigure does not cause the Fair Tree algorithm to run immediately, even if switching from a different algorithm. You may have to wait until the next iteration as defined by PriorityCalcPeriod .

## Level Fairshare Calculation [#fairshare](https://slurm.schedmd.com/fair_tree.html)
The Level Fairshare equation is described below. Under-served associations
will have a value greater than 1.0. Over-served associations will have a value
between 0.0 and 1.0.
```text
LF = S / U
```
LF
is the association's Level Fairshare
S
also known as Shares Norm, S is the association's assigned shares
normalized to the shares assigned to itself and its siblings:
`S = Sraw self / Sraw self+siblings`
U
also known as Effective Usage, U is the association's usage normalized to
the account's usage:
`U = Uraw self / Uraw self+siblings`
U and S are in the range `0.0 .. 1.0` . LF is in the
range `0.0 .. infinity`.

## Introduction[#intro](https://slurm.schedmd.com/fair_tree.html)

An equation is used to calculate a Level Fairshare value for each

Below is a concise, actionable explanation of how Slurm’s Fair Tree fair‑share (account shares) and “effective usage” work, how they are computed, what they mean for job priority, and how to inspect/tune them.

What Fair Tree is (high level)
- Fair Tree is the default fair‑share algorithm used by Slurm to rank users (and accounts) for scheduling priority.  
- It treats the account/user structure as a rooted ordered tree; fair‑share is computed per node in the tree and then the tree is traversed to produce a final ranking of all user associations.
- The result is a per‑user FairShare factor (0..1) used by the priority/multifactor plugin (combined with age, QOS, etc.).

Core quantities and formulas
- Each association (account or user association node) has:
  - Sraw — assigned shares (the administrator sets these via sacctmgr).
  - Uraw — raw usage (from the Slurm accounting DB; units depend on the site's configured usage measure — CPU/GPU hours or other TRES).

- Normalize a node’s shares and usage among its siblings:
  - S = Sraw_self / (sum of Sraw for self + siblings)
  - U = Uraw_self / (sum of Uraw for self + siblings)

- Level Fairshare (LF) for a node:
  - LF = S / U
  - LF > 1.0 => “under‑served” (node has more shares than recent usage)
  - LF < 1.0 => “over‑served” (node has had more usage than its share)

How these values become a per-user fairshare factor
- For each internal tree node, children are sorted by their LF (highest first).
- A depth‑first pre‑order traversal of the tree (visiting children in LF order) assigns a rank to each user association.
- Final FairShare factor for a user = (user rank) / (total number of user associations). The top ranked user receives value 1.0; lower ranks get smaller values.
- Users under a higher‑LF account will all rank above users under a lower‑LF sibling account (so shares at higher tree levels dominate ordering).

Special cases and practical notes
- If an association and its siblings have zero usage (Uraw sum = 0), Level FS for those children is treated as infinity; those associations get top ranking (they are considered entirely under‑served).
- Fair Tree ranks all associations (active or inactive). This can amplify the effect of assigned shares, so admin teams should plan share assignments.
- The final priority also depends on other priority weights (PriorityWeightFairshare, age, QOS, etc.). Fair Tree gives a factor that the priority plugin multiplies by its configured weight.
- scontrol reconfigure does not necessarily cause an immediate recompute; priorities are recalculated on the schedule defined by PriorityCalcPeriod.

Example (simple numbers)
- Two sibling accounts: A (Sraw=80) and B (Sraw=20). So S_A = 80/(80+20)=0.8, S_B = 0.2.
- Suppose recent usage Uraw_A = 400 CPUh, Uraw_B = 600 CPUh. U_A = 400/(400+600)=0.4, U_B = 0.6.
- LF_A = 0.8 / 0.4 = 2.0 (under‑served); LF_B = 0.2 / 0.6 ≈ 0.33 (over‑served).
- All users under account A will rank higher than users under account B. Within A, the same LF method is applied between users to order them.

How to inspect and what to use
- Inspect fairshare and Level FS: sshare -l   (shows FairShare, Level FS, usage)
- View shares and associations: sacctmgr show assoc (or sacctmgr list)
- View usage (historical accounting): sacct or sreport (for CPU/GPU hours)
- For detailed association info or job details: scontrol show assoc / scontrol show job
- If you want to see why a pending job is not starting, use squeue (and scontrol show job for detail).

Practical admin/user guidance
- Admins: set shares at appropriate tree levels (coarse at top, finer lower) to avoid unintended effects. Be aware Fair Tree ranks all associations; adding many small associations can affect ordering.
- Tune PriorityWeightFairshare if fairshare domination is too strong compared to other priority factors.
- If some users/accounts appear under‑served (LF >> 1), they will get higher priority until their usage increases; conversely, over‑served nodes (LF << 1) will be deprioritized.
- Use sshare -l and sreport to monitor effective usage and adjust shares rather than repeatedly changing priorities manually.

References / quick commands
- Read the formal algorithm and derivation: Slurm Fair Tree docs (fair_tree.html) — useful for exact traversal and ranking behavior.
- Useful commands:
  - sshare -l
  - sacctmgr show assoc
  - sacct (usage history)
  - sreport (usage summaries)

If you want, I can:
- Show your cluster’s current fairshare and Level FS (I can run sshare -l for your cluster), or
- Walk through a concrete example using your site’s share assignments and recent usage to show which accounts/users are currently under‑ or over‑served.

updated host info and finish normally.

## INCLUDE MODIFIERS[#SECTION_INCLUDE-MODIFIERS](https://slurm.schedmd.com/slurm.conf.html)
The "include" key word can be used with modifiers within the specified
pathname. These modifiers would be replaced with cluster name or other
information depending on which modifier is specified. If the included file
is not an absolute path name (i.e. it does not start with a slash), it will
searched for in the same directory as the slurm.conf file.
%c [#OPT_%c](https://slurm.schedmd.com/slurm.conf.html) Cluster name specified in the slurm.conf will be used.
EXAMPLE
```text
ClusterName=linux include /home/slurm/etc/%c_config # Above line interpreted as # "include /home/slurm/etc/linux_config"
```

## DESCRIPTION[#SECTION_DESCRIPTION](https://slurm.schedmd.com/slurmdbd.conf.html)
slurmdbd.conf is an ASCII file which describes Slurm Database
Daemon (SlurmDBD) configuration information.
The file will always be located in the same directory as the slurm.conf .
The contents of the file are case insensitive except for the names of nodes

## Age Factor[#age](https://slurm.schedmd.com/priority_multifactor.html)
Note: Computing the age factor requires the installation
and operation of the [Slurm Accounting Database](https://slurm.schedmd.com/accounting.html).
The age factor represents the length of time a job has been sitting in the
queue and eligible to run. In general, the longer a job waits in the queue, the
larger its age factor grows. However, the age factor for a dependent job will
not change while it waits for the job it depends on to complete. Also, the age
factor will not change when scheduling is withheld for a job whose node or time
limits exceed the cluster's current limits.
At some configurable length of time ( PriorityMaxAge ), the age factor
will max out to 1.0.

Good question — scheduling and accounting are tightly linked in Slurm. Below is a concise, actionable overview of the most relevant slurm.conf / slurmdbd / sacctmgr settings and where they interact, plus checks and common pitfalls.

High-level components
- slurmctld (scheduler): governed by slurm.conf and priority plugin settings.
- slurmd (node agents): report usage and enforce cgroups.
- slurmdbd (accounting DB daemon): stores historical usage and is required for fairshare, age, and many accounting-based features.
- sacctmgr / sreport / sshare / sprio: admin tools to inspect and manage accounting, shares, and priorities.

Scheduling configuration (slurm.conf and plugins)
1. Priority plugin
- PriorityType
  - Common value: priority/multifactor — the Multifactor plugin composes priority from age, fairshare, job size, QOS, partition, site factors, and requested TRES.
- Priority weights (how factors combine)
  - PriorityWeightAge, PriorityWeightFairshare, PriorityWeightJobSize, PriorityWeightPartition, PriorityWeightQOS, etc.
  - The composite job priority = site_factor + PriorityWeightAge*age_factor + PriorityWeightFairshare*fairshare_factor + ... (weights are numeric).
- PriorityFlags
  - Toggles behavior (examples: NO_FAIR_TREE to use classic fairshare, SMALL_RELATIVE_TO_TIME, etc.).
- PriorityDecayHalfLife
  - Controls decay of historical usage for fairshare. Example: 7-0 means a 7‑day half-life. 0 disables decay (requires other usage reset policy).
- PriorityCalcPeriod / PriorityUsageResetPeriod / PriorityMaxAge
  - Control recalculation cadence, when usage is reset, and the max age factor value.

2. Fairshare and accounting dependency
- Fairshare requires slurmdbd (AccountingStorage) and properly configured association shares.
- sacctmgr is used to set "Fairshare" (Share) values on accounts/users/associations.
- If you want fairshare-based scheduling, ensure AccountingStorageType points to slurmdbd and slurmdbd is running.

3. QOS and partition factors
- QOS definitions (sacctmgr) can set priorities, limits, preemption behavior, and priority caps.
- Partition factors and per-partition PriorityWeightPartition influence job order by partition.

4. Job size / age / nice / site factors
- PriorityFavorSmall (YES/NO) controls whether small jobs get more priority.
- Age factor grows while a job is eligible to run; PriorityMaxAge caps it.
- Site / job_submit plugins allow custom site_factor or submission-time modifications.

5. Preemption and backfill
- PreemptType / PreemptMode / PreemptExemptTime set how preemption works (requeue, suspend, preempt).
- Backfill: the scheduler supports backfilling; relevant settings live in scheduler plugin parameters (multifactor scheduling uses scheduler logic and backfill capability).

6. TRES-based weighting
- You can weight specific TRES (e.g., GPUs, CPUs) via TRES weights so jobs requesting expensive TRES are evaluated differently.

Accounting configuration (slurmdbd, slurm.conf, job accounting)
1. AccountingStorage
- slurm.conf keys:
  - AccountingStorageType=accounting_storage/slurmdbd
  - AccountingStorageHost / Port /User /Loc depending on DB backend
  - AccountingStorageEnforce: controls enforcement level on job submit (values like associations, all, nojobs, nosteps). Use to block submissions that violate associations/limits.
- slurmdbd.conf: DB connection settings, auth, and retention configuration.

2. Job usage collection and completion logging
- JobAcctGatherType (e.g., jobacct_gather/linux) and JobAcctGatherFrequency: configure how resource usage (RSS, maxrss, CPU) is gathered.
- JobCompType / JobCompLoc (job completion logging plugin) — where completion records are sent if not using slurmdbd.

3. sacctmgr associations, accounts, QOS
- Use sacctmgr to create accounts, users, set DefaultQOS, set Share/Fairshare, set limits (GrpJobs, GrpTRES, etc.).
- Grp* limits are checked when considering starting jobs — these can block allocation if limits would be exceeded.
- DefaultQOS, QOSMaxJobs, QOSMaxSubmitJobs etc. control per-user/ per-account behavior.

4. Reporting and tools
- sshare shows fairshare and effective shares.
- sprio shows priority breakdown per job and the active weights.
- sreport generates accounting usage (CPU/GPU-hours) reports.
- sacct for historical job records; sacct requires accounting data (slurmdbd or jobcomp to storage).

Practical examples (typical lines)
- slurm.conf (examples)
  - PriorityType=priority/multifactor
  - PriorityDecayHalfLife=7-0
  - PriorityWeightAge=1000
  - PriorityWeightFairshare=10000
  - PriorityFavorSmall=YES
  - AccountingStorageType=accounting_storage/slurmdbd
  - AccountingStorageHost=slurmdbd.example.edu
  - AccountingStorageEnforce=associations
  - JobAcctGatherType=jobacct_gather/linux
  - JobAcctGatherFrequency=30
- sacctmgr (examples)
  - sacctmgr add account mygroup Cluster=clustername Description="Research group"
  - sacctmgr modify account mygroup set Fairshare=100
  - sacctmgr modify user alice set DefaultAccount=mygroup

Checks and diagnostics (read-only commands)
- scontrol show config — view current slurm.conf settings (PriorityType, AccountingStorageType, JobAcctGatherType).
- sprio -w — view current priority weights and plugin behavior.
- sshare -l — check fairshare allocation and recent usage.
- sdiag — scheduler diagnostics and backfill statistics.
- scontrol ping — check controller responsiveness.
- sacctmgr list associations — inspect accounts, shares, and limits.

Common pitfalls and recommendations
- Fairshare/age requires slurmdbd; without it fairshare/age factors are not computed.
- If PriorityDecayHalfLife is 0 you must manage usage resets (PriorityUsageResetPeriod).
- Changing slurm.conf requires restart or SIGHUP of slurmctld to take effect; slurmdbd config changes require restart of slurmdbd.
- AccountingStorageEnforce can block users unintentionally — test changes in a staging environment first.
- Ensure JobAcctGatherType is enabled and frequent enough to capture required metrics (increase frequency for finer accounting).
- When tuning weights, use sprio and sshare to observe results and iterate: small changes to PriorityWeightFairshare can have large effects.
